lessons.label: Scalars, Vectors, and Reference Frames

sections.heading: Two kinds of quantity
sections.body: Physics splits every measured quantity into two families. A scalar is fully described by a magnitude and a unit alone: mass (68 kg), temperature (293 K), time (12 s), distance traveled (5 km). A vector needs magnitude AND direction to mean anything: velocity (25 m/s, due north), force (10 N, downward), displacement (3 m, at 30 degrees above the horizontal). Saying "the car's velocity is 25 m/s" is an incomplete statement in physics the same way giving someone a distance without a direction ("go 5 blocks") leaves them unable to actually get anywhere. Vectors are usually drawn as arrows: length encodes magnitude, orientation encodes direction. In print, vectors are marked with an arrow or boldface (v-vector, or v) to distinguish them from the scalar speed |v|.

sections.heading: Adding vectors: tip-to-tail and components
sections.body: Vectors do not add like ordinary numbers. Tip-to-tail addition places the tail of the second vector at the tip of the first; the resultant is the arrow from the first tail to the last tip. This works graphically for any number of vectors but is imprecise by hand. The algebraic equivalent, component addition, is what physicists actually compute with: resolve each vector into perpendicular x- and y-components (Ax = A cos(theta), Ay = A sin(theta) for a vector at angle theta from the x-axis), add components of the same axis separately (Rx = Ax + Bx, Ry = Ay + By), then recombine with the Pythagorean theorem (R = sqrt(Rx^2 + Ry^2)) and inverse tangent (theta = atan2(Ry, Rx)) to recover magnitude and direction. Component addition is exact and scales to any number of vectors in 2D or 3D, which is why it replaces tip-to-tail arrows for real calculation.

sections.heading: Why a reference frame comes first
sections.body: A position, velocity, or displacement is meaningless until you fix a reference frame: an origin (a zero point) and a set of axes (a direction called positive). "The ball is at x = 5" only means something once you have said where x = 0 is and which way x increases. This is not pedantry — choosing the frame is a real physics decision. A ball thrown upward has positive velocity in an up-positive frame and negative velocity in a down-positive frame; the physical motion is identical, only the bookkeeping changed. Sign errors from an unstated or inconsistently applied reference frame are one of the most common sources of wrong answers in introductory mechanics, which is why every solved problem should open by declaring the origin and positive direction before any number is written down.

lessons.workedExample: A hiker walks 3.0 km east, then 4.0 km north. Using components with east as +x and north as +y: total displacement Rx = 3.0 km, Ry = 4.0 km. Magnitude R = sqrt(3.0^2 + 4.0^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5.0 km. Direction theta = atan(4.0/3.0) = 53 degrees north of east. Note the distance walked (the scalar path length) is 3.0 + 4.0 = 7.0 km, while the displacement (the vector) has magnitude only 5.0 km — the two are genuinely different quantities, and only the vector answer specifies a direction.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair-project judge asks "is that a vector or a scalar?" whenever a student reports speed, force, or motion, because conflating the two is the fastest way to reveal shaky fundamentals. A student who reports a bare number for something that is physically a vector ("the object moved 5 meters" without direction, when direction was measured) has thrown away real data. Judges also probe reference frames directly: "what did you define as positive?" A confident, stated answer signals the student understands that the frame is a choice, not a fact of nature — and that choosing it wrong doesn't make the answer wrong, only forgetting to choose it does.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a vector quantity, not a scalar?

options.text: Mass
Displacement
Distance traveled
Temperature

explanations.a: Mass is fully specified by a magnitude alone (kg) — it has no direction, so it is a scalar.
explanations.b: Correct: displacement is a net change in position and requires both a magnitude and a direction to be meaningful.
explanations.c: Distance traveled is total path length, a magnitude-only scalar (it never needs a direction to be reported).
explanations.d: Temperature is a magnitude-only scalar; there is no direction associated with 293 K.

questions.prompt: A vector has components Ax = 6 m and Ay = 8 m. What is its magnitude?

options.text: 2 m

explanations.a: That is Ax + Ay added like scalars, which is not how vector magnitude works.
explanations.b: Correct: magnitude = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 m.
explanations.c: That is Ay minus Ax, which has no physical meaning for magnitude.
explanations.d: That is Ax times Ay, not the Pythagorean combination that gives magnitude.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of adding two vectors by the component method.

items.text: Resolve each vector into x- and y-components
Add the x-components together and the y-components together
Recombine the summed components using the Pythagorean theorem for magnitude
Use inverse tangent to find the resultant's direction

questions.explanation: You must break each vector into components before you can add same-axis components; only after that sum exists can you recombine it into a magnitude, and direction is found last from the summed components.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct classification.

right.text: Vector (needs direction)
Scalar (magnitude only)
Vector (needs direction)
Scalar (magnitude only)

questions.explanation: Velocity and force both require a direction to be fully specified, so they are vectors; speed (velocity's magnitude) and time are fully described by a single number, so they are scalars.

lessons.label: Distance vs Displacement

sections.heading: Two answers to "how far did it go?"
sections.body: Distance is the total length of the path traveled — a scalar that only ever increases or stays flat as an object moves, never decreases, because every step of motion adds to it regardless of direction. Displacement is the vector from the starting position to the ending position — it depends only on where you began and where you ended, not on the path taken between them. Walk 100 m east then 100 m back west: the distance traveled is 200 m, but the displacement is 0 m, because you ended up exactly where you started. This is not a rounding artifact; it is the defining difference between the two quantities, and it is why a runner who does 8 laps of a 400 m track has run a distance of 3200 m but has a displacement of zero.

sections.heading: Sign conventions in one dimension
sections.body: In 1D motion along a line, displacement reduces to a signed number once a positive direction is chosen (Section on reference frames covers why that choice must come first). If a car starts at x = 2 m and ends at x = -3 m, its displacement is delta-x = x_final - x_initial = -3 - 2 = -5 m: negative because the net motion was in the negative direction, regardless of how it got there. Distance, by contrast, is always reported as a non-negative number — it is the sum of the absolute values of every leg of the trip, so a car that drives from x=2 to x=-3 and then back to x=0 has traveled a distance of |(-3)-2| + |0-(-3)| = 5 + 3 = 8 m, even though its net displacement from start to finish is only x_final - x_initial = 0 - 2 = -2 m.

sections.heading: Why velocity is built on displacement, not distance
sections.body: Average velocity is defined as displacement divided by time, not distance divided by time — because velocity is meant to capture net progress in a direction, and only displacement carries that directional, cancel-when-you-backtrack information. If velocity were defined using distance instead, an object that returns exactly to its starting point after a long, winding trip would show a large nonzero "velocity," which contradicts the physical fact that its position, on net, did not change at all. Average speed, defined as distance over time, is the quantity that stays large in that scenario — and the two numbers (average velocity's magnitude and average speed) are only equal when motion is one-directional with no backtracking or curving.

lessons.workedExample: A robot on a 1D track starts at x = 0 m. It moves to x = 6 m, then reverses and moves to x = 2 m, taking 10 s total. Distance traveled = 6 m (leg one) + |2-6| m (leg two) = 6 + 4 = 10 m. Displacement = x_final - x_initial = 2 - 0 = +2 m. Average speed = distance/time = 10 m / 10 s = 1.0 m/s. Average velocity = displacement/time = 2 m / 10 s = 0.2 m/s. The large gap between 1.0 m/s and 0.2 m/s exists entirely because the robot backtracked; without the reversal the two numbers would coincide.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask for both distance and displacement when a project reports "how far" something moved, because reporting only one — especially distance dressed up as if it were the vector answer — hides backtracking, drift, or oscillation that the raw number conceals. A student who can produce both figures and explain why they differ (or confirm they are equal because the path had no reversals) shows they understand what each number actually measures rather than pattern-matching a formula.

questions.prompt: A cyclist rides 3 laps around a circular track that is 400 m in circumference, ending at the same point she started. What is her displacement?

options.text: 0 m
Cannot be determined without knowing her speed

explanations.a: 1200 m is the total distance traveled (3 x 400 m), not the displacement.
explanations.b: 400 m would be one lap's distance, but displacement only depends on start and end position.
explanations.c: Correct: since she ends exactly where she started, the net change in position — displacement — is zero, regardless of how far she rode.
explanations.d: Displacement depends only on start and end position, not on speed; it can be determined here without any speed information.

questions.prompt: In a 1D reference frame with rightward as positive, an object moves from x = 5 m to x = -2 m. What is its displacement?

explanations.a: The magnitude 7 is right but the sign is wrong: the object moved in the negative direction overall.
explanations.b: Correct: displacement = x_final - x_initial = -2 - 5 = -7 m, negative because the net motion was leftward.
explanations.c: This neither matches the correct magnitude nor accounts for the negative net direction.
explanations.d: The sign is right but the magnitude is wrong; the correct computation is -2 - 5 = -7, not -3.

questions.prompt: Match each description to distance or displacement.

left.text: Always reported as a non-negative number
Can be zero even after a long trip
Depends only on start and end position
Sums the length of every leg of the path, including backtracking

right.text: Distance
Displacement
Displacement
Distance

questions.explanation: Distance is a scalar path-length total that only grows and is always non-negative; displacement is a vector fixed entirely by the starting and ending position, so it can be zero (or even negative in 1D) regardless of how convoluted the path was.

questions.prompt: Order these steps to compute distance and displacement for a multi-leg 1D trip.

items.text: Record the position at the start and at the end of each leg
Sum the absolute value of the change in position for every leg to get distance
Subtract the very first position from the very last position to get displacement
Compare the two results to see whether the trip involved any backtracking

questions.explanation: You need every leg's endpoints recorded first; distance requires summing each leg's absolute change, displacement requires only the overall first and last position, and comparing the two final numbers is the last step that reveals whether backtracking occurred.

lessons.label: Velocity and Speed

sections.heading: Average velocity and average speed
sections.body: Average velocity is v_avg = delta-x / delta-t: the displacement divided by the elapsed time, a vector that points in the direction of net motion. Average speed is total distance / delta-t, a scalar that is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of the average velocity, with equality only when the motion never reverses direction or curves back on itself. These two numbers are frequently confused in casual speech ("the car's speed was -5 m/s" is not valid usage; speed is never negative) but rigorously distinct in physics, matching the distance-vs-displacement split from the previous lesson.

sections.heading: Instantaneous velocity as a slope
sections.body: Average velocity over a long interval can hide a lot: a car could average 0 m/s over an hour by driving out and back, despite briefly hitting 30 m/s. Instantaneous velocity fixes this by shrinking the interval toward zero: v = lim(delta-t to 0) of (delta-x / delta-t), the calculus derivative dx/dt. Graphically, average velocity is the slope of a secant line connecting two points on a position-vs-time (x-t) graph; instantaneous velocity is the slope of the line tangent to the x-t curve at a single instant. Where the x-t graph is a straight line, average and instantaneous velocity are identical everywhere along it, because the tangent slope never changes. Where the x-t graph curves, the tangent slope changes point to point, meaning the object's velocity is genuinely changing (it is accelerating), and the secant slope between any two points is just an average that smooths over that variation.

sections.heading: Speed as the magnitude of velocity
sections.body: Instantaneous speed is defined as the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity vector: speed = |v|. In 1D this just means dropping the sign — a velocity of -8 m/s corresponds to a speed of 8 m/s. In 2D or 3D, speed is the length of the velocity vector computed the same way any vector magnitude is computed, sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2). Because speed discards direction, two objects can have identical speed while having very different (even opposite) velocities — this is precisely why a speedometer, which reads speed, cannot tell you whether a car is heading north or south.

lessons.workedExample: A ball's position is given by x(t) = 2t^2 (meters, t in seconds) for the first 3 seconds. Average velocity from t=0 to t=3: delta-x = x(3) - x(0) = 2(9) - 0 = 18 m, so v_avg = 18 m / 3 s = 6 m/s. Instantaneous velocity is the derivative v(t) = dx/dt = 4t; at t = 3 s, v(3) = 12 m/s — notably different from the 6 m/s average, because the ball is speeding up (the x-t curve is getting steeper), so the instantaneous rate at the endpoint exceeds the average rate over the whole interval.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the average-vs-instantaneous distinction because it is where students confuse a single-number summary with the full time-resolved behavior of a system. A student who reports only a study's average velocity, when the underlying process clearly sped up or slowed down partway through, has hidden the most scientifically interesting part of the data. A judge asking "what was it doing at t = 3 seconds specifically, not on average?" is testing whether the student ever looked at the slope of their own x-t graph rather than just computing one endpoint-to-endpoint ratio.

questions.prompt: On an x-t graph, instantaneous velocity at a specific time is represented by:

options.text: The slope of the secant line between two distant points
The slope of the line tangent to the curve at that instant
The area under the curve up to that instant
The x-value of the curve at that instant

explanations.a: A secant line between two distant points gives an average velocity over that interval, not the instantaneous value at a single point.
explanations.b: Correct: instantaneous velocity is the limit of the secant slope as the interval shrinks to zero, which is exactly the tangent line's slope.
explanations.c: The area under an x-t curve is not a standard kinematic quantity used for velocity; area under a v-t curve gives displacement instead.
explanations.d: The x-value at that instant is the position, not velocity, which is about the rate of change of position.

questions.prompt: An object has instantaneous velocity -6 m/s. What is its instantaneous speed?

options.text: -6 m/s
0 m/s
6 m/s
Speed cannot be found without more information

explanations.a: Speed is a scalar magnitude and is never reported as negative; -6 m/s is a velocity, not a speed.
explanations.b: The object is still moving (nonzero velocity), so its speed is not zero.
explanations.c: Correct: speed is the magnitude of velocity, |-6 m/s| = 6 m/s.
explanations.d: Speed follows directly from velocity's magnitude; no additional information is needed.

questions.prompt: Match each formula or concept to what it computes.

right.text: Average velocity
Average speed
Instantaneous velocity
Instantaneous speed

questions.explanation: Average velocity divides net displacement by elapsed time; average speed divides total path length by elapsed time; instantaneous velocity is the calculus limit of that ratio as the interval shrinks to zero; and instantaneous speed is simply the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity vector.

questions.prompt: Order these from smallest scope (a single instant) to largest scope (the whole trip's average).

items.text: Instantaneous velocity at one specific moment
Average velocity over a short 1-second interval
Average velocity over the entire trip

questions.explanation: Instantaneous velocity describes a single point in time with zero interval width; a short interval average covers a small window around that point; the whole-trip average smooths over the entire journey and has the widest scope of the three.

lessons.label: Acceleration

sections.heading: Acceleration as the rate of change of velocity
sections.body: Average acceleration is a_avg = delta-v / delta-t, the change in velocity divided by the elapsed time — a vector, with units of m/s^2. Instantaneous acceleration is the calculus derivative a = dv/dt = lim(delta-t to 0) of delta-v/delta-t, exactly mirroring how instantaneous velocity is the derivative of position. On a velocity-vs-time (v-t) graph, instantaneous acceleration at any moment is the slope of the tangent line to the curve at that point, and average acceleration over an interval is the slope of the secant line connecting the interval's endpoints. A straight-line v-t graph means constant acceleration; a curving v-t graph means the acceleration is itself changing over time.

sections.heading: Acceleration can point against velocity
sections.body: Because acceleration and velocity are independent vectors, they are not required to point the same way. When acceleration points in the same direction as velocity, the object speeds up. When acceleration points opposite to velocity, the object slows down — this is often loosely called "deceleration," but that is not a separate physical quantity; it is simply acceleration with a sign or direction opposite the current velocity. A car braking while moving in the positive direction has a negative acceleration; the same negative acceleration applied to a car already moving in the negative direction would instead speed it up in that negative direction. The sign of acceleration alone never tells you whether an object is speeding up or slowing down — you must compare the sign of acceleration to the sign of velocity.

sections.heading: Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration
sections.body: A common misconception is that acceleration only exists when speed changes. But acceleration is defined from the velocity vector, not just its magnitude, and velocity changes if EITHER magnitude OR direction changes. An object moving in a circle at perfectly constant speed is still accelerating, because its direction is continuously changing, which means its velocity vector is continuously changing even though |v| stays fixed. This acceleration points toward the center of the circle (centripetal acceleration, covered in a later unit) and is what keeps the object curving rather than flying off in a straight line. The general lesson: always check the full velocity vector, not just its magnitude, before concluding acceleration is zero.

lessons.workedExample: A car moving in the positive direction at 20 m/s brakes uniformly to a stop in 4 s. Average acceleration = delta-v / delta-t = (0 - 20) / 4 = -5 m/s^2. The acceleration is negative while the velocity is positive (opposite signs), confirming the car is slowing down, not reversing or speeding up — consistent with braking. If the same -5 m/s^2 acceleration continued to act after the car stopped, the car would then begin speeding up in the negative direction, illustrating that the sign of acceleration alone never tells you "slowing down" without also knowing the current sign of velocity.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges test the sign-of-acceleration misconception directly, often with a question like "if acceleration is negative, is the object slowing down?" A student who answers "it depends on the direction it's currently moving" demonstrates real command of vectors; a student who answers a flat "yes" reveals they have memorized "negative acceleration = deceleration" as a rule rather than derived it from vectors. Judges also like to ask about circular or curved motion at constant speed, since "is it accelerating?" trips up students who equate acceleration with a changing speedometer reading rather than a changing velocity vector.

questions.prompt: An object moves in the negative direction and has negative acceleration. What is happening to its speed?

options.text: It is speeding up
It is slowing down
It is constant
It cannot be determined

explanations.a: Correct: velocity and acceleration point in the same direction (both negative), so the object speeds up in the negative direction.
explanations.b: Slowing down requires acceleration opposite in sign to velocity; here both are negative, meaning they align.
explanations.c: A nonzero acceleration means the velocity's magnitude is changing, so speed is not constant.
explanations.d: It can be determined by comparing the signs of velocity and acceleration, which here match.

questions.prompt: A satellite moves in a perfect circle at a constant 7.5 km/s. Is it accelerating?

options.text: No, because its speed never changes
Yes, because its velocity's direction is continuously changing
No, because acceleration only applies to objects that speed up
Only at the exact moments it changes direction

explanations.a: Speed staying constant is not sufficient; acceleration depends on the full velocity vector, which includes direction.
explanations.b: Correct: even at constant speed, a continuously changing direction means velocity is continuously changing, which is by definition an acceleration.
explanations.c: Acceleration is any change in the velocity vector, including a direction change at constant speed, not just speeding up.
explanations.d: In uniform circular motion, direction changes continuously at every instant, not just at isolated moments.

questions.prompt: Order these v-t graph features from describing zero acceleration to describing the largest-magnitude constant acceleration.

items.text: A perfectly flat (horizontal) v-t line
A straight v-t line with a gentle slope
A straight v-t line with a steep slope

questions.explanation: A flat v-t line has zero slope, meaning zero acceleration; a gentle slope is a small constant acceleration; a steep slope is a larger-magnitude constant acceleration, since slope on a v-t graph directly equals acceleration.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the correct acceleration/velocity relationship.

right.text: Acceleration and velocity point the same way
Acceleration and velocity point opposite ways
Acceleration is zero
Acceleration is nonzero, directed toward the center of the curve

questions.explanation: Speeding up requires acceleration aligned with velocity; slowing down requires it opposed; truly constant velocity (fixed magnitude AND direction) has zero acceleration; and curving at constant speed still has nonzero acceleration because direction is changing, directed toward the curve's center.

lessons.label: The Constant-Acceleration Kinematic Equations

sections.heading: The SUVAT equations and their one big assumption
sections.body: When acceleration is constant, five quantities — displacement (s), initial velocity (u), final velocity (v), acceleration (a), and time (t) — are linked by four standard equations, often nicknamed SUVAT: (1) v = u + at; (2) s = ut + (1/2)at^2; (3) v^2 = u^2 + 2as; (4) s = ((u+v)/2)t. Every one of these is derived from the definitions of average velocity and average acceleration under a single load-bearing assumption: acceleration is constant over the interval in question. If acceleration varies with time, these equations give wrong answers and calculus (integrating a(t)) is required instead. Constant acceleration is common in idealized problems (free fall near Earth's surface, ignoring air resistance) but is an approximation, not a universal law — always check whether it is a defensible assumption for the situation before reaching for SUVAT.

sections.heading: Picking the right equation
sections.body: Each SUVAT equation is missing exactly one of the five variables (s, u, v, a, t), which is the practical key to choosing one: list what you know, list what you want, and pick the equation that excludes the variable you neither know nor need. Equation (1) excludes s, useful when displacement isn't given or needed. Equation (2) excludes v, useful for finding position without knowing final velocity. Equation (3) excludes t, uniquely useful when time is neither known nor asked for. Equation (4) excludes a, useful when acceleration is unknown but assumed constant. A common student error is trying to solve a problem with an equation that doesn't isolate the target variable cleanly, or accidentally using an equation that requires a quantity that was never given, generating an unsolvable or nonsensical result.

lessons.workedExample: A car starts from rest (u = 0 m/s) and accelerates at a constant a = 3 m/s^2 for t = 5 s. Find its displacement and final velocity. Since s, v, a, u, and t are all in play but s is unknown and not needed for finding v, start with equation (1): v = u + at = 0 + (3)(5) = 15 m/s. For displacement, use equation (2), which doesn't require v: s = ut + (1/2)at^2 = (0)(5) + (0.5)(3)(25) = 37.5 m. Check with equation (3): v^2 = u^2 + 2as -> 15^2 = 0 + 2(3)(37.5) -> 225 = 225. The cross-check confirms both answers are internally consistent.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on whether a student can justify using SUVAT at all — "was your acceleration actually constant, or are you assuming it for convenience?" — because misapplying constant-acceleration equations to a system with varying acceleration (a rocket burning fuel, a car with changing engine force) produces confidently wrong numbers. A judge who asks "which of the five variables did you not use, and why did you pick that equation?" is testing whether the student chose deliberately from the five-variable structure or just guessed an equation that had the right-looking letters in it.

questions.prompt: All four SUVAT equations share which required assumption?

options.text: The object starts from rest
Acceleration is constant over the interval
The motion is in two dimensions
Air resistance is significant

explanations.a: Starting from rest (u=0) is a special case sometimes seen in problems, not a requirement of the equations themselves.
explanations.b: Correct: SUVAT is derived assuming acceleration does not change during the interval; varying acceleration invalidates all four equations.
explanations.c: SUVAT is most often applied in 1D (or component-wise in higher dimensions) but dimensionality is not the defining assumption.
explanations.d: Air resistance being significant would typically make acceleration non-constant, working against the equations rather than being required.

questions.prompt: You know initial velocity, final velocity, and acceleration, but not time or displacement, and you want displacement. Which SUVAT equation should you use?

options.text: v = u + at

explanations.a: This equation solves for v or a or t, not for s — it doesn't even contain the displacement variable.
explanations.b: This requires t, which is unknown here, so it can't be used directly without an extra step.
explanations.c: Correct: this is the only equation that excludes time entirely, matching exactly the known quantities (u, v, a) and the unknown you want (s).
explanations.d: This also requires t, which is not known, making it unusable without first solving for time.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving a constant-acceleration kinematics problem.

items.text: Confirm acceleration can be treated as constant over the interval
List which of the five variables (s, u, v, a, t) are known and which is wanted
Select the SUVAT equation that excludes the one variable neither known nor needed
Solve algebraically and check the answer against a second equation

questions.explanation: You must first justify the constant-acceleration assumption, then inventory knowns and unknowns, then pick the equation structurally matched to that inventory, and finally solve and cross-check — using the equations before confirming the assumption risks applying them somewhere invalid.

questions.prompt: Match each SUVAT equation to the variable it excludes.

right.text: Excludes s
Excludes v
Excludes t
Excludes a

questions.explanation: v = u + at has no displacement term (excludes s); s = ut + (1/2)at^2 never uses final velocity (excludes v); v^2 = u^2 + 2as has no time term (excludes t); and s = ((u+v)/2)t never uses acceleration directly (excludes a).

lessons.label: Free Fall and g

sections.heading: The near-surface constant g
sections.body: Near Earth's surface, objects in free fall (falling under gravity alone, with air resistance neglected) accelerate downward at a nearly constant rate g approximately equal to 9.8 m/s^2 (more precisely about 9.81 m/s^2 at sea level at mid-latitudes; the value varies slightly, roughly 9.78 to 9.83 m/s^2, with latitude and altitude because Earth is not a perfect sphere and rotates). This constant acceleration means free fall is a direct, standard application of the SUVAT equations from the previous lesson, with acceleration a fixed at magnitude g and direction always toward the Earth's center (downward, for near-surface problems).

sections.heading: Galileo and the mass-independence of free fall
sections.body: Aristotelian physics held that heavier objects fall faster. Galileo Galilei argued, via a thought experiment and reportedly (though the historical record on the literal Leaning Tower of Pisa demonstration is disputed by historians) through experiment, that in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass. The reasoning: gravitational force scales with mass (F = mg), but so does inertia (resistance to acceleration, via F = ma), and mass cancels between the two, leaving acceleration a = g independent of mass. This was dramatically confirmed on the airless Moon in 1971, when Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a feather and a geologic hammer simultaneously and both struck the lunar surface at the same instant — with no atmosphere to slow the feather, mass-independence held exactly.

sections.heading: Sign choices and the symmetry of rise and fall
sections.body: Vertical free-fall problems require choosing up-positive or down-positive before writing any equation (the reference-frame lesson's rule applies directly). In an up-positive frame, g is entered as a = -9.8 m/s^2 regardless of whether the object is rising or falling, since gravity always pulls downward; in a down-positive frame, a = +9.8 m/s^2 throughout. A ball thrown straight up returns to its launch height with a speed equal in magnitude to its launch speed (by energy conservation and the constant-acceleration symmetry of the motion), and the time to rise to the peak equals the time to fall back down from the peak to the launch height — a direct consequence of the v = u + at relationship being linear and symmetric about the peak, where instantaneous velocity is exactly zero.

lessons.workedExample: A ball is thrown straight up at 14.7 m/s from ground level. Using up-positive, a = -9.8 m/s^2. Time to reach the peak (where v = 0): from v = u + at, 0 = 14.7 + (-9.8)t, so t = 1.5 s. Maximum height: s = ut + (1/2)at^2 = (14.7)(1.5) + (0.5)(-9.8)(1.5)^2 = 22.05 - 11.025 = 11.025 m. By the rise-fall symmetry, the ball takes another 1.5 s to fall back to ground level, landing with speed 14.7 m/s downward (magnitude equal to the launch speed) — total flight time 3.0 s.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask free-fall questions to check both the numeric habit (using g approximately 9.8 m/s^2, not 10 or 9.81 inconsistently within one calculation) and the conceptual habit (declaring a sign convention before computing). A judge who asks "why does a heavier ball not hit the ground first in your trial?" is testing whether the student can explain mass-independence causally (mass cancels between force and inertia) rather than simply citing it as a fact. Judges also probe rise-fall symmetry: asking for the time to fall from the peak without redoing the whole calculation checks whether the student grasps the symmetry as a shortcut, not just a coincidence.

questions.prompt: In a vacuum, a bowling ball and a feather are dropped from the same height at the same instant. What happens?

options.text: The bowling ball lands first because it is heavier
The feather lands first because it is lighter
They land at the same instant
It depends on their exact shapes

explanations.a: Mass cancels out of free-fall acceleration (F=mg and F=ma give a=g independent of mass), so a heavier object does not fall faster in a vacuum.
explanations.b: The same mass-cancellation logic rules out the lighter object falling faster in a vacuum.
explanations.c: Correct: with no air resistance, all objects share the same free-fall acceleration g, so mass-independent objects released together land together, as demonstrated on the Moon by Apollo 15 in 1971.
explanations.d: Shape only matters because of air resistance; in a true vacuum there is no drag, so shape does not affect the outcome.

questions.prompt: A ball thrown straight up takes 2.0 s to reach its peak. Ignoring air resistance, how long does it take to fall back down to the launch height?

options.text: It cannot be determined without the launch speed

explanations.a: Half the rise time would violate the rise-fall symmetry of constant-acceleration motion.
explanations.b: Correct: by the symmetry of constant downward acceleration about the zero-velocity peak, the fall time back to launch height equals the rise time, 2.0 s.
explanations.c: Double the rise time is not what symmetry predicts; that would only be the case if fall time were somehow independent of rise time, which it is not here.
explanations.d: The symmetry argument holds regardless of the specific launch speed, so it can be determined from the rise time alone.

questions.prompt: Match each free-fall fact to its correct description.

right.text: Approximately 9.8 m/s^2 downward near Earth's surface
All objects fall with the same acceleration absent air resistance
Confirmed mass-independent free fall in a vacuum (on the Moon)
Must be chosen (up- or down-positive) before writing kinematic equations

questions.explanation: g is the near-surface free-fall acceleration constant; Galileo's claim was mass-independence of free-fall acceleration; the Apollo 15 lunar demonstration confirmed it directly since the Moon has no atmosphere; and every free-fall problem needs an explicit sign convention before numbers are plugged in.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of a ball thrown straight up and caught again at the same height it was launched from.

items.text: Ball leaves the hand moving upward at maximum speed
Ball slows down as it rises, decelerating under gravity
Ball reaches the peak with instantaneous velocity equal to zero
Ball speeds up as it falls back down under gravity
Ball is caught at the launch height moving downward at the same speed it was thrown

questions.explanation: The ball starts at its fastest upward speed, continuously slows under constant downward acceleration until it momentarily stops at the peak, then speeds up on the way back down, returning to the launch height with a speed matching its initial launch speed by rise-fall symmetry.

lessons.label: Relative Motion and Galilean Velocity Addition

sections.heading: Velocity depends on who's watching
sections.body: Velocity is always measured relative to some reference frame, and a frame is itself often moving relative to other frames. A passenger walking forward at 1.5 m/s inside a train that itself moves at 20 m/s relative to the ground is moving at 21.5 m/s relative to the ground, but only 1.5 m/s relative to the train. Neither number is "more correct" than the other; they are simply velocities measured in different reference frames, and both are physically valid descriptions of the same motion. This is Galilean relative motion: velocities measured in different frames are related by simple vector addition, as long as the frames move at constant velocity relative to each other (non-accelerating, or "inertial," frames).

sections.heading: Galilean velocity addition
sections.body: The general rule: if frame B moves with velocity v(B rel A) relative to frame A, and an object moves with velocity v(object rel B) relative to frame B, then the object's velocity relative to frame A is v(object rel A) = v(object rel B) + v(B rel A) — ordinary vector addition. This holds in both 1D (where it reduces to signed-number addition) and 2D/3D (where it requires full component addition, as in the vectors lesson). The classic "boat crossing a river" problem is the 2D version: a boat's velocity relative to the ground is the vector sum of its velocity relative to the water (however the pilot steers and throttles it) and the water's velocity relative to the ground (the current) — the boat can be pointed straight across the river and still drift downstream, because the current's velocity adds on top of the boat's own heading.

sections.heading: Even 'at rest' is relative
sections.body: A direct consequence of Galilean addition is that there is no universal, frame-independent notion of being 'at rest' or of a single 'true' velocity. An object at rest in one frame has nonzero velocity in any frame that itself moves relative to the first. A coffee cup sitting still on an airplane tray table has zero velocity relative to the plane but roughly 250 m/s relative to the ground below (the plane's cruising speed), and a different nonzero velocity again relative to the Sun (adding Earth's rotation and orbital motion). All of these are simultaneously true and physically valid; physics answers 'velocity relative to what frame,' never 'velocity, full stop.' This principle of relativity (that the laws of motion take the same form in any inertial frame) is Galilean in origin and, updated for the constancy of light speed, becomes the seed of Einstein's special relativity.

lessons.workedExample: A boat's engine pushes it at 4.0 m/s relative to the water, aimed directly across a river (perpendicular to the bank). The river's current flows at 3.0 m/s parallel to the bank. Taking across-river as the x-axis and downstream as the y-axis: boat velocity relative to water = (4.0, 0) m/s; water velocity relative to ground = (0, 3.0) m/s. By Galilean addition, boat velocity relative to ground = (4.0, 0) + (0, 3.0) = (4.0, 3.0) m/s. Magnitude = sqrt(4.0^2 + 3.0^2) = 5.0 m/s, at an angle atan(3.0/4.0) = 37 degrees downstream of straight across — the boat visibly drifts downstream even though the pilot steered it straight across relative to the water.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up relative motion when a project involves any moving platform or medium (currents, wind, a moving vehicle carrying an instrument) to check whether the student measured and reported velocity relative to the correct, clearly stated frame. A judge asking "relative to what?" after any velocity claim is testing the same reference-frame discipline from the first lesson of this unit, now applied to a second, moving frame rather than a fixed one — and a student who can decompose an observed velocity into 'object relative to medium' plus 'medium relative to ground' is demonstrating they understand the addition rule causally, not just as a memorized boat-and-river formula.

questions.prompt: A passenger walks forward at 1.2 m/s inside a train moving at 25 m/s relative to the ground (same direction). What is the passenger's velocity relative to the ground?

options.text: 25 m/s

explanations.a: This subtracts the passenger's velocity from the train's, which would be correct only if the passenger walked backward relative to the train, not forward.
explanations.b: 1.2 m/s is the passenger's velocity relative to the train, not relative to the ground.
explanations.c: Correct: by Galilean addition, velocity relative to ground = velocity relative to train + train's velocity relative to ground = 1.2 + 25 = 26.2 m/s.
explanations.d: 25 m/s is only the train's velocity; it ignores the passenger's own walking velocity relative to the train.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the Galilean principle of relative motion?

options.text: Every object has one true velocity, measurable independent of any reference frame
Velocity is only meaningful once a reference frame is specified, and differs between frames
Only objects on Earth's surface can be said to be at rest
Relative motion only applies to objects moving faster than 100 m/s

explanations.a: This is exactly what Galilean relativity denies: there is no single frame-independent 'true' velocity.
explanations.b: Correct: velocity is always relative to a chosen frame, and the same object can have different, equally valid velocities measured in different frames.
explanations.c: Rest is frame-dependent everywhere, not a special property of Earth's surface; an object at rest on Earth still moves relative to the Sun.
explanations.d: Galilean velocity addition applies at any speed well below light speed, with no minimum threshold.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving a boat-crossing-a-river (2D relative velocity) problem using Galilean addition.

items.text: Identify the boat's velocity relative to the water as a vector
Identify the water's (current's) velocity relative to the ground as a vector
Add the two vectors by components to get the boat's velocity relative to the ground
Compute the resultant's magnitude and direction from the summed components

questions.explanation: Both contributing velocities (boat-relative-to-water and water-relative-to-ground) must be identified first, then combined by Galilean vector addition, and only after summing the components can the final magnitude and direction be extracted.

questions.prompt: Match each relative-motion scenario to the frame in which the stated velocity is measured.

left.text: A coffee cup at rest on an airplane's tray table
The same coffee cup moving at roughly 250 m/s
A swimmer moving at 1.5 m/s relative to pool water
A walker moving at 1.2 m/s relative to the train car

right.text: Measured relative to the airplane
Measured relative to the ground
Measured relative to the water
Measured relative to the train

questions.explanation: The cup is at rest only relative to the plane's own frame, while its ~250 m/s figure is relative to the ground below; likewise the swimmer's and walker's stated speeds are relative to the moving medium or vehicle they are directly measured against, not the ground.

lessons.label: Force and the Free-Body Diagram

sections.heading: Force as an interaction, not a property
sections.body: A force is a directed push or pull that arises from an interaction between two objects — a table pushes up on a book, a rope pulls up on a bucket, Earth pulls down on both. Force is never a property that an object simply "has" the way mass or color is; it always has a source and a target, which is why every force can be named as "X on Y" (gravity on the box, tension on the rope, friction on the tire). Because force is a vector, it carries both magnitude and direction, and multiple forces acting on the same body combine by vector addition, not by simple arithmetic. The single vector sum of every force acting ON a chosen object is called the net force, and it is the net force — not any individual push or pull — that determines how that object's motion changes.

sections.heading: Choosing the system and finding every force
sections.body: Solving almost any mechanics problem starts with the same decision: pick one object (the "system") and ask what is touching it or acting on it at a distance. Contact forces include the normal force from a surface, tension from a string, friction from a surface, and applied pushes; the one common field force at this level is gravity (weight), acting even without contact. A frequent error is including a force that the chosen body exerts on something else — by Newton's third law, that force belongs to a different free-body diagram entirely. Systematically walking around the object — what is touching it below, above, to the sides, and is anything pulling it via a string or field — is the reliable way to avoid missing or double-counting a force.

sections.heading: Why the free-body diagram is the core tool
sections.body: A free-body diagram (FBD) represents the chosen object as a single point or box and draws every external force acting on it as an arrow from that point, roughly scaled to relative magnitude and pointed in the correct direction — with no forces that the object exerts on other things, and no forces from objects not actually touching or interacting with it. The value of the FBD is that it converts a paragraph of physical description into a clean geometric picture that can be resolved into x- and y-components and fed directly into Newton's second law. Many of the most common mechanics errors — a sign flip, a missing friction term, a double-counted weight — can often be traced back to a free-body diagram that was skipped or drawn carelessly, which is why experienced problem-solvers draw one even for problems that seem simple enough to do in their head.

lessons.workedExample: A 2 kg block sits at rest on a horizontal table. To find every force on the block: gravity pulls it down with weight W = mg = 2 * 9.8 = 19.6 N. The table cannot pull, only push, so it exerts a normal force N straight up on the block's bottom surface. No string or applied push is present, and the block is not touching anything else, so those are the only two forces. The free-body diagram is a dot with one arrow down (19.6 N, gravity) and one arrow up (N, normal force). Because the block is not accelerating vertically, Newton's second law requires the vertical net force to be zero, so N = 19.6 N — the diagram alone, resolved along the vertical axis, delivers the answer without needing any other equation.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "can you draw the forces on just this object?" is testing whether a student's physical intuition is disciplined or just vibes. It is easy to say a system "feels" forces in some hand-wavy sense; it is much harder to name each force by its source, direction, and type, and to exclude forces the object exerts on something else. A student who draws a clean, correctly labeled free-body diagram before writing any equation signals that their subsequent algebra is built on a checked foundation rather than a guess, which is exactly what a judge is trying to distinguish.

questions.prompt: A force is best described as:

options.text: A directed push or pull arising from an interaction between two objects
A scalar property that every moving object possesses
The total energy an object has due to its motion

explanations.a: Correct: force always has a source and a target object, and it is a vector with magnitude and direction.
explanations.b: Force is a vector, not a scalar, and it is not a property an object owns in isolation — it requires an interaction with something else.
explanations.c: That describes kinetic energy, a different quantity computed from mass and speed, not force.

questions.prompt: When drawing a free-body diagram for a block resting on a ramp, which force should NOT appear on the diagram?

options.text: The normal force the ramp exerts on the block
The weight of the block
The force the block exerts on the ramp

explanations.a: The normal force acts ON the block from the ramp, so it belongs on the block's free-body diagram.
explanations.b: Weight acts on the block via gravity, so it belongs on the diagram.
explanations.c: Correct: the force the block exerts ON the ramp is the third-law partner of the normal force and acts on the ramp, not the block — it belongs on a different object's diagram.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for correctly identifying the forces on a chosen object.

items.text: Choose a single object as the system
Check what is touching the object on every side
Check for field forces acting at a distance (gravity)
Draw each force as an arrow from the object, excluding forces the object exerts on others

questions.explanation: You must first fix which object you are analyzing, then search contact forces, then field forces, and only then draw the diagram, being careful to exclude any force the object exerts outward.

questions.prompt: Match each force type to its correct description.

right.text: Push exerted perpendicular to a contacting surface
Pull exerted along a taut string or rope
Pull exerted by gravity, acting without contact

questions.explanation: Normal force is a contact push perpendicular to the surface; tension is a contact pull along a string; weight is gravity's non-contact pull.

lessons.label: Newton's First Law and Inertia

sections.heading: Inertia and the break from Aristotle
sections.body: For nearly two thousand years, the Aristotelian view of motion held that objects need a continuous force to keep moving, and that their "natural" state is rest — a rock stops rolling because it "wants" to return to rest, and a cart stops because the ox stops pulling. Galileo challenged this with idealized experiments: he rolled balls down one incline and up another, noticing that the ball always rose to nearly the same height it started from, and reasoned that if the second incline were made flatter and flatter, and eventually perfectly horizontal and frictionless, the ball would roll forever at constant speed, never needing anything to sustain its motion. This inertial reasoning — that steady straight-line motion requires no force to maintain it, only friction and air resistance to destroy it — was Galileo's central conceptual leap, and Newton formalized it as his first law roughly 50 years later in the 1687 Principia.

sections.heading: The first law and equilibrium
sections.body: Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest, or moves in a straight line at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force. The key quantity is net force, the vector sum of every force acting on the object: if that sum is exactly zero, the object is in equilibrium, and equilibrium includes both a book sitting still on a table and a hockey puck sliding at constant speed across frictionless ice — both have zero net force, even though one is moving and one is not. This is precisely why the first law is sometimes called the "law of inertia": inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its velocity, and the first law says that in the absence of net force, that tendency simply wins and velocity stays exactly as it was, in both speed and direction.

sections.heading: Inertia scales with mass, not motion
sections.body: The first law also introduces mass as the measure of inertia — how strongly an object resists a change in velocity when a net force is applied. A loaded shopping cart is harder to start moving and harder to stop than an empty one purely because it has more mass and therefore more inertia; this has nothing to do with weight in the everyday sense of gravity, since the same cart has the same inertia (and would be equally hard to accelerate) even on the Moon, where its weight is a sixth as much. This distinction — that inertia depends on mass alone, independent of gravitational environment — becomes essential once weight and mass are formally separated in a later lesson, and it is the reason astronauts in orbit, effectively weightless, still find it hard to shove a heavy equipment rack into motion.

lessons.workedExample: A hockey puck slides across a stretch of very smooth ice at a constant 4 m/s in a straight line. A student asks what force keeps it moving. Applying the first law: since the puck's velocity is not changing (constant speed, constant direction), the net force on it must be zero — friction and air resistance are small enough on ice to be nearly negligible over that stretch, so no forward-pushing force is needed or present. Contrast this with a puck sliding across dry pavement: it visibly decelerates, so its net force is nonzero (kinetic friction acting backward), and Newton's first law correctly predicts that once that net backward force finally stops it, it will then stay at rest until something pushes it again — matching Galileo's insight that it is friction, not the absence of a "push," that ends motion.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge often asks a version of "what force keeps a moving object going?" specifically because the naive, Aristotelian-flavored answer — that motion needs a sustaining push — is the most common misconception even among students who can state Newton's laws by rote. A strong answer explains that constant-velocity motion implies zero net force, not zero force sustaining it, and can point to friction or air resistance as the force that would be needed to change that motion, not maintain it. This distinguishes a student who has memorized "F=ma" from one who understands why the first law was a genuine conceptual break from millennia of intuition.

questions.prompt: According to Newton's first law, an object moving at constant velocity in a straight line has:

options.text: Zero net force acting on it
A single large force pushing it forward
No forces acting on it at all

explanations.a: Correct: constant velocity (equilibrium) requires the vector sum of all forces to be zero, though individual forces may still be present and simply cancel.
explanations.b: A forward push is not required to sustain constant velocity motion; this is the Aristotelian misconception Galileo and Newton overturned.
explanations.c: Individual forces (like gravity and a normal force, or friction and an applied force) can still exist and simply cancel to a net of zero — "no forces" is too strong a claim.

questions.prompt: Mass, as the measure of inertia, describes:

options.text: How strongly an object resists a change in its velocity
The gravitational pull an object experiences
How fast an object naturally returns to rest

explanations.a: Correct: inertia is resistance to acceleration, and mass is the quantitative measure of that resistance, independent of gravity.
explanations.b: That describes weight, a force that depends on local gravity and equals mass times gravitational acceleration — not inertia itself.
explanations.c: The first law explicitly denies that objects have a natural tendency toward rest; that was the Aristotelian view it replaced.

questions.prompt: Order these historical/logical steps in the development of the law of inertia.

items.text: Aristotelian view: motion requires a continuous sustaining force
Galileo's inclined-plane experiments suggest motion persists longer as friction is reduced
Galileo generalizes: on a frictionless horizontal surface, motion would continue forever
Newton formalizes this as the first law in the Principia (1687)

questions.explanation: The Aristotelian starting point was challenged by Galileo's incline experiments, generalized by Galileo into frictionless inertial motion, and then formally stated by Newton decades later.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to whether the object is in equilibrium (net force zero) or not.

left.text: A book sitting still on a table
A puck sliding at constant speed on frictionless ice
A car speeding up from a stoplight

right.text: Equilibrium — net force is zero
Equilibrium — net force is zero
Not equilibrium — net force is nonzero

questions.explanation: Both the still book and the constant-speed puck have zero net force (equilibrium, whether at rest or moving); the accelerating car has a nonzero net force.

lessons.label: Newton's Second Law (F = ma)

sections.heading: Net force, mass, and acceleration
sections.body: Newton's second law states that the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: F_net = ma. This is a vector equation, meaning it holds independently along every direction — the net force in the x-direction produces acceleration only in x, and likewise for y, which is why free-body diagrams are resolved into x- and y-components before the second law is applied. The law also defines what acceleration means physically: it is not motion itself, and not even speed, but the rate at which velocity changes, so an object can have a large net force and a large acceleration while still moving slowly (or even momentarily at rest), as happens at the top of a ball's toss when gravity still pulls it downward even though its velocity is briefly zero.

sections.heading: Mass as inertia, made quantitative
sections.body: Where the first law introduced mass qualitatively as the source of an object's resistance to changing velocity, the second law makes that resistance precise: for a fixed net force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass, so doubling the mass while keeping the applied force the same halves the resulting acceleration. This is why identical forces produce very different outcomes on different objects — a given push accelerates an empty shopping cart far more than a loaded one — and it is the operational definition of inertial mass — apply a known force, measure the resulting acceleration, and divide — even though in practice mass is usually measured by comparison on a balance rather than this direct method. The second law therefore does double duty, serving both as a predictive tool (given F and m, find a) and as a measurement principle (given F and a, find m).

sections.heading: The newton as a derived unit
sections.body: The SI unit of force, the newton (N), is defined directly from the second law rather than independently: one newton is the force required to accelerate a 1 kg mass at 1 m/s^2, so 1 N = 1 kg*m/s^2. This makes force a derived unit built from the three SI base units of mass, length, and time, and it means that any answer for a net force problem can be dimensionally checked by confirming that kg*m/s^2 appears on both sides of the equation. Because F=ma ties together force, mass, and acceleration so tightly, most second-law problems reduce to the same three-part process: draw the free-body diagram, sum forces along each axis to get F_net in that direction, then divide by mass to solve for acceleration (or rearrange to solve for an unknown force).

lessons.workedExample: A 1200 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 8 seconds on a level road, with negligible friction and air resistance in this idealized case. First find acceleration: a = delta-v / delta-t = 20 / 8 = 2.5 m/s^2. Applying the second law, the net forward force the engine and tires must produce is F_net = ma = 1200 * 2.5 = 3000 N. If a student is instead told the engine produces 3600 N of forward force and the road/air resistance together push back with 600 N, the net force is 3600 - 600 = 3000 N, consistent with the same acceleration — showing that F=ma always refers to the NET force, the vector sum after all opposing forces are subtracted, not any single force in isolation.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe F=ma because students frequently plug in a single given force without checking whether it is actually the net force, or forget to resolve the equation along the correct axis when multiple forces point in different directions. A strong answer explicitly identifies which forces were summed to get F_net before dividing by mass, and can explain why doubling the mass at constant force halves the acceleration rather than treating the relationship as an arbitrary formula. This concept is also a favorite because it connects cleanly to a testable numeric prediction, so a judge can ask a student to defend a specific acceleration or force value, not just recite the equation.

questions.prompt: If the net force on a 4 kg object is 20 N, its acceleration is:

explanations.a: Correct: a = F/m = 20 N / 4 kg = 5 m/s^2.
explanations.b: This results from multiplying F and m instead of dividing; a = F/m, not F*m.
explanations.c: This is m/F instead of F/m: 4/20 = 0.2. The correct ratio is F/m = 20/4 = 5.

questions.prompt: One newton is defined as the force needed to:

options.text: Accelerate a 1 kg mass at 1 m/s^2
Lift a 1 kg mass at constant velocity on Earth
Stop a 1 kg mass moving at 1 m/s instantly

explanations.a: Correct: this is the direct SI definition, 1 N = 1 kg*m/s^2, derived straight from F=ma.
explanations.b: Lifting at constant velocity requires a force equal to weight (mg, about 9.8 N on Earth for 1 kg), not exactly 1 N, and it depends on local gravity.
explanations.c: Stopping "instantly" is not a well-defined finite force, since a true instant means infinite deceleration; the newton is defined via a specific acceleration, not a stopping scenario.

questions.prompt: Order the standard steps for solving a Newton's second law problem.

items.text: Draw the free-body diagram for the chosen object
Resolve each force into x- and y-components along chosen axes
Sum the components along each axis to find F_net in that direction
Divide F_net by mass to solve for acceleration (or solve for an unknown force)

questions.explanation: You must identify all forces first (FBD), then resolve them into components along your chosen axes, then sum each axis to get net force, and only then apply F=ma to solve.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct SI unit.

right.text: newton (kg*m/s^2)
kilogram
m/s^2

questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons, itself defined from kg*m/s^2; mass is measured in kilograms; acceleration is measured in meters per second squared.

lessons.label: Newton's Third Law and Interaction Pairs

sections.heading: Interaction pairs act on different bodies
sections.body: Newton's third law states that whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object simultaneously exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction back on the first. These two forces are called an interaction pair (or action-reaction pair), and the single most important fact about them is that they act on two DIFFERENT objects, never on the same one. This is precisely why third-law pairs never cancel each other out in a free-body diagram: a free-body diagram is drawn for one chosen object, and by definition only one member of any interaction pair can appear on it — the other member acts on the other object entirely, and belongs on that object's own diagram.

sections.heading: The classic misconception, and how it fails
sections.body: A common error treats the third law as explaining why an object doesn't move — "the table pushes up on the book as hard as gravity pulls down, so they cancel and the book stays put." This description is correct about the numbers but wrong about the reasoning: those two forces (gravity on the book, normal force on the book) are NOT a third-law pair, because they both act on the book and they come from different sources — gravity's partner is the book's gravitational pull on Earth, and the normal force's partner is the book pushing down on the table. The book's equilibrium is actually a first/second-law fact (net force on the book happens to be zero), while the third-law pairs are gravity-on-book paired with book's-pull-on-Earth, and table-pushes-book paired with book-pushes-table — four distinct forces, two genuine pairs, none of which cancel within either object's own diagram.

sections.heading: Third-law pairs in propulsion
sections.body: The third law explains a whole class of self-propulsion that otherwise looks paradoxical: how can pushing on something make you move if forces always come in equal-and-opposite pairs? Walking works because a foot pushes backward against the ground, and the ground's third-law reaction pushes the foot (and the walker) forward — the propulsive force acting on the walker's body comes from the ground, not from the walker's own muscles directly. Swimming follows the same logic with water instead of ground, and rocket thrust follows it with expelled exhaust gas: the rocket pushes hot gas backward out of its nozzle, and the gas pushes the rocket forward with equal force, which is also why rockets work in the vacuum of space with no air or ground to push against at all — the reaction partner is the expelled propellant itself, not the surrounding medium.

lessons.workedExample: A swimmer pushes backward on the water with her hands and feet with a force of 300 N. By the third law, the water simultaneously pushes forward on the swimmer with exactly 300 N. These two 300 N forces do NOT cancel, because they act on different objects: the swimmer's push acts on the water, and the water's push acts on the swimmer. To find the swimmer's acceleration, only the force acting ON the swimmer matters — treating the swimmer (mass 60 kg) as the system, F_net = 300 N forward (ignoring drag for simplicity) gives a = F/m = 300/60 = 5 m/s^2 forward. A student who instead reasons "the forces are equal and opposite so nothing happens" has confused a third-law pair (two different objects) with an equilibrium condition (which requires summing forces on ONE object).
lessons.judgeFraming: This is one of the most heavily tested concepts because the third law is simultaneously easy to state and easy to misapply — nearly every student can recite "equal and opposite," but many will then incorrectly cancel two forces acting on the SAME object because they sound like a matched pair. A judge who asks "why doesn't a rocket need air to push against" or "why do the ground-reaction and gravity forces on a walker not cancel as a third-law pair" is directly testing whether a student can correctly identify which object each force in a pair acts on. Getting this right is a strong signal that a student's mental model of forces is precise rather than pattern-matched.

questions.prompt: A book rests on a table. The gravitational force on the book and the normal force on the book are:

options.text: A Newton's third law interaction pair
Two separate forces that happen to be equal in this equilibrium case, but are NOT a third-law pair
The same force described two different ways

explanations.a: A true third-law pair requires the two forces to have different sources acting on different objects; gravity-on-book and normal-on-book both act on the book, so they cannot be a third-law pair.
explanations.b: Correct: they act on the same object (the book) and happen to be equal because the book is in vertical equilibrium (first/second law), not because of the third law.
explanations.c: They arise from entirely different interactions (Earth's gravitational pull vs. the table's contact push) and are not the same force at all.

questions.prompt: A rocket in the vacuum of space can still accelerate forward because:

options.text: It pushes expelled exhaust gas backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward by the third law
It pushes against the surrounding vacuum
Its engines generate forward thrust without needing a reaction partner

explanations.a: Correct: the reaction partner is the expelled propellant itself, not any surrounding medium, so thrust works even with nothing external to push against.
explanations.b: A vacuum has no matter to push against; it cannot provide a reaction force.
explanations.c: The third law always requires a reaction partner; the rocket's forward thrust is the direct reaction to the backward push on the exhaust gas.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for correctly analyzing a walking step using the third law.

items.text: The foot pushes backward against the ground
The ground exerts an equal, opposite forward force on the foot
That forward ground-reaction force acts on the walker's body
The walker accelerates forward due to this external force

questions.explanation: The foot's backward push on the ground causes the ground's forward third-law reaction on the foot, which then propels the walker's whole body forward.

questions.prompt: Match each force to its correct Newton's third law partner.

left.text: Rocket engine pushes exhaust gas backward

right.text: Water pushes swimmer's hand forward
Exhaust gas pushes rocket forward
Book pulls Earth upward (equal gravitational force)

questions.explanation: Every third-law pair swaps which object exerts and which receives the force while keeping magnitude equal and direction opposite: hand-on-water pairs with water-on-hand, rocket-on-gas pairs with gas-on-rocket, and Earth-on-book pairs with book-on-Earth.

lessons.label: Weight, Mass, Normal Force, and Tension

sections.heading: Weight versus mass
sections.body: Mass (measured in kilograms) is an intrinsic property of an object — a measure of how much matter it contains and how strongly it resists acceleration — and it does not change when the object moves to a different location. Weight is a force, W = mg, produced by gravity acting on that mass, and because g varies by location (about 9.8 m/s^2 at Earth's surface, about 1.6 m/s^2 on the Moon, and essentially zero in deep space far from any large body), the same object's weight changes even though its mass stays fixed. A 70 kg astronaut has the same 70 kg mass on the Moon as on Earth, and would resist a push exactly as strongly in either place, but their weight drops from about 686 N on Earth to about 112 N on the Moon — a distinction that matters because everyday language conflates "weight" and "mass" in a way physics does not.

sections.heading: The normal force is a constraint force
sections.body: The normal force is what a surface exerts on an object in contact with it, always perpendicular to that surface, and it is a constraint force: its magnitude is whatever is needed to prevent the object from passing through the surface, not a fixed value tied to the object's weight. On a flat, horizontal surface with no other vertical forces, the normal force does equal mg, but this equality breaks the moment other vertical forces or accelerations are introduced — a person in an elevator accelerating upward feels a normal force greater than mg, a block on an incline has a normal force less than mg (specifically mg*cos(theta) for a frictionless incline), and someone pulled upward by a rope with tension greater than their weight would have a normal force of exactly zero, having left the surface entirely.

sections.heading: Tension in ideal strings, and apparent weight
sections.body: Tension is the pulling force transmitted through a string, rope, or cable, and for an idealized (massless, inextensible) string, the tension has the same magnitude at every point along its length and pulls inward on whatever it is attached to at both ends. This idealization is why a single pulley can redirect a rope's pull without changing its magnitude, a fact used constantly in connected-system problems. Apparent weight — what a scale actually reads — is really just the normal force (or scale-reading tension) the body experiences, and in an accelerating elevator it departs from true weight mg: accelerating upward increases the scale reading above mg, accelerating downward decreases it below mg, and free-fall (elevator cable cut) drives it to exactly zero, the sensation commonly called weightlessness even though gravity, and true weight, are still fully present.

lessons.workedExample: A 60 kg person stands on a bathroom scale inside an elevator accelerating upward at 2 m/s^2. Choosing the person as the system, two vertical forces act: weight W = mg = 60*9.8 = 588 N downward, and the scale's normal force N upward. Newton's second law along the vertical axis gives N - W = ma, so N = W + ma = 588 + (60*2) = 708 N. The scale reads 708 N (about 72.2 kg-equivalent), higher than the person's true weight of 588 N, because upward acceleration requires an upward net force, meaning the normal force must exceed weight. If the elevator instead accelerated downward at 2 m/s^2, the same equation gives N = 588 - 120 = 468 N, a lighter apparent weight, correctly predicting the familiar "stomach drop" sensation as an elevator starts descending.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges lean on elevator and incline scenarios specifically because they force a student to prove the normal force is not simply "equal to mg by definition" — a shortcut that works only in the single special case of a flat surface with zero vertical acceleration. A student who can derive N from Newton's second law in an accelerating frame, correctly distinguishing apparent weight (what a scale reads) from true weight (mg, which never changes with acceleration), demonstrates real command of the constraint-force idea rather than a memorized formula. This also opens naturally into questions about why astronauts in orbit are "weightless" despite gravity still acting on them, a frequent judge follow-up.

questions.prompt: A 70 kg person travels from Earth (g = 9.8 m/s^2) to the Moon (g = 1.6 m/s^2). Which statement is correct?

options.text: Their mass stays 70 kg; their weight decreases from about 686 N to about 112 N
Both their mass and weight decrease proportionally
Their mass decreases but their weight stays the same

explanations.a: Correct: mass is intrinsic and location-independent; weight = mg changes because g changes with location.
explanations.b: Mass does not change with location; only weight, which depends on local g, changes.
explanations.c: This reverses the correct relationship — mass is constant, and it is weight that depends on g and therefore location.

questions.prompt: On a frictionless incline at angle theta, the normal force on a block of weight mg is:

options.text: mg*cos(theta), less than mg
mg, the same as on a flat surface
mg*sin(theta), the component along the incline

explanations.a: Correct: only the component of weight perpendicular to the incline is balanced by the normal force, which is mg*cos(theta) and is less than mg for theta between 0 and 90 degrees.
explanations.b: The normal force equals mg only on a flat horizontal surface with no other vertical forces; tilting the surface changes this.
explanations.c: mg*sin(theta) is the component of weight along the incline's surface (driving the block to slide), not the perpendicular component balanced by the normal force.

questions.prompt: Order these apparent-weight scenarios in an elevator from lowest scale reading to highest, for a person of true weight mg.

items.text: Elevator in free fall (cable cut): scale reads zero
Elevator accelerating downward: scale reads less than mg
Elevator at rest or constant velocity: scale reads exactly mg
Elevator accelerating upward: scale reads more than mg

questions.explanation: Apparent weight ranges from zero in free fall, through less-than-mg when accelerating downward, to exactly mg at constant velocity or rest, up to more-than-mg when accelerating upward.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct description.

right.text: Location-independent measure of inertia, in kg
Force from gravity, W = mg, changes with location
Uniform pulling force along a massless, inextensible string

questions.explanation: Mass is an intrinsic, location-independent property; weight is the gravitational force that depends on local g; tension is the uniform pull transmitted through an idealized string.

lessons.label: Friction: Static and Kinetic

sections.heading: Static friction is self-adjusting and capped
sections.body: Static friction is the force that prevents two surfaces in contact from sliding relative to each other, and its defining feature is that it is self-adjusting: it automatically takes on whatever value, up to a maximum, is needed to keep the object from moving, exactly like a normal force resisting penetration. That maximum is given by f_s,max = mu_s * N, where mu_s is the coefficient of static friction (a property of the two surfaces in contact) and N is the normal force pressing them together. Below that maximum, static friction can be anything from zero up to f_s,max — a book sitting still on a slightly tilted table has some nonzero static friction holding it in place, but far less than the maximum the surfaces could provide, which is why gently increasing the tilt eventually causes it to slip once the required friction exceeds mu_s * N.

sections.heading: Kinetic friction and why mu_s is at least mu_k
sections.body: Once sliding begins, static friction is replaced by kinetic friction, which (unlike static friction) has a single fixed value rather than a self-adjusting range: f_k = mu_k * N, where mu_k is the coefficient of kinetic friction, opposing the direction of relative sliding. Experimentally, mu_s is almost always greater than or equal to mu_k for a given pair of surfaces, which is why it typically takes a noticeably larger push to get a heavy box sliding than it takes to keep it sliding once moving — one common explanation is that stationary surfaces have more time for microscopic contact points to settle and bond, an effect that weakens once sliding begins, though the precise microscopic origin of mu_s being at least mu_k is more complex and still an active area of study in tribology. This is also why a heavy object can seem to jerk into motion suddenly: the moment the applied force barely exceeds f_s,max, the resisting force drops to the smaller f_k, and the net forward force jumps up.

sections.heading: The friction cone and measuring mu from an incline
sections.body: Because static friction is capped at mu_s * N while the normal force itself depends on the angle of an incline, there is a maximum angle beyond which no coefficient of static friction can prevent sliding — visualized as a friction cone, the range of applied-force directions within which static friction can still hold an object still. This gives a clean, direct experimental method for measuring mu_s: place an object on a surface and slowly raise the angle theta until it just begins to slip. At that critical angle theta_c, the component of gravity along the incline (mg*sin(theta_c)) exactly equals the maximum static friction (mu_s * mg*cos(theta_c)), and the mg cancels algebraically to give the strikingly simple result mu_s = tan(theta_c) — a single angle measurement yields the coefficient directly, with no need to measure mass, weight, or force at all.

lessons.workedExample: A student places a wooden block on an adjustable wooden ramp and slowly raises the angle until the block just starts to slide, recording theta_c = 20.6 degrees. Using mu_s = tan(theta_c) = tan(20.6 degrees) ≈ 0.376, a plausible value for wood-on-wood contact.
