To verify, she also measures kinetic friction directly: on the same ramp held at the critical angle, once nudged into sliding the block does not stay at constant velocity but accelerates slightly, confirming mu_k < mu_s for this surface pair; she computes mu_k separately by finding the angle at which the sliding block moves at exactly constant velocity (mg*sin(theta) = mu_k*mg*cos(theta), so mu_k = tan(theta) at THAT lower angle), and finds mu_k ≈ 0.31, numerically less than mu_s ≈ 0.376 as friction theory predicts.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "why did you need a bigger push to start the box moving than to keep it moving" is testing whether a student understands that static and kinetic friction are genuinely different forces with different governing rules, not the same phenomenon at two different speeds. The tan(theta_c) = mu_s incline method is a favorite probe because it requires connecting a force-balance argument to a simple trigonometric result, and a judge can ask a student to derive it live, checking whether they truly understand why the mass cancels out of the final formula rather than having memorized the answer.

questions.prompt: Static friction, as opposed to kinetic friction, is best described as:

options.text: Self-adjusting up to a maximum value of mu_s * N
A single fixed value of mu_s * N whenever two surfaces touch
Always larger than the applied force, so objects never start moving

explanations.a: Correct: static friction adjusts to match the applied force up to the cap f_s,max = mu_s * N, unlike kinetic friction which is fixed at mu_k * N once sliding.
explanations.b: This describes kinetic friction's fixed nature; static friction instead ranges from zero up to that maximum.
explanations.c: Once the applied force exceeds f_s,max, the object DOES begin to move — static friction has a cap, not infinite resistance.

questions.prompt: In the incline-slipping method for measuring mu_s, the critical angle theta_c satisfies:

options.text: mu_s = tan(theta_c)
mu_s = sin(theta_c)
mu_s = mg*cos(theta_c)

explanations.a: Correct: at the critical angle, mg*sin(theta_c) = mu_s*mg*cos(theta_c); the mg cancels, leaving mu_s = sin(theta_c)/cos(theta_c) = tan(theta_c).
explanations.b: sin(theta_c) alone omits the cos(theta_c) term from the normal force side of the balance, so it is not the correct relationship.
explanations.c: mu_s is a dimensionless ratio, not a force, so it cannot equal mg*cos(theta_c), which has units of force.

questions.prompt: Order the events as an increasing force is applied to a block resting on a surface with friction.

items.text: Applied force is small; static friction matches it exactly, block stays still
Applied force approaches f_s,max = mu_s*N; static friction is near its cap
Applied force exceeds f_s,max; the block begins to slide
Friction drops to the smaller kinetic value f_k = mu_k*N as sliding continues

questions.explanation: Static friction self-adjusts up to its maximum, the block slips once applied force exceeds that maximum, and friction then drops to the smaller kinetic value during sliding.

questions.prompt: Match each friction concept to its correct formula or relationship.

right.text: f_s,max = mu_s * N
f_k = mu_k * N
mu_s is typically greater than or equal to mu_k

questions.explanation: Maximum static friction and kinetic friction share the same form (coefficient times normal force), but the static coefficient is typically the larger of the two.

lessons.label: Applying the Laws to Connected Systems

sections.heading: System versus isolated-body analysis
sections.body: When two or more objects are connected — by a rope over a pulley, by direct contact, or stacked on top of each other — there are two valid strategies for applying Newton's second law, and choosing the right one (or combining both) is the core skill of this lesson. Treating the whole connected group as ONE system works when you only need the shared acceleration and the connection forces (tension, contact force) are internal to the system and therefore cancel out of that single equation; this is faster but cannot tell you the value of those internal forces. Isolating each body separately and writing F_net = ma for each one individually is slower but necessary whenever an internal force itself (like the tension in a specific rope, or the contact force between two blocks) is part of what's being asked for — the two approaches are not competitors but complementary tools applied to different questions.

sections.heading: The Atwood machine
sections.body: The classic Atwood machine consists of two masses, m1 and m2, connected by a string over a frictionless, massless pulley, with m1 > m2 so the system accelerates with m1 falling and m2 rising. Treating the system as a whole (a valid shortcut here because both masses share the same magnitude of acceleration, connected by an inextensible string), the net driving force is the difference in weights, (m1 - m2)g, moving a total inertia of (m1 + m2), giving a = (m1 - m2)g / (m1 + m2). To find the tension, however, you must isolate a single mass, since tension is an internal force that cancelled out of the whole-system equation: applying F_net = ma to m2 alone (which accelerates upward) gives T - m2*g = m2*a, solvable once a is already known from the system equation.

sections.heading: Inclines and stacked blocks
sections.body: A block on an incline connected by a string over a pulley to a hanging mass follows the same two-stage logic: the whole-system equation balances the hanging weight against the incline component of the other block's weight (and friction, if present) to find the shared acceleration, while isolating either block individually and resolving forces along and perpendicular to its own relevant axis (the incline's surface for the block on the ramp, vertical for the hanging mass) reveals the tension and normal force. Stacked blocks add a further wrinkle: if a bottom block is pushed and a top block rides on it via friction alone (no rope), the top block's acceleration is capped by the maximum static friction it can receive from the bottom block — isolating the top block shows that if the required friction to keep it moving with the bottom block would exceed mu_s * N, the blocks instead slide relative to each other, and kinetic friction (a smaller, fixed value) takes over for the top block's actual, smaller acceleration.

lessons.workedExample: An Atwood machine has m1 = 5 kg and m2 = 3 kg over a frictionless, massless pulley. Treating the system as a whole: a = (m1 - m2)g / (m1 + m2) = (5-3)(9.8) / (5+3) = 19.6/8 = 2.45 m/s^2, with m1 accelerating downward and m2 upward at that shared magnitude. To find the tension, isolate m2 (accelerating upward at 2.45 m/s^2): T - m2*g = m2*a, so T = m2*(g + a) = 3*(9.8 + 2.45) = 3*12.25 = 36.75 N. As a check, isolating m1 instead (accelerating downward) should give the same T: m1*g - T = m1*a, so T = m1*(g - a) = 5*(9.8 - 2.45) = 5*7.35 = 36.75 N — matching exactly, confirming the whole-system acceleration and the single, shared string tension are mutually consistent.
lessons.judgeFraming: Connected-system problems are a favorite because they cannot be brute-forced by memorizing one formula — a judge can ask for acceleration first, then immediately follow up asking for a specific internal force like tension or the contact force between two blocks, which forces the student to demonstrate they know WHEN the whole-system shortcut applies and when it is necessary to isolate a body instead. A student who correctly explains why the whole-system approach cannot yield the tension (because tension is internal and cancels out of that equation) shows they understand the structure of the method, not just its arithmetic, which is exactly the depth a fair judge is listening for.

questions.prompt: For an Atwood machine with m1 > m2 over a frictionless, massless pulley, treating the whole system as one object can directly give you:

options.text: The shared acceleration of both masses, but not the string tension
Both the acceleration and the tension
The tension, but not the acceleration

explanations.a: Correct: tension is an internal force between the two masses and cancels out of the whole-system equation, so only acceleration is directly available; tension requires isolating one mass.
explanations.b: Tension cannot be found from the whole-system equation alone, since it is internal to the system and cancels out.
explanations.c: The whole-system approach gives acceleration directly; it is tension, not acceleration, that requires isolating a single body.

questions.prompt: A block rides on top of another block that is being pushed and accelerates it via friction alone (no rope). If the required friction to keep them moving together would exceed mu_s * N, then:

options.text: The top block slides relative to the bottom block, and kinetic friction (a smaller value) governs its actual, smaller acceleration
The blocks continue moving together regardless, since friction always adjusts to whatever is needed
The bottom block stops moving entirely

explanations.a: Correct: static friction is capped at mu_s * N; once the required friction would exceed that cap, sliding begins and the smaller, fixed kinetic friction takes over.
explanations.b: Static friction is self-adjusting only up to its maximum; it cannot exceed mu_s * N no matter what acceleration would be 'needed.'
explanations.c: Nothing in this scenario stops the bottom block; the mismatch causes relative sliding between the two blocks, not a halt of the whole system.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving an Atwood machine problem for both acceleration and tension.

items.text: Confirm the string is inextensible, so both masses share the same magnitude of acceleration
Treat the two masses as one system and solve a = (m1-m2)g/(m1+m2)
Isolate one mass and write its own F_net = ma equation, using the acceleration just found
Solve that single-body equation for the tension T

questions.explanation: The shared-acceleration assumption justifies the whole-system shortcut, which yields acceleration; tension then requires isolating one body and solving its individual equation using that already-known acceleration.

questions.prompt: Match each connected-system quantity to the correct analysis approach needed to find it.

left.text: Shared acceleration of an Atwood machine
String tension in an Atwood machine
Contact force between two pushed, touching blocks

right.text: Whole-system equation (internal forces cancel)
Isolate one mass individually
Isolate one of the two blocks individually

questions.explanation: Shared acceleration comes from the whole-system shortcut since internal forces cancel; both tension and the contact force between blocks are internal forces that require isolating one body to solve for.

lessons.label: Work and the Work-Energy Theorem

sections.heading: Work is a dot product, not just "effort"
sections.body: In physics, work has a strict definition: W = F * d * cos(theta), where F is the magnitude of a constant force, d is the magnitude of the displacement, and theta is the angle between the force vector and the displacement vector. This is the scalar (dot) product of the force and displacement vectors, F-vec dot d-vec. The formula punishes intuition in a specific way: if you push hard on a wall that does not move, d = 0, so W = 0, no matter how tired you get. If you carry a heavy box at constant height across a room, the force you exert (upward, supporting weight) is perpendicular to the displacement (horizontal), so cos(90 degrees) = 0 and W = 0 again. Physics work is not effort or time spent; it is force projected onto the direction something actually moves.

sections.heading: Positive, negative, and zero work
sections.body: The sign of cos(theta) sets the sign of the work, and the sign tells you what the force does to an object's motion. When theta is between 0 and 90 degrees, cos(theta) is positive: the force has a component along the direction of motion and does positive work, adding kinetic energy. When theta is exactly 90 degrees, the force does zero work, changing direction but not speed (this is how the normal force behaves on flat ground, and how gravity behaves on a satellite in a circular orbit). When theta is between 90 and 180 degrees, cos(theta) is negative: the force opposes the motion and does negative work, removing kinetic energy. Kinetic friction sliding against motion is the standard example of negative work.

sections.heading: The work-energy theorem: a shortcut around forces
sections.body: The work-energy theorem states that the NET work done on an object (the sum of the work done by every force acting on it) equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = KE_final - KE_initial. This is derived from Newton's second law and kinematics, but once derived it lets you skip acceleration entirely. If you know all the forces and the distance over which they act, you can find a final speed without ever computing acceleration or time. This is especially powerful when the net force is not constant (a spring, an incline with varying friction), where a straight kinematics approach would require calculus but an energy approach does not. It also generalizes cleanly to multiple forces acting at once: you do not need to find the net force vector first, you can compute each force's work separately and simply add the (signed) results, since work is a scalar. That additive property is what makes the theorem practical for real, multi-force systems like a sled being pulled uphill against both gravity and friction simultaneously.

lessons.workedExample: A 10 kg sled starts at rest on a horizontal surface. A person pulls it with a constant horizontal force of 40 N over a distance of 5 m; friction opposes the motion with a constant force of 15 N. Work by the pull: W_pull = 40 * 5 * cos(0 degrees) = 200 J (positive). Work by friction: W_friction = 15 * 5 * cos(180 degrees) = -75 J (negative). Net work: W_net = 200 - 75 = 125 J. By the work-energy theorem, 125 J = (1/2)(10 kg)(v^2) - 0, so v^2 = 25 and v = 5 m/s. Note this required no acceleration or time calculation at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about work versus force because the sign confusion is diagnostic: a student who says friction does "negative work" understands that work is directional and tied to displacement, not just magnitude of force. A judge probing an experiment involving pulleys, inclines, or braking will often ask, "which forces did positive work and which did negative work, and how do you know?" A vague answer that treats work as a synonym for force reveals a surface-level grasp; naming the angle between each force and the displacement, and its sign, reveals real command of the concept.

questions.prompt: A student carries a bag at constant height while walking across a flat room. How much work does her upward supporting force do on the bag?

options.text: Zero, because the force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement
Positive, because she is exerting effort the whole time
Negative, because gravity is pulling the bag down

explanations.a: Correct: W = F * d * cos(theta) with theta = 90 degrees between the vertical support force and the horizontal displacement gives cos(90) = 0, so work is zero regardless of how much force is applied.
explanations.b: Effort and physics work are different things. Muscular fatigue does not appear in W = F * d * cos(theta); only the force component along the displacement does.
explanations.c: Gravity's work depends on gravity's own angle to displacement, not on the supporting force. Here the relevant force is the one exerted BY the student, and it is perpendicular to the motion.

questions.prompt: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals:

options.text: Its change in kinetic energy
Its change in momentum
The total force acting on it

explanations.a: Correct: W_net = KE_final - KE_initial, derived from Newton's second law integrated over distance.
explanations.b: Change in momentum equals impulse (force times TIME), a related but distinct theorem from work (force times DISTANCE).
explanations.c: Work is not a force; it has units of joules (force times distance), and the theorem relates it to an energy quantity, not to force itself.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of solving for a final speed using the work-energy theorem instead of kinematics.

items.text: Identify every force acting on the object
Compute the work done by each force using F * d * cos(theta)
Sum the individual works to get the net work
Set the net work equal to the change in kinetic energy and solve for speed

questions.explanation: You must first know which forces act before you can compute each one's work; only after summing all the individual works do you have the net work to plug into W_net = change in KE.

questions.prompt: Match each force scenario to the sign of the work it does on the object.

left.text: A force pushing in the same direction as motion
The normal force on an object sliding along a flat, horizontal floor

right.text: Positive work
Negative work
Zero work

questions.explanation: A force aligned with motion (theta = 0) does positive work; friction opposing motion (theta = 180) does negative work; the normal force on flat ground is perpendicular to horizontal displacement (theta = 90) and does zero work.

lessons.label: Kinetic Energy

sections.heading: Why the square, not just v
sections.body: Kinetic energy is defined as KE = (1/2) m v^2, where m is mass and v is speed. The factor of 1/2 falls out of the work-energy derivation (integrating F = ma over distance), but the v^2 is the part that matters for intuition. Energy depends on speed quadratically, not linearly, and this quadratic dependence comes directly from integrating F = ma over distance, the same derivation (integral of F dx = integral of m v dv = (1/2) m v^2) that also yields the work-energy theorem, so it is baked into the definition of kinetic energy itself, not a separate consequence of the theorem: a constant braking force removes kinetic energy at a rate set by distance, not time, and KE itself scales with v^2. This is not a minor mathematical detail; it is the reason braking distances and crash severities scale far more steeply with speed than intuition expects (wind-turbine power is even steeper still, scaling as v^3, because the mass of air flowing through the turbine each second also grows with v).

sections.heading: Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy
sections.body: If speed doubles, v^2 becomes (2v)^2 = 4v^2, so kinetic energy quadruples, not doubles. This has a direct, testable consequence for braking distance. If a car's brakes apply roughly the same braking force regardless of speed, the work-energy theorem says the stopping distance is proportional to the initial kinetic energy (since a fixed braking force does work proportional to distance to remove that energy). So a car going twice as fast needs roughly four times the distance to stop, not twice. This is why speed limits on highways are so much more consequential than they feel: going from 30 to 60 mph is not "twice as dangerous," it is roughly four times the stopping distance and four times the collision energy.

sections.heading: A scalar quantity that depends on your frame
sections.body: Kinetic energy is a scalar: it has a magnitude but no direction, unlike velocity or momentum. This makes it easier to work with in some ways (no components to track, no need to resolve a vector sum before squaring), but it hides an important subtlety: KE is not invariant, it depends on the reference frame of the observer, because v itself depends on the reference frame. A passenger sitting still inside a train moving at 30 m/s has zero kinetic energy relative to the train but a large kinetic energy relative to the ground. There is no single "true" kinetic energy for an object; there is only kinetic energy relative to a stated frame, and every energy calculation implicitly picks one (almost always the ground, or lab frame, in an introductory course). This matters in practice whenever a problem involves two moving objects, such as a ball thrown from inside a moving car: the ball's kinetic energy relative to the car and relative to the road are both legitimate numbers, but they are different numbers, and a problem must specify which frame it wants before "the" kinetic energy has a single meaning.

lessons.workedExample: A 1500 kg car traveling at 20 m/s has KE = (1/2)(1500)(20^2) = 300,000 J. The same car at 40 m/s (double the speed) has KE = (1/2)(1500)(40^2) = 1,200,000 J, exactly four times as much, confirming the v^2 relationship. If the brakes supply a constant force of 6000 N, the work-energy theorem gives stopping distance d = KE / F: at 20 m/s, d = 300,000 / 6000 = 50 m; at 40 m/s, d = 1,200,000 / 6000 = 200 m, four times farther, not twice as far, for only double the speed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the v^2 relationship because it separates students who memorized a formula from students who understand its consequences. A student presenting a project on vehicle safety, wind energy, or sports biomechanics who can say "kinetic energy quadruples, so a small speed increase matters far more than it looks like it should" is applying the science, not reciting it. A judge will often ask a follow-up like "if speed increases by 50% instead of doubling, what happens to kinetic energy?" (answer: multiply by 1.5^2 = 2.25, not 1.5) to check whether the quadratic relationship, not just the doubling case, has actually been internalized.

questions.prompt: If an object's speed doubles and its mass stays the same, its kinetic energy:

options.text: Doubles
Quadruples
Stays the same

explanations.a: Doubling would be true if KE were proportional to v, but KE = (1/2)m v^2 is proportional to v-squared.
explanations.b: Correct: (2v)^2 = 4v^2, so KE quadruples when speed doubles, holding mass constant.
explanations.c: KE strongly depends on speed; it cannot stay the same when speed changes and mass is fixed.

questions.prompt: A passenger sits motionless in her seat on a train moving at 30 m/s relative to the ground. Her kinetic energy is:

options.text: Zero in every reference frame, since she isn't moving her arms or legs
Zero relative to the train, but large relative to the ground, because KE depends on the observer's frame
Undefined, because kinetic energy only applies to rigid objects like vehicles, not people

explanations.a: Kinetic energy depends on velocity RELATIVE TO A FRAME, not on internal motion of limbs; she is moving relative to the ground even while sitting still relative to the train.
explanations.b: Correct: KE = (1/2)mv^2 uses whatever v is in the chosen frame. Relative to the train she has v = 0, so KE = 0 in that frame; relative to the ground she has v = 30 m/s, so KE is large in that frame.
explanations.c: Kinetic energy applies to any mass with a defined velocity in some frame, people included; there is nothing special about rigidity.

questions.prompt: Assuming a constant braking force, match each change in initial speed to its effect on stopping distance.

right.text: Stopping distance multiplies by 4
Stopping distance multiplies by 9
Stopping distance multiplies by 1/4

questions.explanation: With a constant braking force, distance is proportional to kinetic energy, which is proportional to v^2: 2^2 = 4, 3^2 = 9, and (1/2)^2 = 1/4.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps that connect a change in speed to a change in stopping distance.

items.text: Write kinetic energy as KE = (1/2) m v^2
Note that a constant braking force does work W = F * d to remove that kinetic energy
Set W equal to KE and solve: d = m v^2 / (2F)
Conclude that stopping distance d is proportional to v^2, so doubling v quadruples d

questions.explanation: The chain starts from the KE formula, applies the work-energy theorem to relate braking work to the KE removed, solves algebraically for distance, then reads off the proportionality to v^2.

lessons.label: Potential Energy: Gravitational and Elastic

sections.heading: Gravitational PE and the arbitrary zero
sections.body: Near Earth's surface, gravitational potential energy is PE_grav = m g h, where h is height above some chosen reference level. The critical, often-missed detail is that h, and therefore PE_grav, has no fixed zero point; you choose the reference level (the floor, the tabletop, sea level) and everything is measured relative to it. This is not a flaw in the formula, it is a feature: physics only ever cares about CHANGES in potential energy (delta-PE), because those changes are what convert to kinetic energy or work. A book on a table has a different numeric PE_grav depending on whether you measure h from the floor or from the tabletop, but the change in PE_grav as it falls to the floor is the same either way, because the reference level cancels out of any subtraction.

sections.heading: Hooke's law and elastic potential energy
sections.body: A spring stretched or compressed by a distance x exerts a restoring force F = -kx, where k is the spring constant (units N/m) and the negative sign shows the force always points back toward equilibrium, opposite the displacement. Because this force is not constant (it grows as x grows), the work needed to stretch the spring is not simply F times x; it is the area under the F-versus-x graph, which is a triangle, giving elastic potential energy PE_elastic = (1/2) k x^2. Like gravitational PE, elastic PE is stored energy available to do work later, released as the spring returns toward x = 0.

sections.heading: Conservative forces and path independence
sections.body: Gravity and the spring force share a defining property: they are CONSERVATIVE forces, meaning the work they do on an object moving between two points does not depend on the path taken, only on the start and end positions. A hiker who climbs a mountain by a long, winding trail does the same net work against gravity as one who climbs a short, steep face to the identical summit; only the change in height matters. This is exactly why a potential energy function can be written for them at all; a well-defined PE(position) only exists for conservative forces. Friction and air drag are non-conservative: the work they do depends on the actual path length (a longer path means more friction work), so no potential energy function exists for them. This distinction is why gravitational and elastic PE can be added into a single conserved "mechanical energy" total, while frictional losses cannot; they must instead be tracked separately as energy leaving the mechanical system, the subject of the unit's final lesson.

lessons.workedExample: A spring with k = 200 N/m is compressed x = 0.15 m: elastic PE = (1/2)(200)(0.15^2) = 2.25 J, ready to launch a small object when released. Separately, a 0.5 kg book sits on a shelf h = 2 m above the floor: PE_grav = (0.5)(9.8)(2) = 9.8 J, measured with the floor as the zero reference. If the reference is instead set at the tabletop 0.8 m below the shelf (so the tabletop sits 1.2 m above the floor), h becomes 0.8 m and PE_grav = (0.5)(9.8)(0.8) = 3.92 J, a different NUMBER, but the change in PE as the book falls to the floor, 9.8 J either way once you subtract consistently (floor reference: 9.8 J to 0 J; tabletop reference: 3.92 J to -5.88 J), is identical, confirming that the reference level itself carries no physical meaning.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask where the "zero" of potential energy is because it exposes whether a student understands PE as a bookkeeping tool for changes in energy, or mistakes it for an absolute physical quantity like mass. A student who can say "I set h = 0 at the launch point because only the CHANGE in PE matters for this problem" demonstrates real command; a student who insists a specific numeric PE value is "the" potential energy, without naming their reference, has not grasped it. For spring-based projects (catapults, dampers), judges also probe whether students realize F = -kx is not constant, which is why (1/2)kx^2, not kx^2 or F times x, is the correct stored energy.

questions.prompt: A student measures a ball's gravitational PE using the floor as the reference level, then a classmate re-measures using the tabletop (0.8 m higher) as the reference. What happens to the CHANGE in PE as the ball falls to the floor?

options.text: It stays the same in both reference-level choices, because only the reference point's numeric value shifts, not the physical drop
It changes, because a different reference level means a genuinely different amount of energy was released
It becomes undefined, since PE has no true zero

explanations.a: Correct: absolute PE values shift with the reference level, but the DIFFERENCE between two PE values (the change) is reference-independent, since the same constant offset appears in and cancels out of both.
explanations.b: The physical process (the ball dropping the same real height) doesn't change just because you relabeled your coordinate system; the released energy is a physical fact, not a labeling artifact.
explanations.c: PE having no fixed zero does not make it undefined; it means only differences are physically meaningful, and those differences are perfectly well defined.

questions.prompt: In Hooke's law, F = -kx, the negative sign indicates that:

options.text: The spring force always points opposite the displacement, back toward equilibrium
The spring constant k is a negative number
The formula only applies when the spring is compressed, not stretched

explanations.a: Correct: F = -kx is a RESTORING force; whichever way you displace the spring (positive x or negative x), the force points the other way, back toward x = 0.
explanations.b: k itself is a positive physical constant describing stiffness; the negative sign is built into the formula, not into the value of k.
explanations.c: F = -kx applies to both stretching (x positive) and compressing (x negative); in both cases the force opposes the displacement.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that derive elastic potential energy PE = (1/2)k x^2 from Hooke's law.

items.text: Write the spring force magnitude as F = kx, which grows linearly with displacement
Recognize that since F is not constant, work cannot be found as simply F times x
Find the work as the area under the F-versus-x graph, a triangle with base x and height kx
Compute that triangular area as (1/2)(x)(kx) = (1/2)k x^2

questions.explanation: You must first note the force grows with x, then recognize that a non-constant force rules out the simple F times x shortcut, then use the area-under-the-graph method, which finally evaluates to (1/2)k x^2.

questions.prompt: Match each force to whether it is conservative or non-conservative.

right.text: Conservative (path-independent, has a PE function)
Non-conservative (path-dependent, no PE function)

questions.explanation: Gravity and the spring force do work that depends only on start and end position, so each has a well-defined potential energy; friction's work depends on the length of the path traveled, so it has no potential energy function.

lessons.label: Conservation of Mechanical Energy

sections.heading: KE plus PE stays constant, if the forces cooperate
sections.body: Mechanical energy is defined as the sum E_mech = KE + PE. When the ONLY forces doing work on a system are conservative (gravity, an ideal spring), that sum stays constant throughout the motion, even though KE and PE individually trade off. As an object falls, PE_grav decreases and KE increases by exactly the same amount; at the bottom of a pendulum swing, all the initial PE has become KE, and at the top of the return swing, it has all become PE again. This is the conservation of mechanical energy, and it is a direct consequence of the work-energy theorem applied to a system where the only forces present are conservative: if W_net = W_conservative and W_conservative = -delta-PE by definition, then W_net = delta-KE, so delta-KE + delta-PE = 0.

sections.heading: A shortcut around forces, angles, and curved paths
sections.body: Conservation of mechanical energy is often far easier than a force analysis, especially for curved paths like a rollercoaster loop or a swinging pendulum, where the direction (and sometimes magnitude) of the net force changes continuously. Rather than integrating Newton's second law along a curve, you compare energy at just two points: initial and final. A rollercoaster car released from height h1 with negligible friction arrives at any lower height h2 with the same speed regardless of the track's shape in between, because only h1 and h2 (not the path) matter for gravitational PE, a direct consequence of gravity being a conservative force.

sections.heading: When the shortcut breaks down
sections.body: The conservation shortcut is only valid when non-conservative forces (friction, air drag, an external push) do zero or negligible work. Real rollercoasters have friction and air resistance, so the true final speed is always slightly less than the frictionless prediction; the energy method still works, but you must subtract the energy lost to those forces (covered in the next lesson) rather than assuming pure KE-PE trade-off. A useful habit is to state the assumption explicitly before applying the shortcut: "treating friction and air resistance as negligible over this short drop" is a defensible, falsifiable claim a judge can evaluate, while silently assuming it is not. Knowing when to reach for the shortcut versus when to add a dissipation term is itself part of using the concept correctly, not just applying the formula.

lessons.workedExample: A pendulum of mass 0.3 kg is pulled back and released from a height 0.2 m above the lowest point of its swing, with negligible air resistance. At the release point, KE = 0 and PE_grav = mgh = (0.3)(9.8)(0.2) = 0.588 J, so total mechanical energy is 0.588 J. At the lowest point, all of that has converted to KE (since h = 0 there): (1/2)(0.3)v^2 = 0.588, giving v^2 = 3.92 and v is approximately 1.98 m/s. A force-based approach would require integrating a continuously changing tension and gravity component along the arc, far more work for the identical answer.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask when a student chose energy conservation over a force analysis because it tests engineering judgment, not just formula recall. A strong answer names the specific reason the shortcut applied here ("the track curves, so the net force direction keeps changing, but only the start and end heights matter for energy") and, critically, states which forces were assumed negligible (usually friction and air resistance) and why that assumption is reasonable for this experiment. A student who applies conservation of energy without ever mentioning what could break it (friction, a motor doing work, air drag at high speed) has memorized a formula, not understood its domain of validity.

questions.prompt: Conservation of mechanical energy (KE + PE = constant) is valid for a system when:

options.text: Only conservative forces (like gravity or an ideal spring) do work on the system
The object moves at constant speed throughout
The path is a straight line

explanations.a: Correct: the KE-PE trade-off only balances exactly when non-conservative forces like friction do zero work; any energy lost to friction breaks the simple sum.
explanations.b: Constant speed would mean constant KE, which is a special case, not the general condition; mechanical energy conservation allows KE to change as long as PE changes to compensate.
explanations.c: Path shape is irrelevant to whether energy is conserved; a curved frictionless track conserves mechanical energy just as well as a straight frictionless one.

questions.prompt: A student uses conservation of energy to predict a rollercoaster car's speed at the bottom of a hill, but the real measured speed is noticeably lower than predicted. The most likely explanation is:

options.text: Friction and air resistance did negative work, removing some mechanical energy that the frictionless model ignored
The height measurement must be wrong, since energy is always exactly conserved
The car's mass changed between the top and bottom of the hill

explanations.a: Correct: real tracks always have some friction and drag; these non-conservative forces convert part of the mechanical energy to heat and sound, so the actual final KE is lower than the frictionless prediction.
explanations.b: Total energy (including heat) is always conserved, but MECHANICAL energy specifically is not conserved once non-conservative forces act, so a height measurement error is not the most likely cause of a small, expected shortfall.
explanations.c: Mass does not change during a rollercoaster ride; this does not explain a systematically lower speed.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving a frictionless pendulum-release problem using energy conservation.

items.text: Choose a reference level (typically the lowest point of the swing) where PE = 0
Compute the initial mechanical energy as PE_grav at the release height (KE = 0 there)
Set the mechanical energy at the lowest point (all KE, since PE = 0) equal to the initial mechanical energy
Solve the resulting equation for the unknown speed

questions.explanation: A reference level must be fixed before any PE can be numerically computed; only then can you state the initial energy, equate it to the final energy, and solve algebraically.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the better solution method.

left.text: Finding final speed on a curved, frictionless track with a continuously changing slope
Finding the exact acceleration at one instant on an incline with a known friction coefficient

right.text: Energy conservation (compare only start and end states)
Newton's second law force analysis (need forces at that instant)

questions.explanation: Energy methods shine when only the start and end states matter and the path is complicated; force methods are needed when the question asks about an instantaneous quantity like acceleration at a specific point.

lessons.label: Power

sections.heading: Power is the RATE of doing work
sections.body: Power measures how quickly work is done or energy is transferred: P = W / t, with units of watts (W), where one watt equals one joule per second. Because power divides work by time, two engines can do the identical amount of work (deliver the identical amount of energy) and still have very different power ratings, if one takes far longer to do it. This is the entire reason power exists as a separate quantity from energy: energy answers "how much," power answers "how fast." A crane and a hand-crank winch can both lift the same 1000 kg beam the same 10 m (identical work, identical energy transferred), but the crane does it in 5 seconds and the winch in 5 minutes, a power difference of exactly 60-fold.

sections.heading: P = F v: power from force and velocity
sections.body: For an object moving at velocity v under an applied force F in the direction of motion, power can also be written as P = F * v, derived by substituting d = v*t into W = F*d and dividing by t. This form is often more directly useful than P = W/t because it applies instantaneously: at any moment, an engine's power output equals the driving force it currently applies times the current speed. This is why a car's engine can produce huge power at highway speed with a modest force, or huge force at low speed (starting from a stop) with modest power, since the two trade off for the same power rating.

sections.heading: Average versus instantaneous power
sections.body: P = W/t computed over an entire time interval gives AVERAGE power; P = F*v evaluated at one specific moment gives INSTANTANEOUS power. The two agree only when power output is constant throughout the interval; otherwise average power is the total energy divided by total time, smoothing over moment-to-moment variation. This is why an athlete's sprint is often measured by both peak (instantaneous) power output, useful for judging explosive capability, and average power sustained over a race, useful for judging endurance; the two numbers measure genuinely different things and a project comparing athletes or motors should specify which one it reports. A car's advertised horsepower is a peak figure reached only in a narrow band of engine speeds, not a number the engine sustains continuously across its whole operating range, which is a common source of confusion when comparing it to a sustained average, such as an engine's rated towing power over a long climb.

lessons.workedExample: A motor lifts a 50 kg mass a height of 3 m in 5 seconds at constant velocity. The work done is W = mgh = (50)(9.8)(3) = 1470 J, so the average power is P = W/t = 1470/5 = 294 W. Since the lift is at constant velocity, v = 3 m / 5 s = 0.6 m/s, and the lifting force must equal the weight, F = mg = 490 N. Checking with the instantaneous formula: P = F*v = (490)(0.6) = 294 W, matching the average exactly, because the velocity (and therefore the power) was constant throughout the lift.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about power, rather than just energy, when a project involves any kind of engine, motor, or athletic performance, because rating a device by total energy alone is meaningless without a time frame; a car battery can deliver hundreds of amps for a few seconds to start an engine yet takes hours to fully recharge, so its momentary power output and its total stored energy tell a judge two very different things about what the battery is suited for. A judge will often ask a student to distinguish average from instantaneous power for their specific device ("was that peak power or sustained power?"), because conflating the two is one of the most common errors in a project's data reporting, and catching it signals a student who understands what they measured rather than just what number their sensor displayed.

questions.prompt: Two motors each lift an identical 200 kg crate to the identical height of 4 m. Motor A takes 8 seconds; Motor B takes 2 seconds. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both motors do the same amount of work, but Motor B has four times the average power
Motor B does four times as much work as Motor A, since it finishes faster
Both motors have the same power, since they did the same work

explanations.a: Correct: work only depends on force and distance (W = mgh here), so both motors do identical work; power is work divided by TIME, so the motor that takes 1/4 the time delivers 4 times the power for the same work.
explanations.b: Work depends on mass, gravity, and height, none of which differ between the two motors; time does not enter the work calculation at all.
explanations.c: Equal work does not imply equal power unless the time taken is also equal; here the times differ by a factor of 4, so the powers differ by a factor of 4.

questions.prompt: A sprinter's power output rises sharply for the first 2 seconds of a race and then levels off for the remaining 8 seconds. A report that states only her AVERAGE power over the full 10 seconds would:

options.text: Understate her peak (instantaneous) power output during the initial burst
Correctly capture every moment of her performance, since average power accounts for all variation
Overstate her power output, since average power is always higher than instantaneous power

explanations.a: Correct: averaging smooths out the high initial burst with the lower sustained phase, so the reported average is necessarily lower than the true peak power reached during the burst.
explanations.b: Averaging by definition discards moment-to-moment detail; it reports total energy over total time, not the shape of the power-versus-time curve.
explanations.c: There is no general rule that average power exceeds instantaneous power; here it is the reverse, the peak instantaneous power exceeds the average.

questions.prompt: Match each formula or unit to what it represents.

right.text: 1 joule of energy transferred per second
Instantaneous power from force and current velocity
Average power from total work over a time interval

questions.explanation: The watt is defined as J/s; P = F*v gives power at one instant using the current force and velocity; P = W/t gives average power by spreading total work across the whole interval.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for computing a motor's average power from a lifting task.

items.text: Compute the work done using W = m * g * h
Measure the total time t the lift took
Divide work by time, P = W / t, to get average power
Optionally cross-check with P = F * v using the constant lifting speed

questions.explanation: Work must be computed first, timing measured second, then the two combined for average power; the instantaneous-power cross-check is an optional final verification step, not part of the core calculation.

lessons.label: Non-Conservative Forces and Energy Dissipation

sections.heading: Friction and drag convert mechanical energy to heat
sections.body: Kinetic friction and air or fluid drag are non-conservative forces: they always do negative work on a moving object (opposing its motion) and that work does not reappear as recoverable mechanical energy. Instead, it is converted into thermal energy, warming the surfaces in contact (and the surrounding air, for drag) along with a small amount of sound. This conversion is not reversible in any practical sense; a block slowed by friction does not spontaneously speed back up as the surfaces cool, even though the total energy involved is unchanged. This one-directional quality is why friction and drag are called DISSIPATIVE: they scatter organized, useful mechanical energy into disorganized thermal motion of countless molecules.

sections.heading: The generalized work-energy relationship
sections.body: The clean statement KE + PE = constant only holds when non-conservative forces do zero work. The more general and always-true relationship is: the work done by non-conservative forces equals the CHANGE in total mechanical energy, W_nc = E_mech,final - E_mech,initial. Since non-conservative forces like friction almost always remove energy, W_nc is typically negative, meaning E_mech decreases: some of the initial KE + PE is not present at the end because it left the mechanical system as heat. This equation is the direct generalization of the work-energy theorem from the frictionless case: it lets you solve real problems (a block sliding down a rough incline, a pendulum slowly losing amplitude to air resistance) by explicitly accounting for the energy that leaves the mechanical "budget".

sections.heading: Nothing is actually lost: a preview of the first law
sections.body: It is tempting to say friction "destroys" energy, but this is imprecise. Total energy, mechanical plus thermal (plus any other form present), is always conserved; friction merely converts a highly organized, easily reusable form (bulk kinetic or potential energy) into a highly disorganized, essentially unrecoverable form (random molecular kinetic energy, i.e., heat). This foreshadows the first law of thermodynamics, covered later, which states that energy is conserved for any closed system once every form, mechanical AND thermal, is counted. "Lost" mechanical energy in an introductory mechanics problem really means "transferred out of the mechanical accounting into heat," not annihilated. This is also why brake rotors on a car get hot after repeated stops: every joule of kinetic energy removed by braking friction has to go somewhere, and it goes into raising the thermal energy, and therefore the temperature, of the rotors and pads themselves.

lessons.workedExample: A 4 kg block slides down a rough ramp, dropping a height of 2 m, and arrives at the bottom moving at 5 m/s. If the ramp were frictionless, energy conservation would predict v = sqrt(2 * 9.8 * 2), about 6.26 m/s. Instead: initial mechanical energy (all PE, since it starts at rest) is E_i = mgh = (4)(9.8)(2) = 78.4 J. Final mechanical energy (all KE, at the bottom) is E_f = (1/2)(4)(5^2) = 50 J. The work done by friction is W_friction = E_f - E_i = 50 - 78.4 = -28.4 J. That 28.4 J did not vanish; it left the block-and-ramp mechanical system as heat generated at the sliding surfaces.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about energy "loss" to friction because it is one of the most common places student explanations quietly become unscientific, casually saying energy "disappeared" or was "wasted" without saying where it went. A strong answer names the destination explicitly (heat at the contact surfaces, or heat and sound for air drag) and, ideally, gives a number for W_nc computed from measured initial and final mechanical energy. A judge probing a project with any friction, drag, or damping (a car crash test, a parachute, a pendulum with a swinging weight) is checking whether the student treats "energy conservation" as a global law that always holds (once heat is counted) rather than a formula that occasionally breaks.

questions.prompt: A sliding block loses 30 J of mechanical energy to kinetic friction. What is the most physically accurate description of that 30 J?

options.text: It was converted into thermal energy (heat) at the sliding surfaces, not destroyed
It was destroyed, since energy conservation only applies to frictionless systems
It was converted directly back into potential energy

explanations.a: Correct: non-conservative forces convert mechanical energy into other forms, chiefly heat (and a little sound); total energy, mechanical plus thermal, is still conserved.
explanations.b: Energy conservation is a completely general law; it is MECHANICAL energy specifically, not total energy, that is not conserved when non-conservative forces act.
explanations.c: Friction does not restore energy to a usable mechanical form (like PE); the conversion to heat is effectively one-directional in practice.

questions.prompt: The relationship W_nc = E_mech,final - E_mech,initial is best described as:

options.text: A generalization of the work-energy idea that accounts for energy leaving the mechanical system via non-conservative forces
A special case that only applies when there is no friction present
An equation for computing total energy, including heat, directly

explanations.a: Correct: when W_nc = 0 (no non-conservative work), this reduces to E_mech,final = E_mech,initial, the simple conservation case; when W_nc is nonzero, it tells you exactly how much mechanical energy left the system.
explanations.b: The opposite is true: this equation is most useful precisely WHEN friction or drag is present; without them it reduces to the simpler conservation law.
explanations.c: The equation tracks only mechanical energy (KE + PE) before and after; it identifies how much left as heat via W_nc, but does not itself compute a total energy including heat.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving a block-on-a-rough-incline problem using the non-conservative work relationship.

items.text: Compute the initial mechanical energy (KE + PE) at the top of the incline
Compute the final mechanical energy (KE + PE) at the bottom, using the measured or given final speed
Subtract to find W_nc = E_mech,final - E_mech,initial
Interpret the negative result as mechanical energy converted to heat by friction

questions.explanation: Both endpoint mechanical energies must be established before they can be subtracted to isolate the non-conservative work, which is then interpreted physically as heat generated by friction.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the correct sign or size of W_nc (work done by non-conservative forces).

left.text: A frictionless pendulum swinging with no air resistance
A block sliding to a stop on a rough floor
A motor actively pushing an object forward, adding energy beyond gravity or springs

right.text: W_nc = 0
W_nc is negative (removes mechanical energy)
W_nc is positive (adds mechanical energy)

questions.explanation: With no non-conservative forces acting, W_nc is zero and mechanical energy is exactly conserved; friction removes mechanical energy (negative W_nc); an external motor doing positive work on the system adds mechanical energy (positive W_nc).

units.label: Momentum, Impulse, and Center of Mass

lessons.label: Linear Momentum

sections.heading: Momentum as a vector: p = mv
sections.body: Linear momentum is defined as p = mv, the product of an object's mass and its velocity. Because velocity is a vector, momentum is a vector too, always pointing in the same direction the object is moving, with units of kilogram-meters per second (kg·m/s). This matters more than it first appears: two objects can have identical mass and identical speed yet completely different momentum if they are moving in different directions, and momentum vectors from different objects can partially or fully cancel when added together, the way a loaded cart moving right and an identical cart moving left, combined, carry zero net momentum even though both are in motion. Momentum is one of physics' great conserved quantities, meaning the total momentum of an isolated system never changes over time even as individual objects within it speed up, slow down, or change direction through their interactions with one another.

sections.heading: Momentum and kinetic energy scale differently with velocity
sections.body: Momentum and kinetic energy both depend on mass and velocity, but not in the same way, and confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes in mechanics. Momentum scales linearly with velocity (p = mv), so doubling an object's speed exactly doubles its momentum. Kinetic energy scales with the square of velocity (KE = ½mv² = p²/2m), so doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy. This means a heavy, slow object and a light, fast object can carry equal momentum while carrying wildly different kinetic energy, or vice versa. Momentum tells you how hard something is to stop (how much impulse is required); kinetic energy tells you how much work that object could do, or how much energy would be released, if it were brought to rest.

sections.heading: Newton's second law in its original form: F = dp/dt
sections.body: Newton did not originally state his second law as F = ma; expressed in modern notation, his law is F = dp/dt, force equals the rate of change of momentum, though he described it in words and geometric reasoning rather than the algebraic form used today. When an object's mass stays constant, dp/dt = m(dv/dt) = ma, so the familiar F = ma formula falls right out as a special case. But the momentum form is more general and is required whenever mass itself changes over time, such as a rocket burning through its fuel, a raindrop growing by condensation as it falls, or a chain being lifted link by link onto a table. In those cases, F = ma alone gives the wrong answer, because it ignores the momentum carried away or added by the changing mass; only F = dp/dt correctly accounts for both the mv change from acceleration and the mv change from mass gain or loss.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.057 kg tennis ball leaves a fast serve at 51 m/s. Its momentum is p = mv = 0.057 × 51 ≈ 2.9 kg·m/s, while its kinetic energy is KE = ½mv² = 0.5 × 0.057 × 51² ≈ 74 J. Compare a 7 kg bowling ball rolling at 2 m/s: p = 7 × 2 = 14 kg·m/s, roughly 4.8 times the tennis ball's momentum, but KE = 0.5 × 7 × 2² = 14 J, only about 1/5.3 (roughly 19%) of the tennis ball's kinetic energy. The heavy, slow ball is harder to stop (more momentum) but carries less kinetic energy; the light, fast ball is easier to stop but packs a bigger energetic punch, because kinetic energy scales as v² while momentum only scales as v. Newton's F = dp/dt form describes the racket-ball contact too — it reduces to F = ma here since the racket's and ball's masses are constant during contact, unlike genuinely variable-mass systems such as a rocket.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe momentum versus kinetic energy because the two are easy to conflate but describe genuinely different physical questions: how hard is this to stop, versus how much energy could it release. A team that can explain why a heavy slow truck and a light fast bullet might share momentum but not energy (or vice versa) demonstrates real conceptual command rather than formula memorization. Judges may also ask when F = ma stops being valid, testing whether students know Newton's original F = dp/dt form and can name a concrete variable-mass system, like a rocket, where the distinction is not just academic.

questions.prompt: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s and a 4000 kg truck moving at 5 m/s have the same magnitude of momentum. Which statement is correct about their kinetic energies?

options.text: They also have equal kinetic energies, since equal momentum means equal energy.
The car has more kinetic energy than the truck.
The truck has more kinetic energy than the car.

explanations.a: Incorrect: momentum is linear in v while kinetic energy is quadratic in v (KE = p²/2m), so equal p with different m gives different KE.
explanations.b: Correct: KE = p²/2m. With equal p = 20,000 kg·m/s, the lighter car (1000 kg) gets KE = 20000²/(2×1000) = 200,000 J versus the truck's 20000²/(2×4000) = 50,000 J — four times less mass means four times more kinetic energy for the same momentum.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the smaller mass in KE = p²/2m makes KE larger, not smaller, for the same momentum — so the car, not the truck, has more kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: For which situation is the F = dp/dt form of Newton's second law required rather than the simpler F = ma?

options.text: A ball thrown straight up, where only its speed changes
A rocket that is continuously burning and ejecting fuel, so its mass decreases over time
A book sliding at constant velocity across a frictionless table

explanations.a: Incorrect: with constant mass, F = dp/dt reduces algebraically to F = ma, so the simpler form works fine here.
explanations.b: Correct: when mass itself changes with time, dp/dt = d(mv)/dt is not simply m(dv/dt); the product rule adds a term from dm/dt, so F = ma alone is insufficient and the momentum form is required.
explanations.c: Incorrect: constant velocity and constant mass mean dp/dt = 0 = F, which F = ma also gives directly — no special form is needed.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct property.

right.text: Scales linearly with v and is a vector
Scales with v² and is a scalar
Scalar; the magnitude of the velocity vector

questions.explanation: Momentum is mass times the velocity vector, so it is a vector that grows in direct proportion to v; kinetic energy depends on v² and has no direction, making it a scalar; speed is simply the scalar magnitude of the velocity vector itself.

questions.prompt: Two identical 0.5 kg balls each move at 4 m/s, one heading north and the other heading south. What is the magnitude of their total combined momentum?

options.text: 4 kg·m/s
0 kg·m/s
2 kg·m/s

explanations.a: Incorrect: this would be the sum of the magnitudes (2+2=4), but momentum is a vector — opposite directions must be added as opposite signs, not just magnitudes.
explanations.b: Correct: because momentum is a vector, the northward momentum (+2 kg·m/s) and southward momentum (-2 kg·m/s) cancel exactly, giving a total momentum of 0, even though both balls are moving fast.
explanations.c: Incorrect: 2 kg·m/s is the magnitude of just one ball's momentum, not the vector sum of both.

lessons.label: Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem

sections.heading: Impulse: the time-integrated force
sections.body: Impulse is defined as J = FΔt for a constant force, or more generally J = ∫F dt for a force that varies over the collision, which is exactly the area under a force-versus-time graph. Impulse is a vector with the same units as momentum, newton-seconds (N·s), which are dimensionally identical to kg·m/s. Starting from Newton's second law in its momentum form, F = dp/dt, and integrating both sides over the time interval of an interaction gives ∫F dt = Δp, or J = Δp: the impulse-momentum theorem. This says the total impulse delivered during an interaction equals the resulting change in momentum, regardless of the exact shape of the force pulse over time — only the total area under the curve matters for how much momentum changes, not how tall or narrow that curve is.

sections.heading: Reading a force-time graph
sections.body: Because impulse equals the area under an F-t curve, two very different-looking collisions, a short sharp spike or a long gentle bump, can deliver exactly the same impulse and therefore the same change in momentum, as long as their areas match. This is the key insight that separates impulse from peak force: peak force tells you about the single worst instant of a collision, while impulse (the area) tells you about the total momentum change over the whole event. A collision's average force can then be found by dividing the fixed impulse by the collision's duration, F_avg = J/Δt, which is the relationship that makes controlling collision time such a powerful safety tool.

sections.heading: Why extending contact time lowers peak force
sections.body: If a required momentum change Δp is fixed by the physics of a situation (a car must go from 15 m/s to 0, say), then the impulse J needed to cause it is also fixed, since J = Δp. Because J = F_avg × Δt, stretching out Δt necessarily shrinks the average force required to deliver that same fixed impulse. This is exactly why airbags, crumple zones, and a padded catch of a fast ball all work: none of them reduce the momentum that must be absorbed, but each extends the time over which that momentum change happens, cutting the peak force transmitted to a passenger, a car body, or a set of hands. The same principle explains why a batter or tennis player follows through after contact rather than stopping the swing abruptly.

lessons.workedExample: A 1500 kg car traveling at 15 m/s strikes a wall and stops. The impulse-momentum theorem gives J = Δp = m(v_f - v_i) = 1500 × (0 - 15) = -22,500 kg·m/s, fixed by the car's mass and speed change alone. If the car body were rigid and stopped in Δt = 0.05 s, the average force would be F = J/Δt = 22,500/0.05 = 450,000 N. With a crumple zone stretching the same stop to Δt = 0.15 s, the required impulse is unchanged, but F = 22,500/0.15 = 150,000 N, a threefold drop in peak force for an identical change in momentum. The crumple zone does not reduce how much momentum must be absorbed; it only changes how quickly, which is exactly the lever the impulse-momentum theorem predicts.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this concept because many students can recite that airbags reduce injury without connecting it to any physics, when the real insight is that the required impulse (and thus momentum change) is fixed by mass and speed, and only the collision's duration is under an engineer's control. A strong answer explains that safety devices extend Δt rather than somehow reducing Δp, and can read a force-time graph to identify that area, not peak height, is what equals impulse — a distinction judges often test directly with a sketched graph.

questions.prompt: On a force-versus-time graph for a collision, what quantity is represented by the area under the curve?

options.text: The peak force during the collision
The impulse delivered, equal to the change in momentum
The average velocity during the collision

explanations.a: Incorrect: the peak force is just the graph's highest point, not the area — a short, tall spike and a long, low bump can enclose the same area (and thus deliver the same impulse) despite very different peak forces.
explanations.b: Correct: impulse J = ∫F dt is exactly the area under a force-time curve, and by the impulse-momentum theorem this area equals the momentum change Δp, no matter the pulse's shape.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the area under an F-t graph has units of force times time (N·s), not velocity — that quantity is impulse/momentum, not average velocity.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps used to explain why a car's crumple zone reduces injury in a crash.

items.text: Determine the required momentum change Δp from the car's mass and impact speed
Recognize the impulse J needed equals that fixed Δp, by the impulse-momentum theorem
Note that a crumple zone increases the collision's duration Δt
Conclude the average force F = J/Δt must drop, since J is unchanged but Δt is larger

questions.explanation: You start from the fixed momentum change the crash requires, recognize that this fixes the total impulse needed, then note that a crumple zone stretches the time over which that same impulse is delivered, which necessarily lowers the average force.

questions.prompt: A tennis player follows through after contact instead of stopping the swing abruptly at impact. How does this connect to the impulse-momentum theorem?

options.text: By keeping the racket in contact longer, the player can deliver the same large impulse to the ball using a smaller peak force, with more control over the force's direction.
Follow-through has nothing to do with impulse; it only affects the racket's kinetic energy, not the ball's momentum.
Follow-through reduces the total impulse delivered to the ball, which is why it makes the shot gentler.

explanations.a: Correct: for a required momentum change Δp = J, a longer contact time Δt means the average force F = J/Δt can be smaller and more controlled while still delivering the full impulse — the same principle that makes crumple zones and airbags effective, just working in the direction of adding momentum rather than removing it.
explanations.b: Incorrect: the racket-ball interaction is precisely a force acting over the ball's contact time, so it is a textbook impulse-momentum scenario, not something unrelated to it.
explanations.c: Incorrect: follow-through does not reduce the ball's total momentum change — the ball still leaves the racket with the momentum the swing's total impulse gave it; what changes is how that impulse is delivered (lower peak force, more control), not its total size.

questions.prompt: Which pair of units is equivalent to a unit of impulse?

options.text: N·s and kg·m/s
N·m and Joules
kg·m/s² only

explanations.a: Correct: impulse J = FΔt has units of newton-seconds, and since 1 N = 1 kg·m/s², a newton-second reduces to 1 kg·m/s² × s = 1 kg·m/s — the same units as momentum, confirming J = Δp dimensionally.
explanations.b: Incorrect: N·m is a unit of work/energy (Joules), not impulse — impulse involves force times time, not force times distance.
explanations.c: Incorrect: kg·m/s² is the unit of force (equivalent to a newton) with no time factor, not impulse.

lessons.label: Conservation of Momentum

sections.heading: Momentum conservation from Newton's third law
sections.body: For any two objects that interact only with each other, Newton's third law guarantees the force object A exerts on B is equal and opposite to the force B exerts on A at every instant. Since impulse is force integrated over the same time interval for both objects, their impulses are equal and opposite too, meaning the momentum gained by one object exactly matches the momentum lost by the other. When you sum momentum over the whole system, these internal forces cancel completely, no matter how violent or complicated the interaction is: a gentle push, a high-speed collision, or an explosion. That cancellation is why the total momentum of an isolated system never changes over time, even while individual objects inside it speed up, slow down, or reverse direction.

sections.heading: Zero net external force is the actual condition
sections.body: Strictly speaking, total momentum stays constant precisely when the net external force on the chosen system is zero, or more precisely, when the external force component along a given direction is zero. Real systems are almost never free of every external force in every direction; gravity, for instance, constantly acts on a system of colliding balls. But if collision forces are enormous compared to gravity or friction over the brief instant of impact, or if only a horizontal momentum component is being tracked where gravity contributes nothing at all, momentum conservation can still apply exactly along that axis, even though it clearly would not apply vertically.

sections.heading: Choosing your system well
sections.body: Applying conservation of momentum well is mostly about choosing which objects belong inside the system so that unwanted forces become internal and cancel, leaving only forces that are genuinely zero or safely negligible as external. Leave out an object that is actually exerting a force, such as a wall a ball bounces off or the Earth in a recoil problem, and momentum will appear to vanish or appear from nowhere, because an unaccounted external force is quietly doing work on the boundary you drew too narrowly. Include unnecessary objects and the problem becomes needlessly complicated. A well-chosen system turns conservation of momentum into a powerful shortcut that sidesteps needing to track every internal force in detail.

lessons.workedExample: Two ice skaters at rest, one of mass 50 kg and the other 70 kg, push off from each other on frictionless ice. Because the ice removes friction and gravity is balanced by the ice's normal force, the horizontal momentum of the two-skater system is conserved and starts at zero. If the 50 kg skater moves off at 3 m/s in one direction, conservation of momentum requires 50(3) + 70(v2) = 0, so v2 = -150/70 ≈ -2.14 m/s: the heavier skater moves the opposite way, at about 71% of the lighter skater's speed. The push itself, an internal action-reaction pair by Newton's third law, never appears explicitly in the final answer, because choosing the two-skater system as closed let that internal force cancel out of the bookkeeping entirely, leaving only the requirement that total momentum stay at its starting value of zero.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe system-choice and the internal-versus-external distinction because misapplying momentum conservation, most often by forgetting an external force like friction, a wall, or the ground, is the single most common analysis error in collision and recoil problems. A strong team explicitly states which objects they included in their system and why the net external force is zero or negligible along the direction they are analyzing, rather than invoking momentum conservation as an unexplained shortcut that happens to give the right number.

questions.prompt: Why do internal forces cancel out when you sum the total momentum of a system?

options.text: By Newton's third law, internal action-reaction force pairs are equal and opposite at every instant, so their impulses cancel when summed over the whole system.
Internal forces are always much weaker than external forces, so we ignore them.
Internal forces only act for an instant, so their total impulse is negligible.

explanations.a: Correct: for every internal force one part of the system exerts on another, Newton's third law guarantees an equal and opposite reaction force on the first part over the identical time interval, so their impulses are equal and opposite and cancel exactly when the whole system's momentum is added up, not because they are small or brief.
explanations.b: Incorrect: internal forces such as an explosion or a hard collision can be enormous, far larger than typical external forces like friction — they cancel because of their action-reaction pairing, not their size.
explanations.c: Incorrect: many internal forces, like a sustained push, act for extended times, not instants, yet they still cancel because of the third-law pairing, not brevity.

questions.prompt: A ball rolls off a table and bounces off the floor. A student wants to apply momentum conservation to 'the ball' alone during the bounce. Why does this fail?

options.text: Because the floor exerts an external force (the bounce force) on the ball-only system, so the ball's momentum alone is not conserved during the bounce.
Because momentum conservation never applies to bouncing objects.
Because the ball is not a closed system unless it is also in contact with a wall.

explanations.a: Correct: if you draw the system boundary around the ball alone, the floor is outside that boundary, so the normal force from the floor during the bounce is an external force to that system — it is exactly what changes the ball's momentum and makes it bounce, so 'ball alone' is not a system with zero net external force.
explanations.b: Incorrect: momentum conservation can still be applied correctly to bouncing problems — the trick is choosing the system (such as ball plus floor plus Earth) so the bounce force becomes internal, not abandoning the principle.
explanations.c: Incorrect: contact with a wall is irrelevant here; the issue is that the floor's force on the ball is external to a ball-only system, regardless of any wall.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for correctly applying conservation of momentum to a two-object interaction.

items.text: Define which objects are included inside the system
Check whether the net external force on that system is zero (or negligible) along the direction of interest
Write total momentum before the interaction equal to total momentum after
Solve for the unknown velocity or mass

questions.explanation: You cannot check whether external force is zero until you have decided what is inside versus outside the system, and you cannot legitimately set 'before' momentum equal to 'after' momentum until that zero-external-force condition is confirmed; only then does solving the resulting equation make sense.

questions.prompt: Match each system description to the momentum-conservation situation it illustrates.

left.text: Two ice skaters pushing off on frictionless ice (horizontal direction)
A single car braking to a stop on a rough road
A rocket together with all of its expelled exhaust gas

right.text: A genuinely closed system with zero net external horizontal force
Momentum is NOT conserved for this system because an external force (friction) acts on it
A closed system even though large internal thrust forces act between its parts

questions.explanation: The frictionless skaters have no external horizontal force, so their combined momentum is conserved; the braking car alone is not closed because road friction is an external horizontal force removing its momentum; the rocket-plus-exhaust system is closed despite violent internal thrust forces, because thrust is an internal action-reaction pair between the rocket and the gas it expels.

lessons.label: Elastic vs Inelastic Collisions (Foundations)

sections.heading: Momentum: conserved in every collision
sections.body: Total momentum is conserved in every collision, elastic, inelastic, or perfectly inelastic, as long as the chosen system is closed, meaning no net external force acts on it. This is a direct consequence of Newton's third law: whatever forces the colliding objects exert on each other during contact are internal to the system and cancel exactly when summed. Momentum conservation does not care whether the objects bounce apart cleanly, crumple and separate, or stick together permanently; it holds regardless of how much kinetic energy is lost during the collision, because it depends only on the internal forces canceling, not on what those forces do to the objects' shapes or internal energy.

sections.heading: Kinetic energy: conserved only in elastic collisions
sections.body: An elastic collision is one in which total kinetic energy is exactly the same before and after, meaning KE_before = KE_after; the colliding objects bounce apart without any permanent deformation, as in idealized billiard-ball or gas-molecule collisions. An inelastic collision converts some kinetic energy into heat, sound, or permanent deformation, so KE_after is less than KE_before, even though momentum is still exactly conserved. A useful special case is an elastic head-on collision between two equal masses: the moving object comes to a complete stop and the initially stationary object moves off with exactly the first object's original velocity, the velocities simply swap, which is the mechanism behind a Newton's cradle.

sections.heading: Perfectly inelastic collisions: objects stick together
sections.body: A perfectly inelastic collision is the case where the colliding objects stick together and move off as one combined mass with a single common final velocity. Because there is only one unknown final velocity to find, momentum conservation alone, m1v1 + m2v2 = (m1+m2)v_f, is enough to fully solve the problem without needing any information about energy. Kinetic energy is not conserved in this case; in fact, a perfectly inelastic collision loses the maximum possible amount of kinetic energy consistent with the given masses and initial velocities, and that loss can be computed afterward as a downstream check, once v_f is already known from momentum alone.

lessons.workedExample: A 2000 kg railcar moving at 5 m/s couples with a stationary 3000 kg railcar. Because momentum is conserved in every collision, (2000)(5) + (3000)(0) = (2000+3000)v_f, giving v_f = 10,000/5000 = 2 m/s for the combined 5000 kg train. Kinetic energy, however, is not conserved: KE_before = ½(2000)(5²) = 25,000 J, while KE_after = ½(5000)(2²) = 10,000 J, a loss of 15,000 J, 60% of the initial kinetic energy, converted into heat and sound in the coupling mechanism and structural deformation. This is the signature of a perfectly inelastic collision: momentum conservation alone, one equation with one unknown v_f, fully determines the outcome, and the large kinetic energy loss falls out afterward as a consequence rather than something that must be separately assumed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the kinetic-energy-loss distinction because a common misconception is that momentum itself is somehow 'lost' in an inelastic collision, when actually momentum is exactly conserved and only kinetic energy decreases. A strong team can explain that 'conserved' behaves differently for the two quantities: universally for momentum in any closed system, but only for kinetic energy specifically in the elastic case. Judges may also probe whether a student recognizes why perfectly inelastic problems can be solved with momentum conservation alone, without ever needing an energy equation.

questions.prompt: In a perfectly inelastic collision between two railcars that couple together, what happens to momentum and kinetic energy?

options.text: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy decreases.
Momentum decreases, but kinetic energy is conserved.

explanations.a: Incorrect: kinetic energy is not conserved in a perfectly inelastic collision — deformation, heat, and sound carry away energy even though momentum stays exactly the same.
explanations.b: Correct: momentum is conserved in every collision because it follows from Newton's third law regardless of what happens to the colliding objects, while kinetic energy in a perfectly inelastic collision drops because energy is converted to heat, sound, and permanent deformation as the objects stick together.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum is exactly conserved in collisions (assuming a closed system) — it is kinetic energy, not momentum, that decreases in inelastic collisions.
