questions.prompt: Two identical billiard balls collide elastically head-on: ball A moves at 4 m/s and strikes stationary ball B. What are their velocities immediately after, assuming a perfectly elastic 1D collision?

options.text: A moves at 4 m/s, B stays at 0 m/s (nothing changes).
A stops (0 m/s) and B moves off at 4 m/s.
Both move together at 2 m/s.

explanations.a: Incorrect: this would mean no interaction actually occurred, which contradicts a collision taking place; checking momentum and kinetic energy conservation together rules this out as the outcome of a real elastic collision.
explanations.b: Correct: for an elastic head-on collision between equal masses, the classic result is that the velocities swap — the moving ball stops and transfers all its velocity to the initially stationary, identical ball; this satisfies both momentum conservation (4=0+4) and kinetic energy conservation (KE_before = ½m(4 m/s)² = KE_after = ½m(4 m/s)²).
explanations.c: Incorrect: both moving together at 2 m/s conserves momentum but is the perfectly INELASTIC result, not the elastic one — its kinetic energy, ½(2m)(2²)=4m, is less than the initial ½m(4²)=8m, so it fails to conserve KE and cannot be the elastic outcome.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving a perfectly inelastic collision problem (two objects that stick together).

items.text: Write total momentum before the collision using each object's individual mass and velocity
Set that total equal to the combined mass moving at one common final velocity
Solve algebraically for the single unknown final velocity
Optionally compute kinetic energy before and after to find the energy lost

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation is set up first and solved for the one unknown, the shared final velocity, since that alone fully determines a perfectly inelastic outcome; only after finding that velocity can you go on to compute kinetic energy before and after to see how much energy was lost, a separate, optional follow-up calculation.

questions.prompt: Match each described collision to its type.

left.text: Two steel balls collide and bounce apart with no measurable loss of total kinetic energy
A bullet embeds itself in a wooden block and they move off together
Two cars collide, crumple somewhat, but separate afterward still moving at different (nonzero) velocities, with less total kinetic energy than before

right.text: Elastic collision
Perfectly inelastic collision
Inelastic collision (but not perfectly inelastic)

questions.explanation: No kinetic energy loss and separate final velocities mark the steel-ball collision as elastic; the bullet and block moving off together with one shared final velocity is the defining signature of a perfectly inelastic collision; the cars losing some kinetic energy to crumpling but still separating with two different final velocities is inelastic but not perfectly inelastic, since the objects do not end up moving as one.

lessons.label: Center of Mass

sections.heading: The mass-weighted average position
sections.body: The center of mass of a system is defined as x_cm = Σ(m_i x_i)/Σm_i, a mass-weighted average position, with analogous formulas for the y and z directions, or written compactly as a vector r_cm = Σm_i r_i / M. It behaves like an ordinary average except that each position is weighted by how much mass sits there, so heavier pieces pull the center of mass toward themselves. For a simple example, a 2 kg mass at x = 0 m and a 3 kg mass at x = 5 m give x_cm = (2×0 + 3×5)/5 = 3 m, noticeably closer to the heavier mass than the simple geometric midpoint (2.5 m) would be. Uniform, symmetric objects have their center of mass at the obvious geometric center, a rod's midpoint or a disk's center, while irregular or composite objects can be broken into simple known pieces and combined with the same weighted-average formula.

sections.heading: The center of mass moves as if all mass and all force acted there
sections.body: For any system of particles, summing Newton's second law over every particle shows that F_net,ext = M a_cm: the net external force on the whole system equals the total mass times the acceleration of the center of mass alone (this is derived in full in the next lesson). This means that no matter how complicated a system's internal motion is, particles spinning, colliding, or rearranging, its center of mass follows a trajectory set only by the net external force, exactly as if the system were a single point particle of mass M. A classic illustration is a spinning wrench tossed through the air: every point on the tumbling wrench traces a complicated looping path, except its center of mass, which traces a smooth, simple parabola, identical to a thrown ball's, because gravity is the only external force acting on the system.

lessons.workedExample: The Earth (mass ≈ 5.97 × 10^24 kg) and Moon (mass ≈ 7.35 × 10^22 kg) orbit their common center of mass, called the barycenter, separated by about 384,400 km center-to-center. Measuring from Earth's center, x_cm = (m_moon × d)/(m_earth + m_moon) = (7.35×10^22 × 384,400 km)/(5.97×10^24 + 7.35×10^22) ≈ 4,670 km. Since Earth's radius is about 6,371 km, this barycenter sits inside the Earth itself, roughly 1,700 km below the surface — the Moon is only about 1.2% of Earth's mass, so it pulls the shared center of mass only a modest distance from Earth's own center rather than to some point in empty space between them. As the Moon orbits, it is really Earth's own center that traces a small monthly circle around this interior point, while the barycenter itself moves smoothly around the Sun.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about center of mass because it is easy to confuse with a simple geometric center, and testing it reveals whether a student understands that center of mass can lie outside an object's physical material entirely, as with a ring or an L-shaped bracket, or buried deep inside one member of a two-body system, as with the Earth-Moon barycenter. A well-prepared team can locate the center of mass for asymmetric or composite objects and can explain why the center of mass's trajectory ignores whatever internal deformation, spin, or rearrangement is happening within the system.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg mass sits at x = 0 m and a 6 kg mass sits at x = 4 m on a massless rod. Where is the center of mass?

options.text: x = 2 m (the midpoint)
x = 3 m
x = 1 m

explanations.a: Incorrect: the midpoint (2 m) would only be correct if the two masses were equal; since the 6 kg mass is three times heavier, the center of mass is pulled much closer to it, not left at the simple geometric midpoint.
explanations.b: Correct: x_cm = (2×0 + 6×4)/(2+6) = 24/8 = 3 m, closer to the heavier 6 kg mass, as expected for a mass-weighted average.
explanations.c: Incorrect: 1 m would place the center of mass closer to the LIGHTER mass, which is backwards — the center of mass is always pulled toward the heavier object, not away from it.

questions.prompt: Where is the center of mass of a uniform ring (like a hula hoop) located?

options.text: On the ring material itself, at any point around the circumference
At the geometric center of the ring, in the empty space it encloses
A ring has no well-defined center of mass because its mass is spread around a circle

explanations.a: Incorrect: no single point on the ring's material is special enough to be the mass-weighted average of the whole ring — by symmetry, the true weighted average lands in the middle, not on the material.
explanations.b: Correct: by the symmetry of a uniform ring, the mass-weighted average of all the positions around the circle lands exactly at the geometric center, even though there is no actual mass there — center of mass is a mathematical average position, not a location that must contain material.
explanations.c: Incorrect: every mass distribution has a well-defined center of mass computed from Σm_i r_i / M, including a ring; the calculation is well-defined even though the answer falls in empty space.

questions.prompt: Match each object to the correct description of its center of mass location.

left.text: An L-shaped bracket made of uniform material

right.text: At the geometric midpoint of the object
In empty space, outside the solid material of the object
Inside the more massive of two orbiting bodies, off-center from its middle

questions.explanation: A uniform rod's mass-weighted average sits at its midpoint by symmetry; an L-shaped bracket's center of mass typically falls in the open space inside the L's corner, not on the material itself; the Earth-Moon barycenter lies inside the Earth, several thousand kilometers from Earth's own geometric center, because Earth is far more massive than the Moon.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to find the center of mass of a composite object made of several simple pieces.

items.text: Divide the object into simple pieces whose individual centers of mass and masses are already known
Record the position and mass of each piece's individual center of mass
Compute the mass-weighted average position across all pieces using x_cm = Σ(m_i x_i)/Σm_i
Confirm the total mass used in the denominator equals the sum of all the pieces' masses

questions.explanation: You must first break the composite shape into simple, known pieces, then note where each piece's own center of mass sits and how much it weighs, before those values can be combined with the weighted-average formula, whose denominator should be checked against the total mass of every included piece.

lessons.label: Newton's Laws for Systems of Particles

sections.heading: External force sets the center of mass's acceleration
sections.body: Writing Newton's second law separately for every particle in a system and summing all of those equations together shows that internal forces cancel in pairs by Newton's third law, leaving F_net,ext = M a_cm: the net external force on the whole system equals the total mass times the acceleration of the system's center of mass. This is a system-level version of F = ma. No matter how complex the internal motion, particles colliding, rotating, or vibrating relative to one another, the center of mass behaves exactly like a single point particle of mass M acted on only by the sum of the external forces, completely ignoring whatever is happening internally.

sections.heading: Internal forces cannot move the center of mass
sections.body: Because internal forces cancel in pairs, no internal push, explosion, or rearrangement of a system's parts can change the system's total momentum or shift its center of mass's trajectory, as long as the system stays closed, meaning no mass enters or leaves and no new external force appears. This explains the classic fireworks-shell example: a shell explodes into fragments mid-flight, but if gravity is the only external force acting on the system, the fragments' combined center of mass keeps following the exact same parabolic arc the intact shell would have followed, right up until fragments start hitting the ground or air resistance on individual light fragments becomes significant enough to matter.

sections.heading: Rockets: internal thrust versus external forces
sections.body: A rocket's thrust comes from expelling propellant mass backward. If the system is defined as rocket plus expelled propellant together, the thrust force the engine exerts on the exhaust gas and the reaction force the gas exerts back on the rocket form an internal action-reaction pair: they cancel in the combined system's total momentum and cannot, by themselves, move that combined system's center of mass. What does accelerate is the rocket by itself, because expelling mass is exactly how a subsystem can gain momentum despite the whole system's internal-force cancellation: the rocket deliberately sheds mass (and momentum) to the exhaust, so its own momentum changes even though the combined rocket-plus-exhaust system's center of mass moves only under genuine external forces like gravity and atmospheric drag.

lessons.workedExample: A 2 kg firework shell is launched and, ignoring air resistance, follows a parabolic path. At its apex, 80 m high and moving horizontally at 20 m/s, it explodes into several fragments due to an internal charge. The explosion exerts only internal forces on the shell's pieces, equal and opposite by Newton's third law, so it cannot change the system's total momentum or push its center of mass off the original parabolic path. Even though individual fragments now fly off in wildly different directions and speeds, the mass-weighted average of all the fragments' positions continues along x_cm(t) = x0 + 20t and y_cm(t) = 80 - ½(9.8)t², exactly as if the explosion had never happened, because gravity, not the explosion, is the only external force acting on the system as a whole.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because many students believe an explosion or an internal push can somehow accelerate or redirect a system's overall motion, when in fact only external forces move the center of mass. Testing the fireworks or rocket-recoil scenario reveals whether a student can correctly separate what moves an individual part, internal forces that redistribute momentum among the parts, from what moves the system as a whole, only external forces, via F_net,ext = M a_cm, which is exactly the distinction a judge is listening for in a strong explanation.

questions.prompt: A firework shell explodes in mid-air with no other forces besides gravity acting on the system. What happens to the trajectory of the fragments' combined center of mass?

options.text: It continues along the same parabolic path the intact shell would have followed.
It suddenly changes direction due to the explosion's force.
It stops moving momentarily at the instant of explosion, then resumes.

explanations.a: Correct: the explosion is an internal force (fragments push on each other via Newton's third law pairs), so it cannot change the total momentum or the center of mass's motion; only gravity, the external force, continues to act, so the center of mass keeps following the same parabola as before.
explanations.b: Incorrect: an internal force like an explosion redistributes momentum among the fragments but cancels out in the total, so it cannot redirect the system's overall (center-of-mass) trajectory — individual fragments change direction, but their combined average does not.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum does not 'freeze' at the moment of an internal explosion — the center of mass's velocity is continuous because the explosion contributes zero net impulse to the system as a whole.

questions.prompt: For a rocket-plus-expelled-exhaust system (ignoring gravity and drag), what causes the combined system's total momentum to be conserved even while the rocket accelerates forward?

options.text: The thrust force is internal to the rocket-plus-exhaust system, so it is an equal-and-opposite pair that cancels in the total, even though it changes the rocket's own momentum by itself.
The rocket's engine somehow avoids exerting any force on the exhaust gas.
Momentum is not actually conserved for rockets; that is why they need fuel.

explanations.a: Correct: the engine pushes the exhaust gas backward, and by Newton's third law the gas pushes the rocket forward with an equal and opposite force; as an internal action-reaction pair within the combined rocket-plus-exhaust system, these forces cancel in the total momentum sum, so the combined system's momentum and center-of-mass motion are set only by true external forces, even though the rocket subsystem alone clearly speeds up.
explanations.b: Incorrect: the engine must exert a real force on the exhaust gas to expel it; that force, and its Newton's-third-law reaction on the rocket, is exactly what produces thrust.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum is absolutely conserved for the combined rocket-plus-exhaust system; fuel is needed because the rocket, as a subsystem that loses mass, gains forward momentum only by giving equal-and-opposite momentum to the ejected exhaust, not because conservation fails.

questions.prompt: Match each force description to whether it can change the trajectory of a closed system's center of mass.

left.text: An internal explosion splitting the system into fragments
Two parts of the system pushing off each other (like a rocket's thrust on its own exhaust)
Gravity from outside the system acting on its total mass

right.text: Cannot change the center of mass's trajectory, only redistributes momentum among the system's parts
Cannot change the center of mass's trajectory, by Newton's third law it is an internal action-reaction pair
Can and does change the center of mass's trajectory, since it is external to the system

questions.explanation: An explosion and an internal push are both internal to the system and cancel in the total momentum sum by Newton's third law, so neither can move the center of mass; gravity acting from outside the system is a genuine external force and is exactly what sets the center of mass's acceleration, per F_net,ext = M a_cm.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps that lead from Newton's second law for individual particles to F_net,ext = M a_cm for a whole system.

items.text: Write Newton's second law (F = dp/dt) separately for every particle in the system
Sum these equations over all particles, splitting each particle's total force into internal and external contributions
Recognize that all internal forces cancel in pairs by Newton's third law, leaving only the sum of external forces
Identify the remaining sum as M times the acceleration of the system's center of mass

questions.explanation: The derivation starts from each particle's own equation of motion, sums them while separating internal from external contributions, cancels the internal pairs using Newton's third law, and finally recognizes that what remains is exactly the definition of the center of mass's acceleration times the total mass.

lessons.label: SI Units and Base Quantities

sections.heading: Seven base units, infinite derived units
sections.body: The International System of Units (SI) defines seven base units, each tied to a base quantity: the meter (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, ampere (A) for electric current, kelvin (K) for temperature, mole (mol) for amount of substance, and candela (cd) for luminous intensity. Every other unit in mechanics is derived by combining these through multiplication and division: velocity is m/s, force is kg*m/s^2 (named the newton, N), energy is kg*m^2/s^2 (the joule, J), and pressure is N/m^2 (the pascal, Pa). Because a derived unit is just base units in disguise, you can always expand a named unit like the newton back into kg, m, and s to check an equation's consistency — this is the seed of dimensional analysis, covered next.

sections.heading: Why a shared standard matters
sections.body: Reproducibility is the currency of experimental science: a result is only useful if another lab, using the same defined units, can attempt to replicate it and compare numbers directly. Before standardization, units like the foot or the pound varied by region and even by trade guild, making cross-lab comparison meaningless. The SI solves this by fixing each base unit to something universal and (as of 2019) unchanging, rather than to a physical artifact that could degrade, be damaged, or drift with age.

sections.heading: The 2019 redefinition: units anchored to constants, not objects
sections.body: For over a century, the kilogram was defined by a single platinum-iridium cylinder locked in a vault near Paris (the International Prototype Kilogram); mass standards worldwide were only as good as that one object's mass, which itself drifted by tens of micrograms over decades. On 20 May 2019, the SI abandoned all physical artifacts. The kilogram, ampere, kelvin, and mole were redefined by fixing exact numerical values for four fundamental constants: the Planck constant h = 6.62607015 x 10^-34 J*s, the elementary charge e = 1.602176634 x 10^-19 C, the Boltzmann constant k = 1.380649 x 10^-23 J/K, and the Avogadro constant N_A = 6.02214076 x 10^23 mol^-1. A kilogram is now realized experimentally with a Kibble balance, which balances mechanical and electrical power to back out mass from h. The practical payoff for a student lab: your instruments are calibrated, directly or indirectly, against constants of nature that any lab on Earth (or off it) can in principle reproduce, not against a jar in France.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures the force needed to stretch a spring and reports 2.4 N. Expanding the newton into base units, 2.4 N = 2.4 kg*m/s^2. If she instead measured mass on a scale calibrated in pounds and length with a meter stick, mixing unit systems, her force calculation would require a conversion factor (1 lb = 0.453592 kg) at every step, multiplying opportunities for arithmetic error. By working entirely in SI from the start (kg, m, s), every derived quantity, force, energy, power, drops out with correct units automatically, with no hidden conversion factors buried in the numbers.
lessons.judgeFraming: A science fair judge checks units almost reflexively, because a correct number with the wrong or missing unit is scientifically meaningless (a report of "4.2" for a spring constant tells the judge nothing without N/m attached). Judges also probe whether a student understands WHY SI is used, not just that it is the convention: expect a question like "why not just use the units your equipment displays by default?" A strong answer names reproducibility, comparability with published literature (which is virtually all SI), and the fact that derived-unit arithmetic only stays clean when everything upstream is already in base SI units.

questions.prompt: The newton (N), the SI unit of force, expands into which combination of base units?

options.text: kg*m/s^2
kg*m^2/s^2
kg/m*s

explanations.a: Correct: F = ma, so force = mass (kg) times acceleration (m/s^2), giving kg*m/s^2.
explanations.b: kg*m^2/s^2 is the joule (energy), one factor of length too many for force.
explanations.c: kg/(m*s) is not a standard derived mechanical unit and has the wrong structure for F = ma.

questions.prompt: What changed about the kilogram on 20 May 2019?

options.text: It was redefined by fixing the exact numerical value of the Planck constant instead of referencing a physical artifact.
Its numerical value was increased slightly to match new precision measurements.
It was replaced entirely by the gram as the SI base unit of mass.

explanations.a: Correct: the kilogram is now realized via a Kibble balance using the fixed value h = 6.62607015 x 10^-34 J*s, retiring the Paris artifact.
explanations.b: The redefinition fixed h's numerical value by definition; it did not change what a kilogram physically weighs in any perceptible way.
explanations.c: The kilogram remains the SI base unit of mass; only its method of realization changed.

questions.prompt: Match each SI base quantity to its base unit.

right.text: meter (m)
second (s)
ampere (A)
mole (mol)

questions.explanation: These are four of the seven SI base units; the other three (kilogram for mass, kelvin for temperature, candela for luminous intensity) are not tested here.

questions.prompt: Order these historically, from the artifact-based kilogram standard to today's constant-based standard.

items.text: The kilogram is defined by a single platinum-iridium cylinder kept in a vault in France
Metrologists measure the Planck constant with extreme precision using Kibble balances
The CGPM votes to fix an exact numerical value for the Planck constant
Labs worldwide realize the kilogram from h using Kibble balances, with no physical artifact involved

questions.explanation: The artifact standard came first; precise measurement of h enabled fixing its value by definition, which then let labs realize the kilogram from that constant rather than from an object.

lessons.label: Dimensional Analysis

sections.heading: Dimensions as a sanity check
sections.body: Every mechanical quantity can be expressed in terms of three fundamental dimensions: mass [M], length [L], and time [T]. Velocity has dimension [L][T]^-1, acceleration [L][T]^-2, force [M][L][T]^-2, and energy [M][L]^2[T]^-2. Dimensional analysis exploits a simple rule: an equation can only be physically valid if both sides have identical dimensions, and you can only add or subtract quantities that share the same dimension. This gives a fast, free check on any formula before you touch lab equipment: if the left and right sides do not match dimensionally, the equation is definitely wrong (though matching dimensions does not prove an equation is right, since a dimensionless numerical constant can hide anywhere).

sections.heading: Deriving a proportionality from dimensions alone
sections.body: Dimensional analysis can also predict the FORM of a relationship before you know the exact physics. Suppose you suspect a pendulum's period T depends on its length L, gravitational acceleration g, and possibly mass m: T = k * L^a * g^b * m^c for some dimensionless constant k. Matching dimensions on both sides ([T]^1 = [L]^a * ([L][T]^-2)^b * [M]^c) forces a + b = 0 for length, -2b = 1 for time, and c = 0 for mass, since mass appears nowhere on the left. Solving gives b = -1/2, a = 1/2, c = 0, so T = k * sqrt(L/g), with mass dropping out entirely. This matches the real physics: for small oscillations, the exact result is T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g), so dimensional analysis alone correctly predicted the L/g dependence and the irrelevance of mass, leaving only the constant 2*pi undetermined.

sections.heading: Catching errors before lab time is wasted
sections.body: The practical payoff is speed: checking dimensions on paper takes thirty seconds, while discovering an algebra error after an hour of data collection wastes the whole session. A common failure mode is dropping or misplacing an exponent during algebraic rearrangement, for example solving for g from a pendulum's period and accidentally leaving an extra factor of L or T. Plugging the rearranged formula's dimensions back through catches this instantly, because the result will not simplify to [L][T]^-2 as gravitational acceleration requires. Dimensional analysis cannot catch a wrong dimensionless constant (a 2*pi swapped for a pi, for instance), so it complements but never replaces checking your derivation against a known formula or a trusted reference.

lessons.workedExample: A student rearranges T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) to solve for g and gets g = 4*pi^2*L/T (missing the square on T). Checking dimensions: the right side is [L]/[T], which is a velocity, not an acceleration. Since g must have dimension [L][T]^-2, the dimensional mismatch flags the algebra error immediately, before she plugs in her measured L and T and reports a nonsensical value for g in m/s instead of m/s^2. Correcting to g = 4*pi^2*L/T^2 gives [L]/[T]^2, matching acceleration, and only then does she proceed to compute a number from her data.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use dimensional analysis as a quick, formula-independent probe of understanding: they can ask a student to check the dimensions of a result on the spot, without needing to verify the full derivation. A student who can instantly say "my answer is in m/s, but I'm solving for an acceleration, so I have an algebra error somewhere" demonstrates real command of the physics, not memorized formula plugging. Judges are also alert to students who treat a dimensionally-consistent answer as automatically correct; a sharp judge may ask "could this equation be dimensionally fine but still numerically wrong," testing whether the student understands that dimensional analysis only bounds the possible form, leaving constants like 2*pi undetermined.

questions.prompt: What is the SI dimension of energy, expressed in [M], [L], [T]?

explanations.a: Correct: energy = force x distance = ([M][L][T]^-2)([L]) = [M][L]^2[T]^-2, matching the joule = N*m.
explanations.b: [M][L][T]^-2 is the dimension of force (the newton), one factor of length short of energy.
explanations.c: [M][L]^2[T]^-1 has the wrong power of time; energy's time exponent is -2, not -1.

questions.prompt: A student derives that period T is proportional to L^a * g^b for a pendulum and finds a = 1/2, b = -1/2 by matching dimensions. What can dimensional analysis NOT tell her?

options.text: The exact numerical constant (such as 2*pi) multiplying the expression
That mass does not appear in the final relationship
That the exponent on L must be positive

explanations.a: Correct: dimensional analysis fixes the exponents but is blind to any dimensionless multiplicative constant; that requires the full physical derivation (or experiment) to pin down.
explanations.b: Dimensional analysis DOES reveal this: mass has no dimension left to balance on the right side once length and time are fixed, forcing its exponent to zero.
explanations.c: The sign and value of the exponent on L (here +1/2) IS determined by the dimensional matching equations, so this is something dimensional analysis does tell her.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for using dimensional analysis to derive a proportionality like T = k*L^a*g^b.

items.text: Write the dimensions [M][L][T] for every quantity in the proposed relationship
Set up equations matching the exponent of each dimension on both sides
Solve the resulting system of equations for the unknown exponents
Note that the leading dimensionless constant k remains undetermined by this method

questions.explanation: You must first list dimensions, then equate exponents dimension-by-dimension, then solve for the exponents algebraically; only after solving do you recognize the constant k is left unfixed.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct SI dimension.
questions.explanation: Velocity is distance per time, acceleration is velocity per time (distance per time squared), and force is mass times acceleration.

lessons.label: Significant Figures, Precision vs Accuracy

sections.heading: Significant figure rules for calculations
sections.body: Significant figures communicate how precisely a number is known: 2.40 m implies precision to the nearest centimeter, while 2.4 m implies only the nearest tenth of a meter, even though the two numbers are mathematically equal. When multiplying or dividing measured quantities, the result is rounded to the same number of significant figures as the input with the FEWEST significant figures, because a calculation cannot manufacture precision that no input possessed. When adding or subtracting, the rule instead tracks decimal places: the result is rounded to the same number of decimal places as the least-precise input. These are different rules for different operations, and mixing them up (for example applying the sig-fig-count rule to a sum) is a common source of over-precise, misleading results.

sections.heading: Precision and accuracy are independent
sections.body: Precision describes how tightly repeated measurements of the same thing cluster together (low scatter, high repeatability), while accuracy describes how close the average of those measurements is to the true value. The two are logically independent: a stopwatch with a sticky button might give period measurements of 2.05 s, 2.06 s, 2.05 s, and 2.06 s for the same pendulum swing, tight and precise, but if a consistent 0.3-second human reaction-time lag inflates every reading, the true period is 1.75 s and every measurement is inaccurate despite being precise. The classic dartboard analogy makes this concrete: darts clustered tightly in one corner (precise, inaccurate), darts scattered evenly around the bullseye (accurate on average, imprecise), and darts clustered tightly on the bullseye (both precise and accurate) are three genuinely different experimental situations requiring different fixes: precision improves with more careful technique or a better instrument, accuracy improves by identifying and removing a systematic bias.

sections.heading: Reporting to an instrument's resolution
sections.body: A measurement should never claim more precision than the instrument delivered. A meter stick with millimeter markings supports readings estimated to the nearest tenth of a millimeter (one digit of interpolation beyond the smallest marked division is the conventional rule), so reporting 1.2345 m from a millimeter-marked meter stick overstates the instrument's actual resolution. Conversely, under-reporting, writing 1.2 m when the stick clearly resolves to 1.234 m, throws away real information the instrument provided. Matching the reported digits to the instrument's actual resolution, no more, no less, is a discipline every subsequent lesson on timing instruments and sensors in this unit depends on.

lessons.workedExample: A student times 10 pendulum swings with a stopwatch reading to 0.01 s and gets a total of 20.14 s, dividing by 10 for a period of 2.014 s. But the stopwatch's real limiting factor is her own reaction time (about +/-0.2 s per press), not its 0.01 s display resolution, so reporting 2.014 s vastly overstates her precision; 2.0 s is closer to honest. Separately, she repeats the 10-swing trial five times and gets totals of 20.1, 20.3, 20.0, 20.2, and 20.1 s, tightly clustered (precise). But her lab partner, using a photogate, gets 19.4 s consistently. The 0.7-second gap suggests her stopwatch technique has a systematic bias (reaction-time lag), an accuracy problem that no amount of repeating the stopwatch trial can fix, since repetition only improves precision.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges specifically listen for whether a student conflates precision and accuracy, because it is one of the most common conceptual gaps in student science fair projects. A student who says "my results were very precise, so they must be accurate" reveals a misunderstanding a judge will probe further, asking what independent check (a different instrument, a known reference value, a second observer) was used to establish accuracy rather than just repeatability. Judges also check sig-fig discipline as a proxy for whether a student actually understands their own instrument's limits, since a result reported to five decimal places from a meter stick signals the student copied a calculator's output without thinking about what the equipment could actually resolve.

questions.prompt: A student multiplies a length measured as 4.52 m (3 sig figs) by a length measured as 2.1 m (2 sig figs). How many significant figures should the reported area have?

explanations.a: Correct: for multiplication, the result is limited to the sig-fig count of the LEAST precise input, which is 2.1 m with 2 significant figures.
explanations.b: 3 sig figs matches the more precise input (4.52 m), but the result cannot exceed the precision of the less precise input.
explanations.c: 5 is simply the sum of both inputs' sig-fig counts, which is not how multiplication's sig-fig rule works.

questions.prompt: A digital scale gives the same mass reading, 15.02 g, for five repeated measurements of an object whose true mass (verified on a certified reference scale) is 14.50 g. This scenario best illustrates:

options.text: High precision, low accuracy
Low precision, high accuracy
High precision and high accuracy

explanations.a: Correct: the five readings are tightly clustered (high precision) but consistently 0.52 g away from the verified true value (low accuracy), indicating a systematic offset like an uncalibrated zero.
explanations.b: The readings are identical across trials, which is the definition of high, not low, precision.
explanations.c: The readings are off from the true value by a consistent 0.52 g, so accuracy is low, not high, despite the precision being high.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the measurement property it primarily illustrates.

left.text: Repeated trials cluster tightly but consistently miss the certified reference value
Repeated trials scatter widely but average close to the certified reference value
Reporting 1.2345 m from a meter stick marked only in millimeters

right.text: Poor accuracy (systematic bias)
Poor precision (random scatter)
Overclaiming instrument resolution

questions.explanation: Tight clustering away from the true value is a systematic (accuracy) problem; wide scatter that still averages correctly is a random (precision) problem; reporting more digits than the instrument resolves overstates precision regardless of accuracy.

questions.prompt: Order these numbers from FEWEST to MOST significant figures.
questions.explanation: 2.1 has 2 significant figures, 2.10 has 3 (the trailing zero after the decimal is significant), and 2.100 has 4 (both trailing zeros after the decimal count).

lessons.label: Timing and Tracking Instruments

sections.heading: Stopwatches and ticker-tape timers
sections.body: A handheld stopwatch measures elapsed time between two button presses, and its display resolution (often 0.01 s) is almost never the limiting error source; human reaction time, typically 0.15-0.3 s per press, dominates instead, and because both a start and a stop press are needed, the total timing uncertainty from reaction time alone can approach half a second. A ticker-tape timer sidesteps human reaction time by punching (or spark-marking) dots onto a paper tape at a fixed, mechanically or electrically controlled interval, commonly 1/50 s (a timer running on 50 Hz AC mains) or 1/60 s (60 Hz mains). Because the interval is set by the timer's own oscillation rather than a person's reflexes, ticker tape trades away reaction-time error for a different resolution limit: the spacing between dots, and any friction the tape itself introduces as it is pulled through the timer.

sections.heading: Photogates
sections.body: A photogate uses an infrared beam and a light sensor: when an object interrupts the beam, the photogate's timer starts or stops, with a resolution on the order of microseconds to milliseconds, essentially eliminating human reaction time from the measurement entirely. Its dominant error instead comes from gate width, the physical thickness of whatever object breaks the beam. A photogate measuring "instantaneous" velocity actually measures average velocity across the width of the flag (a small card mounted on the moving object) as it crosses the beam, so a wider flag or a faster-accelerating object introduces more averaging error. Narrower flags and faster sampling reduce this error but can never eliminate it, since the gate always measures over some finite width.

sections.heading: Video and phone motion tracking
sections.body: Software like Tracker (free, open-source video analysis software) lets a student mark an object's position frame-by-frame in a recorded video, then automatically computes velocity and acceleration from the position-versus-time data. Its resolution is set by the video's frame rate (commonly 30 or 60 frames per second for a phone, meaning positions are known only every 1/30 or 1/60 s) and by pixel resolution translated into real-world distance via a calibration object of known size placed in frame. Motion blur at high speeds and the difficulty of precisely marking a moving object's center each frame are its dominant error sources, distinct from a photogate's gate-width error or a stopwatch's reaction-time error.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to measure a cart's speed down a 1-meter ramp. With a stopwatch, human reaction time (about +/-0.2 s on each of the start and stop presses) swamps a run that only takes about 1.5 s, giving roughly +/-25% timing uncertainty. Switching to a photogate pair at the top and bottom of the ramp, resolution improves to milliseconds, but a 1 cm-wide flag crossing the gate at high speed still introduces a few percent averaging error. Switching again to phone video tracked frame-by-frame at 30 fps gives position data every 0.033 s, letting her fit a smooth velocity-versus-time curve across many points rather than a single two-point average, trading gate-width error for frame-rate resolution and manual-marking error instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe instrument choice because picking the right tool for the claimed precision is a marker of experimental sophistication. A student who reports a photogate-measured speed to four significant figures while their air track has visible friction, or who uses a stopwatch for a sub-second event and reports the result to 0.01 s, has not thought about which error source actually dominates their setup. A strong answer names the SPECIFIC dominant error for the instrument used (reaction time, gate width, or frame rate) and explains why it, rather than the instrument's raw display resolution, sets the true uncertainty on the result.

questions.prompt: What is the dominant source of timing error when using a handheld stopwatch to time a short event?

options.text: Human reaction time in pressing start and stop
The stopwatch's internal display resolution
The frame rate of the stopwatch's internal clock

explanations.a: Correct: reaction time (roughly 0.15-0.3 s per press, doubled across start and stop) is far larger than the stopwatch's 0.01 s display resolution for most short events.
explanations.b: The display resolution (e.g. 0.01 s) is real but tiny compared to human reaction time; it is not the dominant error source.
explanations.c: A stopwatch's internal clock does not have a "frame rate" in the relevant sense; that concept applies to video tracking, not stopwatches.

questions.prompt: A photogate measures a cart's speed as it crosses a beam interrupted by a flag mounted on the cart. What is the photogate's dominant error source, distinct from a stopwatch's?

options.text: Averaging the velocity over the finite width of the flag as it crosses the beam
Human reaction time in starting and stopping the gate
The video frame rate used to record the crossing

explanations.a: Correct: because the flag has finite width, the photogate measures an average velocity across that width rather than a truly instantaneous velocity, introducing gate-width error.
explanations.b: A photogate's electronic beam-break eliminates human reaction time from the start/stop measurement entirely; that is precisely its advantage over a stopwatch.
explanations.c: Frame rate is a video-tracking concept; a photogate does not record video and has no frame rate.

questions.prompt: Match each timing instrument to its dominant source of error.

right.text: Human reaction time on start/stop presses
Averaging over the physical width of the flag crossing the beam
Frame rate limiting how often position is sampled, plus manual marking error

questions.explanation: Each instrument trades away the previous instrument's dominant error for a new, distinct one: reaction time, then gate width, then frame rate and marking precision.

questions.prompt: Order these timing methods from LEAST precise (most timing uncertainty) to MOST precise for capturing a fast, sub-second event.

items.text: Handheld stopwatch (human-triggered start/stop)
Phone video tracked frame-by-frame at 30 fps
Photogate pair with electronic beam-break timing

questions.explanation: The stopwatch's reaction-time error (tenths of a second) is largest; 30 fps video resolves to about 0.033 s per frame; a photogate's electronic timing resolves to milliseconds or better, making it the most precise of the three for a fast event.

lessons.label: Sensors and Calibration

sections.heading: Common mechanics sensors
sections.body: A force sensor (load cell) uses a strain gauge, a resistor bonded to a flexible metal element, whose electrical resistance changes measurably as the element bends under load; that resistance change is converted to a force reading in newtons. An ultrasonic motion detector emits high-frequency sound pulses and times their echo off a moving object (similar in principle to a photogate but continuous rather than a single beam-break), computing position versus time and, by differentiation, velocity and acceleration. An accelerometer, often a MEMS (micro-electromechanical systems) device built into a phone, measures acceleration directly by detecting the tiny displacement of an internal proof mass under inertial force, without needing to differentiate position data at all.

sections.heading: Calibrating against a known standard
sections.body: A sensor's raw output (often a voltage or a digital count) is meaningless in physical units until it is calibrated against something with a known, trusted value. For a force sensor, this typically means hanging a series of calibrated masses (each with a known weight, mg) and recording the sensor's output at each, then fitting a line (output vs. known force) to convert future raw readings into newtons; a sensor calibrated at only one point cannot detect a nonlinear response, so multiple calibration points across the expected range are preferred whenever practical. For a motion detector, calibration might mean placing an object at a precisely measured, tape-measured distance and confirming the sensor reports that same distance.

sections.heading: Zeroing, taring, and removing a systematic offset
sections.body: Zeroing (or taring) sets a sensor's reading to zero under a known reference condition, typically no load, before data collection begins. Skipping this step is a classic source of a systematic offset: if a force sensor reads +0.3 N with nothing attached, every subsequent reading in the session is shifted +0.3 N high, a constant bias that no amount of repeated trials will average away, since it affects every trial identically (this is exactly the accuracy problem from Lesson 3, not a precision problem). Recognizing a systematic offset requires comparing the sensor's zero-load reading, or its readings against an independently known value, rather than just checking whether repeated readings agree with each other; two readings can agree perfectly and both still be wrong by the same fixed amount.

lessons.workedExample: A student calibrates a force sensor by hanging 50 g, 100 g, 150 g, and 200 g calibrated masses and recording sensor outputs of 0.51 N, 0.99 N, 1.52 N, and 1.96 N respectively (expected: 0.49 N, 0.98 N, 1.47 N, 1.96 N using g = 9.8 m/s^2). A linear fit through these points gives a calibration slope close to 1, but with a small positive intercept, revealing a systematic offset of roughly +0.02 N even at zero apparent load. She re-zeros the sensor with nothing attached before her actual trials, which resets that offset to zero, then re-verifies with the 100 g mass to confirm the corrected reading lands close to 0.98 N before trusting the sensor for her real pendulum-force data.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about calibration because an uncalibrated or unzeroed sensor is one of the most common, and most fixable, sources of bad data in student projects, and a project that never mentions calibration invites the question directly. A judge may ask "how do you know your sensor was reading correctly?" expecting a specific answer: calibrated against known masses or known distances, zeroed before each session, and ideally re-checked partway through data collection to catch drift. A student who calibrated once at a single point, rather than across a range, or who never re-zeroed between sessions, should be able to say so and explain what error that choice could introduce.

questions.prompt: A force sensor reads +0.3 N with nothing attached to it. What should the student do before collecting data?

options.text: Zero (tare) the sensor so it reads 0 N under no load before starting trials
Ignore it, since 0.3 N is small and will average out over repeated trials
Subtract 0.3 N only from the final averaged result at the end of the experiment

explanations.a: Correct: zeroing under the known no-load reference condition removes the systematic offset before it can bias every subsequent measurement.
explanations.b: A constant offset affects every single trial identically, so repeating trials does NOT average it away; that only works for random error, not systematic bias.
explanations.c: Subtracting it only from the final average, rather than zeroing before each measurement, still leaves the offset embedded in every individual reading and any calculation done before that final subtraction.

questions.prompt: Which sensor measures acceleration directly, without needing to differentiate position-versus-time data?

options.text: An accelerometer
An ultrasonic motion detector
A force sensor

explanations.a: Correct: an accelerometer (e.g. a phone's MEMS sensor) detects the displacement of an internal proof mass under inertial force, giving acceleration directly.
explanations.b: An ultrasonic motion detector measures position (distance via echo timing) versus time; velocity and acceleration must be computed by differentiating that position data.
explanations.c: A force sensor measures force directly via a strain gauge; acceleration would need to be derived using F = ma if mass is known, not measured directly.

questions.prompt: Match each sensor to what it physically measures.

right.text: Resistance change in a bending strain gauge, converted to newtons
Time for a sound pulse to echo off a moving object, converted to distance
Displacement of an internal proof mass under inertial force

questions.explanation: Each sensor converts a different physical effect (strain, echo timing, proof-mass displacement) into the quantity it reports.

questions.prompt: Order the correct steps for calibrating a force sensor against known masses.

items.text: Zero the sensor with no load attached
Hang a series of calibrated masses across the expected range and record each output
Fit a line through the known-force vs. sensor-output points
Use the fitted line to convert future raw sensor readings into newtons

questions.explanation: Zeroing establishes the no-load baseline first; then multiple known masses are applied and recorded; a line is fit through those points; only then is the fit used to interpret future readings.

lessons.label: Controlling a Mechanics Experiment

sections.heading: Independent, dependent, and controlled variables
sections.body: In a controlled experiment, the independent variable is the one the experimenter deliberately changes (for example, a pendulum's release angle), the dependent variable is the one measured in response (the period), and controlled variables are every other factor held fixed across trials (string length, bob mass, air currents in the room) so that any observed change in the dependent variable can be attributed to the independent variable alone. A common student mistake is changing two variables at once, for example both the pendulum's length and its release angle between trials, which makes it impossible to attribute a period change to either one individually; this is sometimes called confounding, and it is the single fastest way to invalidate an otherwise careful experiment.

sections.heading: Repeated trials beat random error, not systematic error
sections.body: Random error (small, unpredictable fluctuations, like slightly different reaction-time lags on different stopwatch presses) scatters results above and below the true value roughly symmetrically, so averaging many trials genuinely reduces its effect on the reported mean, with the standard error shrinking roughly as 1/sqrt(N) for N trials. Systematic error (a consistent bias in one direction, like an uncalibrated sensor offset from Lesson 5) does not average away no matter how many trials are run, because it shifts every trial the same way. Recognizing which kind of error dominates a given result determines the fix: more trials for random error, better calibration or a redesigned protocol for systematic error.

sections.heading: Mechanics-specific confounders and how a protocol handles them
sections.body: Classic mechanics experiments carry predictable confounders. Friction (at a pivot, along a track, in bearings) systematically drains energy the idealized model does not account for, biasing results like a pendulum's amplitude decay or a cart's measured acceleration; a defensible protocol either minimizes friction (air tracks, low-friction pivots) or explicitly measures and corrects for it rather than ignoring it. Air resistance similarly matters more for light, large-surface-area objects (a falling piece of paper) than dense compact ones (a steel ball), so a protocol should justify why it was or was not a significant factor for the specific object used. Inconsistent release (a hand-released cart given an accidental push, or a pendulum bob released at slightly different angles across trials) introduces variability that is easy to blame on "random error" but is actually a controllable procedural flaw; a release mechanism (a barrier, a electromagnet, a consistent visual guide) removes it. Timing lag, covered in Lesson 4, is addressed by choosing an instrument whose dominant error is small relative to the effect being measured, and by being explicit in the writeup about which error source that instrument leaves uncorrected.

lessons.workedExample: A student investigates how ramp angle affects a cart's acceleration. Her independent variable is ramp angle; her dependent variable is measured acceleration (from photogates); her controlled variables are cart mass, ramp surface, and starting position on the ramp, all held fixed across the five angles she tests. She notices her cart appears to accelerate less than the frictionless prediction a = g*sin(theta) predicts at every angle, a systematic gap rather than random scatter, which she correctly attributes to track friction rather than random timing error, since the gap is consistent in direction and magnitude across repeated trials at each angle. She adds a friction term to her model (a = g*sin(theta) - mu*g*cos(theta)) and fits mu from her data instead of discarding the friction-affected results, turning a confounder into a measured and reported parameter.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about variable control because it is the structural backbone of a valid experiment: a project that changed two variables at once, or that cannot say what was held constant, has a result that cannot support its conclusion no matter how careful the individual measurements were. Judges also specifically probe whether a student can distinguish random from systematic error IN THEIR OWN DATA, asking something like "your five trials at 30 degrees all came in below the predicted value, why more trials instead of investigating friction?" A student who identifies friction, air resistance, inconsistent release, or timing lag as the specific confounder at play, and explains what their protocol did about it, demonstrates real experimental design rather than a plug-and-chug measurement exercise.

questions.prompt: A student changes both a pendulum's string length AND its release angle between trials, then reports how period changed. What is the main problem?

options.text: The two changed variables are confounded, so a period change cannot be attributed to either one individually
The period will now be measured in the wrong units
Nothing; changing more variables per trial makes the experiment more efficient

explanations.a: Correct: with two independent variables changing simultaneously, any observed period change could be due to either (or both), making the result impossible to interpret causally.
explanations.b: Units are unaffected by how many variables are changed at once; this is a design flaw, not a units error.
explanations.c: Changing multiple variables at once may save time but destroys the ability to attribute the result to a specific cause, which is the entire point of a controlled experiment.

questions.prompt: A cart's measured acceleration on a ramp is consistently about 8% lower than the frictionless prediction, across every trial and every angle tested. This pattern is best explained by:

options.text: A systematic error, likely track friction, not random measurement scatter
Random error, which will disappear if more trials are averaged
An error in the sig-fig rounding of the final reported acceleration

explanations.a: Correct: a consistent gap in the same direction across every trial and every condition is the signature of a systematic error like friction, not random scatter.
explanations.b: Random error would show up as scatter ABOVE and below the prediction that shrinks with averaging; a consistent one-directional gap does not average away.
explanations.c: Sig-fig rounding affects reported precision, not a real, physically consistent 8% shortfall in measured acceleration.

questions.prompt: Match each mechanics confounder to a protocol choice that addresses it.

left.text: Friction at a pivot or along a track
Inconsistent release of a cart or pendulum bob
Air resistance on a falling object

right.text: Use an air track or low-friction pivot, or measure and model friction explicitly
Use a consistent release mechanism (barrier, electromagnet, visual guide) instead of releasing by hand
Use a dense, compact object where air resistance is negligible, or justify why it is not

questions.explanation: Each mechanics confounder has a specific, addressable protocol fix rather than being an unavoidable source of noise.

questions.prompt: Order these actions as a student designs a controlled ramp-angle experiment, from first to last.

items.text: Identify ramp angle as the independent variable and acceleration as the dependent variable
Hold cart mass, ramp surface, and starting position fixed across all trials
Run repeated trials at each angle and check whether results scatter randomly or show a consistent directional gap from the prediction
If a consistent directional gap appears, investigate a specific systematic cause (such as friction) rather than just averaging more trials

questions.explanation: Variable roles must be defined first, controls fixed second, then data collected and examined for its error pattern, and only then does a consistent bias prompt investigating a specific systematic cause rather than more repetition.

lessons.label: Systematic vs Random Error

sections.heading: Two very different kinds of "wrong"
sections.body: Every measurement has error, but not all error behaves the same way. Random error is unpredictable scatter: repeat the same measurement under the same conditions and you get slightly different numbers each time, sometimes too high, sometimes too low, with no consistent direction. It comes from things you cannot fully control — a human's reaction time on a stopwatch, tiny air currents disturbing a balance, the exact instant your eye judges a needle has stopped swinging. Systematic error is different: it is a bias that pushes every single reading in the SAME direction by roughly the same amount. A ruler with a worn-down end reads every length too short; a balance that was never zeroed reads every mass a fixed amount too high; a thermometer with a manufacturing offset reads every temperature 2°C hot. Systematic error does not average out because it is not random — it is baked into the instrument or method itself.

sections.heading: Why averaging cures one and not the other
sections.body: Averaging many trials works specifically because random fluctuations are equally likely to land above or below the true value, so they cancel as you add more trials — the mean converges toward the true value and your precision (how tightly clustered your estimate is) improves. But averaging a mis-zeroed balance's readings a hundred times still gives you a hundred readings that are all shifted by the same offset; the mean of a biased population is still biased. This is the practical reason the distinction matters: random error is a precision problem, fixed by collecting more data. Systematic error is an accuracy problem, fixed only by finding the source of the bias and correcting it — calibrating the instrument against a known standard, re-zeroing it, or applying a known correction factor to every reading after the fact.

sections.heading: Spotting each one in practice
sections.body: A useful diagnostic: if your repeated trials scatter noticeably around a central value, you have random error and can characterize it with a standard deviation. If instead your instrument's readings are suspiciously tight (low scatter) but disagree with a trusted reference measurement or with theory in one consistent direction, suspect a systematic bias. The two often coexist in the same experiment — a timing measurement can have both reaction-time jitter (random) and a stopwatch that runs 2% fast (systematic) — and a careful experimenter reports evidence for each separately rather than lumping all disagreement into one vague "error bar." One classic classroom test for a suspected systematic bias is to measure a known, certified reference value on the same instrument: if the instrument reads the reference wrong by a consistent amount, that same offset is almost certainly present, in the same direction, on every other reading that instrument has produced.

sections.heading: Precision and accuracy are not the same word
sections.body: These two error types map onto a distinction physicists insist on: PRECISION describes how tightly repeated measurements cluster together, while ACCURACY describes how close those measurements are to the true value. Readings can be highly precise (tight scatter, small random error) yet wildly inaccurate (systematic bias pushes the whole cluster away from the truth) — imagine a tight group of arrows all missing the target's center in the same direction. Naming which failure mode you have dictates the fix: more trials buy you precision, calibration buys you accuracy, and conflating the two wastes effort, like collecting a hundred more trials on a mis-zeroed balance.

lessons.workedExample: A class weighs a wooden block eight times on a digital balance, getting (in grams): 150.3, 149.8, 150.5, 150.1, 150.0, 149.9, 150.4, 150.2. The mean is 150.15 g with a standard deviation of about 0.24 g, giving a standard error of the mean of about 0.09 g — averaging the eight trials has tightened the estimate to 150.15 ± 0.09 g. But the balance was never tared and reads 0.3 g high on an empty pan, a systematic offset the students discover by weighing a certified 100.0 g reference mass and getting 100.3 g. No amount of averaging removes that 0.3 g; only re-zeroing the balance (or subtracting the known offset) corrects it, giving a true mass near 149.85 g.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge will ask a very specific question: "If you ran this measurement 50 more times, would that fix the problem you just described?" A student who has genuinely internalized the distinction answers instantly and correctly — yes for random error, no for systematic error — and can name what WOULD fix a systematic bias (calibration against a known standard). A student who has only memorized the vocabulary tends to hedge or say "more data always helps," which reveals they have not connected the concept to what averaging actually does mathematically: cancel scatter, not shift.

questions.prompt: A digital scale is never zeroed and reads 0.4 g high no matter what is weighed. This is best described as:

options.text: Systematic error — a consistent bias that needs calibration, not more trials
Random error — it will shrink if you average more trials
Not really error, just a rounding difference

explanations.a: Correct: the offset shifts every single reading by the same amount in the same direction, which is the signature of systematic error.
explanations.b: Wrong direction of reasoning: random error scatters around the true value and shrinks under averaging; a constant +0.4 g offset does not, since averaging a biased set of numbers just gives you a precise but still-biased mean.
explanations.c: A 0.4 g offset on every reading is a real, consistent bias, not a rounding artifact — it changes every recorded mass by a fixed amount.

questions.prompt: Match each source of error to its type.

left.text: A balance never tared before use
Human reaction time starting/stopping a stopwatch
A thermometer manufactured with a permanent +2°C offset
Table vibration causing slightly different balance readings each trial

right.text: Systematic — fixed by calibration
Random — reduced by averaging repeated trials

questions.explanation: An un-tared balance and a manufacturing offset both bias every reading the same way (systematic); reaction time and vibration jitter differently from trial to trial (random).

questions.prompt: Why doesn't averaging many trials reduce systematic error?

options.text: Because systematic error shifts every reading in the same direction by about the same amount, so the bias survives in the mean
Because you need at least 30 trials before averaging works at all
Because random error is always larger than systematic error, so it dominates the average

explanations.a: Correct: averaging cancels fluctuations that go both directions; a bias that pushes every reading the same way has nothing to cancel against.
explanations.b: The 30-trials idea is a rule of thumb from statistics for other purposes; it has nothing to do with why systematic bias resists averaging.
explanations.c: The relative sizes of random vs systematic error vary by experiment — systematic error is not always smaller, and either way it does not average out.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for diagnosing and correcting a suspected systematic error in a balance.

items.text: Notice that repeated readings are unusually tight but disagree with a trusted reference value
Weigh a certified reference mass on the same balance to check for an offset
Confirm the size and direction of the consistent offset
Re-zero the balance or apply a correction factor to future and past readings

questions.explanation: You first notice tight-but-wrong readings, then test against a known standard, confirm the bias, and only then correct the instrument or the data.

lessons.label: Reporting Uncertainty

sections.heading: Mean, standard deviation, and the standard error of the mean
sections.body: Once you have several repeated trials of a measurement, three numbers summarize them. The MEAN is the simple average, your single best estimate of the true value. The STANDARD DEVIATION (SD) measures how spread out the individual trials are around that mean — a small SD means your trials clustered tightly, a large SD means they scattered widely. The STANDARD ERROR OF THE MEAN (SEM) is a different quantity that people frequently confuse with SD: it measures how precisely you know the MEAN itself, and it equals SD divided by the square root of the number of trials, N. This square-root relationship is the mathematical reason more trials help: doubling N does not halve your uncertainty, it shrinks it by a factor of √2, so going from 4 trials to 16 trials (4× the data) only cuts the SEM in half.

sections.heading: The value ± uncertainty convention
sections.body: A measured result is reported as "value ± uncertainty," where the uncertainty is usually the SEM if you are reporting how well you know an average, or a directly estimated reading uncertainty (like half the smallest scale division) for a single careful measurement. On a graph, this uncertainty becomes an error bar: a vertical (or horizontal) line segment through each data point showing the range the true value plausibly falls within. Whether error bars represent one SD, one SEM, or something else should always be stated — an unlabeled error bar is close to useless to another scientist trying to judge your result.

sections.heading: Rounding: matching precision to what you actually know
sections.body: A measurement of 1.4123456 ± 0.0116 seconds is dishonest — it claims far more precision than the data support. The convention is to round the UNCERTAINTY first, to one or occasionally two significant figures, and then round the measured value to match that same decimal place. So an SEM of 0.0116 s rounds to 0.01 s (one sig fig), and the mean rounds to match: 1.41 ± 0.01 s, not 1.412 ± 0.0116 s. Reporting extra digits past the uncertainty implies you know something you don't; this is called false precision, and it is one of the most common mistakes graders look for. The same discipline applies in reverse: rounding TOO aggressively, say to 1.4 ± 0.01 s, throws away real information by dropping the mean to a coarser decimal place than the uncertainty actually supports. The rule of thumb — uncertainty gets one or two sig figs, and the central value's last reported digit lines up with the uncertainty's — keeps a result honest in both directions, neither overclaiming nor underclaiming what the data show.

sections.heading: Choosing SD vs SEM for the error bar
sections.body: Which of the two — SD or SEM — belongs on a graph depends on the question being asked. To show how much any individual measurement is expected to vary, plot the SD. To show how well you know the AVERAGE — the number you would actually quote as your result — plot the SEM, which is always smaller than the SD by a factor of √N. Mixing these up confuses comparisons between labs: two groups reporting "the same" measurement can look inconsistent if one plotted SD and the other SEM, even though their underlying data agree.

lessons.workedExample: A student times a ball's fall over five trials: 1.42, 1.38, 1.45, 1.40, 1.41 seconds. The mean is 1.412 s. The standard deviation of the five trials is about 0.026 s, describing how much any single trial scattered from the average. Dividing by √5 gives a standard error of the mean of about 0.012 s — how precisely the AVERAGE itself is known, tighter than any one trial. Following the rounding convention, the uncertainty 0.012 s rounds to one significant figure (0.01 s), and the mean is rounded to match that decimal place, giving a final reported result of t = 1.41 ± 0.01 s.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges routinely ask a student to point to their error bars and explain, in one sentence, what they represent — standard deviation of the raw trials, or standard error of the mean. A student who cannot answer, or who reports a result like "1.412386 ± 0.0116284 s," is signaling that the number was copied from a calculator screen rather than understood. The fix a judge wants to see is fluent: name which quantity the error bar is, then justify the rounding — that a measurement is only as precise as its stated uncertainty allows.

questions.prompt: The standard error of the mean (SEM) is calculated as:

options.text: SD divided by the square root of N
SD multiplied by the square root of N
SD divided by N
SD squared, divided by N

explanations.a: Correct: SEM = SD / √N, which is why more trials shrink the uncertainty in the mean, but only as the square root of N.
explanations.b: Multiplying by √N would make the uncertainty grow with more trials, the opposite of what averaging accomplishes.
explanations.c: Dividing by N (not √N) would shrink the uncertainty too fast — quadrupling N would cut this quantity to a quarter, not a half.
explanations.d: This is neither the definition of SD nor SEM; squaring SD gives the variance, which is not divided by N to get SEM.

questions.prompt: A mean travel time comes out to 1.412 s with an SEM of 0.0116 s. Following the round-the-uncertainty-first convention, this should be reported as:

explanations.a: Correct: 0.0116 rounds to one significant figure (0.01), and the mean is rounded to the same decimal place (hundredths), giving 1.41 ± 0.01 s.
explanations.b: This reports far more digits than the uncertainty justifies — false precision that implies a level of knowledge the data does not support.
explanations.c: The mean is rounded to the wrong decimal place; it should match the uncertainty's decimal place (hundredths), not be truncated further to tenths.
explanations.d: The uncertainty itself is rounded to two significant figures where the convention calls for one (or at most two, consistently), and it should read 0.01, not 0.012.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it describes.

right.text: Measures the spread of the individual trials about the average
Measures how precisely the average itself is known; shrinks as √N grows
The graphical line segment showing an uncertainty on a plotted point
The single best estimate of the true value, found by averaging the trials

questions.explanation: SD describes trial-to-trial spread, SEM describes how well the average is pinned down, the error bar is how that uncertainty is drawn, and the mean is the central estimate itself.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for computing and reporting a measured value with its uncertainty.

items.text: Record each individual trial's value
Compute the mean of all trials
Compute the standard deviation of the trials
Divide the standard deviation by √N to get the SEM
Round the SEM to 1–2 sig figs and report as mean ± SEM at matching precision

questions.explanation: Raw trials feed the mean, the mean feeds the standard deviation, the standard deviation feeds the SEM, and only at the end is everything rounded for the final report.

lessons.label: Propagation of Uncertainty

sections.heading: Two different combination rules
sections.body: Most physical quantities you care about are not measured directly — they are calculated from two or more measured quantities, each with its own uncertainty. The rule for combining those uncertainties depends entirely on what arithmetic operation connects them. For a SUM or DIFFERENCE, like a length found as L = L2 − L1, the conservative (worst-case) rule is to add the ABSOLUTE uncertainties: if L1 = 5.0 ± 0.1 cm and L2 = 12.0 ± 0.2 cm, then L = 7.0 ± 0.3 cm (0.1 + 0.2). This holds whether you are adding or subtracting — the simple-addition rule treats the worst possible case, where both measurements happen to be off in the direction that makes the error largest, so it never understates the uncertainty. (When your two measurements' errors are genuinely independent and random, statisticians instead combine them in quadrature, Δf = √((ΔL1)² + (ΔL2)²), which is smaller because independent errors partially cancel on average — you'll see this noted again below, but for fair-project reporting the simple-addition bound is the safer default and the one judges expect.)

sections.heading: Products, quotients, and the exponent rule
sections.body: For a PRODUCT or QUOTIENT, like a density ρ = m/V, the same conservative logic applies to RELATIVE (percent) uncertainties instead of absolute ones: you add them. First convert each absolute uncertainty to a percentage of its own value, add those percentages, then convert the total percentage back to an absolute uncertainty on the final answer. A third case extends this: for a quantity raised to a POWER, x^n, the relative uncertainty in x is multiplied by the exponent n — not added, multiplied — because each factor of x in the product contributes its own relative uncertainty. This is why volumes computed from a radius (V ∝ r³) are far more sensitive to radius uncertainty than the radius measurement itself suggests: a 2.5% uncertainty in r becomes a 7.5% uncertainty in V.

sections.heading: Why the rules differ
sections.body: The underlying reason sums use absolute error while products use relative error comes from calculus (the derivative of a sum distributes uncertainty additively in absolute terms, while the derivative of a product distributes it additively in relative terms), but you do not need calculus to apply the rules correctly — you need to correctly identify which operation combines your measured quantities and apply the matching rule. Both rules as taught here (simple addition, whether of absolute or relative uncertainty) are the worst-case bound: they assume both errors line up in the least favorable direction, which is why they're the safer choice to report even though independent random errors typically partially cancel and would combine to something a bit smaller in quadrature. Mixing the rules up — adding absolute uncertainties through a division, for instance — is one of the most common uncertainty-propagation errors, and it usually produces an answer that is wildly too large or too small.

sections.heading: Multi-step calculations and the dominant term
sections.body: Real calculations often chain several operations together — a pendulum's g might be found from a period-squared-over-length slope that itself came from timing and length measurements, each with propagated uncertainty. The rule for handling this is to propagate one operation at a time, working from the innermost calculation outward, applying whichever rule (absolute-add or relative-add) matches each individual step. A useful shortcut for checking whether a calculation is even worth refining further: once uncertainties are combined, one input's contribution is often much larger than the others', and shrinking the smaller contributors further barely changes the final uncertainty. Spotting that dominant term tells you where additional careful measurement would actually improve your result, rather than spending effort tightening an input that was never the bottleneck.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures a solid's mass as m = 24.5 ± 0.2 g and its volume as V = 8.0 ± 0.3 cm³. Since density is a quotient (ρ = m/V), relative uncertainties add: 0.2/24.5 = 0.8% for mass, 0.3/8.0 = 3.8% for volume, totaling 4.6%. The density itself is 24.5/8.0 = 3.06 g/cm³, so the absolute uncertainty is 4.6% of 3.06 ≈ 0.14 g/cm³, giving ρ = 3.06 ± 0.14 g/cm³. Separately, a sphere's radius is measured as r = 2.00 ± 0.05 cm, a 2.5% relative uncertainty; since V ∝ r³, the volume's relative uncertainty is 2.5% × 3 = 7.5%, applied to V = (4/3)πr³ ≈ 33.5 cm³ to give V = 33.5 ± 2.5 cm³.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing propagation skill will hand a student a derived quantity — density, a spring constant, a period-squared — and ask them to state the final uncertainty out loud, showing the intermediate percentages. The tell that separates real understanding from memorized formulas is whether the student correctly identifies WHICH rule applies before calculating: sum/difference gets absolute addition, product/quotient gets relative addition, and a power multiplies the relative uncertainty by the exponent. A student who plugs numbers into the wrong rule, or forgets the exponent multiplication entirely, reveals they never learned why the rules differ, only that rules exist.

questions.prompt: Match each type of calculation to its uncertainty-combination rule.

left.text: Sum or difference (e.g., L = L2 − L1)

right.text: Add the ABSOLUTE uncertainties
Add the RELATIVE (percent) uncertainties
Multiply the relative uncertainty by the exponent

questions.explanation: Sums and differences propagate uncertainty in absolute terms; products and quotients propagate it in relative (percent) terms; a power multiplies that relative uncertainty by the exponent.

questions.prompt: A sphere's radius is r = 2.00 ± 0.05 cm, a 2.5% relative uncertainty. What is the relative uncertainty in its volume, V = (4/3)πr³?

explanations.a: Correct: the power rule multiplies the relative uncertainty by the exponent, so 2.5% × 3 = 7.5%.
explanations.b: This forgets to multiply by the exponent at all — it just copies the radius's relative uncertainty onto the volume unchanged.
explanations.c: This doubles the relative uncertainty (2.5% × 2) instead of multiplying by the correct exponent, 3, for a cubic relationship.
explanations.d: This multiplies by 9 (as if the exponent were squared to 3²) instead of by 3, overstating the propagated uncertainty.
