questions.prompt: For m = 24.5 ± 0.2 g and V = 8.0 ± 0.3 cm³, with ρ = m/V ≈ 3.06 g/cm³, the correctly propagated absolute uncertainty in ρ is closest to:

options.text: 0.14 g/cm³
0.5 g/cm³
0.02 g/cm³
0.20 g/cm³

explanations.a: Correct: relative uncertainties (0.8% + 3.8% = 4.6%) applied to ρ = 3.06 g/cm³ give about 0.14 g/cm³.
explanations.b: This simply adds the two ABSOLUTE uncertainties (0.2 + 0.3), the rule for a sum or difference, not for a quotient like density.
explanations.c: This uses only the mass's relative uncertainty (0.8% of 3.06) and ignores the volume's contribution entirely.
explanations.d: This copies the absolute uncertainty in mass (0.2 g) directly onto the density's units without ever propagating it through the division.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for propagating uncertainty through a density calculation ρ = m/V.

items.text: Find the relative uncertainty in mass by dividing its absolute uncertainty by the mass
Find the relative uncertainty in volume by dividing its absolute uncertainty by the volume
Add the two relative uncertainties to get the total relative uncertainty in density
Multiply the total relative uncertainty by the calculated density to get the absolute uncertainty
Report the density as value ± absolute uncertainty

questions.explanation: Each input's relative uncertainty is found first, then added (since density is a quotient), then converted back to an absolute uncertainty on the final density value for reporting.

lessons.label: Fitting a Straight Line

sections.heading: Why one line beats one point
sections.body: If a physical law predicts a linear relationship between two quantities you can measure, collecting several (x, y) pairs and fitting ONE line through all of them is far more powerful than computing a physical constant from a single data point. A single point carries all of that trial's random error into your answer undiluted. A line fit across many points lets each point's random scatter partially cancel against the others, the same averaging logic that makes a mean more reliable than one trial. The fitted line has two describable features: its SLOPE and its Y-INTERCEPT, and a physical law usually predicts a specific value or expected sign for each.

sections.heading: The least-squares idea
sections.body: The standard way to fit "the best" line is least-squares regression: among all possible straight lines, it picks the one that minimizes the sum of the squares of the RESIDUALS — the vertical distances between each data point and the line. Squaring before summing does two things: it makes every residual positive so points above and below the line don't cancel each other out, and it penalizes large deviations more heavily than small ones, so the fit is pulled toward avoiding any single badly-missed point. In practice this fit is computed by a calculator, spreadsheet, or graphing software, which also reports an uncertainty on the slope and intercept themselves — numbers you should read off and report, not just the central slope value.

sections.heading: Reading a physical constant off the slope
sections.body: The real payoff of fitting a line is that its slope (and sometimes intercept) IS a physical constant, once you know the equation relating your axes. Plot force vs extension for a spring and the slope is the spring constant k. Plot period-squared vs pendulum length and the slope relates to gravitational acceleration g. A near-zero intercept, when theory predicts one should pass through the origin, is itself evidence the physical model fits; a stubbornly nonzero intercept where none is expected is a clue toward an uncorrected systematic error, like a spring that was already slightly stretched before x was defined as zero.

sections.heading: Spanning a wide range beats clustering points
sections.body: A fit is only as reliable as the range of x-values feeding it. Five data points clustered in a narrow window near one end of your instrument's range give the regression very little leverage to pin down the slope precisely — small random errors in y translate into large swings in the fitted slope when the x-values are all nearly identical. Spreading measurements across the widest practical range of x sharpens the slope estimate substantially, because the fit can distinguish a steep line from a shallow one far more confidently when the data spans a broad baseline. This is why a well-designed experiment plans its measured x-values in advance to cover the full usable range of the apparatus, rather than conveniently clustering them wherever measurements happen to be easiest to take.

lessons.workedExample: A student stretches a spring with five different hanging masses and measures the extension x for each, recording (x, F) pairs. Entering the five points into a least-squares regression (spreadsheet or graphing calculator) returns a best-fit line F = (50.4 N/m)·x + 0.02 N, with R² = 0.997. The slope, 50.4 N/m, is read directly as the spring constant k — not from any single (x, F) pair, but as the value that best fits all five points simultaneously. The intercept, 0.02 N, is close enough to zero to be consistent with Hooke's law F = kx having no offset, supporting the conclusion that the spring behaves linearly over the tested range.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask, "Why didn't you just calculate k from your best trial?" The answer a strong student gives is that a single point has no way to distinguish a genuinely typical measurement from an unlucky outlier, while a least-squares fit uses every point's information and reports its own uncertainty on the slope. Judges are also alert to students who report a slope value with no attached uncertainty and no comment on the intercept — a fit is only fully interpreted once both the slope's physical meaning and the intercept's consistency (or inconsistency) with theory have been addressed.

questions.prompt: The best-fit (least-squares) line is the one that minimizes:

options.text: The sum of the squares of the vertical distances (residuals) between the data points and the line
The sum of the absolute (unsquared) distances between the points and the line
The number of data points that fall exactly on the line
The horizontal distance between the first and last data point

explanations.a: Correct: least-squares regression minimizes the sum of squared residuals, which keeps deviations from canceling and penalizes large misses.
explanations.b: Minimizing absolute (unsquared) distances is a different, less common fitting method (least absolute deviations), not the standard least-squares fit.
explanations.c: A best-fit line is not chosen by counting points exactly on it — with continuous, noisy data, expecting exact hits is unrealistic and not the goal.
explanations.d: The spread between the first and last x-value has nothing to do with how well the line fits the data in between.

questions.prompt: A student fits F vs x for a spring and gets a slope of 50.4 N/m with a near-zero y-intercept. The best interpretation is:

options.text: The spring constant k is about 50.4 N/m, and the near-zero intercept is consistent with Hooke's law having no offset
The 50.4 N/m value is only valid at the single largest extension tested
The near-zero intercept means the fit is unreliable and should be discarded
A single (x, F) data point would have given a more trustworthy value of k

explanations.a: Correct: the slope is the best estimate of k across the whole data set, and an intercept near zero matches the theoretical prediction of no offset.
explanations.b: The slope characterizes the whole linear trend across all tested extensions, not just the single largest one.
explanations.c: A near-zero intercept, when theory predicts zero, is a GOOD sign for the fit, not evidence it is unreliable.
explanations.d: A single point carries all of that trial's random error undiluted, whereas the fit combines information from every point.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for extracting a physical constant from a linear fit.

items.text: Collect several (x, y) data pairs spanning a wide range
Plot the data and perform a least-squares regression
Read the slope (and its uncertainty) from the fit
Relate the slope to the physical constant via the underlying equation
Report the constant together with its propagated uncertainty

questions.explanation: Data collection comes first, then the regression, then reading the slope, then interpreting it physically, and finally reporting it with an honest uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Match each fit feature to what it tells you.

left.text: The slope of the fitted F vs x line
The y-intercept of the fitted F vs x line
A single (x, F) data point on its own

right.text: The best overall estimate of the spring constant k, using all the data
Expected near zero if F = kx holds with no built-in offset
An unreliable estimate of k on its own, since it carries one trial's full random error

questions.explanation: The slope is the constant of interest, the intercept is a consistency check against the theoretical model, and any single point is too noisy to trust alone.

lessons.label: The Linearization Trick

sections.heading: Making a curve look like a line
sections.body: Many physical laws are not linear in the variables you directly measure, but they can be made linear by plotting the RIGHT combination of variables instead of the raw ones. A pendulum's period follows T = 2π√(L/g), which is a square-root relationship between T and L — plotting T vs L directly gives a curve, and reading a slope off a curve is meaningless. But squaring both sides gives T² = (4π²/g)·L, which IS linear: plotting T² (y-axis) against L (x-axis) gives a straight line through the origin with slope 4π²/g. The same trick recovers g from the fit's slope, this time with the averaging and uncertainty benefits of a full line fit instead of one data point.

sections.heading: A second example: uniformly accelerated motion
sections.body: The distance a uniformly accelerating object covers from rest follows s = ½at², quadratic in time. Plotting s vs t gives a curve (a parabola), but plotting s (y-axis) against t² (x-axis) gives a straight line through the origin with slope a/2, so twice the slope recovers the acceleration a directly. The general recipe is always the same: start from the nonlinear law, algebraically identify which POWER or COMBINATION of your measured quantities turns the relationship into y = mx (+ b), compute that transformed quantity for every data point, and only then fit a line to the transformed data.

sections.heading: Checking the linearization actually worked
sections.body: Choosing the right transformed axes is necessary but not sufficient — you should still check that the transformed data actually falls on a straight line, and that the line behaves as theory predicts, such as passing through (or very near) the origin when the underlying law has no additive constant. If T² vs L does NOT pass through the origin, that is informative: it may mean a systematic error (like measuring L to the center of the pendulum bob instead of the pivot) rather than a failure of the T ∝ √L relationship itself. Linearization turns "does this messy curve match the law?" into the much easier, much more diagnostic question "is this straight line straight, and does it pass through where I expect?"

sections.heading: Not every law linearizes the same way
sections.body: Different physical relationships call for different transformations, and part of the skill is recognizing which one applies. A quantity that decays exponentially, like radioactive activity vs time, linearizes not by squaring or taking a power but by plotting the LOGARITHM of the quantity against time, since ln(A) = ln(A0) − λt is linear in t with slope −λ. A quantity following an inverse-square law, like light intensity vs distance from a point source, linearizes by plotting intensity against 1/distance². The common thread across every case is the same: solve the equation algebraically until one side is a bare constant times a single transformed variable, then plot that transformed variable, rather than assuming squaring is always the right move.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures period T for pendulum lengths L = 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80, 1.00 m, getting T = 0.90, 1.27, 1.55, 1.80, 2.01 s. Squaring each period gives T² = 0.81, 1.61, 2.40, 3.24, 4.04 s². Plotting T² (y) vs L (x) produces a straight line through the origin with a least-squares slope of about 4.05 s²/m. Since theory predicts slope = 4π²/g, the student solves g = 4π²/slope = 39.48/4.05 ≈ 9.75 m/s², matching the accepted value closely — a result the raw, curved T vs L plot could never have delivered as cleanly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often hand a student a nonlinear formula they haven't seen linearized before and ask, "What would you plot on each axis to get a straight line, and what would the slope mean?" This tests whether the student understands the general recipe — identify the power or combination that makes y = mx — rather than having simply memorized that "pendulums use T² vs L." A strong answer also volunteers what the expected intercept should be and what a nonzero intercept would suggest, showing the linearization is being used as a diagnostic tool, not just a plotting convenience.

questions.prompt: To turn T = 2π√(L/g) into a straight line through the origin whose SLOPE equals 4π²/g, you should plot:

options.text: T² (y-axis) vs L (x-axis)
T (y-axis) vs L (x-axis)
T (y-axis) vs √L (x-axis)
L (y-axis) vs T (x-axis)

explanations.a: Correct: squaring both sides gives T² = (4π²/g)L, a line through the origin in T² vs L with the exact slope 4π²/g.
explanations.b: T vs L is still curved (a square-root relationship), so no meaningful slope can be read off it.
explanations.c: T vs √L is also a straight line, but its slope is 2π/√g, a different quantity than the 4π²/g asked for here — a valid linearization, but not this one.
explanations.d: Plotting L vs T just swaps the axes of the still-curved T vs L relationship; it does not linearize anything.

questions.prompt: A ball rolls from rest with s = ½at². Plotting s (y-axis) vs t² (x-axis) gives a line whose slope equals:

options.text: a
2a
a²

explanations.a: Correct: s = (a/2)·t² is already in the form y = m·x with x = t², so the slope m is exactly a/2.
explanations.b: This forgets the factor of ½ in the original equation — the slope of s vs t² is half the acceleration, not the acceleration itself.
explanations.c: This doubles the correct slope; a/2 doubled would only equal a, not 2a.
explanations.d: Squaring a is not part of this linear relationship at all; the slope is linear in a, not quadratic.

questions.prompt: In the pendulum data set, T² vs L gives a least-squares slope of about 4.05 s²/m. What is g?

options.text: g = 4π² / slope ≈ 9.75 m/s²
g = slope / 4π² ≈ 0.10 m/s²
g = 4π² × slope ≈ 160 m/s²
g = slope ≈ 4.05 m/s²

explanations.a: Correct: since slope = 4π²/g, solving for g gives g = 4π²/slope = 39.48/4.05 ≈ 9.75 m/s², matching the workedExample's fitted value.
explanations.b: This inverts the relationship backwards — dividing slope by 4π² instead of dividing 4π² by slope gives a physically nonsensical result.
explanations.c: This multiplies instead of dividing, giving a value roughly 16× too large to be Earth's gravitational acceleration.
explanations.d: This skips the 4π² factor entirely and just reports the slope itself, which has units of s²/m, not m/s².

questions.prompt: Order the general steps of the linearization trick.

items.text: Start with the nonlinear physical law relating two measured quantities
Algebraically identify a transformed variable pair proportional to each other
Compute the transformed variable for every data point
Plot the transformed variables and check for a straight line through the expected intercept
Extract the physical constant from the slope

questions.explanation: The nonlinear law comes first, then the algebraic transformation is identified, then applied point-by-point, then plotted and checked, and only then is the constant read off.

questions.prompt: Match each nonlinear law to the axes that linearize it.

right.text: Plot T² vs L
Plot s vs t²
Plot v vs t (already linear, no transform needed)

questions.explanation: The pendulum and kinematics laws need a variable transformed (T squared, t squared) to become linear; the velocity equation is already linear in t and needs no transformation.

lessons.label: Residuals, R-squared, and Judging a Fit

sections.heading: What R² actually measures
sections.body: R² (the coefficient of determination) is the fraction of the variance in your y-values that the fitted model explains, ranging from 0 (the model explains none of the trend) to 1 (the model fits every point exactly). An R² of 0.95 means 95% of the spread in y is accounted for by the fitted line's dependence on x, with 5% left over as unexplained scatter. It is tempting to treat a high R² as proof that the chosen model — a straight line, say — is the CORRECT model, but R² only measures how tightly points cluster around whatever line was fit; it says nothing about whether a straight line was even the right shape to try in the first place.

sections.heading: Residual plots: the real diagnostic
sections.body: A residual is the difference between each data point's actual y-value and the value the fitted line predicts at that x. Plotting these residuals against x is far more diagnostic than staring at R² alone. If a straight line is truly the right model, the residuals should scatter randomly above and below zero with no pattern. If instead the residuals show a systematic shape — consistently positive at both ends and negative in the middle, or a clear upward or downward curve — that pattern reveals curvature in the true relationship that the straight line missed, even while R² stays deceptively high, because over a limited range a curve can still look nearly straight.

sections.heading: Asking whether the fit really supports the claim
sections.body: A responsible conclusion doesn't stop at reporting R²; it asks whether the data honestly supports the physical law being tested. This means checking the residual plot for pattern, confirming the fit's intercept matches what theory predicts (near zero when it should be), and being willing to say "a line captures most of the trend, but the residuals suggest the true relationship has some curvature we have not accounted for" rather than overclaiming confirmation. A good fit report treats R² as one piece of evidence among several, not a single number that settles the question.

sections.heading: A low R² is not automatically a failure
sections.body: It is worth separating a low R² caused by genuine random measurement noise from a low R² caused by a wrong model shape, because they call for opposite responses. If the residuals scatter randomly around zero with no pattern, but the scatter is simply large relative to the trend, the model shape (a straight line) may still be entirely correct — the fix is tighter measurement technique or more trials, not a different model. But if a low R² comes paired with a clear residual pattern, the model itself needs rethinking. Treating every low R² as "bad data" without checking the residuals for pattern risks discarding a perfectly valid linear model just because the underlying measurement had more random noise than hoped.

lessons.workedExample: A student drops a small parachute-carrying object and records distance fallen s against time t over a narrow window, then fits s vs t (not t²) with a straight line, getting R² = 0.987 — a number that looks excellent at a glance. But plotting the residuals (actual s minus the line's predicted s) against t reveals a clear U-shape: residuals are positive at the earliest and latest times and negative in the middle. That pattern is the signature of a quadratic relationship (s = ½at²) being approximated by a line over a range too narrow to show the curve by eye. The high R² was misleading; the residual plot correctly reveals the straight-line model is wrong, and the fix is to plot s vs t² instead, as covered in linearization.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love this topic because it exposes a subtle trap: a student who reports "R² = 0.99, so the fit is excellent" without ever looking at a residual plot has not actually verified their model, only its correlation strength. A fair judge will ask to see the residual plot specifically, or ask "what would convince you the straight-line model is wrong, even with a high R²?" The strong answer names a systematic pattern in the residuals — not a lower R² — as the thing that would falsify the linear model, showing the student understands R² and residual analysis answer different questions.

questions.prompt: R² represents:

options.text: The fraction of the variance in y explained by the fitted model
The probability that the fitted model is the physically correct one
The average size of the residuals
The slope of the best-fit line

explanations.a: Correct: R² quantifies how much of the y-variation the model's dependence on x accounts for, from 0 to 1.
explanations.b: R² says nothing about whether the chosen model FORM (e.g., linear vs quadratic) is physically correct — a high R² can come from fitting the wrong shape over a narrow range.
explanations.c: R² is not the average residual size; it is a normalized ratio comparing explained to total variance, unrelated to residual units.
explanations.d: The slope is a separate output of the fit describing the line's steepness; R² describes how well the whole line matches the scatter, not its steepness.

questions.prompt: A straight-line fit to genuinely curved data can still show R² = 0.98 over a limited range. What is the best way to check whether the line is really the right model?

options.text: Plot the residuals (data minus fit) against the independent variable and look for a systematic pattern
Trust the R² value, since 0.98 is already very high
Report R² with more decimal places to be more precise
Only check for problems when R² is below 0.90

explanations.a: Correct: a residual plot reveals systematic curvature that a summary statistic like R² can hide, especially over a narrow data range.
explanations.b: This is exactly the trap the lesson warns about — a high R² can coexist with a badly mismatched model shape.
explanations.c: Adding decimal places to R² does not reveal anything about model shape; the issue is a missing diagnostic step, not insufficient precision.
explanations.d: A high R² can still hide a wrong model shape, so the residual check is worth doing regardless of how high R² already is.

questions.prompt: In a residual plot, a clear U-shaped (or otherwise curved) pattern in the residuals indicates:

options.text: The fitted model (e.g., a straight line) is missing systematic curvature in the true relationship
The data has too much random error to ever be useful
Residuals are supposed to always form a U-shape when a fit is good
The fit is perfect, since the residuals are small in magnitude

explanations.a: Correct: a systematic residual pattern means the model form does not fully capture the trend, even if individual residuals are small.
explanations.b: A patterned residual plot points to a wrong model shape, not simply excessive random noise — random error would scatter residuals with no pattern.
explanations.c: A good fit should show residuals scattered randomly around zero with NO pattern; a U-shape is a red flag, not the goal.
explanations.d: Small residuals combined with a clear pattern still indicate a systematic mismatch — size and pattern are separate issues.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for judging whether a linear fit is trustworthy.

items.text: Perform the least-squares fit and compute R²
Compute the residual for every data point
Plot the residuals against the independent variable
Check whether the residuals scatter randomly around zero or show a pattern
Conclude whether the straight-line model is appropriate or a different model is needed

questions.explanation: R² comes first as a summary statistic, but the real judgment requires computing, plotting, and inspecting residuals before concluding whether the model form is trustworthy.

questions.prompt: Match each fit scenario to the correct conclusion.

left.text: High R² with residuals scattered randomly around zero
High R² with a clearly curved residual pattern
Low R² with residuals scattered randomly around zero

right.text: The linear model is well supported by the data
The linear model is likely the wrong shape, despite the high R²
The linear trend explains little of the variation, but the model shape may still be appropriate

questions.explanation: R² alone cannot distinguish these cases; the residual pattern (or lack of one) is what tells you whether the model's SHAPE, not just its fit strength, is trustworthy.

lessons.label: Outliers and Anomalous Data

sections.heading: Spotting a suspect point
sections.body: An outlier is a data point that lies unusually far from the trend the rest of your data follows — visibly off the line on a scatter plot, or showing an unusually large residual compared to the typical scatter of the other points. Noticing one is straightforward; the hard part is deciding what to do about it. A point being inconvenient — it makes your fit look worse, or moves your computed constant further from the textbook value — is never, by itself, a reason to remove it. Every data point you legitimately collected represents a real measurement, and silently discarding the ones you don't like is a form of data manipulation, even if unintentional.

sections.heading: When exclusion is and isn't justified
sections.body: The one legitimate reason to exclude a point is a specific, identifiable procedural or instrumental failure tied to that particular trial — the timer was started early because someone bumped the table, a reading was mistranscribed and cannot be recovered, the sample was visibly contaminated. In each case there is a concrete CAUSE, documented ideally at the time of the experiment (in a lab notebook), not invented after the fact to justify removing an inconvenient point. If a point looks anomalous but no specific cause can be found, the honest choice is to keep it in the analysis and report it as an unexplained deviation, not quietly drop it.

sections.heading: Documenting the decision honestly
sections.body: Whatever you decide, the decision itself belongs in your report: which point (if any) was excluded, the specific reason, and ideally how the result changes with and without it. This transparency lets another scientist judge whether your exclusion was reasonable, and protects against the appearance (or reality) of cherry-picking data to fit a hoped-for conclusion. Fields with major reproducibility problems have repeatedly traced errors back to undocumented, post-hoc exclusion of "inconvenient" data points — the discipline of writing down the reason, every time, is what separates rigorous science from wishful curve-fitting.

sections.heading: Reporting the fit both ways when in doubt
sections.body: When a point's status is genuinely ambiguous — a plausible cause exists but isn't certain — the most defensible move is often to report the analysis twice: once with the point included, once excluded, showing how much the conclusion actually depends on that single point. If the fitted slope and constant barely change either way, the point wasn't decisive and the ambiguity matters little. If the conclusion flips entirely depending on whether the point is kept, that itself is important information worth stating plainly, since it means the experiment may need more data before the result can be trusted either way. This kind of transparent, both-ways reporting is generally viewed far more favorably by judges and reviewers than a single, confidently stated number that hides how fragile it actually is.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs ten trials timing a pendulum's period, and nine trials cluster tightly around 1.40 s. Trial 6 reads 2.10 s. Checking her lab notebook, she finds a note written at the time: "trial 6 — table bumped mid-swing, pendulum's motion visibly disturbed." Because this is a specific, contemporaneously documented procedural failure, she excludes trial 6 and reports the mean and SD from the remaining nine trials, explicitly stating in her report that one trial was excluded and why. Had she instead noticed trial 6 was simply the furthest from the others with no recorded cause, the correct choice would have been to keep it in the average and note the unexplained scatter honestly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe outlier decisions specifically because this is where scientific honesty is tested most directly. A fair judge will ask, "Why did you exclude this point, and when did you decide to exclude it — before or after you saw how it affected your result?" A strong answer points to a documented, trial-specific cause recorded independent of the outcome. A weak answer says something like "it just looked wrong" or, worse, admits the point was removed because it improved R² — which a judge will correctly identify as cherry-picking, regardless of how good the resulting fit looks.

questions.prompt: A researcher notices a data point far from the trend and, without investigating any cause, deletes it because the fit looks better without it. This is:

options.text: Not good practice — points should not be excluded just because they are inconvenient, only for a documented, specific reason
Good practice, since outliers always ruin an otherwise good fit
Required practice — all outliers must be removed before fitting a line
Irrelevant, since outliers never meaningfully affect a linear fit

explanations.a: Correct: excluding a point solely because it improves the fit, with no independent cause identified, is a form of cherry-picking, not legitimate data cleaning.
explanations.b: An outlier is not automatically "ruining" a fit — it may be a genuine, real measurement that the model simply does not (yet) explain.
explanations.c: There is no blanket rule requiring removal of every unusual point; removal requires a specific, documented justification tied to that trial.
explanations.d: A single far-off point can noticeably shift a least-squares slope, especially with few data points, so outliers are not automatically harmless.

questions.prompt: Which of the following IS a legitimate justification for excluding a data point?

options.text: A lab notebook entry shows the timer was started early because the table was bumped during that specific trial
The point just doesn't fit the trend as well as the researcher would like
Removing the point makes R² noticeably higher
The point happens to be the smallest value recorded in the data set

explanations.a: Correct: a specific, documented procedural failure tied to that trial is exactly the kind of cause that justifies exclusion.
explanations.b: Personal preference about how well a point fits the trend is not a documented cause — it is exactly the temptation the lesson warns against.
explanations.c: Improved R² is an outcome of removing the point, not a reason for removing it — using the outcome to justify the removal is circular.
explanations.d: Simply being the smallest (or largest) value is not evidence of an error; extreme-but-genuine measurements are still valid data.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for handling a suspected outlier responsibly.

items.text: Notice a point that lies unusually far from the trend or has an unusually large residual
Check the lab notebook or procedure for a specific cause tied to that trial
Decide whether the cause found is a genuine, documented procedural or instrumental error
If justified, exclude the point and record the reason; if not, keep it in the analysis
Report the fit and conclusions with the decision (and its reason) disclosed either way

questions.explanation: Noticing the point comes first, then investigating a specific cause, then judging whether that cause is legitimate, then acting on that judgment, and finally reporting the decision transparently.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to the correct verdict.

left.text: A point excluded after finding a documented instrument malfunction for that trial
A point excluded only because its removal raises R²
A far-off point kept in the analysis because no specific cause could be found
A point excluded after confirming it was a data-entry transcription error

right.text: Legitimate exclusion — a specific, documented cause was found
Not legitimate — this is cherry-picking to improve the fit
Correct practice — honest reporting of an unexplained deviation

questions.explanation: Exclusions justified by a documented, trial-specific cause (malfunction, transcription error) are legitimate; exclusion based only on improving a summary statistic is cherry-picking; an unexplained point should be kept and reported honestly.

lessons.label: Motion Graphs I: Position-Time

sections.heading: Slope is velocity, not speed of the pen
sections.body: A position-time (x-t) graph plots where an object is at each instant, and its slope is the single most important thing you can read off it: slope equals average velocity over that interval, and the slope of the tangent line at a point equals instantaneous velocity there. A positive slope means the object is moving in the positive direction you defined; a negative slope means it is moving the opposite way, not that it is slowing down. Steepness encodes speed. A steep line means large displacement per unit time, so a fast object; a gentle line means a slow one. Students often confuse a graph that looks like it is going "down" with an object that is slowing down, but a straight line with negative slope describes constant velocity in the negative direction, no acceleration at all.

sections.heading: Curvature signals acceleration
sections.body: A straight-line segment on an x-t graph means the slope, and therefore the velocity, is not changing: zero acceleration. Curvature is what encodes acceleration. A curve that bends upward with increasing steepness (concave up while slope is positive) means velocity is increasing in the positive direction: positive acceleration. A curve flattening out as it rises means the object is still moving forward but slowing down, so acceleration is negative even though position keeps increasing. This is the classic trap: position can keep increasing while velocity decreases, whenever the graph is concave down but still sloping upward.

sections.heading: Rest, direction reversal, and reading the story
sections.body: A horizontal (flat) segment means zero slope, so zero velocity: the object is momentarily or persistently at rest, not "not moving because nothing is drawn." A turning point, a local maximum or minimum in x, is where the slope crosses zero, meaning the object reverses direction at that instant, even though its position value there is not itself special. To read a position-time graph fluently: scan for flat spots (rest), read the sign of the slope in each region (direction), compare steepness across regions (relative speed), and look for curvature (whether it is speeding up or slowing down within a direction).

lessons.workedExample: A cart's x-t graph rises steeply and straight from t=0 to t=2s (constant fast rightward velocity), then curves and flattens between t=2s and t=4s reaching a peak x-value at t=4s (decelerating, then momentarily at rest), then descends steeply and straight from t=4s to t=6s (constant leftward velocity, opposite sign). Velocity was positive and constant, then positive and shrinking to zero, then negative and constant. The cart never had zero velocity except at the instant t=4s, the single turning point, even though its position was largest there.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use position-time graphs to separate students who memorized "slope equals velocity" from students who can apply it under a twist. A common probe: show a curve that is still rising but flattening, and ask whether the object is speeding up or slowing down. A student fixated on "position is increasing" will wrongly say speeding up; a student reading slope will correctly say slowing down, because the tangent's steepness is shrinking even as x keeps climbing. Naming the turning point as a direction reversal, not a stop-and-restart, is another tell of real fluency versus rote pattern-matching.

questions.prompt: On a position-time graph, a curve that rises but becomes progressively less steep indicates the object is:

options.text: Speeding up in the positive direction
Slowing down while still moving in the positive direction
At rest
Moving in the negative direction

explanations.a: Speeding up would make the curve steeper over time, not flatter; a flattening rise means the slope, and thus the velocity, is shrinking.
explanations.b: Correct: position is still increasing (slope stays positive) but the decreasing steepness means velocity is decreasing in magnitude, i.e. slowing down.
explanations.c: Rest requires a slope of exactly zero, a flat horizontal segment, not merely a small positive slope.
explanations.d: Negative direction requires a negative slope; a rising curve has positive slope throughout this description.

questions.prompt: A local maximum on an x-t graph (a peak) tells you that at that instant:

options.text: The object is at its farthest point from the origin permanently
The object's velocity is zero and it is reversing direction
The object's acceleration is zero
The object has stopped moving for the rest of the motion

explanations.a: A peak only means it is the farthest point locally, in that region of the graph; the object can travel farther in the negative direction or in a later positive excursion.
explanations.b: Correct: the slope crosses zero at a smooth local max, meaning instantaneous velocity is zero there, and the sign of slope flips from positive to negative, a direction reversal.
explanations.c: Acceleration relates to curvature (how slope changes), not to the slope's value itself; acceleration can be nonzero exactly at the peak.
explanations.d: The peak marks only an instant of zero velocity, not a permanent stop; motion resumes immediately in the opposite direction in the typical case.

questions.prompt: Order these x-t graph features from what requires the LEAST information to read to the MOST (simplest visual cue to most subtle):

items.text: A flat (horizontal) segment: object at rest
A straight line's slope sign: direction of constant-velocity motion
A straight line's steepness compared to another line: relative speed
Curvature of a bending segment: whether the object is speeding up or slowing down

questions.explanation: Flatness is the most immediate visual cue (zero slope); sign of a straight slope is the next simplest read; comparing steepness across two lines takes a relative judgment; reading curvature to infer acceleration is the most subtle skill, requiring you to track how slope itself changes.

questions.prompt: Match each position-time graph feature to what it indicates about the object's motion.

right.text: Object at rest (zero velocity)
Fast, constant-velocity motion
Speeding up in the positive direction
Instant of zero velocity and direction reversal

questions.explanation: Zero slope is rest; a large constant slope is fast constant velocity; slope increasing while positive (concave up, rising) means speeding up; and a smooth peak or trough is where slope passes through zero, marking a direction reversal.

lessons.label: Motion Graphs II: Velocity-Time and Acceleration-Time

sections.heading: Slope of v-t is acceleration
sections.body: On a velocity-time (v-t) graph, the same logic from position-time graphs shifts up one derivative: slope now equals acceleration. A straight line with constant positive slope means constant positive acceleration (uniformly speeding up in the positive direction, or slowing down if velocity is negative and becoming less negative). A flat horizontal line on a v-t graph means zero acceleration, i.e., constant velocity, which could be a large constant speed, not necessarily rest. Do not confuse a flat v-t line (constant, possibly fast, motion) with a flat x-t line (rest); they mean opposite things because they are graphs of different quantities.

sections.heading: Area under v-t is displacement
sections.body: The area between a v-t curve and the time axis, counted as positive above the axis and negative below, equals the displacement over that interval. This is why a v-t graph is often more useful than an x-t graph for finding how far something traveled: you compute area with geometry (rectangles for constant velocity, triangles for constant acceleration, trapezoids for general straight segments) rather than reading positions directly. If velocity is negative for part of the interval, that region's area subtracts from the total displacement, even though the object is still moving (distance traveled, unlike displacement, would add the magnitudes instead).

sections.heading: Area under a-t is change in velocity; translating between graphs
sections.body: The same rule steps up again: the area under an acceleration-time (a-t) graph equals the change in velocity, Δv, over that interval, by the same logic (a-t is the derivative of v-t, so its integral, area, recovers Δv). A full mastery move is translating consistently across all three graphs: a parabolic x-t segment (curving smoothly) corresponds to a straight-sloped v-t segment, which corresponds to a flat a-t segment (constant acceleration). A cusp or sudden slope change in x-t corresponds to a sudden jump in v-t, which corresponds to a spike (or undefined point) in a-t. Being able to sketch one graph from another, region by region, matching slopes to areas, is the core skill this unit builds toward.

lessons.workedExample: A v-t graph shows velocity rising in a straight line from 0 to 8 m/s over 4 s, then holding flat at 8 m/s from t=4s to t=6s, then dropping in a straight line back to 0 over 2 s (t=6s to t=8s). Slope in phase one is (8-0)/4 = 2 m/s^2 (constant positive acceleration); phase two has slope 0 (zero acceleration, constant velocity); phase three has slope (0-8)/2 = -4 m/s^2 (constant negative acceleration, braking). Displacement is the total area: a triangle (1/2)(4)(8)=16 m, a rectangle (2)(8)=16 m, and a triangle (1/2)(2)(8)=8 m, for a total of 40 m. The corresponding a-t graph is three flat segments at +2, 0, and -4 m/s^2.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges lean on v-t and a-t graphs because the area-equals-displacement rule is easy to state but easy to misapply under time pressure, especially when velocity dips negative or the shape is a trapezoid rather than a clean triangle or rectangle. A strong answer breaks an irregular v-t curve into geometric pieces, computes each area with correct sign, and sums them, rather than eyeballing a total. A weaker answer confuses area under v-t (displacement) with the value of v-t itself (instantaneous velocity), or forgets that a negative-velocity region subtracts rather than adds to net displacement.

questions.prompt: A v-t graph is a horizontal line at v = 6 m/s for 5 seconds. What is true during this interval?

options.text: The object is at rest
The object moves at constant velocity with zero acceleration
The object is accelerating at 6 m/s^2
The displacement over the interval is zero

explanations.a: Rest means v = 0; a flat line at v = 6 m/s means constant nonzero speed, not rest.
explanations.b: Correct: a horizontal v-t line has zero slope, meaning zero acceleration, while the constant height means constant velocity.
explanations.c: The value 6 m/s is the velocity, not the slope; the slope of a flat line is zero, so acceleration is 0 m/s^2, not 6.
explanations.d: Displacement is the area under the line, a rectangle of height 6 and width 5, equal to 30 m, not zero.

questions.prompt: On an a-t graph, the shaded area under the curve between two times represents:

options.text: The total distance traveled
The displacement
The change in velocity, Δv
The change in acceleration

explanations.a: Distance traveled is what you'd get from the area under a v-t (not a-t) graph, taking all regions as positive.
explanations.b: Displacement is the area under a v-t graph, not an a-t graph; a-t is one derivative higher.
explanations.c: Correct: because a-t is the rate of change of velocity, its area over an interval recovers the net change in velocity, Δv, across that interval.
explanations.d: The area gives Δv, a single number for the interval; it does not directly represent how acceleration itself changed within the interval (that would be curvature of the a-t graph, if it were curved).

questions.prompt: Order the steps to find total displacement from an irregularly-shaped v-t graph made of straight segments.

items.text: Break the graph into simple geometric regions (rectangles, triangles, trapezoids) at each slope change
Compute the signed area of each region, negative where the curve is below the time axis
Sum all signed areas across the full interval
Report the sum as the net displacement over that interval

questions.explanation: You first segment the curve at each change in slope, then find each piece's signed area (respecting sign below the axis), then add the signed areas together, and that running total is the net displacement.

questions.prompt: Match each motion-graph relationship to what it computes.

right.text: Instantaneous velocity
Instantaneous acceleration
Displacement
Change in velocity, Δv

questions.explanation: Each graph's slope is the derivative of the plotted quantity (x-t slope gives velocity, v-t slope gives acceleration), while each graph's area is the integral (v-t area gives displacement, a-t area gives Δv).

lessons.label: Projectile Trajectories on a Plot

sections.heading: The parabola comes from two independent motions
sections.body: Plot a projectile's height y against its horizontal position x (not against time) and, ignoring air resistance, you get a parabola. That shape is a direct consequence of combining two independent motions: constant horizontal velocity (x grows linearly with time, x = v_x t) and uniformly accelerated vertical motion under gravity (y = y_0 + v_y0 t - (1/2) g t^2). Because horizontal position is linear in time, you can substitute t = x / v_x into the vertical equation, and a linear-in-t vertical position becomes quadratic in x, which is exactly a parabola on the y-vs-x plot. Galileo was the first to establish this decomposition rigorously in his 1638 work Two New Sciences, showing that horizontal and vertical motions could be analyzed as independent components that combine to produce the curved path.

sections.heading: Reading independence directly off the plot
sections.body: The plot itself shows the independence: mark equal time intervals along the trajectory (imagine strobe-flash dots), and the horizontal spacing between consecutive dots stays constant throughout the flight, because horizontal velocity does not change. The vertical spacing between dots, however, shrinks going up (decelerating against gravity), reaches its smallest value at the very top, and then grows again coming down (accelerating downward) mirroring the ascent. This is the visual signature that horizontal motion is uniform while vertical motion is uniformly accelerated, layered onto one curve.

sections.heading: Symmetry, apex, and range
sections.body: For a projectile launched and landing at the same height, the trajectory is symmetric about the apex: time to rise equals time to fall, the launch and landing speeds are equal in magnitude, and the launch and landing angles are mirror images (equal magnitude, opposite sign) of each other relative to the horizontal. The apex is where vertical velocity, v_y, is instantaneously zero, so the trajectory's slope (dy/dx) is exactly zero there, a flat tangent at the peak, even though horizontal velocity, and therefore speed, is nonzero at that instant. Range (horizontal distance at landing) and maximum height both depend on launch angle and speed; for a fixed launch speed on level ground, range is maximized at a 45-degree launch angle in the no-air-resistance case.

lessons.workedExample: A ball is launched at 20 m/s at 30 degrees above horizontal from ground level (g = 9.8 m/s^2). v_x0 = 20 cos(30°) ≈ 17.3 m/s (constant throughout flight); v_y0 = 20 sin(30°) = 10 m/s. Time to apex: v_y0/g ≈ 1.02 s, so total flight time (symmetric) ≈ 2.04 s. Max height: v_y0^2/(2g) ≈ 5.1 m. Range: v_x0 × total time ≈ 17.3 × 2.04 ≈ 35.3 m. On the y-vs-x plot, the curve rises smoothly to a peak at x ≈ 17.7 m (half the range, by symmetry), y ≈ 5.1 m, with a flat tangent exactly there, then descends as a mirror image back to y = 0 at x ≈ 35.3 m.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges test projectile plots to see whether a student truly separates the two motions or is pattern-matching a parabola formula. A sharp probe: point to the apex on the graph and ask what is true and false there. A student who knows the decomposition says vertical velocity is zero (flat tangent) but horizontal velocity, hence speed, is not zero, so the projectile is still moving fast at the peak, just not moving up or down that instant. Another probe is symmetry: change the launch and landing heights so they differ, and ask a student to sketch the (now asymmetric) curve, testing whether they understand symmetry is a consequence of matched launch/landing height, not a universal law of projectiles.

questions.prompt: At the apex of a projectile's y-vs-x trajectory plot (level launch and landing), which statement is correct?

options.text: Both horizontal and vertical velocity are zero
Vertical velocity is zero, but horizontal velocity is not, so speed is nonzero
Horizontal velocity is zero, but vertical velocity is not
Acceleration is zero at the apex

explanations.a: If both were zero the projectile would stop mid-air; horizontal velocity is constant throughout flight and does not vanish at the apex.
explanations.b: Correct: the apex is defined by v_y = 0 (the moment vertical motion reverses), while v_x stays at its constant launched value, so the object is still moving horizontally at full speed.
explanations.c: Horizontal velocity is constant the entire flight because there is no horizontal force (ignoring air resistance); it never reaches zero mid-flight.
explanations.d: Gravity acts throughout the entire flight, including exactly at the apex, giving a constant downward acceleration of g at every instant, not zero.

questions.prompt: Why does a projectile's y-vs-x plot come out as a parabola rather than some other curve?

options.text: Because gravity pulls diagonally on the projectile
Because x is linear in time while y is quadratic in time, and substituting t(x) makes y quadratic in x
Because air resistance curves the path symmetrically
Because horizontal and vertical velocities are always equal

explanations.a: Gravity acts straight down (vertically) on a projectile near Earth's surface; it does not pull diagonally.
explanations.b: Correct: x = v_x t is linear, so t = x/v_x; substituting into y = y_0 + v_y0 t - (1/2)g t^2 produces a quadratic (parabolic) relationship between y and x.
explanations.c: This unit's analysis explicitly ignores air resistance; the parabola arises from gravity and kinematics alone, and air resistance, if included, actually distorts the path away from a true parabola.
explanations.d: Horizontal and vertical velocities are generally different and change differently over time (horizontal constant, vertical changing); they are not required to be equal.

questions.prompt: Order these events in a level-launch, level-landing projectile's flight, from launch to landing.

items.text: Launch: vertical velocity is at its maximum upward value
Vertical velocity decreases toward zero as the projectile rises
Apex: vertical velocity is exactly zero, tangent to the path is flat
Vertical velocity becomes increasingly negative as the projectile falls, landing at the same speed magnitude as launch

questions.explanation: The projectile starts with its greatest upward vertical velocity, that velocity shrinks under gravity's constant deceleration until it hits zero at the apex, and then it grows in magnitude in the downward direction symmetrically until landing.

questions.prompt: Match each projectile-motion feature to its correct description.

right.text: Constant velocity, no horizontal acceleration
Uniformly accelerated by gravity, g downward
Vertical velocity is zero; tangent to the curve is flat
Rise time equals fall time; launch and landing speeds and angle magnitudes match

questions.explanation: Horizontal motion is unaccelerated and constant-velocity; vertical motion is uniformly accelerated by gravity; the apex is where vertical velocity crosses zero, giving a flat tangent; and equal launch/landing heights produce a trajectory symmetric in time, speed, and angle about the apex.

lessons.label: Force vs Displacement Curves

sections.heading: Area under F-x is work
sections.body: Work done by a force as an object moves is defined as W = ∫F dx along the path, so on a force-versus-displacement (F-x) graph, the area between the force curve and the displacement axis equals the work done by that force over that interval. This mirrors the v-t area rule from earlier motion graphs: whenever one quantity is the integral (accumulated sum) of another with respect to a variable, its value equals the area under that other quantity's graph against that variable. For a constant force, the F-x graph is a horizontal line, and the "area" is simply a rectangle, recovering the familiar W = F × d formula as a special case of the more general area rule.

sections.heading: The spring's triangular area
sections.body: An ideal spring obeys Hooke's Law, F = -kx for the restoring force, or F = kx for the magnitude of the applied force needed to stretch or compress it a distance x from equilibrium, where k is the spring constant (units N/m). Plotted as applied force versus displacement, this is a straight line through the origin with slope k, so the region under the line from 0 to some displacement x is a triangle with base x and height kx. The area of that triangle, (1/2) × base × height = (1/2)(x)(kx) = (1/2)kx^2, is exactly the work done stretching or compressing the spring that distance, which is also the elastic potential energy stored in it. Robert Hooke published this linear force-extension relationship in 1676 (as an anagram he later revealed as "ut tensio, sic vis" — as the extension, so the force), and it remains the standard first-order model for elastic materials within their linear range.

sections.heading: Reading work from an arbitrary, variable force
sections.body: Real forces are frequently not constant and not linear, so their F-x graphs can be irregular curves. The general method for extracting work stays the same: partition the graph into small enough strips that each looks locally like a rectangle or trapezoid, sum the signed areas of each strip (negative where force opposes the direction of displacement), and the total is the net work. This is precisely how a numerical integration (like the trapezoidal rule) approximates the exact integral, and it is why F-x plots from real experimental data (a rubber band's nonlinear stretch, a variable-thrust rocket engine's force curve) can still yield an accurate work value even without a closed-form force equation.

lessons.workedExample: A student stretches a spring with k = 40 N/m from x=0 to x=0.15 m. The F-x graph is a straight line from (0,0) to (0.15, 6) since F = kx = 40(0.15) = 6 N at full stretch. The area under this line is a triangle: (1/2)(0.15)(6) = 0.45 J, matching the formula (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)(40)(0.15)^2 = 0.45 J. If she then attaches a nonlinear rubber band whose F-x graph curves upward more steeply past x=0.1 m (stiffening), she cannot use the triangle formula; instead she divides the graph into narrow vertical strips, estimates each strip's average height, sums the strip areas, and that sum, larger than the equivalent spring's 0.45 J because the rubber band demands more force per additional stretch, gives the actual work done.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe F-x graphs to check whether students understand work as an area (a general geometric/calculus idea) rather than having memorized only the constant-force formula W = Fd. A telling question: given a curved, non-triangular F-x plot, can the student describe how to estimate the work without an equation, i.e., by partitioning into strips and summing areas? Another common probe swaps in a spring and asks why the work is (1/2)kx^2 rather than kx^2 (the full rectangle) — testing whether the student recognizes the triangular, not rectangular, shape of a linear force-extension relationship, since force grows only up to its final value, not throughout the whole motion.

questions.prompt: On a force-displacement graph, the work done by the force over an interval is given by:

options.text: The value of the force at the end of the interval
The slope of the force curve
The area between the curve and the displacement axis
The average of the force values at each end of the interval, without regard to shape

explanations.a: The endpoint force value alone ignores everything that happened over the rest of the interval; work depends on the whole accumulated area, not one instant.
explanations.b: Slope of the F-x curve is a rate of change of force with distance, not directly meaningful as work; area, not slope, corresponds to the integral that defines work.
explanations.c: Correct: work is defined as the integral of force with respect to displacement, W = ∫F dx, which is exactly the area under the F-x curve.
explanations.d: Simple averaging of endpoints only gives the correct area for a straight-line (linear) force curve; for a genuinely curved F-x relationship it would misstate the true area/work.

questions.prompt: A spring with spring constant k is stretched from 0 to displacement x. Why is the work done (1/2)kx^2 and not kx^2 (the full rectangle of height kx and width x)?

options.text: Because the spring only stores half of the work as potential energy
Because the applied force grows linearly from 0 up to kx, so the region under the line is a triangle, half the rectangle's area
Because friction removes half the energy
Because kx^2 is only correct for compression, not stretching

explanations.a: For an ideal (lossless) spring, all the work done goes into stored elastic potential energy; the factor of 1/2 comes from geometry, not from energy being lost or split.
explanations.b: Correct: since F = kx starts at 0 and increases linearly to kx as displacement goes from 0 to x, the F-x graph is a triangle, and a triangle's area is half the corresponding rectangle's area, giving (1/2)kx^2.
explanations.c: This scenario describes an ideal spring with no friction mentioned; the 1/2 factor is a purely geometric consequence of the linear force-extension relationship, not a loss term.
explanations.d: Hooke's Law and its (1/2)kx^2 energy result apply symmetrically to both stretching and compression of an ideal spring within its linear range.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding the work done by a variable (non-constant, non-linear) force from its F-x graph.

items.text: Partition the displacement axis into narrow strips
Approximate the force as roughly constant (or use a trapezoid) within each narrow strip
Compute the signed area of each strip, negative if force opposes displacement
Sum all strip areas to approximate the total work

questions.explanation: Numerical integration of an irregular F-x curve works by slicing the axis into small strips, treating the force as locally simple (constant or linear) within each strip, computing each strip's signed area, and adding them all to approximate the total work integral.

questions.prompt: Match each force-displacement scenario to the shape of its F-x graph and the resulting work formula.

left.text: Constant force F over distance d
Ideal spring stretched from 0 to x (F = kx)

right.text: Rectangle; work = F × d
Triangle through the origin; work = (1/2)kx^2
Irregular shape; work found by numerically summing strip areas

questions.explanation: A constant force gives a flat horizontal F-x line, a rectangle whose area is F×d; an ideal spring's linear F=kx relationship gives a triangle with area (1/2)kx^2; and a genuinely irregular force curve requires numerically summing many small strip areas to estimate the work.

lessons.label: Energy-Exchange Curves

sections.heading: KE and PE trading off along a track
sections.body: Plot kinetic energy (KE) and potential energy (PE) against position for an object moving along a track (a roller coaster, a pendulum, a ball rolling in a bowl), and in the absence of friction or air resistance you see the two curves as mirror images of each other: wherever PE is high, KE is low, and vice versa, because energy is converting from one form to the other, not being created or destroyed. As the object descends, gravitational PE (= mgh, with h measured from a reference level) converts into KE (= (1/2)mv^2); as it climbs, KE converts back into PE. The two curves cross where KE = PE, and each curve's individual shape traces out the mgh and (1/2)mv^2 values at every position along the path.

sections.heading: The flat total-energy line, or the sloping one
sections.body: If you plot total mechanical energy (KE + PE) against position for an ideal, frictionless system, you get a perfectly flat horizontal line: this is the graphical statement of conservation of mechanical energy, whose rigorous mathematical treatment traces back to Daniel Bernoulli's work on vis viva in Hydrodynamica (1738) and Lagrange's systematic formulation in Mécanique analytique (1788), with Gustave Coriolis formalizing the modern definitions of work and kinetic energy in 1829, and William Rankine coining the terms "potential energy" (1853) and "the conservation of energy" (1850) shortly after. Any energy that leaves the KE+PE ledger in a real system, most commonly to friction, air resistance, or sound and heat, is called dissipation, and it shows up on the graph as a total-energy line that slopes downward over position or time rather than staying flat. The steeper that downward slope, the faster energy is being dissipated (analogous to how the slope of a v-t graph reveals acceleration): a shallow, nearly flat decline suggests a system close to ideal (like a well-designed pendulum in air), while a steep decline flags substantial energy loss (like a block sliding to a stop on a rough floor).

sections.heading: Finding maximum speed from the KE curve
sections.body: Because KE = (1/2)mv^2 is a strictly increasing function of speed for a fixed mass, the position where the KE curve reaches its peak is exactly the position of maximum speed along the path, with no need to separately compute or plot velocity. On a pendulum's energy-vs-angle plot, KE peaks (and PE bottoms out) at the lowest point of the swing, the equilibrium position, which is indeed where a pendulum bob moves fastest. This lets you read off "where is it going fastest" directly from an energy diagram, a genuinely useful shortcut, without ever writing down a velocity equation.

lessons.workedExample: A 2 kg cart on a frictionless track starts at rest at height 5 m (PE = mgh = 2(9.8)(5) = 98 J, KE = 0, total = 98 J). Partway down, at height 2 m, PE = 2(9.8)(2) = 39.2 J, so by conservation KE = 98 - 39.2 = 58.8 J, giving v = sqrt(2×58.8/2) = sqrt(58.8) ≈ 7.67 m/s. At the bottom (h=0), PE = 0 and KE = 98 J, its maximum, so the cart is moving fastest there: v = sqrt(2×98/2) = sqrt(98) ≈ 9.9 m/s. Plotted against position, the PE and KE curves cross where each equals 49 J (at h=2.5 m), and the flat 98 J total-energy line confirms no energy was lost, consistent with the frictionless assumption.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use energy-exchange graphs to test whether a student treats conservation of energy as a bookkeeping tool they can read visually, not just an equation to plug into. A sharp probe: given a total-energy line that slopes downward, ask what physically must be happening and where the slope is steepest. A strong answer identifies dissipation (friction, drag) and reads the steepest decline as the region of fastest energy loss, perhaps where a rough patch or greatest speed against air resistance occurs. A second common probe asks students to locate maximum speed purely from a KE-vs-position curve, testing whether they understand that KE's peak IS the speed's peak, without needing to derive velocity separately.

questions.prompt: On a frictionless track, a plot of total mechanical energy (KE + PE) versus position should look like:

options.text: A curve mirroring the KE curve
A flat horizontal line
A line sloping steadily downward
A curve identical to the PE curve

explanations.a: The KE curve itself rises and falls as the object speeds up and slows down; total energy does not mirror KE, it stays constant while KE and PE individually vary.
explanations.b: Correct: with no friction or drag, mechanical energy is conserved, so KE + PE sums to the same constant value at every position, a flat line.
explanations.c: A downward-sloping total-energy line indicates dissipation (friction, drag), which contradicts the frictionless assumption given in the question.
explanations.d: PE alone changes with height and generally is not constant along the track, so a flat total-energy line cannot be identical to the (non-constant) PE curve.

questions.prompt: On a KE-vs-position graph for an object moving along a track, the position of maximum speed corresponds to:

options.text: Wherever PE is at its own local peak
Wherever the KE curve reaches its highest value
Wherever the total-energy line is steepest
It cannot be determined from a KE curve alone

explanations.a: A PE peak is where the object is highest and (in a conservative system) moving slowest, the opposite of where speed is maximal.
explanations.b: Correct: since KE = (1/2)mv^2 increases monotonically with speed, the KE curve's maximum value corresponds exactly to the position of maximum speed.
explanations.c: Steepness of the total-energy line indicates the rate of energy dissipation, not the object's speed at that point; a flat total-energy line has no meaningful slope to reference at all in an ideal system.
explanations.d: It can be determined directly: because KE is a monotonic function of speed, the KE curve's own peak is sufficient to identify the location of maximum speed.

questions.prompt: A pendulum released from the side swings down and back up its arc. Order these positions from lowest KE to highest KE.

items.text: Release point (maximum height, momentarily at rest)
Partway down the swing, still above the lowest point
The very bottom of the swing (equilibrium position)

questions.explanation: KE is zero at the release point (all energy is PE there), grows as the pendulum descends and PE converts to KE, and reaches its maximum at the bottom of the swing where all the initial PE has become KE.

questions.prompt: Match each energy-graph feature to what it indicates.

left.text: Point where KE and PE curves cross

right.text: Conservative system; mechanical energy is conserved
Dissipative system losing energy to friction or drag
Position of maximum speed
Position where KE equals PE

questions.explanation: A flat total-energy line signals no energy loss (conservative system); a downward slope signals dissipation; the KE curve's peak marks the fastest point; and wherever the KE and PE curves intersect, by definition, KE equals PE at that position.

lessons.label: Oscillation Traces and Phase Portraits

sections.heading: Amplitude, period, and the decay envelope
sections.body: A displacement-versus-time trace of an oscillator (a mass on a spring, a pendulum, a plucked string) directly displays amplitude, the maximum displacement from equilibrium, as the height of each peak, and period, the time for one complete cycle, as the horizontal spacing between successive peaks (or successive same-phase points). For ideal, undamped simple harmonic motion (SHM), the trace is a clean sine or cosine wave with constant amplitude and constant period forever. Real oscillators lose energy to friction, air resistance, or internal damping, so their amplitude shrinks cycle by cycle; that shrinking is visualized by an envelope, typically a smooth exponential decay curve (Ae^{-γt}), drawn tangent to each peak, that bounds the oscillation from above and below. The period itself stays nearly constant for light damping, while the amplitude envelope collapses toward zero, which is why a plucked guitar string's trace shows evenly-spaced peaks of steadily shrinking height rather than peaks that spread further apart.

sections.heading: The phase portrait: velocity versus position
sections.body: A phase portrait plots an oscillator's velocity against its position (rather than either quantity against time), and for ideal SHM this traces out a closed ellipse (a circle, if velocity and position are scaled to matching units): the system returns to exactly the same (x, v) state every period, so the same closed loop is retraced forever. This works because SHM's total mechanical energy, (1/2)kx^2 + (1/2)mv^2, is conserved and constant, and the equation for a constant sum of an x^2 term and a v^2 term is exactly the equation of an ellipse in the x-v plane. The size of the ellipse encodes the amplitude and total energy: a larger ellipse means a larger-amplitude, higher-energy oscillation.

sections.heading: What a phase plot reveals that a time trace hides
sections.body: A displacement-time trace shows you the history of position and, indirectly, the shrinking envelope of a damped system, but a phase portrait shows the state-space behavior directly: for a damped oscillator, instead of retracing the same closed ellipse, the trajectory spirals slowly inward toward the origin (v=0, x=0, the state of rest), and the tightness of that inward spiral visually communicates the damping rate in a single unified picture, without needing to separately read amplitude decay against a time axis. A phase portrait also instantly reveals things a time trace makes hard to see at a glance, such as whether the system is losing energy steadily (a smooth spiral) or in sudden jumps (a spiral with abrupt kinks), and it generalizes to more complex or chaotic systems where a simple time trace becomes visually unreadable, and the phase-space trajectory (even if intricate, as with a chaotic strange attractor) still reveals structure that a time trace hides.

lessons.workedExample: A mass-spring system with amplitude 0.2 m and light damping is released from rest at x=0.2 m. Its displacement-time trace shows peaks at 0.2 m, then roughly 0.17 m, then 0.145 m one period later, each successive peak about 85% of the previous one, tracing a decaying exponential envelope with period staying close to 1.2 s throughout. Its phase portrait (v vs x) starts at the point (0.2, 0) on the horizontal axis (maximum displacement, zero velocity) and spirals clockwise and inward: each loop is slightly smaller than the last, matching the same 85%-per-cycle shrinkage seen in the time trace, until the trajectory converges toward the origin as the oscillation dies out.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges reach for phase portraits specifically because they separate students who have only memorized "SHM looks like a sine wave" from students who understand oscillation as a dynamical system with a state (position and velocity together). A revealing probe: show an undamped phase portrait (a closed ellipse) beside a lightly damped one (an inward spiral) and ask what physical difference distinguishes them. A strong answer names energy loss over each cycle, connects the tightening spiral to a shrinking-amplitude envelope on the corresponding time trace, and can explain why the closed ellipse in the ideal case reflects constant total energy, (1/2)kx^2 + (1/2)mv^2, being conserved.

questions.prompt: On a displacement-time trace of a lightly damped oscillator, the amplitude envelope is typically:

options.text: A straight line decreasing linearly
A smooth exponential decay curve bounding the peaks
Constant, matching an undamped oscillator
A curve that increases over time

explanations.a: Damping in most simple mechanical oscillators (viscous/light damping) produces an exponential, not linear, decay in amplitude over successive cycles.
explanations.b: Correct: light damping typically yields amplitude that decays as Ae^{-γt}, an exponential curve, tangent to each successive peak of the oscillation.
explanations.c: A constant-amplitude trace describes an undamped, ideal oscillator; a damped one loses amplitude cycle by cycle, so its envelope is not constant.
explanations.d: Damping removes energy from the system over time, so amplitude shrinks, not grows; an increasing envelope would indicate energy being added, not damping.

questions.prompt: In a phase portrait (velocity vs. position) of an ideal, undamped simple harmonic oscillator, the trajectory is:

options.text: A straight line through the origin
A spiral converging to the origin
A closed ellipse retraced every period
A single point at the origin

explanations.a: A straight line would mean velocity and position are always proportional, which is not how SHM behaves; velocity and position are 90 degrees out of phase in SHM, producing a curve, not a line.
explanations.b: A spiral converging to the origin describes a damped oscillator losing energy over time, not an ideal, undamped one that conserves energy.
explanations.c: Correct: because total energy (1/2)kx^2 + (1/2)mv^2 is exactly conserved in ideal SHM, the (x, v) state traces a fixed-size ellipse, retraced identically every period.
explanations.d: A single point would mean the system is permanently at rest with no motion at all, not an oscillating system.

questions.prompt: Order these oscillator behaviors from most energy retained to least energy retained, based on their phase-portrait signature.

items.text: Undamped SHM: closed ellipse retraced forever
Lightly damped: slow inward spiral over many cycles
Heavily damped: rapid inward spiral collapsing in a few cycles
Fully at rest: trajectory has converged to the origin

questions.explanation: An undamped system never loses energy (constant ellipse); light damping loses energy slowly (a gently tightening spiral); heavy damping loses energy quickly (a rapidly tightening spiral); and once the trajectory reaches the origin, all mechanical energy is gone and the system is at rest.

questions.prompt: Match each displacement-time trace feature to what it reveals.

left.text: An exponential curve bounding the peaks

right.text: Gives the period
Reveals the damping rate

questions.explanation: On a displacement-time trace, the horizontal spacing between successive peaks gives the period, while an exponential curve bounding the peaks reveals the damping rate.

questions.prompt: Match each phase portrait feature to what it reveals.

left.text: The size of a closed loop
How tightly a trajectory spirals inward

right.text: Reveals the oscillation's total energy
Reveals the damping rate

questions.explanation: On a phase portrait (velocity vs. position), the size of a closed loop reveals the oscillation's total energy, while how tightly the trajectory spirals inward reveals the damping rate.

lessons.label: Galileo, Inclined Planes, and Falling Bodies

sections.heading: Diluting gravity to make it measurable
sections.body: Aristotle had claimed for two thousand years that heavier objects fall faster, in direct proportion to their weight. Galileo challenged this with a thought experiment before he ever ran a formal test: tie a heavy stone and a light stone together. By Aristotle's rule the combined body should fall faster than the heavy stone alone, since it is now heavier, but the slow light stone should also drag on the fast heavy one and slow it down. The rule contradicts itself, and Galileo concluded both stones must fall at the same rate. The problem was proving it. Free fall from a reasonable height took under a second, far too fast for the era's water clocks and pulse-counting to time precisely. Galileo's fix was to dilute gravity rather than fight the clock: he rolled bronze balls down long, smooth, grooved wooden ramps tilted at a shallow angle. A gentler slope meant a slower, more measurable version of the same uniformly accelerated motion that governs a vertical drop, just stretched out in time.

sections.heading: The odd-number rule and distance proportional to t squared
sections.body: Using a water clock, timing by weighing the water that drained through a narrow spout, Galileo marked how far the ball had traveled at the end of each equal time interval. The distances covered in successive equal intervals came out in the ratio 1:3:5:7:9, the sequence of odd numbers. That pattern is the fingerprint of uniformly accelerated motion: if total distance from rest grows as d = (1/2)at^2, then the distance covered in interval n alone is proportional to n^2 - (n-1)^2 = 2n-1, exactly the odd numbers. Galileo reported repeating the trial roughly a hundred times at different ramp angles and ball weights, always recovering the same ratio, which is why Two New Sciences treats this as an empirical law rather than a one-off demonstration.

sections.heading: The Leaning Tower story versus the real evidence
sections.body: The image most people associate with Galileo, dropping two different-mass balls off the Leaning Tower of Pisa to show they land together, is almost certainly legend. The only source for it is a biography written decades later by his secretary and first biographer, Vincenzo Viviani; Galileo's own writings never mention it. The real case against Aristotle is the far less cinematic inclined-plane data published in Two New Sciences (1638), Galileo's last book, written and smuggled out of Italy while he was under Inquisition-ordered house arrest for defending a heliocentric universe. It is methodical, quantitative, and repeatable, the actual birth of experimental physics, while the tower drop, whether or not it happened, was never Galileo's own evidence for his law.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a ball rolls from rest down a ramp and travels 5 cm during the first equal time interval. If motion is uniformly accelerated, total distance after n intervals is d = 5n^2 cm, so after 1, 2, 3, and 4 intervals the ball has gone 5, 20, 45, and 80 cm. The distance covered in each interval alone is the difference between consecutive totals: 5, 15, 25, and 35 cm, a ratio of 1:3:5:7, exactly Galileo's odd-number rule. A student replicating this with a track, a marble, and a slow-motion camera can reproduce Galileo's result in minutes; the historical achievement was doing it with a water clock and getting the ratio right by hand, without calculus, decades before Newton formalized acceleration.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about Galileo because it is the cleanest case study in experimental design: he could not test the law he wanted directly, so he engineered a slowed-down version he could measure, then reasoned back to the real case. A student who explains WHY the ramps were used, to slow motion within timing precision rather than because the law was different on a slope, shows real methodological understanding.
