questions.prompt: Order the steps of the T-squared-vs-L pendulum lab for measuring g.

items.text: Measure the period T at several distinctly different lengths L, each period averaged over many swings
Compute T^2 for each length
Plot T^2 (vertical axis) against L (horizontal axis) and fit a straight line
Compute g = 4*pi^2 divided by the fitted slope

questions.explanation: Raw (L, T) data must be collected first; only then can T be squared for each length; those T^2 values are what get plotted and fitted to a line, whose slope is finally converted into g.

questions.prompt: Match each lab practice to the specific error it protects against.

left.text: Timing 20 swings and dividing, instead of timing one
Using several different lengths and fitting a line, instead of one (L, T) pair
Measuring L from the pivot to the bob's CENTER of mass, not to the top of the bob

right.text: Random error from human reaction-time in starting and stopping a stopwatch
A single unlucky measurement dominating the whole estimate
A systematic (consistent) error in the independent variable itself

questions.explanation: Averaging over many swings dilutes random reaction-time error; fitting across several distinct lengths prevents any one scattered data point from dominating the slope; measuring L to the bob's actual center of mass (not its top or edge) avoids a consistent, repeated error baked into every length value.

lessons.label: The Physical (Compound) Pendulum

sections.heading: When the point-mass idealization breaks down
sections.body: A meter stick pivoted at one end, a swinging door, or a person on a playground swing all violate the simple pendulum's core assumption: their mass is spread out over a size comparable to the distance to the pivot, not concentrated at one point. These are physical pendulums (also called compound pendulums), rigid bodies free to rotate about a fixed axis that does not pass through their center of mass, oscillating under gravity. The point-mass formula T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) simply does not apply to them, because it was derived assuming all the restoring torque and all the rotational inertia live at a single distance L from the pivot.

sections.heading: The physical pendulum period formula
sections.body: For a rigid body pivoted at point O, gravity acting at the center of mass (a distance d from the pivot) creates a restoring torque tau = -mgd*sin(theta) about the pivot, which for small theta becomes tau approximately equals -mgd*theta. The rotational analog of Newton's second law, tau = I*alpha (with alpha = d^2(theta)/dt^2), gives I*d^2(theta)/dt^2 = -mgd*theta, where I is the body's moment of inertia about the pivot axis (not about its center of mass). This is again the SHM equation, with angular frequency omega = sqrt(mgd/I) and period T = 2*pi*sqrt(I/(mgd)). Both I and d depend on the specific shape and pivot point of the object, so unlike the simple pendulum, there is no single "length" built into the formula until one is defined.

sections.heading: The equivalent simple-pendulum length
sections.body: Defining L_eq = I/(m*d) lets the physical pendulum's period be written in the exact same form as the simple pendulum's: T = 2*pi*sqrt(L_eq/g). Physically, L_eq is the length a point-mass simple pendulum would need in order to swing with the identical period as the real, extended object. This is precisely what a grandfather clock's adjustable bob is for: sliding the bob along the pendulum rod changes both I and d together, retuning L_eq (and therefore the clock's period) without needing to change the rod's physical length at all.

lessons.workedExample: A uniform rod of length 1.00 m and mass 0.50 kg is pivoted at one end. Its moment of inertia about that end is I = (1/3)*m*L^2 = (1/3)(0.50)(1.00)^2 = 0.1667 kg*m^2, and its center of mass sits at d = L/2 = 0.50 m from the pivot. The period is T = 2*pi*sqrt(I/(mgd)) = 2*pi*sqrt(0.1667/(0.50*9.81*0.50)) = 2*pi*sqrt(0.1667/2.4525) = 2*pi*sqrt(0.06796) = 2*pi*(0.2607) = 1.64 s. A simple pendulum of the same 1.00 m overall length would instead have T = 2*pi*sqrt(1.00/9.81) = 2.01 s, about 22-23% longer than the rod's period, because most of the rod's mass sits closer to the pivot than a point bob at the very tip would, giving the rod less rotational inertia per unit of restoring torque.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the physical pendulum to see whether a student can identify WHEN the simple pendulum formula stops applying, not just recite the physical pendulum formula on demand. A strong answer names the two ingredients, moment of inertia about the actual pivot and the pivot-to-center-of-mass distance, and explains that L_eq is the length of an equivalent point-mass pendulum rather than any length that literally exists on the object. Any student building a device with an extended swinging arm (a robot limb, a trebuchet arm) should expect this question the moment they claim a period without justifying which model they used.

questions.prompt: Which formula gives the small-angle period of a physical (compound) pendulum?

options.text: T = 2*pi*sqrt(I/(mgd)), where I is the moment of inertia about the pivot and d is the pivot-to-center-of-mass distance
T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g), using the object's total physical length as L
T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/(gd))

explanations.a: Correct: this follows from tau = I*alpha applied to the restoring torque -mgd*theta, giving angular frequency omega = sqrt(mgd/I) and period T = 2*pi*sqrt(I/(mgd)).
explanations.b: The simple pendulum formula assumes a point mass; using an extended object's overall physical length in it ignores how the object's mass is actually distributed and generally gives the wrong period.
explanations.c: This omits the moment of inertia I entirely and has the wrong quantity, m, in the wrong place; it is not derivable from tau = I*alpha.

questions.prompt: What does the "equivalent simple-pendulum length" L_eq = I/(m*d) physically represent?

options.text: The length a point-mass simple pendulum would need to swing with the same period as the real object
The literal distance from the pivot to the far end of the object
The distance from the pivot to the object's center of mass

explanations.a: Correct: substituting L_eq into T = 2*pi*sqrt(L_eq/g) reproduces the physical pendulum's actual period, so L_eq is defined as exactly the point-mass pendulum length that matches it.
explanations.b: L_eq is generally different from the object's overall physical dimensions; for the uniform rod example, L_eq = (2/3)*L, shorter than the rod's actual length.
explanations.c: That distance is d, a separate quantity that appears inside the formula for L_eq but is not itself L_eq.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that derive the physical pendulum's period.

items.text: Write the restoring torque about the pivot, tau = -mgd*sin(theta)
Apply the small-angle approximation, tau approximately equals -mgd*theta
Apply the rotational form of Newton's second law, tau = I*d^2(theta)/dt^2
Identify omega^2 = mgd/I and write T = 2*pi*sqrt(I/(mgd))

questions.explanation: The exact torque must be written first, then linearized for small angles, before it can be substituted into the rotational equation of motion, from which the angular frequency and period are finally read off.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity in the physical pendulum formula T = 2*pi*sqrt(I/(mgd)) to its physical role.

right.text: Moment of inertia of the object about the actual pivot axis
Distance from the pivot to the object's center of mass
Length of the point-mass simple pendulum with the identical period

questions.explanation: I captures how the object's mass is rotationally distributed about the pivot, d is simply how far the center of mass sits from that pivot, and combining them as L_eq = I/(m*d) yields the length of an equivalent point-mass pendulum with the same period.

lessons.label: Large-Amplitude Pendulums and Anharmonicity

sections.heading: The period is not actually constant
sections.body: Beyond a few tens of degrees, a real pendulum's period grows measurably beyond the small-angle prediction T0 = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g). A pendulum released from 90 degrees has a genuinely, measurably longer period than an identical pendulum (same L, same g) released from 5 degrees. This directly breaks the clean isochronism celebrated in Lesson 3: "the period does not depend on amplitude" turns out to be strictly a small-angle statement, not a universal fact about pendulums, and the underlying motion at large amplitude is no longer simple harmonic at all, since it is no longer described by a single sine or cosine function of time.

sections.heading: How much longer, and why
sections.body: Lesson 2 introduced Bernoulli's first-order correction, T approximately equals T0*(1 + theta_max^2/16), which is accurate for modest amplitudes and grows slowly at first (a quadratic dependence on amplitude), matching the roughly 1% figure near 23 degrees. But the true growth accelerates well beyond what this first term alone captures: at theta_max = 45 degrees the period is about 4% longer than T0, and at theta_max = 90 degrees it is about 18% longer. The physical reason is that near the extreme turning points of a wide swing, the restoring torque (proportional to sin(theta)) grows much more slowly than theta itself does, so the pendulum's angular acceleration weakens there and it lingers near the top of each swing, while it still rushes quickly through the bottom; that extra lingering time at the extremes is what stretches out the period.

sections.heading: The exact answer needs elliptic integrals
sections.body: Integrating the full nonlinear equation of motion exactly gives T = 4*sqrt(L/g) * K(sin(theta_max/2)), where K is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, a function with no elementary closed form, historically evaluated from numerical tables and today computed by software. Bernoulli's correction formula from Lesson 2 is simply the leading terms of a Taylor expansion of this exact K-function result for small theta_max. No student is expected to evaluate an elliptic integral by hand; the point to take away is qualitative but important: pushed to large amplitude, the pendulum problem leaves the tidy world of simple harmonic motion altogether and becomes a genuinely different, still fully deterministic and still periodic, kind of motion.

lessons.workedExample: A pendulum of length L = 1.00 m is released from 90 degrees instead of a small angle. The small-angle prediction is T0 = 2*pi*sqrt(1.00/9.81) = 2.006 s. Using the known result that T/T0 approximately equals 1.18 at this amplitude (from the exact elliptic-integral formula), the actual period is close to T = 2.006*1.18 = 2.37 s, about 0.36 s (18%) longer than the small-angle prediction. A student who assumed simple harmonic motion held at 90 degrees and used T0 directly would mistime this swing by more than a third of a second on every single cycle.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up large-amplitude pendulums when a project's demonstration involves a wide swing (a wrecking-ball-style release-from-the-nose safety demo, a swing set, a trebuchet arm), asking directly whether the period changes with how far the pendulum swings. A strong answer states clearly that it does, that the period GROWS with amplitude once small-angle conditions are left behind, and can name the physical reason (weaker restoring torque relative to displacement near the turning points). An answer that insists isochronism holds at any amplitude reveals the small-angle caveat from Lesson 2 was never really understood, only memorized as an unconditional rule.

questions.prompt: As release amplitude grows well beyond the small-angle regime, the actual pendulum period compared to T0 = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g):

options.text: Grows steadily longer
Shrinks steadily shorter
Stays exactly equal to T0 at any amplitude

explanations.a: Correct: both the first-order Bernoulli correction and the exact elliptic-integral result show the period growing with amplitude, reaching about 18% longer than T0 at a 90-degree release angle.
explanations.b: The correction term is always positive; no standard pendulum treatment predicts a period shorter than the small-angle value.
explanations.c: Exact equality to T0 at any amplitude (perfect isochronism) is only true in the idealized small-angle limit, not at large amplitude.

questions.prompt: What mathematical function gives the pendulum's EXACT period at any amplitude, without the small-angle approximation?

options.text: The complete elliptic integral of the first kind
A Bessel function
A Legendre polynomial

explanations.a: Correct: T = 4*sqrt(L/g)*K(sin(theta_max/2)), where K is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, gives the exact period at any amplitude, with the Bernoulli series as its small-amplitude Taylor expansion.
explanations.b: Bessel functions solve a different class of problems (such as radially symmetric wave equations); they are not the function that appears in the exact pendulum period.
explanations.c: Legendre polynomials appear in other physics contexts, such as multipole expansions, but are not the function governing the exact large-amplitude pendulum period.

questions.prompt: Physically, WHY does the pendulum's period grow at large amplitude?

options.text: Near the extreme turning points, the restoring torque grows more slowly than the angle itself, so the pendulum lingers there longer
Gravity becomes measurably weaker as the bob swings farther from vertical
Air resistance dominates the motion at large swing angles

explanations.a: Correct: sin(theta) grows more slowly than theta as theta increases, so the restoring torque (and hence angular acceleration) weakens near a wide swing's extremes, extending the time spent there.
explanations.b: Gravitational acceleration g is treated as constant regardless of the pendulum's swing angle; it does not change with theta in this analysis.
explanations.c: This lesson's large-amplitude correction is a purely conservative, frictionless-pivot result; air resistance is a separate effect covered in Lesson 7 and is not the cause of this particular period growth.

questions.prompt: Order these release amplitudes by increasing period elongation relative to T0 = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g).

items.text: 5 degrees (negligible elongation)
23 degrees (about 1% elongation)
45 degrees (about 4% elongation)
90 degrees (about 18% elongation)

questions.explanation: Period elongation grows with amplitude and accelerates faster than the simple theta_max^2/16 estimate at larger angles, moving from negligible at 5 degrees, to about 1% at 23 degrees, about 4% at 45 degrees, and about 18% at a full 90-degree release.

lessons.label: Damping in Real Pendulums

sections.heading: Where the energy goes
sections.body: Every real pendulum loses mechanical energy over time through two dominant channels. Air (or other fluid) drag acts on the moving bob and string, opposing velocity and converting kinetic energy into heat in the surrounding air. Pivot friction, whether from a bearing, a knife-edge support, or a string that flexes slightly with each swing, dissipates energy at the support itself. Both mechanisms steadily drain the pendulum's total mechanical energy (kinetic plus gravitational potential), which is why an undriven real pendulum always eventually comes to rest, unlike the idealized, frictionless simple pendulum of Lesson 1.

sections.heading: How the amplitude shrinks
sections.body: For light damping, the standard model is an exponentially decaying envelope, theta(t) approximately equals theta0*e^(-t/tau)*cos(omega*t + phi), where tau sets the timescale of the decay. A hallmark of this light-damping regime is that consecutive amplitude peaks shrink by roughly the same FRACTION swing after swing, not by a fixed number of degrees; a 1% loss per swing at large amplitude is roughly a 1% loss per swing at small amplitude too, at least until damping becomes strong enough that the exponential model itself breaks down. Because both kinetic and potential energy scale with amplitude squared, the pendulum's total mechanical ENERGY decays twice as fast (in the exponent) as its amplitude envelope does.

sections.heading: Timing strategy: measure before drag wins
sections.body: Because a real pendulum's amplitude is always quietly shrinking, and Lesson 6 showed that period itself depends on amplitude once swings are not small, careful experimenters make two deliberate choices. First, they start with a genuinely small amplitude (well under the roughly 15-degree range where the amplitude-period coupling from Lesson 6 is negligible), so gradual decay barely perturbs the period even as it continues. Second, they time many consecutive periods starting immediately after release, while the amplitude is still closest to its known initial value, and average those periods together, rather than letting the pendulum run for a long time and averaging periods measured deep into the decay, when the true amplitude (and, at borderline angles, the true period) has already drifted from what was assumed. Both choices protect the same idealization, that the measurement matches an undamped, small-angle pendulum, from a slow, real-world imperfection that would otherwise sneak into the result unnoticed.

lessons.workedExample: A pendulum's peak swing angle is measured at 8.0 degrees at release and has decayed to 5.2 degrees after 40 complete periods (roughly 80 s, with T approximately 2.0 s). The fractional amplitude decay per swing is (5.2/8.0)^(1/40) = 0.650^(0.025); taking logarithms, ln(0.650)/40 = -0.01077, so the per-swing multiplier is e^(-0.01077) = 0.9893, about a 1.07% amplitude loss per swing. Since even the starting 8.0-degree amplitude keeps the small-angle period error close to 0.1% (well under the ~1% threshold that matters, per Lesson 2), the pendulum's period stays essentially fixed across this entire 80-second run, which is exactly what justifies timing and averaging all 40 periods together.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up damping to check whether a student recognizes their real apparatus is not the idealized, frictionless pendulum their formulas assume, and can justify the specific measurement window they chose. A strong answer names both loss mechanisms (air drag and pivot friction) and explicitly connects the choice of small starting amplitude and early timing window to protecting the small-angle and constant-period assumptions from Lessons 2 and 6, rather than offering a vague "friction slows it down eventually." This question often follows directly after a g-measurement result, testing whether error sources are understood as connected, not listed independently.

questions.prompt: What are the two dominant energy-loss channels for a real, undriven swinging pendulum?

options.text: Air (fluid) drag on the bob and string, and friction at the pivot or support
Variation in local gravitational acceleration and magnetic damping
Thermal expansion of the string and the bob's own internal vibrations

explanations.a: Correct: drag opposing the bob's motion through the surrounding air, and friction at the pivot or support, are the two dominant mechanisms that convert a real pendulum's mechanical energy into heat.
explanations.b: Local g does not meaningfully change during a lab timescale, and ordinary pendulums (absent an added magnet) are not subject to magnetic damping; neither is a standard energy-loss channel here.
explanations.c: Thermal expansion and internal bob vibrations are not the standard, dominant sources of mechanical energy loss in a typical swinging pendulum.

questions.prompt: For light damping, how does the pendulum's total mechanical ENERGY decay compare to how its amplitude decays?

options.text: Energy decays twice as fast (in the exponent) as amplitude, since energy scales with amplitude squared
Energy and amplitude decay at exactly the same rate
Energy decays more slowly than amplitude

explanations.a: Correct: since kinetic and potential energy both scale as amplitude squared, an amplitude envelope decaying as e^(-t/tau) corresponds to an energy envelope decaying as e^(-2t/tau), twice as fast in the exponent.
explanations.b: Because energy depends on amplitude SQUARED, not amplitude itself, energy cannot decay at the same rate as amplitude except in the trivial case of no damping at all.
explanations.c: Energy decays faster than amplitude, not more slowly, precisely because of the squared relationship between them.

questions.prompt: Why do careful experimenters time periods right after release rather than late in a long run?

options.text: Because the amplitude, and the conditions it assumed, is closest to its known initial value right after release, minimizing drift from decay
Because a pendulum needs a warm-up period before it swings correctly
Because periods measured later in a run are always mathematically faster

explanations.a: Correct: timing shortly after release captures periods while the amplitude (and hence, at borderline angles, the period itself) is closest to the initial, best-characterized state, before ongoing decay changes it.
explanations.b: An ideal or well-built pendulum requires no physical warm-up; this is a measurement-error consideration, not a mechanical one.
explanations.c: There is no general rule that later periods run faster; whether the period drifts at all, and in which direction, depends on whether amplitude is in the regime where Lesson 6's amplitude-period coupling matters.

questions.prompt: Match each measurement choice to the specific issue it protects against, connecting back across the unit.

left.text: Starting with a small initial amplitude
Timing many periods immediately after release, not late in the run
Averaging total time over many swings, not timing just one

right.text: Keeps the actual period close to the small-angle prediction, since large amplitude makes period grow (Lessons 2 and 6)
Avoids averaging together periods measured at meaningfully different, decaying amplitudes
Reduces the relative size of fixed human reaction-time timing error (Lesson 4)

questions.explanation: A small starting amplitude keeps the period near its small-angle value despite Lesson 6's amplitude dependence; timing early avoids blending periods from measurably different decayed amplitudes; and averaging over many swings, as in Lesson 4, dilutes fixed reaction-time uncertainty regardless of damping.

lessons.label: The SHM Equation of Motion

sections.heading: The defining equation
sections.body: Simple harmonic motion is not defined by what an object looks like as it moves back and forth; it is defined by one equation: a = -omega^2 x, where omega (the angular frequency, in rad/s) is a positive constant. This says the acceleration at every instant is directly proportional to the displacement from equilibrium, and always points back toward equilibrium (the minus sign). It is a second-order linear differential equation, and that word "linear" is doing the real work: any system whose acceleration obeys this exact form, no matter what physical mechanism produces it, is executing SHM by definition. The physics (springs, pendulums, circuits) only tells you what omega equals; the mathematics of the motion afterward is identical across all of them.

sections.heading: Where the equation comes from physically
sections.body: For a mass on an ideal spring, Hooke's law gives the restoring force F = -kx, and Newton's second law gives F = ma. Combining them: ma = -kx, so a = -(k/m) x. Matching this to a = -omega^2 x gives omega^2 = k/m, purely from the spring constant and the mass. For a pendulum of length L swinging through a small angle theta, the tangential restoring acceleration is a = -(g/L) theta for small theta, giving omega^2 = g/L. Note the word "small": this pendulum result is a linearization that only holds when sin(theta) is well approximated by theta itself, valid to within about 2% for angles under roughly 20 degrees.

sections.heading: Recognizing SHM versus merely periodic motion
sections.body: Not every back-and-forth motion is SHM. A ball dropped and bouncing elastically off a floor is periodic, but its acceleration is a constant -g throughout each flight, not proportional to -x measured from any fixed equilibrium point, so it is not SHM. A large-angle pendulum is also periodic but obeys a = -(g/L) sin(theta), which is not linear in theta, so it fails the definition too. This distinction matters because true SHM has a special property called isochronism: because omega is a fixed constant independent of amplitude, the period T = 2*pi/omega is the same no matter how big or small the oscillation is. The large-angle pendulum loses this property; its period measurably lengthens as the swing amplitude grows, which is exactly why it is not SHM.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.40 kg block on a spring with k = 250 N/m is pulled to x = 0.05 m and released. Newton's second law with Hooke's law gives ma = -kx, so a = -(k/m)x = -(250/0.40)x = -625x, matching a = -omega^2 x with omega^2 = 625 s^-2, so omega = 25 rad/s and T = 2*pi/25 approximately 0.251 s. Now compare a large-angle pendulum released from 60 degrees: its acceleration is a = -(g/L) sin(theta), which is NOT of the form a = -omega^2 x (it is -omega^2 sin(theta), not -omega^2 theta), so it is only approximately SHM for small theta, and its period actually depends on amplitude, unlike the spring's.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the SHM equation itself, rather than jumping straight to the sinusoidal solution, because the equation is where structural understanding lives: can a student look at an unfamiliar system's acceleration expression and correctly say whether it is or is not SHM, and explain why? A common trap is a student who calls anything periodic "SHM" out of habit. A strong answer names isochronism (period independent of amplitude) as the diagnostic consequence of a genuinely linear a = -omega^2 x relationship, and can point to the large-angle pendulum as a case where that property visibly breaks down.

questions.prompt: Which of the following acceleration equations describes simple harmonic motion?

options.text: a = -9x
a = -9 (a constant)

explanations.a: Correct: this is linear in x with a negative proportionality constant, exactly matching a = -omega^2 x with omega^2 = 9.
explanations.b: Not SHM: the acceleration depends on x squared, not x itself, so it is not linear and does not match a = -omega^2 x.
explanations.c: Not SHM: a constant acceleration (like free fall) does not depend on displacement at all, so there is no restoring behavior toward an equilibrium point.

questions.prompt: A true SHM oscillator with a fixed omega is released from a small amplitude and, separately, from a much larger amplitude. What happens to the period T in each case?

options.text: T is the same in both cases (isochronism)
T is longer for the larger amplitude
T is shorter for the larger amplitude

explanations.a: Correct: T = 2*pi/omega depends only on omega, which is fixed by the physical system (like k/m), not on how far it was pulled back. This amplitude-independence is called isochronism.
explanations.b: This is what happens for a large-angle pendulum, which is NOT true SHM precisely because its restoring acceleration is not linear in displacement.
explanations.c: SHM period does not shrink with amplitude either; that would also violate the fixed-omega definition of SHM.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that derive the SHM equation of motion for a mass on an ideal spring.

items.text: State Hooke's law: the spring force is F = -kx
State Newton's second law: F = ma
Combine the two to get ma = -kx
Divide by mass: a = -(k/m)x, matching a = -omega^2 x with omega^2 = k/m

questions.explanation: You need both force laws stated before you can combine them into ma = -kx, and only after combining can you isolate a and identify omega^2 = k/m by comparison with the defining SHM equation.

questions.prompt: Match each system to its restoring-acceleration behavior.

right.text: a = -(k/m)x, exact SHM for any amplitude
a = -(g/L)theta, approximately SHM only because sin(theta) is close to theta for small theta
a = -(g/L)sin(theta), a real restoring acceleration but NOT SHM; period grows with amplitude

questions.explanation: An ideal spring's restoring force is exactly linear in x at every amplitude; a small-angle pendulum is linear only as an approximation valid for small swings; a large-angle pendulum keeps the true sin(theta) dependence, which is not linear and breaks isochronism.

lessons.label: The Solution x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi)

sections.heading: Verifying the solution
sections.body: The function x(t) = A cos(omega*t + phi) is claimed to solve a = -omega^2 x. Check it by differentiating twice: the first derivative is v(t) = -A*omega*sin(omega*t + phi), and the second derivative is a(t) = -A*omega^2*cos(omega*t + phi). Since A*cos(omega*t + phi) is just x(t) again, this reads a(t) = -omega^2 * x(t), exactly the defining equation. This works for ANY choice of the two constants A and phi, which makes sense: a second-order differential equation always needs exactly two free constants to pin down a unique solution, and here those two constants are the amplitude and the phase.

sections.heading: What each parameter controls
sections.body: The amplitude A is the maximum displacement from equilibrium; it sets the height of the trace but does not affect its timing at all. The angular frequency omega (rad/s) is fixed by the physical system itself, such as omega = sqrt(k/m) for a spring, and controls how rapidly the whole pattern repeats; it is not something you choose by how you release the oscillator. The phase constant phi (radians) sets where in the cycle the oscillator sits at t = 0, shifting the entire trace earlier or later in time without changing its shape or size.

sections.heading: Period and frequency
sections.body: Because cosine repeats every 2*pi radians of its argument, the motion repeats when omega*t increases by 2*pi, giving the period T = 2*pi/omega. The ordinary frequency f, in cycles per second (Hz), is f = 1/T = omega/(2*pi), so omega = 2*pi*f. It is easy to conflate omega and f since both describe "how fast" the oscillation goes, but they differ by a factor of 2*pi and have different units: omega is in radians per second, f is in cycles per second.

lessons.workedExample: For x(t) = 0.2*cos(4t + pi/3) in SI units, read off A = 0.2 m, omega = 4 rad/s, phi = pi/3 (60 degrees). At t = 0: x(0) = 0.2*cos(60 degrees) = 0.2*0.5 = 0.1 m. The period is T = 2*pi/4 approximately 1.571 s, and the frequency is f = omega/(2*pi) approximately 0.637 Hz. At t = 0.5 s, the argument is 4(0.5) + pi/3 = 3.047 rad (about 174.6 degrees), and cos(174.6 degrees) is approximately -0.996, so x(0.5) approximately -0.199 m, very close to the negative extreme -A, as expected since the argument is nearly at pi (180 degrees).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges test whether a student can read A, omega, and phi directly off a written x(t) expression or a graph, and correctly compute T and f from omega, rather than treating the formula as an opaque black box. They also probe the conceptual split: can the student explain that omega is baked into the physical system (spring constant, mass, or pendulum length) while A and phi come from how the oscillator happened to be launched? Confusing which parameter is which, especially mixing up omega with f, is the most common failure judges look for.

questions.prompt: In x(t) = A*cos(omega*t + phi), which parameter is fixed by the physical properties of the oscillator (like spring constant and mass) and NOT by how it is released?

options.text: A
omega
phi

explanations.a: Incorrect: amplitude A depends on how far the oscillator is pulled back or how hard it is pushed at release, which is an initial condition, not a fixed property of the system.
explanations.b: Correct: omega = sqrt(k/m) for a spring (or sqrt(g/L) for a small-angle pendulum) is set entirely by the system's physical parameters, independent of how you start the motion.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the phase constant phi depends on the initial position and velocity at release, which is also an initial condition, not a fixed system property.

questions.prompt: For x(t) = 0.3*cos(2t - pi/2) in SI units, what are the amplitude and angular frequency?

options.text: A = 0.3 m, omega = 2 rad/s
A = 2 m, omega = 0.3 rad/s
A = 0.3 m, omega = pi/2 rad/s

explanations.a: Correct: the coefficient in front of cosine is the amplitude (0.3 m) and the coefficient multiplying t inside the cosine is the angular frequency (2 rad/s).
explanations.b: Incorrect: this swaps the roles, treating the coefficient of t as the amplitude and the leading coefficient as omega.
explanations.c: Incorrect: pi/2 is part of the phase term, not the angular frequency; the angular frequency is the coefficient multiplying t, which is 2.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that verify x(t) = A*cos(omega*t + phi) solves a = -omega^2*x.

items.text: Differentiate x(t) once to get v(t) = -A*omega*sin(omega*t + phi)
Differentiate v(t) again to get a(t) = -A*omega^2*cos(omega*t + phi)
Notice that A*cos(omega*t + phi) is just x(t) again, so a(t) = -omega^2*x(t)
Confirm this matches the defining equation a = -omega^2*x for every value of t

questions.explanation: You must take the first derivative before the second, then recognize the second derivative's cosine term is x(t) itself before you can state that the result matches the defining SHM equation.

questions.prompt: Match each parameter of x(t) = A*cos(omega*t + phi) to what changing it alone does to the graph.

right.text: Changes the maximum height (and depth) of the trace, leaving its timing unchanged
Compresses or stretches the trace along the time axis, changing how many cycles fit per second
Slides the entire trace left or right along the time axis without changing its shape or size

questions.explanation: Amplitude only scales the vertical extent; angular frequency only rescales the time axis (changing T = 2*pi/omega); phase only translates the pattern in time, since cos(omega*t + phi) and cos(omega*t) have identical shape offset by a time delay of -phi/omega.

lessons.label: Phase and Initial Conditions

sections.heading: Two constants, two conditions
sections.body: A second-order differential equation like a = -omega^2 x needs exactly two pieces of information to pin down a unique motion: the initial position x(0) and the initial velocity v(0). Setting t = 0 in x(t) = A*cos(omega*t + phi) and v(t) = -A*omega*sin(omega*t + phi) gives x(0) = A*cos(phi) and v(0) = -A*omega*sin(phi). Solving this pair for the unknowns gives A = sqrt(x(0)^2 + (v(0)/omega)^2) by squaring and adding both equations, and tan(phi) = -v(0)/(omega*x(0)) by dividing them.

sections.heading: Two clean special cases
sections.body: Two launches are especially common. Released from rest at the extreme (v(0) = 0, x(0) = A): the equations give phi = 0, so x(t) = A*cos(omega*t), the simplest possible trace, like pulling a spring back and letting go. Launched from equilibrium with a push (x(0) = 0, v(0) not zero): the equations force cos(phi) = 0, giving phi = -pi/2 (moving in the +x direction) or phi = +pi/2 (moving in the -x direction), and the cosine form becomes equivalent to a plain sine, x(t) = plus-or-minus A*sin(omega*t). Both are the same SHM family, just entering the cycle at different points.

sections.heading: Resolving the quadrant ambiguity
sections.body: The equation tan(phi) = -v(0)/(omega*x(0)) alone does not determine phi uniquely, because tangent repeats every pi radians, so a calculator's arctan gives one of two possible angles that differ by 180 degrees. The fix is to check the sign of each original equation separately: cos(phi) must have the same sign as x(0), and sin(phi) must have the opposite sign from v(0) (since v(0) = -A*omega*sin(phi)). Whichever of the two candidate angles satisfies both sign conditions is the correct phi; skipping this check is the single most common phase-constant error.

lessons.workedExample: A block on a spring (omega = 5 rad/s) is at x(0) = 0.1 m when it is given a push of v(0) = +0.5 m/s. Amplitude: A = sqrt(0.1^2 + (0.5/5)^2) = sqrt(0.01 + 0.01) = sqrt(0.02) approximately 0.141 m. Phase ratio: tan(phi) = -0.5/(5*0.1) = -1, so the candidates are phi = -45 degrees or phi = 135 degrees. Check signs: x(0) > 0 requires cos(phi) > 0, and v(0) > 0 requires sin(phi) < 0. Only phi = -45 degrees (-pi/4 rad) satisfies both (cos(-45) is positive, sin(-45) is negative), so phi = -pi/4 is the answer, not 135 degrees.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this step because plugging into tan(phi) blindly is a well-known trap: a calculator returns only one of two mathematically valid angles, and only checking the signs of x(0) and v(0) against cos(phi) and sin(phi) resolves which one is physically correct. A student who reports a phase constant without that quadrant check, or who conflates "starts at rest" with "starts at equilibrium," reveals they memorized a formula rather than understood where a cosine trace actually begins its cycle.

questions.prompt: An oscillator is released from rest at its maximum positive displacement. What is its phase constant phi (using x(t) = A*cos(omega*t + phi))?

options.text: phi = 0
phi = pi/2
phi = pi

explanations.a: Correct: cos(0) = 1, so x(0) = A (maximum positive displacement) and sin(0) = 0, so v(0) = 0 (released from rest). Both match.
explanations.b: Incorrect: phi = pi/2 gives x(0) = A*cos(pi/2) = 0, meaning the oscillator starts at equilibrium, not at maximum displacement.
explanations.c: Incorrect: phi = pi gives x(0) = A*cos(pi) = -A, the maximum NEGATIVE displacement, not the positive one.

questions.prompt: An oscillator starts at x(0) = 0 moving in the +x direction. What is its phase constant phi (using x(t) = A*cos(omega*t + phi))?

options.text: phi = -pi/2
phi = +pi/2
phi = 0

explanations.a: Correct: v(0) = -A*omega*sin(phi) must be positive, so sin(phi) must be negative; phi = -pi/2 gives sin(-pi/2) = -1, making v(0) = +A*omega, matching the +x motion, while cos(-pi/2) = 0 matches x(0) = 0.
explanations.b: Incorrect: phi = +pi/2 also gives x(0) = 0, but sin(+pi/2) = +1 makes v(0) negative, meaning motion in the -x direction, the opposite of what is described.
explanations.c: Incorrect: phi = 0 gives x(0) = A, not 0, so the oscillator would not be starting at equilibrium at all.

questions.prompt: Match each launch scenario to its phase constant phi.

left.text: Starts at x = 0 moving in +x direction
Starts at x = 0 moving in -x direction

right.text: phi = 0
phi = pi
phi = -pi/2
phi = +pi/2

questions.explanation: Each pairing follows from evaluating x(0) = A*cos(phi) and v(0) = -A*omega*sin(phi) at the given phi and checking it reproduces the described starting position and direction of motion.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding A and phi from known initial conditions x(0) and v(0).

items.text: Write the two definitions x(0) = A*cos(phi) and v(0) = -A*omega*sin(phi)
Square both equations and add them to eliminate phi, solving for A
Divide the velocity equation by the position equation to get tan(phi) = -v(0)/(omega*x(0))
Check the signs of x(0) and v(0) to pick the correct quadrant for phi

questions.explanation: You need both defining equations written down before you can eliminate phi to solve for A, and before you can divide them to isolate tan(phi); the sign check for the correct quadrant only makes sense as a final step after a candidate phi has been computed.

lessons.label: Velocity and Acceleration as Derivatives

sections.heading: Differentiating the position trace
sections.body: Starting from x(t) = A*cos(omega*t + phi), one derivative gives the velocity, v(t) = -A*omega*sin(omega*t + phi), and a second derivative gives the acceleration, a(t) = -A*omega^2*cos(omega*t + phi). Because the cosine term is exactly x(t) again, this last expression is also just a(t) = -omega^2*x(t), which is a built-in consistency check: differentiating the assumed solution twice must reproduce the defining equation of motion, and it does.

sections.heading: Where each quantity peaks
sections.body: The velocity's magnitude peaks at |v|_max = A*omega, and this happens exactly when x = 0, at equilibrium, because that is where sin(omega*t+phi) reaches plus-or-minus 1 in the velocity expression while cos does the same in x only at the turning points, not here. Physically, equilibrium is where all the oscillator's mechanical energy is kinetic. The acceleration's magnitude peaks at |a|_max = A*omega^2, at the turning points x = +A or x = -A, where the restoring force (and hence acceleration) is strongest, even though velocity is momentarily zero there.

sections.heading: The 90-degree relationships
sections.body: Differentiating a sinusoid shifts its phase by 90 degrees (a quarter cycle) forward, since -sin(theta) equals cos(theta + 90 degrees). Applying this once shows velocity leads displacement by 90 degrees; applying it a second time shows acceleration leads velocity by another 90 degrees, which means acceleration is a full 180 degrees, or antiphase, relative to displacement itself (which is exactly what the minus sign in a = -omega^2*x already says: acceleration always points opposite to displacement). This 90-degrees-per-derivative chain is a general feature of any single-frequency sinusoidal motion, not something special to springs.

lessons.workedExample: Continuing the block from the phase lesson (A approximately 0.1414 m, omega = 5 rad/s, phi = -pi/4): the peak speed is v_max = A*omega = 0.1414*5 approximately 0.707 m/s, and the peak acceleration magnitude is a_max = A*omega^2 = 0.1414*25 approximately 3.54 m/s^2. Checking consistency at t = 0: v(0) = -A*omega*sin(-pi/4) = -0.707*(-0.707) = 0.5 m/s, matching the given initial push exactly. And a(0) = -omega^2*x(0) = -25*0.1 = -2.5 m/s^2, which is smaller in magnitude than a_max, as expected since the block starts away from equilibrium but not yet at the turning point.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask for v(t) and a(t) not to test mechanical calculus but to see whether a student connects each derivative's peak location to energy: can they explain that speed peaks at equilibrium because that is where all the mechanical energy is kinetic, and acceleration peaks at the turning points because that is where the restoring force is strongest even though the object is momentarily still? They also probe the sign relationship directly: a student who can explain, without algebra, why acceleration always points opposite to displacement (it is the restoring force divided by mass) has understood the physics, not just executed the derivative.

questions.prompt: At which position is the SPEED of an SHM oscillator at its maximum?

options.text: x = 0 (equilibrium)
x = +A
x = -A

explanations.a: Correct: v(t) = -A*omega*sin(omega*t+phi) reaches its maximum magnitude A*omega exactly when the sine term is plus-or-minus 1, which coincides with x = A*cos(omega*t+phi) = 0.
explanations.b: Incorrect: at x = +A the cosine term is at its own maximum, which forces the sine term (and hence velocity) to zero, not to its maximum.
explanations.c: Incorrect: at x = -A the same logic applies; the object is momentarily at rest at this turning point.

questions.prompt: At which position is the magnitude of ACCELERATION at its maximum?

options.text: x = 0 (equilibrium)
x = +A or x = -A (the turning points)
Acceleration magnitude is constant everywhere in SHM

explanations.a: Incorrect: since a(t) = -omega^2*x(t), acceleration is zero exactly where x is zero, at equilibrium, not maximum there.
explanations.b: Correct: a = -omega^2*x is largest in magnitude wherever |x| is largest, which is at the turning points x = plus-or-minus A, where the restoring force is strongest.
explanations.c: Incorrect: acceleration varies continuously with position in SHM since it is directly proportional to displacement; it is not constant.

questions.prompt: In SHM, velocity leads displacement in phase by:

options.text: 90 degrees
180 degrees
0 degrees (in phase)

explanations.a: Correct: differentiating a cosine shifts its phase forward by 90 degrees, since v(t) = -A*omega*sin(omega*t+phi) equals A*omega*cos(omega*t+phi+90 degrees).
explanations.b: 180 degrees is the phase relationship between acceleration and displacement, not velocity and displacement; acceleration is a second derivative, adding another 90 degrees on top of velocity's lead.
explanations.c: Incorrect: velocity and displacement reach their extremes at different times (velocity is zero exactly where displacement is extreme, and vice versa), so they are not in phase.

questions.prompt: Starting at the positive extreme, order these four states of an SHM oscillator as it moves through one full cycle.

items.text: At x = +A: velocity is zero, acceleration is at its most negative
At x = 0 moving in the -x direction: velocity is at its most negative, acceleration is zero
At x = -A: velocity is zero, acceleration is at its most positive
At x = 0 moving in the +x direction: velocity is at its most positive, acceleration is zero

questions.explanation: Starting at the positive turning point, the oscillator swings back through equilibrium moving in the negative direction, reaches the negative turning point, then swings back through equilibrium moving in the positive direction to complete the cycle.

lessons.label: The Reference Circle

sections.heading: SHM as a shadow
sections.body: Imagine a point P moving counterclockwise at constant angular speed omega around a circle of radius A. Its angular position at time t is theta(t) = omega*t + phi_0, where phi_0 is its starting angle. Now project P straight down onto a horizontal axis: the projection's coordinate is x = A*cos(theta(t)) = A*cos(omega*t + phi_0), which is exactly the SHM solution. In other words, SHM is nothing more than the one-dimensional shadow, or projection, of an ordinary point moving at constant speed around a circle.

sections.heading: Reading A, omega, and phi off the circle
sections.body: This single picture packages all three SHM parameters into one moving arrow. The radius of the circle IS the amplitude A. The angular speed at which the arrow sweeps around the circle IS the angular frequency omega. The arrow's starting angle, measured from the positive x-axis, IS the phase constant phi. This geometric view makes some comparisons far easier than the trig formula alone, for instance comparing two oscillators of different phase is just comparing the angles of two arrows on the same circle at a given instant.

sections.heading: Projecting velocity and acceleration too
sections.body: The reference point P also carries a tangential velocity vector of constant magnitude A*omega, always perpendicular to its radius; projecting this vector onto the x-axis gives v(t) = -A*omega*sin(theta), matching the SHM velocity exactly. P also has a centripetal acceleration vector of constant magnitude A*omega^2, always pointing from P toward the circle's center; projecting that gives a(t) = -A*omega^2*cos(theta), matching the SHM acceleration. So the entire kinematic package of SHM, position, velocity, and acceleration together, is just the shadow of one point in honest two-dimensional uniform circular motion, viewed edge-on.

lessons.workedExample: A reference circle has radius A = 0.2 m, and its point sweeps at omega = 3 rad/s starting at phi_0 = pi/6 (30 degrees) at t = 0. At t = 1 s, the angle is theta = 3(1) + pi/6 = 3.524 rad (about 201.9 degrees). The projected position is x = 0.2*cos(201.9 degrees) approximately -0.186 m. The tangential speed is A*omega = 0.6 m/s, and its x-component gives the SHM velocity: v = -A*omega*sin(201.9 degrees) approximately 0.224 m/s. Checking consistency, the SHM acceleration should be a = -omega^2*x = -9*(-0.186) approximately 1.67 m/s^2, matching a direct projection of the centripetal acceleration, -A*omega^2*cos(201.9 degrees) approximately 1.67 m/s^2.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the reference circle to test spatial intuition beyond memorized formulas: can a student explain, purely from the picture (not algebra), why speed is maximum at x = 0 (the tangential velocity there points straight along the horizontal, fully contributing to the x-projection) and zero at x = plus-or-minus A (the tangential velocity there points straight up or down, perpendicular to the projection axis, contributing nothing to it)? A student who can reason this way from the circle, rather than only from the derivative formulas, demonstrates a deeper geometric grasp that the derivative approach alone does not reveal.

questions.prompt: In the reference circle model, the radius of the circle corresponds to which SHM quantity?

options.text: The amplitude A
The period T
The phase constant phi

explanations.a: Correct: the projection of a point at radius A onto the x-axis ranges from -A to +A, exactly matching the SHM amplitude.
explanations.b: Incorrect: the period is related to how fast the point sweeps around the circle (via omega), not to the circle's size.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the phase constant is the point's starting angle on the circle, not the circle's radius.

questions.prompt: The angular speed at which the reference point sweeps around the circle corresponds to which SHM quantity?

options.text: The angular frequency omega
The amplitude A
The phase constant phi

explanations.a: Correct: theta(t) = omega*t + phi_0 is literally the point's angular position, and its rate of change, omega, is by construction the same omega that appears in the SHM solution.
explanations.b: Incorrect: amplitude is a fixed length (the radius), not a rate; it does not describe how fast the point moves around the circle.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the phase constant is a fixed starting angle, not the rate at which the angle changes over time.

questions.prompt: At the instant the reference point crosses the very top of the circle (theta = 90 degrees), what is happening to the projected velocity v?

options.text: v is at its maximum magnitude
v is zero
v is at half its maximum magnitude

explanations.a: Correct: at the top of the circle the radius points straight up, so the tangential velocity (perpendicular to the radius) points purely horizontally, meaning all of it projects onto the x-axis, giving the maximum |v|. This also matches x = A*cos(90 degrees) = 0, equilibrium, where speed peaks.
explanations.b: Incorrect: v is zero when the tangential velocity is purely vertical, which happens at theta = 0 or 180 degrees (the turning points x = plus-or-minus A), not at the top of the circle.
explanations.c: Incorrect: there is no reason for the projection to be at exactly half its maximum at this particular angle; the projected velocity is a sine function of theta and reaches its full magnitude here.

questions.prompt: Match each reference-circle element to the SHM quantity it represents.

left.text: Tangential speed of the point, A*omega

right.text: Amplitude of the oscillation
Instantaneous phase of the oscillation
Maximum speed of the oscillator
Maximum acceleration of the oscillator

questions.explanation: Each circle quantity projects directly onto its SHM counterpart: the fixed radius becomes the fixed amplitude, the changing angle becomes the changing phase, and the two constant-magnitude circular motion vectors (tangential velocity and centripetal acceleration) become the peak values that the projected v(t) and a(t) never exceed.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for constructing the reference-circle picture of a given SHM motion.

items.text: Draw a circle of radius A
Place a point on the circle at angle phi, measured from the positive x-axis, to represent t = 0
Let the point revolve around the circle at constant angular speed omega
At each instant, project the point straight onto the x-axis to read off x(t)

questions.explanation: The circle's size must be set first (radius A), then the starting position placed on it (angle phi), then the rotation rate applied (omega), and only then does projecting the moving point onto the axis generate the SHM trace x(t).

lessons.label: The Phase Portrait

sections.heading: Plotting v against x
sections.body: Instead of plotting x or v against time, plot velocity v (vertical axis) against position x (horizontal axis) at each instant, an image called a phase portrait. Since x = A*cos(theta) and v = -A*omega*sin(theta) share the same theta = omega*t + phi, eliminating theta using cos^2(theta) + sin^2(theta) = 1 gives (x/A)^2 + (v/(A*omega))^2 = 1, the equation of an ellipse with horizontal semi-axis A and vertical semi-axis A*omega. As time runs, the point (x, v) traces this same ellipse over and over, once per period, moving clockwise: starting at (A, 0), x decreases while v first becomes negative.

sections.heading: The ellipse encodes energy
sections.body: The total mechanical energy of the oscillator, E = (1/2)*k*A^2 = (1/2)*m*omega^2*A^2, is a single fixed number set by A and omega. Rewriting the ellipse equation as (1/2)*k*x^2 + (1/2)*m*v^2 = E shows that every point on the ellipse has exactly this same total energy: the trajectory is a literal contour of constant energy in (x, v) space, kinetic and potential energy trading off continuously as the point moves around it. A bigger ellipse (larger A) means more stored energy; the ellipse's aspect ratio, A*omega to A, is fixed by the oscillator's own omega, but its overall size scales with amplitude and hence with energy.

sections.heading: Area of the ellipse
sections.body: The area enclosed by an ellipse is pi times the product of its two semi-axes: Area = pi * A * (A*omega) = pi*omega*A^2. Since E = (1/2)*m*omega^2*A^2, substituting A^2 = 2E/(m*omega^2) gives Area = 2*pi*E/(m*omega), meaning the enclosed area is directly proportional to the total mechanical energy for a fixed oscillator (fixed m and omega). This is not just a curiosity: this enclosed area hints at the true action variable of more advanced mechanics, J = E/omega, which is instead defined using the canonical (x, p = m*v) phase space rather than the (x, v) plane used here (so it differs from Area/(2*pi) computed above by a factor of the mass m); the true action stays remarkably constant even when a system's parameters are changed slowly, a preview of ideas that reappear throughout physics beyond introductory SHM.

lessons.workedExample: A block of mass m = 0.5 kg on a spring with k = 200 N/m oscillates with amplitude A = 0.05 m. Its angular frequency is omega = sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(400) = 20 rad/s, so its phase-portrait ellipse has semi-axes A = 0.05 m and A*omega = 1 m/s. The enclosed area is pi*A*(A*omega) = pi*0.05*1 approximately 0.157 (units of m times m/s). The total mechanical energy is E = (1/2)*k*A^2 = (1/2)*200*0.0025 = 0.25 J. Checking the area-energy relation: Area = 2*pi*E/(m*omega) = 2*pi*0.25/(0.5*20) = 1.571/10 approximately 0.157, matching the direct ellipse-area calculation exactly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up the phase portrait to see if a student can read the STATE of an oscillator instantly from a single snapshot point on the (x, v) plane, without needing a stopwatch or a timeline: for example, a point at (0, -A*omega) means the mass is passing through equilibrium moving in the negative direction at its maximum speed. They may also ask what happens to the portrait if friction removes energy over time: the ellipse spirals inward toward the origin as A shrinks. This tests whether the student treats the picture as a live readout of the system's energy, not merely a decorative alternative to the x(t) graph.

questions.prompt: What shape does an ideal (undamped) SHM oscillator trace in the (x, v) phase plane?

options.text: An ellipse with semi-axes A and A*omega
A perfect circle of radius A regardless of omega
A straight line through the origin

explanations.a: Correct: (x/A)^2 + (v/(A*omega))^2 = 1 is the equation of an ellipse with horizontal semi-axis A and vertical semi-axis A*omega, and these two are equal only in the special case omega = 1 rad/s.
explanations.b: Incorrect: this is only true in the special case omega = 1 rad/s, where A*omega happens to equal A; in general the vertical and horizontal semi-axes differ.
explanations.c: Incorrect: a straight line would mean v is always proportional to x with a fixed sign, which is not the case since v and x reach their extremes at different times.

questions.prompt: If friction slowly removes energy from a real oscillator, what happens to its phase portrait over many cycles?

options.text: It spirals inward toward the origin
It spirals outward, away from the origin
It stays exactly the same fixed ellipse

explanations.a: Correct: losing energy means E, and therefore A, shrinks cycle by cycle, so the traced ellipse gets smaller and smaller, spiraling in toward the origin (the point of zero displacement and zero velocity, zero energy).
explanations.b: Incorrect: outward spiraling would mean the oscillator is gaining energy over time, which does not happen under friction; friction removes energy.
explanations.c: Incorrect: a fixed, unchanging ellipse only describes an idealized undamped oscillator with no energy loss, which is not what friction produces.

questions.prompt: For a fixed oscillator (fixed mass m and angular frequency omega), the area enclosed by its phase-portrait ellipse is proportional to:

options.text: The amplitude A alone
The total mechanical energy E
The period T

explanations.a: Incorrect: the area is pi*omega*A^2, which is proportional to A^2, not to A alone.
explanations.b: Correct: substituting A^2 = 2E/(m*omega^2) into Area = pi*omega*A^2 gives Area = 2*pi*E/(m*omega), directly proportional to E when m and omega are fixed.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the period T = 2*pi/omega does not depend on the amplitude or energy at all in true SHM (isochronism), so it cannot be what the ellipse's area tracks.

questions.prompt: Match each point on the phase-portrait ellipse to the physical state of the oscillator it represents.

right.text: At the positive extreme, momentarily at rest
Passing through equilibrium moving in the -x direction at maximum speed
At the negative extreme, momentarily at rest
Passing through equilibrium moving in the +x direction at maximum speed

questions.explanation: Each point's x-coordinate gives the position and its v-coordinate gives the velocity at that instant, so (A, 0) is the positive turning point (v = 0), (0, -A*omega) is equilibrium moving at maximum negative speed, and so on around the ellipse.

questions.prompt: Starting at (A, 0), order these four phase-portrait states as the point moves clockwise around the ellipse through one full cycle.

items.text: (0, -A*omega)
(0, +A*omega)

questions.explanation: Starting at the rightmost point (A, 0), the phase point moves clockwise: down to the bottom (0, -A*omega), across to the leftmost point (-A, 0), up to the top (0, +A*omega), and back to the start, completing one full period.

lessons.label: The Damping Force

sections.heading: A force that fights velocity, not position
sections.body: In an ideal spring-mass oscillator, the only force is the restoring force F = -kx, which depends solely on displacement and would let the system oscillate forever at constant amplitude. Real oscillators do not do this: a pendulum in air slows down, a plucked guitar string quiets, a car bouncing after a pothole settles. The missing piece is a damping force that resists motion whenever the object moves, and does no work when it sits still. The simplest and most common model is linear (viscous) damping, F_damping = -b v, where v is velocity and b is a damping coefficient (units kg/s, or N*s/m). This force law describes an object moving slowly through a fluid, air, oil, or water, where the fluid's viscosity supplies drag proportional to speed, a regime exemplified by Stokes' law for a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid. Because F_damping depends on velocity's sign, it always opposes whichever direction the object is currently moving, whether that is outward or inward, so it removes mechanical energy on every pass through the cycle rather than storing it like the spring force does. Adding this term to Newton's second law gives the governing equation of a damped oscillator: m d2x/dt2 + b dx/dt + kx = 0. Every damped-oscillation lesson in this unit is built by solving different regimes of that one equation.

sections.heading: Where the energy goes
sections.body: Because F_damping = -bv, the instantaneous power it removes from the oscillator is P = F_damping * v = -b v squared, always negative (energy leaving) whenever the mass is moving, and exactly zero at the instants the mass reverses direction and v = 0. That -bv squared term converts kinetic energy into heat via the microscopic friction between the object and the surrounding medium, molecules of air or oil being sheared and jostled. Averaged over a full cycle, this steady bleed of energy is what shrinks the oscillation's amplitude cycle after cycle, even though the frequency and period barely change (later lessons quantify by how little). Not all resistive forces are linear in v: dry (Coulomb) friction has constant magnitude regardless of speed and only depends on the sign of v, while aerodynamic drag at higher speeds scales with v squared. Engineers choose whichever force law fits the physical mechanism doing the damping, a submerged dashpot is well modeled as linear, while a fast-moving projectile in air is not. This unit uses the linear model throughout because it is the one that yields a clean, exactly solvable exponential-envelope solution.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.50 kg mass hangs from a spring with k = 200 N/m and sits submerged in a light oil that supplies a damping coefficient b = 4.0 kg/s. Its natural angular frequency is omega0 = sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(400) = 20 rad/s. At the instant it passes through equilibrium moving at v = 1.0 m/s, the damping force is F = -bv = -4.0 N, and the instantaneous power is P = F * v = -b v squared = -4.0 W: negative because it is the power delivered to the mass by the damping force, meaning 4.0 W is simultaneously leaving the mechanical system as heat in the oil. Over many cycles, that steady loss is what will shrink the visible swing. Because b is small compared to what full stopping would require (about 20 kg/s, found in Lesson 3), this system stays underdamped: it keeps oscillating while quietly losing energy.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing damping usually starts with the force law itself: can the student say why F = -bv depends on velocity rather than displacement, and explain that it does zero work at the endpoints of a swing (where v = 0) and maximum negative work at top speed through equilibrium? The follow-up is almost always energy: where does the lost mechanical energy physically go? "It gets smaller" is not an answer; "it converts to heat in the fluid or friction interface, proportional to b v squared" is. Students who can also name that this is a linear/viscous model, not the only possible damping law, signal they understand it as a model choice, not a law of nature.

questions.prompt: The damping force F = -bv is exactly zero at which point in an oscillation?

options.text: The equilibrium position, where displacement is zero
The turning points, where velocity is zero
It is never exactly zero during real motion

explanations.a: Wrong direction: at equilibrium the mass is moving fastest, so the damping force is at its largest magnitude there, not zero.
explanations.b: Correct: F = -bv depends only on velocity, and velocity is zero at the turning points, so the damping force vanishes there too.
explanations.c: It genuinely is zero at each turning point, for an instant, before the mass reverses and speeds up again.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to build the governing equation of a damped oscillator.

items.text: Identify the spring's restoring force, F_spring = -kx
Identify the velocity-proportional damping force, F_damping = -bv
Sum the forces via Newton's second law, F_net = m a
Obtain the governing equation m x'' + b x' + kx = 0

questions.explanation: The two individual force laws are identified first, then combined through F_net = ma, which is what actually produces the single second-order differential equation that every later lesson solves in a different damping regime.

questions.prompt: Match each resistive-force regime to its mathematical form.

left.text: Viscous drag at low speed (Stokes' law regime, e.g. oil or thick air)

right.text: F is proportional to -v (linear in speed)
F has constant magnitude, direction set only by the sign of v
F is proportional to -v squared (quadratic in speed)

questions.explanation: Linear damping (F = -bv) is the model used throughout this unit because it applies to slow motion through a viscous fluid; dry friction and high-speed drag follow different force laws and would not produce a clean exponential envelope.

questions.prompt: The instantaneous power removed from the oscillator by a linear damping force is:

options.text: P = -b v
P = -b v squared
P = -b x squared

explanations.a: That is the force itself, not the power; power requires multiplying the force by velocity.
explanations.b: Correct: P = F * v = (-bv)(v) = -b v squared, always removing energy whenever the mass is moving.
explanations.c: Power dissipated by a velocity-dependent force depends on velocity, not displacement squared.

lessons.label: Underdamped Motion

sections.heading: Oscillation trapped inside a shrinking envelope
sections.body: Solving m x'' + b x' + kx = 0 when the damping is light enough (formally, when b is less than the critical value found in Lesson 3) gives a solution of the form x(t) = A0 e^(-gamma t) cos(omega_d t + phi), where gamma = b/(2m) is the decay rate. This is the underdamped case, and it is by far the most common regime for everyday oscillators: a plucked guitar string, a struck bell, a pendulum swinging in air, a car's suspension after most bumps. The cosine term keeps producing genuine back-and-forth oscillation, while the e^(-gamma t) factor multiplying it is a smoothly shrinking envelope that pinches the peaks closer to zero on each swing. If you plot x(t), the curve looks exactly like an ordinary cosine wave trapped between two mirror-image exponential curves, plus and minus A0 e^(-gamma t), that squeeze together over time. The oscillation touches each envelope curve, but not quite at its own peaks, the peak of x(t) occurs slightly before it touches the envelope, a detail that matters for careful data analysis but not for the qualitative picture: you get real oscillation, with monotonically shrinking amplitude, forever (in the ideal linear model) but never oscillation that simply stops or overshoots and comes back only once.

sections.heading: Why the frequency shifts, and why it barely does
sections.body: Damping does more than shrink the amplitude, it also slightly lowers the oscillation frequency. The damped angular frequency is omega_d = sqrt(omega0 squared - gamma squared), always a little less than the natural (undamped) frequency omega0 = sqrt(k/m). Physically, the resistive force is fighting the restoring force on every swing, so the mass takes infinitesimally longer to complete each cycle than it would if damping were absent. For most real oscillators this shift is small enough to ignore: light damping means gamma is much smaller than omega0, so the correction is a fraction of a percent for a gently damped pendulum or a lightly plucked guitar string. The shift only becomes dramatic as b approaches the critical damping value from below, at which point omega_d falls toward zero, the oscillation gets slower and slower until it stops oscillating altogether right at the critical damping boundary (Lesson 3). Two other quantities in x(t) = A0 e^(-gamma t) cos(omega_d t + phi) are set purely by the starting conditions and do not decay: the phase phi (when the clock is started relative to the motion), and, notably, omega_d itself is constant in time, only the amplitude envelope A0 e^(-gamma t) changes as the cycles pass.

lessons.workedExample: Take the oiled spring-mass system from Lesson 1: m = 0.50 kg, k = 200 N/m, b = 4.0 kg/s, so omega0 = 20 rad/s and gamma = b/2m = 4.0 per second. The damped frequency is omega_d = sqrt(400 - 16) = sqrt(384), about 19.6 rad/s, roughly 2% below omega0, a shift small enough that a stopwatch timing a few cycles would barely catch it. The envelope, however, is very noticeable: A(t) = A0 e^(-4.0t), so after just t = 0.25 s the amplitude has fallen to A0 e^(-1), about 37% of A0, a visible drop in barely one damped period (T_d = 2 pi / omega_d, about 0.32 s). This system is a case where the frequency is nearly untouched but the amplitude collapses quickly, exactly the signature of underdamped motion with a modest quality factor.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use underdamped motion to test whether a student conflates "the oscillation is dying out" with "the oscillation is slowing down." They are different: omega_d is fixed once b, m, and k are fixed, while only the envelope A0 e^(-gamma t) changes cycle to cycle. A sharp question is: does the time between successive zero-crossings change as the amplitude decays? A student who understands the model says no, the period stays essentially T_d = 2 pi / omega_d throughout, only slightly longer than the undamped period, while the visible swing height shrinks geometrically. A student who says the oscillation gradually slows down and stops, like a spinning top losing energy, has the wrong mental model.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes omega_d relative to omega0 for underdamped motion?

options.text: omega_d is always greater than omega0
omega_d is always slightly less than omega0
omega_d equals omega0 exactly; only the amplitude changes

explanations.a: omega_d = sqrt(omega0 squared - gamma squared) is always less than omega0 for any nonzero damping, never greater.
explanations.b: Correct: subtracting a positive gamma squared under the square root always pulls omega_d below omega0.
explanations.c: Damping does shift the frequency, just by a small amount when damping is light; it is not exactly omega0.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity in x(t) = A0 e^(-gamma t) cos(omega_d t + phi) to how it behaves over time.

right.text: Decays exponentially cycle after cycle
Stays constant at sqrt(omega0 squared - gamma squared)
Fixed once by the initial conditions, does not change with time

questions.explanation: Only the envelope shrinks with time; the damped frequency and the phase are both constants of the motion once the system's parameters and starting conditions are set.

questions.prompt: Order these envelope values by the time at which they occur, earliest to latest, where tau = 1/gamma is the time constant.

items.text: t = tau, A is about 0.37 A0
t = 2 tau, A is about 0.14 A0
t = 3 tau, A is about 0.05 A0

questions.explanation: The envelope A0 e^(-t/tau) falls monotonically, so equal steps of one time constant occur in this chronological order with amplitude shrinking by roughly the same factor, 1/e, at each step.

questions.prompt: For the same m and k, if the damping coefficient b is halved, what happens to omega_d?

options.text: It moves closer to omega0
It moves further from omega0
It stays exactly the same

explanations.a: Correct: halving b halves gamma = b/2m, and a smaller gamma squared subtracted under the square root pulls omega_d closer to omega0.
explanations.b: Less damping means less of a frequency shift, not more; this describes the opposite effect.
explanations.c: omega_d depends on gamma, so changing b does change omega_d, just by a small amount when damping is already light.

lessons.label: Critical Damping and Overdamping

sections.heading: The dividing line: critical damping
sections.body: As the damping coefficient b grows, gamma = b/2m grows too, and the damped frequency omega_d = sqrt(omega0 squared - gamma squared) shrinks toward zero. The special value where omega_d reaches exactly zero, where gamma = omega0, is called critical damping, and it occurs at b_c = 2 m omega0 = 2 sqrt(mk). At this exact value, the system no longer oscillates at all: displaced from equilibrium and released, it returns directly to zero without crossing it, and does so in the shortest possible time of any non-oscillating return. This is why critical damping is the design target for systems that must settle fast without bouncing: an analog voltmeter needle should swing to the correct reading and stop, not oscillate around it; a door closer should shut the door promptly without letting it swing back open or slam. Mathematically, critical damping is the boundary case of the governing equation where the characteristic equation has a repeated real root, giving a solution of the form x(t) = (A + Bt) e^(-gamma t), a decaying exponential multiplied by a linear term, rather than the cosine of the underdamped case or the sum of two separate exponentials of the overdamped case.

sections.heading: Past the boundary: overdamping
sections.body: When b exceeds b_c (equivalently gamma is greater than omega0), the system is overdamped: the resistive force is now strong enough that the characteristic equation has two distinct real roots, and the solution is a sum of two decaying exponentials, x(t) = C1 e^(-r1 t) + C2 e^(-r2 t), with no oscillation at all. Overdamped return is also monotonic and non-oscillating, but it is slower than critical damping, the smaller of the two decay rates (the slow exponential) dominates at late times and drags the return out. A heavily oil-damped screen door that creeps shut over several seconds, or a very stiff shock absorber that lets a car body sink back down sluggishly after a big bump, are overdamped: safe from bouncing, but sluggish. Real automotive shock absorbers are usually deliberately set a little underdamped rather than critically or over-damped, a damping ratio around zeta = 0.2 to 0.4, because a small, quickly vanishing oscillation after a bump gives a more comfortable ride than either a bouncy, lightly damped car or a harsh, overdamped one that transmits more of the bump directly to the frame before it dissipates.

lessons.workedExample: Return to the m = 0.50 kg, k = 200 N/m spring system. Its critical damping coefficient is b_c = 2 sqrt(mk) = 2 sqrt(0.50 times 200) = 2 sqrt(100) = 20 kg/s. Lesson 1's oil bath supplied only b = 4.0 kg/s, a damping ratio zeta = b/b_c = 0.20, solidly underdamped, consistent with the visible oscillation found there. If that same mass were instead placed in a much thicker fluid giving b = 20 kg/s, it would sit exactly at critical damping and return to equilibrium from a displaced start with no overshoot, in minimum time. Push b higher still, to 40 kg/s (zeta = 2.0), and the same mass becomes overdamped: it still returns without oscillating, but measurably more slowly, because the dominant slow exponential decay rate is now smaller than gamma was at critical damping.
lessons.judgeFraming: Because underdamped, critically damped, and overdamped sound like a spectrum of "more damping is always better," judges probe whether students actually understand the trade-off. A strong answer distinguishes speed of return (critical damping is fastest with no overshoot) from what most consumer systems actually use (cars are intentionally underdamped for comfort, accepting one or two small bounces). Expect a question like "why not just make every shock absorber critically damped?", testing whether the student can connect the math (zeta around 0.2 to 0.4 gives a fast-feeling-but-not-harsh response) to the engineering trade-off between speed, overshoot, and how directly a passenger feels the bump.

questions.prompt: Critical damping is defined as the damping level at which:

options.text: The damped frequency omega_d first reaches zero, and return to equilibrium is fastest without overshoot
The system oscillates with maximum amplitude
Energy loss per cycle is zero

explanations.a: Correct: this is the boundary gamma = omega0, where the solution stops oscillating and returns to equilibrium in the shortest non-oscillating time.
explanations.b: Critical damping produces no oscillation at all, so there is no amplitude of oscillation to maximize.
explanations.c: Energy loss per cycle is not zero at critical damping; damping is at its most consequential there, not absent.

questions.prompt: Order these three systems, all sharing the same m and k, from fastest to slowest return toward equilibrium.

items.text: Critical damping: b = b_c
Moderately overdamped: b = 2 b_c
Heavily overdamped: b = 5 b_c

questions.explanation: Critical damping gives the fastest possible non-oscillating return; increasing b further beyond b_c shrinks the dominant (slower) decay rate, so return time increases monotonically as b grows past b_c.

questions.prompt: Match each damping regime to a real-world example of its behavior.

right.text: Door closer or analog meter needle: settles fastest, no overshoot or oscillation
Heavy screen-door closer or stiff dashpot: settles slowly, no overshoot
Car suspension with zeta around 0.2 to 0.4: one or two small bounces, then fast decay

questions.explanation: Critical damping is the fastest non-oscillating case; overdamping trades away that speed for extra margin against oscillation; light underdamping accepts a small bounce in exchange for a response most people perceive as comfortable rather than harsh.

questions.prompt: Compared to critical damping, an overdamped system with a much larger b returns to equilibrium:

options.text: Faster
At the same speed
More slowly

explanations.a: Critical damping is already the fastest non-oscillating return possible; increasing b past that point cannot make it faster.
explanations.b: The return time changes as b increases past b_c; it does not stay fixed at the critical-damping value.
explanations.c: Correct: a larger b shrinks the slower of the two decay rates in the overdamped solution, stretching out the return time.

lessons.label: The Decay Envelope and Time Constant

sections.heading: The envelope as its own exponential
sections.body: Whatever the fine oscillatory details, the amplitude of any underdamped oscillator falls along a clean exponential envelope, A(t) = A0 e^(-t/tau), where the time constant tau = 1/gamma = 2m/b sets the pace of decay. tau has units of time and a direct physical meaning: it is the time for the envelope to fall to 1/e, about 36.8%, of its starting value. After 2 tau the envelope has fallen to about 13.5%, after 3 tau to about 5.0%, after 5 tau to under 1%, the five-time-constant rule used across physics and engineering to call a decaying process essentially finished. Because tau depends only on m and b (not on k or the initial amplitude), doubling the mass while keeping the same fluid doubles tau, while doubling the damping coefficient halves it, a system in thicker oil or with more friction decays faster, exactly as intuition expects, and the relationship is linear, not merely qualitative.

sections.heading: Reading tau off real data, and counting cycles
sections.body: In a lab, tau is usually extracted by recording peak displacements over time, a motion sensor tracking a swinging pendulum, or an oscilloscope trace of a ringing circuit, and finding the time for the peak envelope to shrink to 1/e of its start, or more robustly, by plotting the natural log of amplitude against t: since ln A(t) = ln A0 minus t/tau, that plot is a straight line whose slope is minus 1/tau, and fitting a line through several peaks is far less noisy than trusting any single measured amplitude.
