A separate and physically important question is how many oscillations fit inside one time constant, since that determines whether the decay is obvious to the eye, a handful of swings, or so gradual it looks almost like an undamped oscillator, thousands of swings. That count is N = tau / T_d, which for light damping is closely tied to the quality factor Q covered in Lesson 5 (N is approximately Q / pi). A heavily damped system might lose noticeable amplitude within a single swing, tau comparable to or shorter than the period, while a lightly damped bell or tuning fork can complete hundreds or thousands of cycles before its envelope visibly shrinks, the same exponential law, just running on a vastly different clock.

lessons.workedExample: A student records a pendulum's swing amplitude with a motion sensor: 10.0 cm at t = 0, and 3.7 cm at t = 5.0 s. Since 3.7/10.0 is about 0.37, close to 1/e, that 5.0 s interval is one time constant, so tau is about 5.0 s and gamma = 1/tau = 0.20 per second. Checking the trace, the pendulum completes about 10 full swings in those 5.0 s, so the period is T about 0.50 s and N = tau/T = 10 oscillations fit inside one time constant, a lightly damped system whose decay is gradual enough to be easy to see but slow enough to take many careful cycles to measure well. To reduce noise, the student instead plots ln(amplitude) against time for all 10 peaks and fits a line; the slope's reciprocal magnitude gives a more reliable tau of about 4.8 s than the two-point estimate alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: The classic confusion judges probe for is mixing up the time constant tau with the oscillation period T, two very different timescales that both have units of seconds. A judge may ask directly: if I told you the pendulum's period is 0.5 seconds, do you now know how fast the amplitude is decaying? The correct answer is no, period and decay rate are set by different physical quantities (k and m set T; b and m set tau), and a well-prepared student should be ready to describe the ln(A) versus t linear-fit method as the honest way to measure tau from noisy real data rather than eyeballing one point.

questions.prompt: The time constant tau is the time for the amplitude envelope to fall to approximately:

options.text: 50% of its initial value
36.8% (1/e) of its initial value
Zero

explanations.a: 50% is the definition of a half-life, a different (though related) way of describing exponential decay, not the time constant.
explanations.b: Correct: tau is defined so that A(tau) = A0 e^(-1), which is about 36.8% of the starting amplitude.
explanations.c: An exponential decay only reaches exactly zero as time goes to infinity, never at a single finite time like tau.

questions.prompt: Match each elapsed number of time constants to the approximate fraction of amplitude remaining.

right.text: About 36.8% remaining
About 13.5% remaining
About 5.0% remaining
Under 1% remaining

questions.explanation: Each additional time constant multiplies the remaining amplitude by another factor of 1/e, about 0.368, so the fraction remaining drops geometrically: 36.8%, 13.5%, 5.0%, and under 1% after five time constants.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of extracting tau reliably from decaying lab data.

items.text: Record the peak displacement of each swing over time
Plot the natural log of each peak amplitude versus time
Fit a straight line through the plotted points
Take tau as the negative reciprocal of the fitted slope

questions.explanation: Raw peak data comes first, then the log transform that linearizes exponential decay, then a line fit that averages out noise across many peaks, then converting the fitted slope into tau.

questions.prompt: Doubling the mass m, while keeping the same damping coefficient b and spring constant k, will:

options.text: Double tau
Halve tau
Leave tau unchanged

explanations.a: Correct: tau = 2m/b, so doubling m with b fixed doubles tau directly.
explanations.b: Halving tau would require increasing b or decreasing m, not increasing m.
explanations.c: tau depends explicitly on m, so changing the mass while holding b fixed does change tau.

lessons.label: The Quality Factor Q

sections.heading: Q as a ratio of energy stored to energy lost
sections.body: The quality factor Q packages how good, how lightly damped, an oscillator is into a single dimensionless number. The formal definition is Q = 2 pi times (energy stored in the oscillator) divided by (energy lost per cycle), which is equivalent to saying Q is (energy stored) divided by (energy lost per radian of oscillation), since one full cycle covers 2 pi radians of phase. In terms of the damping parameters already defined, Q = omega0 / (2 gamma) = m omega0 / b, a large Q means gamma is small compared to omega0, meaning the oscillator loses only a small fraction of its stored energy on each swing, exactly the light-damping condition for the approximations used in Lessons 2 and 4. Because energy is proportional to amplitude squared, and amplitude decays as e^(-gamma t), energy decays twice as fast, as e^(-2 gamma t); the fractional energy lost in one radian of phase works out to be almost exactly 1/Q for large Q, which is the cleanest way to see why the two ways of stating the definition, the energy ratio and omega0/(2 gamma), are the same number.

sections.heading: What Q looks like in real systems
sections.body: Quality factor spans enormous ranges across ordinary and specialized oscillators. A car's shock absorber is deliberately built with Q of only about 1.25 to 2.5 (zeta around 0.2 to 0.4), light-to-moderate underdamping that lets a bump produce one or two quickly-vanishing bounces rather than a harsh, fully non-oscillating overdamped response. A plucked guitar or violin string typically has Q in the hundreds to about 1,000, you hear dozens to hundreds of audible cycles before the note visibly fades, the string's Q kept modest by soundboard coupling and mounting losses. A tuning fork, built specifically to ring cleanly at one pitch with no comparable coupling loss, reaches a noticeably higher Q, roughly 2,000 to a few thousand. Quartz crystal resonators, the timekeeping element in ordinary watches and computer clocks, achieve Q on the order of 10,000 to several hundred thousand, and beyond a million in specialized high-precision resonators, by vibrating in a near-vacuum enclosure with almost no frictional loss, which is precisely why they hold time so precisely, the sharper the resonance, the more stable the frequency. This same Q shows up again once driven (forced) oscillators are introduced: a high-Q system not only rings for a long time when struck, it also responds with a very narrow, tall resonance peak when driven near its natural frequency, while a low-Q system responds broadly across a wide range of driving frequencies but with a much shorter, gentler peak, the same number describing both the free-decay behavior and the driven-response sharpness.

lessons.workedExample: For the recurring m = 0.50 kg, k = 200 N/m, b = 4.0 kg/s system, omega0 = 20 rad/s and gamma = 4.0 per second, so Q = omega0 / (2 gamma) = 20/8.0 = 2.5, a fairly low quality factor. Using N approximately equal to Q/pi from Lesson 4, that predicts only about 0.8 oscillations before the amplitude falls by 1/e, consistent with the earlier finding that this system's envelope drops to 37% of its starting value in barely one damped period. Contrast that with a tuning fork at Q about 2,000: the same N approximately Q/pi relation predicts roughly 640 audible oscillations before the amplitude falls by 1/e, which is exactly why a struck tuning fork rings clearly for several seconds while this oil-damped spring visibly dies within a fraction of a second.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges reach for Q to test whether a student can connect a single number to two different observable behaviors at once: how many cycles you can count before a struck system visibly quiets, and how sharp or broad its resonance peak is when driven. A good answer explains both from the same Q = omega0/(2 gamma), rather than treating "rings a long time" and "sharp resonance" as unrelated facts. A likely follow-up: why does a quartz watch crystal need a very high Q? The answer is that a sharp, stable resonance is what lets the driving circuit lock onto one precise frequency rather than drifting.

questions.prompt: A high quality factor Q corresponds to:

options.text: Heavy damping and a fast-dying oscillation
Light damping, with many visible oscillations before the amplitude decays
An oscillator with no natural frequency

explanations.a: That describes low Q, not high Q; heavy damping shrinks Q = omega0/(2 gamma) because gamma grows large.
explanations.b: Correct: high Q means gamma is small relative to omega0, so the amplitude decays slowly and many cycles remain visible.
explanations.c: Q is defined in terms of omega0 and gamma; it requires a natural frequency to exist, not the absence of one.

questions.prompt: Q = omega0 / (2 gamma) is equivalent to which energy-based definition?

options.text: 2 pi times energy stored, divided by energy lost per cycle
Energy stored multiplied by energy lost per cycle
Energy lost per cycle, divided by energy stored

explanations.a: Correct: this is the standard definition, and it reduces algebraically to omega0/(2 gamma) for a linearly damped oscillator.
explanations.b: Multiplying the two energies together does not give a dimensionless ratio and is not the definition of Q.
explanations.c: This ratio is inverted; it is proportional to 1/Q rather than Q itself.

questions.prompt: Match each system to its approximate quality factor.

right.text: Q of order 1.25 to 2.5 (deliberately underdamped: one or two quick bounces, not fully non-oscillating)
Q in the hundreds to low thousands
Q in the tens of thousands to over a million

questions.explanation: These three systems span roughly six orders of magnitude in Q: shock absorbers are engineered to be lightly underdamped so bumps die out in one or two quick bounces rather than ringing, guitar strings ring audibly for seconds, and quartz resonators are built to hold an almost undamped, extremely stable resonance.

questions.prompt: Order these systems from lowest to highest quality factor Q.

items.text: Automobile shock absorber
Guitar string
Tuning fork
Quartz crystal resonator

questions.explanation: Shock absorbers are deliberately underdamped for a controlled bounce or two rather than a harsh non-oscillating settle (Q of order 1.25 to 2.5); guitar strings ring for seconds but lose energy through soundboard coupling (Q in the hundreds to about 1,000); tuning forks are purpose-built single-mode resonators with far less coupling loss, so they out-ring a guitar string (Q roughly 2,000 to a few thousand); quartz resonators, isolated from friction in a near-vacuum, reach the highest Q of the group.

lessons.label: Logarithmic Decrement

sections.heading: Turning peak ratios into a damping measurement
sections.body: The logarithmic decrement delta is a practical bridge between what an experimenter can actually measure, the heights of successive amplitude peaks on a decaying trace, and the damping parameters (gamma, tau, Q) defined mathematically in earlier lessons. Because the envelope is a clean exponential, A(t) = A0 e^(-gamma t), the ratio of any two peaks exactly one damped period T_d apart is always the same number, regardless of which peak pair you pick: x_n / x_(n+1) = e^(gamma T_d). Taking the natural log of that constant ratio defines the logarithmic decrement, delta = ln(x_n / x_(n+1)) = gamma T_d. This is powerful precisely because it requires no knowledge of m, k, or b individually, only two peak heights and the period read directly off a recorded trace, making it one of the most common ways damping is actually measured in an undergraduate or research lab, from mechanical pendulums to electrical RLC circuits to structural vibration testing on real buildings and bridges. Once delta is known, gamma = delta / T_d follows immediately, and for lightly damped systems delta connects directly to the quality factor via delta approximately pi / Q, exact for gamma much smaller than omega0, since T_d approximately equals the undamped period in that limit.

sections.heading: Averaging over many peaks for a cleaner number
sections.body: A single pair of peaks is noisy, reading two heights off a hand-drawn or slightly jittery trace carries measurement error that a single ratio does not average away. The standard refinement is to measure n periods apart instead of one: delta_n = (1/n) ln(x0 / x_n), which divides the total logarithmic drop over n periods by n, smoothing out any single bad peak reading and typically giving a more reliable delta than the two-adjacent-peaks version. This method rests on one testable assumption: that the underlying damping really is linear (proportional to velocity), because only linear damping produces a perfectly exponential envelope with a constant peak-to-peak ratio. If a plot of ln(x_n) against n curves rather than falling in a straight line, that is itself evidence the damping law is not the simple F = -bv model, for instance, dry friction or high-speed aerodynamic drag would produce a systematically different peak-ratio pattern, not a constant one. In that sense, the logarithmic decrement doubles as both a damping measurement and a built-in consistency check on the linear-damping assumption underlying every other lesson in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: An oscillating cart on a track is filmed decaying from a push; successive peak positions are 5.00 cm and 4.00 cm, one damped period (T_d = 0.50 s) apart. The logarithmic decrement is delta = ln(5.00/4.00), about 0.223. From that, gamma = delta / T_d, about 0.446 per second. Since the damping is light, omega_d is approximately omega0 = 2 pi / T_d, about 12.57 rad/s, giving Q = omega0 / (2 gamma), about 14.1, a moderate quality factor, visible as roughly Q/pi, about 4 to 5, clearly shrinking oscillations before the cart's swing is hard to see against track friction. To sanity-check the single-peak-pair estimate, the student also reads the 5th peak at 1.55 cm and computes delta_5 = (1/5) ln(5.00/1.55), about 0.234, close to but not identical to the two-peak value, illustrating exactly why averaging over more periods, rather than trusting one pair, is the more trustworthy method when real data carries measurement noise.
lessons.judgeFraming: Logarithmic decrement is a favorite for judges because it is a genuine lab skill, not just algebra: it tests whether a student can go from a raw decaying trace to a real damping number without ever measuring b or m directly, and whether they know why averaging over several peaks (delta_n) beats trusting one adjacent pair. A sharp follow-up is what a non-straight-line ln(amplitude)-versus-cycle-number plot would mean, a student who says that would indicate the damping is not actually linear in velocity, perhaps dominated by dry friction instead, is demonstrating they understand delta as a diagnostic, not just a formula to plug numbers into.

questions.prompt: The logarithmic decrement delta is defined as:

options.text: ln(x_n / x_(n+1)), the natural log of the ratio of two successive peak amplitudes one period apart
The difference between two successive peak amplitudes
The period of oscillation

explanations.a: Correct: delta is the natural log of the ratio of consecutive peaks, which stays constant because the envelope is a clean exponential.
explanations.b: A simple subtraction of amplitudes is not constant from peak to peak and does not isolate the damping rate the way the log-ratio does.
explanations.c: The period T_d is a separate quantity, needed alongside delta to compute gamma, but it is not what delta itself measures.

questions.prompt: Why is delta_n = (1/n) ln(x0/x_n), averaged over several periods, generally preferred over a single adjacent-peak ratio?

options.text: It is required by the mathematical definition of gamma
It averages out measurement noise from any single peak reading
It removes the need to know the period

explanations.a: gamma can be computed from a single peak pair just fine mathematically; averaging is a measurement-quality choice, not a mathematical requirement.
explanations.b: Correct: spreading the log-ratio over many periods dilutes the effect of any one noisy peak reading, giving a steadier estimate.
explanations.c: The period is still needed afterward to convert delta_n into gamma; averaging over peaks does not eliminate that step.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of measuring damping in the lab using the logarithmic decrement.

items.text: Record the oscillator's decaying displacement over time
Identify the heights of successive amplitude peaks
Compute delta = ln(x_n/x_(n+1)), or average over several periods
Convert delta to gamma (and Q) using delta = gamma T_d

questions.explanation: The raw decaying trace is captured first, then peak heights are read off it, then those heights are combined into the logarithmic decrement, and only then is that number converted into the physical damping rate.

questions.prompt: Match each observed pattern in the data to what it indicates about the damping.

left.text: ln(peak amplitude) versus cycle number falls on a straight line
ln(peak amplitude) versus cycle number visibly curves
Successive peak ratios are large (large delta)

right.text: Damping is well modeled as linear (viscous), F = -bv
Damping is not simply linear in velocity, e.g. dry friction or v-squared drag dominates
Heavy damping; the envelope collapses within just a few oscillations

questions.explanation: A straight-line log-amplitude plot is the signature of a constant peak-to-peak ratio, which only linear damping produces; curvature signals a different force law; and a large delta means each cycle loses a large fraction of amplitude, the hallmark of heavy damping.

lessons.label: Forced (Driven) Oscillation

sections.heading: Adding a periodic push to the equation of motion
sections.body: Every real oscillator you have studied so far -- a mass on a spring, a pendulum -- moves on its own once displaced and released, ringing at its natural angular frequency omega_0 = sqrt(k/m). A driven oscillator adds an external periodic force to that system, so the equation of motion becomes m x'' + b x' + k x = F0 cos(omega t). The new term F0 cos(omega t) is under the experimenter's control: omega is whatever frequency you choose to push, shake, or pump the system at, and it has no obligation to match omega_0. This distinction -- drive frequency omega versus natural frequency omega_0 -- is the single most important idea in this unit, because nearly every later lesson (resonance, the amplitude curve, Q, engineering dampers) is really just asking what happens as omega is swept toward, through, and past omega_0.

sections.heading: Transient fades, steady state locks to the drive
sections.body: The full solution to that equation is a sum of two pieces. The transient is the homogeneous solution left over from however the motion started; it oscillates near the damped natural frequency omega_d = sqrt(omega_0^2 - (b/2m)^2) and its envelope decays exponentially as e^(-bt/2m), set entirely by the damping, not by the drive. The steady-state term is the particular solution forced by F0 cos(omega t), and it oscillates forever at exactly the drive frequency omega, with an amplitude and phase lag that depend on how far omega sits from omega_0. Because the transient dies out but the steady-state term does not, any driven system observed for more than a few damping time constants shows motion at the drive frequency alone -- the system's own natural pitch has been swamped by whatever frequency is being fed into it.

sections.heading: Beats during the transition, when omega is close to omega_0
sections.body: While both pieces are still present, something more interesting than a simple decay can appear: if the drive frequency omega happens to sit close to the natural frequency omega_0, the transient (oscillating near omega_0) and the steady-state term (oscillating at omega) add together as two nearly-equal-frequency sinusoids, producing a beating envelope -- the total amplitude visibly swells and shrinks at the difference frequency |omega - omega_0| while the whole pattern simultaneously decays. This is the same beat phenomenon that appears when two tuning forks of slightly different pitch are struck together, except here the "two frequencies" are the transient and the steady state of a single driven oscillator rather than two separate objects, and one of the two beating frequencies is dying out even as the beats occur, so the beating is itself a temporary feature of the approach to steady state, not a permanent one.

lessons.workedExample: A mass m = 0.50 kg on a spring with k = 50 N/m gives omega_0 = sqrt(50/0.50) = 10 rad/s (f0 ~ 1.59 Hz). Damping b = 0.50 kg/s gives an amplitude-envelope time constant tau = 2m/b = 2.0 s for the transient. The system is driven at f = 2.0 Hz (omega ~ 12.57 rad/s), off resonance. After t = 3*tau = 6.0 s, the transient's amplitude has fallen to e^(-3) ~ 5% of its starting value -- effectively gone. From that point on, a stopwatch and a strobe would show the mass oscillating at 2.0 Hz, the drive frequency, even though nothing about the spring or mass changed and the system's own natural frequency is still 1.59 Hz.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe forced oscillation because it is easy to blur natural and drive frequency into one vague idea of "the frequency." A fair judge asks what frequency the mass is oscillating at two seconds after the drive starts versus twenty seconds after, expecting the answer to change from a mix (transient + steady state) to purely the drive frequency, and expects the student to justify the shift with the damping time constant rather than a guess. A student who can also state that the transient's frequency depends on damping while the steady-state frequency depends only on the driver has correctly separated the two competing behaviors this equation contains.

questions.prompt: Long after a driven oscillator's transient has decayed away, the system oscillates at:

options.text: The natural frequency omega_0 of the mass-spring system
The drive frequency omega imposed by the external force
The damped natural frequency omega_d

explanations.a: omega_0 governs the transient's oscillation, but the transient is exactly the part that has decayed away by then.
explanations.b: Correct: the steady-state particular solution oscillates forever at the drive frequency omega, regardless of omega_0, once the transient is gone.
explanations.c: omega_d is the frequency of the decaying transient term, not of the surviving steady-state motion.

questions.prompt: Order the sequence of events after a periodic driving force is switched on for a damped oscillator initially at rest.

items.text: The driving force switches on; both a transient and a steady-state term are present
The transient's amplitude decays exponentially at a rate set by the damping
After several damping time constants, the transient becomes negligible
The motion is essentially pure steady-state oscillation at the drive frequency

questions.explanation: The transient and steady-state terms coexist from the start; damping erodes only the transient over time, leaving pure drive-frequency motion once enough time constants have passed.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to what actually sets its value.

left.text: Rate at which the transient's amplitude shrinks

right.text: The external drive frequency, omega
The damped natural frequency, omega_d
The damping coefficient b (via e^(-bt/2m))

questions.explanation: Steady-state motion tracks the driver; the transient's own oscillation frequency comes from the damped natural frequency; how fast that transient fades is set purely by the damping coefficient.

lessons.label: Resonance at the Natural Frequency

sections.heading: Why amplitude peaks near omega = omega_0
sections.body: As the drive frequency omega is swept, the steady-state amplitude A(omega) = F0 / sqrt(m^2(omega_0^2 - omega^2)^2 + b^2 omega^2) is small when omega is far from omega_0 and grows large as omega approaches omega_0 -- this buildup is resonance. The underlying reason is energetic, not just algebraic: the rate at which the driving force delivers power to the oscillator is P = F v, and power delivered over a full cycle is largest when the force F(t) and the velocity v(t) are in phase with each other, rising and falling together. At exactly omega = omega_0, the steady-state phase lag between the driving force and the displacement is 90 degrees -- and because velocity always leads displacement by 90 degrees for sinusoidal motion, a 90-degree lag between force and displacement means force and velocity are perfectly in phase. That is the condition for maximum average power input, which is why the sharpest buildup in amplitude clusters right around the natural frequency.

sections.heading: In-phase pushes add; mistimed pushes cancel
sections.body: A push timed to match the system's own rhythm adds a small increment of energy every cycle, and with only weak damping to drain it back out, that energy accumulates cycle after cycle until amplitude grows large -- exactly how a small periodic push, timed to the swing's own period, builds a large arc from a child's swing. A push at any other frequency drifts in and out of phase with the motion: sometimes it helps, sometimes it fights the velocity and removes energy, and the net work done over many cycles stays small. This is why resonance is described as the frequency at which energy transfer is most efficient, not simply the frequency at which the system happens to move a lot -- efficiency of energy input is the cause, and large amplitude is the effect.

sections.heading: A historical warning: marching feet as an accidental driver
sections.body: Resonant buildup does not require a deliberate driver; any sufficiently regular, sufficiently in-tune periodic force will do, which is why the British Army still orders troops to break step crossing a bridge. On April 12, 1831, seventy-four soldiers of the 60th Rifle Corps marched four-abreast across the Broughton Suspension Bridge near Manchester; their footfalls happened to land near the bridge's own natural frequency, and as the deck began to sway, some soldiers reportedly fell into step with the swaying rather than against it, reinforcing it further. A corner of the bridge dropped some sixteen to eighteen feet into the river below. No one died (the water was shallow), but the British Army thereafter required troops to break step on bridges, and the same lesson was learned again, far more fatally, when marching was cited as a contributing factor in the 1850 collapse of the Angers Bridge in France.

lessons.workedExample: Using the same system as the previous lesson (m = 0.50 kg, k = 50 N/m so omega_0 = 10 rad/s, b = 0.50 kg/s, F0 = 2.0 N): at resonance the steady-state amplitude is A(omega_0) = F0/(b*omega_0) = 2.0/(0.50*10) = 0.40 m. Driven instead at f = 2.0 Hz (omega ~ 12.57 rad/s, the same off-resonance case from Lesson 1), the amplitude works out to roughly 0.067 m -- about six times smaller. Nothing about the spring, mass, or driving force's strength changed between the two cases; only the timing of the push relative to the system's own rhythm did, and that timing alone accounts for the sixfold difference in how large the oscillation grows.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on resonance because students often describe it as "the frequency where amplitude is biggest" without being able to say why. A strong answer explains resonance through energy transfer -- force and velocity in phase, maximizing average power delivered per cycle -- rather than treating the amplitude formula as a black box. Expect a question like "why does pushing a swing exactly out of step with its motion fail to build amplitude, even if you push just as hard?", which tests whether the student understands that it is the phase relationship between force and velocity, not the force's strength, that determines whether energy accumulates.

questions.prompt: At resonance (drive frequency = natural frequency), the driving force and the oscillator's velocity are:

options.text: In phase with each other, maximizing average power delivered
90 degrees out of phase, minimizing power delivered
180 degrees out of phase, removing energy from the system

explanations.a: Correct: at resonance the force leads the displacement by 90 degrees, and since velocity itself leads displacement by 90 degrees, force and velocity align -- maximizing P = Fv averaged over a cycle.
explanations.b: A 90-degree lag exists between force and displacement, not between force and velocity; that specific phase relationship is what puts force and velocity in phase, not out of phase.
explanations.c: 180 degrees out of phase would mean the force actively opposes the velocity every instant, draining energy -- the opposite of what happens at resonance.

questions.prompt: A child's swing is pushed with small, equal-strength pushes. Pushing exactly in step with the swing's own period builds a large arc; pushing at a random, mismatched rhythm does not. What explains the difference?

options.text: In-step pushes are physically stronger than mismatched ones
In-step pushes stay in phase with the velocity cycle after cycle, so their work adds up instead of partially canceling
Mismatched pushes violate conservation of energy

explanations.a: The push strength (force magnitude) is stated to be the same in both cases; strength is not what differs.
explanations.b: Correct: only when pushes stay synchronized with the velocity does each one do positive work, so energy accumulates; mismatched timing means some pushes help and some fight the motion, netting little gain.
explanations.c: Energy is always conserved; mismatched pushes simply fail to add net energy efficiently, they do not violate any conservation law.

questions.prompt: Order these drive frequencies for the Lesson-1 system (omega_0 = 10 rad/s) from smallest to largest resulting steady-state amplitude.

items.text: omega = 30 rad/s (far above resonance)
omega = 12.57 rad/s (moderately above resonance)
omega = 10 rad/s (exactly at resonance)

questions.explanation: Amplitude grows as the drive frequency approaches the natural frequency and is largest exactly at resonance (omega = omega_0 = 10 rad/s); frequencies further from omega_0 produce smaller steady-state amplitude.

lessons.label: Amplitude and Phase Response Curves

sections.heading: The amplitude curve: a peak centered near omega_0
sections.body: Plotting the steady-state amplitude A(omega) = F0 / sqrt(m^2(omega_0^2 - omega^2)^2 + b^2 omega^2) against drive frequency omega produces a single peak: amplitude is small at low omega, rises to a maximum near omega_0, and falls again at high omega. For light damping the peak sits essentially at omega_0 and is tall and narrow; heavier damping shifts the peak very slightly below omega_0, and flattens and broadens it. In the limit of very strong damping the peak can disappear altogether, leaving a curve that falls monotonically as omega increases. This single curve -- built from nothing but the response of a mass-spring-damper system to a range of drive frequencies -- is the experimental signature engineers and physicists actually measure to characterize a resonant system, rather than measuring omega_0 or b directly.

sections.heading: The phase curve: a 0-to-180-degree sweep
sections.body: Alongside amplitude, the steady-state phase lag phi between the driving force and the displacement also changes systematically with omega, following tan(phi) = b*omega / (m(omega_0^2 - omega^2)), with phi running from 0 to 180 degrees. Well below resonance (omega << omega_0) the oscillator has time to follow the force almost instantly, so phi is close to 0 degrees -- displacement tracks force. Exactly at resonance (omega = omega_0) the denominator vanishes and phi = 90 degrees exactly, regardless of how much or little damping is present. Well above resonance (omega >> omega_0) the oscillator is too sluggish to keep up and ends up moving essentially opposite to the force, so phi approaches 180 degrees. The amplitude curve alone cannot distinguish a system driven just below resonance from one driven just above it, since both can sit at similar amplitude on either side of the peak; the phase curve resolves that ambiguity, because phi is below 90 degrees on one side and above 90 degrees on the other.

sections.heading: Damping steepens or softens the same 0-to-180 sweep
sections.body: The fixed point phi = 90 degrees at omega = omega_0 does not depend on damping, but how quickly phi swings from near 0 degrees to near 180 degrees around that point does. Lightly damped systems (high Q, from the next lesson) pass through the whole 0-to-180-degree range in a very narrow band of frequencies close to omega_0, so the phase curve looks almost like a vertical step at resonance; heavily damped systems spread the same 0-to-180-degree swing across a much wider range of omega, giving a gentle, gradual slope. In the lab, phase lag is commonly read off an oscilloscope by displaying the driving force on one axis and the displacement (or a proportional signal) on the other -- this produces a Lissajous figure that is a straight diagonal line when phi is 0 or 180 degrees, a perfect circle or ellipse with axes aligned to the screen when phi is 90 degrees, and a tilted ellipse at intermediate phases, giving an immediate visual readout of phi without needing to time the force and displacement peaks separately.

lessons.workedExample: Using the recurring system (m = 0.50 kg, omega_0 = 10 rad/s, b = 0.50 kg/s): at omega = 5 rad/s, tan(phi) = (0.50*5)/(0.50*(100-25)) = 2.5/37.5 = 0.067, giving phi ~ 3.8 degrees -- displacement almost tracks the force. At omega = 10 rad/s (resonance), the denominator (omega_0^2 - omega^2) is exactly zero, so phi = 90 degrees regardless of the numerator. At omega = 20 rad/s, the denominator (100-400) = -300 is negative, so phi lands past 90 degrees; working through the quadrant gives phi ~ 176 degrees -- the mass now moves almost exactly opposite to the driving force. The phase swings from near 0 degrees to near 180 degrees while sweeping omega from 5 to 20 rad/s, passing through exactly 90 degrees at resonance.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the phase curve specifically because students who have memorized "resonance = amplitude peak" often cannot say anything about phase at all. A fair probe is: "if I tell you only that the phase lag is 90 degrees, what do you know about the drive frequency?" -- testing whether the student recognizes phi = 90 degrees as the unambiguous, damping-independent signature of exact resonance, more reliable than reading an amplitude peak off a noisy graph. A student who can also explain why phase resolves the below-resonance/above-resonance ambiguity that amplitude alone cannot has demonstrated real command of the driven-oscillator picture.

questions.prompt: At exactly the resonant drive frequency (omega = omega_0), the phase lag between driving force and displacement is:

options.text: 0 degrees
90 degrees
180 degrees

explanations.a: 0 degrees describes the low-frequency limit (omega much less than omega_0), where displacement tracks the force almost instantly.
explanations.b: Correct: at omega = omega_0 the denominator of tan(phi) vanishes, fixing phi at exactly 90 degrees independent of the damping value.
explanations.c: 180 degrees describes the high-frequency limit (omega much greater than omega_0), where the oscillator moves essentially opposite to the force.

questions.prompt: Order these drive frequencies (for omega_0 = 10 rad/s) from smallest phase lag to largest.

items.text: omega = 5 rad/s
omega = 10 rad/s
omega = 20 rad/s

questions.explanation: Phase lag increases monotonically with drive frequency: near 0 degrees well below resonance, exactly 90 degrees at resonance, and approaching 180 degrees well above resonance.

questions.prompt: Match each drive-frequency regime to its approximate phase lag.

right.text: Phase lag near 0 degrees
Phase lag exactly 90 degrees
Phase lag near 180 degrees

questions.explanation: The phase lag sweeps monotonically from near 0 degrees far below resonance, through exactly 90 degrees at resonance, to near 180 degrees far above resonance.

lessons.label: Q, Sharpness, and Bandwidth

sections.heading: Q measures how sharp the resonance peak is
sections.body: The quality factor Q = m*omega_0 / b is a dimensionless number that captures, in a single figure, how pronounced a system's resonance is. High-Q systems (tuning forks and quartz crystals reach Q in the thousands to millions) have amplitude curves with a tall, narrow peak: a small change in drive frequency near omega_0 causes a large change in response. Low-Q systems (a heavily damped door closer or a car's shock absorber, with Q of order 1 or less) have a broad, shallow response curve, or none at all -- amplitude barely depends on which frequency, within a wide range, is doing the driving. Q also controls how long a system keeps ringing once the drive is removed: energy decays with time constant tau = m/b, and a high-Q system, having a long tau relative to its own oscillation period, continues oscillating audibly or visibly for many cycles before dying out, while a low-Q system stops almost immediately. This same Q can equivalently be defined without reference to bandwidth at all, as Q = 2*pi * (energy stored in the oscillation) / (energy dissipated per cycle); the two definitions -- one from the shape of the frequency response, one from energy bookkeeping in the time domain -- describe the same physical property and agree closely for the underdamped, moderate-to-high-Q systems this unit deals with, because a system that loses only a small fraction of its energy each cycle is exactly the system that can hold a sharp, well-defined resonant frequency.

sections.heading: Bandwidth: the trade-off between selectivity and robustness
sections.body: The width of the resonance peak, called the bandwidth (delta-omega, measured between the two frequencies where the response has fallen to a set fraction of its peak value), is related to Q by delta-omega = omega_0 / Q. A high Q therefore means a narrow bandwidth: the system is highly selective, responding strongly only to frequencies very close to omega_0, which is exactly the property that makes high-Q resonators useful as frequency filters -- a radio tuner's LC circuit, or a wine glass that shatters only at one particular pitch. But that same selectivity is a liability if the frequency of interest is not known precisely, or drifts: a high-Q system can almost completely miss a signal that is only slightly off-frequency, and it responds sluggishly, taking many cycles to build up or die away. A low-Q system trades away sharp selectivity for robustness -- it responds acceptably across a wide range of frequencies and settles almost instantly, which is precisely why shock absorbers and vibration isolators are deliberately built with low Q rather than high Q.

lessons.workedExample: For the recurring system (m = 0.50 kg, omega_0 = 10 rad/s, b = 0.50 kg/s), Q = m*omega_0/b = (0.50*10)/0.50 = 10. Bandwidth delta-omega = omega_0/Q = 10/10 = 1 rad/s, or about 0.16 Hz around f0 ~ 1.59 Hz -- a moderately sharp peak. Compare two extremes built from the same mass and spring: a tuning fork with Q ~ 1000 would have a bandwidth roughly 100 times narrower (about 0.0016 Hz), ringing audibly for seconds after being struck; a critically damped shock absorber with Q ~ 0.5 would show no distinct peak at all, responding almost equally across a wide range of frequencies and settling within a fraction of a cycle -- illustrating the same selectivity-versus-robustness trade-off at opposite ends of the Q scale.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use Q to test whether a student can reason about trade-offs rather than just optimizing one number. A natural probe is: "why wouldn't you just build every resonant sensor or filter with the highest Q possible?" -- the strong answer names the cost directly: narrow bandwidth means the system misses off-frequency signals and responds slowly, so high Q is only the right design choice when the frequency of interest is precisely known and stable. Expect follow-up questions asking the student to name a real system that deliberately uses low Q (a shock absorber) and one that deliberately uses high Q (a tuning fork or radio filter), and to justify each choice by its purpose.

questions.prompt: A system with very high Q, compared to one with low Q, has a resonance peak that is:

options.text: Taller and narrower, with a smaller bandwidth
Shorter and wider, with a larger bandwidth
The same shape, just centered at a different frequency

explanations.a: Correct: Q = omega_0/delta-omega, so a larger Q directly means a narrower bandwidth and, since less energy is dissipated per cycle, a taller peak.
explanations.b: This describes a LOW-Q system, the opposite of the high-Q case asked about.
explanations.c: Q changes the peak's height and width, not merely its center frequency, which is set by omega_0 independent of Q.

questions.prompt: A vibration isolator (like a shock absorber) is deliberately engineered to have LOW Q. What is the design benefit of that choice?

options.text: It responds strongly only to one very specific frequency, filtering out all others
It rings for a very long time after being disturbed, storing energy efficiently
It responds moderately and predictably across a broad range of frequencies and settles quickly, rather than resonating sharply at one

explanations.a: That describes a HIGH-Q system's sharp selectivity, the opposite of what a low-Q isolator is built for.
explanations.b: Long ringing is a hallmark of high Q (long energy-decay time constant), not the low-Q behavior an isolator needs.
explanations.c: Correct: low Q trades sharp selectivity for a broad, robust response and fast settling, avoiding a dangerous resonant buildup at any particular road or engine frequency.

questions.prompt: Match each real system to its approximate Q regime.

right.text: Very high Q (10^3 to 10^6): extremely narrow, selective response
High Q (~10^2 to 10^3): rings audibly for seconds
Low Q (~1 or less): broad, non-resonant, fast-settling response

questions.explanation: Frequency-selective devices like tuners push Q as high as possible for sharpness; a tuning fork sits in the high-but-lower range, ringing audibly; shock absorbers are deliberately built with low Q so they do not resonate at all.

lessons.label: Resonance in Engineering: Dampers and Suspension

sections.heading: Tuned mass dampers: fighting resonance with a second oscillator
sections.body: Tall buildings sway at their own natural frequency when pushed by wind gusts or earthquakes, and if that push happens to arrive rhythmically near the building's natural frequency, the same resonant buildup covered earlier in this unit can grow the sway to uncomfortable or even dangerous amplitudes. A tuned mass damper (TMD) counters this by adding a second, independent mass-spring-damper system, tuned so its own natural frequency closely matches the building's problematic sway mode. When the building sways, the TMD's mass swings in a way that lags and works against the building's motion, and its own damper bleeds that motion away as heat, pulling resonant energy out of the primary structure instead of letting it accumulate. Taipei 101, completed in 2004, carries the most famous public example: a 660-metric-ton steel sphere about 5.5 meters (18 feet) across, suspended by eight cables between roughly the 87th and 92nd floors and functioning as a giant pendulum whose cable length is tuned to match the tower's own sway period. It is reported to cut wind- and earthquake-induced sway by roughly 30 to 40 percent, and is visible to the public through the observation deck.

sections.heading: Suspension: shifting and damping resonance rather than eliminating it
sections.body: A car's suspension is also a driven-oscillator problem: the sprung mass of the car body sits on springs with a natural bounce frequency typically around 1 to 1.5 Hz, while the unsprung mass of each wheel sits on the much stiffer tire, giving a much higher "wheel hop" natural frequency, often in the 10-15 Hz range. Road bumps, expansion joints, and washboard surfaces act as a driving force at a frequency set by vehicle speed and bump spacing; if that drive frequency happened to sit near either natural frequency with too little damping, the resulting resonance could bounce the car dangerously. Shock absorbers (dashpots) add damping deliberately -- lowering the effective Q of both the body-bounce and wheel-hop modes -- which flattens and broadens the amplitude response curve exactly as in Lesson 4, trading away a small amount of ride comfort (which favors light damping) for controlled, non-resonant behavior across the whole range of speeds and road conditions a car actually encounters (which favors heavier damping). Worn or failed shock absorbers do not change the car's spring stiffness or its natural frequency at all; what they lose is precisely the damping term b, so Q silently climbs back up and the suspension becomes able to resonate again at whatever bump frequency happens to match omega_0 -- which is why a car that visibly keeps bouncing for several cycles after a single pothole, rather than settling in one or two, is a textbook sign of underdamped (high-Q) shocks rather than a spring problem.

lessons.workedExample: Model a car body as a mass-spring-damper system with a natural bounce frequency near f0 ~ 1.2 Hz. Driving over a washboard dirt road with regularly spaced ridges, a car traveling at a particular speed hits ridges at a rate that can coincide with 1.2 Hz -- exactly the resonance condition from Lesson 2. Worn-out shock absorbers (low b, hence high Q) let that coincidence build a large, uncomfortable, and unsafe bounce that can even reduce tire contact with the road. Fresh shock absorbers restore a higher b (lower Q), which -- following the bandwidth relation delta-omega = omega_0/Q from Lesson 4 -- broadens and flattens the response curve so no single washboard speed produces a dangerous resonant peak, even though the car's natural frequency of 1.2 Hz has not changed at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe engineering applications of resonance to see whether a student can connect an abstract amplitude-versus-frequency curve to a design decision with real consequences. A fair question is: "why not just make a building or a car infinitely stiff so it never resonates?" -- the strong answer explains that stiffness alone only shifts omega_0, it does not remove resonance, and that damping (controlling Q and bandwidth) is the tool that actually controls how sharply and dangerously a structure responds near whatever natural frequency it has. A student who names the Taipei 101 damper's function (opposing sway, tuned to the tower's period, dissipating energy as heat) rather than just its size shows real transfer from the physics to the engineering.

questions.prompt: A tuned mass damper reduces a building's sway primarily by:

options.text: Making the building infinitely stiff so it has no natural frequency at all
Adding a second oscillator, tuned near the building's natural sway frequency, that works against the sway and dissipates the energy
Blocking wind from reaching the building entirely

explanations.a: No real structure is infinitely stiff, and stiffness alone would only change omega_0, not eliminate resonance; the TMD works by a completely different mechanism.
explanations.b: Correct: the TMD is a second mass-spring-damper system tuned to the building's sway frequency, and its damper converts resonant energy pulled from the building into heat.
explanations.c: Wind still reaches and pushes the building; the TMD does not block the driving force, it counters and dissipates the response to it.

questions.prompt: Why do engineers add damping (via shock absorbers) to a car's suspension rather than just accepting whatever natural frequency the springs alone would give?

options.text: Damping increases the natural frequency so bumps are felt less often
Damping lowers Q, broadening and flattening the resonance response so no single road-bump frequency causes a dangerous amplitude buildup
Damping has no effect on resonance, it only affects top speed

explanations.a: Damping does not meaningfully change the natural frequency (which is set by mass and spring stiffness); its main effect is on Q and the shape of the response curve.
explanations.b: Correct: lower Q means a larger bandwidth relative to peak height -- a broader, flatter response -- so resonant buildup at any one bump frequency is suppressed.
explanations.c: Damping directly controls the sharpness of resonant response (Lesson 4's Q and bandwidth), which is very much relevant to ride safety, independent of top speed.

questions.prompt: Match each engineered system to the design goal it primarily addresses.

right.text: Counters and dissipates resonant sway energy near the structure's own natural frequency
Lowers Q to broaden the response and avoid dangerous resonant bounce
Sets the sprung mass's natural bounce frequency in the first place

questions.explanation: The TMD is a secondary resonator that opposes and drains sway energy; the shock absorber controls damping (Q) rather than frequency; the spring itself is what determines the body's natural bounce frequency.

lessons.label: Seismometers and Resonant Sensors

sections.heading: A mass that (almost) doesn't move
sections.body: A classic seismometer is a mass suspended by a spring or pendulum inside a frame that is bolted directly to the ground. When the ground shakes, the frame moves with it, but the suspended mass, by inertia, tends to lag behind -- and the key to how well it lags depends on comparing the frequency of the ground motion to the seismometer's own natural frequency omega_0. For ground-motion frequencies well above omega_0 (fast shaking relative to how quickly the mass itself would naturally oscillate), the mass behaves almost as if fixed in space while the frame and ground move underneath it, and the relative displacement measured between mass and frame -- via a coil-and-magnet or capacitive pickup -- closely tracks the actual ground displacement. Below omega_0, the mass simply follows the ground along with the frame, and the relative-motion signal used to detect shaking becomes weak. This is the same amplitude-versus-frequency relationship from Lesson 3, just read in the opposite direction: for a seismometer, the useful regime is drive frequencies well ABOVE the instrument's own omega_0.

sections.heading: Choosing omega_0 and damping for the signal you want
sections.body: To record long-period surface waves from large earthquakes, which can have periods of tens to hundreds of seconds, a seismometer needs its own natural frequency far below those signal frequencies -- historically achieved with long-period pendulum suspensions, and in modern instruments achieved electronically: broadband seismometers like the Streckeisen STS-2 use force-feedback electronics to extend the effective natural period out to roughly 120 seconds, something no practical mechanical pendulum could match. Damping is chosen deliberately near critical (a damping ratio around 0.6 to 0.7) rather than very light, which flattens the response curve near omega_0 (avoiding a false resonant peak that would distort recorded amplitudes) and lets the instrument settle quickly after a large jolt rather than ringing. Modern MEMS accelerometers, found in smartphones and used in citizen-seismology networks, use micro-machined mass-spring resonators with natural frequencies in the kilohertz range, operated in the opposite regime from a seismometer -- well BELOW their own omega_0 -- so the mass's displacement stays directly proportional to acceleration rather than showing a resonant response. The tiny suspended proof mass in a MEMS device (often just tens to hundreds of micrograms) is etched from silicon and its position is read out capacitively, through an interleaved comb of electrodes whose capacitance changes as the mass shifts; because the whole sensor is smaller than a grain of rice, its natural frequency is naturally very high, which is exactly what a below-resonance accelerometer needs -- the same fabrication constraint that makes MEMS devices cheap and mass-producible also happens to place them in the correct operating regime for phone-based earthquake detection apps.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a seismometer needs to sense surface waves with a period of about T = 20 s (f = 0.05 Hz), requiring its own natural frequency well below that, say f0 = 0.01 Hz (T0 = 100 s). A simple pendulum achieving T0 = 100 s would need a length L = g*(T0/2*pi)^2 = 9.8*(100/6.283)^2 ~ 2,480 meters -- taller than any building, and obviously impossible to build as a swinging mechanical pendulum. This is exactly why real broadband instruments abandon a long mechanical pendulum in favor of force-feedback electronics: a short, stiff mechanical spring paired with an electronic feedback loop can synthesize the same very-low effective natural frequency (and the flat, high-fidelity response above it) without needing a two-and-a-half-kilometer pendulum arm.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about seismometer design because it forces a student to apply the amplitude-and-phase relationships from earlier lessons in an unfamiliar direction -- choosing omega_0 relative to a target signal frequency rather than avoiding resonance. A sharp question is: "why would a smartphone's accelerometer and a broadband seismometer choose opposite relationships between their own natural frequency and the frequencies they measure?" A strong answer explains that a seismometer needs signal frequencies ABOVE omega_0 so the mass stays inertially still, while an accelerometer needs signal frequencies BELOW its own omega_0 so displacement tracks acceleration proportionally rather than resonating -- the same physics, deliberately exploited in two different regimes for two different jobs.

questions.prompt: For a mechanical seismometer to accurately record ground motion at a given frequency, that ground-motion frequency should be:

options.text: Well above the seismometer's own natural frequency omega_0, so the suspended mass stays nearly still in space
Exactly equal to omega_0, so resonance amplifies the signal
Well below omega_0, so the mass follows the ground exactly

explanations.a: Correct: in that regime the mass is essentially inertially fixed while the frame moves with the ground, so the relative displacement recorded closely tracks true ground motion.
explanations.b: Driving right at resonance would distort recorded amplitudes rather than faithfully reproducing them, which is why seismometers are damped to avoid a sharp resonant peak.
explanations.c: If the mass follows the ground exactly, there is no relative motion between mass and frame to measure, and the instrument records almost nothing.

questions.prompt: Why do modern broadband seismometers use electronic force-feedback instead of simply building a very long mechanical pendulum to get a very low natural frequency?

options.text: A pendulum long enough for a ~100-second natural period would need to be on the order of kilometers long, which is impractical
Mechanical pendulums cannot have a natural frequency at all
Electronic feedback is simply cheaper, with no physical advantage

explanations.a: Correct: T0 = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) means a ~100 s period needs L on the order of 2,500 m, far beyond what any physical pendulum suspension could achieve.
explanations.b: Mechanical pendulums absolutely have a natural frequency, set by their length; the issue is that a sufficiently low one is physically impractical to build.
explanations.c: The advantage is physical, not merely economic: feedback electronically synthesizes an effective natural frequency no reasonably sized mechanical pendulum could reach.

questions.prompt: Match each sensor to the frequency regime it deliberately operates in, relative to its own natural frequency omega_0.

left.text: Broadband seismometer, sensing long-period surface waves

right.text: Signal frequencies well ABOVE omega_0 (mass stays inertially still)
Signal frequencies well BELOW omega_0 (displacement tracks acceleration proportionally)

questions.explanation: A seismometer needs a very low omega_0 so target earthquake frequencies sit above it, keeping the mass inertially still; an accelerometer needs a much higher omega_0 so its operating frequencies sit below it, keeping response proportional rather than resonant.

lessons.label: Tacoma Narrows: Resonance or Flutter?

sections.heading: The collapse
sections.body: The original Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State opened on July 1, 1940, and quickly earned the nickname "Galloping Gertie" for the vertical undulations, sometimes several feet high, that rippled along its deck even in modest winds -- motion engineers had noticed but judged tolerable. On the morning of November 7, 1940, sustained winds of roughly 40-42 mph produced the usual vertical rippling, but around 11:00 a.m. the motion abruptly transformed into a violent torsional (twisting) oscillation, with the deck rotating as much as 45 degrees from one edge to the other. That twisting mode tore at the structure for roughly an hour before the center span broke apart and fell into the water below. No one died in the collapse itself (a dog left in a car was the only casualty), but the dramatic newsreel footage made it one of the most widely studied structural failures in engineering history.

sections.heading: The textbook explanation: simple resonance
sections.body: For decades after the collapse, introductory physics and engineering textbooks presented Tacoma Narrows as a clean, dramatic illustration of exactly the kind of forced resonance covered earlier in this unit: wind blowing at a frequency that happened to match the bridge's natural torsional frequency, pumping in energy cycle after cycle just as a well-timed push builds a swing's amplitude, until the response grew catastrophically large. This story is appealing precisely because it maps so directly onto the F0 cos(omega t) driven-oscillator model from Lesson 1 -- a single external periodic force locked onto omega_0.

sections.heading: The modern understanding: self-excited aeroelastic flutter
sections.body: In a 1991 paper in the American Journal of Physics ("Resonance, Tacoma Narrows bridge failure, and undergraduate physics textbooks"), engineers K. Yusuf Billah and Robert Scanlan argued that the simple-resonance story is physically wrong, and had been propagated uncritically through textbooks for fifty years. Real wind on November 7, 1940 was fairly steady, not oscillating periodically at any particular frequency the way an idealized F0 cos(omega t) driver does, so there was no external rhythm to match. What actually destroyed the bridge was aeroelastic flutter: a self-excited instability in which the deck's own twisting motion changes the aerodynamic forces the wind exerts on it, and above a critical wind speed that feedback loop effectively supplies negative aerodynamic damping -- the airflow does net positive work on the twisting motion rather than resisting it, so any small twist is reinforced and grows, even under a wind that is not itself periodic. Flutter and forced resonance can look similar (both produce runaway growing amplitude at a specific natural frequency) but they are mechanistically distinct: resonance needs an external periodic driver matched to omega_0, while flutter is fed by the structure's own motion feeding back into the force acting on it.

lessons.workedExample: Contrast two everyday analogues. A child's swing pushed by a person at the same instant each cycle is classic forced resonance: the periodic external driver (the push) is matched to the swing's own period, exactly the F0 cos(omega t) model from Lesson 1. A bowed violin string is closer to flutter: the bow does not push periodically at the string's natural frequency; instead, a steady bow motion combined with stick-slip friction feedback between bow and string self-excites a sustained oscillation at the string's natural frequency. Modern bridge design reflects the flutter lesson directly: engineers now test scale models of proposed deck cross-sections in wind tunnels to find the critical flutter onset wind speed, rather than only checking whether the bridge's natural frequency might coincide with a periodic gust frequency.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Tacoma Narrows specifically because the "simple resonance" story is so widely known that repeating it, unexamined, is a red flag for surface-level science. A fair judge asks the student to name the actual mechanism (aeroelastic flutter, not forced resonance) and to explain the physical distinction: flutter is a self-excited, feedback-driven instability sustained by fairly steady wind, while forced resonance strictly requires an external periodic driving force tuned to the natural frequency. A student who can also cite that this correction traces to Billah and Scanlan's 1991 paper, and that engineers responded by wind-tunnel-testing deck cross-sections for flutter onset, shows they engaged with the real history rather than the simplified textbook version.

questions.prompt: According to the modern engineering understanding (Billah and Scanlan, 1991), the Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse is best explained as:

options.text: Classic forced resonance, where a periodically oscillating wind force matched the bridge's natural frequency
Aeroelastic flutter, a self-excited instability where the deck's own twisting motion fed back into the aerodynamic forces acting on it
A simple material defect in the steel cables, unrelated to oscillation

explanations.a: This is the traditional textbook story Billah and Scanlan specifically challenged; the wind on the day of collapse was fairly steady, not periodic at a matching frequency.
explanations.b: Correct: flutter is a feedback instability where the structure's own motion alters the aerodynamic forces on it, allowing runaway growth even under fairly steady wind.
explanations.c: The failure was a dynamic instability in the deck's response to wind, not a static material or cable defect.

questions.prompt: What is the key physical difference between forced resonance and aeroelastic flutter, even though both can produce runaway growing amplitude?

options.text: There is no real difference; they are two names for the same phenomenon

Forced resonance requires an external periodic force matched to omega_0; flutter is sustained by feedback between the structure's own motion and the forces acting on it, without needing a periodic external driver
Flutter only happens underwater, never in air

explanations.a: They are mechanistically distinct even though both can produce large, growing amplitude -- one needs a matched external periodic drive, the other is self-sustaining through feedback.
explanations.b: Correct: this is precisely the distinction Billah and Scanlan drew, and why calling Tacoma Narrows simple resonance is now considered a physics misconception.
explanations.c: Aeroelastic flutter is named for its role in aerodynamics (airflow feedback) and occurs in air, including on aircraft wings and long-span bridges; it is not restricted to water.

questions.prompt: Order the events of November 7, 1940 at the Tacoma Narrows Bridge.

items.text: Sustained wind of roughly 40-42 mph produces the bridge's usual vertical rippling motion
The motion abruptly transitions into violent torsional (twisting) oscillation
The deck twists as much as 45 degrees and tears at the structure for about an hour
The center span breaks apart and falls into the water

questions.explanation: The bridge's familiar vertical undulation preceded the sudden shift into torsional flutter, which then progressively damaged the structure until the center span finally failed.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to the description that fits it.

right.text: Amplitude grows because an external periodic force is tuned to the system's natural frequency
Amplitude grows because the structure's own motion feeds back into the force acting on it, under fairly steady driving conditions
American Journal of Physics paper correcting the widespread textbook explanation of the 1940 collapse

questions.explanation: Forced resonance depends on a matched external periodic driver; flutter is a self-excited feedback instability that needs no periodic driver; Billah and Scanlan's 1991 paper is the source of the modern correction to the simple-resonance textbook story.

lessons.label: Galileo and Pendulum Isochronism

sections.heading: A Swinging Lamp in Pisa Cathedral
sections.body: The story goes that a young Galileo, around 1583 and supposedly a bored medical student, watched an oil lamp swinging in Pisa Cathedral and timed its swings against his own pulse, noticing that as the arc decayed the time per swing stayed roughly the same. Like the more famous Leaning Tower drop, this vivid anecdote comes only from a biography written decades later by Galileo's secretary, Vincenzo Viviani, not from anything Galileo himself wrote down. Historians treat it with the same caution they give the tower story: charming, plausible, and unverifiable. What is not legend is the physical claim Galileo actually tested, refined, and published.

sections.heading: The Law of the Pendulum
sections.body: Galileo's documented contribution appears in Two New Sciences (1638): a pendulum's period depends on the square root of its length and is essentially independent of both the bob's mass and, for the modest swing angles he could time by hand, its amplitude, a property he called "isochronism." He supported this by comparing pendulums of equal length but different weight, and by timing swings of different but modest amplitude against each other and against his own pulse, finding no detectable difference within the precision available to him.

sections.heading: An Idealization, and an Unbuilt Clock
sections.body: Isochronism is only approximately true. For small swing angles the period is very nearly constant, but as amplitude grows the true period lengthens measurably, a fact Galileo's pulse-timing could not have caught but calculus later would. In 1641, blind and confined under Inquisition-ordered house arrest in his final year, Galileo dictated a design for a pendulum-regulated clock to his son Vincenzo, but his son Vincenzo lost enthusiasm for the project after Galileo's death in 1642 and did not resume it for years; not until 1649 did he begin construction, a build that itself stalled, unfinished, when Vincenzo died later that same year. The idea remained proven in principle but unbuilt, until a Dutch mathematician picked it up.

lessons.workedExample: The small-angle period is T0 = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g); for L = 1 m, T0 is about 2.01 s. At a 15-degree swing, the true period differs from T0 by just under half a percent (about 0.4%), undetectable by pulse-timing, which is why Galileo could reasonably believe isochronism was exact. At a 90-degree swing, though, the true period is about 18% longer than T0, roughly 2.37 s instead of 2.01 s, a gap a modern stopwatch or photogate catches easily but Galileo's methods never could. This is the concrete boundary of his claim: correct and useful at small amplitude, measurably wrong at large amplitude.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges test this because it is the clean case of an idealization mistaken for an exact law: Galileo's isochronism is right to within his instruments' precision but wrong as amplitude grows, and a fair judge wants a student who states both halves, the correct small-angle behavior and the amplitude-dependent correction, rather than treating "isochronism" as an absolute truth. A student who can also explain that the swinging-lamp story itself is uncorroborated legend, distinct from the small-angle law he actually published and tested, demonstrates the same source-literacy this unit rewards throughout.

questions.prompt: What did Galileo actually establish about a pendulum's period, and to what precision does it hold?

options.text: For small swing angles, period depends on length (not mass) and amplitude has almost no effect; the amplitude-independence breaks down measurably at large angles
The period is exactly independent of amplitude at any swing angle, an exact law with no exceptions
The period depends primarily on the mass of the bob, with length as a secondary factor

explanations.a: Correct: Galileo's published law is a small-angle result; at large amplitude the true period grows measurably longer than his prediction.
explanations.b: Wrong: exactness at every amplitude is false. The true period lengthens noticeably at large swing angles (about 18% longer at 90 degrees).
explanations.c: Wrong: a simple pendulum's period is independent of the bob's mass; it depends on length and gravity, not mass.

questions.prompt: Order these events in Galileo's engagement with the pendulum.

items.text: Galileo reportedly times a swinging cathedral lamp against his pulse (traditionally dated to around 1583, per Viviani's later biography)
Galileo publishes the length-dependent, near-amplitude-independent law of the pendulum in Two New Sciences (1638)
Galileo, blind and under house arrest, dictates a pendulum clock design to his son Vincenzo (1641)
Galileo dies before the clock is built (1642)

questions.explanation: The cathedral-lamp anecdote is dated earliest in Galileo's life; the formal law came decades later in his 1638 book; the clock design followed in 1641, near the very end of his life; his death in 1642 left the clock unbuilt.

questions.prompt: Match each claim about Galileo's pendulum work to its correct status.

left.text: Small-angle period independent of amplitude and mass
Period stays exactly constant at any amplitude, even 90 degrees

right.text: Legend from Viviani's biography, not from Galileo's own writings
Verified law published in Two New Sciences (1638)
False; the true period grows with amplitude, about 18% longer at 90 degrees than the small-angle prediction

questions.explanation: The lamp story is unverified legend; the small-angle law is Galileo's real, published, and tested result; exact amplitude-independence at all angles is false, since real pendulum period grows with swing angle.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't Galileo detect that a pendulum's period actually depends slightly on amplitude?

options.text: His hand and pulse timing precision was far coarser than the small percentage differences involved at the modest amplitudes he tested
He deliberately avoided testing large amplitudes because he suspected the law would fail
Amplitude has literally zero effect on period at any angle, so there was nothing to detect

explanations.a: Correct: at the modest amplitudes achievable by hand, the true correction is well under 1%, far below what pulse-timing could resolve.
explanations.b: Wrong: there is no evidence Galileo avoided large-amplitude tests out of suspicion; his instruments simply could not resolve the effect at any amplitude he used.
explanations.c: Wrong: amplitude does affect period at large angles; the effect is real and measurable, just too small to catch with 17th-century pulse-timing at modest amplitude.

lessons.label: Huygens and the Pendulum Clock

sections.heading: From Verge-and-Foliot to Pendulum
sections.body: Before Huygens, mechanical clocks used verge-and-foliot escapements with no natural timekeeping element built in, and they drifted badly, commonly losing or gaining up to about 15 minutes a day, far too imprecise for serious astronomical timing. Christiaan Huygens, working with clockmaker Salomon Coster in The Hague, applied Galileo's pendulum principle to a working escapement and had a functioning pendulum clock built in 1656, patented in the Netherlands in 1657. Accuracy jumped roughly sixtyfold, down to about 15 seconds a day.

sections.heading: Horologium Oscillatorium (1673)
sections.body: Huygens's major treatise, published in 1673, went far beyond a workshop notebook. It gave a rigorous mathematical theory of pendulum motion, including the physical (compound) pendulum, defined the "center of oscillation" as the length of an equivalent simple pendulum for a real, extended swinging body, and formalized, with the mathematics of evolutes and involutes, the tautochrone result and cycloidal-cheek design Huygens had actually worked out over a decade earlier, around 1659-1661.

sections.heading: Cycloidal Cheeks and True Isochronism
sections.body: Huygens proved mathematically that Galileo's isochronism is only a small-angle approximation for a circular arc: a pendulum bob swinging on a circle takes measurably longer at large amplitude. He then solved a stronger version of the problem, finding the one curve whose descent time is exactly independent of starting point, the tautochrone, and proving it is a cycloid. Because the evolute of a cycloid is another cycloid, he built clocks whose suspension string was flanked by curved metal "cheeks" shaped like a cycloid; as the string swung, it wrapped against the cheeks, forcing the bob to trace a cycloidal path rather than a circular arc, making its period genuinely constant regardless of amplitude, in principle even for wide swings, not just Galileo's small ones.

lessons.workedExample: The classic "seconds pendulum," whose half-swing takes exactly 1 s so its full period is T = 2 s, needs a length L = g*(T/2*pi)^2 = 9.8*(2/6.283)^2, about 0.993 m (roughly 39 inches), long used as a reference length standard. In practice, Huygens's escapement already limited swings to just a few degrees, where circular-arc error is under 1%, so the cheeks gave more theoretical elegance than everyday accuracy gain. What they did prove was that the tautochrone problem had a real, buildable solution, a result that fed directly into the calculus of variations that followed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Huygens's cheeks because they test whether a student separates an engineering fix from its practical payoff: the cycloidal cheeks are a mathematically exact solution to amplitude-dependence, yet real escapements already kept swings small enough that circular-arc error was tiny, so the practical accuracy gain was modest. A strong answer separates "Huygens proved true isochronism is achievable in principle, via the cycloid and the tautochrone problem" from "the cheeks meaningfully improved his clocks' day-to-day accuracy": the historical driver of the roughly sixtyfold accuracy jump was coupling a natural pendulum oscillator to the escapement in the first place, not the cheeks.

questions.prompt: What mathematical curve did Huygens prove is the true tautochrone (equal-descent-time curve), leading to the cycloidal cheeks?

options.text: A cycloid
A circle
A parabola

explanations.a: Correct: Huygens proved the cycloid is the tautochrone, and since its evolute is another cycloid, cycloidal cheeks force a swinging bob onto that exact curve.
explanations.b: Wrong: a circular arc is what an ordinary pendulum swings on, and that path is exactly what causes amplitude-dependent period, the problem the cheeks were built to fix.
explanations.c: Wrong: the parabola is not the tautochrone solution; Huygens's proof specifically identifies the cycloid.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the development of the pendulum clock.

items.text: Pre-Huygens verge-and-foliot clocks drift by up to about 15 minutes a day
Huygens and clockmaker Salomon Coster build the first working pendulum clock (1656)
Huygens proves the cycloid is the tautochrone curve and adds cycloidal cheeks to his clocks
Huygens publishes the full mathematical theory in Horologium Oscillatorium (1673)

questions.explanation: Poor pre-existing clock accuracy motivated the 1656 pendulum clock; the cycloidal-cheeks refinement followed as Huygens worked out the amplitude-dependence problem; the full published theory came last, in 1673.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Huygens's pendulum theory to its correct definition.

right.text: Length of an equivalent simple pendulum for a real, extended (physical) pendulum
Curve on which descent time is independent of starting point, proven to be a cycloid
Curved metal guides that force a swinging string to trace a cycloid, making period amplitude-independent

questions.explanation: Center of oscillation reduces a real pendulum's motion to an equivalent simple pendulum length; the tautochrone is the equal-time curve Huygens proved to be a cycloid; the cheeks are the physical mechanism that imposes that cycloidal path.

questions.prompt: What was the main practical driver of Huygens's roughly sixtyfold accuracy improvement over pre-pendulum clocks?

options.text: Coupling a natural pendulum oscillator, whose period is set by length and gravity, to the escapement, rather than relying on an escapement with no natural timekeeping element
The cycloidal cheeks, since without them the clock would have been no more accurate than a verge-and-foliot clock
Huygens's use of a heavier pendulum bob, since heavier pendulums keep time more accurately

explanations.a: Correct: the pendulum itself, with its length-set natural frequency, is what gave the escapement a stable timekeeping reference; the cheeks were a later, secondary refinement.
explanations.b: Wrong: the cheeks came after the accuracy jump already existed from coupling the pendulum to the escapement, and at the small swing angles used, circular-arc error was already under 1%.
explanations.c: Wrong: a simple pendulum's period does not depend on bob mass; only its length and local gravity set the period.

lessons.label: Hooke's Law and the Spring

sections.heading: An Anagram to Protect Priority
sections.body: Robert Hooke, who would become the Royal Society's Curator of Experiments, had worked out the linear relationship between a spring's stretch and the force it exerts by around 1660, but delayed full publication while he explored applications to clocks, watches, and instruments, and wanted to establish priority without handing competitors the finished result. In 1676, in an appendix to a book on telescope design (A Description of Helioscopes), he published the finding only as the scrambled anagram "ceiiinosssttuv," a common 17th-century tactic for claiming a discovery date without disclosing its content. Two years later, in De Potentia Restitutiva, or Of Spring (1678), he revealed the solution: "Ut tensio, sic vis," Latin for "as the extension, so the force."

sections.heading: The Linear Restoring Force
sections.body: In modern notation, Hooke's law is F = -kx: the force a spring exerts is proportional to its displacement x from equilibrium and directed opposite that displacement, hence restoring, with k the spring constant in newtons per meter. This is precisely the force law that, combined with Newton's second law F = ma, generates simple harmonic motion: it produces the differential equation whose solution is sinusoidal motion with angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m), independent of amplitude, the same amplitude-independence Galileo found empirically for pendulums, now derived from an exact force law rather than observed within instrument precision.

sections.heading: Where the Law Breaks
