sections.body: Hooke's law is not a universal law of nature; it is the leading-order, linear approximation to how real elastic materials behave, valid only up to a material's proportional (elastic) limit. Stretch a spring gently and release it, and it returns to its original length; stretch it past the elastic limit and it deforms permanently, the force-extension curve bends away from a straight line, and F = -kx no longer applies. Every real oscillator, a spring, a guitar string, a diving board, is Hooke's-law linear only within some restricted amplitude range, a theme that returns when oscillators are pushed into their nonlinear regime.

lessons.workedExample: A spring with k = 200 N/m holds a mass of 0.50 kg. Its angular frequency is omega = sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(400) = 20 rad/s, giving a period T = 2*pi/omega, about 0.314 s, and frequency f, about 3.18 Hz. Separately, checking Hooke's law directly: a 10 N force applied to this spring should stretch it x = F/k = 10/200 = 0.05 m (5 cm). If the measured stretch instead came out as 7 cm under that same 10 N, that mismatch would signal the spring has moved past its elastic limit into a nonlinear regime, where k = 200 N/m no longer describes its behavior.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about Hooke's law because it is the single force law underlying essentially all of simple harmonic motion, so a student needs to state it correctly (F = -kx, restoring, linear) and know its history, the anagram and the 1678 decoding, without conflating "Hooke's law" with a universal law of elasticity. The sharper follow-up a judge often asks is what happens past the elastic limit: a student who can say the restoring force stops being linear, the SHM equations stop applying, and the oscillator's frequency becomes amplitude-dependent shows they understand SHM as a regime, not a fact about all springs.

questions.prompt: What does "Ut tensio, sic vis," the phrase Hooke published in 1678, assert?

options.text: The restoring force of a spring is proportional to its extension
The period of oscillation is proportional to the square root of mass
Tension in a string is inversely proportional to its length

explanations.a: Correct: "as the extension, so the force" is the Latin statement of the linear force-extension law now written F = -kx.
explanations.b: Wrong: that statement describes a period-mass relationship, not what Hooke's phrase asserts about force and extension.
explanations.c: Wrong: Hooke's phrase is about force being proportional to extension, not an inverse relationship with string length.

questions.prompt: Why did Hooke first publish his 1660 discovery only as the anagram "ceiiinosssttuv" in 1676?

options.text: To establish priority for the discovery by date while withholding its actual content from rivals
Because the Royal Society required all findings to be submitted in coded form
Because he had not yet worked out the relationship and the anagram was a placeholder

explanations.a: Correct: publishing a scrambled anagram was a recognized 17th-century way to timestamp a discovery without revealing it, protecting priority while Hooke kept developing applications.
explanations.b: Wrong: this was not a Royal Society requirement; it was Hooke's individual choice to protect his own priority claim.
explanations.c: Wrong: Hooke had already worked out the linear relationship around 1660, well before the 1676 anagram publication; he was withholding a finished result, not stalling an unfinished one.

questions.prompt: Order these events in Hooke's spring law and its consequences.

items.text: Hooke works out the linear force-extension relationship for springs (around 1660)
Hooke publishes it only as the scrambled anagram "ceiiinosssttuv" (1676)
Hooke reveals the solution, "Ut tensio, sic vis," in De Potentia Restitutiva (1678)
The linear law F = -kx is combined with F = ma to derive simple harmonic motion with omega = sqrt(k/m)

questions.explanation: Hooke's private discovery came first, followed by the coded anagram, then the plain-language 1678 reveal; only once the force law was public could it be combined with Newton's second law to derive the SHM equation.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Hooke's law and its consequences to its correct description.

right.text: Hooke's law: restoring force proportional to displacement, valid within the elastic limit
Force-extension curve bends nonlinear; deformation becomes permanent (plastic)
Angular frequency of the resulting simple harmonic motion, amplitude-independent within the linear regime

questions.explanation: F = -kx is the linear restoring force itself; exceeding the elastic limit is exactly where that linearity fails and permanent deformation begins; omega = sqrt(k/m) is the amplitude-independent frequency that follows from the linear law while it holds.

lessons.label: Barton's Pendulums and Resonant Coupling

sections.heading: A Driver and a Row of Followers
sections.body: Barton's pendulums, a classroom apparatus associated with the early-20th-century British physicist Edwin H. Barton, consists of one heavy "driver" pendulum swinging from a rigid support, its string or rod also carrying a horizontal cord from which several lighter "follower" pendulums of different lengths hang, often light paper cones or small bobs chosen so their own damping stays small. As the driver swings, it tugs the shared cord back and forth, forcing every follower to oscillate at the driver's frequency rather than each one's own natural frequency.

sections.heading: Amplitude Peaks Where Length Matches
sections.body: Because a simple pendulum's natural frequency depends only on its length, f0 = (1/2*pi)*sqrt(g/L), independent of mass, the follower whose length equals the driver's length has a natural frequency equal to the driving frequency: it is driven exactly at resonance, and its steady-state amplitude grows far larger than any of the others, visibly dwarfing followers whose lengths are shorter or longer. The mismatched followers still move, forced at the driver's frequency, but with far smaller amplitude, the classic amplitude-response curve of a driven, damped oscillator, peaked sharply at resonance and falling off on either side.

sections.heading: Phase Tells the Rest of the Story
sections.body: Amplitude is only half of what the demonstration reveals; phase is the other half. A follower much shorter than the driver, with natural frequency well above the driving frequency, swings essentially in phase with the driver. A follower much longer, with natural frequency well below the driving frequency, swings essentially out of phase, moving opposite the driver at each instant. The resonant follower, whose length matches, lags the driver by about a quarter cycle (90 degrees) at peak amplitude. This full amplitude-and-phase picture is the general signature of any driven, damped oscillator, whether a pendulum, a bridge deck, or an electrical circuit, which is why the demonstration is taught well beyond mechanics courses.

lessons.workedExample: A driver pendulum of length L_d = 1.00 m has natural (and driving) frequency f0 = (1/2*pi)*sqrt(9.8/1.00), about 0.498 Hz, period about 2.01 s. A follower cut to the same 1.00 m length is driven exactly at its own resonance and swings with the largest amplitude in the row, lagging the driver by about a quarter period (roughly 0.5 s). A follower cut to 0.25 m has its own natural frequency f = (1/2*pi)*sqrt(9.8/0.25), about 0.997 Hz, roughly double the driving frequency, so it is driven well off resonance and shows only a small, nearly in-phase wobble. A follower's response is set entirely by how close its own length puts it to the driver's frequency, not by matching mass or amplitude.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use Barton's pendulums to test whether a student separates two things people conflate: matching natural frequency, set purely by pendulum length via f0 = (1/2*pi)*sqrt(g/L), drives large resonant response, while matching mass or bob size does nothing. A sharp judge asks what happens to a follower whose length does not match, expecting an answer about both reduced amplitude and a phase shift, not just "it moves less," and may ask why this exact same math, a peaked, phase-shifting amplitude-response curve, reappears for driven oscillators far outside pendulums, setting up the resonance-versus-flutter distinction the next lesson turns on.

questions.prompt: In Barton's pendulums, which follower shows the largest steady-state amplitude?

options.text: The one whose length matches the driver pendulum's length, because its natural frequency equals the driving frequency
The one with the heaviest bob, because more mass responds more strongly to the driving force
The shortest follower, because shorter pendulums always swing with larger amplitude

explanations.a: Correct: matching length matches natural frequency to the driving frequency, putting that follower exactly at resonance, which is where amplitude peaks.
explanations.b: Wrong: a simple pendulum's natural frequency does not depend on bob mass, so mass alone does not determine which follower resonates.
explanations.c: Wrong: shorter followers are not automatically larger in amplitude; a short follower is only large if its length happens to match the driver's length.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning behind why one follower swings much larger than the rest.

items.text: The driver pendulum swings, forcing every follower via the shared cord to oscillate at the driver's frequency
Each follower's own natural frequency is set only by its length, f0 = (1/2*pi)*sqrt(g/L)
The follower whose length matches the driver's is driven exactly at its own resonance
That follower's steady-state amplitude grows much larger than the others, while lagging the driver by about a quarter cycle

questions.explanation: The driver first imposes a common driving frequency on every follower; each follower's own natural frequency then depends only on its length; the length-matched follower ends up driven at resonance; and resonance is what produces its outsized, phase-lagged amplitude.

questions.prompt: Match each follower's length, relative to the driver, to its resulting phase behavior.

left.text: Much shorter than driver (natural frequency well above driving frequency)
Much longer than driver (natural frequency well below driving frequency)

right.text: Swings essentially in phase with the driver
Lags the driver by about a quarter cycle (90 degrees), largest amplitude
Swings essentially out of phase (opposite the driver)

questions.explanation: A driven oscillator's phase lag relative to its driving force grows from near zero well below resonance, to a quarter cycle exactly at resonance, to nearly a half cycle well above resonance, which maps directly onto the shorter, matched, and longer followers.

questions.prompt: Why does a pendulum's mass not affect which follower resonates in Barton's demonstration?

options.text: A simple pendulum's natural frequency f0 = (1/2*pi)*sqrt(g/L) depends only on length and g, not on the bob's mass
Mass does affect resonance, but the effect is too small to observe in a classroom demonstration
All followers in the apparatus are built with identical mass by design, so mass cannot be tested

explanations.a: Correct: the simple-pendulum period formula has no mass term at all, so resonance is governed purely by length.
explanations.b: Wrong: mass does not merely have a small effect; for an ideal simple pendulum it has exactly zero effect on natural frequency.
explanations.c: Wrong: followers are typically built with different, not identical, masses (light paper cones or small bobs), and the demonstration works regardless of those mass differences.

lessons.label: The Tacoma Narrows Debate Revisited

sections.heading: Galloping Gertie Comes Down
sections.body: The original Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State earned the nickname "Galloping Gertie" for the vertical undulations it developed in modest winds soon after opening in July 1940. On November 7, 1940, in a sustained wind of roughly 40 mph, those vertical undulations gave way to a violent twisting, torsional motion of the roadway, one edge rising as the other fell, and the amplitude grew until the deck tore apart and the center span collapsed into the water below. No people died, though a dog left in a car on the bridge did not survive.

sections.heading: The Textbook Story: Simple Resonance
sections.body: For decades afterward, physics and engineering textbooks explained the collapse as classic resonance: wind blowing past the deck was said to shed vortices at a frequency that happened to match the bridge's natural torsional frequency, pumping in energy cycle after cycle the way a marching column in step can amplify a footbridge's sway, until the amplitude became destructive. It is a tidy, visual, easy-to-teach story, and Barton's-pendulums-style resonance is a genuinely real phenomenon, part of why the explanation stuck for so long.

sections.heading: The Engineering Consensus: Self-Excited Flutter
sections.body: The tidy story is wrong in its mechanism. A widely cited 1991 American Journal of Physics paper by K. Yusuf Billah and Robert Scanlan, "Resonance, Tacoma Narrows Bridge Failure, and Undergraduate Physics Textbooks," laid out the engineering consensus that had already formed among bridge aerodynamicists: the bridge's solid, H-shaped plate-girder deck was aerodynamically unstable, so that as the deck twisted even slightly, the resulting change in airflow around it produced an aerodynamic torque that pushed the twist further in the same direction, a self-reinforcing feedback loop called negative aerodynamic damping. This is self-excited aeroelastic flutter: the growing oscillation is driven by the motion's own effect on the airflow, not by an external wind force oscillating at a matching frequency. The observed torsional oscillation settled near roughly 0.2 Hz just before failure, a frequency the flutter mechanism itself selected, not one the wind was independently vibrating at.

lessons.workedExample: Contrast the two mechanisms concretely. In true forced resonance, as in Barton's pendulums, an external periodic force at frequency f drives a system, and amplitude peaks specifically when f equals the system's natural frequency f0; change the driving frequency and the large response goes away. In self-excited flutter, there is no fixed external driving frequency to tune: a steady wind, not a periodic gust train, supplies energy, and the bridge's own twisting motion continuously reshapes the airflow to keep reinforcing itself, so growth persists at whatever frequency the coupled structure-airflow system naturally settles into, about 0.2 Hz for Tacoma Narrows, so long as wind speed stays above a critical "flutter speed." Below that speed the feedback is stabilizing; above it, any small disturbance grows without needing a matching external frequency at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges return to Tacoma Narrows because it is the clearest case in this unit of a superficially plausible but mechanistically wrong explanation persisting in textbooks for decades, and a fair judge wants the correction stated precisely, not just repeated as "it wasn't resonance." A strong answer names the actual mechanism, self-excited aeroelastic flutter via negative aerodynamic damping, the source of the corrected consensus, Billah and Scanlan's 1991 paper, and the concrete distinction that separates it from resonance: flutter needs no external periodic forcing at a matching frequency, only a steady wind above a critical speed and a structure whose own motion destabilizes the airflow around it.

questions.prompt: What is the modern engineering consensus on why the original Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed in 1940?

options.text: Self-excited aeroelastic flutter: the deck's own twisting motion reshaped the airflow in a way that reinforced further twisting, without needing a wind frequency matched to the bridge's natural frequency
Classic forced resonance: wind vortex shedding happened to match the bridge's natural torsional frequency and pumped in energy like a marching column in step
A manufacturing defect in the suspension cables that had nothing to do with aerodynamics

explanations.a: Correct: Billah and Scanlan's 1991 paper documents the engineering consensus that self-excited flutter, not matched-frequency resonance, caused the collapse.
explanations.b: Wrong: this is the long-taught textbook oversimplification the engineering literature has since corrected; it misidentifies the mechanism as forced resonance rather than self-excited flutter.
explanations.c: Wrong: the failure mechanism was aerodynamic instability of the deck cross-section, not a cable manufacturing defect.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: An external periodic force at a fixed frequency drives amplitude to a peak specifically when that frequency matches the natural frequency
A structure's own motion reshapes the airflow around it, reinforcing further motion above a critical wind speed, with no matching external frequency required
The feedback mechanism by which airflow forces add energy to the oscillation instead of removing it

questions.explanation: Forced resonance requires a periodic driving force at a matching frequency; self-excited flutter needs only steady wind above a critical speed and an aerodynamically unstable structure; negative aerodynamic damping is the specific feedback loop that makes flutter self-reinforcing.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the Tacoma Narrows story.

items.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opens (July 1940) and develops vertical undulations nicknamed "Galloping Gertie"
In roughly 40 mph wind on November 7, 1940, the motion becomes a violent torsional oscillation and the deck collapses
Textbooks for decades explain the collapse as wind-driven resonance matching the bridge's natural frequency
Billah and Scanlan's 1991 paper documents the engineering consensus that the true mechanism was self-excited aeroelastic flutter

questions.explanation: The bridge's early undulating behavior preceded its catastrophic torsional collapse; the (incorrect) resonance explanation dominated textbooks for decades afterward; the corrected flutter-based consensus was formally documented later, in 1991.

questions.prompt: Which observation is hardest to explain under the simple "wind vortex frequency matched bridge frequency" resonance story?

options.text: The bridge failed under a fairly steady sustained wind rather than a wind oscillating in a way that would need to match a fixed frequency precisely
The bridge was made of steel, and steel structures cannot experience resonance at all
The collapse happened in November, a detail resonance theory cannot account for

explanations.a: Correct: a steady wind has no fixed periodic frequency to match a natural frequency against, which is exactly why self-excited flutter, not frequency-matched forced resonance, is the mechanism that fits the observed steady wind conditions.
explanations.b: Wrong: steel structures can and do experience resonance; that is not the issue with the textbook explanation.
explanations.c: Wrong: the month of the collapse has no bearing on distinguishing resonance from flutter; it is not a relevant physical clue.

lessons.label: Nonlinear Oscillators and Open Questions

sections.heading: When the Restoring Force Isn't Linear
sections.body: Every oscillator discussed so far, Hooke's spring, the small-angle pendulum, assumed a restoring force exactly proportional to displacement, F = -kx. Real springs, real pendulums at large amplitude, and real structural elements all deviate from this once displacement grows: the restoring force picks up higher-order terms. The classic model, introduced by German engineer Georg Duffing in a 1918 study of forced vibrations, adds a cubic term, F = -kx - (epsilon)*x^3, where epsilon > 0 describes a "hardening" spring that stiffens at large displacement and epsilon < 0 describes a "softening" spring that weakens.

sections.heading: Frequency Now Depends on Amplitude
sections.body: The single most important consequence of nonlinearity is that oscillation frequency stops being a fixed property of the system and starts depending on amplitude, unlike ideal SHM where omega = sqrt(k/m) regardless of how big the swing is. The large-angle pendulum from the first lesson in this unit is a softening oscillator: at 90-degree amplitude its true period runs about 18% longer than the small-angle prediction, and the period keeps growing as amplitude approaches (but never quite reaches) 180 degrees. A hardening spring shows the opposite trend, running faster at larger amplitude, which shows up experimentally as a resonance peak that leans over rather than standing straight up as driving amplitude increases.

sections.heading: Driven Hard Enough, Nonlinear Oscillators Can Go Chaotic
sections.body: Push a linear oscillator with a periodic external force and, after transients die out, it settles into steady motion at the driving frequency, full stop. Push a nonlinear oscillator like the Duffing oscillator instead, and for the right combination of driving frequency, driving amplitude, and damping, it can undergo period-doubling: the response repeats every two drive cycles instead of one, then every four, then eight, a cascade that in some parameter ranges accumulates into chaos, motion that never exactly repeats and is exquisitely sensitive to starting conditions even though the governing equation is entirely deterministic with no randomness anywhere in it. Mapping exactly where in parameter space a given nonlinear oscillator transitions from periodic to chaotic behavior remains an active area of nonlinear dynamics research, not a settled textbook fact.

lessons.workedExample: Take the large-angle pendulum as a concrete softening-oscillator case. Small-angle prediction: T0 = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g); for L = 1 m, T0 is about 2.01 s. At 15-degree amplitude the correction is under half a percent, effectively unmeasurable by eye. At 90-degree amplitude the true period is about 18% longer, roughly 2.37 s instead of 2.01 s, a difference a stopwatch easily catches. Now imagine periodically driving that same pendulum, pushing it once per cycle, with amplitude and frequency dialed up: at low drive it settles into simple back-and-forth motion at the drive frequency, exactly as a linear oscillator would; past a critical drive strength, real experiments and the Duffing equation modeling them show the motion period-doubling and eventually becoming chaotic, still governed by the same deterministic F = ma, just no longer predictable far into the future from a slightly different starting angle.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges close the unit here because it directly tests whether a student understands SHM as a bounded approximation rather than a universal law: every prior lesson, Hooke's linear F = -kx, Galileo's amplitude-independent period, holds only within a limited displacement range, and a fair judge wants a student who can name the specific breakdown, amplitude-dependent frequency, and its most striking consequence, that deterministic driven nonlinear oscillators can behave chaotically. An answer that just says "real oscillators aren't perfectly linear" without naming a mechanism, a cubic restoring term, a period-doubling route to chaos, misses the depth the earlier landmark lessons were building toward.

questions.prompt: In the Duffing model F = -kx - (epsilon)*x^3, what does a negative epsilon describe?

options.text: A "softening" oscillator whose restoring force weakens at large displacement, so its period grows with amplitude, like the large-angle pendulum
A "hardening" oscillator whose restoring force strengthens at large displacement, so its period shrinks with amplitude
A perfectly linear oscillator identical to the Hooke's-law case, since epsilon only matters when positive

explanations.a: Correct: with epsilon negative, the cubic term -epsilon*x^3 becomes positive for x>0, partially canceling the linear -kx restoring force, so the net restoring force weakens at large displacement, the softening case exemplified by the large-angle pendulum.
explanations.b: Wrong: hardening corresponds to positive epsilon, which strengthens the restoring force at large displacement, the opposite sign described here.
explanations.c: Wrong: any nonzero epsilon, positive or negative, makes the oscillator nonlinear; only epsilon = 0 recovers the pure Hooke's-law case.

questions.prompt: Order the progression from linear approximation to chaotic driven motion.

items.text: A system is modeled with a small-angle or linear approximation where frequency is amplitude-independent
Displacement grows large enough that higher-order, nonlinear terms in the restoring force become significant
The oscillator's frequency begins measurably depending on amplitude (softening or hardening)
Under strong enough periodic driving, the nonlinear oscillator can period-double its way into chaotic motion

questions.explanation: The linear approximation holds only at small displacement; as displacement grows the nonlinear terms become significant, producing amplitude-dependent frequency, and under strong periodic driving that nonlinearity can cascade into period-doubling and chaos.

questions.prompt: Match each nonlinear-oscillator concept to its correct description.

left.text: Softening oscillator (epsilon < 0), e.g. the large-angle pendulum

right.text: Restoring force strengthens at large displacement; frequency increases with amplitude
Restoring force weakens at large displacement; frequency decreases (period grows) with amplitude
A route by which a deterministic nonlinear oscillator's response can become chaotic

questions.explanation: Hardening and softening are opposite-sign nonlinear corrections with opposite effects on frequency versus amplitude; period-doubling is the specific bifurcation cascade by which strong periodic driving can push a nonlinear oscillator into chaos.

questions.prompt: Why can a driven Duffing oscillator behave chaotically even though its governing equation is fully deterministic with no random terms?

options.text: At certain driving parameters the motion becomes extremely sensitive to initial conditions, so nearby starting states diverge into unpredictable long-term trajectories despite the equation being deterministic
The equation actually contains a hidden random noise term that standard notation omits
Chaos in this context just means the motion is very fast, not that it is unpredictable

explanations.a: Correct: deterministic chaos arises from sensitive dependence on initial conditions, not from randomness in the equation; nearby trajectories diverge exponentially, making long-term prediction practically impossible despite a fully deterministic rule.
explanations.b: Wrong: the Duffing equation as written has no random term; chaos here is a property of deterministic nonlinear dynamics, not hidden noise.
explanations.c: Wrong: chaotic motion is not defined by speed; it is defined by aperiodicity and sensitive dependence on initial conditions.

lessons.label: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

sections.heading: Every mass pulls on every other mass
sections.body: In the 1680s Isaac Newton proposed a claim that was radical for its time: the same force that pulls an apple to the ground also holds the Moon in orbit around the Earth and the planets in orbit around the Sun. Before Newton, terrestrial motion (falling objects) and celestial motion (orbiting bodies) were treated as governed by entirely different rules. Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation unified them into a single statement: every particle of mass in the universe attracts every other particle of mass with a force that acts along the straight line connecting their centers. This is not a special property of planets or of large objects — a pencil on a desk and the book beside it attract each other gravitationally, just too weakly to notice.

sections.heading: The inverse-square law
sections.body: The law is written F = G m1 m2 / r^2, where m1 and m2 are the two masses, r is the distance between their centers, and G is the gravitational constant. Two features define the law's shape. First, the force is directly proportional to the product of the masses: double either mass and the force doubles. Second, the force falls off as the inverse square of the separation: double the distance and the force drops to one-quarter; triple it and the force drops to one-ninth. This inverse-square dependence means gravity never truly reaches zero at any finite distance, but it weakens so fast with distance that only enormously massive bodies like planets and stars produce forces large enough to matter over astronomical distances.

sections.heading: A force pair, not a one-way pull
sections.body: Because gravitation follows Newton's third law, the force is always mutual and equal in magnitude: the Earth pulls on you with the same magnitude of force that you pull on the Earth, directed toward each other along the line joining your centers. The reason you fall toward the Earth and the Earth does not visibly fall toward you is not that the forces differ — they are identical in size — but that Newton's second law (a = F/m) gives the enormously more massive Earth a proportionally tiny, imperceptible acceleration compared to yours. Gravity is also always attractive, never repulsive, which distinguishes it from the electric force between charges.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate the gravitational force between two 70 kg people standing 1 m apart (center to center). Using F = G m1 m2 / r^2 with G = 6.674e-11 N m^2/kg^2: F = (6.674e-11)(70)(70)/(1)^2 = 6.674e-11 * 4900 = 3.27e-7 N, about 0.33 micronewtons — roughly the weight of a single small grain of sand, far too small to feel. Now compare the force between the Earth (5.97e24 kg) and one of those people at Earth's radius (6.37e6 m): F = (6.674e-11)(5.97e24)(70)/(6.37e6)^2 ~ 686 N, easily felt as the person's weight. The same law, same constant — the difference is entirely in the size of the masses involved.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this concept wants to see whether a student treats gravitation as a memorized formula or as a physical relationship they can reason about qualitatively. A strong answer explains what happens to the force if one mass triples, or if the distance is halved, without needing to plug numbers into a calculator — because the proportionalities are understood, not just the symbols. Judges often ask why we do not feel the gravitational pull of nearby objects like furniture; a student who can explain that it is a matter of tiny mass rather than a different physical law entirely demonstrates real command of the inverse-square relationship.

questions.prompt: If the distance between two masses is tripled, the gravitational force between them becomes:

options.text: One-third as large
One-ninth as large
Nine times as large

explanations.a: That would be true for a force inversely proportional to r, not r squared — gravitation depends on 1/r^2.
explanations.b: Correct: force scales as 1/r^2, so tripling r divides the force by 3^2 = 9.
explanations.c: This inverts the relationship — increasing distance weakens gravitational force, it does not strengthen it.

questions.prompt: According to Newton's third law applied to gravitation, when the Earth pulls on a falling apple, the apple:

options.text: Pulls back on the Earth with an equal-magnitude force
Exerts no force on the Earth at all
Pulls on the Earth, but with a much smaller force

explanations.a: Correct: gravitational forces come in equal-and-opposite pairs; the apple pulls on the Earth just as hard as the Earth pulls on the apple.
explanations.b: Gravitation is always mutual — if the Earth exerts a force on the apple, the apple must exert a force back, by Newton's third law.
explanations.c: The forces are equal in magnitude; what differs is the resulting acceleration, since the Earth's mass is vastly larger.

questions.prompt: Order these masses by the gravitational force each would exert on a fixed 1 kg test mass at a fixed distance of 1 m, from smallest force to largest.

items.text: A 0.1 kg pebble
A 70 kg person
A 2,000 kg car
A 5.97e24 kg planet (Earth)

questions.explanation: With distance and the test mass held fixed, force is directly proportional to the source mass, so ranking by force is identical to ranking by mass: pebble, person, car, planet.

questions.prompt: Match each change to its effect on gravitational force F = G m1 m2 / r^2.

left.text: Double one mass (m1), keep r fixed
Double the distance r, keep masses fixed
Halve both masses, keep r fixed

right.text: Force doubles
Force drops to one-quarter
Force drops to one-quarter (from the mass product)

questions.explanation: Force is linear in each mass, so doubling one mass doubles F. Force is inverse-square in r, so doubling r quarters F. Halving both masses multiplies the mass product by (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4, so F also quarters.

lessons.label: The Gravitational Constant G

sections.heading: A universal but tiny number
sections.body: The constant G in F = G m1 m2 / r^2 is called the universal gravitational constant because, as far as every experiment to date has shown, it has the same value everywhere in the universe and does not depend on what the masses are made of, their temperature, or any other property. Its accepted value is G = 6.674e-11 N m^2/kg^2 (CODATA recommends 6.67430e-11, with the last couple of digits still the least precisely known of any fundamental constant in physics). Newton's law itself was published in the Principia in 1687, but Newton never measured G numerically — he worked with proportionalities and ratios; G was not measured until more than a century later, in 1798, by Henry Cavendish.

sections.heading: Why gravity feels weak in everyday life
sections.body: G's smallness explains a fact of everyday experience: gravity is by far the weakest of the four fundamental forces. The electric force between two protons is roughly 10^36 times stronger than the gravitational force between them, yet gravity dominates the large-scale structure of the universe — galaxies, stars, planets, orbits — while the electric force is invisible at that scale. The resolution is that electric charge comes in both positive and negative signs and tends to cancel out in bulk matter (a rock has almost exactly as many protons as electrons), whereas mass has no negative counterpart and never cancels — every kilogram of mass in a planet adds to the same one-directional pull.

sections.heading: When gravity becomes noticeable
sections.body: Because G is so small, the F = G m1 m2 / r^2 force is only large enough to notice or measure when at least one of the two masses is astronomically large — a planet, a moon, a star. Between two ordinary human-scale objects, even objects as large as cars or buildings, the gravitational force is far below what any but the most sensitive laboratory instruments can detect, which is precisely why it took until 1798 for anyone to directly measure a gravitational attraction between two objects in a lab rather than infer G indirectly from planetary motion.

lessons.workedExample: Compare the gravitational force between two 1,000 kg cars parked 2 m apart to the electric force between two protons 1 m apart. Gravity: F = (6.674e-11)(1000)(1000)/(2)^2 = 6.674e-11 * 1,000,000 / 4 ~= 1.67e-5 N, still far too small to feel or even measure without specialized equipment. Electric force between two protons: using Coulomb's law with k = 8.99e9 N m^2/C^2 and each proton's charge 1.6e-19 C at r = 1 m, F = (8.99e9)(1.6e-19)^2/(1)^2 ~= 2.3e-28 N. Even without matching separations, the vast difference in magnitude illustrates how differently the forces scale with mass versus charge, and the qualitative point stands: gravity between everyday objects is minuscule, only becoming significant when planet-sized masses are involved.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about G specifically to check whether students understand it as a fixed conversion factor rather than something that varies with the objects involved (a common misconception is confusing G with the local gravitational field strength g near Earth's surface, which does vary with location and altitude). A student who can explain why G's smallness means we never feel the pull of nearby furniture, yet planets still orbit stars reliably, is demonstrating that they grasp the scale argument, not just a memorized numeric value.

questions.prompt: The gravitational constant G is best described as:

options.text: A fixed value that is the same everywhere in the universe, regardless of what the masses are made of
A value that changes depending on the material composition of the masses involved
The same thing as g, the 9.8 m/s^2 acceleration near Earth's surface

explanations.a: Correct: G is a universal constant, believed to have the same value throughout the universe independent of what the masses are made of.
explanations.b: Every gravity experiment to date shows G is independent of material composition, temperature, or other physical properties.
explanations.c: G and g are different quantities: G is a universal constant, while g = GM_Earth/r^2 is a derived, location-dependent field strength.

questions.prompt: Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces, yet it dominates the large-scale structure of the universe mainly because:

options.text: Mass has no negative counterpart, so gravitational attraction never cancels out in bulk matter
G is actually larger than the electric force constant k
Electric forces only exist at very small (atomic) distances

explanations.a: Correct: unlike charge, mass is always positive and additive, so gravitational pull accumulates across every particle in a large body instead of canceling.
explanations.b: G is many orders of magnitude smaller than the electric constant k; gravity's dominance at large scale is not because it is a stronger constant.
explanations.c: Electric forces also obey an inverse-square law extending to any distance; they simply tend to cancel in neutral bulk matter, unlike gravity.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the historical development of universal gravitation, earliest to latest.

items.text: Newton publishes the Principia with F = G m1 m2 / r^2 as a proportionality
The numeric value of G remains unmeasured for over a century
Henry Cavendish measures G directly using a torsion balance
Modern CODATA measurements refine G to a precise recommended value

questions.explanation: Newton (1687) stated the law without a numeric G; G stayed unmeasured until Cavendish's 1798 experiment; later, standards bodies like CODATA have continued refining G's precise value.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct description.

right.text: ~6.674e-11 N m^2/kg^2, the same value everywhere
~9.8 m/s^2, depends on planet mass and radius
Everyday objects have far too little mass to produce a noticeable force

questions.explanation: G is the fixed universal constant in Newton's law; g is a derived, location-specific field strength (g = GM/r^2); and gravity's everyday weakness traces to the small masses of ordinary objects, not to G varying.

lessons.label: The Cavendish Experiment

sections.heading: A force too weak to measure directly
sections.body: By the late 1700s, Newton's law of gravitation was well accepted for explaining planetary orbits, but no one had measured a gravitational attraction between two objects in a laboratory, nor did anyone know the numeric value of G. In 1797-1798, the English scientist Henry Cavendish built an apparatus originally designed by natural philosopher and clergyman John Michell (a pioneer of seismology, who died before completing it) to measure exactly this: the gravitational attraction between two ordinary-sized lead spheres. Cavendish's stated goal was actually to determine the density of the Earth, not G directly — the concept of G as a separate constant came later, but his data can be used to compute it, so the experiment is remembered today as the first measurement of G.

sections.heading: The torsion balance
sections.body: Cavendish's apparatus was a torsion balance: two small lead spheres (about 0.73 kg each) were mounted on the ends of a light 6-foot horizontal rod, which hung suspended from its center by a thin wire. Two much larger lead spheres (about 158 kg each) were brought close to the small spheres from outside. The gravitational attraction between each large-small pair caused the rod to rotate slightly, twisting the suspension wire until the wire's restoring torque balanced the gravitational torque. Because the wire was extraordinarily thin and flexible, even the minuscule gravitational force between the spheres was enough to produce a measurable twist — the twist angle was read using a telescope and scale from another room, since air currents and even the experimenter's body heat could disturb such a delicate measurement.

sections.heading: From a twist angle to the mass of the Earth
sections.body: Once the torsion constant of the wire was calibrated (by timing the balance's natural oscillation period), Cavendish could convert the observed twist into a measured force, and from that force — knowing the masses and separation of the spheres — calculate G. Combining G with the already-known value of g at Earth's surface and Earth's radius (g = GM_Earth/R_Earth^2), he calculated Earth's mass and average density, arriving at a density that his own raw measurements work out to about 5.45 times that of water, remarkably close to the modern accepted value of about 5.51 g/cm^3. This is why the experiment is sometimes described as "weighing the Earth": Cavendish never weighed the Earth directly, but his lab measurement of a small force between lead spheres let him calculate the entire planet's mass.

lessons.workedExample: Cavendish's torsion balance measured a force on the order of 10^-7 N between a large sphere (~158 kg) and a small sphere (~0.73 kg) separated by roughly 0.225 m. Plugging these into F = G m1 m2 / r^2 with the modern G = 6.674e-11 N m^2/kg^2 predicts a force F = (6.674e-11)(158)(0.73)/(0.225)^2 ~= 1.52e-7 N, and running the calculation the other way — solving G = F r^2 / (m1 m2) from that measured force — recovers G ~= 6.674e-11 N m^2/kg^2 almost exactly. That close agreement is the real historical result: the density recoverable from Cavendish's own raw measurements (about 5.45 times water, versus the modern 5.51) was within roughly 1% of today's accepted value, not merely 'in the right ballpark,' which is a testament to how carefully the experiment controlled for disturbances despite using only period-appropriate tools. The experiment's precision came not from powerful instruments but from clever design: a torsion wire is sensitive to forces far smaller than any spring scale of the era could register, and the remote telescope-and-scale readout eliminated the biggest source of disturbance, the experimenter's own presence near the apparatus.
lessons.judgeFraming: This experiment is a favorite for judges because it is a clean case study in experimental ingenuity: a force tens of millions of times weaker than the small sphere's own weight (and billions of times weaker than the weight of the large spheres) was measured using period-appropriate technology. A strong answer explains WHY a torsion balance rather than a spring scale was necessary — the restoring torque of a twisted wire can be made arbitrarily small by making the wire thin, giving the instrument enough sensitivity — and correctly notes that Cavendish's original goal was Earth's density, not a standalone constant called G, which by itself often surprises students who assume the experiment was framed exactly as it is retold today.

questions.prompt: The Cavendish experiment is remembered as significant chiefly because it:

options.text: Provided the first laboratory measurement of a gravitational attraction between ordinary masses, allowing G to be calculated
Was the first experiment to prove that objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass
Discovered gravitational waves for the first time

explanations.a: Correct: Cavendish measured a gravitational force between lab-sized lead spheres, which let him calculate G (and from it, Earth's mass and density).
explanations.b: That describes a different class of experiment (associated with Galileo's inclined-plane and falling-body work), not Cavendish's torsion balance.
explanations.c: Gravitational waves were not detected until LIGO in 2015 using entirely different technology, over two centuries after Cavendish.

questions.prompt: Cavendish used a torsion balance rather than an ordinary spring scale because:

options.text: A thin twisted wire can register forces far smaller than any spring scale of the era could detect
Torsion balances are less expensive to build than spring scales
Spring scales cannot measure any force smaller than about 1 Newton, by definition

explanations.a: Correct: the restoring torque of a thin wire can be made extremely small by design, giving the torsion balance enough sensitivity to detect a roughly 10^-7 N gravitational force.
explanations.b: Cost was not the deciding factor; sensitivity to extremely small forces was the reason for the design choice.
explanations.c: There is no fixed 1 N floor for spring scales in general, but period spring scales lacked the sensitivity needed for a force this small.

questions.prompt: Order the steps Cavendish used to go from an observed twist angle to Earth's mass.

items.text: Calibrate the torsion wire's restoring constant using its natural oscillation period
Measure the twist angle caused by attraction between large and small lead spheres
Convert the twist into a force, then solve F = G m1 m2 / r^2 for G
Combine G with Earth's known radius and surface gravity g to calculate Earth's mass

questions.explanation: The wire had to be calibrated before the twist reading meant anything; the twist gave a force; the force with known masses and separation gave G; and G combined with g = GM/R^2 gave Earth's mass.

questions.prompt: Match each apparatus component to its role in the Cavendish experiment.

left.text: Small lead spheres on the rod

right.text: The masses being gravitationally pulled, whose deflection was measured
The masses providing the attracting gravitational force
Provided the extreme sensitivity needed to detect a tiny force via twisting
Let the experimenter read the result without disturbing the delicate balance

questions.explanation: The small spheres on the rod were pulled by the fixed large spheres; the thin wire's low restoring torque made the tiny gravitational force measurable; and the remote telescope avoided disturbing the balance with air currents or body heat.

lessons.label: Superposition of Gravitational Forces

sections.heading: Gravity from many masses adds as vectors
sections.body: Newton's law as written, F = G m1 m2 / r^2, gives the force between exactly two masses. Real systems almost always involve more than two: a spacecraft near the Earth and Moon simultaneously, an asteroid pulled by the Sun and every planet, a satellite in a multi-body configuration. The principle of superposition resolves this: the net gravitational force on any one mass from several other masses is simply the vector sum of the separate forces each of those masses would exert individually, exactly as if the others were not there. Superposition holds because gravitational forces obey the same rule as any other vector quantity — magnitude and direction combine independently — with no interaction terms between the source masses themselves complicating the sum.

sections.heading: Why vector addition, not scalar addition, matters
sections.body: The critical subtlety is that each individual force has both a magnitude (computed from F = G m1 m2 / r^2 for that pair) and a direction (along the line connecting the two masses, always attractive). Simply adding the magnitudes of several forces and ignoring their directions gives the wrong answer whenever those forces do not all point the same way, which is the common case. The standard method is to resolve each individual force into x- and y-components (or x, y, z in three dimensions), sum the components separately, and only then recombine the summed components into a net magnitude and direction using the Pythagorean theorem and inverse tangent, exactly as with any other force superposition problem in mechanics.

sections.heading: A caveat: uniform spheres and point masses
sections.body: Superposition as stated applies exactly to point masses, and — thanks to the shell theorem covered in the next lesson — also applies exactly to any uniform (or radially-layered) sphere treated as a point mass located at its center, provided you are outside the sphere's surface. This is why the technique is safely usable for planets and stars despite their being extended three-dimensional objects rather than true points: as long as the masses involved are spherically symmetric and you are calculating the force at a point outside all of them, replacing each sphere with an equivalent point mass at its center introduces no error at all.

lessons.workedExample: Three point masses lie on a line: m1 = 4 kg at x = 0, m2 = 9 kg at x = 3 m, and a test mass m3 = 1 kg sits at x = 5 m. Force from m1 on m3 (distance 5 m, pulling toward decreasing x, i.e. in the -x direction): F1 = G(4)(1)/(5)^2 = G(4/25) = 0.16G, direction -x. Force from m2 on m3 (distance 2 m, also pulling toward decreasing x since m2 lies between m1 and m3 at x = 3): F2 = G(9)(1)/(2)^2 = G(9/4) = 2.25G, direction -x. Since both forces point in the same -x direction here, the net force is simply their sum: F_net = 0.16G + 2.25G = 2.41G ~= 2.41 * 6.674e-11 ~= 1.61e-10 N, directed in -x. Had m1 and m2 been on opposite sides of m3, the two forces would point in opposite directions and would need to be subtracted rather than added, which is the more common and more error-prone case.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use multi-body superposition problems specifically to catch students who add force magnitudes without tracking direction — a very common and very wrong shortcut. A strong answer explicitly states the direction of each individual force before combining them, and, for masses not arranged on a single line, explicitly resolves components before summing. Judges will also probe whether a student knows superposition breaks down cleanly for extended non-spherical bodies (irregular asteroids, for instance) unless you integrate over the mass distribution rather than treating it as one point.

questions.prompt: The principle of superposition for gravitational forces states that the net force on a mass from several other masses is:

options.text: The vector sum of the individual forces from each mass, computed as if the others were absent
The sum of the magnitudes of each individual force, regardless of direction
Equal to the force from whichever single mass is largest, ignoring the rest

explanations.a: Correct: each individual pairwise force is computed independently and then combined as a vector sum, respecting each force's direction.
explanations.b: Simply adding magnitudes ignores direction and gives the wrong answer whenever the individual forces do not all point the same way.
explanations.c: All contributing masses matter; ignoring smaller ones can introduce significant error and is not how superposition works.

questions.prompt: Two masses pull on a test mass from exactly opposite directions along the same line. To find the net force, you should:

options.text: Add the two force magnitudes together
Subtract the smaller magnitude from the larger, with the result pointing in the direction of the larger force
Average the two force magnitudes

explanations.a: Adding magnitudes of oppositely-directed vectors gives too large a result; opposite vectors partially cancel rather than reinforcing.
explanations.b: Correct: vectors pointing in opposite directions subtract, and the net force points the same way as the larger individual force.
explanations.c: Averaging is not a valid vector operation for combining forces and has no physical justification here.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for correctly finding the net gravitational force on a mass from several other masses arranged in a plane (not all on one line).

items.text: Compute the magnitude of each individual pairwise force using F = G m1 m2 / r^2
Determine the direction of each individual force (along the line toward the source mass)
Resolve each individual force into x- and y-components
Sum the x-components and y-components separately, then recombine into a net magnitude and direction

questions.explanation: You need each force's size and direction before you can resolve it into components, and only after summing components separately can you recombine them into the net vector.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the correct superposition approach.

left.text: Two source masses pull in the same direction
Two source masses pull in exactly opposite directions
Source masses are not collinear with the test mass

right.text: Add the force magnitudes directly
Subtract the smaller magnitude from the larger
Resolve each force into components before summing

questions.explanation: Same-direction collinear forces add directly; opposite-direction collinear forces subtract; and any non-collinear arrangement requires resolving into components before combining, since simple addition or subtraction of magnitudes no longer applies.

lessons.label: The Shell Theorem

sections.heading: Treating a sphere as a point
sections.body: A planet or star is not a point mass — it is a vast three-dimensional distribution of matter spread throughout a sphere. Strictly, computing the gravitational force it exerts should require summing (integrating) the contribution of every tiny piece of that mass individually, at every different distance and angle from the point being pulled on. Newton proved a remarkable simplification, now called the shell theorem, that makes this unnecessary for any spherically symmetric mass distribution: a uniform (or radially-layered, meaning density can vary with depth as long as each layer is uniform at that depth) spherical shell of mass attracts any external point mass exactly as if the shell's entire mass were concentrated at a single point at its center. This holds true no matter how close the external point is to the shell's surface, as long as it remains outside.

sections.heading: The second half: zero force inside a shell
sections.body: The theorem's second and more surprising result concerns a mass located inside a uniform spherical shell rather than outside it: the net gravitational force from the shell on that interior mass is exactly zero, regardless of where inside the shell the mass sits. This is not because the shell's gravity somehow shuts off — every part of the shell is still pulling on the interior point — but because the closer, smaller-area portion of the shell nearby and the farther, larger-area portion of the shell on the opposite side exert forces that exactly cancel. The nearby mass is stronger per unit area (closer, inverse-square) but spans a smaller solid angle; the far mass is weaker per unit area but spans a proportionally larger solid angle, and the two effects balance perfectly for any point inside.

sections.heading: Why real planets can be treated as points
sections.body: A solid sphere, such as a planet, can be modeled as a nested set of thin concentric shells, from the center out to the surface. For a point outside the entire sphere, the point-mass-at-the-center result from each shell adds up, so the whole sphere attracts external objects exactly as a point mass at its center would — which is why F = G m1 m2 / r^2 can be applied directly to planets, moons, and stars using r as the center-to-center distance, without needing to account for their finite size. For a point inside a uniform sphere (a tunnel through the Earth, say), only the shells interior to that point contribute any net force — the shells outside it, being now "outside-in" from the point's perspective, cancel to zero exactly as the shell theorem predicts.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a spacecraft 10,000 km from the center of a spherical planet of radius 6,000 km and mass 5e24 kg. Because the spacecraft is outside the planet's surface, the shell theorem justifies treating the entire planet as a point mass at its center, so F = G M_planet m_ship / r^2 with r = 10,000 km = 1e7 m applies directly: no correction is needed for the planet's finite size or internal density structure, provided the planet is spherically symmetric (even if density increases toward the core, as Earth's does). Now imagine a probe that drills to a point 3,000 km from the planet's center, still inside the planet. The shell theorem says only the mass interior to 3,000 km contributes to the gravitational pull on the probe; all of the planet's mass in the shell between 3,000 km and 6,000 km from center exerts exactly zero net force on the probe, so the effective attracting mass shrinks dramatically compared to the planet's total mass.
lessons.judgeFraming: The shell theorem is a favorite judge topic because its two halves are frequently confused, and getting them right shows real conceptual command: outside a shell, treat it as a point (nonzero, inverse-square force); inside a uniform shell, the force is exactly zero, not just small. A judge may ask what the gravitational force is at the exact center of a hollow spherical asteroid, expecting the answer "zero, by the shell theorem" rather than an attempt to average distances. Students who can also explain WHY the interior cancellation happens (the near-far, small-area-large-area balance) rather than just quoting the result demonstrate they understand the geometry, not just the conclusion.

questions.prompt: According to the shell theorem, a point mass located OUTSIDE a uniform spherical shell of mass M experiences a gravitational force as if:

options.text: All of the shell's mass were concentrated at its center
Only the nearest point on the shell's surface contributed any force
The force were exactly zero, just as it is for points inside the shell

explanations.a: Correct: for an exterior point, the shell theorem allows the entire shell to be replaced by an equivalent point mass at its center.
explanations.b: The force accounts for the entire shell's mass, not just the nearest patch of surface; using only the nearest point would give the wrong magnitude.
explanations.c: Zero net force applies specifically to points INSIDE a uniform shell, not to points outside it, where the force is nonzero.

questions.prompt: A mass sits exactly at the center of a uniform, hollow spherical shell. The net gravitational force on it from the shell is:

options.text: Zero, because the pulls from every direction around the shell exactly cancel
Very large, because every part of the shell is relatively close
Equal to G times the shell's mass divided by the shell's radius squared, same as if outside

explanations.a: Correct: by symmetry, every element of the shell has an opposite element pulling with exactly equal and opposite force, so the interior net force is zero.
explanations.b: Proximity alone does not determine the net force; symmetric cancellation, not distance, is what drives the result to zero here.
explanations.c: That outside-point formula does not apply to interior points; the interior force is zero regardless of the shell's radius or mass.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps that explain why gravitational force is zero at any point inside a uniform spherical shell.

items.text: Consider a small cone from the interior point extending in both opposite directions to the shell's surface
Note the nearer intersection has a smaller area but is closer (stronger pull per unit mass)
Note the farther intersection has a larger area but is more distant (weaker pull per unit mass)
Recognize the two effects exactly balance for every such cone, so the total net force sums to zero

questions.explanation: The classic proof pairs opposite patches of the shell via a cone from the interior point; the closer patch pulls harder but is smaller in area, the farther patch pulls weaker but is larger in area, and the two effects cancel exactly, for every direction, summing to zero net force.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to the shell theorem result that applies.

left.text: Point outside a uniform spherical shell
Point inside a uniform spherical shell
Point outside a solid uniform sphere (like a planet)
Point inside a uniform solid sphere, partway to the center

right.text: Treat the entire shell as a point mass at the center
Net force from that shell is exactly zero
Treat the entire sphere as a point mass at the center
Only the mass interior to that point contributes any net force

questions.explanation: Outside any shell (or full sphere built from nested shells), treat all its mass as concentrated at the center. Inside a single uniform shell, the net force from that shell is zero. Inside a solid sphere, only the mass at radii smaller than the point's distance from center contributes, since all shells farther out cancel to zero.

lessons.label: Why Inverse-Square?

sections.heading: A geometric picture, not an arbitrary exponent
sections.body: It can look like a coincidence that gravitation, electric force, and light intensity all fall off as 1/r^2, but the exponent is not arbitrary — it is a direct consequence of living in three spatial dimensions. Imagine a mass sitting at the center of empty space, radiating its gravitational "influence" outward equally in every direction, like light from a bare bulb. At any distance r from the source, that influence has spread out over the surface of an imaginary sphere of radius r centered on the source. The surface area of a sphere is 4 pi r^2, so as r grows, the same total amount of "influence" is spread over a rapidly growing area — and the influence per unit area, which is what a test mass at that distance actually feels, is the total divided by 4 pi r^2.

sections.heading: Flux and the conservation of field lines
sections.body: This picture is often formalized using the idea of gravitational field lines or flux: the total number of field lines leaving a mass is fixed by the mass itself and does not depend on how far away you measure them. Picture field lines as spreading radially outward from the source mass, never crossing, never created or destroyed in the empty space around it. At a small sphere near the source, all the lines are packed into a small area, so the line density (lines per unit area) is high; at a larger sphere far away, the same fixed number of lines are spread across a much bigger area (4 pi r^2), so the density is lower. Because the strength of the gravitational field is proportional to this line density, and the density scales as 1/r^2 (fixed total divided by growing area), the field — and hence the force — necessarily scales as 1/r^2 as well.

sections.heading: Why three dimensions produces the square
sections.body: The exponent 2 is tied directly to living in three spatial dimensions, because a sphere's surface area in 3D space scales as r^2 (as opposed to a circle's circumference in 2D space, which scales as r^1). If space had four spatial dimensions, the analogous "surface" enclosing a source would scale as r^3, and gravity would plausibly follow an inverse-cube law instead. This connection between the number of spatial dimensions and the force law's exponent is one reason physicists treat any observed deviation from inverse-square gravity at very small or very large distances as a potential signature of extra dimensions or new physics — the inverse-square law is not an assumption pulled from nowhere, it is what you would expect purely from geometry in the space we observe.

lessons.workedExample: Picture a lightbulb radiating a fixed total power P in every direction. At a sphere of radius r = 1 m around the bulb, that power is spread over area 4 pi(1)^2 = 4 pi m^2, giving an intensity of P/(4 pi) W/m^2. At r = 2 m, the same total power P is spread over 4 pi(2)^2 = 16 pi m^2, four times the area, so the intensity is P/(16 pi) W/m^2, one-quarter as much — exactly the inverse-square falloff, and exactly the same geometric argument that governs gravity: a fixed total quantity (light power, or gravitational flux) spread across a sphere whose area grows as r^2 must have its per-area value fall as 1/r^2. This is why the inverse-square law shows up not just in gravitation but wherever something spreads uniformly outward from a point source through three-dimensional space.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is one of the more conceptually demanding ideas in the segment, and judges use it to separate students who have memorized the formula from those who understand where the exponent comes from. A strong answer connects the exponent 2 explicitly to the fact that a sphere's surface area in three dimensions scales as r^2, rather than treating 1/r^2 as an unexplained empirical fact to be accepted on faith. Judges may also ask what would happen to gravity's exponent in a universe with more spatial dimensions, testing whether the student grasps that the inverse-square law is a geometric consequence of 3D space rather than a special property of gravitational force alone.

questions.prompt: The 1/r^2 dependence of gravitational force arises geometrically because:

options.text: A sphere's surface area grows as r^2, spreading a fixed total influence over an ever-larger area
Mass itself weakens as it moves farther from other masses
G decreases as distance increases

explanations.a: Correct: a fixed quantity of gravitational influence spread over a sphere of area 4 pi r^2 gives a per-area value that falls as 1/r^2.
explanations.b: Mass does not change with distance; the source mass stays the same, only the geometric spreading of its influence changes with r.
explanations.c: G is a universal constant and does not vary with distance; the r-dependence comes entirely from the 1/r^2 term, not from G changing.

questions.prompt: If space had four spatial dimensions instead of three, the geometric argument suggests gravity's force law would most plausibly scale as:

options.text: 1/r^3, because the enclosing "surface" in 4D scales as r^3
1/r^2, unchanged, because gravity is independent of dimensionality
1/r, because higher dimensions weaken the exponent

explanations.a: Correct: the flux/surface-area argument generalizes so that in d spatial dimensions the enclosing hypersurface scales as r^(d-1), giving 1/r^3 in four dimensions.
explanations.b: The whole point of the geometric derivation is that the exponent IS tied to the number of spatial dimensions, so it would not stay unchanged.
explanations.c: Higher dimensions increase, not decrease, how fast the enclosing surface area grows with r, so the exponent gets larger, not smaller.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the flux/geometric argument for why gravitational force scales as 1/r^2.

items.text: A source mass emits a fixed total amount of gravitational "influence" (flux) in all directions
At distance r, that fixed flux has spread over the surface of an imaginary sphere of area 4 pi r^2
The influence per unit area equals the fixed total divided by 4 pi r^2
Since the force felt by a test mass is proportional to this per-area influence, the force scales as 1/r^2

questions.explanation: The argument starts with a fixed total flux from the source, spreads it over a sphere whose area grows as r^2, divides to get a per-area density, and identifies that density with the force felt at that distance — yielding the inverse-square scaling.

questions.prompt: Match each geometric quantity to its scaling with distance r.

left.text: Circumference of a circle (2D enclosing boundary)
Surface area of a sphere (3D enclosing boundary)

right.text: Scales as r^1
Scales as r^2
Scales as 1/r^2

questions.explanation: A circle's circumference (the 2D enclosing boundary) scales as r^1; a sphere's surface area (the 3D enclosing boundary) scales as r^2; and because force is fixed total flux divided by that enclosing area, force in 3D space scales as 1/r^2, the inverse of the sphere's area growth.

units.label: Gravitational Field and Surface Gravity g

lessons.label: The Gravitational Field g = GM/r^2

sections.heading: Force per unit mass: what a field is
sections.body: Newton's law of gravitation gives the force between two specific masses, F = GMm/r^2, but that force depends on BOTH masses — it changes if you swap in a heavier test object. To describe the space around a mass M independent of whatever you might place there, physicists divide the force by the test mass m and define the gravitational field: g = F/m = GM/r^2. The field g is a property of the source mass M and the distance r alone; it has units of force per unit mass (N/kg), which are identical to units of acceleration (m/s^2). At Earth's surface, plugging in G = 6.674x10^-11 N*m^2/kg^2, Earth's mass M = 5.972x10^24 kg, and Earth's mean radius R = 6.371x10^6 m gives g = 9.8 m/s^2 — the number that shows up in every free-fall problem, now understood as a field strength rather than a coincidence.

sections.heading: The field view versus the force view
sections.body: The force view asks: given two specific masses at a specific separation, what push or pull exists between them? The field view instead asks: what does the space around a single mass M look like, at every point, regardless of what (if anything) is ever placed there? The field exists whether or not a test mass is present to feel it — a useful fiction that lets you map out gravity's strength and direction throughout a region once, then multiply by whatever mass you drop in later using F = mg. This is more than notation: it is the same conceptual move used later for electric and magnetic fields, and it sidesteps uncomfortable questions about how one mass 'knows' about another across empty space by localizing the interaction to the field at each point instead.

sections.heading: g as the local free-fall acceleration
sections.body: Because g is force per unit mass, Newton's second law (F = ma) applied to gravity alone gives mg = ma, so a = g — the mass cancels. This is why every object in a vacuum, regardless of its own mass, falls with the same acceleration at a given location: a feather and a hammer released together on the airless Moon hit the ground simultaneously, as Apollo 15 commander David Scott demonstrated on camera in 1971. The field g is therefore simultaneously two things: the force per unit mass that a test object would feel, and the acceleration any free-falling object actually undergoes there. That equivalence — inertial mass and gravitational mass behaving identically — is not obviously guaranteed by the math and becomes a deep clue that later motivates Einstein's equivalence principle.

lessons.workedExample: Using g = GM/r^2 with G = 6.674x10^-11 N*m^2/kg^2, Earth's mass M = 5.972x10^24 kg, and r equal to Earth's mean radius 6.371x10^6 m gives g = 9.82 m/s^2, matching the familiar 9.8 m/s^2. Now move a satellite out to r = 2R (twice Earth's radius, meaning one Earth-radius of altitude above the surface): since g scales as 1/r^2, doubling r cuts g by a factor of 4, giving g = 9.8/4 = 2.45 m/s^2. Note that this calculation needed no information about the satellite's own mass at all — a 10 kg cubesat and a 10,000 kg space station both experience exactly 2.45 m/s^2 at that distance, because the field itself, not the object placed in it, is what was computed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'what's the difference between gravitational force and gravitational field?' is testing whether a student can separate a property of the source (the field, which exists independent of any test object) from an interaction between two specific objects (the force, which requires both). A student who can explain why g does not depend on the mass of the falling object — and connect that to why all objects in vacuum fall at the same rate — shows they understand the field concept rather than having memorized a formula. This distinction also previews why fields are the organizing idea behind electricity and magnetism, so a strong answer here signals transferable physical reasoning, not a memorized fact about Earth specifically.

questions.prompt: The gravitational field g at a point in space is best defined as:

options.text: The force per unit mass a test object would feel at that point
The total gravitational force between two specific named masses
The source mass divided by its own radius

explanations.a: Correct: g = F/m isolates a quantity that depends only on the source mass M and distance r, not on any particular test mass.
explanations.b: That describes the force F = GMm/r^2, which requires knowing BOTH masses involved, unlike the field.
explanations.c: Mass divided by radius is not a physically meaningful gravitational quantity and has the wrong units for a field.

questions.prompt: Because g = GM/r^2 does not include the mass of the object placed at that point, a bowling ball and a marble dropped together in a vacuum will:

options.text: Fall at different accelerations, since the bowling ball is heavier
Fall at the same acceleration, since both feel the same field g at that location
Fall at the same acceleration, but only because air resistance happens to cancel out

explanations.a: This is the common Aristotelian misconception; it ignores that a = g follows once mass cancels out of F = mg = ma.
explanations.b: Correct: since the field is independent of the test mass, F = mg gives a = g for any object, regardless of its own mass.
explanations.c: The scenario specifies a vacuum, so there is no air resistance to cancel; the equal acceleration holds for a deeper reason than that.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to derive an object's free-fall acceleration from Newton's force law of gravitation.

items.text: Write the force law F = GMm/r^2 for a test mass m near source mass M
Divide both sides by the test mass m to isolate a quantity independent of m
Identify the resulting quantity GM/r^2 as the gravitational field g at that point
Set g equal to the local free-fall acceleration of any object placed there

questions.explanation: Dividing the force law by the test mass isolates the field, which Newton's second law then shows is exactly the acceleration any object at that point would experience.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct description.

left.text: A test mass placed in the field

right.text: Measured in newtons; depends on both interacting masses
Measured in m/s^2 (equivalently N/kg); independent of the test mass
Converts the field at its location into an actual force via F = mg

questions.explanation: Force depends on both masses and is measured in newtons; field is force per unit mass, measured in m/s^2, independent of any test mass; the test mass is what the field acts ON to produce a real force.

lessons.label: Why g Varies: Altitude, Latitude, and Rotation

sections.heading: Earth is not a perfect sphere
sections.body: Earth's rotation causes it to bulge slightly at the equator and flatten at the poles: the equatorial radius is about 6,378.1 km while the polar radius is about 6,356.8 km, a difference of roughly 21 km. Since g = GM/r^2 depends on distance from Earth's center, standing at the equator means standing about 21 km farther from the center than standing at a pole — and because g falls off with the square of distance, this alone makes measured gravity weaker at the equator than at the poles, even before rotation is considered.

sections.heading: Rotation adds a centrifugal effect
sections.body: A second, larger effect comes from Earth's spin. An object at the equator is swinging in a circle of radius ~6,378 km once per sidereal day, which requires centripetal acceleration directed toward Earth's center; the true gravitational pull supplies both this centripetal acceleration AND the apparent weight measured on a scale, so the scale reads less than the true gravitational field would predict. This apparent reduction, roughly omega^2 * R ~ 0.034 m/s^2 at the equator, drops to zero at the poles (where an object sits on the rotation axis and needs no centripetal acceleration at all). Combined with the bulge, standard reference values put measured surface gravity at about 9.780 m/s^2 at the equator and about 9.832 m/s^2 at the poles — a roughly half-percent spread entirely explained by shape and spin, with no change in Earth's total mass anywhere.

sections.heading: Gravity also falls with altitude
sections.body: Moving straight up increases r directly, so g weakens continuously with height following the same inverse-square law. Near Earth's surface this gradient is small: about 3.086x10^-6 m/s^2 per meter of altitude (the 'free-air' gradient used in gravity surveys, equivalently 0.3086 milligal per meter). A commercial jet cruising at 10 km loses only about 0.03 m/s^2, about 0.3% of surface gravity — negligible for everyday purposes. But the effect compounds at large altitudes: the International Space Station, orbiting about 400 km up, still experiences roughly 88% of Earth's surface gravity, which is why 'zero gravity' in orbit is a popular misnomer rather than a literal absence of the field (the real explanation is free fall, covered in a later lesson).

lessons.workedExample: Starting from equatorial sea-level gravity of about 9.78 m/s^2, estimate g for a jet cruising at 10 km using the free-air gradient of 3.086x10^-6 m/s^2 per meter: change = 3.086x10^-6 * 10,000 = 0.031 m/s^2, giving g ~ 9.75 m/s^2, essentially unchanged. Now estimate g at the ISS's ~400 km altitude using the full inverse-square law instead of the small-altitude approximation, switching to Earth's average surface gravity (9.8 m/s^2, the standard reference value) rather than the equatorial figure used above: g = 9.8 * (6,371 / 6,771)^2 = 9.8 * (0.941)^2 = 9.8 * 0.885 ~ 8.7 m/s^2. So a plane loses under 1%, while the ISS — often pictured as 'gravity-free' — is still in a field about seven-eighths as strong as at Earth's surface; astronauts there feel weightless because they and the station are continuously falling together, not because gravity vanished.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask why g varies with location to check whether a student conflates 'weaker gravity' with 'Earth got lighter somewhere' rather than correctly attributing the variation to geometry (distance from center) and reference-frame effects (rotation). A strong answer separates the two causes at the surface — the equatorial bulge and the centrifugal effect of spin — and can also reason quantitatively about altitude, correctly predicting that airplane cruising altitude barely matters while orbital altitude matters substantially. This distinction also sets up the common misconception that astronauts in orbit experience 'no gravity,' which a well-prepared student can immediately correct.

questions.prompt: Measured surface gravity is lower at the equator (~9.78 m/s^2) than at the poles (~9.83 m/s^2) mainly because of:

options.text: Earth's equatorial bulge (greater distance from center) plus the centrifugal effect of rotation, both largest at the equator
The equator receiving less sunlight than the poles
The Moon pulling harder on the equatorial bulge than on the poles
