It stays the same regardless of radius
It increases only if the satellite's mass also increases

explanations.a: Correct: T = 2*pi*sqrt(r^3/GM) grows with r^3; a larger orbit means both more distance to travel per lap and a slower required speed, both of which lengthen the period.
explanations.b: Farther-out satellites move SLOWER (v = sqrt(GM/r) decreases with r), not faster, which is part of why their periods are longer.
explanations.c: Period depends strongly on radius through the r^3 term; it is not radius-independent.
explanations.d: The satellite's own mass cancels out of the orbit equations entirely and has no effect on the period, only the central mass M and the radius r matter.

questions.prompt: Kepler's third law for circular orbits, T^2 proportional to r^3, has a constant of proportionality (4*pi^2/GM) that depends on:

options.text: The mass of the central body being orbited
The mass of the orbiting satellite
Both the central mass and the satellite's mass equally
Neither mass, only the orbital radius

explanations.a: Correct: GM in the denominator refers to the mass of the body being orbited (e.g., Earth or the Sun); this is why every satellite around Earth obeys the same T^2/r^3 ratio.
explanations.b: The orbiting satellite's mass canceled out earlier in the derivation (from F_gravity = F_centripetal) and does not appear anywhere in the final period equation.
explanations.c: Only the central mass appears; the satellite's mass was already eliminated, so it cannot contribute to the proportionality constant.
explanations.d: The constant 4*pi^2/GM explicitly contains M, the central mass; radius r is the variable the constant multiplies, not part of the constant itself.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to how it changes when a satellite's orbital radius increases.

left.text: Central mass M in the equations

right.text: Decreases (as 1/sqrt(r))
Increases (as r^(3/2))
Unchanged by a change in orbital radius

questions.explanation: Speed falls as 1/sqrt(r), period rises as r^(3/2) because it combines a slower speed with a longer path, and the central mass M is a fixed property of the planet or star being orbited, independent of any particular satellite's radius.

questions.prompt: Order the algebraic steps that turn T = 2*pi*r/v into Kepler's third law, T^2 proportional to r^3.

items.text: Start from T = 2*pi*r/v
Substitute v = sqrt(GM/r) into the expression for T
Simplify to get T = 2*pi*sqrt(r^3/GM)
Square both sides to get T^2 = (4*pi^2/GM) * r^3

questions.explanation: Beginning from the definition of period in terms of speed and circumference, substituting the circular-orbit speed formula, simplifying the resulting expression, and squaring it produces Kepler's third law in its T^2-versus-r^3 form.

lessons.label: Falling Around the Earth

sections.heading: Newton's cannonball
sections.body: In a thought experiment from his 1728 'A Treatise of the System of the World,' Isaac Newton imagined a cannon on an impossibly tall mountain firing a ball horizontally. A slow ball falls to the ground close to the mountain, following a curved (parabolic) path. Fire it faster, and it lands farther away, because the ground has more time to curve out of the way of a projectile that covers more horizontal distance while falling the same amount. Newton's insight was that this trend has an endpoint: fire the ball fast enough, and the curvature of its falling path matches the curvature of the Earth itself. The ball keeps falling toward the center of the Earth forever, but the ground keeps curving away beneath it at exactly the same rate, so it never gets any closer to the surface. That is an orbit — not an escape from gravity, but a perpetual, unresolved fall.

sections.heading: The speed that makes falling never land
sections.body: The exact speed needed for this to work at the Earth's surface (ignoring air resistance) is the circular-orbit speed evaluated at r = R_Earth = 6,371 km: v = sqrt(GM_Earth / R_Earth) = sqrt(3.986x10^14 / 6.371x10^6) = 7,911 m/s, or about 7.9 km/s (roughly 28,400 km/h). This is sometimes called the first cosmic velocity. Real satellites orbit above the atmosphere, at somewhat larger radii and correspondingly smaller speeds, because atmospheric drag at surface altitude would rapidly slow and deorbit anything moving that fast that low. But the physical idea is identical at every altitude: an orbit is not a place where gravity has been switched off or overcome; it is a trajectory falling toward the planet with just enough sideways speed to keep missing it, indefinitely.

sections.heading: Why this is not merely a metaphor
sections.body: It is tempting to treat 'falling around the Earth' as a loose figure of speech, but the acceleration involved is the genuine, measurable acceleration due to gravity, not an approximation. An orbiting spacecraft's downward acceleration at any given altitude is g(r) = GM_Earth/r^2, calculated exactly the same way as the acceleration of a dropped ball, just evaluated at a larger r. What differs from a simple drop is only the initial sideways velocity; strip that away and the two situations are identical physics. This is also why an orbit requires no engine firing to maintain once established (barring atmospheric drag or other perturbations) — a rocket burns fuel to REACH orbital speed, but once there, gravity alone, doing exactly what it does to any falling object, keeps the spacecraft on its circular path indefinitely, for free.

lessons.workedExample: Check that the geometry actually works out at orbital speed. In 1 second of free fall near Earth's surface, gravity pulls an object down by d = (1/2)*g*t^2 = (1/2)(9.8)(1)^2 = 4.9 meters. At the surface orbital speed of 7,911 m/s, that same object also travels 7,911 meters horizontally in that 1 second. The question is whether the Earth's curved surface has dropped away by about that same 4.9 meters over a horizontal distance of 7,911 meters. Using the small-angle curvature-drop formula, drop = d_horizontal^2 / (2*R_Earth) = (7,911)^2 / (2*6.371x10^6) = 6.258x10^7 / 1.274x10^7 = 4.91 meters. The two numbers match almost exactly (4.9 m of fall versus 4.91 m of surface curvature drop) — direct confirmation that at 7.9 km/s, the ball falls exactly as fast as the ground curves away beneath it, tracing a circular orbit rather than crashing.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the cannonball scenario to catch the widespread misconception that objects in orbit have 'escaped Earth's gravity' or are 'beyond gravity's pull.' A student who explains that an orbiting object is continuously accelerating downward at very close to normal gravitational acceleration, and that the orbit is simply a controlled, endless fall, demonstrates real conceptual mastery. A follow-up a judge might ask is what would happen if the sideways speed were suddenly cut to zero at orbital altitude; the correct answer is that the object would fall essentially straight down, because it was never fighting gravity to begin with, only falling around the planet instead of into it.

questions.prompt: In Newton's cannonball thought experiment, what makes the fired ball go into orbit rather than crash into the ground?

options.text: Its horizontal speed makes the ground curve away beneath it at the same rate it is falling
It becomes lighter and gravity stops pulling on it
Air resistance pushes it upward once it goes fast enough
The cannon fires it above the atmosphere where gravity does not exist

explanations.a: Correct: the ball never stops falling; at orbital speed the curvature of the ground matches the curvature of its fall path, so the distance between the ball and the surface stays constant.
explanations.b: The ball's mass and the strength of gravity acting on it do not change with speed; gravity keeps pulling on it exactly as strongly throughout an orbit.
explanations.c: Air resistance opposes motion and would slow the ball down, not lift it into orbit; real orbits are maintained above the atmosphere precisely to avoid this drag.
explanations.d: Gravity does not switch off at any altitude reachable by a cannonball; it simply weakens gradually with distance, following the inverse-square law, and is still very much present in low Earth orbit.

questions.prompt: The 'first cosmic velocity' (about 7.9 km/s) refers to the circular orbital speed at:

options.text: The Earth's surface radius
The distance to the Moon
Geostationary orbit altitude
The distance the atmosphere ends

explanations.a: Correct: it is v = sqrt(GM_Earth/R_Earth), the circular-orbit speed evaluated at Earth's surface radius, the minimum speed needed for a (idealized, drag-free) orbit right at the surface.
explanations.b: The Moon's orbital speed is much lower, around 1 km/s, because it orbits at a far larger radius where gravity is much weaker.
explanations.c: Geostationary orbit speed is about 3.07 km/s, much lower than the surface value, again because of its far larger radius.
explanations.d: The atmosphere's extent is not what defines this speed; it is defined purely by the geometry of Earth's radius and its gravitational parameter GM.

questions.prompt: An object is in a stable circular orbit and suddenly loses all of its horizontal (sideways) velocity while keeping its altitude. What happens next?

options.text: It falls essentially straight down toward the planet
It continues orbiting normally, since gravity was never the source of its motion
It flies outward away from the planet
It remains stationary at that altitude

explanations.a: Correct: with no sideways speed left to make the ground curve away, gravity simply pulls it straight down, exactly as it would pull any dropped object — confirming that gravity was doing the falling all along, not something the orbit was resisting.
explanations.b: The orbit's continued path depended entirely on that horizontal speed; without it, the geometric trick that produced a circular path (falling versus curving ground) no longer works.
explanations.c: There is no outward force available to push it away; gravity only pulls inward, and nothing opposes that pull once the sideways motion is gone.
explanations.d: An object cannot hover motionless in a gravitational field without some supporting force (like thrust); gravity will accelerate it downward.

questions.prompt: Order Newton's cannonball scenario from slowest cannonball speed to the speed that produces a full circular orbit.

items.text: Cannonball lands close to the mountain, following a short parabolic arc
Cannonball lands farther away as its speed increases
Cannonball's fall path curvature approaches the curvature of the Earth
Cannonball falls forever without landing, tracing a circular orbit

questions.explanation: As launch speed increases from small to the circular-orbit value, the landing point moves progressively farther away until, at exactly the orbital speed, the falling path's curvature matches the planet's curvature and the object never lands at all.

lessons.label: Apparent Weightlessness

sections.heading: Falling together, not escaping gravity
sections.body: Astronauts aboard the International Space Station (ISS) appear to float, which leads many people to assume gravity is absent or negligible in orbit. It is not: at the ISS's altitude of roughly 400 km, gravitational acceleration is g_ISS = GM_Earth/r^2 = 3.986x10^14 / (6.771x10^6)^2 = 8.69 m/s^2, still about 88% of the surface value of 9.8 m/s^2. The astronauts feel weightless not because gravity is weak but because they and the entire station are in free fall together, accelerating downward at the same rate at the same instant. Weight, as something you can feel and a scale can measure, is really the CONTACT force a supporting surface exerts on you to prevent you from falling; a scale under your feet only reads a nonzero number because the floor is pushing up to stop you from accelerating downward at g. In orbit, nothing needs to push on the astronaut, because the astronaut, the station, and everything loose inside it are all accelerating downward together at the same rate, so there is no relative force between them, and thus no felt weight, even though gravity is still pulling on all of them almost as strongly as it does at the surface.

sections.heading: Distinguishing apparent from true weightlessness
sections.body: This state is properly called apparent weightlessness (or microgravity), distinct from true weightlessness, which would require being far enough from every mass that gravitational field strength is genuinely near zero — a condition essentially unreachable anywhere near a planet or star. The same apparent weightlessness happens briefly in a falling elevator, in an airplane flying a parabolic 'vomit comet' trajectory, or for a skydiver before the parachute opens; all are cases of unsupported free fall, just for a few seconds instead of continuously. The ISS is a special case only because its sideways orbital speed keeps it falling around the Earth rather than into it, making the free fall (and the weightlessness) continue indefinitely rather than ending after a few seconds.

lessons.workedExample: Compare gravity felt at the ISS to gravity at the surface. Using g proportional to 1/r^2: g_ISS/g_surface = (R_Earth/r_ISS)^2 = (6,371/6,771)^2 = (0.9409)^2 = 0.885. So g_ISS = 0.885 x 9.8 = 8.67 m/s^2, in close agreement with the direct calculation of 8.69 m/s^2 above (the small difference is rounding). This confirms that an object at ISS altitude experiences about 88% of surface gravity — strong enough that, if the station were to somehow stop moving sideways, everything inside would fall to Earth in minutes, not drift off into space. The floating sensation astronauts describe has nothing to do with weak gravity; it comes entirely from the station and its contents accelerating downward together at that same 8.7 m/s^2, leaving nothing pressing against anything else.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is one of the most commonly mis-explained topics at a science fair, so judges specifically watch for the phrase 'no gravity in space' as a red flag. A strong student response states the actual gravitational acceleration at the relevant altitude (making clear it is not zero) and then explains weightlessness as a free-fall condition rather than an absence of force. A sharper follow-up a judge might pose: would a bathroom scale under an astronaut's feet read zero on the ISS? The correct answer is yes, because the scale and the astronaut are both in free fall together and exert no contact force on each other, which is precisely why weightlessness is 'apparent' rather than a sign that gravity has vanished.

questions.prompt: Astronauts on the ISS appear to float primarily because:

options.text: They and the station are in free fall together at the same acceleration
Gravity is essentially zero at that altitude
The station generates an anti-gravity field
Their bodies have adapted to weigh less over time

explanations.a: Correct: with no relative acceleration between astronaut and station, there is no contact force between them, which is what produces the floating sensation, regardless of how strong gravity is.
explanations.b: Gravity at ISS altitude is about 88% of its surface strength, far from zero; the floating is not due to weak gravity.
explanations.c: No such technology exists; the ISS does not counteract gravity in any way, it simply falls with everything inside it.
explanations.d: Weightlessness is immediate upon entering free fall and has nothing to do with gradual bodily adaptation, though long-duration weightlessness does cause separate physiological effects like bone density loss.

questions.prompt: Approximately what fraction of Earth's surface gravity acts on the ISS at its ~400 km altitude?

options.text: About 88%
About 50%
About 10%
Essentially 0%

explanations.a: Correct: g falls off as 1/r^2, and at only about 6% farther from Earth's center than the surface, the reduction is modest, leaving roughly 88% of surface gravity.
explanations.b: A 50% reduction would require a much larger increase in distance from Earth's center than the ISS's modest 400 km altitude produces.
explanations.c: A drop to 10% would require an orbital radius several times Earth's radius, far beyond low Earth orbit.
explanations.d: Gravity is never zero at any finite distance from a mass; it only approaches zero at very large distances, nowhere near low Earth orbit.

questions.prompt: A bathroom scale is placed under an astronaut's feet aboard the freely orbiting ISS. What does it read?

options.text: Zero, because there is no contact force between the astronaut and the scale
The astronaut's normal Earth weight, since gravity is nearly the same strength
A negative number, because gravity pulls the astronaut away from the scale
It depends on the astronaut's velocity relative to the ISS

explanations.a: Correct: a scale reads the contact (normal) force pressing on it; since the astronaut and scale are both in free fall at the same acceleration, neither presses on the other, so the reading is zero.
explanations.b: A scale reading requires a supporting force resisting gravity; on Earth's surface the ground provides that resistance, but in orbit nothing is resisting the fall, so the reading is not the surface weight.
explanations.c: Scales measure contact force, not gravitational force directly, and contact force cannot be negative in this simple sense; the astronaut simply exerts no force on the scale.
explanations.d: As long as the astronaut and the ISS share the same free-fall acceleration (which orbital mechanics guarantees for objects at the same location), their relative velocity does not change the scale reading.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to whether it produces true weightlessness or apparent (free-fall) weightlessness.

left.text: Person in an elevator with a suddenly cut cable
An object extremely far from all stars and planets

right.text: Apparent weightlessness (still in a gravitational field, but in free fall)
Apparent weightlessness (brief, unsupported free fall)
True weightlessness (negligible gravitational field strength)

questions.explanation: The ISS and a falling elevator both remain within a substantial gravitational field but are in unsupported free fall, producing apparent weightlessness; only being far enough from every mass for gravity to genuinely approach zero counts as true weightlessness.

lessons.label: Geostationary and Geosynchronous Orbits

sections.heading: Matching a satellite's period to Earth's rotation
sections.body: A geosynchronous orbit is any orbit whose period matches Earth's rotation period relative to the distant stars, one sidereal day of 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds (86,164 seconds) — slightly shorter than the familiar 24-hour solar day, because Earth's rotation and its orbit around the Sun combine to make the Sun return to the same position in the sky about 4 minutes later than the stars do. A satellite in such an orbit completes one lap in exactly the time Earth takes to spin once, so as seen from the ground it retraces the same path in the sky every day. If that orbit is also circular and directly above the equator (zero inclination), the satellite appears to hang motionless over a single fixed point on the ground; this special case is a geostationary orbit. Every geostationary orbit is geosynchronous, but most geosynchronous orbits (inclined or elliptical) are not geostationary — they trace a repeating figure-eight-like pattern in the sky instead of holding perfectly still.

sections.heading: Solving for the geostationary altitude
sections.body: Plugging T = 86,164 s into Kepler's third law for a circular orbit, r^3 = GM*T^2 / (4*pi^2), and solving gives r ≈ 42,164 km measured from Earth's center, or an altitude of about 42,164 - 6,378 = 35,786 km above the surface (using Earth's equatorial radius of 6,378 km, since geostationary satellites orbit directly above the equator). This altitude is fixed by physics, not engineering choice — every geostationary satellite, regardless of purpose or country, sits at essentially this one altitude directly above the equator, which is why that narrow equatorial ring is a crowded and internationally regulated piece of orbital real estate. Communications and weather satellites favor this orbit because a ground antenna or dish can point at a fixed spot in the sky permanently, with no motorized tracking needed, and because a single geostationary satellite can maintain continuous, uninterrupted coverage of roughly a third of the globe at once.

sections.heading: The tradeoffs of parking that far out
sections.body: Geostationary orbit's fixed vantage point comes at real costs that make it unsuitable for every mission. The altitude is so large that a round-trip radio signal (ground to satellite and back) takes roughly 240 milliseconds at the speed of light, an unavoidable latency that is noticeable in live voice calls or fast-paced data links, which is one reason many modern broadband constellations (such as low-Earth-orbit internet satellites) accept the cost of thousands of moving satellites and constant ground-antenna tracking in exchange for far lower latency. Geostationary satellites are also far from the poles: because the orbit sits directly above the equator, its signal arrives at a very low angle above the horizon for observers at high latitudes, degrading coverage near the poles regardless of how many satellites are added to the ring.

lessons.workedExample: Derive the geostationary radius from Kepler's third law. With GM_Earth = 3.986x10^14 m^3/s^2 and T = 86,164 s: T^2 = 86,164^2 = 7.424x10^9 s^2. r^3 = (3.986x10^14)(7.424x10^9) / (4*pi^2) = 2.960x10^24 / 39.48 = 7.499x10^22 m^3. Taking the cube root: r = 4.217x10^7 m = 42,170 km, matching the commonly cited value of about 42,164 km (the small gap is rounding in the intermediate arithmetic). Subtracting Earth's radius, 42,170 - 6,371 = 35,799 km, matching the standard figure of 35,786 km altitude to within the same rounding. At this radius, the orbital speed is v = sqrt(GM/r) = sqrt(3.986x10^14/4.217x10^7) = 3,075 m/s, or about 3.07 km/s — far slower than low-Earth-orbit speeds near 7.7 km/s, since geostationary satellites sit roughly 6 times farther from Earth's center.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges often ask why the geostationary altitude is a single specific number rather than a range, to test whether a student understands it as the unique solution to T = 86,164 s in Kepler's third law rather than an arbitrary industry convention. A well-prepared student can also explain why the orbit must be equatorial: any inclination causes the satellite to drift north and south of the equator during each orbit, which breaks the 'fixed point in the sky' property even if the period is correct, illustrating the difference between merely geosynchronous and truly geostationary. Judges may also probe communication latency, since the roughly 71,600 km round trip (up and back down) introduces an unavoidable roughly 240-millisecond signal delay, a real engineering tradeoff for geostationary systems.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a geostationary orbit from a geosynchronous orbit in general?

options.text: Geostationary orbits are circular and equatorial, so the satellite appears fixed over one point
Geostationary orbits are much lower in altitude
Geostationary orbits have no fixed period
There is no real difference between the two terms

explanations.a: Correct: geostationary is the special case of geosynchronous that is also circular and directly above the equator, which is what makes the satellite appear motionless over one ground location.
explanations.b: Both terms refer to the same altitude range (period matching Earth's rotation); the geostationary requirement is about orbital shape and inclination, not altitude.
explanations.c: By definition, both geosynchronous and geostationary orbits share the same fixed period, one sidereal day.
explanations.d: The terms are related but distinct: all geostationary orbits are geosynchronous, but inclined or elliptical geosynchronous orbits are not geostationary.

questions.prompt: The geostationary orbital period is set to one sidereal day (about 23h 56m) rather than exactly 24 hours because:

options.text: The sidereal day matches Earth's rotation relative to the distant stars, which is what determines a fixed point in the sky
24 hours would place the satellite too close to Earth
The 4-minute difference is a rounding convenience with no physical basis
Geostationary satellites actually use a 25-hour period

explanations.a: Correct: a solar day (24 hours) is defined by the Sun's apparent position, which is slightly offset from Earth's true rotation because Earth also moves along its orbit around the Sun; the sidereal day tracks the actual rotation relative to a ground observer's fixed sky position.
explanations.b: The roughly 4-minute difference between sidereal and solar day changes the required radius only slightly, not by an amount that would meaningfully alter 'too close' versus 'far enough.'
explanations.c: The sidereal/solar distinction has a precise physical origin (Earth's orbital motion around the Sun), not an arbitrary convention.
explanations.d: Geostationary satellites use the sidereal day period (about 23h 56m), not 25 hours; using 25 hours would cause the satellite to visibly drift relative to any fixed ground point over time.

questions.prompt: Why do geostationary communications satellites all sit at essentially the same altitude?

options.text: That altitude is the unique solution to Kepler's third law for a period equal to one sidereal day
International law restricts satellites to one specific altitude
Rockets can only reach that altitude efficiently
It is simply the traditional altitude chosen by early satellite engineers

explanations.a: Correct: for a circular orbit, T^2 proportional to r^3 has exactly one radius solution for any given period; requiring a period equal to Earth's sidereal day pins down one specific altitude, about 35,786 km, by physics alone.
explanations.b: Regulation governs the ANGULAR spacing (longitude slots) of satellites within that ring, not the altitude itself, which is fixed by orbital mechanics.
explanations.c: Rockets can reach a wide range of altitudes; the geostationary altitude is chosen for its orbital period property, not launch efficiency.
explanations.d: The altitude follows directly from solving Kepler's third law for the required period; it was calculated, not chosen by convention.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to find the geostationary orbital altitude.

items.text: Identify the required period: one sidereal day, 86,164 seconds
Substitute that period into r^3 = GM*T^2 / (4*pi^2)
Solve for the orbital radius r (about 42,164 km from Earth's center)
Subtract Earth's radius to get the altitude above the surface (about 35,786 km)

questions.explanation: The geostationary altitude is derived by fixing the period to Earth's rotation rate, solving Kepler's third law for the corresponding orbital radius, and then converting that radius (measured from Earth's center) into an altitude above the surface.

lessons.label: Satellites and GPS

sections.heading: Designing an orbit for a purpose
sections.body: Different satellite jobs call for different orbits, chosen by working backward from what the mission needs to the radius and period that deliver it. Low Earth orbit (a few hundred km up, periods near 90 minutes) is favored for Earth-imaging and the ISS because it is cheap to reach and gives high-resolution views, at the cost of passing over any given point only briefly. Geostationary orbit trades altitude for permanence, ideal for communications and weather satellites that need to stare at one region continuously. GPS satellites split the difference with a medium Earth orbit (MEO): a constellation of at least 24 operational satellites near 20,200 km altitude (orbital radius about 26,560 km), chosen so each satellite's orbital period is close to half a sidereal day, about 11 hours 58 minutes. That period means each satellite retraces very nearly the same ground track once every day, and the constellation is arranged across six orbital planes so that a GPS receiver anywhere on Earth can typically see at least four satellites at once, the minimum needed to solve for its own 3D position and clock offset.

sections.heading: Where mechanics meets relativity
sections.body: GPS positioning depends on timing satellite signals to nanosecond precision, which means the atomic clocks aboard GPS satellites must stay synchronized with ground clocks far more precisely than orbital mechanics alone would suggest. Two relativistic effects intrude here, working in opposite directions. General relativity predicts that a clock higher up in a gravitational well (weaker field) runs FASTER than one at the surface, roughly 45.7 microseconds per day faster for GPS's altitude. Special relativity predicts that a clock moving at orbital speed (about 3.87 km/s for GPS) runs SLOWER than a stationary one due to time dilation, by about 7.2 microseconds per day. The two effects don't cancel; the net result is that each GPS satellite's onboard clock runs about 38.5 microseconds per day FASTER than an identical clock on the ground. Left uncorrected, that drift would translate into a growing position error of roughly 10 km per day, useless for navigation. Engineers correct for it before launch, by physically tuning each satellite's atomic-clock oscillator to run slightly slow (offset by about 4.465x10^-10 in relative frequency) so that once combined with the relativistic speed-up, the clock ticks in step with ground time.

lessons.workedExample: Confirm a GPS satellite's orbital period from its radius. With r = 26,560 km = 2.656x10^7 m and GM_Earth = 3.986x10^14 m^3/s^2: v = sqrt(GM/r) = sqrt(3.986x10^14 / 2.656x10^7) = sqrt(1.501x10^7) = 3,874 m/s, matching the commonly cited GPS orbital speed of about 3.87 km/s used in the relativistic time-dilation calculation. The period is T = 2*pi*r/v = (2*pi)(2.656x10^7)/3,874 = 1.669x10^8/3,874 = 43,090 s, which converts to 43,090/3,600 = 11.97 hours, matching the standard figure of 11 hours 58 minutes. This period is intentionally close to half a sidereal day (half of 23h 56m is 11h 58m) so that each satellite passes over nearly the same ground track at the same sidereal time every day, which simplifies both constellation planning and ground-station tracking.
lessons.judgeFraming: GPS is a favorite judge topic because it forces a student to connect two subjects that seem unrelated: circular-orbit mechanics and relativity. A judge will often ask directly why GPS needs relativistic corrections at all, since the speeds and altitudes involved seem 'ordinary.' A strong answer names both competing effects (gravitational blueshift speeding the clock up, velocity time dilation slowing it down), states which one wins (gravity, giving a net ~38.5 microsecond/day gain), and explains the consequence in a way a non-expert can follow: an uncorrected clock drift of tens of microseconds a day would compound into kilometers of position error, since GPS timing errors translate directly into distance errors at the speed of light. A student who can quantify that error chain, not just say 'relativity matters,' stands out.

questions.prompt: GPS satellites are placed in medium Earth orbit with a period near 12 hours mainly so that:

options.text: Each satellite retraces nearly the same ground track roughly once per sidereal day, aiding constellation coverage and tracking
They can avoid all relativistic effects at that altitude
It is the fastest possible orbital period allowed by physics
It matches the period of the Moon's orbit

explanations.a: Correct: a period of about half a sidereal day means the ground track repeats on a predictable daily cycle, which simplifies both operations and the constellation geometry needed for global coverage.
explanations.b: Relativistic effects occur at every altitude and every speed; MEO does not avoid them, it just sets the specific magnitude of the correction GPS engineers must apply.
explanations.c: Much shorter periods are possible at lower altitudes (the ISS orbits in about 90 minutes); 12 hours is a deliberate design choice, not a physical speed limit.
explanations.d: The Moon's orbital period is about 27.3 days, vastly longer than GPS's roughly 12-hour period; there is no direct connection between the two.

questions.prompt: Compared to a stationary clock on the ground, an onboard GPS satellite clock's NET relativistic effect is that it runs:

options.text: Faster overall, because the gravitational (general relativity) effect outweighs the velocity (special relativity) effect
Slower overall, because velocity time dilation dominates
Unaffected, because the two relativistic effects exactly cancel
Faster, but only due to special relativity, with no contribution from general relativity

explanations.a: Correct: the weaker gravity at GPS altitude speeds the clock up by about 45.7 microseconds/day, while orbital velocity slows it by about 7.2 microseconds/day; the gravitational effect is larger, so the net result is roughly 38.5 microseconds/day faster.
explanations.b: The velocity effect (7.2 microseconds/day) is smaller in magnitude than the gravitational effect (45.7 microseconds/day), so it does not dominate the net result.
explanations.c: The two effects are close in general order of magnitude but do not exactly cancel; a substantial net drift of about 38.5 microseconds/day remains.
explanations.d: Both effects contribute; general relativity's gravitational speed-up is actually the larger of the two contributions, not an absent one.

questions.prompt: If GPS engineers did NOT correct for the net relativistic clock drift, the practical consequence would be:

options.text: Growing position errors, since timing errors translate directly into distance errors
No effect, because GPS receivers only use orbital position, not timing
The satellites would fall out of orbit
The satellites' orbital period would change over time

explanations.a: Correct: GPS positioning works by timing how long a signal took to travel from satellite to receiver at the speed of light; an uncorrected clock drift of tens of microseconds per day compounds into a growing position error on the order of kilometers per day.
explanations.b: GPS positioning is fundamentally a timing system: a receiver measures signal travel time from multiple satellites and converts that into distance, so clock accuracy is central, not incidental, to the method.
explanations.c: Clock drift is a timing error, not a mechanical or gravitational effect on the satellite's trajectory; it would not cause the satellite to fall out of orbit.
explanations.d: The orbital period is governed by orbital mechanics (radius and central mass), which is unrelated to the onboard clock's timekeeping accuracy.

questions.prompt: Match each relativistic effect on GPS clocks to its cause and direction.

right.text: Weaker gravity at altitude makes the clock run faster (~45.7 microseconds/day)
Orbital velocity makes the clock run slower (~7.2 microseconds/day)
Clock runs about 38.5 microseconds/day faster overall

questions.explanation: General relativity's weaker-gravity effect speeds the satellite clock up, special relativity's velocity effect slows it down by a smaller amount, and because the gravitational effect is larger, the net result is a clock that runs about 38.5 microseconds per day fast, requiring a pre-launch correction.

lessons.label: Kepler's First Law: Elliptical Orbits

sections.heading: Not circles, but ellipses
sections.body: For nearly two thousand years, astronomers assumed planets moved on circles, because circles were considered the "perfect" shape and any deviation had to be patched with extra circles riding on circles (epicycles). Johannes Kepler broke that assumption using Tycho Brahe's unusually precise naked-eye observations of Mars. When Kepler tried to fit Mars's positions to a circular orbit, he was left with an 8-arcminute discrepancy — tiny, but far larger than Tycho's instruments could have gotten wrong. Rather than dismiss it, Kepler trusted the data and abandoned the circle. In Astronomia Nova (1609), he showed Mars actually traces an ellipse, with the Sun sitting not at the center but at one of the ellipse's two foci. An ellipse is defined by two focal points such that the sum of the distances from any point on the curve to the two foci is constant. A circle is the special case where both foci coincide.

sections.heading: Semi-major axis, eccentricity, perihelion, aphelion
sections.body: Two numbers describe an orbital ellipse's size and shape. The semi-major axis, a, is half the ellipse's longest diameter — essentially the orbit's average radius. The eccentricity, e, is a dimensionless shape parameter running from 0 (a perfect circle) toward 1 (a long, thin sliver); e = 0 means the two foci merge into the center. Because the Sun occupies one focus rather than the middle, a planet's distance from the Sun changes continuously over one orbit. The closest approach is perihelion, at distance a(1-e); the farthest point is aphelion, at distance a(1+e). Earth's orbit is nearly circular (e = 0.0167), so its perihelion (about 147.1 million km, early January) and aphelion (about 152.1 million km, early July) differ by only about 3%. Mercury (e = 0.206) and periodic comets like Halley (e = 0.967) show far more dramatic ellipses.

lessons.workedExample: Earth's semi-major axis is a = 149.6 million km with eccentricity e = 0.0167. Perihelion distance = a(1-e) = 149.6 x 0.9833 = 147.1 million km, reached in early January. Aphelion distance = a(1+e) = 149.6 x 1.0167 = 152.1 million km, reached in early July. Notice the counterintuitive result: the Northern Hemisphere's winter occurs when Earth is closest to the Sun, and its summer when Earth is farthest — proof that orbital distance is not what drives the seasons (axial tilt is), even though Kepler's ellipse does slightly modulate how intense that seasonal effect feels.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the first law to check whether a student's mental model of orbits is a genuine ellipse or a "circle with wobble." A student who says the Sun sits at the orbit's center, or who treats eccentricity as a distance rather than a shape ratio, reveals a shaky foundation everything else in the unit builds on. A strong answer states plainly that the Sun occupies one focus, not the geometric center, and can compute perihelion and aphelion from a and e without hesitation.

questions.prompt: Kepler's First Law states that a planet's orbit is:

options.text: A circle centered on the Sun
An ellipse with the Sun at one focus
An ellipse with the Sun at the center

explanations.a: Kepler specifically rejected the circular-orbit model after Mars's positions disagreed with it by 8 arcminutes.
explanations.b: Correct: the orbit is an ellipse, and the Sun sits at one of its two foci, not at the geometric center.
explanations.c: The center of an ellipse is a different point from either focus (unless e = 0, a circle); the Sun occupies a focus.

questions.prompt: A comet has eccentricity e = 0.9, while a planet has e = 0.05. Compared to the planet's orbit, the comet's orbit is:

options.text: Nearly identical in shape, just a different size
Much more circular
Much more elongated (stretched-out)

explanations.a: Eccentricity is a shape parameter independent of size; 0.9 versus 0.05 describes very different shapes.
explanations.b: Higher eccentricity moves an orbit farther from circular, not closer to it.
explanations.c: Correct: eccentricity closer to 1 means a longer, thinner ellipse, so e = 0.9 is dramatically more elongated than e = 0.05.

questions.prompt: Match each orbital term to its correct definition.

right.text: The closest distance to the Sun, equal to a(1-e)
The farthest distance from the Sun, equal to a(1+e)
Half the ellipse's longest diameter
A shape parameter from 0 (circle) toward 1 (elongated)

questions.explanation: Perihelion and aphelion are the two extreme distances, a(1-e) and a(1+e); the semi-major axis sets the orbit's overall scale, and eccentricity sets how stretched the ellipse is.

questions.prompt: Why did Kepler abandon the circular-orbit model for Mars?

options.text: Because circles were considered philosophically unfashionable
Because Tycho Brahe's data disagreed with circular predictions by 8 arcminutes, more than the data's likely error
Because Newton had already proven orbits must be ellipses

explanations.a: Kepler's decision was driven by trusting the observational data over an aesthetic assumption, not by fashion.
explanations.b: Correct: an 8-arcminute mismatch was too large to be Tycho's instrumental error, so Kepler concluded the circular model itself was wrong.
explanations.c: This is backwards chronologically: Kepler's empirical laws (1609, 1619) predate Newton's Principia (1687) by decades.

lessons.label: Kepler's Second Law: Equal Areas

sections.heading: Equal areas in equal times
sections.body: Kepler's Second Law states that an imaginary line connecting a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals, no matter where the planet is in its orbit. Near perihelion, where the planet is close to the Sun, that thin triangular wedge of swept area must be short and stubby, so the planet has to move quickly along its path to cover it in a given time. Near aphelion, far from the Sun, the wedge is long and thin, so the planet can move slowly and still sweep the same area. The practical consequence: every planet (and every comet) moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion. Earth's orbital speed varies from about 30.29 km/s in early January (near perihelion) to about 29.29 km/s in early July (near aphelion) — only a few percent, because Earth's orbit is nearly circular, but the effect is dramatic for a highly eccentric body like a comet.

sections.heading: The real physics: conservation of angular momentum
sections.body: This law is not a separate rule Kepler invented — it is exactly conservation of angular momentum, expressed geometrically. Gravity is a central force: it always points directly from the planet toward the Sun, along the line connecting them. A force that acts along the radius vector produces zero torque about the Sun, because torque is r x F, and r and F are parallel (or antiparallel). With zero torque, angular momentum L = m v r sin(theta) about the Sun cannot change — it is conserved throughout the orbit. The rate at which the radius vector sweeps area, dA/dt, equals L/(2m), a constant. So as r shrinks near perihelion, v must grow to keep L fixed, and as r grows near aphelion, v must shrink. The equal-areas law is really just angular momentum conservation wearing geometric clothing, and — unlike the elliptical shape of Law 1 — it holds for any central force, not just gravity's inverse-square law.

lessons.workedExample: Earth's perihelion distance is 147.1 million km with speed 30.29 km/s; its aphelion distance is 152.1 million km with speed 29.29 km/s. Because velocity is exactly perpendicular to the radius vector at these two extreme points, angular momentum there simplifies to L = m * r * v. Check conservation: r_peri * v_peri = 147.1M x 30.29 = 4.456 x 10^9 (km^2/s), and r_apo * v_apo = 152.1M x 29.29 = 4.455 x 10^9 — matching to within rounding, confirming r*v stays constant at the orbit's two extreme points exactly as angular momentum conservation predicts.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the second law to see whether a student can name the underlying physics rather than just recite "equal areas, equal times." A strong answer identifies gravity as a central force, explains that a central force exerts zero torque about the Sun, and connects that directly to angular momentum conservation — then predicts correctly that a planet speeds up approaching perihelion. A weak answer treats the law as a stand-alone geometric curiosity disconnected from Newtonian mechanics.

questions.prompt: A planet speeds up as it approaches perihelion because:

options.text: The Sun's gravity does positive work on it as it falls inward, and angular momentum conservation requires v to rise as r falls
Space is less resistant to motion near the Sun
The planet's mass decreases near the Sun

explanations.a: Correct: gravity is a central (zero-torque) force, so angular momentum L = m v r is conserved, forcing v to increase as r decreases.
explanations.b: There is no medium resisting motion in orbital mechanics; the speed change is a direct consequence of angular momentum conservation.
explanations.c: A planet's mass does not change during its orbit; only its distance and speed vary.

questions.prompt: Kepler's Second Law (equal areas in equal times) follows directly from which physical principle?

options.text: Conservation of mechanical energy
Conservation of angular momentum, because gravity is a central force with zero torque about the Sun
Newton's Third Law of action-reaction pairs

explanations.a: Energy conservation explains the vis-viva speed equation, but the equal-areas law specifically is a geometric statement of angular momentum conservation.
explanations.b: Correct: because the gravitational force always points along the Sun-planet line, it produces zero torque, so angular momentum (and hence the areal sweep rate) is constant.
explanations.c: The Third Law concerns paired forces between two bodies; it does not by itself explain why swept area is constant.

questions.prompt: Put the reasoning chain for Kepler's Second Law in the correct logical order.

items.text: Gravity always points directly along the line from the planet to the Sun (a central force)
A central force produces zero torque about the Sun (since r and F are parallel)
With zero torque, the planet's angular momentum L = m v r is conserved throughout the orbit
As the planet's distance r decreases, its speed v must increase to keep L constant
The swept area per unit time, proportional to L, stays the same everywhere in the orbit

questions.explanation: Centrality of the force implies zero torque, which implies conserved angular momentum, which forces speed to trade off against distance, which is exactly the equal-areas law.

questions.prompt: Which of Kepler's three laws holds for ANY central force, not just gravity's specific inverse-square form?

options.text: The First Law (elliptical shape)
The Second Law (equal areas)
The Third Law (T-squared proportional to a-cubed)

explanations.a: The elliptical orbit shape is special to an inverse-square force law; other central forces produce different (often non-closed) paths.
explanations.b: Correct: equal-area sweeping is a consequence of zero torque from ANY central force, regardless of how the force strength depends on distance.
explanations.c: The specific T^2 proportional to a^3 relationship depends on the inverse-square form of gravity, not just centrality.

lessons.label: Kepler's Third Law: T^2 Proportional to a^3

sections.heading: The harmonic law
sections.body: Ten years after publishing the first two laws, Kepler found a third relationship connecting every planet to every other planet in Harmonices Mundi (1619). He discovered that the square of a planet's orbital period, T^2, is directly proportional to the cube of its orbit's semi-major axis, a^3. Formally, for any two objects orbiting the same central body, (T1/T2)^2 = (a1/a2)^3. Kepler found this by painstakingly testing ratios across the six planets known in his time, without any theoretical justification for why it should be true — that explanation would not arrive until Newton, seven decades later. The law is remarkably convenient in solar-system units: if you measure a planet's semi-major axis in astronomical units (AU, Earth's average Sun distance) and its period in Earth years, then T^2 = a^3 almost exactly, because the Sun's mass so overwhelmingly dominates every planet's mass that the general proportionality constant reduces to 1 in these units.

sections.heading: Applying it across the solar system
sections.body: The law lets you predict one orbital quantity from the other without ever measuring both directly. Mercury, at a = 0.387 AU, has T = 0.241 years; check: 0.387^3 = 0.058 and 0.241^2 = 0.058, matching. Jupiter, at a = 5.20 AU, has T = 11.86 years; 5.20^3 = 140.6 and 11.86^2 = 140.7, matching. Neptune, at a = 30.07 AU, has T = 164.8 years; 30.07^3 approx 27,190 and 164.8^2 approx 27,150, matching within the precision of these approximate values. The pattern also carries an important physical insight: farther planets don't just travel a longer path, they also move more slowly (per Kepler's second and third laws combined), so orbital period grows faster than orbital distance — Neptune takes roughly 165 times as long as Earth to orbit the Sun, even though it is only about 30 times farther out.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose an astronomer measures a newly discovered dwarf planet's semi-major axis as a = 68 AU and wants to predict its orbital period without waiting centuries to observe a full orbit. Using T^2 = a^3 in AU-year units: T^2 = 68^3 = 314,432, so T = sqrt(314,432) approx 561 years. This is exactly how astronomers predicted the orbital periods of distant Kuiper Belt objects like Eris (a approx 68 AU, calculated T approx 559 years) long before a single full orbit could be directly observed — a striking demonstration of the third law's predictive power.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges test the third law to see if a student treats "proportional to" as an exponent relationship (doubling a multiplies T^2 by 8) rather than a simple linear scaling. They also check whether the student understands the AU-year shortcut (T^2 = a^3) as a unit convenience specific to objects orbiting the Sun, not a universal constant — a student who tries to apply T^2 = a^3 directly to a moon orbiting Jupiter, without adjusting for Jupiter's very different mass, has missed the point.

questions.prompt: If a planet's semi-major axis doubles, its orbital period increases by a factor of approximately:

options.text: 2.83 (that is, 2 to the power 1.5)

explanations.a: A factor of 2 would be true if T were proportional to a, but Kepler's Third Law relates T-squared to a-cubed, not T to a.
explanations.b: A factor of 4 would apply if a doubling of a quadrupled T^2 directly, but T itself is the square root of a^3, not a^3 itself.
explanations.c: Correct: T^2 proportional to a^3 means T proportional to a^1.5; doubling a scales T by 2^1.5 approx 2.83.

questions.prompt: In AU-year units, T^2 approx a^3 works so cleanly for solar-system planets because:

options.text: The Sun's mass is so much larger than any planet's that the proportionality constant reduces to 1 in these units
AU and years are, by definition, the same physical quantity
Kepler chose these units specifically to force the equation to look simple

explanations.a: Correct: the general form is T^2 = (4pi^2/G(M+m)) a^3; because M (Sun) >> m (planet), the constant simplifies to 1 exactly in AU-year-solar-mass units.
explanations.b: AU is a distance and a year is a time; they are different physical quantities that happen to combine conveniently under this specific proportionality.
explanations.c: Kepler discovered the pattern from data before Newton explained the underlying physics; the unit convenience is a consequence of physics, not a deliberate design choice.

questions.prompt: Order these solar system bodies from SHORTEST to LONGEST orbital period.

items.text: Mercury (a = 0.39 AU)
Earth (a = 1.00 AU)
Mars (a = 1.52 AU)
Jupiter (a = 5.20 AU)
Neptune (a = 30.07 AU)

questions.explanation: Because T^2 is proportional to a^3, orbital period increases monotonically with semi-major axis, so ranking by a exactly ranks by T for objects orbiting the same central body.

questions.prompt: Match each planet to its approximate orbital period, consistent with Kepler's Third Law.

right.text: 0.24 years
1.88 years
11.86 years

questions.explanation: Each pair satisfies T^2 approx a^3 in AU-year units: 0.39^3 approx 0.24^2; 1.52^3 approx 1.88^2; 5.20^3 approx 11.86^2.

lessons.label: Deriving Kepler's Third Law for a Circle

sections.heading: Setting gravity equal to centripetal force
sections.body: Kepler found T^2 proportional to a^3 purely by fitting observations — he had no idea why it was true. Newton showed the relationship is a direct mathematical consequence of his own law of gravitation. Start with the simplest case: a circular orbit of radius r. For an object to move in a circle at constant speed, some net force must continuously pull it toward the center, providing centripetal acceleration v^2/r. For a planet, that force is gravity: F = GMm/r^2, where M is the central mass, m is the orbiting mass, and G is the gravitational constant. Setting gravity equal to the required centripetal force, GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r, the orbiting mass m cancels from both sides — a first hint that orbital motion doesn't depend on the smaller body's mass. Solving for speed gives v = sqrt(GM/r): the orbital speed at radius r depends only on the central mass and the radius, nothing else.

sections.heading: From speed to period — recovering Kepler's law
sections.body: The orbital period is the circumference divided by the speed: T = 2*pi*r / v. Substituting v = sqrt(GM/r) gives T = 2*pi*r / sqrt(GM/r) = 2*pi*sqrt(r^3/GM). Squaring both sides isolates the proportionality Kepler discovered empirically: T^2 = (4*pi^2/GM) * r^3. For a circular orbit, r equals the semi-major axis a, so this is exactly T^2 proportional to a^3 — Kepler's Third Law, derived rather than merely observed. Crucially, the derivation reveals what the empirical "constant of proportionality" actually is: 4*pi^2/GM, a quantity that depends only on the central mass M. That single fact — that the proportionality constant encodes M — is what later lets astronomers turn Kepler's law around and use orbital measurements to weigh unseen masses (the subject of a later lesson in this unit).

lessons.workedExample: Geostationary satellites orbit Earth so that their period matches Earth's 23.93-hour sidereal rotation, making them appear fixed over one point on the equator. Using T^2 = 4*pi^2 r^3 / (GM) with Earth's mass M = 5.97 x 10^24 kg and T = 86,164 s: rearranging gives r^3 = G*M*T^2 / (4*pi^2) = (6.674e-11 x 5.97e24 x 86,164^2) / 39.48 approx 7.49 x 10^22 m^3, so r approx 4.22 x 10^7 m (about 42,200 km from Earth's center, or roughly 35,800 km above the surface) — exactly the well-known geostationary altitude, derived from first principles rather than looked up.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask students to derive, not just quote, Kepler's Third Law because the derivation is direct evidence of deductive reasoning — it shows the student understands that Newton's gravitation and Kepler's empirical pattern are the same physics viewed two ways. A student who can start from F = GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r and arrive at T^2 proportional to r^3 without prompting has demonstrated real command of the material; one who can only state the proportionality has memorized a fact Kepler himself couldn't explain.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that derive Kepler's Third Law for a circular orbit from Newton's gravitation.

items.text: Set gravitational force equal to the required centripetal force: GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r
Cancel the orbiting mass m and solve for speed: v = sqrt(GM/r)
Write the period as circumference over speed: T = 2*pi*r / v
Substitute v and simplify: T = 2*pi*sqrt(r^3/GM)
Square both sides to obtain T^2 = (4*pi^2/GM) r^3

questions.explanation: Each step feeds the next: equating forces gives speed, speed gives period via the circumference, and squaring the period expression exposes the T^2-proportional-to-r^3 relationship.

questions.prompt: In the derived relationship T^2 = (4*pi^2/GM) r^3, the constant 4*pi^2/GM depends on:

options.text: Only the mass of the orbiting body (the satellite or planet)
Only the mass of the central body being orbited
Both the orbiting body's mass and the central body's mass equally

explanations.a: The orbiting body's mass m canceled out of the equation entirely during the derivation; it does not appear in the final constant.
explanations.b: Correct: the orbiting mass cancels, leaving a constant that depends only on G and the central mass M — which is exactly why this relationship can be used to measure M.
explanations.c: The derivation explicitly shows m cancels from both sides of GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r, so the final constant contains no dependence on the orbiting body's mass.

questions.prompt: Why do all geostationary satellites orbit at essentially the same fixed altitude (about 35,800 km above Earth's surface), regardless of the satellite's own mass?

options.text: Because orbital radius, given a required period, depends only on the central mass, not the orbiting satellite's mass
Because heavier satellites are placed higher to balance their extra weight
Because satellite engineers coordinate to avoid collisions at a shared altitude

explanations.a: Correct: since the satellite's mass cancels out of T^2 = 4*pi^2 r^3 / GM, matching Earth's rotation period fixes r uniquely for any satellite mass.
explanations.b: Orbital mechanics doesn't work this way; a heavier satellite at the same radius orbits at the same period as a lighter one, since mass cancels from the equations of motion.
explanations.c: Collision avoidance is a real operational concern, but it is not why the geostationary altitude itself is fixed — that follows purely from matching Earth's rotation period via Kepler's Third Law.

lessons.label: Perihelion and Aphelion Speeds

sections.heading: Vis-viva: speed depends on where you are in the orbit
sections.body: Kepler's Second Law tells you a planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion, but not the actual numbers. The vis-viva equation supplies them: v^2 = GM * (2/r - 1/a), where r is the instantaneous distance from the central body, a is the orbit's semi-major axis, and M is the central mass. It comes from conservation of total mechanical energy: for any bound orbit, the sum of kinetic energy (1/2)mv^2 and gravitational potential energy -GMm/r equals a constant total energy of -GMm/(2a), regardless of where the body sits in its orbit. Rearranging that energy-conservation statement for v produces vis-viva directly. The equation applies at every point along an elliptical orbit, not just at the two extremes — plug in whatever r you're at, along with the orbit's fixed a, and get the instantaneous speed.

sections.heading: Perihelion versus aphelion speeds
sections.body: Applying vis-viva at the two extreme points gives clean formulas. At perihelion, r = a(1-e), and the equation simplifies to v_peri = sqrt[(GM/a) * (1+e)/(1-e)]. At aphelion, r = a(1+e), giving v_apo = sqrt[(GM/a) * (1-e)/(1+e)]. Dividing one by the other shows the ratio of speeds depends only on eccentricity: v_peri / v_apo = (1+e)/(1-e). For Earth's nearly circular orbit (e = 0.0167), that ratio is only about 1.034 — barely a 3% difference, consistent with the 30.29 versus 29.29 km/s figures from Kepler's second law. For a highly eccentric body like a comet, the same ratio can reach into the dozens, meaning the object crawls for years near aphelion and then whips through perihelion in a matter of days.

lessons.workedExample: Halley's Comet has a = 17.8 AU and e = 0.967. Its perihelion distance is a(1-e) approx 0.587 AU (inside Venus's orbit) and its aphelion distance is a(1+e) approx 35.0 AU (beyond Neptune). Using vis-viva with GM_sun = 1.327 x 10^20 m^3/s^2: v_peri = sqrt[(GM_sun/a) x (1+e)/(1-e)] approx 54.5 km/s, and v_apo = sqrt[(GM_sun/a) x (1-e)/(1+e)] approx 0.91 km/s. The comet is nearly 60 times faster at perihelion than at aphelion — it streaks past the inner solar system in weeks, then crawls through the outer darkness for decades before returning, which is exactly why Halley's period is about 76 years despite spending most of that time barely moving.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use vis-viva to test whether a student can connect an abstract equation to physical intuition rather than just plug numbers. A strong answer explains vis-viva as conservation of energy in a different algebraic form, correctly predicts that higher eccentricity produces a bigger perihelion-to-aphelion speed contrast, and can explain WHY (energy conservation trades potential for kinetic energy as the orbiting body falls closer to the central mass) rather than treating the formula as a black box to memorize.

questions.prompt: The vis-viva equation, v^2 = GM(2/r - 1/a), is fundamentally an expression of:

options.text: Conservation of angular momentum
Conservation of total mechanical energy
Newton's Third Law

explanations.a: Angular momentum conservation is Kepler's Second Law; vis-viva is derived from a different conserved quantity, total mechanical energy.
explanations.b: Correct: vis-viva comes directly from setting kinetic plus potential energy equal to the orbit's constant total energy, -GMm/(2a), and solving for v.
explanations.c: The Third Law concerns paired forces between two bodies and is not the source of the vis-viva relationship.

questions.prompt: A comet with e = 0.98 will have a perihelion-to-aphelion speed ratio that is:

options.text: Much larger than a planet's with e = 0.02
About the same as Earth's
Smaller than Earth's, since comets move slowly overall

explanations.a: Correct: since v_peri/v_apo = (1+e)/(1-e), a higher eccentricity produces a dramatically larger speed ratio (about 99 for e=0.98 versus about 1.04 for e=0.02, well above Earth's actual e = 0.0167).
explanations.b: The ratio depends directly and strongly on eccentricity; a comet's much higher e guarantees a much larger speed contrast than Earth's (whose actual eccentricity is only 0.0167).
explanations.c: Comets are not slow overall — near perihelion they can move faster than any planet; it's specifically the RATIO of speeds that grows with eccentricity.

questions.prompt: Match each orbital location to the correct vis-viva expression for speed there.

right.text: sqrt[(GM/a) x (1+e)/(1-e)]
sqrt[(GM/a) x (1-e)/(1+e)]

questions.explanation: Substituting r = a(1-e) into vis-viva gives the perihelion speed formula, r = a(1+e) gives the aphelion speed formula, and dividing the two cancels GM/a to leave a pure eccentricity ratio.

lessons.label: From Newton to Kepler

sections.heading: From guesswork to proof
sections.body: Kepler found his three laws by fitting Tycho Brahe's naked-eye observations, mostly of Mars, without any theory explaining why planets should behave that way — the laws were empirical pattern-matching, brilliant but unexplained. Nearly seventy years later, in the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687), Isaac Newton proved that all three laws follow mathematically from just two ingredients: his three laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation, F = GMm/r^2. Newton's contemporaries Robert Hooke, Edmond Halley, and Christopher Wren had each independently guessed that gravity might follow an inverse-square law, but none of them could prove what orbital shape it would produce. Newton did — using geometric methods (equivalent to solving a differential equation, though he wrote it in classical geometric language), he showed that an inverse-square central force yields orbits that are conic sections: ellipses for bound orbits, parabolas or hyperbolas for unbound ones.

sections.heading: Which law comes from what
sections.body: Newton's proof cleanly separates which physical fact is responsible for each Keplerian law. The Second Law (equal areas) requires only that the force be central — always pointing along the line to the Sun — because that alone guarantees zero torque and conserved angular momentum; it would hold even if gravity obeyed a different distance-dependence. The First Law (closed ellipse with the Sun at a focus) is special to the inverse-square form specifically; a force that fell off differently with distance (say, inverse-cube) would generally NOT produce a closed ellipse at all, but an open, precessing rosette-like path. The Third Law (T^2 proportional to a^3) falls out of combining the inverse-square force with the elliptical geometry, and Newton additionally generalized it to T^2 = 4*pi^2*a^3 / [G(M+m)], revealing that Kepler's "universal constant" actually depends on the central mass — not truly universal across different star systems, only within one system where M barely changes.

lessons.workedExample: Edmond Halley used Newton's proven laws to identify that the bright comets seen in 1531, 1607, and 1682 were the same object, returning on one elliptical orbit obeying Newtonian gravity, rather than three unrelated comets. Applying Kepler's Third Law to the roughly 76-year gap between sightings, Halley calculated the comet's orbit and predicted its return around 1758. The comet reappeared on schedule that December — sixteen years after Halley's own death — becoming one of the most famous confirmations of Newtonian mechanics and earning the comet his name.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "why do Kepler's laws work" specifically to separate a student who memorized three empirical rules from one who understands Newton derived them from deeper physics. A strong answer names which piece of Newton's physics is responsible for which law: centrality of the force for the second law, the specific inverse-square form for the first law, and their combination for the third — and can explain that this is why the third law's "constant" secretly encodes the central mass.

questions.prompt: Match each of Kepler's laws to the Newtonian physics that explains why it holds.

left.text: First Law (elliptical orbit, Sun at a focus)
Second Law (equal areas in equal times)

right.text: Specific to the inverse-square distance-dependence of gravity
Follows from any central force having zero torque about the Sun
Follows from combining the inverse-square force with elliptical orbit geometry

questions.explanation: Only an inverse-square force closes into an ellipse (Law 1); any central force conserves angular momentum (Law 2); and Law 3 emerges specifically from combining the inverse-square force law with the elliptical geometry it produces.

questions.prompt: What is special about the inverse-square form of gravity, specifically, for producing closed elliptical orbits?

options.text: Any central force, regardless of how it depends on distance, produces closed ellipses
Only an inverse-square (or a couple of other special) force laws produce closed, non-precessing elliptical orbits; most other distance-dependences do not
The inverse-square law is required only for circular orbits, not elliptical ones

explanations.a: This is false — centrality alone (needed for Law 2) is a weaker condition than what's needed to guarantee a closed ellipse; most central force laws produce open, precessing paths instead.
explanations.b: Correct: Newton showed the inverse-square law is one of only a couple of special force laws (the other being force proportional to distance) that produce closed elliptical orbits rather than precessing rosette paths.
explanations.c: Circular orbits are a special case of ellipses (e=0) and don't require any special force law to close — any central force with the right speed at a given radius produces a circle.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the historical unification of Kepler and Newton's work.

items.text: Kepler publishes the First and Second Laws in Astronomia Nova (1609)
Kepler publishes the Third Law in Harmonices Mundi (1619)
Newton proves all three laws follow from gravitation and motion in the Principia (1687)
Halley uses Newton's proven laws to predict the 1758 return of his namesake comet

questions.explanation: Kepler's empirical laws came first (1609, then 1619), Newton's theoretical proof followed decades later (1687), and Halley's predictive application came after that, confirmed in 1758.

lessons.label: Weighing a Star or Planet with Kepler

sections.heading: Turning Kepler's third law into a scale
sections.body: The derived relationship T^2 = 4*pi^2*a^3 / (GM) can be rearranged to solve for the central mass instead of the period: M = 4*pi^2*a^3 / (G*T^2). This is one of the most practically important equations in all of astronomy, because it is essentially the only direct way to measure the mass of an object you can't put a probe near or weigh from an orbiting companion's motion (gravitational lensing is another direct dynamical method, but it's mainly used for extended systems like galaxies and clusters). You cannot put a planet or a star on a scale — but if you can measure something orbiting it (a moon, a planet, a star, even a wisp of gas) and determine that orbit's period T and semi-major axis a, Kepler's rearranged third law hands you the central mass without any other assumptions about what the object is made of or how it formed.

sections.heading: From the Sun to a supermassive black hole
sections.body: Using Earth's own orbit (a = 1 AU, T = 1 year) in this formula gives the Sun's mass: about 1.989 x 10^30 kg — essentially the ONLY way the Sun's mass has ever been measured. The same trick, applied to a moon orbiting a planet, gives the planet's mass; Io's orbit around Jupiter (a = 4.22 x 10^8 m, T = 1.769 days) yields Jupiter's mass, about 1.90 x 10^27 kg. The method scales up dramatically: over roughly two decades of adaptive-optics infrared imaging, the teams of Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez tracked a star called S2 completing one full orbit (period about 16 years, semi-major axis about 970 AU) around the compact radio source Sagittarius A* at the Milky Way's center. Plugging those numbers into Kepler's rearranged third law gave a central mass of about 4 million solar masses packed into a region too small for anything but a black hole — decisive evidence that won Genzel and Ghez a share of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.

lessons.workedExample: Io orbits Jupiter with a = 4.217 x 10^8 m and T = 1.769 days = 1.5287 x 10^5 s. Using M = 4*pi^2*a^3 / (G*T^2): a^3 = (4.217e8)^3 approx 7.50 x 10^25 m^3, so the numerator is 4*pi^2 x 7.50e25 approx 2.96 x 10^27. The denominator is G*T^2 = 6.674e-11 x (1.5287e5)^2 approx 1.56. Dividing gives M approx 1.90 x 10^27 kg — matching Jupiter's independently known mass of 1.898 x 10^27 kg to within rounding, confirming the method with an object we can also cross-check by other means.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love this application because it is the concrete payoff of the entire unit: it shows the abstract T^2-proportional-to-a^3 relationship is not just a pattern to recite but an actual measurement tool, used identically to weigh the Sun, Jupiter, and a supermassive black hole. A strong answer states the rearranged formula from memory, correctly identifies that ONLY period and semi-major axis are needed (no assumptions about composition), and can name a real example — the Sun, a Jovian moon, or the S2/Sagittarius A* system — that used exactly this technique.

questions.prompt: Rearranged to solve for the central mass, Kepler's Third Law gives M equal to:

explanations.a: Correct: starting from T^2 = 4*pi^2*a^3/(GM) and solving for M gives M = 4*pi^2*a^3/(G*T^2).
explanations.b: This is the reciprocal of the correct expression, which would have the wrong units and would shrink, not grow, with a larger orbit.
explanations.c: This swaps the roles of a and T from the correct derivation; the semi-major axis, not the period, must be cubed.

questions.prompt: Why is measuring an orbiting star's period and semi-major axis essentially the ONLY way to determine the mass of Sagittarius A*, the Milky Way's central black hole?

options.text: Because a black hole emits no light of its own to directly analyze, so its gravitational pull on something orbiting it is the only observable evidence of its mass
Because black holes are made of a special material that can only be weighed using orbital mechanics
Because Kepler's Third Law only applies to invisible objects

explanations.a: Correct: since a black hole cannot be observed directly, its mass must be inferred indirectly, and Kepler's rearranged third law converts a measured orbit (the S2 star's period and semi-major axis) directly into a central mass.
explanations.b: This isn't about material composition; the method works identically for the Sun, a planet, or a black hole because it only depends on gravity's effect on an orbiting body.
explanations.c: Kepler's Third Law applies to any two-body gravitational system, visible or not; it's simply the ONLY practical tool when the central mass can't be observed directly.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to measure the mass of Sagittarius A* from the S2 star's orbit.

items.text: Track the star S2's position near the galactic center over many years with adaptive-optics imaging
Fit the tracked positions to an elliptical orbit to determine S2's period T and semi-major axis a
Plug T and a into M = 4*pi^2*a^3 / (G*T^2)
Obtain a central mass (about 4 million solar masses) far too great to be anything but a black hole

questions.explanation: Direct observation over years yields the orbit's shape and timing, which are the two inputs Kepler's rearranged third law needs to output a mass, which then supports the black-hole conclusion.

units.label: Orbital Maneuvers, Tides, and Many-Body Gravity

lessons.label: Changing Orbits: The Hohmann Transfer

sections.heading: Two circular orbits, one connecting ellipse
sections.body: A spacecraft sitting in a low circular orbit cannot simply drift up to a higher circular orbit; raising altitude costs energy, and the cheapest way to spend it is the maneuver German engineer Walter Hohmann worked out in 1925. A first, instantaneous burn (a brief rocket firing treated as an impulsive speed change) is applied while the spacecraft is at the point on its low circular orbit where the transfer will begin. That burn does not change position, only speed, but a higher speed at a fixed radius means more orbital energy, which converts the circular path into an elliptical transfer orbit whose perigee (closest point) is the original low orbit and whose apogee (farthest point) is set to exactly reach the radius of the target orbit. The spacecraft then simply coasts, under gravity alone, along that ellipse from perigee to apogee, needing no fuel during the coast itself.

sections.heading: The second burn circularizes
sections.body: Arriving at apogee, the spacecraft is now at the correct radius for the target orbit, but it is still moving on an elliptical path, not a circular one, and by the vis-viva relation an object on an ellipse is moving slower at its apogee than a circular orbit at that same radius requires. A second prograde burn (again speeding up) at apogee adds exactly the velocity needed to convert the elliptical path into a circular orbit at the new, higher radius. Both burns for an outward transfer are therefore speed-ups: the first raises apogee to the target altitude, the second circularizes once there — a transfer to a LOWER orbit instead uses two braking (retrograde) burns in the same two-point pattern.

sections.heading: Minimum energy, not minimum time
sections.body: The Hohmann transfer is the minimum-total-delta-v path between two coplanar circular orbits for most radius ratios, which is precisely why it is the default choice for missions where fuel is scarcer than time — it is emphatically not the fastest transfer, since a spacecraft willing to burn far more propellant could take a more direct, higher-energy path and arrive sooner. For very large radius ratios (roughly beyond about 11.9), a three-burn bi-elliptic transfer can actually use slightly less total delta-v than a Hohmann transfer, at the cost of a much longer flight time, illustrating that "minimum energy" and "minimum time" are frequently competing design goals in real mission planning.

lessons.workedExample: A spacecraft orbits Earth in a circular orbit at r1 = 6678 km (about 300 km altitude) and needs to reach a circular orbit at r2 = 10000 km, using Earth's GM = 398600 km^3/s^2. Circular speed at r1 is v1 = sqrt(398600/6678) ≈ 7.726 km/s. The transfer ellipse has semi-major axis a = (r1+r2)/2 = 8339 km, giving perigee speed v_p = sqrt(398600*(2/6678 - 1/8339)) ≈ 8.459 km/s, so the first burn is Δv1 ≈ 0.733 km/s. At apogee the ellipse speed is v_a = sqrt(398600*(2/10000 - 1/8339)) ≈ 5.650 km/s, while the target circular speed is v2 = sqrt(398600/10000) ≈ 6.313 km/s, so the second burn is Δv2 ≈ 0.663 km/s. Total mission cost: about 1.40 km/s of delta-v.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking a student to justify a Hohmann transfer over some other path is testing whether the student understands that orbital maneuvers are an optimization problem, not a single correct recipe. A strong answer explains why each burn is placed where it is (perigee and apogee of the SAME transfer ellipse, tangent to both circular orbits), computes or at least reasons about delta-v using vis-viva, and can name when a Hohmann transfer stops being optimal (the bi-elliptic case, or when time matters more than fuel). This distinguishes a student who has internalized the energy tradeoffs of orbit-raising from one who has only memorized "two burns, one ellipse."

questions.prompt: What does the first burn of a Hohmann transfer to a higher orbit accomplish?

options.text: It converts the circular orbit into an elliptical transfer orbit whose apogee reaches the target radius
It immediately moves the spacecraft to the target orbit's radius
It circularizes the spacecraft at the new, higher altitude

explanations.a: Correct: the first burn only changes speed at a fixed point, raising orbital energy so the resulting ellipse's apogee equals the target radius.
explanations.b: A burn changes velocity, not position, instantaneously; the spacecraft still has to coast along the ellipse to physically reach the higher radius.
explanations.c: Circularizing happens at the SECOND burn, once the spacecraft has coasted to apogee; the first burn only sets up the transfer ellipse.

questions.prompt: Why is a second burn needed at apogee of the transfer ellipse?

options.text: Because the spacecraft is moving slower there than the circular-orbit speed required at that radius, per the vis-viva relation
Because the first burn used up all the spacecraft's fuel
Because gravity alone would carry the spacecraft back down without any burn

explanations.a: Correct: an object on an ellipse moves slower at apogee than a circular orbit at that same radius requires, so a prograde burn is needed to add the missing speed and circularize.
explanations.b: Fuel remaining is a mission-design detail, not the physical reason a second burn is required; even with fuel to spare, the burn is needed because of the speed mismatch.
explanations.c: Without the second burn the spacecraft would indeed fall back toward perigee, but that is a description of the elliptical orbit's shape, not the reason the second burn adds speed rather than doing nothing.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a Hohmann transfer to a higher circular orbit.

items.text: Spacecraft begins in a low circular orbit
First prograde burn at perigee creates a transfer ellipse reaching the target radius
Spacecraft coasts along the transfer ellipse to apogee
Second prograde burn at apogee circularizes the orbit at the higher radius

questions.explanation: The maneuver starts on the low circular orbit, the first burn sets up the transfer ellipse, the spacecraft coasts (no fuel needed) to apogee, and the second burn circularizes there.
