left.text: Planning an ordinary communications satellite's orbit

right.text: Newtonian gravity alone is sufficient
Newtonian gravity alone is sufficient
General relativity's corrections are required for accuracy
General relativity's corrections are required for accuracy

questions.explanation: Newtonian gravity is accurate enough for structural engineering and ordinary satellite orbit design, where fields are weak and precision demands are modest; GPS clock timing and Mercury's precise perihelion precession are the two classic cases where relativistic corrections are not optional.

lessons.label: Momentum and F = dp/dt

sections.heading: Momentum as the vector a collision actually conserves
sections.body: A collision is a brief, violent exchange of momentum between two objects, and momentum p = mv is a vector: it has both a magnitude and a direction, and its sign matters as much as its size. A ball that bounces off a wall does not lose all its momentum, and it does not merely lose speed; its momentum reverses direction, so the change in momentum is roughly twice the incoming momentum, not zero. Tracking momentum as a signed, directional quantity, rather than treating a collision as if it just removed speed, is the single habit that separates correct collision reasoning from confused reasoning, and it is why every collision problem starts by fixing a positive direction before any numbers are plugged in.

sections.heading: Newton's second law in its original form: F = dp/dt
sections.body: Newton did not originally write his second law as F = ma; in modern notation his law reads F = dp/dt, force equals the rate of change of momentum. When mass is constant, dp/dt = m(dv/dt) = ma, so F = ma falls out as a special case. But collisions are exactly the situation where the momentum form earns its keep: during the brief contact, the force between two colliding bodies is a complicated, rapidly changing function of time that would be difficult to integrate step by step through F = ma. F = dp/dt sidesteps that difficulty by connecting the force directly to the momentum before and after contact, without requiring a detailed model of the force at every instant in between.

sections.heading: Why the momentum form is strictly more general
sections.body: F = dp/dt remains valid even when mass itself changes over time, a case where F = ma silently gives the wrong answer because it assumes mass is fixed. Expanding p = mv with the product rule gives F = m(dv/dt) + v(dm/dt); F = ma only survives if the second term vanishes, which requires dm/dt = 0. Rockets shedding burnt fuel, chains being lifted link by link, and raindrops growing by condensation all have dm/dt ≠ 0, and all require the full momentum form. Collisions between fixed-mass objects are the simpler case, but the underlying law that governs them, F = dp/dt, is the same one that governs these variable-mass systems.

lessons.workedExample: During a 0.5 kg cart's 8 ms collision with a spring bumper, its velocity reverses from +2.0 m/s to −1.6 m/s. Rather than modeling the complicated, rapidly changing contact force instant by instant, F = dp/dt lets you skip straight to the momentum change: p_i = 0.5 × 2.0 = 1.0 kg·m/s, p_f = 0.5 × (−1.6) = −0.8 kg·m/s, so Δp = −1.8 kg·m/s is exactly the net impulse the bumper delivered, no matter what the force curve looked like in between. Contrast this with a variable-mass case: a hopper drops sand onto a conveyor belt moving at a constant 3 m/s, adding mass at 5 kg/s. F = ma predicts zero force is needed, since the belt's own velocity is not changing, but F = dp/dt correctly shows the motor must supply an extra F = v(dm/dt) = 3 × 5 = 15 N to accelerate each new kilogram of sand up to belt speed — a force F = ma cannot explain, because it assumes mass is fixed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe F = dp/dt because it tests whether a student understands why the momentum form is more fundamental, not just an alternate way to write F = ma. A student who can state that F = ma is the special case where dm/dt = 0, and name a concrete system where that assumption fails, such as a rocket or a conveyor belt gaining mass, demonstrates real command of the law's structure. In a collision context specifically, judges also probe whether students track momentum's sign: a student who says a bounced ball merely lost speed, rather than reversing its momentum vector, has missed the point of using p = mv instead of scalar speed in the first place.

questions.prompt: A 0.06 kg ball moving at +12 m/s bounces straight back off a wall and leaves at −10 m/s. What is the magnitude of its change in momentum?

options.text: 0.12 kg·m/s, from the 2 m/s drop in speed
1.32 kg·m/s, from the ball's momentum reversing direction
0 kg·m/s, since the ball returns along the same line it arrived on

explanations.a: Incorrect: this treats momentum as scalar speed and subtracts speeds (12 − 10 = 2), ignoring that momentum is a signed vector quantity.
explanations.b: Correct: Δp = m(v_f − v_i) = 0.06 × (−10 − 12) = 0.06 × (−22) = −1.32 kg·m/s; the magnitude is 1.32 kg·m/s because the momentum reversed sign, not just shrank.
explanations.c: Incorrect: returning along the same line does not mean unchanged momentum; the direction flipped, which is exactly what makes Δp large rather than zero.

questions.prompt: For which situation is the F = dp/dt form of Newton's second law required rather than the simpler F = ma?

options.text: A cart of fixed mass colliding briefly with a bumper, where only its velocity changes
A rocket that is continuously burning and ejecting fuel, so its own mass decreases over time
A book sliding at constant velocity across a frictionless table

explanations.a: Incorrect: with constant mass, F = dp/dt reduces algebraically to F = ma, so the simpler form is sufficient even though the force is complicated during contact.
explanations.b: Correct: when mass itself changes with time, dp/dt = d(mv)/dt is not simply m(dv/dt); the product rule adds a v(dm/dt) term, so F = ma alone is insufficient and the full momentum form is required.
explanations.c: Incorrect: constant velocity and constant mass mean dp/dt = 0 = F, which F = ma also gives directly — no special form is needed here.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that show F = ma is a special case of F = dp/dt.

items.text: Start from F = dp/dt, momentum's general rate-of-change form
Substitute p = mv and apply the product rule: F = m(dv/dt) + v(dm/dt)
Impose the constant-mass condition dm/dt = 0
The second term vanishes, leaving F = m(dv/dt) = ma

questions.explanation: The derivation must begin from the general law, expand the product rule to expose both terms, impose the constant-mass assumption, and only then can the variable-mass term be dropped to recover F = ma.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to the reason it needs the full F = dp/dt form rather than F = ma.

left.text: A rocket burning and ejecting fuel
A chain being lifted onto a table link by link
A book sliding at constant mass across a table

right.text: dm/dt ≠ 0: mass leaves the system, carrying momentum away with it
dm/dt ≠ 0: new mass at rest must be accelerated up to the moving system's speed
dm/dt = 0, so F = dp/dt reduces exactly to F = ma

questions.explanation: The rocket loses mass that carries momentum away with it; the chain gains mass that starts at rest and must be sped up; the sliding book's mass never changes, so the general law collapses to the familiar F = ma.

lessons.label: Impulse as the Area Under a Force-Time Curve

sections.heading: The impulse-momentum theorem
sections.body: Impulse is defined as J = ∫F dt, the integral of force over the time it acts. The impulse-momentum theorem states that this integral equals exactly the change in momentum it produces: J = Δp. This is not a coincidence but a direct consequence of F = dp/dt — integrate both sides over the interval of contact and the right side telescopes to p_f − p_i by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Impulse and momentum therefore share units, kilogram-meters per second (kg·m/s), which is identical to the newton-second (N·s); either unit is correct, and the equivalence is a useful check that a calculation is dimensionally sound.

sections.heading: Reading impulse as an area, not just a formula
sections.body: Because J = ∫F dt is an integral, it has a direct graphical meaning: plot force on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis, and the impulse delivered over any interval is exactly the area under that curve between the interval's endpoints. Real collisions almost never produce a flat, constant force; a bat striking a ball, a foot striking the ground, or two cars crumpling into each other all produce a force that rises from zero, peaks, and falls back to zero as contact begins, intensifies, and ends. Reading impulse off such a graph means computing the area of whatever shape the curve traces — a triangle, a rounded hump, or an irregular blob — not simply reading off one number and multiplying by the total time.

sections.heading: The constant-force shortcut, and why it is a special case
sections.body: The familiar formula J = FΔt is only the area of a rectangle, and it is exact only when the force truly is constant over the interval. Applying J = FΔt to a curve that rises and falls, using either the peak force or some arbitrarily chosen value for F, overstates or understates the true impulse; only the actual area under the actual curve gives the correct answer. This is why physics problems that hand you a real or graphed force-time trace expect geometric reasoning (areas of triangles, trapezoids, or numerically summed strips) rather than a single multiplication.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.2 kg hockey puck slides toward a player's stick at +3 m/s. Contact lasts 6 ms, and the stick's push on the puck rises linearly from 0 to a peak of 380 N (in the negative direction) at 3 ms, then falls linearly back to 0 by 6 ms — a triangular force-time graph. The area of a triangle is ½ × base × height, so the impulse is J = ½ × 0.006 s × 380 N = 1.14 N·s, directed opposite the puck's initial motion. By the impulse-momentum theorem, Δv = J/m = 1.14/0.2 = 5.7 m/s in that same direction, so the puck's final velocity is 3 − 5.7 = −2.7 m/s: it now moves backward at 2.7 m/s. Reading J straight off the graph as an area recovered the exact answer without ever needing to know why the force rose and fell the way it did.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe area-under-the-curve reasoning because the most common error on a real force-time graph is multiplying the peak force by the full contact time, which badly overstates the impulse for anything other than a perfectly rectangular pulse. A student who instead identifies the shape (triangle, trapezoid, or a curve to be estimated) and computes the correct geometric area shows they understand impulse as an integral, not just a memorized formula. This lesson also sets up the next one directly: judges may ask what happens to the peak force if the same triangular area is squeezed into half the time, testing whether the area concept carries over to comparing curves.

questions.prompt: A force rises linearly from 0 to 200 N over 10 ms, then instantly drops to 0. What is the impulse delivered?

options.text: 2.0 N·s, treating it as a rectangle of height 200 N and width 0.010 s
1.0 N·s, the area of the triangle: ½ × 0.010 × 200
20 N·s, multiplying 200 N by 0.010 s and then by 10 for unit conversion

explanations.a: Incorrect: this treats a triangular rise as if it were a rectangle at the peak height the whole time, doubling the true area.
explanations.b: Correct: a linear rise from 0 to a peak forms a triangle, whose area is ½ × base × height = ½ × 0.010 s × 200 N = 1.0 N·s.
explanations.c: Incorrect: there is no factor-of-10 unit conversion needed here; N·s and kg·m/s are numerically identical, so this answer results from an invented extra step.

questions.prompt: Why is J = FΔt (using the peak force) generally the WRONG way to find the impulse from a real, non-rectangular force-time graph?

options.text: Because impulse and momentum do not actually share the same units
Because it computes the area of a rectangle at the peak height, which overstates the true area under a rising-and-falling curve
Because force-time graphs cannot be integrated at all

explanations.a: Incorrect: impulse (N·s) and momentum (kg·m/s) are dimensionally identical; that is not the issue here.
explanations.b: Correct: using the peak force for the entire duration draws a rectangle taller than the real curve everywhere except at the single peak instant, so it always overstates the true area for a rising-and-falling pulse.
explanations.c: Incorrect: force-time graphs absolutely can be integrated, whether analytically (for simple shapes) or numerically (for irregular ones); that is the whole point of this lesson.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding a collision's Δv from a real force-time graph.

items.text: Identify the shape(s) the force-time curve traces during contact
Compute the area under the curve using the correct geometric or numerical method
Set that area equal to the impulse J, and by the theorem, to Δp
Divide Δp by the mass to solve for Δv

questions.explanation: You must first know what shape you are measuring before computing its area, then invoke the impulse-momentum theorem to convert that area into a momentum change, and only then divide by mass to reach a velocity change.

questions.prompt: Match each force-time curve shape to the correct formula for the area (impulse) under it.

left.text: Rectangle (constant force F over duration Δt)
Triangle (force rises linearly to a peak, then falls linearly to 0)
Trapezoid (force rises, holds at a plateau, then falls)

right.text: J = F × Δt
J = ½ × base × peak height
J = ½ × (sum of the two parallel sides) × height

questions.explanation: Each shape's area formula gives its impulse directly: a rectangle's constant force times duration, a triangle's half-base-times-height, and a trapezoid's averaged-parallel-sides formula for a curve with a plateau.

lessons.label: Average versus Peak Force

sections.heading: Defining the average force from the area
sections.body: For any force-time curve, however irregular, the average force over the interval is defined as F_avg = J/Δt = Δp/Δt. This definition is exact, not an approximation: it is simply the constant force that would need to act for the same duration Δt to sweep out the identical area (and therefore deliver the identical impulse) as the real, varying curve. F_avg is a useful summary number precisely because Δp and Δt are usually the two quantities you actually know or can measure; the detailed shape of the force pulse in between is often hidden or hard to observe directly.

sections.heading: Same impulse, wildly different peaks
sections.body: Two very different-looking force-time curves can deliver the identical impulse. A flat-topped, rectangular pulse spread over a long duration can sweep out the same area as a tall, narrow, spiky pulse concentrated into a short duration. Because F_avg = J/Δt depends only on the total area and the total time, both pulses share the same average force if their durations happen to match — but their peak forces can differ enormously, since the spiky pulse must reach a much higher instantaneous force to sweep out the same area in far less time.

sections.heading: Why the peak, not just the average, still matters
sections.body: Materials, tissues, and structures typically fail or deform based on the peak stress or peak force they experience at any single instant, not the time-averaged force over the whole event. Two collisions that deliver identical momentum changes, and therefore identical impulses, can be safe in one case and damaging in the other purely because one pulse concentrates its force into a sharp spike while the other spreads the same area out flatly over more time. This is precisely why the ratio between an event's peak force and its average force, not just the impulse itself, is a meaningful engineering and safety quantity — and it sets up the next lesson's central idea: stretching Δt is the direct lever for lowering both the average AND the peak force for a fixed required Δp.

lessons.workedExample: Two padding materials are each tested to absorb the same 12 N·s impulse from a dropped weight. Pad A produces a roughly rectangular, flat-topped force pulse of F = 300 N lasting Δt = 40 ms (area = 300 × 0.040 = 12 N·s); since a rectangle's peak equals its average, F_peak,A = F_avg,A = 300 N. Pad B is stiffer and produces a triangular, spiky pulse lasting only Δt = 8 ms; because a triangle's area is ½ × base × peak, its peak must satisfy ½ × 0.008 × F_peak = 12, giving F_peak,B = 3000 N — and since a triangle's average is half its peak, F_avg,B = 1500 N. Both pads absorb the identical 12 N·s impulse, yet Pad B's peak force (3000 N) is ten times higher than Pad A's (300 N), purely because the same area was compressed into a fifth of the time and into a peaked, rather than flat, shape.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe average-versus-peak force because it is a genuine and common source of confusion: students often assume that if two collisions have equal impulse, they must be equally forceful or equally safe. A student who can explain that impulse fixes only the area under the curve, while the curve's shape and duration independently determine how concentrated (peaked) that area is, demonstrates real command of the concept. Judges may follow up by asking which single design change — shape or duration — most directly lowers a collision's peak force, previewing the practical lever explored in the next lesson.

questions.prompt: Two force pulses deliver the same impulse over the same total duration Δt, but one is rectangular and the other is triangular. How do their peak forces compare?

options.text: The triangular pulse has a higher peak force than the rectangular one
Both have identical peak forces, since they share the same impulse and duration
The rectangular pulse has a higher peak force than the triangular one

explanations.a: Correct: a rectangle's peak equals its average (F_peak = F_avg), but a triangle's peak is twice its average (F_peak = 2F_avg) for the same area and duration, so the triangular pulse must reach a higher peak.
explanations.b: Incorrect: equal impulse and equal duration force equal AVERAGE force, not equal peak force — the shape of the curve still changes how concentrated that average is at any one instant.
explanations.c: Incorrect: this has the relationship backward; spreading the same area flatly (rectangle) requires a lower peak than concentrating it into a rising-and-falling shape (triangle) over the same duration.

questions.prompt: Why can two collisions with identical impulse (identical Δp) still differ in how much damage they cause?

options.text: Because impulse and momentum change are only loosely related, not equal
Because materials and tissues typically respond to peak force, which can differ enormously between pulses even when the total impulse is the same
Because identical impulse always means identical average force, which always means identical peak force

explanations.a: Incorrect: the impulse-momentum theorem makes J = Δp an exact equality, not a loose relationship.
explanations.b: Correct: peak force, not average force or total impulse, is usually what determines damage, and the same area under a force-time curve can be shaped into a low, flat pulse or a tall, narrow spike.
explanations.c: Incorrect: identical impulse and duration do fix the average force, but the peak force still depends on the curve's shape, which is not determined by the impulse alone.

questions.prompt: Match each force-time pulse shape to the ratio of its peak force to its average force.

left.text: Triangular pulse (linear rise then linear fall)
Half-sine pulse (smooth rise and fall, like many real impacts)

right.text: Peak = 1 × average
Peak = 2 × average
Peak ≈ 1.57 × average (π/2)

questions.explanation: A rectangle's peak equals its average by definition; a triangle's area formula (½ base × height) forces its peak to be twice its average for the same area and base; a half-sine pulse's integral works out to an average of (2/π) times its peak, so its peak is π/2, about 1.57, times its average.

lessons.label: Extending Contact Time to Reduce Force

sections.heading: The one lever you actually control: Δt
sections.body: In a real collision, Δp is usually fixed by physics you cannot change: an object's mass and how much its velocity must change to reach zero (or to reverse) are set by the situation. But F_avg = Δp/Δt shows that Δt is not fixed the same way — it is often a design or technique choice, and because F_avg is inversely proportional to Δt, stretching the contact time even modestly produces a proportional drop in the average force, and typically the peak force as well. Doubling Δt halves F_avg for the identical momentum change; multiplying Δt by ten divides F_avg by ten. This single inverse relationship, not any vague notion of cushioning absorbing energy, is the actual mechanism behind every soft-landing and safety-padding technique.

sections.heading: Concrete techniques that lengthen Δt
sections.body: Bending the knees on landing lets the legs act as a hinge, letting the body's center of mass keep moving downward over a longer path and a longer time before velocity reaches zero, instead of the legs staying rigid and stopping the body almost instantly. Catching a fast ball with give — pulling the glove or hands backward in the direction the ball is already moving as it arrives — extends the time over which the ball decelerates to a stop inside the glove, rather than meeting a hand that stays fixed in place. Cushioned packaging works the same way at a materials level: foam or crumpling cardboard collapses gradually under load, so the packaged object decelerates over the time it takes the material to crush, rather than stopping abruptly against a rigid wall.

sections.heading: The limits of the trick
sections.body: Extending Δt is not unlimited. A landing surface, a glove, or a package only has so much travel distance available before the material bottoms out and behaves rigidly anyway; a car's crumple zone can only be as long as the car itself allows. And in some contexts a very long Δt is undesirable for other reasons — a boxer's glove that gave way completely would fail to deliver a controlled punch at all. The technique's value is always bounded by how much extra time (and the distance that time corresponds to) the situation can physically provide before the same fixed Δp must be absorbed anyway.

lessons.workedExample: A 70 kg person jumps down and lands moving at 4 m/s, coming to rest. The impulse the ground must deliver is fixed by physics: Δp = mΔv = 70 × 4 = 280 kg·m/s. Landing stiff-legged, the body stops in roughly Δt = 0.02 s, giving F_avg = 280/0.02 = 14,000 N — about 20 times the person's own body weight (70 × 9.8 ≈ 686 N). Landing with bent knees stretches the stopping time roughly tenfold, to Δt = 0.2 s, giving F_avg = 280/0.2 = 1,400 N, only about 2 times body weight. The momentum change to be absorbed, 280 kg·m/s, was identical in both cases; only the time over which it was absorbed changed, and the average force dropped by exactly the same factor of ten that the time increased by.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe contact-time extension because the correct explanation is mechanistic (F_avg = Δp/Δt, so a longer Δt divides the force by the same factor) while the common wrong explanation is vague hand-waving about padding 'absorbing the energy' or 'cushioning the blow' without any quantitative content. A student who can state a specific factor — a bent-knee landing that lasts ten times longer than a stiff one experiences roughly a tenth of the average force — demonstrates they understand the relationship rather than reciting a slogan. Judges may also test the boundary of the idea by asking why a technique cannot extend Δt indefinitely, checking whether students recognize the physical limits (available crush distance, need for control) on the trick.

questions.prompt: A padded landing extends the stopping time from 0.03 s to 0.15 s for the same momentum change. By what factor does the average force change?

options.text: It decreases by a factor of 5
It increases by a factor of 5
It stays the same, since the momentum change is unchanged

explanations.a: Correct: F_avg = Δp/Δt, and Δt increased by a factor of 0.15/0.03 = 5, so F_avg decreases by that same factor of 5 for the identical Δp.
explanations.b: Incorrect: F_avg is inversely, not directly, proportional to Δt — a longer stopping time lowers the average force, it does not raise it.
explanations.c: Incorrect: Δp being unchanged is exactly why the force DOES change; F_avg is the ratio Δp/Δt, and stretching Δt while holding Δp fixed necessarily shrinks that ratio.

questions.prompt: Why does bending your knees when landing from a jump reduce the peak force on your body, in mechanistic terms?

options.text: It reduces the total momentum change your body must undergo
It reduces your mass momentarily, lowering the momentum that needs to be absorbed
It lengthens the time (and distance) over which your velocity drops to zero, lowering F_avg = Δp/Δt for the same fixed Δp

explanations.a: Incorrect: your momentum change is fixed by your mass and landing velocity; bending your knees does not change how much momentum must be brought to zero, only how long that takes.
explanations.b: Incorrect: bending your knees does not reduce your mass; mass is unaffected by the technique.
explanations.c: Correct: the joints flexing let the center of mass keep descending over a longer path and time before reaching zero velocity, which lowers F_avg = Δp/Δt because Δp is unchanged but Δt grows.

questions.prompt: Order the causal chain of a bent-knee landing, from initial contact to the reduced force outcome.

items.text: The feet make initial contact with the ground while still moving downward
The knees and hips flex, letting the center of mass keep descending
The time (Δt) over which velocity reaches zero is stretched out
F_avg = Δp/Δt drops because Δp is unchanged but Δt has increased

questions.explanation: Contact must occur first; the joint flexion that follows is what physically stretches the stopping time; that stretched time is what then lowers the average force for the same fixed momentum change.

questions.prompt: Match each technique to the specific mechanism by which it lengthens the stopping time.

left.text: Catching a fast ball with give
Cushioned packaging around a shipped object

right.text: Leg joints flex, letting the body's center of mass keep descending before velocity reaches zero
The hand moves backward in the ball's direction of travel as contact begins, rather than staying fixed
The material gradually collapses under load, so the object decelerates over the crushing distance rather than stopping at a rigid wall

questions.explanation: Each technique achieves the same inverse-force effect through a different physical mechanism: joint flexion, a hand moving with the ball, or a material crushing gradually — but all three work by stretching Δt for the same fixed Δp.

lessons.label: Measuring Impulse with a Force Sensor

sections.heading: What a force sensor actually records
sections.body: A force plate or handheld force sensor typically uses a piezoelectric crystal or a strain-gauge load cell: the crystal generates a tiny voltage proportional to the stress squeezing it, or the gauge's electrical resistance changes as it deforms under load, and either signal is converted into a force reading. Crucially, the sensor does not record a smooth, continuous curve; it samples force at a fixed rate, often 1000 samples per second or more for impact studies, producing a list of discrete (time, force) data points rather than the idealized continuous F(t) curve used in a textbook diagram.

sections.heading: Numerically integrating the trace to recover Δp
sections.body: Because the raw data is a set of discrete points rather than a smooth function, the impulse cannot be read off as a clean geometric area; instead it is approximated with a numerical integration rule. The trapezoidal rule is the most common choice: between each pair of consecutive samples, the curve is approximated by a straight line, and the small trapezoid's area (the average of the two force readings, times the time step) is computed and summed across the whole trace: J ≈ Σ [(F_i + F_i+1)/2] × Δt. As the sampling rate increases and Δt shrinks, this sum converges toward the true integral, which is exactly what the impulse-momentum theorem calls for.

sections.heading: Cross-checking against an independent mΔv measurement
sections.body: A well-designed experiment does not stop at the sensor's own number; it checks the integrated impulse against an independent measurement of momentum change, typically mass times the velocity change measured by photogates or high-speed video tracking before and after contact. Agreement between the two methods, usually within a few percent, validates that the sensor and the numerical integration are trustworthy. Disagreement points to specific, identifiable error sources: a sampling rate too slow to capture a sharp true peak (which flattens and understates the integrated area), sensor drift or an uncalibrated zero-offset, or a sensor whose mechanical bandwidth simply cannot respond fast enough to track a very brief, very sharp force spike.

lessons.workedExample: A force sensor records a bouncing ball's impact at 2 ms intervals: F = 0 N at t = 0 ms, 150 N at 2 ms, 400 N at 4 ms, 150 N at 6 ms, and 0 N at 8 ms. Applying the trapezoidal rule across the four intervals gives J ≈ 0.002 × [(0+150)/2 + (150+400)/2 + (400+150)/2 + (150+0)/2] = 0.002 × (75+275+275+75) = 0.002 × 700 = 1.4 N·s. Independently, a 0.16 kg superball is tracked arriving at −4.0 m/s and rebounding at +4.5 m/s, so mΔv = 0.16 × (4.5 − (−4.0)) = 0.16 × 8.5 = 1.36 kg·m/s. The two methods agree to within about 3%, a discrepancy consistent with the sensor's 2 ms sampling interval slightly under-resolving the true, sharper force peak that occurred somewhere between the 4 ms and 6 ms readings.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe force-sensor experiments to test whether students understand numerical integration as an approximation that converges toward the true impulse as sampling rate increases, rather than treating the sensor's readout as automatically exact. A strong answer names a specific, plausible error source, such as a coarse sampling interval missing the true peak or a sensor's limited mechanical bandwidth, when asked to explain a several-percent gap between the integrated impulse and an independently measured mΔv. Judges may also ask why the trapezoidal rule is preferred over simply summing the raw force readings, checking whether students grasp that trapezoids account for the slope between samples in a way a simple sum does not.

questions.prompt: A force sensor records F = 100 N at t = 0 ms and F = 300 N at t = 10 ms, with nothing recorded in between. Using the trapezoidal rule, what is the estimated impulse over this interval?

explanations.a: Correct: trapezoidal rule gives J ≈ [(F_1+F_2)/2] × Δt = [(100+300)/2] × 0.010 = 200 × 0.010 = 2.0 N·s.
explanations.b: Incorrect: this comes from using only the higher endpoint (300 N) as if it applied for the whole interval, rather than averaging both endpoints.
explanations.c: Incorrect: this comes from summing both endpoints (100+300=400) and multiplying by Δt without taking the average, effectively double-counting the area.

questions.prompt: Increasing a force sensor's sampling rate (recording more points per second during an impact) mainly does what to the trapezoidal-rule estimate of impulse?

options.text: Makes it converge more closely to the true integral, especially for sharp, brief peaks
Has no effect, since the trapezoidal rule already gives the exact answer at any sampling rate
Systematically increases the estimate regardless of the true force curve's shape

explanations.a: Correct: more, closer-together samples mean each trapezoid better approximates the true curve between points, so the sum converges toward the true integral — this matters most for sharp peaks a coarse sampling rate would otherwise flatten and understate.
explanations.b: Incorrect: the trapezoidal rule is only exact for a curve that is itself perfectly straight between samples; for a curved or peaked real force trace, coarser sampling introduces real error.
explanations.c: Incorrect: finer sampling does not systematically bias the estimate in one direction; it reduces the (potentially over- or under-) error by tracking the true curve more closely.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a force-sensor impulse-measurement experiment.

items.text: Zero and calibrate the sensor's baseline before impact
Record the force-time trace during the collision at a fixed sampling rate
Numerically integrate the discrete trace (e.g., with the trapezoidal rule) to estimate J
Compare the estimate against an independently measured mΔv to validate it

questions.explanation: Calibration must happen before any data is trustworthy, then the trace is recorded during the actual event, then that discrete trace is integrated to get an impulse estimate, and only then can that estimate be checked against an independent measurement.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: Generates a small voltage proportional to the mechanical stress squeezing a crystal
Its electrical resistance changes as it physically deforms under load
Approximates area under discrete data points by averaging each pair of consecutive readings

questions.explanation: Piezoelectric sensors convert stress directly into a voltage signal, strain gauges convert physical deformation into a resistance change, and the trapezoidal rule is the numerical method that turns either sensor's discrete samples into an impulse estimate.

lessons.label: Impulse in Sport and Safety

sections.heading: Soft versus jarring landings
sections.body: A trained rolling fall spreads a person's momentum change across a sequence of contact points and a longer total time, instead of stopping the body abruptly at one rigid point. The military parachute landing fall (PLF), for example, is taught as a deliberate five-point sequence: the balls of the feet strike first, then the side of the calf, then the thigh, then the hip and buttock, and finally the side of the back, each point absorbing part of the total momentum change in turn as the body rolls through the fall. A stiff, unrolled landing on the feet alone forces the same total Δp through one joint in a much shorter Δt, which is exactly why the rolled technique is trained: it is the same physics as bent-knee landing, generalized across the whole body and multiple sequential contact points rather than one.

sections.heading: Riding a punch: extending Δt to lower the peak force received
sections.body: A boxer who is struck can either meet the punch with a stationary head, or 'ride' the punch by moving the head and body backward or rotating away as the glove arrives. Riding the punch does not change the momentum the punch delivers, which is fixed by the puncher's fist speed and mass, but it extends the distance and time over which the head decelerates relative to the incoming glove, lowering the peak force and peak acceleration transmitted to the skull. This is the same F_avg = Δp/Δt relationship used for landings and packaging, applied here to reduce injury risk rather than to protect an object.

sections.heading: Follow-through: extending contact to increase the impulse delivered
sections.body: Follow-through inverts the goal of the previous two examples. In a throw, a pitcher's hand stays in continuous contact with (or grip on) the ball through a long wind-up and release motion; coaches who say to 'throw through' the target are asking the athlete not to decelerate the arm early, because a longer time (and distance) over which force is applied to the ball produces a larger impulse, and therefore a higher final ball speed, for the same force the athlete's muscles can generate. In striking sports, the ball or opponent's contact time itself is extremely brief, but a full swing that keeps accelerating into and through contact, rather than one that unconsciously decelerates right before impact to 'aim' the shot, keeps the bat or racket at its highest speed at the moment of contact — maximizing the impulse and momentum transferred for a given swing effort.

lessons.workedExample: A punch delivers a fixed Δp = 6 kg·m/s to an effective head-and-neck mass of about 5 kg, regardless of technique. Meeting the punch with a stiff, stationary chin gives roughly Δt = 5 ms of deceleration, so F_avg = 6/0.005 = 1,200 N. Riding the punch, moving the head backward through about 15 cm over a longer Δt = 25 ms, gives F_avg = 6/0.025 = 240 N — a fivefold reduction in average (and peak) force for the identical momentum delivered by the punch. This is the physical basis for the difference between absorbing a shot cleanly and being staggered or knocked down by the same punch thrown at the same speed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe sport and safety examples specifically because they force a student to hold both directions of F_avg = Δp/Δt in mind at once: landing softly and riding a punch both extend Δt to shrink the force the body receives, while follow-through extends the time force is applied to increase the impulse delivered to a ball. A student who can explain why coaches give what sounds like opposite advice — 'give' on landing but 'drive through' on a throw — using the very same equation solved for two different unknowns, demonstrates genuine command of the relationship rather than a memorized list of separate 'safety tips.' A weak answer treats each example as an unrelated fact rather than recognizing the shared underlying physics.

questions.prompt: A boxer rides a punch by moving the head backward as the glove lands, instead of holding still. What happens to the momentum delivered by the punch, and what happens to the peak force on the head?

options.text: The momentum delivered decreases, and so does the peak force
The momentum delivered stays the same, but the peak force decreases because Δt increases
The momentum delivered stays the same, and so does the peak force, since only speed of the glove matters

explanations.a: Incorrect: the punch's momentum is set by the puncher's fist mass and speed, not by what the receiver's head does; riding the punch does not reduce the momentum thrown at the head.
explanations.b: Correct: Δp is fixed by the incoming punch, but riding it extends Δt (the head keeps moving with the glove longer before stopping relative to it), and F_avg = Δp/Δt drops as a direct result.
explanations.c: Incorrect: peak force depends on Δt as well as Δp; changing how the head moves changes Δt even though the punch's own momentum is unaffected.

questions.prompt: A coach tells a pitcher to 'follow through' rather than stopping the arm right at release. What is the physical reason this increases the ball's speed?

options.text: It reduces the ball's mass at the moment of release
Continuing to apply force through release lengthens the time (and distance) over which the hand accelerates the ball, increasing the impulse delivered for the same muscular force
It has no physical effect on ball speed and is purely a stylistic habit

explanations.a: Incorrect: the ball's mass is fixed and unaffected by the throwing motion.
explanations.b: Correct: not decelerating the arm early keeps force being applied to the ball over a longer stretch of the motion, and a longer time of applied force means a larger impulse J = ∫F dt for the same force capability, which directly raises the ball's final momentum and speed.
explanations.c: Incorrect: follow-through has a real, quantifiable physical effect through the impulse-momentum relationship; it is not merely stylistic.

questions.prompt: Order the five points of contact, as trained, in a rolling parachute landing fall (PLF).

items.text: Balls of the feet
Side of the calf
Thigh
Hip and buttock
Side of the back

questions.explanation: The trained PLF sequence rolls the momentum change through the body from the feet upward, each point picking up part of the deceleration in turn: feet, then calf, then thigh, then hip and buttock, and finally the side of the back.

questions.prompt: Match each technique to its goal within the F_avg = Δp/Δt relationship.

left.text: Rolling through a parachute landing across five contact points
A boxer riding a punch by moving the head back
A pitcher following through instead of stopping the arm at release

right.text: Extend Δt to reduce the peak force the body receives, for a fixed incoming Δp
Extend the time force is applied to increase the impulse (and momentum) delivered to the ball, for a given muscular force

questions.explanation: Rolling and riding a punch both extend Δt to shrink the force a body receives from a fixed incoming momentum change, while follow-through extends the time force is applied to grow the impulse and momentum delivered outward to the ball — the same equation, solved for two different goals.

units.label: Conservation of Momentum in One Dimension

lessons.label: Conservation of Momentum from Newton's Third Law

sections.heading: Internal forces come in canceling pairs
sections.body: Conservation of momentum is not a separate law bolted onto Newton's mechanics; it is a direct consequence of Newton's third law. When two objects collide, object A exerts a force on object B, and by the third law, object B simultaneously exerts a force on A that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction: F(A on B) = -F(B on A). These two forces act for exactly the same duration, because they exist only while the objects are in contact (or otherwise interacting), so the impulse each object receives, J = FΔt, is also equal and opposite: J(on B) = -J(on A). Since impulse equals the change in momentum, Δp(B) = -Δp(A), which means B's momentum gain is exactly A's momentum loss. Add the two changes together and they cancel: Δp(A) + Δp(B) = 0, so the total momentum of the two-object system is unchanged by the collision, no matter how complicated, violent, or messy the interaction is at the microscopic level.

sections.heading: Why internal forces never touch the total
sections.body: This cancellation is not a coincidence specific to collisions; it is completely general. In any system of interacting bodies, every internal force appears as a third-law pair, and when you sum F = dp/dt over the whole system, every internal pair contributes zero to the net force because the two members of each pair cancel identically. What survives the sum is only the net external force acting on the system from outside. This gives the general law: dP_total/dt = F_external,net, where P_total is the vector sum of every object's momentum. If no net external force acts on a system — or if the external forces are negligible over the timescale considered — then dP_total/dt = 0, and total momentum is a constant of the motion. Momentum conservation is therefore a bookkeeping law: internal forces can shuffle momentum between the pieces of a system, but they can never create or destroy it, because every internal push has an equal and opposite internal push somewhere else in the same system.

sections.heading: Momentum conservation versus energy conservation
sections.body: It is worth being precise about what does and does not survive a collision. Total momentum is conserved in every collision where external forces are negligible, elastic or not. Total kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions; in inelastic collisions, some kinetic energy converts to heat, sound, or permanent deformation, yet momentum conservation holds regardless, because it follows from the third law alone and makes no assumption about how the contact forces vary with deformation or time. This is why momentum conservation is such a powerful problem-solving tool: it applies even when you know almost nothing about the details of the contact forces during the (often extremely brief and complicated) collision itself.

lessons.workedExample: Two students on frictionless carts, A (60 kg) at rest and B (40 kg) moving at 3 m/s toward A, collide and stick together. During contact, A pushes B backward with some complicated, time-varying force, and by the third law B pushes A forward with the exact negative of that force at every instant. Because the forces are equal and opposite and act for the same contact time, the impulses are equal and opposite, so momentum lost by B exactly equals momentum gained by A. Total momentum before: p = 0 + 40(3) = 120 kg·m/s. Since Δp(A) = -Δp(B), total momentum after is still 120 kg·m/s, giving a common final velocity v = 120/(60+40) = 1.2 m/s — obtainable without ever knowing the actual shape of the contact force curve.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this derivation because many students can quote 'momentum is conserved' without knowing why it is true, and a project that invokes conservation as an unexplained rule reads as memorized rather than understood. A student who can trace the logic from the third law, through equal-and-opposite impulses, to canceling momentum changes shows they understand conservation as a consequence, not an axiom. Judges will also test the boundary: ask what happens if a wall (an external object) is part of the collision, since then the wall's reaction force is external to the two-cart system and momentum of the carts alone need not be conserved.

questions.prompt: Why does Newton's third law guarantee that total momentum is conserved in a two-body collision with no external forces?

options.text: Because the two objects always end up with equal final velocities
Because the equal-and-opposite contact forces act for the same time, giving equal-and-opposite impulses that cancel when the momentum changes are summed
Because kinetic energy is always conserved in a collision, and momentum follows from energy

explanations.a: Incorrect: equal final velocities only happens in a perfectly inelastic (sticking) collision; momentum is conserved in every collision, elastic or not, regardless of the final velocities.
explanations.b: Correct: equal magnitude, opposite direction, same duration forces give equal-and-opposite impulses, so Δp(A) = -Δp(B), and the sum of momentum changes is zero.
explanations.c: Incorrect: kinetic energy conservation is a separate, stricter condition true only for elastic collisions; momentum conservation follows from the third law alone and holds even when energy is not conserved.

questions.prompt: In F(A on B) = -F(B on A), what must also be true for the resulting impulses to be exactly equal and opposite?

options.text: The two forces must act for the same duration, Δt
The two objects must have equal mass
The collision must be elastic

explanations.a: Correct: impulse is J = FΔt; since the forces are exerted through the same contact interval, equal-and-opposite forces integrated over the same Δt give equal-and-opposite impulses.
explanations.b: Incorrect: mass does not need to be equal — impulses cancel because of the forces and shared contact time, not because of matching mass; unequal masses just mean unequal velocity changes for the same impulse.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the impulse cancellation, and thus momentum conservation, holds for both elastic and inelastic collisions; elasticity only concerns whether kinetic energy is also conserved.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps that derive momentum conservation from Newton's third law.

items.text: State the third law: F(A on B) = -F(B on A) during contact
Both forces act over the same contact time, so J(on B) = -J(on A)
Impulse equals change in momentum, so Δp(B) = -Δp(A)
Sum the changes: Δp(A) + Δp(B) = 0, so total momentum is unchanged

questions.explanation: The derivation starts from the third law's force pair, converts equal-and-opposite forces over equal time into equal-and-opposite impulses, converts impulse into momentum change, then sums to show the total is conserved.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its conservation status in a real (possibly inelastic) collision with no external forces.

left.text: Total kinetic energy of the system
Sum of all internal contact forces at any instant

right.text: Always conserved, because it follows from the third law alone
Conserved only in the special case of an elastic collision
Always sums to zero, because internal forces occur in equal-and-opposite pairs

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation is unconditional given no external forces; kinetic energy conservation is the extra, optional condition defining an elastic collision; internal force pairs cancel identically by the third law at every instant.

lessons.label: Defining a Closed System

sections.heading: Choosing the boundary is the whole trick
sections.body: Momentum conservation only holds for the total momentum of a system with no net external force acting on it. In practice, that means the entire skill of applying conservation correctly is choosing the system boundary so that whatever forces cross it are either genuinely absent or small enough, for the timescale of interest, to ignore. Draw the boundary too narrowly — around just one of two colliding carts, say — and the other cart's push is an external force, so that single cart's momentum is not conserved on its own. Draw the boundary around both carts together, and the cart-on-cart forces become internal, third-law pairs that cancel, leaving the pair's total momentum conserved. The physics does not change; only what counts as 'internal' versus 'external' changes, and that choice is entirely up to the person setting up the problem.

sections.heading: Why brief collisions make gravity and friction negligible
sections.body: Real collisions are almost never perfectly closed, because gravity and friction are always present. The reason momentum conservation still works so well for collisions is the impulse-time argument: impulse is J = FΔt, and while gravity and friction act continuously, a hard collision — a bat hitting a ball, two carts crashing — typically lasts only a few milliseconds. The contact force during that brief window is often hundreds or thousands of times larger than gravity or friction, so the contact impulse dwarfs the impulse gravity or friction can deliver in that same tiny Δt. This is why 'closed system' is usually a good approximation during the collision itself, even though the system is clearly not closed if you track it for a full second before and after.

sections.heading: When the ground or a pivot breaks closure
sections.body: Closure fails, and momentum is genuinely not conserved for the object alone, whenever an external object supplies a large, sustained, or otherwise non-negligible force during the interaction. A ball bouncing off the floor is not a closed system for the ball alone: the floor (rigidly attached to the Earth, for practical purposes infinitely massive) delivers whatever impulse is needed to reverse the ball's momentum, and that impulse comes from outside the ball. A bat swung by a batter is not free to recoil over the full swing — the grip and stance deliver a sustained external force before, during, and after the hit — so the bat-ball system is not closed if tracked over the whole swing. During the brief ~1 ms of contact itself, however, the grip's impulse has too little time to act, similar to how gravity is negligible during a brief collision (see the ball-and-bat treatment in this lesson's worked example). Recognizing these cases early prevents the classic error of writing a momentum conservation equation for a system that a wall, pivot, axle, or the ground is quietly pumping momentum into or out of.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.15 kg baseball moving at 40 m/s is struck by a bat and leaves at 50 m/s in the opposite direction, all in about 0.7 ms of contact. Naively summing the ball's momentum before and after gives Δp = 0.15(50) - 0.15(-40) = 7.5 - (-6.0) = 13.5 kg·m/s, which looks like momentum was 'created' — but the ball alone is not a closed system, since the bat, gripped by a batter braced against the ground, supplies exactly that impulse from outside. If instead the system is redefined as ball-plus-bat-plus-batter-plus-Earth, momentum is conserved, but that system is too unwieldy to be useful. In practice, the correct closed system for this problem is ball-and-bat during the brief 0.7 ms of contact only, ignoring the ground reaction through the batter's feet as negligible on that short timescale — a boundary choice, not a law of physics, that makes the arithmetic tractable.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe system boundaries because a shockingly common error is writing 'momentum is conserved' for an object that is visibly interacting with something massive and external, like the ground or a clamp, without noticing. A team that explicitly states its system boundary and justifies why the chosen boundary makes external forces negligible (via the Δt argument, or genuine isolation like frictionless carts) demonstrates real command of when the shortcut applies. Judges may ask 'conserved for what system, exactly, and why is the [ground/pivot/friction] excluded?' — a question a student who only memorized the momentum formula cannot answer.

questions.prompt: Why is momentum conservation still a good approximation for a bat-ball collision that lasts only about 1 millisecond, even though gravity acts on the ball the whole time?

options.text: Gravity does not act on objects during a collision
The contact force is so much larger than gravity that gravity's impulse (FΔt) over the brief contact time is negligible compared to the contact impulse
Momentum conservation ignores gravity by definition, regardless of timescale

explanations.a: Incorrect: gravity acts continuously on every object regardless of what else is happening; it is never literally switched off during a collision.
explanations.b: Correct: impulse is force times time; with Δt on the order of a millisecond, even a modest force like gravity contributes a tiny impulse compared to the huge contact force, so it is a good approximation, not an exact law, to neglect it.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum conservation applies exactly only to genuinely closed systems; neglecting gravity is a justified approximation based on the short timescale, not something the law does automatically.

questions.prompt: A ball bounces off a rigid, fixed floor. Why is momentum not conserved for the ball alone during the bounce?

options.text: Because the floor exerts an external force on the ball, delivering an impulse from outside the ball's own system
Because bouncing always violates the third law
Because the ball loses kinetic energy on every bounce

explanations.a: Correct: the floor, attached to the effectively infinite mass of the Earth, is outside the 'ball' system boundary, so its force on the ball is external and can change the ball's momentum without violating conservation of the ball-plus-floor-plus-Earth system.
explanations.b: Incorrect: the third law is not violated; the floor does push back on the ball equal and opposite to the ball's push on the floor, but the floor is external to the ball-alone system, so the ball's own momentum still changes.
explanations.c: Incorrect: kinetic energy loss (an inelastic bounce) is a separate issue from momentum conservation; even a perfectly elastic bounce still changes the ball's momentum because the floor exerts an external force.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to whether momentum is conserved for the stated system.

left.text: Two frictionless carts colliding; system = both carts
A bat swung by a grounded batter hits a ball; system = ball alone
A firecracker at rest explodes into fragments; system = all fragments

right.text: Conserved — no significant external force on the chosen system
Not conserved — a large external force (through the bat/batter/ground) acts on this system

questions.explanation: The two-cart system and the all-fragments system are each closed (their mutual forces are internal), but the ball alone is not closed because the bat, anchored through the batter to the ground, exerts an external force on it.

questions.prompt: Order these systems from narrowest (most likely to have unaccounted external forces) to broadest (most likely to be truly closed).

items.text: Just the ball, ignoring the bat entirely
Ball and bat together, ignoring the batter's grip
Ball, bat, and batter, ignoring the batter's feet on the ground
Ball, bat, batter, and the entire Earth

questions.explanation: Each step folds in the next external object that was previously supplying an outside force, moving from the narrowest, most externally-influenced boundary to the broadest, most nearly closed system.

lessons.label: Recoil: Guns, Rockets, and Skaters

sections.heading: Recoil is momentum conservation starting from zero
sections.body: Recoil is the special, and conceptually cleanest, case of momentum conservation where a system starts at rest — total momentum zero — and then some internal process (an explosion, a spring release, a muscular push) separates it into two or more pieces moving apart. Because total momentum must remain zero (no external force, closed system), the pieces must carry momenta that sum to zero: if one piece gets momentum p in one direction, the rest of the system must collectively carry momentum -p in the opposite direction. With just two pieces, this means m1v1 = -m2v2, so the lighter piece always moves away faster and the heavier piece always moves away slower, in exact inverse proportion to their masses.

sections.heading: Rifles, skaters, and the mass ratio
sections.body: A rifle firing a bullet is a textbook recoil pair: before firing, the rifle-plus-bullet system is at rest, so total momentum is zero. After firing, the bullet (small mass) moves forward at high speed, and the rifle (large mass) recoils backward at low speed, satisfying m(bullet)v(bullet) = m(rifle)v(rifle,recoil). A typical rifle bullet might be 5-15 grams to a rifle's several kilograms — a mass ratio on the order of 1:300 to 1:1000 — so the rifle's recoil speed is a small fraction of the bullet's muzzle speed, though it still delivers a noticeable kick to the shooter's shoulder because the rifle's momentum magnitude equals the bullet's. A skater pushing off a second, stationary skater on ice works identically: both skaters were at rest (zero total momentum), and after the push each moves away with momentum equal in size and opposite in direction, so the lighter skater ends up moving faster.

sections.heading: The rocket idea, qualitatively
sections.body: A rocket is recoil happening continuously rather than in one instant: at every moment, the rocket engine ejects a small mass of hot gas backward at high speed, and by the same zero-total-momentum logic, the rocket body gains a small forward momentum to balance it. Because this happens continuously as fuel burns, the rocket's mass decreases over time even as its momentum keeps being nudged forward by each new puff of ejected gas, which is why rockets need the full F = dp/dt form of Newton's second law (Lesson 1's point) rather than the constant-mass F = ma. The qualitative takeaway that matters at this level: a rocket does not need air or anything to 'push against' — it works in the vacuum of space precisely because it only needs to conserve momentum with the gas it ejects, not with any external medium.

lessons.workedExample: A 4.5 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet at a muzzle velocity of 300 m/s. Before firing, total momentum is zero. After firing, conservation requires m(bullet)v(bullet) + m(rifle)v(rifle) = 0, so v(rifle) = -m(bullet)v(bullet)/m(rifle) = -(0.010)(300)/4.5 ≈ -0.67 m/s. The rifle recoils backward at about 0.67 m/s — much slower than the bullet's 300 m/s, because the mass ratio is 450:1, but the rifle's momentum magnitude, 4.5 × 0.67 ≈ 3.0 kg·m/s, exactly matches the bullet's, 0.010 × 300 = 3.0 kg·m/s. A shooter feels this as a sharp kick because, while the recoil speed is small, the rifle's momentum is not — and stopping that momentum against the shoulder in a short time requires a noticeable force.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe recoil scenarios because they test whether a student truly grasps that momentum conservation constrains speeds through the mass ratio, not through some vague notion that 'action equals reaction' just means equal speeds. A student who can correctly explain why the light bullet moves much faster than the heavy rifle, despite their very different masses — because it is their momenta, not their masses, that are equal — shows real fluency. Judges may also probe the rocket case to check that a student does not think rockets need to push against air, since that misconception, though common, gets the physics backward: rockets work by ejecting mass, not by shoving against a medium.

questions.prompt: A rifle (mass M) at rest fires a bullet (mass m, m << M) forward. Which statement correctly compares their recoil momenta, speeds, and kinetic energies?

options.text: The rifle and bullet have equal momentum magnitude, but the bullet has much higher speed and much higher kinetic energy than the rifle
The rifle and bullet have equal speed, but the bullet has more momentum
The rifle and bullet have equal kinetic energy, but different momentum

explanations.a: Correct: zero initial momentum forces mv(bullet) = Mv(rifle) in magnitude, but since m << M, v(bullet) >> v(rifle); and since KE = p²/2mass with equal p, the much smaller bullet mass gives it much greater kinetic energy too.
explanations.b: Incorrect: equal speed would require m1v1 = -m2v2 to fail for unequal masses, but momentum conservation from zero total momentum requires equal MOMENTUM magnitude, not equal speed, and with unequal masses the speeds must differ.
explanations.c: Incorrect: equal momentum with unequal mass means unequal kinetic energy (KE = p²/2mass), so the lighter bullet actually has much more kinetic energy than the rifle, not the same.

questions.prompt: Why can a rocket accelerate in the vacuum of space, where there is no air to push against?

options.text: Because it is not actually in a true vacuum; trace gases provide the needed push
Because momentum conservation only requires the rocket and its ejected exhaust gas to balance each other; no external medium is needed
Because rockets in space rely on solar wind for propulsion

explanations.a: Incorrect: rockets function in genuine vacuum; this misconception (that they need something to push against) is common but not how the physics works.
explanations.b: Correct: recoil only requires that the ejected mass (gas) and the remaining mass (rocket) conserve total momentum between themselves; since space contributes no external momentum change, this internal exchange works with or without surrounding air.
explanations.c: Incorrect: solar wind is far too weak to be the propulsion mechanism for a chemical or ion rocket; the actual mechanism is momentum conservation with the ejected propellant.

questions.prompt: Match each recoil scenario to the correct outcome given zero initial total momentum.

left.text: Two skaters of very different mass push apart from rest
Two skaters of equal mass push apart from rest
A rocket continuously ejects exhaust gas backward

right.text: The lighter skater moves away much faster than the heavier skater
Both skaters move away at equal speed in opposite directions
The rocket gains forward momentum continuously as mass is continuously ejected backward

questions.explanation: With m1v1 = m2v2 in magnitude from zero total momentum, unequal masses give unequal speeds (inversely proportional to mass), equal masses give equal speeds, and a rocket applies the same logic continuously as it burns fuel.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps used to find a rifle's recoil speed from its bullet's muzzle speed.

items.text: Note the rifle-bullet system starts at rest, so total momentum is zero
Write conservation as m(bullet)v(bullet) + m(rifle)v(rifle) = 0
Solve for v(rifle) = -m(bullet)v(bullet)/m(rifle)
Interpret the negative sign as recoil in the direction opposite the bullet

questions.explanation: The zero-momentum starting condition sets up the conservation equation, which is then algebraically solved for the unknown recoil velocity, whose sign is interpreted as motion opposite the bullet's.

lessons.label: One-Dimensional Collision Bookkeeping

sections.heading: Why a sign convention is not optional
sections.body: One-dimensional collision problems fail more often from sign errors than from any misunderstanding of the physics. Because momentum is a vector, and in 1D a vector only has two possible directions, every velocity in a collision problem must be assigned a signed value relative to one chosen positive direction, fixed before any arithmetic begins. A common convention is "rightward positive, leftward negative," but the specific choice does not matter — what matters is applying it with total consistency to every object, both before and after the collision, including objects that reverse direction (whose sign must flip) and objects initially at rest (whose sign is simply zero, contributing nothing to the sum). Skipping this step and reasoning about direction in words only, mid-calculation, is where most 1D collision errors are born; writing the convention down first turns a source of confusion into a fixed reference every subsequent number must respect.

sections.heading: The before-and-after table
sections.body: A systematic table with one row per object and one column each for mass, velocity before, momentum before, velocity after, and momentum after turns a potentially confusing problem into pure bookkeeping. The organizing equation is always the same: sum of momentum before equals sum of momentum after, m1v1i + m2v2i = m1v1f + m2v2f, where every v carries its sign. Filling in the known values (masses are always given or measurable; at least three of the four velocities are usually given or asked for) and solving for the one unknown converts almost any 1D collision problem into straightforward algebra, provided the sign convention was applied consistently when the knowns were entered. The table also makes it easy to spot-check the answer afterward: compute the total momentum column both before and after using the solved value, and confirm the two totals match, since a real arithmetic slip almost always shows up as a mismatch between those two sums.

sections.heading: Reading the algebra: what a negative answer means
sections.body: When solving for an unknown final velocity, a negative result is not an error to be discarded — it is physically meaningful information that the object ends up moving in the negative direction (opposite whatever was chosen as positive), which is a completely normal and common outcome, for example when a light object bounces backward off a much heavier one. Students who assume all answers should come out positive, and flip a genuinely negative result to make it 'look right,' introduce an error where none existed. The correct habit is to interpret the sign, not discard it: state which direction the resulting velocity actually points, consistent with the convention fixed at the start of the problem.

lessons.workedExample: A 2 kg cart moving right at 3 m/s (+3 m/s) collides with a 3 kg cart moving left at 1 m/s (-1 m/s); after the collision the 2 kg cart moves at -0.6 m/s (found from a separate measurement or given). Using m1v1i + m2v2i = m1v1f + m2v2f: (2)(3) + (3)(-1) = (2)(-0.6) + (3)v2f, so 6 - 3 = -1.2 + 3v2f, giving 3 = -1.2 + 3v2f, so v2f = 4.2/3 = 1.4 m/s. The table format makes the bookkeeping explicit: cart 1 goes from +3 to -0.6 m/s (it bounces back, as the negative sign correctly indicates), and cart 2 goes from -1 to +1.4 m/s (it reverses direction too, now moving right). Total momentum before, 6 + (-3) = 3 kg·m/s, matches total momentum after, -1.2 + 4.2 = 3 kg·m/s, confirming the arithmetic.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe sign-convention discipline because it is the single most common place a student's 1D momentum solution silently goes wrong, and a judge can catch a sign error in seconds by asking a student to state their convention and re-derive one velocity's sign from the physical picture. A student who sets up a clean before-and-after table, states the convention explicitly, and correctly interprets a negative final velocity as 'moving in the other direction' rather than discarding the sign demonstrates real procedural mastery, which judges value as much as conceptual explanation because it is what actually produces correct answers under pressure.

questions.prompt: In solving a 1D collision problem, you calculate a final velocity of -2.5 m/s for an object that was initially moving in the positive direction. What should you do?

options.text: Report it as -2.5 m/s and interpret it as the object now moving in the negative direction
Flip the sign to +2.5 m/s, since velocities describing final states should be positive
Discard the result as an arithmetic error and redo the problem

explanations.a: Correct: the sign is physically meaningful and should be kept and interpreted, not discarded — a negative final velocity correctly indicates the object reversed direction relative to the original positive convention.
explanations.b: Incorrect: there is no rule that final velocities must be positive; flipping the sign to force a 'nicer-looking' answer introduces an error and misrepresents the object's actual direction of motion.
explanations.c: Incorrect: a negative final velocity is a common, physically valid outcome (e.g., a light object bouncing backward off a heavy one), not automatically a sign of an arithmetic mistake.

questions.prompt: Why must a sign convention (e.g., rightward positive) be fixed BEFORE plugging any values into the momentum conservation equation?

options.text: Because momentum is a vector, and inconsistent signs for objects moving in different directions will corrupt the sum on both sides of the equation
Because the equation only works if all objects move in the same direction
Because a sign convention is a formality with no effect on the numerical answer

explanations.a: Correct: since m1v1i + m2v2i = m1v1f + m2v2f sums signed vector quantities, any object assigned the wrong sign relative to the fixed convention will corrupt the total on whichever side it appears, producing a wrong final answer.
explanations.b: Incorrect: the equation applies to objects moving in the same or opposite directions equally well, as long as each velocity's sign is correctly assigned relative to the convention.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the sign convention directly determines whether each velocity is entered as positive or negative, which directly changes the numerical result of the sum.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving a 1D collision problem using the before-and-after table method.

items.text: Fix a sign convention (e.g., rightward positive) before assigning any values
Fill in known masses and signed velocities before the collision for each object
Write the conservation equation, sum of momentum before equals sum after
Solve algebraically for the one unknown velocity, keeping its sign
Interpret the sign of the solved velocity as a physical direction

questions.explanation: The convention must be fixed first so every subsequent value is entered consistently; then knowns are tabulated, the conservation equation is written and solved, and finally the resulting sign is translated back into a physical direction.

questions.prompt: Match each described outcome to the correct signed velocity, given a rightward-positive convention.

left.text: An object bounces backward after moving rightward into a collision
An object continues moving rightward, but slower, after the collision
An object is stationary in the lab frame

right.text: A negative final velocity
A smaller positive final velocity than its initial velocity
A velocity of exactly zero

questions.explanation: Reversing direction relative to rightward-positive gives a negative sign, slowing down while still moving rightward keeps the sign positive but reduces the magnitude, and no motion at all is exactly zero regardless of convention.

lessons.label: Explosions as Reverse Collisions

sections.heading: Running the collision equation backward
sections.body: An explosion is, mathematically, a collision run in reverse: instead of separate objects coming together and (possibly) merging, one object separates into two or more pieces flying apart. The same conservation equation applies with the same logic — no external force acts during the brief separation, so total momentum before the explosion equals total momentum after. The "before" state is almost always simpler than in a typical collision, because the single unexploded object is very often at rest, making total momentum before exactly zero, exactly as in the recoil cases of Lesson 3. Explosions are therefore best understood as a generalization of two-piece recoil to three, four, or many fragments, and the same brief-interval argument from Lesson 2 applies here too: as long as the separation happens quickly, external forces like gravity or air resistance deliver negligible impulse during the explosion itself, even though they will matter for each fragment's subsequent flight.

sections.heading: Why the pieces don't all move the same way
sections.body: With more than two fragments, the individual fragment velocities are no longer forced by momentum conservation alone — a single vector equation (or one equation per direction) cannot uniquely determine many unknown fragment velocities, so additional information (measured speeds or directions for all but one fragment, or symmetry arguments) is needed to fully solve the problem. What conservation does guarantee, regardless of how many fragments there are or how the energy released is distributed among them, is that the vector sum of every fragment's momentum equals the system's total momentum before the explosion. If that total was zero, the fragments' momenta must sum to zero collectively, even though individual fragments can carry very different momenta from one another depending on their mass and how the explosive energy happened to distribute.

sections.heading: Explosions convert stored energy into kinetic energy, unlike inelastic collisions
sections.body: It is useful to contrast explosions with the inelastic collisions covered elsewhere in this branch. In an inelastic collision, kinetic energy is lost, converted to heat, sound, and deformation. In an explosion, the reverse happens: some form of stored energy — chemical energy in a propellant, elastic energy in a spring, nuclear energy in a fission event — converts into kinetic energy of the separating fragments, so total kinetic energy after an explosion is typically much greater than before (which was often zero, since the unexploded object was at rest). Momentum conservation says nothing about this energy release one way or the other; it only constrains how the resulting kinetic energy gets divided among the fragments' momenta, not how much total kinetic energy appears from the stored energy source.

lessons.workedExample: A 6 kg object at rest explodes into three fragments in a horizontal plane. Fragment A (1 kg) flies off at 12 m/s in the +x direction; fragment B (2 kg) flies off at 9 m/s in the +y direction; fragment C (3 kg) is unmeasured. Since total momentum must remain zero (the object started at rest), the x-momentum of C must cancel A's: 1(12) + 3v(Cx) = 0, so v(Cx) = -4 m/s. Likewise the y-momentum of C must cancel B's: 2(9) + 3v(Cy) = 0, so v(Cy) = -6 m/s. Fragment C's speed is √(4² + 6²) = √52 ≈ 7.2 m/s, directed into the third quadrant (negative x, negative y) — found entirely from momentum conservation without any direct measurement of fragment C, because with two unknowns (Cx and Cy) and two independent component equations (x and y), the system is exactly determined, so the two known fragments' momenta pin down C's momentum exactly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe explosions because students often correctly recite that momentum is conserved in a collision but hesitate when the direction is reversed — pieces flying apart rather than together — even though the identical equation applies. A student who confidently sets total momentum before (often zero) equal to the vector sum of fragment momenta after, and who understands why extra measured fragments are needed once there are more than two pieces, demonstrates that they grasp momentum conservation as a general principle rather than a memorized collision-specific recipe. Judges may also ask where the kinetic energy of the fragments came from, testing whether the student distinguishes momentum conservation (always holds) from energy conservation (requires tracking the stored-energy source).

questions.prompt: A firework shell at rest explodes into many fragments. What does momentum conservation guarantee about the fragments?

options.text: All fragments must move at the same speed
The vector sum of all fragment momenta must equal zero, the shell's momentum before exploding
All fragments must have equal mass

explanations.a: Incorrect: fragments generally have different masses and receive different shares of the released energy, so their speeds are typically different; only the vector sum of momenta is constrained, not individual speeds.
explanations.b: Correct: since the shell started at rest, total momentum before the explosion was zero, and momentum conservation requires the fragments' momenta to sum to zero after, regardless of how many fragments there are or how their masses differ.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum conservation places no requirement on the fragments' masses; fragments are commonly very unequal in size.

questions.prompt: How does the energy balance of a typical explosion differ from that of an inelastic collision?

options.text: An explosion converts stored (chemical, elastic, or nuclear) energy into kinetic energy, so total kinetic energy after typically exceeds that before; an inelastic collision converts kinetic energy into heat/sound/deformation, so kinetic energy after is less than before
Both processes conserve kinetic energy exactly, just like momentum
An explosion always loses kinetic energy, just like an inelastic collision

explanations.a: Correct: explosions are essentially the reverse of inelastic collisions in terms of energy — stored energy becomes kinetic energy (an increase) in an explosion, while kinetic energy is lost to other forms in an inelastic collision (a decrease).
explanations.b: Incorrect: kinetic energy conservation only applies to elastic collisions; neither typical explosions nor inelastic collisions conserve kinetic energy, though momentum is conserved in both.
explanations.c: Incorrect: this describes inelastic collisions, not explosions; explosions gain kinetic energy from a stored energy source, they do not lose it.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the correct total momentum immediately before the described event.

left.text: A stationary grenade explodes into fragments
A moving 5 kg cart at 4 m/s collides and merges with a stationary cart
