A rocket at rest on a launchpad ignites and begins ejecting exhaust

right.text: Zero total momentum
Nonzero total momentum, equal to the moving object's momentum

questions.explanation: Both the stationary grenade and the stationary rocket start with zero total momentum, so momentum conservation constrains their pieces to sum to zero after; the moving cart starts with nonzero momentum, which the merged system retains.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to find an unmeasured fragment's momentum from an explosion of an object initially at rest into three fragments, given two fragments' momenta.

items.text: Confirm the object was at rest, so total momentum before is zero
Write the two known fragments' momentum components
Set the sum of all three fragments' momentum components equal to zero
Solve for the unknown fragment's momentum components
Convert the unknown fragment's momentum components into a speed and direction

questions.explanation: Establishing the zero-momentum starting condition justifies setting the fragment sum to zero; the known fragments' components are then subtracted out algebraically to isolate, then interpret, the unknown fragment's momentum.

lessons.label: When Momentum Is Not Conserved

sections.heading: The shortcut has a condition attached
sections.body: Every conservation statement in this unit carries an implicit clause: 'provided no significant net external force acts on the system.' That clause is not decoration — it is the entire reason momentum conservation is sometimes exactly right and sometimes badly wrong for a given problem. Recognizing when the clause fails is as important a skill as applying the conservation equation itself, because a student who reflexively writes m1v1i + m2v2i = m1v1f + m2v2f for every problem involving colliding objects, without checking whether the system is actually closed, will get some problems correct by luck and others wrong with total confidence.

sections.heading: Fixed pivots and sustained friction as external-force culprits
sections.body: A bat swung around a fixed pivot — a batter's wrists and shoulders, effectively anchoring one end — cannot recoil freely the way an unattached bat could; the pivot supplies whatever external force is needed to keep that end (approximately) fixed, so linear momentum of the ball-bat system is not conserved if tracked from the start of the swing through the follow-through, even though angular momentum about the pivot may be a more useful conserved quantity in that scenario (a topic for rotational mechanics). During the brief instant of contact itself, the pivot's impulse has too little time to act and can be neglected, just as gravity can be neglected during a brief collision — the failure of closure shows up only once the pivot's force has had enough time to deliver a non-negligible impulse. Sustained friction is a different failure mode: unlike a brief, large collision force that dwarfs friction over a millisecond of contact, a slow process — like two train cars coupling while both are already rolling and decelerating under a long friction force from the tracks — lets friction accumulate a non-negligible impulse over the extended time involved, so momentum measured well before and well after is not conserved, only momentum measured immediately before and immediately after the coupling itself, on the short timescale where friction's impulse is still small.

sections.heading: Gravity over long times, and the practical test
sections.body: Gravity is the clearest illustration that whether a force 'breaks' momentum conservation depends entirely on the timescale considered. During a bat-ball collision lasting under a millisecond, gravity's impulse is negligible and momentum conservation for the ball-bat system works beautifully. But track a thrown ball's momentum from the moment it leaves a hand to the moment it lands a full second later, and gravity has delivered a large, entirely non-negligible impulse (Δp = mgΔt) the whole time, so of course the ball's momentum at landing differs from its momentum at launch — vertical momentum is clearly not conserved over that timescale, because gravity is an external force acting continuously. The practical test is always the same: identify every force acting on the chosen system, and ask whether each one's impulse (FΔt, using the actual duration of the process being analyzed) is negligible compared to the internal forces or momenta involved. If yes, momentum conservation is a safe and powerful shortcut. If no, it is the wrong tool, and Newton's second law (or a direct impulse-momentum calculation including the external force) must be used instead.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.15 kg baseball is thrown horizontally at 30 m/s and caught 1.2 seconds later after falling under gravity, with no air resistance considered for simplicity. Over this 1.2 s flight, gravity delivers a vertical impulse of Δp(y) = mgΔt = 0.15 × 9.8 × 1.2 ≈ 1.8 kg·m/s to the ball, so its vertical momentum goes from 0 (thrown horizontally) to about 1.8 kg·m/s downward at catching — momentum is clearly not conserved vertically over this 1.2 second flight, because gravity is a continuously acting external force with plenty of time to deliver a substantial impulse. Contrast this with the same ball's 0.7 ms bat collision from Lesson 2: gravity's impulse over that much shorter time is only mgΔt = 0.15 × 9.8 × 0.0007 ≈ 0.001 kg·m/s, utterly negligible next to the roughly 13.5 kg·m/s impulse the bat delivers — which is exactly why momentum conservation is an excellent approximation for the brief collision but a poor one for the full second-plus flight.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the limits of momentum conservation because a student who can correctly identify a case where the shortcut does NOT apply, and explain why in terms of the size and duration of the external force's impulse, demonstrates a level of understanding well beyond formula application. This is often where projects lose credibility: a team that conserves momentum across a scenario with an obvious external force (a fixed pivot, an extended frictional slide, a long flight under gravity) without acknowledging the approximation reveals that they applied the equation without checking its precondition. Judges will specifically ask 'what breaks this here?' expecting a named external force and a rough justification of why its impulse is or is not negligible on the relevant timescale.

questions.prompt: A batter's bat is anchored through a fixed grip and stance. Why is linear momentum of the ball-bat system alone NOT well conserved if tracked from the start of the swing through the follow-through?

options.text: Because the batter's grip and stance exert a significant external force on the bat over that extended time, which is outside the ball-bat system boundary
Because bats are too light for momentum conservation to apply
Because the collision is elastic, and elastic collisions never conserve momentum

explanations.a: Correct: over the full swing, the fixed grip/stance is an external constraint outside the chosen ball-bat system, delivering an external force whose impulse accumulates over that longer time and that momentum conservation for that system does not account for. During the brief instant of contact alone, that same impulse is negligible, which is why ball-and-bat works as a closed system for just the collision.
explanations.b: Incorrect: mass has no bearing on whether momentum conservation applies; conservation depends on whether external forces are negligible, not on how heavy the objects are.
explanations.c: Incorrect: elastic collisions conserve BOTH momentum and kinetic energy for a closed system; the issue here is that the pivot/grip makes the system not closed in the first place, unrelated to elasticity.

questions.prompt: Why does gravity's effect on a ball's momentum depend so strongly on the timescale being considered?

options.text: Gravity's impulse is Δp = FΔt; over a very short Δt (like a millisecond collision) its impulse is tiny, but over a long Δt (like a full second of flight) its impulse accumulates and becomes significant
Gravity only acts on objects that have been in flight for more than one second
Gravity's strength changes depending on how fast the object is moving horizontally

explanations.a: Correct: impulse scales directly with elapsed time for a roughly constant force like gravity near Earth's surface, so the same force delivers a negligible impulse over a millisecond but a substantial one over a second or more.
explanations.b: Incorrect: gravity acts continuously on every object in flight from the very first instant, not only after some threshold time has passed.
explanations.c: Incorrect: gravitational acceleration near Earth's surface (about 9.8 m/s²) does not depend on an object's horizontal speed.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the reason momentum conservation fails (or nearly fails) for the stated system.

left.text: A bat anchored by a batter's fixed grip strikes a ball
Two train cars couple while decelerating under friction over many seconds
A ball's momentum is compared at launch versus one second later

right.text: An external force through the pivot/grip acts on part of the system
Friction's impulse accumulates to a non-negligible size over the long duration
Gravity's impulse accumulates to a non-negligible size over the long duration

questions.explanation: The pivot case fails because of a genuinely external force outside the system; the other two fail because a normally-negligible continuous force (friction, gravity) is given enough time to deliver a significant impulse.

questions.prompt: Order the practical checks used to decide whether momentum conservation safely applies to a given system and timescale.

items.text: Identify every force acting on the chosen system
Determine the duration Δt over which the process is being analyzed
Estimate each force's impulse, FΔt, over that duration
Compare each external force's impulse to the internal forces/momenta involved
Apply conservation only if external impulses are negligible by that comparison

questions.explanation: Correctly judging whether conservation applies requires first listing the forces, fixing the relevant timescale, converting each force to an impulse using that timescale, comparing magnitudes, and only then deciding the shortcut is valid.

lessons.label: What Elastic Means

sections.heading: Two conservation laws, not one
sections.body: Momentum is conserved in every collision, elastic or not, as long as no net external force acts during the impact — that follows straight from Newton's third law, since the force each object exerts on the other is equal and opposite at every instant of contact. What makes a collision elastic is a second, stronger condition: kinetic energy is also conserved. Total KE before the collision equals total KE after, with none diverted into heat, sound, or permanent deformation. Momentum conservation alone under-determines the outcome of a collision — many final-velocity pairs satisfy it. Adding kinetic energy conservation supplies the second equation needed to pin down a unique answer, which is why elastic collisions are solvable exactly while general inelastic ones require an extra piece of information such as the coefficient of restitution.

sections.heading: An idealization with real-world footholds
sections.body: No macroscopic collision is perfectly elastic — some energy always leaks into sound waves, internal vibration, and microscopic deformation, however briefly. But some collisions come remarkably close. Hard, low-deformation materials colliding briefly and rebounding cleanly — steel ball bearings and billiard balls — lose only a few percent of their kinetic energy per bounce, and treating them as elastic gives accurate predictions with far less algebra than tracking every joule of loss. A superball, with a lower restitution (e ~ 0.8-0.9), loses a more noticeable fraction — roughly 20 to 35 percent per bounce — while still bouncing far higher than a clay or sand-filled ball. At the molecular scale, elastic collisions are not an approximation at all: kinetic theory treats collisions between simple gas molecules as exactly elastic, which is what lets an ideal gas maintain a stable temperature and pressure indefinitely in an isolated container without spontaneously cooling down.

sections.heading: Naming the spectrum with the coefficient of restitution
sections.body: The coefficient of restitution, e, is the ratio of the relative speed of separation after impact to the relative speed of approach before it. Elastic collisions have e = 1: the objects separate exactly as fast as they approached. A perfectly inelastic collision, where the objects stick together and move as one, has e = 0 — the maximum possible kinetic energy loss for a given momentum. Everything else — a dropped rubber ball, a car fender, a tennis serve — falls somewhere between, with 0 < e < 1. Framing collisions on this single dial makes elastic and perfectly inelastic collisions the two clean endpoints of the same physical picture, rather than unrelated special cases.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.5 kg cart moving at 2 m/s collides with an identical stationary 0.5 kg cart on a frictionless track. Case A: the carts have magnetic bumpers and repel without touching, separating at 2 m/s relative speed (e = 1). Because the masses are equal, the collision is a clean velocity exchange: the first cart stops, and the second cart moves off at 2 m/s. Kinetic energy before is 0.5(0.5)(2)^2 = 1.0 J, and kinetic energy after is entirely in the second cart, 0.5(0.5)(2)^2 = 1.0 J — conserved exactly, confirming the collision is elastic. Case B: the carts instead have Velcro bumpers and lock together, moving off at a shared 1 m/s. Momentum is conserved in both cases (1.0 kg m/s before and after), but Case B's final KE is only 0.5(1.0)(1)^2 = 0.5 J — half the energy vanished into the Velcro's deformation, so e = 0 and the collision is perfectly inelastic.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing this concept is checking whether a student conflates momentum conservation, which holds for essentially all collisions, with kinetic energy conservation, which is the specific, restrictive signature of an elastic collision. The strongest answers state both conservation laws separately and explain why momentum survives collisions that KE does not — the internal contact forces are equal and opposite regardless of what happens to the objects' shapes, but shape changes can absorb energy. A judge will often ask for a real system that is only approximately elastic, since claiming perfect elasticity for any everyday macroscopic collision is a common overreach worth catching.

questions.prompt: Which quantity is conserved in essentially every collision (elastic or inelastic), given no external force during impact?

options.text: Momentum
Kinetic energy
Both momentum and kinetic energy
Neither, in general

explanations.a: Correct: Newton's third law makes the contact forces equal and opposite at every instant, so total momentum is conserved regardless of whether the collision is elastic.
explanations.b: Kinetic energy conservation is the extra, restrictive condition that defines an elastic collision specifically — it does not hold for inelastic collisions.
explanations.c: Both being conserved is the special elastic case, not the general rule for all collisions.
explanations.d: Momentum conservation is quite general (absent external forces); it is not true that neither quantity is conserved.

questions.prompt: A collision in which the two objects stick together and move off with a common final velocity is called:

options.text: Elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Partially elastic

explanations.a: Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy and the objects separate afterward; sticking together is the opposite extreme.
explanations.b: Correct: objects moving off together with one shared final velocity is the defining feature of a perfectly inelastic collision, e = 0.
explanations.c: There is no standard category called 'partially elastic' with this defining feature; sticking together specifically names the perfectly inelastic case.

questions.prompt: Match each collision type to its defining property.

right.text: e = 1; momentum and kinetic energy both conserved
e = 0; objects stick together, maximum KE lost for the given momentum
0 < e < 1; momentum conserved, some KE lost to heat, sound, deformation

questions.explanation: Elastic sits at e = 1 with both conservation laws holding; perfectly inelastic sits at the opposite endpoint e = 0 with objects sticking together; nearly all everyday collisions land in between, conserving momentum but leaking some kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: Why does kinetic theory model collisions between simple gas molecules as elastic?

options.text: Because molecules are electrically attracted to each other during impact
Because an isolated gas at constant temperature does not spontaneously lose kinetic energy over time, which matches what elastic collisions predict
Because molecules never actually make contact, so no energy transfer is possible

explanations.a: Electrical attraction is not the basis for the elastic-collision assumption in kinetic theory, and treating collisions as attractive would not itself guarantee energy conservation.
explanations.b: Correct: if molecular collisions steadily drained kinetic energy, an isolated gas would cool on its own, which is not observed; treating collisions as elastic is consistent with a gas holding steady temperature and pressure.
explanations.c: Kinetic theory does model molecules as making contact (or interacting at very short range) during a collision; the elastic assumption concerns what happens to energy during that interaction, not whether contact occurs.

lessons.label: The One-Dimensional Elastic Collision Equations

sections.heading: Two equations, two unknowns
sections.body: For a head-on, one-dimensional elastic collision between mass m1 (initial velocity v1) and mass m2 (initial velocity v2), two conservation laws hold simultaneously: momentum, m1v1 + m2v2 = m1v1' + m2v2', and kinetic energy, (1/2)m1v1^2 + (1/2)m2v2^2 = (1/2)m1v1'^2 + (1/2)m2v2'^2. That is two equations in the two unknowns v1' and v2', so the system is fully solvable — no extra information about the materials is needed, unlike a general inelastic collision where the outcome depends on how much energy is lost.

sections.heading: The shortcut: approach speed equals separation speed
sections.body: Solving the pair directly means factoring a quadratic energy equation, which is messy. The standard shortcut rearranges the KE equation as a difference of squares, m1(v1^2 - v1'^2) = m2(v2'^2 - v2^2), factors each side, and divides by the corresponding momentum equation m1(v1 - v1') = m2(v2' - v2). The mass terms cancel, leaving v1 + v1' = v2 + v2', which rearranges to v1 - v2 = -(v1' - v2'), or equivalently v1 - v2 = v2' - v1'. In words: the relative velocity at which the two objects approach each other before the collision equals the relative velocity at which they separate afterward. This is exactly the coefficient-of-restitution statement from the previous lesson with e = 1, but derived here directly from the two conservation laws rather than assumed.

sections.heading: Solving for the final velocities
sections.body: Combining the relative-velocity relation with momentum conservation as a linear system (no more quadratics) gives closed-form results: v1' = ((m1 - m2) / (m1 + m2)) v1 + (2 m2 / (m1 + m2)) v2, and v2' = (2 m1 / (m1 + m2)) v1 + ((m2 - m1) / (m1 + m2)) v2. These two formulas are the master equations for every 1D elastic collision problem; every special case in this unit — equal masses, a light projectile on a heavy target, a heavy projectile on a light target — is just these formulas evaluated at a particular mass ratio. Notice that the two formulas are mirror images of each other: swapping the labels 1 and 2 everywhere turns one into the other, which is exactly what physical symmetry demands, since nothing about the derivation privileged one object over the other.

sections.heading: Two independent checks for every answer
sections.body: Because the derivation used both conservation laws, a completed 1D elastic collision problem carries two built-in checks that a general (inelastic) collision problem does not. First, plug the computed v1' and v2' back into the momentum equation and confirm the total matches the initial momentum — a check that catches simple arithmetic slips. Second, plug them into the kinetic energy equation and confirm the total energy matches — a check that specifically catches an error in applying the elastic condition itself, since a mistake that preserves momentum but not energy often means the relative-velocity relation was applied incorrectly or skipped. Together the two checks make elastic collision problems unusually self-verifying compared to most other mechanics problems, where only one conservation law is typically available to check the work.

lessons.workedExample: A 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s strikes a stationary 1 kg cart head-on and elastically. Using the formulas with m1 = 3, v1 = 4, m2 = 1, v2 = 0: v1' = ((3-1)/(3+1))(4) = (2/4)(4) = 2 m/s, and v2' = (2*3/4)(4) = (6/4)(4) = 6 m/s. Check momentum: before, 3(4) + 1(0) = 12 kg m/s; after, 3(2) + 1(6) = 6 + 6 = 12 kg m/s. Check kinetic energy: before, 0.5(3)(16) = 24 J; after, 0.5(3)(4) + 0.5(1)(36) = 6 + 18 = 24 J. Check the relative-velocity rule: approach speed was 4 - 0 = 4 m/s; separation speed is 6 - 2 = 4 m/s. All three checks agree.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge wants to see that a student can actually execute the two-conservation-law solution rather than just quoting it — plugging numbers into the closed-form formulas and then independently verifying both momentum and kinetic energy afterward. The relative-velocity shortcut (approach speed equals separation speed) is worth stating explicitly and checking numerically, since it is the fastest sanity check available and shows the student understands where it comes from — a direct algebraic consequence of the two conservation laws, not a separate assumption bolted on.

questions.prompt: In a 1D elastic collision, what relation, derived from combining momentum and kinetic energy conservation, avoids having to solve a quadratic equation directly?

options.text: The relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation
Total kinetic energy doubles after the collision
The two final velocities must be equal to each other

explanations.a: Correct: factoring the KE equation as a difference of squares and dividing by the momentum equation yields v1 - v2 = v2' - v1', a linear relation that replaces the need to solve the quadratic directly.
explanations.b: Kinetic energy is conserved (stays the same), not doubled — doubling would violate the defining condition of an elastic collision.
explanations.c: The two final velocities are generally different from each other; nothing in the derivation forces them to be equal (equal final velocities only appear in special limiting cases, not in general).

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to derive the closed-form final-velocity formulas for a 1D elastic collision.

items.text: Write momentum conservation: m1v1 + m2v2 = m1v1' + m2v2'
Write kinetic energy conservation and factor it as a difference of squares
Divide the factored energy equation by the momentum equation to get v1 - v2 = v2' - v1'
Solve the linear system of the relative-velocity relation and momentum conservation for v1' and v2'

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation and the factored energy equation are each set up first; dividing one by the other produces the linear relative-velocity relation, which then combines with momentum conservation as a solvable linear system for the two unknowns.

questions.prompt: In the worked example (3 kg at 4 m/s strikes a stationary 1 kg cart elastically), what is the 1 kg cart's final velocity?

options.text: 2 m/s
4 m/s
6 m/s
8 m/s

explanations.a: 2 m/s is the 3 kg cart's final velocity, v1', not the 1 kg cart's.
explanations.b: 4 m/s was the initial velocity of the 3 kg cart, not either final velocity.
explanations.c: Correct: v2' = (2m1/(m1+m2))v1 = (6/4)(4) = 6 m/s, confirmed by both the momentum and energy checks.
explanations.d: 8 m/s would overshoot the momentum budget; total momentum after the collision must still equal 12 kg m/s, and 3(2)+1(8)=14 does not balance.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, the carts approached each other at a relative speed of 4 m/s. What is their relative speed of separation afterward?

options.text: 2 m/s
4 m/s
6 m/s
0 m/s

explanations.a: 2 m/s is v1' alone, not the difference between the two final velocities.
explanations.b: Correct: v2' - v1' = 6 - 2 = 4 m/s, exactly matching the 4 m/s approach speed, as the elastic collision relation requires.
explanations.c: 6 m/s is v2' alone, not the relative separation speed.
explanations.d: A separation speed of 0 would mean the carts end up moving together, which is the perfectly inelastic case, not this elastic one.

lessons.label: Equal Masses Exchange Velocities

sections.heading: Setting m1 = m2 in the master equations
sections.body: Substitute m1 = m2 = m into the general 1D elastic collision formulas from the previous lesson. The (m1 - m2)/(m1 + m2) term in the v1' formula becomes 0/2m = 0, and the 2m2/(m1+m2) term becomes 2m/2m = 1, so v1' = v2. Symmetrically, v2' = v1. The two objects simply trade velocities — whatever the first object was doing, the second object does after the collision, and vice versa. This is not an approximation or a special trick; it falls directly out of the general formulas at the specific mass ratio of 1.

sections.heading: The clean case: one moving, one at rest
sections.body: The most common version has m2 initially at rest (v2 = 0). Then v1' = 0 and v2' = v1: the incoming object stops dead, and the object it struck moves off with exactly the incoming object's original velocity. This is the physical basis of the classic pool 'stun shot,' where a cue ball striking an object ball squarely comes to a near-complete stop while the object ball takes off with the cue ball's speed — real cue and object balls are close enough to equal mass and close enough to elastic (coefficient of restitution roughly 0.92-0.98) that the stop is often dramatic and nearly complete, though spin and slight mass or elasticity differences prevent a perfectly clean stop in practice.

sections.heading: The exchange holds even when both objects are already moving
sections.body: The v1' = v2, v2' = v1 swap is not limited to the case of a stationary target — it holds for any two equal masses with any initial velocities, including head-on approaches where both objects are moving toward each other with opposite-signed velocities. If a 1 kg cart moving at +3 m/s collides elastically with an identical 1 kg cart moving at -1 m/s, the formulas still give a clean exchange: the first cart leaves at -1 m/s and the second leaves at +3 m/s, each one simply taking on the other's incoming velocity, sign included. This generality is easy to miss if the rule is memorized only from the stationary-target example, but it falls out of the same substitution m1 = m2 = m regardless of what v1 and v2 happen to be.

sections.heading: Why this case matters beyond billiards
sections.body: Equal-mass velocity exchange is the building block behind more elaborate demonstrations, including Newton's cradle, where a chain of equal-mass balls passes an incoming velocity down the line one clean swap at a time. It is also a useful sanity check on the general 1D formulas: any solution to a two-mass elastic collision problem should reduce to this simple exchange the moment the masses are set equal, and if a derivation does not reduce that way, it has an error somewhere.

lessons.workedExample: Two identical 0.17 kg pool balls collide head-on and elastically: the cue ball approaches at 2.5 m/s and strikes a stationary object ball squarely. Applying v1' = v2 = 0 and v2' = v1 = 2.5 m/s, the cue ball should stop completely and the object ball should roll away at 2.5 m/s. Checking momentum: before, 0.17(2.5) + 0.17(0) = 0.425 kg m/s; after, 0.17(0) + 0.17(2.5) = 0.425 kg m/s, balanced. Checking kinetic energy: before, 0.5(0.17)(2.5)^2 = 0.531 J; after, 0.5(0.17)(2.5)^2 = 0.531 J for the object ball alone, balanced. In practice a real cue ball creeps forward slightly after the hit because e is close to but not exactly 1, and because friction with the felt begins acting immediately.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes whether a student sees the equal-mass exchange as a direct consequence of the general equations rather than a memorized special rule. A strong answer derives v1' = v2 and v2' = v1 from the mass ratio (m1-m2)/(m1+m2) = 0 rather than asserting it, and can explain why the real-world version (a cue ball's near-complete stop) is only approximate — because real balls are not perfectly elastic and are not perfectly identical in mass, so the exchange is close but not exact. A judge may also ask what changes if the masses are only nearly equal, testing whether the student understands this as a limiting case rather than an all-or-nothing rule.

questions.prompt: In a 1D elastic collision with m1 = m2, and m2 initially at rest, what happens to m1 after the collision?

options.text: m1 comes to a complete stop, and m2 moves off with m1's original velocity
m1 continues forward at half its original velocity
Both masses move off together at half the original velocity

explanations.a: Correct: with equal masses, the (m1-m2)/(m1+m2) coefficient on v1' vanishes, so v1' = 0 and v2' = v1 — a full velocity exchange.
explanations.b: Halving the velocity would violate both momentum and kinetic energy conservation for this equal-mass case; the correct result is a full stop, not a partial slowdown.
explanations.c: Moving off together describes a perfectly inelastic collision (e = 0), not an elastic one; elastic equal-mass collisions produce a clean exchange, not a merger.

questions.prompt: The equal-mass velocity exchange is the physical basis for which classic pool/billiards result?

options.text: The stun shot, where a cue ball striking an object ball squarely comes to a near-complete stop
The massé shot, where heavy spin curves the cue ball's path
The break shot spreading the rack across the table

explanations.a: Correct: the stun shot's near-complete stop of the cue ball is the real-world signature of the equal-mass velocity exchange, since cue and object balls have nearly equal mass and a high coefficient of restitution.
explanations.b: The massé shot relies on imparted spin and friction with the felt, not on the equal-mass exchange described here.
explanations.c: A break shot involves many simultaneous multi-body collisions and spreads energy across the whole rack; it is not the clean two-body exchange this lesson describes.

questions.prompt: Match each mass scenario (m1 initially moving, m2 initially at rest) to its elastic-collision outcome.

right.text: Velocities exchange exactly: m1 stops, m2 takes m1's original velocity
m1 barely slows down; m2 flies off at roughly twice m1's original velocity
m1 bounces back at roughly its original speed reversed; m2 barely moves

questions.explanation: Equal masses give a clean velocity swap; a much heavier projectile keeps going near its original speed while flinging the light target off at roughly double that speed; a much lighter projectile rebounds off a nearly stationary heavy target with its speed reversed.

questions.prompt: Why is the equal-mass velocity exchange essential to how a real Newton's cradle produces its 'balls in equal balls out' effect?

options.text: Because equal masses make every pairwise collision in the chain a clean velocity swap, letting momentum and energy pass ball to ball without distortion
Because equal masses are required for momentum to be conserved at all
Because equal masses prevent the balls from touching each other

explanations.a: Correct: since each collision in the chain is between equal masses, each one is a full stop-and-swap, so the incoming velocity threads cleanly down the row of touching balls.
explanations.b: Momentum conservation does not require equal masses — it holds for any masses, given no external force during impact.
explanations.c: The balls in a Newton's cradle are touching (or nearly touching) precisely so the collision chain can propagate; equal mass has nothing to do with whether they touch.

lessons.label: Light Hits Heavy, Heavy Hits Light

sections.heading: Limit one: a light projectile hits a very heavy, stationary target
sections.body: Take the general formulas from lesson 2 and let m2 grow much larger than m1, with m2 initially at rest (v2 = 0). The coefficient on v1' in v1' = ((m1-m2)/(m1+m2))v1 approaches -1 as m2/m1 approaches infinity, so v1' approaches -v1: the light object bounces straight back with essentially its original speed, just reversed in direction. Meanwhile v2' = (2m1/(m1+m2))v1 approaches 0, since the numerator stays finite while the denominator grows without bound — the heavy target barely moves at all. This is the elastic-collision model of a ball bouncing off a wall or a massive fixed obstacle: the wall does not need to be literally infinite in mass, just much larger than the ball, for the approximation to be excellent.

sections.heading: Limit two: a heavy projectile hits a very light, stationary target
sections.body: Now reverse the roles: let m1 grow much larger than m2, with m2 initially at rest. The v1' coefficient (m1-m2)/(m1+m2) approaches +1, so v1' approaches v1 — the heavy object barely slows down at all. But v2' = (2m1/(m1+m2))v1 approaches 2v1 as m1/m2 approaches infinity, since m1 dominates both the numerator and denominator, leaving the ratio 2m1/m1 = 2. The light target is flung forward at roughly twice the heavy projectile's original speed — a factor that surprises many students, who expect the light object to simply match the heavy one's speed rather than exceed it. This double-speed result is exact only in the limit; for any finite mass ratio the light target's departure speed is slightly less than 2v1, approaching that value ever more closely as the mass ratio grows.

sections.heading: Reading the limits as a single mass-ratio dial
sections.body: Both limits are the same formula, m2/m1 dialed to two extremes. At m2/m1 = 1 (equal masses), the target takes exactly v1 and the projectile stops (lesson 3). Turning the dial toward a much lighter target pushes the target's departure speed up toward 2v1, while turning it toward a much heavier target pushes the target's speed down toward 0 and reflects the projectile backward. The equal-mass case sits exactly halfway between these two limiting behaviors, which is a useful way to remember all three regimes as one continuous family rather than three unrelated facts.

sections.heading: Recognizing the limits in familiar situations
sections.body: The heavy-target limit shows up whenever a small, fast object strikes something effectively fixed: a hailstone bouncing off pavement, a rubber ball off a brick wall, or an alpha particle scattering off a massive atomic nucleus (the same near-elastic, heavy-fixed-target picture Rutherford's team used, in modified form, to infer that atoms have a small dense nucleus). The light-target limit shows up whenever something massive strikes something nearly negligible in mass: a bowling ball through a stack of ping-pong balls, a car tapping an empty soda can, or a bat's barrel meeting a ball, where the bat is effectively far more massive at the instant of contact and the ball leaves substantially faster than the bat's swing speed alone would suggest.

lessons.workedExample: A 7.26 kg bowling ball moving at 4 m/s strikes a stationary 0.0027 kg ping-pong ball head-on and elastically. Since m1 >> m2, use the light-target limit: v2' approaches 2v1 = 8 m/s for the ping-pong ball, and v1' approaches v1 = 4 m/s for the bowling ball (a tiny, near-undetectable slowdown). Exact formulas confirm this closely: v2' = (2)(7.26)/(7.26+0.0027) (4) = 7.9970 m/s, essentially 8 m/s. Now reverse it: a 0.0027 kg ping-pong ball at 4 m/s strikes a stationary 7.26 kg bowling ball. Since m1 << m2 this time, the ping-pong ball rebounds at essentially -4 m/s (bounces straight back at nearly its original speed), while the bowling ball's exact final velocity, (2)(0.0027)/(7.2627)(4) = 0.003 m/s, is immeasurably small.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing this concept wants to see the two limiting cases derived from the same general formula, not memorized as separate facts — and specifically wants the student to catch the factor-of-two result for a light stationary target, since intuition often (wrongly) predicts the light object simply matches the heavy projectile's speed. A strong answer also states which physical assumption drives each limit (m2/m1 to infinity versus m1/m2 to infinity) and can sanity-check the bowling-ball-versus-ping-pong-ball example numerically rather than just qualitatively.

questions.prompt: As m2/m1 approaches infinity (a light projectile strikes a very massive, stationary target), the projectile's final velocity approaches:

options.text: -v1 (same speed, reversed direction)

explanations.a: Correct: as m2 dominates, (m1-m2)/(m1+m2) approaches -1, so v1' approaches -v1 — the light projectile bounces straight back.
explanations.b: 0 describes what happens to the heavy target's velocity in this limit, not the light projectile's, which keeps nearly all its speed (reversed).
explanations.c: 2v1 is the light-target result from the opposite limit (heavy projectile, light target), not this case.

questions.prompt: As m1/m2 approaches infinity (a heavy projectile strikes a very light, stationary target), the light target's final velocity approaches:

options.text: v1

explanations.a: v1 is what the heavy projectile's own final velocity approaches (it barely slows), not the light target's, which moves faster than the projectile did.
explanations.b: Correct: v2' = (2m1/(m1+m2))v1 approaches 2v1 as m1 dominates both numerator and denominator, leaving the ratio at 2.
explanations.c: 0 would describe a light target that barely moves, which is the opposite of what happens — the light target is flung forward faster than the incoming projectile.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, a 7.26 kg bowling ball at 4 m/s strikes a stationary 0.0027 kg ping-pong ball head-on, elastically. Approximately what speed does the ping-pong ball leave with?

options.text: 2 m/s
4 m/s
8 m/s
16 m/s

explanations.a: 2 m/s is half the bowling ball's initial speed, which does not match the light-target limit of roughly double the incoming speed.
explanations.b: 4 m/s would mean the ping-pong ball just matches the bowling ball's speed; the light-target limit predicts roughly double that, not equal.
explanations.c: Correct: with m1 >> m2, v2' approaches 2v1 = 2(4) = 8 m/s, matching the exact formula's result of about 7.9970 m/s.
explanations.d: 16 m/s would require a factor of four, not the factor of two that the light-target limit actually gives.

questions.prompt: Three head-on elastic collisions all have the same projectile incoming speed v against a stationary target, but different target masses relative to the projectile. Order the target's final departure speed from slowest to fastest.

items.text: Target mass much greater than projectile mass (heavy, fixed-like target)
Target mass equal to projectile mass
Target mass much less than projectile mass (light target)

questions.explanation: A very heavy target barely moves (final speed near 0); an equal-mass target takes exactly the incoming speed v; a very light target is flung off at roughly 2v — the target's departure speed rises monotonically as the target gets lighter relative to the projectile.

lessons.label: Newton's Cradle Done Right

sections.heading: Why momentum conservation alone is not enough
sections.body: Swing two balls of mass m and speed v into a stationary row of touching balls at the other end of a five-ball cradle. Momentum conservation by itself permits an outcome most people never see: a single ball leaving the far end at speed 2v, since m(2v) = 2mv matches the incoming momentum 2mv exactly. Momentum conservation also permits three balls leaving at (2/3)v each, since 3m(2v/3) = 2mv also balances. Momentum conservation is satisfied by an entire family of outcomes, which is why it cannot, on its own, explain why a real cradle reliably produces exactly two balls leaving at speed v each.

sections.heading: Kinetic energy conservation picks the winner
sections.body: Checking kinetic energy eliminates every outcome but one. The incoming KE is 2 * (1/2)mv^2 = mv^2. The single-ball-at-2v outcome gives (1/2)m(2v)^2 = 2mv^2 — double the available energy, impossible. The three-balls-at-(2/3)v outcome gives 3*(1/2)m(2v/3)^2 = (2/3)mv^2 — too little energy, also impossible for an elastic chain. Only the two-balls-at-v outcome, 2*(1/2)mv^2 = mv^2, matches the incoming energy exactly. Since the balls in a real cradle are hard and nearly elastic (small energy loss per contact), the two-out result is the only one consistent with both conservation laws holding almost exactly, which is why it is what actually happens.

sections.heading: The chain mechanism: repeated equal-mass swaps
sections.body: Physically, the middle balls in the cradle barely move at all — the incoming momentum and energy propagate down the chain as a rapid sequence of pairwise, nearly elastic, equal-mass collisions, each one a clean velocity swap of the kind described in lesson 3. Ball 1 hits ball 2 and stops while ball 2 takes its velocity; ball 2 (now moving) instantly hits ball 3 and stops while ball 3 takes the velocity; and so on down the line, until the last ball or balls in the row are free to actually move away, since there is nothing beyond them to collide with. Two balls entering means two velocity packets threading through the chain, so two balls exit; the middle balls act as an efficient but nearly motionless relay.

lessons.workedExample: Two balls (each mass m) swing in at speed v and strike a stationary row of three touching balls (five total). Testing the single-ball-out hypothesis: momentum needs mu = 2mv, so u = 2v, but then KE = (1/2)m(2v)^2 = 2mv^2 while the incoming KE was only 2*(1/2)mv^2 = mv^2 — the hypothesis manufactures energy from nothing, so it is physically impossible. Testing three-balls-out at speed w each: momentum needs 3mw = 2mv, so w = (2/3)v, giving KE = 3*(1/2)m(2v/3)^2 = (2/3)mv^2, which is less than the incoming mv^2 — energy would have to vanish with nowhere to go, also impossible for a chain that is nearly elastic. Only two balls out at speed v each balances both momentum (2mv = 2mv) and energy (mv^2 = mv^2) exactly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about Newton's cradle wants to see momentum conservation checked first, alternative outcomes proposed, and then kinetic energy conservation used to rule them out — because momentum alone is not restrictive enough to explain the cradle's behavior, and a student who stops at momentum has not actually explained anything. The strongest answers also connect the observed outcome to the chain-of-equal-mass-swaps mechanism from the equal-masses lesson, since that is what makes the two-out result physically executable rather than merely arithmetically permitted. A judge may probe what happens with an odd number of balls in, or with unequal ball sizes, to test whether the reasoning generalizes.

questions.prompt: Two balls (mass m, speed v each) swing into a stationary row of three touching balls. Momentum conservation alone would permit a single ball leaving the far end at speed 2v. Why is this outcome actually ruled out?

options.text: It violates kinetic energy conservation — a single ball at 2v carries twice the incoming kinetic energy
It violates momentum conservation as well
It is not ruled out; this is in fact what happens in a real cradle

explanations.a: Correct: (1/2)m(2v)^2 = 2mv^2, twice the incoming kinetic energy of mv^2, so this outcome would create energy from nothing.
explanations.b: Momentum is exactly conserved by this hypothesis (m(2v) = 2mv matches); the problem is with kinetic energy, not momentum.
explanations.c: Real cradles reliably send out two balls at speed v each, not one ball at 2v — the single-ball-at-2v outcome is not observed because it is not physically possible.

questions.prompt: Which outcome satisfies both momentum and kinetic energy conservation when two balls (mass m, speed v) swing into a stationary row?

options.text: One ball leaves at speed 2v
Two balls leave at speed v each
All five balls drift together at 2v/5

explanations.a: This satisfies momentum (m(2v) = 2mv) but fails kinetic energy conservation, delivering twice the available energy.
explanations.b: Correct: momentum checks out (2mv = 2mv) and kinetic energy checks out (mv^2 = mv^2) exactly, matching what real cradles produce.
explanations.c: All balls moving together describes a perfectly inelastic outcome (like the balls fusing), which is inconsistent with the nearly elastic, hard-contact behavior of real cradle balls.

questions.prompt: Physically, what mechanism lets the cradle 'know' to send out exactly two balls rather than one?

options.text: The chain propagates as a sequence of nearly elastic, equal-mass pairwise collisions, each a clean velocity swap, so the incoming momentum and energy pass ball to ball down the line
The strings that support the balls transmit information about how many balls entered
Friction between the balls selects which outcome occurs

explanations.a: Correct: each ball-to-ball contact behaves like the equal-mass velocity exchange from lesson 3, relaying the incoming velocity packets down the chain until they reach balls free to depart.
explanations.b: The strings only constrain each ball's swing; they play no role in transmitting momentum or energy between balls, which happens entirely through direct contact.
explanations.c: Friction is a minor loss mechanism in a well-made cradle, not the reason two balls specifically exit; the outcome is set by conservation laws acting through the collision chain, not by friction.

questions.prompt: Match each proposed outcome for the two-balls-in cradle to what it does or does not violate.

left.text: Two balls leave at v each

right.text: Satisfies momentum; violates kinetic energy conservation by delivering too much KE
Satisfies both momentum and kinetic energy conservation exactly
Satisfies momentum; violates kinetic energy conservation by delivering too little KE

questions.explanation: One ball at 2v conserves momentum (2mv) but doubles the kinetic energy to 2mv^2; two balls at v conserve both exactly; three balls at (2/3)v conserve momentum but only carry (2/3)mv^2, less than the mv^2 available — both wrong outcomes fail energy conservation, in opposite directions.

lessons.label: Elastic Collisions in the Real World

sections.heading: Near-elastic macroscopic collisions
sections.body: No everyday collision is perfectly elastic, but some come close enough that the elastic model predicts outcomes accurately. Billiard and pool balls, made of hard phenolic resin, collide with a measured coefficient of restitution around 0.92 to 0.98 — typically 92 to 98 percent of the kinetic energy survives a ball-on-ball hit, with the rest lost to sound, minor deformation, felt friction, and conversion of translational motion into spin. Superballs, made of high-resilience synthetic rubber (polybutadiene), are a classic classroom demonstration of near-elastic bouncing: their vertical coefficient of restitution off a hard floor is commonly cited around 0.8 to 0.9, high enough that they visibly recover most of a drop height on each bounce, in sharp contrast to a clay ball or a sand-filled 'sad ball,' which stops almost dead on impact.

sections.heading: Truly elastic collisions at the molecular scale
sections.body: The elastic model is not an approximation for collisions between monatomic gas molecules such as helium, neon, or argon. These atoms have no internal rotational or vibrational modes to absorb energy, so a collision between two of them has nowhere for kinetic energy to go except into the atoms' translational motion — the collision is, to a very good approximation, exactly elastic. This is why kinetic theory can treat molecular collisions as elastic without qualification and still correctly predict that an insulated ideal gas maintains constant pressure and temperature indefinitely. Polyatomic gas molecules complicate the picture slightly, since some collision energy can shuttle into rotation or vibration, but total energy is still conserved across the whole gas even when individual collisions are not purely translationally elastic.

sections.heading: Where the elastic model deliberately fails
sections.body: Some engineered systems are built specifically to be inelastic. A car's crumple zones are designed to deform permanently on impact, converting kinetic energy into structural damage and heat rather than into a rebound — that absorption is what keeps the deceleration forces on occupants survivable, since a highly elastic car (bouncing back at near its impact speed) would subject its occupants to a second violent jolt. The general rule of thumb is that the elastic model works best for hard, minimally-deforming materials in brief contact (steel, glass, rigid plastics, or atoms with no internal structure), and works worst for soft, energy-absorbing materials or long, grinding contacts, where a coefficient-of-restitution or fully inelastic treatment is the physically honest choice.

lessons.workedExample: A classroom superball with coefficient of restitution e = 0.9 is dropped from rest at height h = 1.0 m. Just before impact, v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 * 9.8 * 1.0) = 4.43 m/s. Since e is the ratio of rebound speed to impact speed for a bounce off a fixed, much heavier floor, the rebound speed is v' = e*v = 0.9 * 4.43 = 3.99 m/s, and the new bounce height is h' = v'^2/(2g) = (3.99)^2 / 19.6 = 0.81 m. Notice h'/h = e^2 = 0.81, a general shortcut: bounce height ratio equals the square of the coefficient of restitution. A perfectly elastic ball (e = 1) dropped the same way would return to the full 1.0 m, while a ball with e = 0 (like wet clay) would not bounce at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing this concept wants a student who can rank real materials and systems on the elastic-to-inelastic spectrum with actual numbers or mechanisms, not just labels — citing a billiard ball's coefficient of restitution, explaining why monatomic gas collisions are essentially exactly elastic (no internal energy modes to absorb energy), and explaining why crumple zones are intentionally the opposite. A weak answer calls something 'basically elastic' without justification; a strong one names the physical reason energy is or is not conserved in that specific system, and recognizes that engineered inelasticity (as in a car) can be a safety feature rather than a design flaw.

questions.prompt: Which of these is closest to a perfectly elastic collision in everyday physics?

options.text: A car crash into a crumple zone
Two billiard balls colliding
A ball of wet clay hitting the floor

explanations.a: Crumple zones are deliberately designed to be highly inelastic, converting kinetic energy into deformation rather than conserving it.
explanations.b: Correct: billiard balls have a measured coefficient of restitution around 0.92-0.98, close to the elastic ideal of 1.0.
explanations.c: Wet clay sticks and stops on impact, close to the perfectly inelastic extreme (e near 0), the opposite of elastic.

questions.prompt: Why are car crumple zones deliberately engineered to make a collision inelastic?

options.text: To conserve momentum more precisely than an elastic collision would
To convert kinetic energy into deformation and heat rather than a rebound, reducing the forces experienced by occupants
To increase the coefficient of restitution as close to 1 as possible

explanations.a: Momentum is conserved in essentially any collision, elastic or not; crumple zones don't improve momentum conservation, they change where the kinetic energy goes.
explanations.b: Correct: absorbing kinetic energy into permanent deformation avoids a violent elastic rebound, which would otherwise subject occupants to a second sharp deceleration.
explanations.c: Crumple zones intentionally push the coefficient of restitution toward 0, not toward 1 — the opposite of what this option claims.

questions.prompt: A demonstration superball with coefficient of restitution e = 0.9 is dropped from h = 1.0 m. Approximately how high does it bounce back?

explanations.a: 1.0 m would require e = 1 (perfectly elastic); this ball has e = 0.9, so it loses some height.
explanations.b: 0.9 m would be the result if bounce height scaled linearly with e; it actually scales with e squared.
explanations.c: Correct: bounce height ratio equals e^2, so h' = (0.9)^2 (1.0 m) = 0.81 m, matching the direct kinematic calculation.
explanations.d: 0.5 m would correspond to a much lower coefficient of restitution, roughly e = 0.71, not 0.9.

questions.prompt: Which gas molecules undergo collisions closest to perfectly elastic?

options.text: Large polyatomic molecules with many vibrational modes
Monatomic gases like helium and argon, which have no internal rotational or vibrational modes
Any gas molecules, regardless of structure, as long as the gas is at high pressure

explanations.a: Polyatomic molecules can shuttle collision energy into rotation or vibration, making individual collisions less purely translationally elastic than monatomic ones.
explanations.b: Correct: with no internal modes to absorb energy, a monatomic collision has nowhere for kinetic energy to go except back into translational motion, making it essentially exactly elastic.
explanations.c: Pressure affects how often molecules collide, not whether individual collisions are elastic; the presence or absence of internal energy modes is what matters.

units.label: Inelastic Collisions and the Coefficient of Restitution

lessons.label: Perfectly Inelastic Collisions

sections.heading: Sticking together: one final velocity, not two
sections.body: A perfectly inelastic collision is one in which the colliding objects stick together and move off with a single shared final velocity. Momentum is still conserved, as in any closed collision, because Newton's third law makes the internal force pair between the two objects cancel — so as long as external forces contribute negligible impulse over the short collision time, total momentum before equals total momentum after, regardless of what happens to kinetic energy. For two objects with masses m1 and m2 and initial velocities v1 and v2, conservation of momentum gives m1v1 + m2v2 = (m1 + m2)v_f, so the shared final velocity is v_f = (m1v1 + m2v2) / (m1 + m2). Because the two objects end up moving as one, this is a single unknown, one equation, one answer — solving a perfectly inelastic collision is algebraically the simplest case in all of collision mechanics, even though it is the most energetically destructive.

sections.heading: Why this is the maximum-KE-loss case
sections.body: Among all collisions between two given objects with given initial momenta, the perfectly inelastic outcome is the one that loses the most kinetic energy while still conserving momentum. This is not a coincidence of definition; it falls directly out of the algebra. Total momentum fixes the velocity of the system's center of mass, and KE splits into a center-of-mass piece (which momentum conservation forces to be the same in every allowed outcome) plus a piece describing relative motion between the two objects. When the objects stick together, their relative velocity is driven to exactly zero, which is the minimum relative KE possible — zero. Any other outcome, including a bounce, leaves some relative motion and therefore retains more of that relative-KE piece. Sticking is the floor, not an arbitrary case; you cannot lose more KE than a perfectly inelastic collision loses while still obeying momentum conservation.

sections.heading: One equation is never enough for two unknowns
sections.body: A common student error is trying to find two separate final velocities from a single momentum equation in an inelastic problem — that is only solvable when a second, independent piece of information is supplied, such as a given coefficient of restitution or a stated final velocity for one object. In the perfectly inelastic special case, the objects moving together supplies that missing information for free: v1_f = v2_f = v_f collapses two unknowns into one, which is exactly why the perfectly inelastic case is solvable by momentum conservation alone, while a general partially-inelastic or elastic collision needs momentum conservation plus one more relationship (either energy conservation, for the elastic case, or a restitution coefficient, for everything in between). Recognizing 'they stick together' as physics shorthand for 'v1_f = v2_f' — rather than as a separate rule to memorize — is what lets a student see the perfectly inelastic case as one instance of the same two-equation collision framework used everywhere else, not an unrelated special formula.

lessons.workedExample: A 1200 kg car traveling east at 18 m/s rear-ends a stationary 1000 kg car, and the bumpers lock so the two vehicles move off together. Taking east as positive, momentum conservation gives v_f = (m1v1 + m2v2)/(m1+m2) = (1200 × 18 + 1000 × 0)/(1200+1000) = 21,600/2200 ≈ 9.8 m/s east. Both cars now move together at 9.8 m/s — not 18 m/s and not 0 m/s, but a single shared value determined entirely by the total momentum divided by the total mass. Notice that the answer used only conservation of momentum; no energy equation was needed, because the sticking condition itself supplied the second constraint (v1_f = v2_f) that made the algebra solvable with one unknown.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the perfectly inelastic case because it is the cleanest test of whether a student actually understands what conservation of momentum does and does not guarantee. A strong answer states plainly that momentum is conserved in every collision, elastic or not, and that kinetic energy is a separate bookkeeping question decided by the collision's physical details, not by the conservation laws themselves. Judges often follow up by asking a team to defend WHY sticking together is the maximum-energy-loss outcome rather than just accepting it as a rule, which separates memorized formulas from real command of the center-of-mass argument.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s collides with and sticks to a stationary 1 kg cart. What is their common final velocity?

options.text: 4 m/s
3 m/s
1 m/s

explanations.a: Incorrect: 4 m/s would require the mass added at rest to contribute nothing to slowing the system, which ignores that momentum must be shared across the combined mass.
explanations.c: Incorrect: this divides by the wrong mass or drops a factor; the combined mass is 4 kg, not 12 kg, so the correct quotient is 12/4 = 3 m/s.

questions.prompt: Why is a perfectly inelastic collision solvable from momentum conservation alone, without a separate energy equation?

options.text: Because kinetic energy happens to be conserved in this special case
Because the sticking condition (v1_f = v2_f) supplies the second equation needed, collapsing two unknowns into one
Because perfectly inelastic collisions violate momentum conservation, so energy conservation is used instead

explanations.a: Incorrect: kinetic energy is NOT conserved in an inelastic collision — it is a maximum-loss case, the opposite of conserved.
explanations.b: Correct: with two unknown final velocities and only one momentum equation, the problem is underdetermined until sticking together forces v1_f = v2_f, turning it into one unknown solvable by momentum alone.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum conservation holds in every collision, sticking or not; it is never violated, and it is momentum, not energy, that solves this case.

questions.prompt: Match each collision feature to the perfectly inelastic case.

left.text: Final velocities of the two objects
Kinetic energy lost, relative to all momentum-conserving outcomes

right.text: Equal to each other (objects move as one)
Exactly equal to the total momentum before the collision
Maximum possible, among outcomes consistent with momentum conservation

questions.explanation: Sticking together forces one shared final velocity; momentum conservation is unconditional and unaffected by sticking; and driving relative velocity to zero removes the maximum amount of relative kinetic energy allowed by momentum conservation.

lessons.label: How Much Kinetic Energy Is Lost

sections.heading: Computing the loss directly
sections.body: Once the final velocities of a collision are known, the kinetic energy lost is simply KE_before minus KE_after, computed the same way for every collision: KE = ½mv² summed over every object, both before and after. This number is never negative for a real collision — kinetic energy can only stay the same (elastic) or decrease (inelastic); it cannot spontaneously increase in a closed collision with no external energy input: total energy is still conserved either way (the first law), but converting disordered thermal energy spontaneously back into ordered kinetic energy would require entropy to decrease, which the second law of thermodynamics forbids. Reporting a percentage lost, ΔKE/KE_before × 100%, is often more informative than the raw joule figure, because it shows how energetically violent the collision was independent of the objects' absolute size. A useful habit is computing KE_before and KE_after as two entirely separate calculations, each from the ordinary ½mv² formula applied to whatever velocities are known at that instant, rather than trying to shortcut the subtraction through momentum, which carries no direct information about energy at all.

sections.heading: Where the missing energy actually goes
sections.body: The lost kinetic energy is not destroyed; it is converted into other forms of energy that the simple before/after KE bookkeeping does not track. The dominant sink is usually permanent deformation — bending metal, crushing foam, tearing fibers — which stores energy in broken and rearranged intermolecular bonds, ultimately dissipated as heat as those materials settle. A meaningful fraction becomes heat directly from friction at the contact surface, and a small fraction radiates away as sound, the audible crunch or thud of impact. In collisions between very hard, elastic-like objects (steel ball bearings, billiard balls) these losses are small and the collision looks nearly elastic; in collisions between soft or crushable objects (clay, a car's front end) losses dominate and the collision looks close to perfectly inelastic. A smaller but real sink is vibration left behind in each object after separation — a struck bell or a rung tuning fork keeps ringing well after contact ends, carrying away kinetic energy as internal oscillation that outlasts the collision itself and only slowly bleeds off as heat and sound.

sections.heading: A useful diagnostic: KE lost versus e = 0 vs e = 1 limits
sections.body: The energy lost in any real collision falls between two bounds set by the fully elastic case (zero loss) and the perfectly inelastic case (maximum loss, computed in the previous lesson). Comparing a measured energy loss against these two bounds is a fast diagnostic for how close a real collision came to either extreme, without needing to solve the full velocity equations. A collision losing 5% of its initial KE behaves almost elastically; one losing 95% behaves almost like a perfectly inelastic stick. This bracketing is the conceptual bridge to the coefficient of restitution, which formalizes exactly where between these two extremes a given collision falls, using velocities rather than energies.

lessons.workedExample: Two 0.5 kg clay balls collide head-on, each at 6 m/s, and stick together. Before: KE = ½(0.5)(6²) + ½(0.5)(6²) = 9 + 9 = 18 J. Total momentum is zero (equal masses, opposite velocities), so the stuck-together final velocity is v_f = 0/(1.0) = 0 m/s, and KE_after = ½(1.0)(0²) = 0 J. All 18 J is lost — a 100% loss, the extreme case of a symmetric head-on perfectly inelastic collision where the objects end up completely at rest. That energy did not vanish: it went into flattening and deforming the two clay balls at the point of impact, plus a small amount of heat and the dull thud heard on contact.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe kinetic energy loss because it is a frequent source of a specific misconception: that momentum conservation implies energy conservation, when in fact the two are independent bookkeeping systems that only agree in the special elastic case. A well-prepared student computes both KE_before and KE_after explicitly, states a numeric or percentage loss, and can name a physical destination for that energy (deformation, heat, sound) rather than treating it as having vanished. Judges may also ask why the lost KE is never negative, testing whether the student connects the result to the second law of thermodynamics (spontaneously turning disordered thermal energy back into ordered kinetic energy would require entropy to decrease) rather than treating it as a memorized fact.

questions.prompt: In any real, closed collision with no external energy input, the kinetic energy after the collision compared to before can be:

options.text: Greater than before, if the objects are elastic enough
Equal to or less than before, never greater
Always exactly half of the initial value

explanations.a: Incorrect: kinetic energy cannot spontaneously increase in a closed collision with no external energy source — total energy is still conserved either way, but converting disordered thermal energy back into ordered kinetic energy would require entropy to decrease, which the second law of thermodynamics forbids.
explanations.b: Correct: KE_after ≤ KE_before always; equality holds only for a perfectly elastic collision, and every other real collision loses some KE to deformation, heat, and sound.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the fraction lost depends entirely on the specific collision (materials, geometry, speed) — there is no universal fixed fraction like one-half.

questions.prompt: Two identical 0.5 kg balls collide head-on at 6 m/s each and stick together, ending at rest. Where did the 18 J of lost kinetic energy go?

options.text: It was destroyed, since energy is not exactly conserved in inelastic collisions
It converted into deformation energy, heat, and sound at the point of impact
It transferred entirely into the balls' rotational kinetic energy

explanations.a: Incorrect: total energy is always conserved; kinetic energy specifically is not, because some of it converts to other forms rather than vanishing.
explanations.b: Correct: the missing KE is converted, not destroyed — dominant sinks are permanent deformation (broken/rearranged bonds), friction heat at the contact surface, and a small amount of radiated sound.
explanations.c: Incorrect: nothing in the problem describes the balls spinning after collision, and rotational KE is not the typical dominant sink for a head-on translational collision like this one.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for computing and interpreting kinetic energy lost in a collision.

items.text: Compute total KE_before using ½mv² for every object
Solve for final velocities using momentum conservation (plus any needed second equation)
Compute total KE_after using the final velocities
Report ΔKE = KE_before − KE_after, and compare it to the elastic (0) and perfectly inelastic (maximum) bounds

questions.explanation: You need the initial KE and the final velocities (from momentum conservation) before you can compute the final KE, and only then can the loss be computed and placed between the elastic and perfectly inelastic bounds.

lessons.label: The Coefficient of Restitution e

sections.heading: Defining e from separation and approach speeds
sections.body: The coefficient of restitution, e, is defined as the ratio of the relative speed of separation to the relative speed of approach: e = |v2_f − v1_f| / |v1_i − v2_i|. It is a dimensionless number, always between 0 and 1 for a physically real collision, that measures how much of the relative motion between two colliding objects survives the collision. Unlike momentum, which is conserved in a closed collision because internal force pairs cancel (with negligible external impulse over the collision time), e is not a conservation law; it is an empirical parameter, measured or estimated for a given pair of materials and impact condition, that supplies the second equation needed to solve a collision problem once momentum conservation alone is not enough. Isaac Newton himself introduced this ratio in the Principia (1687), measuring it experimentally with pendulum-suspended balls made of compressed wool, cork, steel, and glass and finding the ratio differed clearly by material, an empirical result he reported without a theoretical derivation, since deriving e from first principles requires the material physics of stress, strain, and internal damping that was not developed until much later.

sections.heading: The two limits: e = 1 and e = 0
sections.body: When e = 1, the relative speed of separation exactly equals the relative speed of approach — this is precisely the condition that defines a perfectly elastic collision, and it can be shown algebraically that e = 1 combined with momentum conservation reproduces the standard elastic-collision velocity formulas exactly. When e = 0, the objects have zero relative speed after the collision, meaning they move off with the same final velocity — exactly the definition of a perfectly inelastic collision from the earlier lessons. Every real collision falls somewhere in this range, 0 ≤ e ≤ 1, which is why e functions as a continuous dial between the two idealized extremes rather than a binary switch between 'elastic' and 'inelastic' collision types.

sections.heading: Using e to solve a general collision
sections.body: Given e for a specific collision, momentum conservation (one equation) plus the restitution relation v2_f − v1_f = −e(v2_i − v1_i) (a second, independent equation) together fully determine both final velocities — no separate energy equation is needed, because e itself already encodes how much relative kinetic energy the collision retains. The minus sign matters: it enforces that if the objects approach each other, they must separate (or at minimum have zero relative velocity) rather than continuing to close the gap, which is physically required for a completed collision. This two-equation system is the general-purpose tool for 1D collision problems: elastic and perfectly inelastic are simply e = 1 and e = 0 plugged into the same machinery.

lessons.workedExample: A 2 kg cart moving at 5 m/s strikes a stationary 3 kg cart, and the collision has a measured coefficient of restitution e = 0.6. Momentum conservation: 2(5) + 3(0) = 2v1_f + 3v2_f, so 10 = 2v1_f + 3v2_f. Restitution: v2_f − v1_f = −e(v2_i − v1_i) = −0.6(0 − 5) = 3 m/s. Substituting v1_f = v2_f − 3 into the momentum equation: 10 = 2(v2_f − 3) + 3v2_f = 5v2_f − 6, so v2_f = 3.2 m/s and v1_f = 0.2 m/s. Check: relative separation speed = |3.2 − 0.2| = 3 m/s, relative approach speed = |5 − 0| = 5 m/s, and 3/5 = 0.6 = e, confirming the solution is consistent with the given restitution coefficient.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the coefficient of restitution because it is the concept that unifies elastic and inelastic collisions into a single continuous framework rather than two disconnected special cases, and testing whether a student can set up and solve the two-equation system (momentum plus restitution) reveals whether they understand collisions structurally rather than by memorized formula. A judge may hand a team an e value between 0 and 1 and ask for both final velocities on the spot, which is a direct test of whether the momentum-and-restitution system, not just the two textbook extremes, has actually been internalized.

questions.prompt: What does a coefficient of restitution of e = 0.6 tell you about a collision?

options.text: 60% of the kinetic energy is conserved
The relative speed of separation is 60% of the relative speed of approach
The objects stick together with 60% probability

explanations.a: Incorrect: e relates to relative SPEEDS, not directly to kinetic energy fractions; the fraction of KE retained is generally e² only in special symmetric cases, not e itself in general.
explanations.b: Correct: e is defined as relative separation speed divided by relative approach speed, so e = 0.6 means the objects fly apart at 60% of the speed at which they came together.
explanations.c: Incorrect: e is a deterministic ratio of speeds for a given collision, not a probability of any outcome.

questions.prompt: Which value of e corresponds to a perfectly elastic collision, and which to a perfectly inelastic collision?

options.text: e = 1 is elastic; e = 0 is perfectly inelastic
e = 0 is elastic; e = 1 is perfectly inelastic
e = 1 is elastic; e = 1 is also perfectly inelastic, since both conserve momentum

explanations.a: Correct: e = 1 means separation speed equals approach speed (no relative KE lost, elastic); e = 0 means zero separation speed (objects move together, perfectly inelastic).
explanations.b: Incorrect: this reverses the two limits — e = 0 is the objects sticking together (perfectly inelastic), and e = 1 is the fully bouncy elastic case.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum conservation holds at every value of e, so it cannot be what distinguishes elastic from inelastic; the two cases are correctly distinguished by e = 1 versus e = 0, not by momentum conservation alone.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its role in solving a general 1D collision with a given e.

right.text: Always holds exactly, in every collision
Supplies the second independent equation needed to solve for two unknown final velocities
An empirically measured parameter, not derived from a conservation law

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation is unconditional; the restitution relation is the extra equation that, together with momentum, pins down both final velocities; and e itself is measured for real materials rather than derived from first principles.

lessons.label: Measuring e from Bounce Height

sections.heading: Deriving e = sqrt(h_rebound / h_drop)
sections.body: A ball dropped onto a stationary, immovable floor is a special case of the general collision framework: the floor's mass is effectively infinite and its velocity stays zero throughout, before and after. The restitution relation e = |v_separation| / |v_approach| then simplifies to e = v_rebound / v_drop, the ball's upward speed right after the bounce divided by its downward speed right before. Using free-fall kinematics, a ball dropped from height h hits the floor with speed v_drop = sqrt(2gh_drop), and a ball leaving the floor at v_rebound rises to height h_rebound = v_rebound²/(2g), so v_rebound = sqrt(2g·h_rebound). Substituting both into the restitution ratio gives e = sqrt(2g·h_rebound) / sqrt(2g·h_drop) = sqrt(h_rebound / h_drop) — the g cancels entirely, leaving a formula that needs only two height measurements. It is worth noting this also means e² is exactly the fraction of kinetic energy retained through the bounce in this specific, single-object-off-a-fixed-floor case, since KE is proportional to height in free fall; that convenient shortcut (KE_after/KE_before = e² = h_rebound/h_drop) does NOT generalize to arbitrary two-body collisions, only to a bounce off an effectively immovable surface.

sections.heading: Why this is such a good experiment
sections.body: This derivation makes bounce-height testing one of the cheapest, most accurate ways to measure a coefficient of restitution in a classroom or lab: no force sensors, no high-speed camera, and no timing electronics are required, only a meter stick or a phone's slow-motion video and a fixed drop height. Because e depends on the SQUARE ROOT of a height ratio, height measurement errors are damped by a factor of two when propagated to e — a 4% error in a measured height produces only about a 2% error in e, which is one of the reasons this method remains standard for regulating sports equipment (tennis balls, basketballs) despite far more sophisticated alternatives existing. The same setup can be extended to compare surfaces or balls directly: dropping the same ball onto concrete, wood, and grass from an identical height and comparing the three rebound heights isolates the surface's contribution to e without needing to know any absolute material property in advance.

sections.heading: Sources of uncertainty and how to control them
sections.body: The dominant sources of error are judging the exact top of the rebound by eye, an uneven or non-rigid floor (a soft mat effectively changes the 'floor' being tested), air resistance on a light or high-drag ball, and any spin imparted on the drop that couples some translational energy into rotation and back unpredictably. Best practice is to drop the ball from rest (no initial push, which could add horizontal velocity or spin), use a rigid and level floor, and repeat the trial multiple times, reporting the mean bounce height and its standard deviation rather than a single trial, since e derived from a single bounce carries whatever measurement noise that one trial happened to have.

lessons.workedExample: A student drops a basketball from h_drop = 1.80 m onto a hardwood gym floor and measures a rebound height of h_rebound = 1.01 m, averaged over five trials with a standard deviation of 0.03 m. The coefficient of restitution is e = sqrt(h_rebound/h_drop) = sqrt(1.01/1.80) = sqrt(0.561) ≈ 0.749, consistent with the NBA/NCAA specification that a properly inflated basketball, dropped from 6 ft (72 in), should rebound to between 49 and 54 inches — about 68% to 75% of its drop height, corresponding to e roughly between 0.82 and 0.87 — here the ball is bouncing noticeably deader than that spec range, which is exactly the kind of quantitative comparison bounce-height testing is designed to make possible.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the bounce-height method because it is a rare case where the underlying physics (kinematics plus the restitution definition) directly produces a simple, testable, and CHEAP experimental protocol, and asking a student to derive e = sqrt(h_rebound/h_drop) from scratch tests whether they understand restitution as speeds, not just as a formula to memorize. A strong team also reports uncertainty from repeated trials and can name a specific confound, like ball spin or floor rigidity, that a single-trial measurement would miss — showing they understand this as a real experimental method, not just an algebra exercise.

questions.prompt: A ball dropped from 2.0 m rebounds to a height of 0.5 m. What is its coefficient of restitution with the floor?

explanations.a: Incorrect: 0.25 is the height ratio h_rebound/h_drop = 0.5/2.0 itself, but e is the SQUARE ROOT of that ratio, not the ratio directly.
explanations.b: Correct: e = sqrt(h_rebound/h_drop) = sqrt(0.5/2.0) = sqrt(0.25) = 0.5.
