explanations.c: Incorrect: 0.71 ≈ sqrt(0.5), which mistakenly uses h_rebound alone (in some unit) rather than the ratio h_rebound/h_drop = 0.25 under the square root.

questions.prompt: Why does the bounce-height method for measuring e remain popular despite more sophisticated alternatives (force sensors, high-speed video)?

options.text: It requires only simple height measurements, is cheap, and height errors are damped by the square root in the formula
It is the only method that gives an exact value of e with zero uncertainty
It works even when the floor is soft, springy, or uneven, unlike other methods

explanations.a: Correct: e = sqrt(h_rebound/h_drop) needs only a drop height and a rebound height, cheap and simple to measure, and because e depends on a square root, height measurement errors are roughly halved in their effect on e.
explanations.b: Incorrect: no experimental method gives zero uncertainty; bounce-height testing still has real error sources like judging peak height by eye and air resistance.
explanations.c: Incorrect: a soft, springy, or uneven floor actually corrupts this method, since the derivation assumes an effectively rigid, immovable floor whose own motion can be ignored.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the bounce-height derivation of e = sqrt(h_rebound/h_drop).

items.text: Note the floor is effectively infinite mass and stays at rest, so e reduces to v_rebound/v_drop
Use free-fall kinematics to write v_drop = sqrt(2g·h_drop)
Use free-fall kinematics to write v_rebound = sqrt(2g·h_rebound)
Divide the two speed expressions; the factor of 2g cancels, leaving e = sqrt(h_rebound/h_drop)

questions.explanation: The floor's infinite effective mass simplifies the restitution ratio to a single speed ratio first, then each speed is expressed via kinematics from its respective height, and only then does dividing them cancel the 2g and leave the clean height-ratio formula.

lessons.label: The Ballistic Pendulum

sections.heading: Two physics regimes stitched into one device
sections.body: The ballistic pendulum, invented by English mathematician Benjamin Robins and published in his 1742 book New Principles of Gunnery, was the first instrument able to measure a projectile's speed with real precision, well before high-speed timing electronics existed. A projectile (originally a musket ball) is fired into a large, softer block hanging at rest from cords, embeds itself, and the combined block-plus-projectile swings upward on the pendulum's arc. The device deliberately combines two DIFFERENT physical processes: the embedding itself is a perfectly inelastic collision, governed by momentum conservation (with kinetic energy lost to deformation as the projectile buries itself), while the subsequent swing upward is governed by conservation of mechanical energy, since a smoothly swinging pendulum has no significant energy-dissipating collision happening within it. Before Robins, gunners and artillerists had no reliable way to know how fast a ball actually left the muzzle; his device let ballistics become a genuinely quantitative science, and New Principles of Gunnery is often credited as the work that founded the modern, mathematically grounded study of projectile motion in weapons.

sections.heading: Stage 1 — the embedding (momentum only)
sections.body: If a projectile of mass m strikes a stationary block of mass M and embeds itself, momentum conservation gives mv = (m+M)V, where v is the projectile's pre-impact speed (the ultimate target of the whole measurement) and V is the shared velocity of the block-plus-projectile immediately after embedding, before the pendulum has swung at all. Critically, energy conservation CANNOT be applied across this stage — this collision is perfectly inelastic and loses a large, unmeasured amount of kinetic energy to deforming the block and projectile, so any attempt to relate v directly to the pendulum's swing height using energy alone, skipping the momentum step, gives a wrong answer. Notice that the fraction of kinetic energy lost in this embedding is typically enormous, often well over 99% for a light, fast bullet embedding in a heavy block, yet the device still yields an exact bullet speed, because the measurement never depends on knowing how much energy was lost, only on momentum being conserved regardless of how much energy was lost.

sections.heading: Stage 2 — the swing (energy only)
sections.body: Once the block and embedded projectile are moving together at speed V, the pendulum's swing to some maximum height h is a separate, ordinary event where mechanical energy IS conserved, because the string tension does no work and air resistance/friction at the pivot are treated as negligible: ½(m+M)V² = (m+M)gh, giving V = sqrt(2gh). Combining both stages gives the full solution: measure the swing height h, compute V = sqrt(2gh) from energy conservation, then compute the original bullet speed v = (m+M)V/m from momentum conservation. Getting the ORDER right, momentum first across the lossy collision, energy second across the lossless swing, is the entire conceptual content of the device.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.010 kg bullet is fired into a 4.99 kg wooden block (total mass after embedding: 5.00 kg) hanging from cords. The block-bullet system swings up to a maximum height of h = 0.12 m. Stage 2 (energy, swing only): V = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 × 9.8 × 0.12) = sqrt(2.352) ≈ 1.53 m/s. Stage 1 (momentum, embedding only): v = (m+M)V/m = (5.00 × 1.53)/0.010 ≈ 765 m/s. This two-stage method recovers a bullet speed of roughly 765 m/s from nothing more than a mass ratio and a swing height measured with a protractor or ruler — no timing equipment at all, which is exactly why Robins' device was revolutionary in 1742.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the ballistic pendulum because it is a compact test of whether a student can correctly identify WHICH conservation law applies to WHICH stage of a multi-stage process, a skill that generalizes far beyond this one device. The classic trap is applying energy conservation straight through the embedding collision, which silently produces a wrong (too-low) bullet speed because it ignores the large, real kinetic energy loss in that perfectly inelastic stage. A judge asking 'why can't you just conserve energy for the whole process' is testing exactly this distinction, and a strong answer names the embedding as the lossy, momentum-only stage explicitly.

questions.prompt: In a ballistic pendulum, which conservation law applies during the swing stage (after the bullet has embedded), and which during the embedding stage itself?

options.text: Energy conservation applies to both stages
Momentum conservation applies to the embedding; energy conservation applies to the swing
Energy conservation applies to the embedding; momentum conservation applies to the swing

explanations.a: Incorrect: the embedding is a perfectly inelastic collision that loses kinetic energy to deformation, so energy conservation does not hold across that stage.
explanations.b: Correct: the embedding conserves momentum only (energy is lost to deformation); the swing afterward conserves mechanical energy only (no further collision occurs).
explanations.c: Incorrect: this reverses the two stages — the lossy, momentum-only event is the embedding, and the lossless, energy-only event is the swing.

questions.prompt: Why would applying energy conservation across the ENTIRE process (embedding plus swing) give a wrong bullet speed?

options.text: Because gravity does not act during the swing
Because the embedding collision is perfectly inelastic and loses a large, unaccounted amount of kinetic energy to deformation
Because momentum is not actually conserved during the embedding

explanations.a: Incorrect: gravity is exactly what drives the swing and is central to the energy equation used in stage 2 — it is not the source of the error.
explanations.b: Correct: skipping the momentum step and applying energy across the whole process silently assumes no KE was lost in the embedding, when in fact a large amount was lost to deforming the block and bullet.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum IS conserved during the embedding (as in every collision); the error comes from wrongly assuming energy is ALSO conserved there, which it is not.

questions.prompt: Order the correct solution procedure for a ballistic pendulum problem, given the swing height h and both masses.

items.text: Apply energy conservation to the swing to find V, the post-embedding speed, from V = sqrt(2gh)
Apply momentum conservation to the embedding to relate the bullet's initial speed v to V
Solve for v = (m+M)V/m, the original bullet speed

questions.explanation: Because the swing height is the only direct measurement available, energy conservation on the swing must be used first to back out V, and only then can momentum conservation on the embedding be used to solve for the original bullet speed v.

lessons.label: The Coefficient of Restitution Is Not a Constant

sections.heading: e depends on impact speed
sections.body: Despite being called a 'coefficient,' e is not a fixed material property the way density or specific heat is — it typically DECREASES as impact speed increases. At low speeds, most materials deform elastically (like a spring) and return most of that stored energy back into the bounce, giving a relatively high e. At higher speeds, the material is driven past its elastic limit into plastic (permanent) deformation, which absorbs energy irreversibly as heat and structural change rather than releasing it back, so a harder-thrown ball or a faster impact tends to bounce back with proportionally less of its approach speed than a gentler one, even off the identical surface. This is exactly why quoting a single e for 'a golf ball' or 'a baseball' is only meaningful alongside the impact speed it was measured at — equipment regulators test at specified speeds precisely to make comparisons between products fair and reproducible.

sections.heading: e depends on temperature
sections.body: Temperature changes a material's stiffness and internal damping, so a colder ball generally has a lower e than the same ball warm, which is why a basketball feels noticeably 'dead' outdoors in winter and needs extra inflation pressure to compensate, and why baseballs stored in a cold clubhouse are measurably less lively than the same balls at room temperature. This is a real, quantified effect in sports regulation: several ball sports specify a minimum storage or testing temperature precisely because e (and therefore bounce height, feel, and game-relevant behavior) is temperature-dependent, not a fixed number that can be tested once and assumed forever after. The mechanism is the same rubbery-polymer physics behind why a cold rubber band snaps rather than stretches: below a material's characteristic transition temperature, internal friction between polymer chains rises sharply, converting far more of an impact's energy into heat rather than into elastic rebound.

sections.heading: e depends on materials and geometry, not just 'the ball'
sections.body: The coefficient of restitution is a property of a COLLISION PAIR, not of either object alone — the same ball has a different e bouncing off concrete, wood, sand, or grass, because e depends on both objects' stiffness, damping, and how their geometries interact at the contact point (a glancing versus head-on impact, a flat surface versus a curved one). This is why sports equipment regulations specify not just a ball's construction but the exact test surface, drop height, and temperature: a bat's 'trampoline effect' (an unusually high effective e from a springy barrel wall) is regulated for baseball and softball precisely because manufacturers could otherwise engineer bats that behave like an artificially higher-e collision pair than the sport intends, giving batted balls extra unearned speed.

lessons.workedExample: A rubber ball is tested at three impact speeds onto the same concrete floor: at 2 m/s its measured e is 0.85, at 8 m/s its measured e drops to 0.78, and at 15 m/s it drops further to 0.68. A student incorrectly assumes e = 0.85 (the low-speed value) applies at all speeds and predicts a rebound height for a ball dropped from 3 m (impact speed sqrt(2×9.8×3) ≈ 7.67 m/s, close to the 8 m/s trial) using h_rebound = e² × h_drop = 0.85² × 3 ≈ 2.17 m. Using the correct, speed-appropriate e = 0.78 instead gives h_rebound = 0.78² × 3 ≈ 1.83 m, a meaningfully lower and more accurate prediction — a nearly 20% overestimate results from treating e as a single constant rather than a function of impact speed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the speed- and temperature-dependence of e specifically because it exposes a subtle but common misconception: treating a measured coefficient of restitution as a fixed material constant that transfers unchanged to a different impact condition. A strong team explicitly caveats any quoted e value with the conditions it was measured under (speed, temperature, surface) and can explain the underlying mechanism, elastic versus plastic deformation setting the speed dependence, rather than citing the trend as an unexplained empirical curiosity. This also connects directly to real sports-equipment regulation, which judges may reference to test whether the physics generalizes beyond a textbook ball-drop scenario.

questions.prompt: As the impact speed of a collision increases, the coefficient of restitution e for most real materials tends to:

options.text: Stay exactly constant, since e is a fixed material property
Increase, since faster impacts transfer more energy into the bounce
Decrease, as the material is driven from elastic into plastic (permanent) deformation

explanations.a: Incorrect: e is an empirical, condition-dependent parameter, not a fixed material constant like density — it varies measurably with impact speed for real materials.
explanations.b: Incorrect: this has the trend backwards; faster impacts push materials past their elastic limit, INCREASING irreversible energy loss, not decreasing it.
explanations.c: Correct: higher-speed impacts drive more of the deformation into the plastic (permanent, energy-absorbing) regime rather than the elastic (energy-returning) regime, lowering e.

questions.prompt: Why do some ball sports specify a minimum testing or storage temperature for their balls?

options.text: Because temperature has no real effect on bounce, and the rule is purely traditional
Because a colder ball is generally stiffer and less lively, giving a lower coefficient of restitution and a different bounce than intended
Because cold temperatures increase e, making a colder ball bounce too high

explanations.a: Incorrect: temperature measurably changes a material's stiffness and internal damping, which directly affects e — the rule reflects real physics, not tradition alone.
explanations.b: Correct: colder balls tend to have lower e (feel 'dead'), which is why regulations pin down a testing/storage temperature so bounce behavior stays consistent and game-appropriate.
explanations.c: Incorrect: this reverses the direction — cold generally LOWERS e for most ball materials, it does not raise it.

questions.prompt: Match each variable to how it affects the coefficient of restitution e.

left.text: Same ball, different contact surface (e.g. concrete vs. sand)

right.text: Generally lowers e, from more plastic (permanent) deformation
Generally lowers e, from reduced material liveliness/increased stiffness
Gives a genuinely different e, since e describes the collision PAIR, not the ball alone

questions.explanation: Higher speed drives more permanent deformation, lowering e; colder material is stiffer and less resilient, also lowering e; and because e is a property of the colliding PAIR, changing the surface changes e even with the identical ball.

lessons.label: Crash Safety: Crumple Zones and Energy Absorption

sections.heading: Engineering a car to be deliberately inelastic
sections.body: Modern car design deliberately makes the front and rear sections of a vehicle LESS elastic (lower effective restitution) than a rigid structure would be, because a low-restitution, highly deformable structure absorbs far more kinetic energy through permanent crushing than a stiff, bouncy structure would. This is the opposite of what naive intuition might suggest: a car that stayed perfectly rigid and 'bounced off' a wall (high e, closer to elastic) would transmit a much larger peak force to its occupants than one that crumples and stays partially in contact for longer, even though the crumpled car looks far more dramatically damaged afterward. The visible destruction of a crumple zone is not a design failure; it is the entire safety mechanism working as intended.

sections.heading: The engineering history: Béla Barényi
sections.body: The crumple zone concept was patented by engineer Béla Barényi, first in 1937 and then in a fully developed form as Mercedes-Benz patent DBP 854157 on 28 February 1952, describing a vehicle body divided into three zones: a rigid, non-deforming passenger safety cell in the center, flanked by front and rear sections deliberately engineered to crush and absorb energy in a collision. Barényi's insight directly overturned the prevailing wisdom of the time, that a 'safe' car body needed to be as rigid as possible throughout. Mercedes-Benz's W111 'Fintail' sedan, introduced in 1959, was the first production car to fully implement the patented safety-cell-plus-crumple-zone design, and the same three-zone principle, rigid cell plus deformable crush structures, remains the basis of automotive crash safety engineering today.

sections.heading: Connecting restitution and impulse: two views of the same mechanism
sections.body: The crumple zone's benefit can be described in two equivalent physics languages. In restitution terms, a low e means the car's structure absorbs (rather than returns) most of the relative kinetic energy of the collision, sparing the passenger compartment from having to reverse direction sharply. In impulse terms (from the impulse-momentum theorem, J = FΔt = Δp), the car's required momentum change is fixed by its mass and speed regardless of structure, but crumpling stretches the collision's duration Δt, which lowers the average force F = Δp/Δt transmitted through the structure to the occupants for that same fixed momentum change. These are not two competing explanations; a structure engineered for a lower effective e is, mechanically, exactly the kind of structure that extends contact time and therefore lowers peak force — restitution and impulse describe the same crash from two different, mutually consistent angles. Modern designs push this further with crash structures engineered to crumple in a controlled, staged sequence (front rails folding in a predetermined accordion pattern) rather than buckling unpredictably, which keeps the deceleration curve smoother and more survivable than either a purely rigid or a randomly collapsing structure would achieve.

lessons.workedExample: A 1400 kg car crashes into a rigid barrier at 15 m/s and comes to rest. A poorly engineered, nearly rigid front end stops the car's momentum change of Δp = 1400 × 15 = 21,000 kg·m/s over a very short crush distance and time, say Δt = 0.03 s, giving an average force F = Δp/Δt = 21,000/0.03 = 700,000 N transmitted toward the passenger compartment. An engineered crumple zone extending the collision to Δt = 0.12 s (a factor of four longer, achieved by allowing roughly a meter of front-end crush rather than a few centimeters) delivers the identical fixed impulse of 21,000 kg·m/s, but now F = 21,000/0.12 = 175,000 N — a fourfold reduction in the peak force reaching the rigid passenger cell, purely from stretching out the time over which the same unavoidable momentum change occurs.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe crumple-zone physics because it is one of the clearest, highest-stakes real-world applications of collision mechanics, and it tests whether a student can connect two representations, restitution (energy absorption) and impulse (force-time tradeoff), as one coherent mechanism rather than two disconnected facts to memorize. A strong answer explicitly states that the crushed metal is not evidence of a failed design but is the mechanism doing its job, and can quantify the tradeoff (fixed momentum change, but tunable Δt and therefore tunable peak force) rather than describing safety only in qualitative terms. Judges may also ask why a perfectly rigid, bouncy (high-e) car would be MORE dangerous, testing whether the counterintuitive direction of the result is genuinely understood.

questions.prompt: Why is a car engineered to have a LOW effective coefficient of restitution in its front structure, rather than a high one?

options.text: A low e means the structure absorbs more collision energy through permanent deformation rather than bouncing it back, and extends the collision's duration, lowering peak force on occupants
A low e makes the car lighter, which is the only goal of crumple zone design
A low e has no real safety benefit; crumple zones exist mainly to reduce repair costs

explanations.a: Correct: low restitution absorbs energy as permanent deformation instead of returning it as a bounce, and mechanically this corresponds to a longer collision duration Δt, which lowers peak force for the same fixed momentum change.
explanations.b: Incorrect: crumple zone design is about energy absorption and collision duration, not primarily about vehicle weight.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the safety benefit is real and physics-based (lower peak force on occupants), not a cost-related side effect; repair cost is a secondary consequence, not the design goal.

questions.prompt: Béla Barényi's key patented insight, developed into Mercedes-Benz patent DBP 854157 (1952), was to divide a car body into which zones?

options.text: A uniformly rigid body throughout, with no deformable sections
A rigid central passenger safety cell flanked by deformable front and rear crumple zones
A uniformly soft, deformable body throughout, including the passenger area

explanations.a: Incorrect: this describes the OLDER design philosophy Barényi's patent overturned, which assumed uniform rigidity was inherently safer.
explanations.b: Correct: Barényi's design used a rigid, non-deforming passenger safety cell in the center, with front and rear zones deliberately engineered to crumple and absorb energy.
explanations.c: Incorrect: making the passenger area itself deformable would remove the protective rigid cell that keeps the occupant survival space intact — only the front/rear sections are meant to crush.

questions.prompt: Match each physics description of a crumple zone to its equivalent framing.

left.text: What stays fixed regardless of crumple design

right.text: A low effective e means energy is absorbed by deformation rather than returned as a bounce
Extending the collision's duration Δt lowers the average force for a fixed impulse
The total momentum change Δp, set by the car's mass and impact speed

questions.explanation: The two framings describe the identical physical mechanism from different angles — restitution language emphasizes energy absorption, impulse language emphasizes the force-time tradeoff — while the required momentum change itself is fixed by mass and impact speed no matter how the structure is designed.

lessons.label: Momentum Is a Vector: Conserving Components

sections.heading: One vector law, two scalar bookkeepers
sections.body: Conservation of momentum is a vector statement: the total momentum vector of an isolated system is the same before and after any interaction. In one dimension that vector has only one component, so "conserved" means a single number stays fixed. In two dimensions the momentum vector has an x-component and a y-component, and the vector law is equivalent to two independent scalar laws holding at once: total p_x before equals total p_x after, AND total p_y before equals total p_y after. These two equations do not trade off against each other — a collision cannot conserve x-momentum by borrowing from y-momentum. Each axis keeps its own books, which is what makes 2D problems solvable at all: instead of one vector equation with an unknown magnitude and unknown direction, you get two ordinary scalar equations.

sections.heading: Choosing axes and resolving velocities
sections.body: Because the x and y equations are independent, you are free to choose any pair of perpendicular axes — but once chosen, every velocity in the problem must be resolved into components along those same axes before you add anything. A puck moving at speed v and angle theta above the x-axis contributes v·cos(theta) to the x-sum and v·sin(theta) to the y-sum for each object involved, and it is momentum components — mass times velocity component — that get summed, not speeds or angles directly. A frequent setup convenience: orient the x-axis along the incoming projectile's initial velocity, which makes its initial p_y exactly zero and removes one term from every equation, leaving only the target and post-collision velocities to resolve.

sections.heading: Two equations, several unknowns
sections.body: A generic 2D collision problem has up to four unknowns after the collision (each object's post-collision speed and direction, or equivalently each object's v_x and v_y), but conservation of momentum supplies only two equations, one per axis. That is not enough to solve a fully unknown two-body 2D collision outright — you need additional information, such as one final angle measured experimentally, an elastic-collision assumption (which adds a kinetic-energy equation), or a stated fraction of energy lost. Recognizing this counting problem — two conservation equations versus up to four unknowns — is what tells you whether a 2D collision problem is solvable as stated or needs one more given quantity.

lessons.workedExample: A 2.0 kg puck moves at 3.0 m/s in the +x direction and strikes a stationary 2.0 kg puck. After the collision, puck A moves off at 2.0 m/s at 30 degrees above the x-axis. Conservation gives: initial p_x = 2.0(3.0) = 6.0 kg·m/s, initial p_y = 0. Puck A's components after: p_Ax = 2.0(2.0)cos(30°) = 3.46 kg·m/s, p_Ay = 2.0(2.0)sin(30°) = 2.0 kg·m/s. Since total p_x and p_y must each still equal their initial values, puck B must carry p_Bx = 6.0 − 3.46 = 2.54 kg·m/s and p_By = 0 − 2.0 = −2.0 kg·m/s. Puck B's speed is √(2.54² + 2.0²)/2.0 ≈ 1.62 m/s, at an angle arctan(−2.0/2.54) ≈ −38.2° (below the x-axis) — the two axes were solved completely independently.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the component-conservation setup because it is the single most common place students go wrong in 2D mechanics: adding speeds or momenta directly instead of resolving into x and y first, or letting an x-direction result leak into the y-equation. A student who can state cleanly that momentum conservation in 2D is really two separate scalar laws, and can explain why the number of unknowns can exceed the number of conservation equations, shows they understand the vector nature of momentum rather than pattern-matching a formula. Judges may ask what extra piece of data (an angle, an elastic assumption) was needed to make a particular problem solvable.

questions.prompt: In a 2D collision with no external forces, which statement is correct?

options.text: Total momentum magnitude is conserved, but its direction can change.
The x-component and y-component of total momentum are each conserved separately.
Only the component of momentum along the incoming object's initial direction is conserved.

explanations.a: Incorrect: momentum is a vector and both its magnitude and direction stay fixed for an isolated system, not just magnitude.
explanations.b: Correct: the vector conservation law is equivalent to two independent scalar equations, one for total p_x and one for total p_y, both holding before and after.
explanations.c: Incorrect: conservation holds along ANY chosen axis, not only the direction of initial motion — that direction is just a common convenient choice.

questions.prompt: A fully unspecified 2D two-body collision (both objects' final speeds and directions unknown) has how many unknowns compared to the number of independent momentum-conservation equations available?

options.text: 4 unknowns, 2 equations — more unknowns than equations
2 unknowns, 2 equations — exactly solvable
4 unknowns, 4 equations — exactly solvable

explanations.a: Correct: each object's final velocity has 2 unknowns (e.g., v_x and v_y, or speed and angle), giving 4 total, while momentum conservation supplies only 2 scalar equations (x and y) — extra information is needed to fully solve it.
explanations.b: Incorrect: 2 unknowns would only be true if one object's final velocity were already fully known, which is not the generic case.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum conservation in 2D never supplies more than 2 independent scalar equations, regardless of how many unknowns exist.

questions.prompt: Match each setup choice to its effect on the algebra.

left.text: Orienting x-axis along the incoming object's velocity
Resolving each velocity into components before summing

right.text: Makes the initial p_y term equal to zero
Ensures momentum components, not speeds, are what get added
Supplies one additional (kinetic-energy) equation

questions.explanation: Aligning the x-axis with the incoming velocity zeroes out its y-component; resolving every velocity into x/y components before adding is what makes vector addition valid; assuming an elastic collision contributes the kinetic-energy conservation equation needed to close the unknown count.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for setting up a 2D collision problem using component conservation.

items.text: Choose a pair of perpendicular x and y axes
Resolve every object's velocity into x and y components
Write separate conservation equations for total p_x and total p_y
Solve the two scalar equations (with any extra given data) for the unknowns

questions.explanation: Axes must be fixed before anything can be resolved into components; components must be resolved before they can be summed into per-axis conservation equations; those equations are then solved last, using whatever extra data (an angle, an elastic assumption) closes the unknown count.

lessons.label: Glancing Collisions

sections.heading: What makes a collision "glancing"
sections.body: A head-on collision sends both objects along the same line before and after — a genuinely one-dimensional problem. A glancing (off-center) collision happens when the objects do not meet dead-center: the line connecting their centers at the moment of contact, called the line of impact, is offset from the incoming object's direction of travel. Because real contact forces between round or curved bodies act along that line of impact (normal to the surfaces at the contact point), an off-center hit pushes momentum sideways as well as forward, and both objects fly off at some deflection angle rather than continuing straight through or bouncing straight back.

sections.heading: Impact parameter sets the geometry
sections.body: The offset distance between the incoming object's undeflected path and the target's center is called the impact parameter, b. When b = 0 the collision is head-on (1D); as b increases toward the sum of the two objects' radii, the hit becomes more glancing, and the deflection angles shrink because more of the contact is tangential rather than along the direction of approach. At the extreme, b equal to or greater than the sum of the radii means the objects miss entirely. This single geometric parameter — how far off-center the objects meet — is what a full mechanics treatment uses to predict the scattering angles, though a two-body momentum-only version of the problem (like a checkpoint problem) usually supplies one final angle as data rather than deriving it from b.

sections.heading: Momentum still separates into two independent axes
sections.body: Regardless of how glancing the collision is, the same rule from the previous lesson applies without modification: total p_x and total p_y are each conserved separately. What changes with the degree of "glance" is simply how the momentum gets redistributed between the axes — a nearly head-on collision transfers almost all momentum along the original line of motion with only a small sideways deflection, while a strongly glancing collision transfers relatively more momentum sideways and leaves the incoming object only slightly slowed along its original direction. Billiards players exploit exactly this: aiming for a large or small impact parameter controls how much the cue ball deflects versus how much speed it hands off to the object ball.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.17 kg billiard ball moving at 2.0 m/s strikes a second, identical stationary ball off-center. After the glancing collision, the cue ball deflects to 25° above its original line of motion at 1.4 m/s. Using p_x and p_y conservation: initial p_x = 0.17(2.0) = 0.34 kg·m/s, initial p_y = 0. Cue ball after: p_x = 0.17(1.4)cos25° = 0.216 kg·m/s, p_y = 0.17(1.4)sin25° = 0.101 kg·m/s. Object ball must supply p_x = 0.34 − 0.216 = 0.124 kg·m/s and p_y = 0 − 0.101 = −0.101 kg·m/s, giving speed = √(0.124² + 0.101²)/0.17 ≈ 0.94 m/s at angle arctan(−0.101/0.124) ≈ −39.2° — a moderately glancing hit, well short of head-on (which would send the object ball straight ahead at 2.0 m/s and stop the cue ball — a separate 1D elastic-collision result, not covered in this unit).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe glancing collisions to see whether a student understands that deflection is a geometric consequence of where contact occurs, not a separate rule from momentum conservation. A strong answer connects the impact parameter to the size of the deflection angle and can explain why a strongly off-center hit transfers more sideways momentum than a nearly head-on one. Judges may also ask what happens as the impact parameter approaches the sum of the two radii (the objects barely graze, deflection angles shrink toward zero) versus approaches zero (the collision becomes effectively 1D), checking that the student sees glancing and head-on as two ends of one continuous geometric spectrum.

questions.prompt: What physically distinguishes a glancing (off-center) collision from a head-on collision?

options.text: Glancing collisions do not conserve momentum, only head-on ones do.
In a glancing collision, the line connecting the objects' centers at contact is offset from the incoming direction of travel, so momentum is redirected sideways.
Glancing collisions only occur between objects of different mass.

explanations.a: Incorrect: momentum conservation is a universal law for isolated systems and applies to glancing collisions exactly as it does to head-on ones.
explanations.b: Correct: the offset line of impact means the contact force is not aligned with the incoming velocity, so the collision redistributes momentum into a sideways (y) component as well as forward (x).
explanations.c: Incorrect: glancing collisions can occur between any masses, equal or unequal — what matters is geometric offset (impact parameter), not mass ratio.

questions.prompt: As the impact parameter b increases from 0 toward the sum of the two objects' radii, what happens to the collision?

options.text: It becomes more head-on and deflection angles shrink toward zero.
It becomes more glancing, and at b equal to the sum of the radii the objects miss entirely.
The impact parameter has no effect on the collision geometry.

explanations.a: Incorrect: b = 0 is the head-on case; INCREASING b moves away from head-on, toward more glancing (and eventually a total miss), the opposite of this claim.
explanations.b: Correct: larger offset means more of the contact force is tangential rather than along the approach direction, so the collision becomes more glancing, until b reaches the sum of the radii and the objects no longer make contact at all.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the impact parameter is precisely the geometric quantity that sets how glancing versus head-on a collision is.

questions.prompt: Match each impact-parameter regime to its collision character.

right.text: Head-on, effectively one-dimensional collision
Glancing collision with sideways deflection on both objects
No contact occurs at all

questions.explanation: Zero offset means the contact force acts directly along the line of approach (1D, head-on); any positive offset less than the sum of the radii produces a genuine off-center hit with sideways momentum transfer; an offset at or beyond the sum of the radii means the objects' surfaces never touch.

questions.prompt: Order these collisions from LEAST glancing (most head-on) to MOST glancing, based on impact parameter b (with r = the sum of the two objects' radii).

items.text: b just under r

questions.explanation: Larger impact parameter means a more off-center hit and a more glancing collision, so ordering by increasing b from 0 up to just under the sum of the radii orders the collisions from head-on to nearly missing entirely.

lessons.label: Equal-Mass Elastic 2D Collisions Separate at 90 Degrees

sections.heading: The billiards result
sections.body: When two objects of EQUAL mass collide elastically in 2D, and one of them starts at rest, a striking geometric fact holds regardless of the impact parameter (as long as the collision is genuinely off-center, not head-on): the two objects' velocity vectors after the collision are perpendicular to each other — the angle between their paths is exactly 90 degrees. This is why, in billiards and pool, a cue ball that strikes an object ball off-center appears to peel away at a right angle from the object ball's departure path; skilled players use this as a first-order aiming reference, adjusting for cue-ball spin and friction ("throw") that pull the real angle a few degrees off the idealized 90 degrees. It only holds for equal masses and only for perfectly elastic collisions; unequal masses or any kinetic-energy loss break the exact 90-degree result.

sections.heading: Why the geometry works: a proof sketch
sections.body: Let the moving ball have initial velocity v0 and mass m, striking an identical stationary ball of mass m. Momentum conservation gives m·v0 = m·v1 + m·v2, i.e., v0 = v1 + v2 (the initial velocity vector equals the vector sum of the two final velocities). Elastic collision means kinetic energy is also conserved: ½m·v0² = ½m·v1² + ½m·v2², i.e., v0² = v1² + v2² (as scalar magnitudes squared). Now square the vector momentum equation: v0² = (v1 + v2)·(v1 + v2) = v1² + v2² + 2(v1·v2), where v1·v2 is the dot product. Comparing this to the energy equation v0² = v1² + v2² forces 2(v1·v2) = 0, so v1·v2 = 0 — and a zero dot product between two nonzero vectors means they are perpendicular. The proof uses only vector algebra applied to the two conservation laws together; neither law alone gives the result.

sections.heading: Where the rule breaks down
sections.body: The 90-degree separation depends on three conditions holding simultaneously: equal masses, an elastic collision (KE exactly conserved), and the target starting at rest. Change any one and the clean right-angle result disappears. Unequal masses skew the angle away from 90 degrees (heavier-onto-lighter and lighter-onto-heavier bend it in opposite directions). Any inelasticity — energy lost to heat, sound, or deformation — means the energy equation no longer matches the squared-momentum equation exactly, so the dot product v1·v2 is no longer forced to zero and the angle drifts below 90 degrees as more energy is lost (in a perfectly inelastic collision the objects do not separate at all, so the angle concept does not even apply). A moving target, rather than one at rest, also breaks the specific algebra used in the proof sketch above.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.16 kg cue ball moving at 3.0 m/s strikes an identical, stationary 0.16 kg object ball off-center in a perfectly elastic collision. The cue ball deflects to 25° above its original direction. Because the two final velocity vectors form a right triangle with v0 as the hypotenuse (v1 = v0·cos25° and v2 = v0·sin25°, from the perpendicularity proof), the cue ball's speed after is v1 = 3.0·cos25° ≈ 2.72 m/s, and the object ball's speed is v2 = 3.0·sin25° ≈ 1.27 m/s at exactly 25° − 90° = −65° (65° below the original line, on the other side). Checking momentum: p_x = 0.16(2.72·cos25° + 1.27·cos(−65°)) = 0.16(2.465 + 0.537) = 0.16(3.00) = 0.48 kg·m/s, matching the original 0.16(3.0) = 0.48 exactly; p_y = 0.16(2.72·sin25° − 1.27·sin65°) = 0.16(1.149 − 1.149) = 0, also matching. Kinetic energy checks too: ½(0.16)(3.0²) = 0.72 J equals ½(0.16)(2.72² + 1.27²) ≈ 0.72 J — the 90° geometry, momentum, and energy all agree simultaneously, exactly as the proof guarantees.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this result because it is one of the few places in introductory mechanics where a clean, memorable geometric fact (90 degrees, always, for these specific conditions) emerges from combining two separate conservation laws — and because it is easy to over-generalize. A strong student states the THREE conditions precisely (equal mass, elastic, target initially at rest) rather than reciting "90 degrees" as a blanket rule, and can walk through why squaring the momentum equation and comparing it to the energy equation is what forces the dot product to zero. Judges often ask what happens to the angle if the collision loses even a little kinetic energy, testing whether the student understands the proof rather than just the punchline.

questions.prompt: Under which THREE conditions does an off-center 2D collision guarantee the two objects separate at exactly 90 degrees?

options.text: Equal masses, elastic collision, target initially at rest
Any masses, elastic collision, target initially at rest
Equal masses, any energy loss allowed, target initially at rest

explanations.a: Correct: the proof requires equal masses (so the mass cancels out of both conservation equations identically) AND an elastic collision (so KE is exactly conserved) AND a stationary target (so the algebra reduces cleanly) — all three together force the dot product of the final velocities to zero.
explanations.b: Incorrect: unequal masses break the exact 90° result, even if the collision is perfectly elastic and the target starts at rest.
explanations.c: Incorrect: any kinetic energy loss breaks the energy-conservation equation used in the proof, so the angle is no longer forced to exactly 90 degrees.

questions.prompt: In the proof sketch, squaring the vector momentum equation v0 = v1 + v2 and comparing it to the scalar energy equation v0² = v1² + v2² leads directly to which conclusion?

options.text: v1 · v2 = 0, meaning the two final velocity vectors are perpendicular
v1 = v2, meaning the two objects move at equal speeds
v1 + v2 = 0, meaning the two objects move in exactly opposite directions

explanations.a: Correct: squaring the momentum equation gives v0² = v1² + v2² + 2(v1·v2); subtracting the energy equation v0² = v1² + v2² leaves 2(v1·v2) = 0, so v1·v2 = 0, which for two nonzero vectors means they are perpendicular.
explanations.b: Incorrect: nothing in the proof forces the final speeds to be equal — only their directions are constrained to be perpendicular, not their magnitudes.
explanations.c: Incorrect: v1 + v2 = 0 would mean the vectors are equal and opposite, which is a different (and generally false) geometric relationship than perpendicularity.

questions.prompt: Match each change to the collision setup with its effect on the 90-degree separation result.

left.text: Target is moving instead of at rest

right.text: Angle skews away from 90° depending on the mass ratio
Angle drifts below 90° as more energy is lost
The specific algebraic proof no longer applies as derived

questions.explanation: Unequal mass prevents the clean cancellation in the momentum-squared-versus-energy comparison, skewing the angle; lost kinetic energy means the energy equation no longer matches the squared-momentum equation exactly, so the dot product is no longer forced to zero and the angle falls below 90°; a moving target changes the initial conditions the proof sketch assumed, requiring a different derivation.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of the proof that equal-mass elastic collisions with a stationary target separate at 90 degrees.

items.text: Write momentum conservation as a vector equation: v0 = v1 + v2
Write kinetic energy conservation as a scalar equation: v0² = v1² + v2²
Square the vector momentum equation to get v0² = v1² + v2² + 2(v1·v2)
Compare to the energy equation to conclude v1·v2 = 0, so the vectors are perpendicular

questions.explanation: Both conservation laws must be written down first; squaring the momentum equation introduces the cross term 2(v1·v2); only then can it be compared against the independently-stated energy equation to isolate and conclude v1·v2 = 0, the perpendicularity condition.

lessons.label: Two-Dimensional Explosions and Fragmentation

sections.heading: Explosions are collisions run backward
sections.body: An explosion or fragmentation event — one object breaking apart into two or more pieces — conserves momentum by exactly the same vector law as a collision, just with the roles reversed: instead of separate objects merging their momenta into a combined final state, one combined initial momentum splits apart into separate pieces. If the original object was at rest, its total momentum was zero, so the VECTOR SUM of all the fragments' momenta after the explosion must also equal zero — not that each fragment has zero momentum individually, but that the fragments' momentum vectors, added tip-to-tail, return exactly to the starting point. This is why a firework shell launched (nearly) straight up, which bursts at the top of its arc where its velocity is momentarily zero, scatters sparks in a roughly symmetric pattern in every direction: any given spark's momentum is balanced by the combined momentum of all the others.

sections.heading: Internal forces and the invisible energy source
sections.body: The forces that drive an explosion apart — a spring releasing, a chemical reaction, a compressed gas expanding — are internal to the system, meaning they occur between parts of the system rather than being applied from outside. Newton's third law guarantees that internal forces come in equal-and-opposite pairs, and it is exactly this pairing that keeps total momentum unchanged even as the system violently rearranges itself and gains a large amount of kinetic energy. That kinetic energy comes from somewhere else entirely — stored chemical, elastic, or pressure energy converted during the explosion — and is NOT conserved the way momentum is; an explosion typically ends with far more total kinetic energy in the fragments than the system had before it broke apart, which is the opposite pattern from an inelastic collision losing kinetic energy.

sections.heading: Solving for a missing fragment
sections.body: If a system explodes into pieces and every fragment's momentum is known except one, the missing fragment's momentum vector can be found directly: it must be whatever vector, added to all the known fragments, brings the total back to the original momentum (zero, if the object started at rest). Component by component, the unknown fragment's p_x is minus the sum of all other fragments' p_x (plus the original p_x if the object was moving before it broke apart), and likewise for p_y. This is precisely how investigators reconstruct fragmentation events after the fact — from debris field data giving most fragments' masses and velocities, the momentum of an unrecovered or unmeasured piece can be inferred by vector subtraction.

lessons.workedExample: A 6.0 kg object at rest explodes into three fragments in a horizontal plane. Fragment A (2.0 kg) moves at 4.0 m/s due east (+x). Fragment B (1.0 kg) moves at 3.0 m/s due north (+y). Find fragment C's (3.0 kg) velocity. Total initial momentum is zero, so p_Ax + p_Bx + p_Cx = 0 and p_Ay + p_By + p_Cy = 0. p_Ax = 2.0(4.0) = 8.0, p_Bx = 0, so p_Cx = −8.0 kg·m/s. p_Ay = 0, p_By = 1.0(3.0) = 3.0, so p_Cy = −3.0 kg·m/s. Fragment C's velocity components: v_Cx = −8.0/3.0 = −2.67 m/s, v_Cy = −3.0/3.0 = −1.0 m/s, giving speed = √(2.67² + 1.0²) ≈ 2.85 m/s at angle arctan(−1.0/−2.67) ≈ 200.5° (into the third quadrant, roughly southwest) — found entirely by vector subtraction, without ever needing to know the energy released.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe explosions because they test whether a student truly understands momentum as a VECTOR sum rather than a scalar quantity that simply must "balance out" loosely. A student who states precisely that the vector sum of fragment momenta must equal the original momentum (zero for an at-rest object) — not that each fragment individually has zero momentum, and not that the fragments' speeds must be equal — demonstrates real command. Judges may also probe the energy side: unlike an inelastic collision, an explosion typically INCREASES total kinetic energy, drawn from stored chemical, elastic, or pressure energy, and a good answer keeps that source explicit rather than treating kinetic energy as automatically conserved alongside momentum.

questions.prompt: An object at rest explodes into three fragments in a plane. What must be true about the fragments' momenta?

options.text: Each fragment individually must have zero momentum.
The vector sum of all three fragments' momenta must equal zero.
All three fragments must move at the same speed.

explanations.a: Incorrect: individual fragments typically have large, nonzero momenta — it is only their VECTOR SUM that must return to zero, not each piece separately.
explanations.b: Correct: since the object started at rest with zero total momentum, and momentum is conserved, the fragments' momentum vectors must add (tip-to-tail) back to zero, even though each one is individually large.
explanations.c: Incorrect: nothing about momentum conservation requires equal speeds; fragments of different mass moving at different speeds can still have momentum vectors that sum to zero.

questions.prompt: What happens to total kinetic energy during a typical explosion, and where does it come from?

options.text: Total KE stays exactly conserved, just like momentum.
Total KE typically decreases, lost as heat and sound.
Total KE typically increases, drawn from stored chemical, elastic, or pressure energy released during the explosion.

explanations.a: Incorrect: unlike momentum, kinetic energy is NOT automatically conserved in an explosion — internal forces conserve momentum via Newton's third law, but energy bookkeeping is separate.
explanations.b: Incorrect: this describes an inelastic collision, the opposite scenario — explosions typically gain kinetic energy rather than lose it.
explanations.c: Correct: an explosion converts stored energy (chemical reaction, compressed spring, expanding gas) into the kinetic energy of the flying fragments, so total KE after is usually much greater than before.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity in an explosion to how it behaves.

left.text: Total momentum (vector sum of all fragments)
The forces driving the fragments apart

right.text: Conserved exactly, equal to the pre-explosion value
Typically increases, fed by stored energy
Internal, occurring in equal-and-opposite third-law pairs

questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved because the driving forces are internal and obey Newton's third law in equal-and-opposite pairs, which is also exactly why those forces cannot change total momentum even as they release stored energy that increases the fragments' total kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding a missing fragment's velocity after a 2D explosion, given the other fragments' masses and velocities.

items.text: Compute each known fragment's momentum components (p_x, p_y)
Sum the known fragments' p_x and p_y components separately
Subtract that sum from the original total momentum to get the missing fragment's p_x and p_y
Divide the missing fragment's momentum components by its mass to get its velocity components

questions.explanation: Individual fragment momenta must be computed before they can be summed; the sum of known fragments must be found before it can be subtracted from the (usually zero) original total to isolate the unknown fragment's momentum; only once that momentum is known can it be divided by the fragment's mass to recover its velocity.

lessons.label: Solving a 2D Collision Step by Step

sections.heading: The standard method, laid out as a checklist
sections.body: Every solvable 2D collision problem follows the same sequence regardless of the specific numbers: (1) sketch the situation and choose axes, typically with x along the incoming object's initial velocity; (2) list every given quantity — masses, initial speeds and directions, and whatever single piece of extra information (one final angle, an elastic assumption, a stated energy loss) makes the problem solvable; (3) write the x-momentum and y-momentum conservation equations separately, substituting known values and leaving unknowns as symbols; (4) use the extra given information to reduce the system to two equations in two unknowns; (5) solve algebraically, then check the answer's magnitude and direction make physical sense. Skipping the checklist — especially step 2, identifying what extra data is given — is the most common source of getting stuck partway through.

sections.heading: Reading the extra given quantity correctly
sections.body: Because two conservation equations alone cannot pin down four unknowns (as established in this unit's first lesson), every solvable 2D problem hides exactly the right amount of extra information somewhere in its wording. Common forms: one object's final direction is stated outright (removing one unknown angle); the collision is stated or implied to be elastic (adding the kinetic-energy equation); the objects are said to stick together (perfectly inelastic, removing an entire object's worth of unknowns since both move together afterward); or a specific fraction of kinetic energy lost is given. Correctly identifying which of these the problem provides, and translating it into an equation, is usually the actual conceptual step — the algebra that follows is mechanical.

sections.heading: Solving the resulting system without losing track of signs
sections.body: Once the equations are written, the algebra itself is where careless sign errors most often creep in. A dependable approach is to isolate the unknown angle from each momentum equation separately — for instance, writing v2·cosθ2 as an expression in v1 from the x-equation and v2·sinθ2 as another expression in v1 from the y-equation — then use the identity sin²θ2 + cos²θ2 = 1 to eliminate θ2 entirely and leave a single equation in v1 alone. Squaring and adding this way is a standard trick precisely because it removes an awkward trigonometric unknown without ever needing to solve for the angle directly along the way. Whatever unknown emerges from that combined equation (v1 in the cart example) can then be substituted back into either momentum equation to recover the remaining unknowns, including the angle, via an inverse tangent — always checking that the resulting angle lands in the correct quadrant given the signs of both components.

lessons.workedExample: A 3.0 kg cart moving at 4.0 m/s in the +x direction collides with a 5.0 kg stationary cart. After the collision, the two carts move apart, with the 3.0 kg cart deflected at 40° above the x-axis. The collision is given as elastic. Step 1-2: axes chosen, masses/speeds/angle given, elastic assumption noted. Step 3: p_x: 3.0(4.0) = 3.0·v1·cos40° + 5.0·v2·cosθ2; p_y: 0 = 3.0·v1·sin40° + 5.0·v2·sinθ2; KE: ½(3.0)(4.0²) = ½(3.0)v1² + ½(5.0)v2². Step 4-5: three equations, three unknowns (v1, v2, θ2) — solving simultaneously (substituting the momentum equations into each other to eliminate θ2, then combining with the energy equation) yields v1 ≈ 3.46 m/s and v2 ≈ 1.56 m/s at θ2 ≈ −58.6° (below the x-axis, opposite side from the light cart, satisfying both momentum axes and energy conservation simultaneously: p_x ≈ 3.0(3.46)cos40° + 5.0(1.56)cos58.6° ≈ 7.95 + 4.06 ≈ 12.0 kg·m/s, and KE ≈ 1.5(3.46)² + 2.5(1.56)² ≈ 17.95 + 6.08 ≈ 24.0 J — three equations for three unknowns, exactly closed by the elastic assumption).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use full worked problems to see whether a student has an actual METHOD rather than a memorized formula for one specific case. A strong presentation names each step out loud — what axes were chosen and why, what extra given quantity closed the unknown count, which equations came from momentum versus energy — rather than jumping straight to a final number. Judges frequently interrupt a worked solution partway through to ask "what would change if this were inelastic instead" or "what if the given angle were for the heavier object instead," testing whether the student understands the method well enough to adapt it, not just execute one memorized path.

questions.prompt: Order the standard steps for solving a 2D collision problem.

items.text: Sketch the situation and choose axes
List all given quantities, including the extra piece of information beyond basic momentum
Write separate x- and y-momentum conservation equations
Use the extra given information to close the system, then solve algebraically

questions.explanation: Axes must be fixed before quantities can be listed in a consistent frame; the given quantities (including the crucial extra piece of data) must be identified before the conservation equations can be written with knowns substituted in; the equations must exist before the extra information can be used to close and solve the system.

questions.prompt: A 2D collision problem gives both masses, both initial velocities, and states that the objects stick together on impact. Why is this problem solvable despite involving a 2D collision?

options.text: "Sticking together" means the two final velocities are identical, reducing four unknowns (two objects' v_x and v_y) to just two (one shared v_x and v_y).
Sticking together makes the collision elastic, adding a kinetic-energy equation.
It is not actually solvable without an additional given angle.

explanations.a: Correct: a perfectly inelastic (stick-together) collision means both objects share one final velocity, so instead of 4 unknowns there are only 2 (the shared v_x and v_y), exactly matching the 2 momentum-conservation equations available.
explanations.b: Incorrect: sticking together is the definition of a PERFECTLY INELASTIC collision, which loses the maximum possible kinetic energy — it does not add an energy equation, it removes unknowns instead.
explanations.c: Incorrect: no additional angle is needed because the stick-together condition itself supplies enough constraint (reducing to 2 unknowns) to match the 2 available equations.

questions.prompt: In the worked cart example, why were three equations (two momentum, one energy) needed to solve for v1, v2, and θ2?

options.text: Because there were exactly three unknowns to solve for, and the elastic assumption supplied the third equation beyond the two momentum equations.
Because momentum conservation alone always requires three equations in 2D.
Because the problem was actually overdetermined and one equation was redundant.

explanations.a: Correct: the unknowns were v1, v2, and theta2 — three unknowns in total — and momentum conservation supplies only two equations (x and y); the elastic assumption's kinetic-energy equation was exactly the third equation needed to close the system.
explanations.b: Incorrect: momentum conservation in 2D always supplies exactly two equations (x and y), never three — the third equation here came from the separate elastic-collision assumption, not from momentum itself.
explanations.c: Incorrect: three equations for three unknowns is exactly determined, not overdetermined — dropping any one of the three would leave the system unsolvable.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of extra given information to the unknown-count effect it has on a 2D collision problem.

right.text: Removes exactly one unknown angle
Adds one kinetic-energy equation
Forces both objects to share one final velocity, removing two unknowns

questions.explanation: A stated final angle directly removes one degree of freedom; an elastic assumption contributes an entirely new equation (kinetic energy) rather than removing an unknown; a stick-together (perfectly inelastic) condition collapses two separate final velocities into one shared velocity, removing two unknowns at once.

lessons.label: Two-Dimensional Collisions in the Lab

sections.heading: Air tables and coins: making friction negligible
sections.body: Testing 2D momentum conservation experimentally requires nearly eliminating friction, since any external horizontal force (like sliding friction) violates the isolated-system assumption the conservation law depends on. An air table (or air hockey table) forces a thin cushion of air through small holes in its surface, letting pucks glide with only a tiny residual friction from air drag. A cheaper classroom substitute uses coins or discs sliding across a smooth, level, low-friction surface such as glass or a whiteboard, sometimes dusted lightly with something like cornstarch to further cut friction, though this introduces more uncertainty than a true air table. Either way, the setup must be verified level — any slope introduces a small constant acceleration that looks like an external force and will bias every measured collision.

sections.heading: Extracting velocity vectors from video
sections.body: Modern lab work typically uses video tracking software (or a phone's slow-motion camera) to record the collision from directly overhead, then digitizes the position of each puck frame by frame. Dividing the change in position between two frames by the known time interval between frames gives an estimate of instantaneous velocity as a vector — both a magnitude (speed) and a direction — at each moment before and after contact. Because collisions happen fast, video frame rate limits precision: a collision lasting only a few milliseconds may be captured by only one or two frames, in which case velocities just before and just after contact (rather than during) are what get measured and compared, treating the collision itself as instantaneous.

sections.heading: Drawing and checking the vector diagram
sections.body: Once before- and after-collision velocities are measured for both pucks, the standard check draws all momentum vectors (mass times velocity, to scale) on a single diagram: the two initial momentum vectors added tip-to-tail should reach the same point as the two final momentum vectors added tip-to-tail, since total momentum must be conserved. Any gap between where the initial sum ends and where the final sum ends represents experimental error — from friction, measurement uncertainty in position or timing, or a collision that was not perfectly isolated (bumping the table, air currents). A well-executed lab typically closes this gap to within a few percent of the total momentum magnitude; discrepancies of tens of percent usually indicate a systematic problem, like an untracked friction source or a tilted table, rather than random measurement noise.

lessons.workedExample: Two 0.020 kg coins slide on a low-friction glass surface. Coin A, initially moving at 0.80 m/s in the +x direction, strikes stationary coin B off-center. Video tracking at 240 frames per second gives coin A's post-collision displacement over 5 frames as (0.010 m, 0.006 m), and coin B's as (0.014 m, -0.006 m) over the same 5 frames (elapsed time = 5/240 = 0.0208 s). Coin A's final velocity: (0.010/0.0208, 0.006/0.0208) = (0.48, 0.29) m/s. Coin B's final velocity: (0.014/0.0208, -0.006/0.0208) = (0.67, -0.29) m/s. Momentum check: initial p = (0.020·0.80, 0) = (0.016, 0) kg·m/s. Final p = 0.020·(0.48+0.67, 0.29-0.29) = 0.020·(1.15, 0.0) = (0.023, 0.0) kg·m/s. The x-component is off by about 0.007 kg·m/s (roughly 44% high), flagging a likely tracking or timing error worth rechecking rather than treating as conserved.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe lab methodology because it tests whether a student can connect the abstract conservation law to what a real, imperfect measurement looks like. A strong answer names specific, controllable error sources — table tilt, frame-rate-limited timing precision, friction from the sliding surface — rather than vaguely citing "experimental error," and can explain concretely how the before/after momentum vector diagram exposes those errors as a visible gap. Judges often ask what a large discrepancy (well beyond a few percent) would suggest, checking whether the student distinguishes a systematic problem worth re-examining the setup for (a tilted table, an untracked collision with the table edge) from ordinary small random measurement noise.

questions.prompt: Why is an air table (or a similarly low-friction surface) essential for a 2D collision lab testing momentum conservation?

options.text: It makes the pucks move faster, which is easier to film.
Friction is an external horizontal force, and momentum conservation only holds for a system with no net external force.
It has no real purpose beyond making the demonstration look more impressive.

explanations.a: Incorrect: speed is not the reason for using an air table — the point is eliminating a force that would violate the conservation law being tested, not filming convenience.
explanations.b: Correct: momentum conservation assumes the system is isolated from external forces; sliding friction is exactly such an external force, so minimizing it (via an air cushion) keeps the measured system close enough to isolated for the law to hold as expected.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the air cushion serves a specific physical purpose (removing an external force that would otherwise bias the measurement), not just visual effect.

questions.prompt: In video-tracking a fast collision, why are the velocities "just before" and "just after" contact measured rather than a velocity "during" contact?

options.text: Because velocity during contact is undefined in physics.
Because the collision typically lasts only a few milliseconds, often shorter than one or two camera frame intervals, so it is effectively treated as instantaneous.
Because momentum is only conserved before and after collisions, never during them.

explanations.a: Incorrect: velocity during contact is a perfectly well-defined physical quantity — it is just extremely hard to resolve with typical video frame rates.
explanations.b: Correct: contact forces act over a very short time, often shorter than the interval between video frames, so the camera cannot resolve the motion DURING contact — only the states just before and just after, which is exactly what conservation of momentum compares anyway.
explanations.c: Incorrect: momentum is instantaneously always defined and, for an isolated system, its TOTAL value does not change even during the brief contact interval — it is a measurement limitation, not a physical restriction on when conservation applies.

questions.prompt: Match each lab error source to its likely effect on the momentum vector diagram.

left.text: Camera frame rate is too low for the collision speed
Residual friction from the sliding surface

right.text: A consistent, direction-biased gap between initial and final momentum sums
Larger uncertainty in the computed velocity vectors from position/time division
A gradual, speed-dependent loss of momentum magnitude between measurement points

questions.explanation: A tilt introduces a small constant acceleration in a fixed direction, producing a consistent directional bias in the vector diagram; low frame rate limits the precision of the position-over-time division used to compute velocity, inflating uncertainty rather than biasing direction; friction continuously drains kinetic energy and momentum in the direction opposing motion, showing up as a gradual magnitude loss rather than a one-time offset.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a video-tracked 2D collision lab, from setup to conclusion.

items.text: Level the low-friction surface and position the overhead camera
Record the collision and digitize each puck's position frame by frame
Compute before- and after-collision velocity vectors from position and known frame time
Draw the momentum vector diagram and check whether the initial and final sums match within experimental error

questions.explanation: The surface must be leveled and the camera positioned before any useful recording can happen; position data must be digitized from the recording before velocities can be computed from displacement over frame time; only once velocity vectors exist can they be converted to momentum and checked against each other on the diagram.

units.label: Center of Mass and the Zero-Momentum Frame

lessons.label: The Center of Mass of a System

sections.heading: Averaging Position by Mass
sections.body: The center of mass of a system of particles is the single point that behaves as though all the system's mass were concentrated there and all external forces applied there. For a system of N particles with masses m_i at positions r_i, its position is defined as a mass-weighted average: r_cm = (sum of m_i r_i) / (sum of m_i) = (sum of m_i r_i) / M, where M is the total mass. This is not simply the geometric center of the object -- if the masses aren't distributed evenly, the center of mass shifts toward the heavier concentration. A baseball bat's center of mass sits closer to the thick barrel end than to the thin handle; a wrench's is offset from its geometric middle; a donut's center of mass is a point of empty air at the center of the hole, since no mass exists exactly there yet the mass distribution around it is symmetric. The one-dimensional case, two masses on a line, makes the weighting obvious: doubling one mass while holding positions fixed pulls the center of mass twice as far toward that side. This weighted-average idea generalizes cleanly to continuous mass distributions by replacing the sum with an integral, but for the collision problems in this segment, systems of two or a few discrete masses are what matter.

sections.heading: The Velocity of the Center of Mass
sections.body: Because r_cm is itself a position, it has its own velocity, found by differentiating: v_cm = dr_cm/dt = (sum of m_i v_i) / M. Multiply both sides by M and the numerator becomes something instantly recognizable: M v_cm = sum of m_i v_i = sum of p_i = p_total, the system's total momentum. This is the single most useful fact about center-of-mass velocity: it is total momentum divided by total mass, so tracking v_cm and tracking p_total are the same bookkeeping task viewed two ways. It also means the center of mass moves at a single well-defined velocity even while the individual particles that make it up move at wildly different velocities in different directions -- two masses can be approaching each other, receding from each other, or orbiting each other, and the center of mass calculated from their momenta still glides along one straight-line trajectory at one constant speed, provided no external force acts. That last clause is the subject of the next lesson: it turns out that during a collision, the internal forces the colliding bodies exert on each other cannot change v_cm at all, however violently they collide.

lessons.workedExample: Two carts sit on a frictionless track: cart A has mass 2 kg at position x = 0 m, cart B has mass 3 kg at position x = 5 m. The center of mass sits at x_cm = (2(0) + 3(5))/(2+3) = 15/5 = 3.0 m -- closer to the heavier cart, as expected. Now give the carts velocities: A moves at +4 m/s, B moves at -1 m/s (they are approaching each other, headed for a collision). The center-of-mass velocity is v_cm = (2(4) + 3(-1))/5 = (8-3)/5 = +1.0 m/s. Equivalently, total momentum is p = 2(4)+3(-1) = 5 kg m/s, and dividing by total mass M = 5 kg gives the same 1.0 m/s. The carts collide, but until they do, the point x = 3 m marked on the track drifts steadily rightward at exactly 1.0 m/s.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a team to locate a system's center of mass is testing whether 'average position' has been understood as mass-weighted rather than geometric. A team that places the center of mass at the midpoint of two unequal masses, ignoring the weighting, reveals they've memorized a formula without internalizing what it means. A stronger answer explains why heavier objects pull the center of mass toward themselves, and connects center-of-mass velocity to total momentum divided by total mass in one step rather than two separate calculations. Judges also probe edge cases -- asking for the center of mass of an object with a hole, like a donut or a horseshoe -- because those cases expose whether a student thinks of it as a physical piece of material or a purely mathematical bookkeeping point.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg mass sits at x = 0 m and a 6 kg mass sits at x = 4 m. Where is the system's center of mass?

options.text: x = 2 m (the geometric midpoint)
x = 3 m
x = 1 m
x = 4 m

explanations.a: The midpoint ignores the mass weighting entirely -- it would only be correct if both masses were equal.
explanations.b: Correct: x_cm = (2(0) + 6(4)) / (2+6) = 24/8 = 3 m, pulled toward the heavier 6 kg mass as expected.
explanations.c: This underweights the heavier mass's pull on the center of mass rather than overweighting it.
explanations.d: This places the center of mass exactly at the heavier mass's location, ignoring that the lighter mass still contributes some pull.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for computing a system's center-of-mass velocity from its individual particles.

items.text: Identify the mass and velocity of each particle in the system
Multiply each particle's mass by its velocity to get its momentum
Sum the individual momenta to get the total momentum
Divide the total momentum by the system's total mass

questions.explanation: You need each particle's mass and velocity before computing its momentum; summing those momenta gives total momentum; dividing by total mass converts total momentum into center-of-mass velocity, since M v_cm = p_total by definition.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its defining expression.

right.text: (sum of m_i r_i) / M, the mass-weighted average position
(sum of m_i v_i) / M, equal to total momentum divided by total mass
M v_cm, equal to the sum of the individual particle momenta

questions.explanation: Position and velocity of the center of mass are both mass-weighted averages (divided by M), while total momentum is that same velocity multiplied back through by M -- the three expressions are three views of the same weighting.

questions.prompt: Why can the center of mass of a donut-shaped object lie at a point with no mass, in the empty hole at its center?

options.text: Because the center of mass is a mass-weighted average position, not a piece of material -- it can fall anywhere the geometry and mass distribution dictate, including empty space.
Because the donut's density is negative at the center, canceling the surrounding material.
Because the center-of-mass formula only applies to solid, hole-free objects, so the donut is a special exception.

explanations.a: Correct: the center of mass is a mathematical bookkeeping point defined by the weighted-average formula. Nothing requires it to sit on actual material, only that the mass distribution around it balances.
explanations.b: Real mass densities are never negative; this isn't how the symmetric hole produces the effect.
explanations.c: The formula applies to any mass distribution, hollow or solid -- the donut is simply a clean example, not an exception.

lessons.label: The Center of Mass Glides Through a Collision

sections.heading: Internal Forces Cancel in Pairs
sections.body: Newton's third law guarantees that whatever force one particle in a system exerts on another, that other particle pushes back with equal magnitude and opposite direction. Sum every internal force pair in a system and they cancel exactly, term by term, regardless of how complicated the interaction is -- a bat striking a ball, two magnets repelling, a spring compressing between two blocks. What survives the sum is only the net external force acting on the system from outside. Newton's second law applied to the whole system states F_net,external = M a_cm, where M is total mass and a_cm is the acceleration of the center of mass. If no external force acts -- the system is isolated, or external forces like gravity and the normal force cancel as they do for objects sliding on a level frictionless track -- then a_cm = 0 and v_cm is constant. This holds during a collision too, not just before and after it. While two carts are physically interacting, compressing springs or crumpling metal between them, those forces are internal to the two-cart system, so they cancel in the sum and cannot budge v_cm even for an instant during the collision itself.

sections.heading: Even Violent, Lossy Collisions Don't Bend the CM Path
sections.body: This has a genuinely surprising consequence: the center of mass moves in a perfectly straight line at perfectly constant speed straight through a collision, no matter how violent or lossy that collision is. A head-on crash that crumples both bumpers and converts a large fraction of kinetic energy into heat, sound, and deformation does not deflect the center of mass by one millimeter from the path it was already on -- because kinetic energy loss is irrelevant to momentum conservation. Momentum conservation follows purely from the absence of net external force; energy conservation is a separate, stronger condition that only elastic collisions satisfy. A perfectly inelastic collision, where the two bodies stick together and move as one afterward, loses the maximum possible kinetic energy consistent with momentum conservation, yet the combined object continues along exactly the trajectory the center of mass was already tracing, at exactly v_cm. This is why v_cm is such a reliable anchor for collision analysis: total momentum, and therefore v_cm, survives untouched, while total kinetic energy is up for grabs depending on how elastic the collision is.

lessons.workedExample: Two carts on a frictionless track approach each other: cart A, 2 kg at +4 m/s, and cart B, 3 kg at -1 m/s. From Lesson 1, v_cm = +1.0 m/s and total momentum is 5 kg m/s. Suppose the carts collide and stick together (perfectly inelastic). Conservation of momentum gives the combined 5 kg mass a final velocity of v_f = 5/5 = 1.0 m/s -- identical to v_cm before the collision. Kinetic energy before: (1/2)(2)(4^2) + (1/2)(3)(1^2) = 16 + 1.5 = 17.5 J. Kinetic energy after: (1/2)(5)(1^2) = 2.5 J. A full 15 J vanished into heat and sound of the crumpling collision, yet the center of mass never wavered from its steady 1.0 m/s drift -- proof that momentum conservation and energy conservation are independent bookkeeping.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this concept by asking what would change if the collision were perfectly elastic instead of perfectly inelastic -- and the correct answer is nothing about v_cm, only the kinetic-energy outcome differs.
