Noether proves that continuous symmetries of the action correspond to conserved quantities (1915, published 1918)
Momentum conservation is understood as a necessary consequence of space having no preferred location, not an independent empirical fact

questions.explanation: The empirical/mathematical discovery of momentum conservation came first in 1668-69, was used without a deeper justification for centuries, and Noether's 1915/1918 theorem finally explained why it must hold given spatial symmetry -- reframing it from a discovered rule into a necessary consequence.

lessons.label: The Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion

sections.heading: Two motions, one object, zero interaction
sections.body: A projectile is anything moving through the air under gravity alone, with air resistance neglected. Galileo's great insight, laid out in his 1638 Two New Sciences, was that a projectile's motion can be split into two independent one-dimensional motions happening at the same time along perpendicular axes. Horizontally, no force acts on the projectile (gravity is purely vertical, and air resistance is ignored), so the horizontal velocity component vx stays exactly constant for the entire flight: vx = v0x always, and horizontal position is just x = v0x * t. Vertically, gravity accelerates the object downward at g = 9.8 m/s^2 the whole time, exactly as if the object had been dropped from rest at that same starting height at that same instant. The two components are computed with entirely separate kinematic equations and never appear in each other's formula — that separability is what makes 2D projectile motion tractable with 1D tools instead of requiring genuinely new physics.

sections.heading: The classic proof: drop versus fire
sections.body: The cleanest demonstration of independence is an apparatus that releases two identical balls at the same instant from the same height: one simply drops straight down, the other is launched horizontally off a spring-loaded track. Both balls hit the floor at exactly the same moment, audibly, every time — regardless of how fast the second ball is launched horizontally. This is not a coincidence; it is a direct consequence of independence. The dropped ball's vertical motion is y = h - (1/2)g*t^2 starting from rest. The fired ball's vertical motion is also y = h - (1/2)g*t^2 starting from rest, because its initial vertical velocity is zero (it was launched purely horizontally) and gravity acts on it identically. The horizontal velocity, however large, contributes nothing to the vertical equation, so the vertical equation — and therefore the fall time — is identical for both balls. Only the horizontal launch speed changes how FAR the second ball travels before landing, never HOW LONG it takes to land.

sections.heading: Why this matters for every later calculation
sections.body: Independence is the reason the entire projectile-motion toolkit works: you solve the vertical problem first (it tells you the time of flight, since only gravity and the vertical launch speed determine when the object returns to a given height), then use that time in the horizontal equation to find range. Mixing the two axes — for example, trying to use v0 (the full launch speed) directly in a vertical equation instead of v0y — is the single most common error introductory students make, and it stems from not internalizing that x and y are two separate, simultaneous stories about the same clock.

lessons.workedExample: A ball is dropped from a 20 m tall building at the same instant a second, identical ball is fired horizontally from the same ledge at 15 m/s. Vertical motion for both: 20 = (1/2)(9.8)t^2, so t = sqrt(40/9.8) = 2.02 s — the same for both balls, since neither has any initial vertical velocity and both feel the same g. The dropped ball lands directly below the ledge. The fired ball, in that same 2.02 s, travels horizontally x = 15 * 2.02 = 30.3 m from the ledge before landing, but it hits the ground at the identical instant as the dropped ball, 2.02 s after release.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who understands mechanics will often ask a student mid-presentation, "if you launched that ball twice as fast, would it take longer to land?" A student who has genuinely internalized independence answers immediately: no, the vertical time of flight depends only on the vertical launch velocity and height, never on horizontal speed. A student who has only memorized formulas often hesitates or guesses that a faster launch means a longer flight, revealing that the two-axis structure was never really understood, just pattern-matched. This question is a favorite precisely because it cannot be answered by algebra alone; it requires knowing WHY the equations are split the way they are.

questions.prompt: Two identical balls are released at the same instant from the same height: one is dropped, one is fired horizontally. Which lands first?

options.text: The dropped ball lands first
The fired ball lands first
They land at the same instant

explanations.a: The dropped ball has no head start — both balls start with zero vertical velocity, so their vertical motions are identical.
explanations.b: Horizontal speed does not affect vertical fall time, because the two axes are independent; the fired ball is not vertically faster.
explanations.c: Correct: both balls start with zero initial vertical velocity and feel the same downward acceleration g, so their vertical (and therefore total) fall times are identical.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the horizontal velocity component of a projectile in flight (no air resistance)?

options.text: It decreases steadily due to gravity
It stays constant throughout the flight
It increases as the object falls
It equals zero at the apex

explanations.a: Gravity has no horizontal component, so it cannot slow the horizontal velocity at all.
explanations.b: Correct: with no horizontal force acting, vx = v0x for the entire flight — this is the core statement of axis independence.
explanations.c: Nothing accelerates the projectile horizontally, so horizontal speed cannot increase either.
explanations.d: The vertical velocity is zero at the apex, not the horizontal one; horizontal velocity is unaffected by height.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps used to prove that a dropped ball and a horizontally-fired ball (same height, same release instant) land simultaneously.

items.text: Note both balls start with zero initial vertical velocity
Note gravity supplies the same vertical acceleration g to both
Conclude the vertical equation y = h - (1/2)g*t^2 is identical for both balls
Conclude both balls reach the ground at the same time t

questions.explanation: Identical initial vertical velocity and identical vertical acceleration together force the vertical position equation to be identical for both balls, which in turn forces the fall time to be identical.

questions.prompt: Match each axis of projectile motion to the force/acceleration acting along it.

right.text: No net force (constant velocity)
Constant downward acceleration g

questions.explanation: With air resistance neglected, only gravity acts on a projectile, and gravity is purely vertical — so the horizontal axis has no net force while the vertical axis has constant acceleration g.

lessons.label: The Parabolic Trajectory

sections.heading: From two linear-in-time equations to one curve
sections.body: Once horizontal and vertical motion are treated separately, each is simple: horizontal position is linear in time, x(t) = x0 + v0x*t, while vertical position is quadratic in time, y(t) = y0 + v0y*t - (1/2)g*t^2. The trajectory — the actual path traced through space, y as a function of x rather than of t — is found by eliminating the time parameter between these two equations. Solving the horizontal equation for t gives t = (x - x0)/v0x; substituting that into the vertical equation produces y as a function of x that contains a t^2 term, which becomes an (x - x0)^2 term. Because x is degree 1 in t, and y is degree 2 in t, the resulting y(x) relationship is necessarily degree 2 in x — a quadratic. A quadratic function of position is, geometrically, a parabola. This is why every projectile with negligible air resistance sweeps out a parabolic arc, from a thrown baseball to a fired cannonball to a stream of water from a garden hose.

sections.heading: Reading the parabola's shape
sections.body: The parabola opens downward (concave down) because the coefficient on the squared term is negative: it is -g/(2*v0x^2), and g is positive. A steeper launch angle produces a narrower, taller parabola because v0x shrinks (more of the launch speed goes into v0y) while v0y grows; a shallower launch angle produces a flatter, wider parabola. The trajectory is also symmetric about a vertical line through its highest point (the apex) whenever launch and landing heights are equal — the rising half and falling half are mirror images in both shape and speed, a direct consequence of gravity being constant and time-reversible in this idealized model.

sections.heading: Where the parabola breaks down
sections.body: This clean parabolic shape assumes no air resistance. Real projectiles — a badminton shuttlecock, a golf ball, an artillery shell at high speed — experience drag that removes energy asymmetrically, making the descending branch steeper and shorter-ranged than the ascending branch would predict; the true path becomes a ballistic curve that is no longer a true parabola. For the speeds and objects typical of AP-level problems (baseballs, arrows, thrown rocks, at speeds well under Mach 1), the parabolic approximation remains excellent, which is why it is the standard first model.

lessons.workedExample: A projectile launches from ground level (x0 = 0, y0 = 0) with v0x = 8 m/s and v0y = 12 m/s. From x = 8t, we get t = x/8. Substituting into y = 12t - 4.9t^2 gives y = 12(x/8) - 4.9(x/8)^2 = 1.5x - 0.0766x^2. This is a downward-opening parabola in x, confirming the trajectory shape without ever needing to plot individual (x, y) points at multiple times — the single equation y(x) = 1.5x - 0.0766x^2 describes the entire path. Setting y = 0 to find where it lands (other than the origin) gives x(1.5 - 0.0766x) = 0, so x = 1.5/0.0766 ≈ 19.6 m, the horizontal range.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge who sees a plotted trajectory will often ask, "how do you know that's actually a parabola and not just a curve that looks like one?" This tests whether the student can derive y(x) algebraically from the two component equations rather than simply recognizing the shape visually. A strong answer shows the elimination-of-time step explicitly; a weak answer says only "it always looks parabolic" without being able to produce the algebra that guarantees it. Judges also value a student who can name the real-world condition (negligible air resistance) under which the parabola is exact, since that shows awareness of the model's limits, not just its result.

questions.prompt: Why is a projectile's trajectory (y as a function of x) shaped like a parabola?

options.text: Because x(t) is quadratic in time and y(t) is linear in time
Because x(t) is linear in time and y(t) is quadratic in time
Because both x(t) and y(t) are linear in time
Because gravity acts equally on both axes

explanations.a: This reverses the actual roles: horizontal position is linear in time (constant velocity), not quadratic.
explanations.b: Correct: eliminating linear-in-t x(t) in favor of x gives a t that is linear in x; substituting into the quadratic-in-t y(t) produces a quadratic-in-x relationship — a parabola.
explanations.c: If both were linear in time, y(x) would also be linear, giving a straight-line path, not a curve — which contradicts observed projectile paths.
explanations.d: Gravity acts only on the vertical axis; the horizontal axis feels no net force, which is exactly why the two equations have different degrees in t.

questions.prompt: For a projectile launched and landing at the same height, the trajectory's rising and falling halves are:

options.text: Mirror images of each other about the apex
Unrelated in shape
Only the same if air resistance is included

explanations.a: Correct: with equal launch/landing heights and constant g, the parabola is symmetric about the vertical line through the apex — the rise mirrors the fall.
explanations.b: The two halves are directly linked by the same quadratic equation and constant acceleration, so they are far from unrelated.
explanations.c: Air resistance is what BREAKS this symmetry in real flight; the idealized (no drag) case is the symmetric one.

questions.prompt: Order the algebra steps that derive the trajectory equation y(x) from the two time-based component equations x(t) and y(t).

items.text: Write x(t) = v0x*t and y(t) = v0y*t - (1/2)g*t^2 separately
Solve the x(t) equation for t in terms of x
Substitute that expression for t into the y(t) equation
Simplify to obtain y as a quadratic function of x

questions.explanation: You start from the two independent time-parameterized equations, isolate t from the simpler (linear) one, substitute it into the other, and simplify — that substitution is exactly what eliminates the time parameter and produces the parabola.

questions.prompt: Match each trajectory feature to its cause.

left.text: Steeper launch angle narrows the parabola
Real trajectories deviate from a true parabola

right.text: The x^2 coefficient -g/(2*v0x^2) is negative
A smaller v0x makes the coefficient -g/(2*v0x^2) more negative, curving the path more sharply per unit of horizontal distance
Air resistance removes energy asymmetrically between rise and fall

questions.explanation: The downward opening comes directly from the negative sign on the squared term; a steeper angle shrinks v0x, which makes the coefficient -g/(2*v0x^2) more negative and produces a narrower (and, since v0y is larger, taller) arc; and air resistance is the real-world effect that breaks the idealized symmetric parabola.

lessons.label: Decomposing the Launch Velocity

sections.heading: One speed, one angle, two components
sections.body: Every projectile problem begins with a launch described by a single speed v0 and a single angle theta measured from the horizontal. Because the physics is done separately on each axis, that one vector must first be split into its horizontal and vertical pieces using basic trigonometry on the right triangle formed by v0 and its projections: v0x = v0 * cos(theta) and v0y = v0 * sin(theta). Here v0 is the hypotenuse of the triangle, v0x is the side adjacent to theta, and v0y is the side opposite theta — exactly the SOH-CAH-TOA relationships from trigonometry, just applied to a velocity vector instead of a length. These two components are then treated as the initial conditions for two completely separate 1D kinematics problems: v0x is plugged into the constant-velocity horizontal equations, and v0y is plugged into the constant-acceleration vertical equations.

sections.heading: Why decomposition always comes first
sections.body: Skipping decomposition and trying to use v0 directly in a kinematics equation is a category error — v0 is a single number describing a diagonal motion, and none of the standard 1D kinematics formulas (which assume motion along one straight line) apply to a diagonal quantity. Decomposition converts one 2D unknown into two independent 1D unknowns that standard formulas can actually handle. This is also why decomposition is always the FIRST step written on a projectile solution: every later quantity — time of flight, range, height, landing speed — is built from v0x and v0y, never from v0 and theta directly.

sections.heading: Special angles and a useful symmetry
sections.body: A few special cases are worth memorizing intuition for: a 0-degree launch (purely horizontal) has v0x = v0 and v0y = 0, so it starts with no vertical velocity at all; a 90-degree launch (straight up) has v0x = 0 and v0y = v0, so it has no horizontal motion and simply becomes a 1D free-fall problem. A 45-degree launch splits evenly, v0x = v0y = v0 * cos(45) = v0 * 0.707, which is also the angle that (on level ground, with no air resistance) maximizes range for a given launch speed. Complementary angles like 30 and 60 degrees produce the same range as each other on level ground, because sin(2*theta) — which range depends on — is the same for theta and 90-theta.

lessons.workedExample: A soccer ball is kicked at v0 = 20 m/s at theta = 35 degrees above the ground. Decomposing: v0x = 20 * cos(35°) = 20 * 0.819 = 16.4 m/s, and v0y = 20 * sin(35°) = 20 * 0.574 = 11.5 m/s. As a check, these should recombine via Pythagoras to the original speed: sqrt(16.4^2 + 11.5^2) = sqrt(269 + 132) = sqrt(401) ≈ 20.0 m/s, confirming the decomposition is consistent. From here, 16.4 m/s becomes the constant horizontal velocity used in x = 16.4*t, and 11.5 m/s becomes the initial vertical velocity used in vertical kinematics — two separate, simple 1D problems.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating a projectile-based experiment (a trebuchet, a catapult, a ball launcher) will frequently ask a student to state v0x and v0y for their design's launch conditions before asking about range or height. This is a quick diagnostic: a student who can immediately produce both components, and explain that v0x uses cosine (the adjacent side) while v0y uses sine (the opposite side), demonstrates fluent command of the setup step every projectile calculation depends on. A student who instead tries to plug the raw launch speed v0 into a vertical equation reveals that decomposition was skipped or misunderstood, which undermines every downstream number in the presentation.

questions.prompt: A ball is launched at v0 = 10 m/s at theta = 90 degrees (straight up). What are v0x and v0y?

options.text: v0x = 10 m/s, v0y = 0 m/s
v0x = 0 m/s, v0y = 10 m/s

explanations.a: This is the decomposition for a 0-degree (purely horizontal) launch, not a 90-degree one.
explanations.b: Correct: at theta = 90 degrees, cos(90°) = 0 so v0x = 0, and sin(90°) = 1 so v0y = v0 = 10 m/s — all the speed is vertical.
explanations.c: That even split (cos = sin = 0.707) only happens at theta = 45 degrees, not 90 degrees.

questions.prompt: Which trigonometric function gives the vertical component v0y of a launch velocity v0 at angle theta from the horizontal?

options.text: v0y = v0 * cos(theta)
v0y = v0 * tan(theta)
v0y = v0 * sin(theta)

explanations.a: Cosine gives the side ADJACENT to theta, which is the horizontal component v0x, not the vertical one.
explanations.b: Tangent relates the two components to each other (v0y/v0x), not either component to the hypotenuse v0 directly.
explanations.c: Correct: sine gives the side OPPOSITE theta in the right triangle, which is the vertical component v0y.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of setting up a projectile problem starting from a stated launch speed and angle.

items.text: Read off the given launch speed v0 and angle theta from the horizontal
Compute v0x = v0 * cos(theta)
Compute v0y = v0 * sin(theta)
Use v0x and v0y as separate inputs to the horizontal and vertical kinematics equations

questions.explanation: The angle and speed must be identified before either component can be computed, and both components must exist before they can be handed off to the separate 1D equations that actually solve the problem.

questions.prompt: Match each launch angle to its horizontal/vertical velocity split.

right.text: v0x = v0, v0y = 0
v0x = 0, v0y = v0

questions.explanation: At 0 degrees cos = 1 and sin = 0 so all speed is horizontal; at 45 degrees cos = sin = 0.707 splitting evenly; at 90 degrees cos = 0 and sin = 1 so all speed is vertical.

lessons.label: Time of Flight and the Apex

sections.heading: The vertical axis alone controls timing
sections.body: Because the horizontal and vertical motions are independent, the total time a projectile spends in the air is determined entirely by the vertical motion — v0y, the launch/landing heights, and g — and never by v0x or the horizontal distance covered. This is a direct consequence of the previous lessons: the vertical equation y(t) = y0 + v0y*t - (1/2)g*t^2 is the only equation that involves time explicitly running out when the object reaches the ground, so solving y(t) = 0 (or y(t) = landing height) for t is the only way to find flight duration.

sections.heading: Time to the apex
sections.body: The apex is the highest point of the trajectory, defined as the instant the vertical velocity component reaches zero — the object has finished rising and is about to start falling, even though it is still moving horizontally at full speed v0x. Using vy(t) = v0y - g*t and setting vy = 0 gives t_apex = v0y / g. This is exactly the same algebra as finding when a ball thrown straight up momentarily stops before falling back, because vertically, a projectile IS a ball thrown straight up with initial speed v0y — the horizontal motion is simply along for the ride and does not affect this calculation at all.

sections.heading: Total flight time on level ground
sections.body: When launch height equals landing height (the common 'level ground' case), the trajectory is symmetric in time about the apex: the time spent rising equals the time spent falling. That means total flight time is exactly twice the time to the apex: T = 2 * t_apex = 2*v0y/g = 2*v0*sin(theta)/g. This symmetry breaks the moment launch and landing heights differ — for example, a ball thrown from a cliff falls for LONGER than it rose, because it has extra height to descend through after returning to launch level, so T = 2*v0y/g only applies to the equal-height case and must be replaced by solving the full quadratic y(t) = 0 otherwise.

lessons.workedExample: A ball is launched from level ground at v0 = 25 m/s, theta = 40 degrees, so v0y = 25*sin(40°) = 25*0.643 = 16.1 m/s. Time to apex: t_apex = 16.1/9.8 = 1.64 s. Total flight time (level ground): T = 2*1.64 = 3.28 s. Check using the full formula directly: T = 2*25*sin(40°)/9.8 = 2*16.1/9.8 = 3.28 s, matching. The apex therefore occurs at exactly the halfway point in time, t = 1.64 s out of the total 3.28 s flight — not at the halfway point in horizontal distance necessarily, but precisely at the time midpoint.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges often ask, "does doubling the launch speed double the flight time?" A student who understands that T = 2*v0*sin(theta)/g is linear in v0 will correctly say yes (for a fixed angle), while a student who has memorized range formulas (which scale with v0-squared) sometimes incorrectly imports that squared relationship into time, revealing confusion between the two different formulas. A second common probe is asking what changes if the ball is launched from a height above the landing point instead of level ground — testing whether the student knows T = 2*v0y/g is a special case, not a universal law, and can identify when the simplification no longer applies.

questions.prompt: A projectile is at its apex. Which statement about its velocity at that instant is correct?

options.text: Both velocity components are zero
The vertical component is zero; the horizontal component equals v0x
The horizontal component is zero; the vertical component equals v0y

explanations.a: The horizontal component never becomes zero mid-flight (no horizontal force acts on the projectile), so this is false.
explanations.b: Correct: the apex is defined by vy = 0, but horizontal velocity is constant throughout the flight and remains v0x at every instant, including the apex.
explanations.c: This reverses the two components; it is the vertical component, not the horizontal one, that vanishes at the apex.

questions.prompt: A projectile is launched from level ground and lands at the same height it started. If the time to reach the apex is 2.0 s, what is the total time of flight?

explanations.a: Halving the apex time has no physical basis; the total flight is longer than the time to the apex, not shorter.
explanations.b: 2.0 s is only the time to reach the apex (the rise), not the full round trip of rise plus fall.
explanations.c: Correct: on level ground the rise and fall take equal time, so total time T = 2 * t_apex = 2 * 2.0 = 4.0 s.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to find total time of flight for a projectile launched and landing at the same height.

items.text: Decompose v0 into v0y = v0*sin(theta)
Set vertical velocity vy = v0y - g*t equal to zero to find t_apex
Recognize that rise time equals fall time on level ground
Double t_apex to get total flight time T

questions.explanation: You need v0y before you can find when vertical velocity zeroes out at the apex; only after establishing the level-ground rise-fall symmetry does doubling t_apex become valid to get T.

questions.prompt: Match each launch/landing scenario to how its total flight time compares to the simple level-ground formula T = 2*v0y/g.

left.text: Launch and landing heights are equal
Launched from a cliff, landing far below
Launched from ground level, landing on a raised platform

right.text: T = 2*v0y/g applies exactly
Actual flight time is longer than 2*v0y/g
Actual flight time is shorter than 2*v0y/g

questions.explanation: Equal heights give the symmetric rise-equals-fall case the formula assumes; landing below launch height adds extra fall time beyond the apex-symmetric case; landing above launch height cuts the fall short, ending the flight before the symmetric point would have.

lessons.label: Velocity and Speed Along the Path

sections.heading: One component frozen, one component reversing
sections.body: At every instant during flight, a projectile has a velocity vector with two components: vx, which is frozen at v0x for the entire flight because nothing acts on the horizontal axis, and vy, which changes continuously according to vy(t) = v0y - g*t. Vy starts positive (moving up, if launched upward), decreases linearly, crosses exactly zero at the apex, and then becomes increasingly negative (moving down) for the remainder of the flight. This means the velocity VECTOR is constantly rotating throughout the flight even though one of its two components never changes — the horizontal 'backbone' stays fixed while the vertical component swings from positive through zero to negative.

sections.heading: Speed is minimized at the apex, not zero
sections.body: A common misconception is that a projectile 'stops' at the top of its arc. It does not — only its vertical velocity component reaches zero there; its horizontal component v0x is completely unaffected and keeps moving at full speed. Total speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, v = sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2). Since vx is constant and vy^2 is smallest (zero) exactly at the apex, total speed IS minimized at the apex — but that minimum value is v0x, not zero, unless the projectile was launched perfectly vertically (in which case v0x = 0 and the object does momentarily stop). For any non-vertical launch, the projectile is always moving at the apex, just moving purely horizontally at that instant.

sections.heading: The direction of motion over time
sections.body: The angle of the velocity vector relative to horizontal, found from arctan(vy/vx), starts at the launch angle theta, decreases toward zero as the object rises (approaching purely horizontal motion at the apex), then continues decreasing into negative angles as the object descends, becoming steeper and steeper below horizontal. On level ground with no air resistance, the landing angle has the same MAGNITUDE as the launch angle (a direct consequence of the same vy-symmetry that makes rise time equal fall time), though the object is now moving downward instead of upward — the path in and the path out mirror each other in angle, even though gravity has been continuously acting the whole time.

lessons.workedExample: A projectile launches at v0 = 30 m/s, theta = 50 degrees, so v0x = 30*cos(50°) = 19.3 m/s and v0y = 30*sin(50°) = 23.0 m/s. At the apex, vy = 0, so total speed = vx = 19.3 m/s — the minimum speed of the whole flight, and clearly not zero. At launch, speed = sqrt(19.3^2 + 23.0^2) = sqrt(372 + 529) = sqrt(901) ≈ 30.0 m/s, matching v0 as expected. On level ground, by symmetry, the landing speed also equals 30.0 m/s (same magnitude as launch speed, direction now angled downward at 50 degrees below horizontal instead of above it) — kinetic energy returns to its starting value once the object returns to its starting height.
lessons.judgeFraming: A favorite judge trap is asking, "what is the projectile's velocity at the top of its arc — is it zero?" Students who answer 'zero' are conflating vertical velocity (which IS zero at the apex) with total velocity (which generally is not). A strong answer distinguishes the two explicitly: 'the vertical component is zero, but the object is still moving horizontally at v0x, so its speed is v0x, not zero, unless it was launched straight up.' This single question efficiently separates students with a component-level understanding of projectile motion from those who have only memorized that 'the apex is where things stop.'

questions.prompt: A ball is launched at an angle of 60 degrees above horizontal (not straight up). At the apex of its trajectory, its speed is:

options.text: Zero
Equal to v0x, the horizontal component of launch velocity
Equal to v0, the full launch speed

explanations.a: Only the vertical velocity component is zero at the apex; the horizontal component is unaffected, so total speed is not zero.
explanations.b: Correct: at the apex vy = 0, so total speed = sqrt(vx^2 + 0^2) = vx = v0x, the minimum speed of the whole flight for a non-vertical launch.
explanations.c: The full launch speed v0 only occurs at launch (and, on level ground, at landing) — the apex speed is smaller because vy has dropped to zero there.

questions.prompt: As a projectile rises from launch to apex (non-vertical launch, no air resistance), what happens to its horizontal velocity component?

options.text: It decreases toward zero
It stays exactly constant
It increases

explanations.a: Nothing acts horizontally on the projectile, so there is no mechanism to decrease vx during the rise.
explanations.b: Correct: with no horizontal force, vx = v0x for the entire flight, rising phase included — only vy changes during the rise.
explanations.c: There is no horizontal acceleration in projectile motion (air resistance neglected), so vx cannot increase either.

questions.prompt: Order the sequence of the vertical velocity component vy from launch to landing (level ground, launched upward at an angle).

items.text: vy is positive and largest in magnitude, at launch
vy decreases steadily toward zero while rising
vy equals exactly zero at the apex
vy becomes increasingly negative while falling, reaching -v0y at landing

questions.explanation: Vy starts at its positive launch value, decreases linearly under gravity, crosses zero at the apex by definition, and continues decreasing into negative territory as the object falls, reaching the negative of its launch value at landing (level ground).

questions.prompt: Match each point in the flight to the sign/value of the vertical velocity component vy.

left.text: At launch (thrown upward at an angle)

right.text: Positive (vy = v0y)
Zero
Negative (vy = -v0y)

questions.explanation: Vertical velocity begins positive at v0y, decreases linearly to zero exactly at the apex by definition, and continues to -v0y by the time the object returns to launch height on level ground.

lessons.label: A Worked Projectile Problem End-to-End

sections.heading: The component method, assembled
sections.body: Every projectile problem, however it is phrased, reduces to the same sequence: decompose v0 into v0x and v0y; solve the vertical problem to get time of flight (and, along the way, time and height of the apex); use that time in the horizontal equation to get range; and, if asked, recombine the final vx and vy to get an impact speed and angle. No new physics appears after Lessons 1 through 5 — this lesson exists purely to show all five steps executed back-to-back on one concrete problem, since stitching the pieces together correctly, in the right order, is where most computational errors actually happen.

sections.heading: Sanity checks that catch the most common mistakes
sections.body: Two checks catch nearly all decomposition and algebra errors. First, vx^2 + vy^2 should recombine (via square root) to v0 at launch and, on level ground, to the same v0 at landing — if it does not, a component was mis-assigned (sine and cosine swapped is the most frequent culprit). Second, the impact angle on level ground should have the same magnitude as the launch angle, just below horizontal instead of above — if a computed impact angle comes out equal to the launch angle in sign as well as magnitude, a sign was dropped somewhere in the vertical velocity calculation. Building these two checks into a routine habit turns projectile problems from error-prone into close to error-proof.

sections.heading: What each output quantity actually depends on
sections.body: It is worth explicitly separating what each final answer is sensitive to: range depends on BOTH v0x and total flight time (which itself comes from v0y), so range is affected by both components and therefore by both v0 and theta. Time of flight and max height depend ONLY on v0y (and g), never on v0x — doubling v0x while holding v0y fixed changes the range but leaves flight time and max height completely untouched. Keeping this dependency map in mind while working a problem prevents the common error of expecting a horizontal-speed change to alter timing, or a vertical-speed change to somehow leave the flight time unaffected.

lessons.workedExample: A projectile is launched from level ground at v0 = 40 m/s, theta = 30 degrees. Step 1 (decompose): v0x = 40*cos(30°) = 40*0.866 = 34.6 m/s; v0y = 40*sin(30°) = 40*0.5 = 20.0 m/s. Step 2 (time of flight): T = 2*v0y/g = 2*20.0/9.8 = 4.08 s. Step 3 (max height): using vy^2 = v0y^2 - 2*g*h at the apex where vy = 0, h_max = v0y^2/(2g) = 20.0^2/(2*9.8) = 400/19.6 = 20.4 m. Step 4 (range): R = v0x * T = 34.6 * 4.08 = 141 m (matching the standard formula R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g = 1600*sin(60°)/9.8 = 1600*0.866/9.8 = 141 m, confirming consistency). Step 5 (impact velocity): at landing, vx = 34.6 m/s (unchanged) and vy = -20.0 m/s (equal magnitude, opposite sign to launch, by level-ground symmetry), so impact speed = sqrt(34.6^2 + 20.0^2) = sqrt(1197 + 400) = sqrt(1597) ≈ 40.0 m/s, at 30 degrees BELOW horizontal — matching the launch speed and angle magnitude exactly, as the symmetry check predicts.
lessons.judgeFraming: In a full presentation, a judge assessing a projectile-based project (a catapult competition, a trajectory-prediction experiment) will usually walk a student through their own calculation live: 'show me how you got that range number, step by step.' What separates a strong defense from a weak one is whether the student narrates the component method in the correct causal order — decompose, then solve vertical for time, then use that time horizontally — rather than reciting a memorized range formula as if it were a separate, unrelated fact. A student who can also state the two sanity checks (component recombination and launch/landing angle symmetry) signals they would catch their own errors, which is exactly the kind of self-checking rigor judges are trained to reward.

questions.prompt: A projectile's launch speed v0 and angle theta are both increased in a way that keeps v0y unchanged, but increases v0x. What happens to the time of flight (level ground)?

options.text: It increases
It decreases
It stays the same

explanations.a: Time of flight depends only on v0y and g, neither of which changed, so it cannot increase.
explanations.b: Time of flight depends only on v0y and g, neither of which changed, so it cannot decrease.
explanations.c: Correct: T = 2*v0y/g depends only on v0y and g; since v0y is unchanged, T is unaffected by any change in v0x, even though range would change.

questions.prompt: In the worked example (v0 = 40 m/s, theta = 30 degrees, level ground), what is the impact speed when the projectile lands?

options.text: About 20.0 m/s
About 34.6 m/s
About 40.0 m/s

explanations.a: 20.0 m/s is only the vertical component magnitude v0y, not the full impact speed.
explanations.b: 34.6 m/s is only the horizontal component v0x, which stays constant but is not the full speed.
explanations.c: Correct: on level ground, by symmetry, impact speed equals launch speed, sqrt(34.6^2 + 20.0^2) ≈ 40.0 m/s.

questions.prompt: Order the five steps of the full component-method solution to a level-ground projectile problem.

items.text: Decompose v0 into v0x = v0*cos(theta) and v0y = v0*sin(theta)
Solve the vertical problem for total time of flight T
Use v0y and T to find maximum height at the apex
Use v0x and T to find horizontal range
Recombine vx and vy at landing to find impact speed and angle

questions.explanation: Decomposition must come first since nothing else can be computed without v0x and v0y; time of flight (from the vertical problem) is needed before both max height and range can be finalized; impact velocity is the last quantity since it depends on having already reached the landing instant.

questions.prompt: Match each final-answer quantity to what it fundamentally depends on.

left.text: Time of flight and maximum height (level ground)

right.text: v0y and g only
Both v0x and v0y (via flight time)

questions.explanation: Time of flight and max height are both purely vertical-axis outcomes, set by v0y and g alone; range multiplies v0x by that same flight time, so it is the one quantity sensitive to both velocity components.

lessons.label: The Range Equation on Level Ground

sections.heading: Splitting the launch into two independent axes
sections.body: A projectile launched at speed v0 and angle theta above the horizontal has an initial horizontal velocity v0x = v0 cos(theta) and an initial vertical velocity v0y = v0 sin(theta). The entire power of projectile analysis comes from treating these two axes as independent: gravity (g = 9.8 m/s^2, directed downward) acts only on the vertical motion, while the horizontal motion has zero acceleration and proceeds at constant velocity v0x for the whole flight. Nothing couples the axes except time — they share the same clock, and that shared clock is what lets you connect "how long the projectile is in the air" (a vertical fact) to "how far it travels" (a horizontal fact).

sections.heading: Time of flight, then range
sections.body: On level ground, the projectile lands at the same height it launched from, so the vertical displacement over the full flight is zero. Starting from y(t) = v0y*t - (1/2)g*t^2 and setting y = 0 gives two roots: t = 0 (the launch instant) and t = 2*v0y/g (the landing instant). That second root is the time of flight, T = 2*v0*sin(theta)/g. Range is just horizontal velocity times time of flight, since horizontal velocity never changes: R = v0x * T = v0*cos(theta) * (2*v0*sin(theta)/g) = 2*v0^2*sin(theta)*cos(theta)/g. Applying the double-angle identity sin(2*theta) = 2*sin(theta)*cos(theta) collapses this to the compact and widely quoted form R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g.

sections.heading: The assumptions baked into the formula
sections.body: R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g is not a universal law of projectiles — it is the answer to a specific, idealized problem, and every assumption that produced it is a place real motion can diverge. It assumes level ground (launch height equals landing height); if a golf ball is launched from a raised tee or a shot put leaves the hand above the ground, this formula does not apply and a full quadratic in y(t) is needed instead. It assumes no air resistance, so a real baseball or badminton shuttlecock, which are strongly affected by drag and sometimes spin-induced lift (the Magnus effect), will show measurably different range and often a different optimal angle than this vacuum prediction. It also assumes g is constant, which is an excellent approximation near Earth's surface but breaks down for very high trajectories. Every one of these idealizations is a deliberate simplification, not an error — it isolates the geometry of the launch angle from every other complicating force.

lessons.workedExample: A soccer ball is kicked at v0 = 20 m/s at theta = 30 degrees above level ground. First find time of flight: T = 2*v0*sin(theta)/g = 2*20*sin(30)/9.8 = 2*20*0.5/9.8 = 20/9.8 = 2.04 s. Range: R = v0x*T = (20*cos(30))*2.04 = (20*0.866)*2.04 = 17.32*2.04 = 35.3 m. Checking with the compact formula: R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g = 400*sin(60)/9.8 = 400*0.866/9.8 = 346.4/9.8 = 35.3 m. Both routes agree, confirming the compact formula is just the two-step derivation folded into one line.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g on a poster will almost always ask the student to derive it, not just quote it, because quoting a memorized formula proves nothing about understanding. The stronger follow-up is "what does this formula assume, and when would it fail?" A student who can name level ground and negligible air resistance, and can say concretely what changes without them (a raised launch point needs a different time-of-flight equation; a windy or spinning ball needs drag terms), demonstrates they understand the model's boundaries rather than having pattern-matched a formula off a reference sheet.

questions.prompt: Why does the range formula R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g only apply on level ground?

options.text: Because gravity only acts on level ground
Because the derivation sets vertical displacement to zero, which is only true when launch and landing heights match
Because horizontal velocity changes when the ground is not level
Because sin(2*theta) is undefined for non-level ground

explanations.a: Gravity acts everywhere near Earth's surface regardless of terrain; that is not the restriction.
explanations.b: Correct: the time-of-flight step solves y(t) = 0, which is only the landing condition when launch height equals landing height.
explanations.c: Horizontal velocity is constant throughout flight in this model regardless of ground level; that assumption does not change with terrain.
explanations.d: sin(2*theta) is a well-defined trigonometric function for any angle; terrain has nothing to do with its definition.

questions.prompt: A projectile launches at v0 = 15 m/s and theta = 40 degrees on level ground with no air resistance. What is its time of flight (g = 9.8 m/s^2)?

explanations.a: This is roughly half the correct time of flight — it looks like only v0y/g was computed, forgetting the factor of 2 for the full up-and-down trip.
explanations.c: This comes from omitting sin(theta) altogether — computing T = 2*v0/g = 30/9.8 = 3.06 s instead of including the sin(40) factor.
explanations.d: This comes from computing T = v0/g = 15/9.8 = 1.53 s, forgetting both the sin(theta) factor and the factor of 2 for the full up-and-down trip.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that derive the range equation from the launch conditions.

items.text: Multiply constant horizontal velocity v0x by time of flight T to get range R
Resolve v0 into v0x = v0*cos(theta) and v0y = v0*sin(theta)
Apply the double-angle identity to write R in the compact sin(2*theta) form
Set vertical displacement y(t) = 0 and solve for the nonzero root, giving time of flight T

questions.explanation: You must first split v0 into components, then use the vertical component to find how long the flight lasts, then use the horizontal component and that duration to get range, and only at the end simplify algebraically with the double-angle identity.

questions.prompt: Match each assumption in the range equation to what it means physically.

right.text: Launch height equals landing height
No drag force decelerates the projectile horizontally
Trajectory stays close enough to Earth's surface that gravitational acceleration does not measurably change

questions.explanation: Level ground means the y=0 landing condition matches the y=0 launch condition; no air resistance means horizontal velocity truly stays constant; constant g requires the trajectory to stay near Earth's surface where gravitational acceleration barely varies.

lessons.label: Why 45 Degrees Maximizes Range

sections.heading: Range is a function of sin(2*theta) alone
sections.body: For a fixed launch speed v0 on level ground, R(theta) = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g. Since v0 and g are held fixed, the entire theta-dependence of range lives inside sin(2*theta). Sine is bounded between -1 and 1 for any input, and it reaches its maximum value of exactly 1 when its argument is 90 degrees. Setting 2*theta = 90 degrees gives theta = 45 degrees. At that angle, R = v0^2*(1)/g = v0^2/g, which is the largest range achievable at that launch speed on level ground. No other angle can do better, because no other angle makes sin(2*theta) larger than 1 — 1 is the ceiling of the sine function itself, not a coincidence of this particular problem.

sections.heading: The calculus view: where the slope of R(theta) is zero
sections.body: The same result falls out of calculus. Take the derivative of R with respect to theta: dR/dtheta = (2*v0^2/g)*cos(2*theta). A maximum (or minimum) occurs where this derivative is zero, which happens when cos(2*theta) = 0, i.e. 2*theta = 90 degrees, i.e. theta = 45 degrees. Checking the second derivative, or simply checking that R is smaller on either side of 45 degrees, confirms this critical point is a maximum rather than a minimum or inflection. Both the calculus argument and the "sine maxes out at 1" argument are really the same fact seen two ways: calculus locates the stationary point, while the sine-bound argument explains directly why that stationary point cannot be beaten.

sections.heading: Symmetric fall-off around the peak
sections.body: Range does not collapse sharply away from 45 degrees — it falls off symmetrically and fairly gently, because sin(2*theta) is a smooth, symmetric curve around its peak at 2*theta = 90 degrees. Launching at 40 degrees or 50 degrees gives sin(80 degrees) = sin(100 degrees) = 0.985, nearly indistinguishable from the peak value of 1. Even at 30 degrees or 60 degrees, sin(60) = sin(120) = 0.866, still 87% of the maximum range. This gentle plateau near the top is why real athletes and engineers do not have to hit exactly 45 degrees to get near-maximum range, and it is also exactly why complementary angles (the next lesson) produce identical ranges — the symmetry that flattens the peak is the same symmetry that pairs up equal-range angles on either side of it.

lessons.workedExample: A trebuchet launches a projectile at v0 = 30 m/s. At theta = 45 degrees: R = v0^2*sin(90)/g = 900*1/9.8 = 91.8 m, the maximum possible range at this speed. At theta = 35 degrees: R = 900*sin(70)/9.8 = 900*0.940/9.8 = 86.3 m, about 94% of the maximum despite being 10 degrees off. At theta = 20 degrees: R = 900*sin(40)/9.8 = 900*0.643/9.8 = 59.0 m, only 64% of the maximum, showing that the plateau near 45 degrees is real but the fall-off accelerates well away from it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing a launch-angle project often ask "why 45 degrees, specifically?" and are listening for whether the student can connect the calculus/geometry argument to the physical answer rather than reciting it as trivia. The stronger answer notes that sin(2*theta) simply cannot exceed 1, so no launch angle can beat theta = 45 degrees at a fixed speed — this is a hard mathematical ceiling, not an empirical trend. A judge may also ask what happens to a real thrown object (a shot put, a javelin) that does not follow the 45-degree rule in practice; the expected answer is that release height and aerodynamic drag shift the true optimum away from 45 degrees, which is a question the next few lessons and later drag-focused material address.

questions.prompt: Why is theta = 45 degrees the range-maximizing angle on level ground with no air resistance?

options.text: Because 45 degrees splits gravity and velocity evenly
Because sin(2*theta) reaches its maximum possible value of 1 exactly when theta = 45 degrees
Because it is the angle where horizontal and vertical velocity are both zero
Because g is smallest at 45 degrees

explanations.a: This is not a real physical mechanism; there is no such thing as gravity and velocity being "split evenly."
explanations.b: Correct: R is proportional to sin(2*theta), and sine cannot exceed 1, which it reaches when its argument is 90 degrees, i.e. theta = 45 degrees.
explanations.c: At theta = 45 degrees, v0x and v0y are equal in magnitude and both nonzero, not zero.
explanations.d: g is a constant near Earth's surface and does not vary with launch angle.

questions.prompt: A projectile is launched at v0 = 25 m/s at theta = 45 degrees on level ground. What is the maximum range (g = 9.8 m/s^2)?

explanations.a: This looks like v0^2/g was divided by an extra factor of 10, or v0 was used instead of v0^2.
explanations.b: Correct: R = v0^2/g at theta = 45 degrees since sin(90) = 1, so R = 625/9.8 = 63.8 m.
explanations.c: This is half the correct answer, as if sin(2*theta) were mistakenly treated as 0.5 instead of 1.
explanations.d: This is double the correct answer, as if an extra factor of 2 were carried through incorrectly.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of the calculus argument that theta = 45 degrees maximizes range.

items.text: Solve to find 2*theta = 90 degrees, so theta = 45 degrees is the critical point
Differentiate to get dR/dtheta = (2*v0^2/g)*cos(2*theta)
Write range as R(theta) = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g
Set the derivative equal to zero, giving cos(2*theta) = 0

questions.explanation: You start from the range function, differentiate it with respect to theta, set the derivative to zero to find where the slope is flat, and solve that equation to locate the critical angle at 45 degrees.

questions.prompt: Match each launch angle to its range relative to the maximum range at the same speed (using sin(2*theta) values).

right.text: 100% of maximum range (sin(90) = 1)
About 87% of maximum range (sin(60) = 0.866)
50% of maximum range (sin(30) = 0.5)

questions.explanation: At 45 degrees, 2*theta = 90 degrees and sine peaks at 1; at 30 degrees, 2*theta = 60 degrees where sine is 0.866; at 15 degrees, 2*theta = 30 degrees where sine is exactly 0.5.

lessons.label: Complementary Angles Give Equal Range

sections.heading: The identity behind the pairing
sections.body: Take two launch angles that add to 90 degrees: theta and (90 - theta). Their ranges are R(theta) = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g and R(90-theta) = v0^2*sin(2*(90-theta))/g = v0^2*sin(180 - 2*theta)/g. The trigonometric identity sin(180 - x) = sin(x) applies directly with x = 2*theta, giving sin(180 - 2*theta) = sin(2*theta). So R(90-theta) = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g = R(theta) exactly. Any two complementary launch angles — 20/70, 30/60, 15/75 — produce identical range at the same launch speed on level ground. This is not an approximation or a near-coincidence; it is an exact algebraic consequence of how sine behaves past 90 degrees.

sections.heading: Two very different trajectories, same landing spot
sections.body: Equal range does not mean equal trajectory. The low angle (theta less than 45 degrees) produces a flat, fast, low-arcing shot: shorter time of flight, lower maximum height, higher horizontal velocity component. The complementary high angle (90 - theta) produces a lofted, slower-looking shot: longer time of flight, greater maximum height, lower horizontal velocity component but higher vertical velocity component. Both land at exactly the same distance because what determines range is the product v0x * T, and swapping theta for (90-theta) swaps v0x and v0y with each other (since cos(90-theta) = sin(theta) and sin(90-theta) = cos(theta)) while the underlying product that generates range stays balanced.

sections.heading: Why this matters tactically
sections.body: This complementary-angle pairing is not just a mathematical curiosity — it shows up directly in sports and artillery. A punter or golfer choosing between a low, fast trajectory and a high, lofted one for the same distance is choosing between two angles that this identity says are range-equivalent, but which differ enormously in hang time, defender reaction time, wind exposure, and how steeply the object comes down. A mortar crew or artillery officer historically used the high-angle, indirect-fire solution (as used by mortars and howitzers firing in high-angle mode) to clear an obstacle or hit a target hidden behind a ridge, and the low-angle ("flat trajectory") solution when a fast, direct, less wind-affected shot was preferred — both hitting the same range table distance from the identical firing table.

lessons.workedExample: A golf ball is launched at v0 = 22 m/s. At theta = 25 degrees: R = 22^2*sin(50)/9.8 = 484*0.766/9.8 = 37.8 m. At the complementary angle theta = 65 degrees: R = 484*sin(130)/9.8 = 484*0.766/9.8 = 37.8 m — identical range, since sin(130) = sin(50) exactly. But time of flight differs sharply: T(25) = 2*22*sin(25)/9.8 = 1.90 s, while T(65) = 2*22*sin(65)/9.8 = 4.07 s — the lofted shot at 65 degrees stays airborne more than twice as long to cover the same horizontal distance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who understands the range equation will often ask a student who only tested one launch angle to predict the range at its complement, without recomputing — this checks whether the student grasps sin(180-x) = sin(x) as a structural feature of the model rather than something to look up per angle. A stronger follow-up asks the student to justify why a coach or engineer might still prefer one of the two complementary angles despite equal range; the expected answer invokes hang time, defender/interception time, wind sensitivity, or angle of descent, showing the student can move from "same range" to "not actually equivalent choices" in a practical sense.

questions.prompt: Why do launch angles of 30 degrees and 60 degrees give the same range at the same launch speed?

options.text: Because sin(60) = sin(120) by the identity sin(180-x) = sin(x)
Because 30 and 60 both round to 45 degrees
Because time of flight is the same for both angles
Because horizontal velocity is the same for both angles

explanations.a: Correct: 2*theta for the two angles are 60 degrees and 120 degrees, and sin(120) = sin(180-60) = sin(60), so the range formula gives an identical value.
explanations.b: Rounding is not a real mathematical justification and 30, 60 do not round to 45.
explanations.c: Time of flight differs between complementary angles — the 60 degree shot stays airborne longer than the 30 degree shot.
explanations.d: Horizontal velocity differs: v0*cos(30) is not equal to v0*cos(60); it is v0x at 30 degrees that equals v0y at 60 degrees, not v0x at both.

questions.prompt: A ball launched at 20 degrees and its complementary angle both hit the same range target. Which statement about the two trajectories is correct?

options.text: They have identical maximum height and identical time of flight
The 70 degree shot has greater maximum height and longer time of flight than the 20 degree shot
The 20 degree shot has greater maximum height than the 70 degree shot
Maximum height cannot be compared without knowing v0

explanations.a: Equal range does not mean equal trajectory shape; height and time of flight both differ between complementary angles.
explanations.b: Correct: the steeper 70 degree angle has a larger vertical velocity component, producing greater maximum height and longer hang time than the low, flat 20 degree shot.
explanations.c: This has the comparison backwards — the steeper (higher) angle produces the greater maximum height, not the flatter one.
explanations.d: The comparison (which angle is higher) can be made without knowing v0's numeric value, since the same v0 applies to both and the steeper angle always wins on height.

questions.prompt: Order the algebraic steps showing R(theta) = R(90-theta).

items.text: Apply the identity sin(180 - x) = sin(x) with x = 2*theta
Write R(90-theta) = v0^2*sin(2*(90-theta))/g
Conclude R(90-theta) = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g = R(theta)
Simplify the angle inside sine: 2*(90-theta) = 180 - 2*theta

questions.explanation: You start from the range formula evaluated at the complementary angle, simplify the argument of sine algebraically, apply the supplementary-angle sine identity, and arrive at the same expression as the original range, proving equality.

questions.prompt: Match each launch style to its complementary-angle description.

right.text: Flat, fast trajectory with short time of flight and low maximum height
Lofted, slower-looking trajectory with long time of flight and high maximum height
Equals sin(2*theta), which is why complementary angles give identical range

questions.explanation: The low angle trades height for horizontal speed; the complementary high angle trades horizontal speed for height and hang time; the identity sin(180-2*theta) = sin(2*theta) is exactly why both produce the same range.

lessons.label: Maximum Height and the Range-Height Trade-off

sections.heading: Deriving maximum height
sections.body: Maximum height occurs at the instant vertical velocity is zero — the top of the arc, where the projectile has stopped rising but not yet begun falling. Using vy^2 = v0y^2 - 2*g*h and setting vy = 0 at the peak: 0 = v0y^2 - 2*g*H, so H = v0y^2/(2*g) = (v0*sin(theta))^2/(2*g). Notice this depends only on the vertical component of the initial velocity, v0*sin(theta) — the horizontal component v0*cos(theta) plays no role in how high the projectile climbs, which is a direct consequence of treating the two axes as independent. Doubling v0 quadruples maximum height, just as it quadruples range, because both formulas scale with v0^2.

sections.heading: Height and range pull in opposite directions
sections.body: Range depends on sin(2*theta), which peaks at theta = 45 degrees, while maximum height depends on sin^2(theta), which peaks at theta = 90 degrees — a straight-up vertical launch, where all the velocity is devoted to climbing and none to horizontal travel. These two optimal angles do not coincide, which is the mathematical statement of the range-height trade-off: at 45 degrees you get maximum range but only a modest height (H = v0^2/(4g) at that angle, which is one-quarter of R's peak value v0^2/g), while pushing theta toward 90 degrees sacrifices range in exchange for climbing higher and staying aloft longer, and pushing theta toward 0 degrees sacrifices both height and hang time for a flat, fast, low shot.

sections.heading: Choosing an angle for the goal, not just the distance
sections.body: This trade-off is why real launch-angle decisions depend on what problem is being solved, not on range alone. A basketball free throw is not aimed for a 45-degree "maximum range" trajectory — it is arced steeper, near 45 to 55 degrees depending on the shooter, to gain a larger entry angle into the hoop and a softer, more forgiving landing on the rim, even though this is not the flattest or fastest path. A mortar or howitzer crew aiming at a target behind a hill deliberately chooses a high angle, well above the range-optimal 45 degrees, to gain height and clear the obstacle, accepting reduced range efficiency. A javelin thrower, by contrast, aims close to but a few degrees below the naive 45-degree optimum (real elite throws cluster around 32 to 36 degrees) because the javelin's aerodynamic lift and the biomechanics of the throwing motion shift the true optimum away from the no-drag textbook answer — hang time and height are not always the goal, and even range itself is not always maximized at exactly 45 degrees once aerodynamics enter.

lessons.workedExample: A basketball is shot at v0 = 8 m/s at theta = 52 degrees. Maximum height: H = (v0*sin(theta))^2/(2*g) = (8*sin(52))^2/(2*9.8) = (8*0.788)^2/19.6 = (6.30)^2/19.6 = 39.7/19.6 = 2.03 m above the release point. Range: R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g = 64*sin(104)/9.8 = 64*0.970/9.8 = 62.1/9.8 = 6.34 m. Compare to launching the same v0 at the range-optimal 45 degrees: R45 = 64*sin(90)/9.8 = 64/9.8 = 6.53 m (only 3% farther) but H45 = (8*sin(45))^2/19.6 = (5.66)^2/19.6 = 32.0/19.6 = 1.63 m, noticeably lower — confirming the shooter traded a small amount of range for meaningfully more height and a steeper, more forgiving entry angle.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the range-height trade-off by asking why a student's model or experiment did not simply use 45 degrees if that maximizes range — the expected answer is that maximum range is not always the goal, and a fair project should state explicitly what quantity it is actually optimizing (height, hang time, entry angle, clearance over an obstacle) rather than defaulting to 45 degrees by habit. A strong student can also state, with the formula, why height and range peak at different angles (sin^2(theta) vs sin(2*theta)) rather than treating the trade-off as a vague qualitative claim.

questions.prompt: Maximum height H = (v0*sin(theta))^2/(2g) depends on which component of the initial velocity?

options.text: Only the horizontal component, v0*cos(theta)
Only the vertical component, v0*sin(theta)
Both components equally
Neither component, only on g

explanations.a: The horizontal component does not appear anywhere in the height formula; it governs range, not height.
explanations.b: Correct: H depends only on v0*sin(theta), the vertical component, because horizontal motion has no effect on how high the projectile climbs.
explanations.c: Only the vertical component appears in the formula; the horizontal component is entirely absent from it.
explanations.d: g appears in the formula but so does v0*sin(theta) squared; height is not independent of launch velocity.

questions.prompt: Why do maximum range and maximum height occur at different launch angles?

options.text: Range depends on sin(2*theta), which peaks at 45 degrees, while height depends on sin^2(theta), which peaks at 90 degrees
They actually occur at the same angle, 45 degrees, for both quantities
Range depends on g while height does not
Height decreases as v0 increases while range increases

explanations.a: Correct: the two quantities are governed by different trigonometric functions of theta with different peak locations, so their optimal angles genuinely differ.
explanations.b: This is false — height keeps increasing all the way to theta = 90 degrees (straight up), well past the range-optimal 45 degrees.
explanations.c: Both range and height formulas include g in the denominator; that is not what separates their optimal angles.
explanations.d: Both height and range increase with v0 (both scale as v0^2); v0 does not explain why their optimal angles differ.

questions.prompt: Order these launch angles from lowest to highest maximum height, for the same v0.

items.text: theta = 90 degrees
theta = 45 degrees
theta = 10 degrees
theta = 75 degrees

questions.explanation: Maximum height depends on sin^2(theta), which increases monotonically from 0 to 90 degrees, so height ranks in the same order as the angle itself across this range.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world launch to the trade-off it is making.

left.text: Basketball free throw arced above 45 degrees
Mortar fired at a steep angle to clear a hill
Football punt kicked low and fast for a quick return coverage window

right.text: Sacrifices some range for a steeper, more forgiving entry angle into the hoop
Sacrifices range-optimal efficiency for extra height needed to clear an obstacle
Sacrifices height and hang time to minimize the time defenders have to react

questions.explanation: Each real launch angle choice is optimizing something other than raw range: entry angle for the free throw, obstacle clearance for the mortar, and short hang time for the low, fast punt.

lessons.label: Hitting a Target: Solving for the Launch Angle

sections.heading: Inverting the range equation
sections.body: Given a required range R and a fixed launch speed v0 on level ground, the range equation R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g can be solved backward for theta. Rearranging: sin(2*theta) = R*g/v0^2. Taking the inverse sine (arcsin) of both sides gives 2*theta = arcsin(R*g/v0^2), so theta = (1/2)*arcsin(R*g/v0^2). This only has a real solution when R*g/v0^2 is between -1 and 1 (arcsin is undefined outside that domain), which means there is a maximum achievable range at that speed — namely R_max = v0^2/g at theta = 45 degrees, as established earlier. If the required range exceeds v0^2/g, no launch angle at that speed can reach the target; the projectile needs more speed, not a different angle.

sections.heading: Two solutions, not one
sections.body: Arcsin returns one principal value, but sine is positive for angles in both the first quadrant (0 to 90 degrees) and the second quadrant (90 to 180 degrees), and sin(x) = sin(180-x) for any x. Since 2*theta ranges from 0 to 180 degrees as theta ranges from 0 to 90 degrees, both 2*theta = arcsin(R*g/v0^2) and 2*theta = 180 - arcsin(R*g/v0^2) are valid solutions, giving two angles: theta1 = (1/2)*arcsin(R*g/v0^2) and theta2 = 90 - theta1. This is exactly the complementary-angle relationship from before, now appearing as the natural consequence of inverting the range equation: except at the single boundary case theta = 45 degrees (where theta1 = theta2), every reachable target below R_max can be hit by two distinct trajectories, a low flat one and a high lofted one.

sections.heading: Choosing between the two solutions in practice
sections.body: Because both solutions land at the same range, choosing between them depends on constraints the range equation alone does not capture. The low-angle solution arrives faster with less hang time and a shallower angle of descent, useful when speed matters or when a flatter trajectory is needed to pass under an obstacle like a net or a tree branch. The high-angle (lofted) solution arrives more slowly but comes down steeper, useful for clearing an obstacle in front of the target, dropping into a target from above, or when a steep, high-arc approach is tactically preferred (as with mortar fire onto a fortified position or a lob shot over a defender's reach in tennis or basketball). In artillery, this is the classic "low-angle vs high-angle solution" a gunnery table provides for a given range: the crew explicitly picks one of the two valid angles based on terrain and tactics, not because the other is wrong.

lessons.workedExample: A target is 40 m away, and launch speed is fixed at v0 = 22 m/s (g = 9.8 m/s^2). Solve sin(2*theta) = R*g/v0^2 = 40*9.8/484 = 392/484 = 0.810. Then 2*theta = arcsin(0.810) = 54.1 degrees, giving theta1 = 27.1 degrees (the low, flat solution). The complementary solution is theta2 = 90 - 27.1 = 62.9 degrees (the high, lofted solution). Checking: at theta1, R = 484*sin(54.1)/9.8 = 484*0.810/9.8 = 40.0 m; at theta2, 2*theta2 = 125.8 degrees and sin(125.8) = sin(180-125.8) = sin(54.2) = 0.810, so R = 40.0 m again — both angles reach the same 40 m target, as the theory predicts.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge handed a project that finds "the" angle to hit a target should ask whether the student checked for a second solution, since silently dropping the complementary angle suggests the student solved the equation mechanically without understanding why arcsin only returns one root out of two physically valid ones. A stronger project explicitly reports both angles and explains, using the specific scenario (obstacle clearance, desired hang time, descent steepness), why one was chosen over the other — that choice is where physical judgment enters a problem that arcsin alone cannot resolve.

questions.prompt: A required range R satisfies R*g/v0^2 greater than 1. What does this mean?

options.text: There are two valid launch angles that reach the target
There is exactly one launch angle, 45 degrees, that reaches the target
No launch angle at this speed can reach the target; a higher v0 is required
The target must be above the launch point

explanations.a: Two valid angles exist only when R*g/v0^2 is strictly between 0 and 1, not greater than 1.
explanations.b: 45 degrees only reaches the target when R*g/v0^2 equals exactly 1 (the maximum-range case), not when it exceeds 1.
explanations.c: Correct: arcsin is undefined for inputs greater than 1, meaning R exceeds the maximum reachable range v0^2/g at that speed; more speed is needed, not a different angle.
explanations.d: This condition is purely about range vs. maximum range at a given speed and says nothing about relative launch/landing height.

questions.prompt: A target requires theta1 = 20 degrees as one solution to the range equation at a fixed v0. What is the complementary second solution?

options.text: 70 degrees
40 degrees
160 degrees
There is no second solution

explanations.a: Correct: theta2 = 90 - theta1 = 90 - 20 = 70 degrees, giving the same range via sin(2*70) = sin(140) = sin(40) = sin(2*20).
explanations.b: 40 degrees is 2*theta1, not the complementary solution theta2 = 90 - theta1.
explanations.c: 160 degrees is not a valid launch angle in this model, since theta is restricted to 0-90 degrees for a projectile launched above level ground.
explanations.d: A second solution exists for any target range strictly below the maximum range v0^2/g; only the boundary case at exactly 45 degrees has a single (repeated) solution.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to find both launch angles that hit a given target range R at fixed v0.

items.text: Check that R*g/v0^2 is between -1 and 1 so a real solution exists
Compute the complementary solution theta2 = 90 - theta1
Rearrange the range equation to isolate sin(2*theta) = R*g/v0^2
Take arcsin to find 2*theta and divide by 2 to get the low-angle solution theta1

questions.explanation: You must isolate sin(2*theta) first, verify the target is actually reachable at that speed, extract the principal (low-angle) solution from arcsin, and only then generate the second, lofted solution from the complementary-angle relationship.

questions.prompt: Match each of the two solutions for hitting a target to its practical trade-off.

left.text: High-angle solution (theta2 = 90 - theta1, greater than 45 degrees)

right.text: Arrives faster with a shallow angle of descent, good for passing under an obstacle
Arrives slower with a steep angle of descent, good for clearing an obstacle or dropping onto a target

questions.explanation: The low-angle solution favors speed and a flat approach; the high-angle solution favors a steep, high-arcing approach at the cost of time in the air.

lessons.label: How Range Scales with Launch Speed

sections.heading: Range grows with the square of launch speed
sections.body: In R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g, launch speed v0 appears squared while theta appears only inside sin(2*theta), which is bounded and does not grow without limit. Holding theta and g fixed, range is directly proportional to v0^2: R = k*v0^2, where k = sin(2*theta)/g is a constant for that angle. This quadratic dependence means range is far more sensitive to launch speed than to almost any other lever available to a thrower or engineer — doubling v0 does not double range, it quadruples it, because (2*v0)^2 = 4*v0^2. Tripling v0 gives nine times the range. This is why even modest gains in launch speed (a stronger throwing arm, a faster bat swing, more powerful gunpowder) produce outsized gains in distance compared to fine-tuning the angle near its already-flat 45-degree peak.

sections.heading: Contrast with time of flight, which scales linearly
sections.body: Time of flight, T = 2*v0*sin(theta)/g, depends on v0 to the first power, not the second. Doubling v0 doubles T, not quadruples it. This linear-versus-quadratic contrast has a direct physical explanation: T is set purely by how long gravity takes to bring the vertical velocity component back to zero and land, a process that scales linearly with how much initial vertical velocity there was to cancel. Range, by contrast, is a product of two quantities that both increase with v0 — a larger v0y means more hang time (linear in v0), and simultaneously a larger v0x means faster horizontal coverage during that time (also linear in v0) — so range, being time multiplied by horizontal speed, inherits the product of two linear-in-v0 factors and ends up quadratic in v0.

sections.heading: Why this dominates real-world performance gains
sections.body: The quadratic sensitivity of range to speed explains real patterns in sports and engineering that a purely angle-focused analysis would miss. A shot put thrower who increases release speed from 13 m/s to 14 m/s, a roughly 7.7% increase, gains about (14/13)^2 - 1 = 16% more range from speed alone — nearly double the percentage gain in speed. This is a large part of why elite throwing and hitting sports emphasize explosive power training to maximize release/exit velocity, while angle is typically tuned to a narrower, near-optimal range (often a few degrees off the naive 45-degree prediction once drag and release height are included) rather than obsessing over each additional degree. Engineers designing a device meant to maximize range — a water rocket, a catapult, a pitching machine — get far more benefit from increasing muzzle velocity than from precisely nailing the launch angle, once that angle is already reasonably close to optimal.

lessons.workedExample: A pitching machine launches balls at theta = 45 degrees. At v0 = 30 m/s: R = 30^2*sin(90)/9.8 = 900/9.8 = 91.8 m. Doubling the speed to v0 = 60 m/s: R = 60^2*sin(90)/9.8 = 3600/9.8 = 367.3 m — exactly four times the original range, confirming the v0^2 scaling. Time of flight, by contrast, only doubles: T(30) = 2*30*sin(45)/9.8 = 4.33 s, while T(60) = 2*60*sin(45)/9.8 = 8.66 s, exactly twice as long, not four times, illustrating that range (quadratic in v0) and time of flight (linear in v0) respond very differently to the same speed increase.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge reviewing a project that varies launch speed should expect the student to state the v0^2 scaling explicitly and predict outcomes from it (e.g., "since I doubled the speed, I expect roughly four times the range") rather than treating each new speed trial as an unrelated data point. This tests whether the student understands the range equation as a genuine quantitative model rather than a black box that gets re-measured for every input. A sharp follow-up question asks the student to contrast this with time of flight's linear scaling, checking whether they can distinguish which physical quantities scale linearly versus quadratically with speed and explain why the difference arises from range being a time-times-velocity product of two v0-dependent terms.

questions.prompt: If launch speed v0 triples while theta and g stay fixed, what happens to range?

options.text: Range triples
Range becomes 9 times larger
Range becomes 6 times larger
Range stays the same, since angle did not change

explanations.a: Range does not scale linearly with v0; it scales with v0^2, so tripling speed does more than triple range.
explanations.b: Correct: R is proportional to v0^2, so tripling v0 multiplies range by 3^2 = 9.
explanations.c: This looks like conflating the earlier doubling-quadruples-range result with tripling — mistakenly computing 3 (the speed multiplier) times 2 (the exponent) = 6, instead of squaring the multiplier (3^2 = 9).
explanations.d: Range depends on both v0 and theta; holding theta fixed does not make range independent of v0.

questions.prompt: Why does time of flight scale linearly with v0 while range scales quadratically?

options.text: Time of flight does not depend on v0 at all
Range is the product of horizontal velocity and time of flight, both of which individually scale linearly with v0
Time of flight depends on v0^2 while range depends on v0
g changes with v0, which affects the two quantities differently

explanations.a: Time of flight does depend on v0: T = 2*v0*sin(theta)/g increases linearly as v0 increases.
explanations.b: Correct: range is horizontal velocity (linear in v0) multiplied by time of flight (also linear in v0), so their product is quadratic in v0.
explanations.c: This has the scalings reversed; time of flight is linear in v0 and range is quadratic in v0, not the other way around.
explanations.d: g is a constant near Earth's surface and does not depend on launch speed at all.

questions.prompt: Order these launch speeds (same angle, same g) from smallest to largest resulting range.
questions.explanation: Since range scales as v0^2 at a fixed angle, and v0^2 is a strictly increasing function of v0 for positive speeds, ranking by v0 directly gives the same ranking as ranking by range.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to how it scales with launch speed v0 (fixed theta and g).

right.text: Scales with v0^2 (quadruples if v0 doubles)
Scales with v0 (doubles if v0 doubles)
Scales with v0^2 (quadruples if v0 doubles)

questions.explanation: Both range (v0^2*sin(2theta)/g) and maximum height ((v0*sin(theta))^2/(2g)) depend on v0 squared, while time of flight (2*v0*sin(theta)/g) depends on v0 to the first power only.

units.label: Projectiles from Heights and onto Slopes

lessons.label: Launching from a Height

sections.heading: Where the symmetric formulas break
sections.body: The compact range formula R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g and the shortcut "time up equals time down" both come from setting vertical displacement y(t) = 0, which is only the landing condition when the projectile lands at the height it launched from. A ball thrown off a cliff, a shot put released above the throwing circle, or a dart flying off a table edge all violate that assumption: the landing point is below the launch point, so the vertical displacement at landing is a nonzero negative number, not zero. Reusing the level-ground formulas in this situation gives a wrong, too-short flight time and a wrong, too-short range, because the projectile actually has extra distance left to fall after it would have hit level ground.

sections.heading: Setting up the general vertical equation
sections.body: The fix is to go back to the full kinematics equation instead of a shortcut. Put the origin at the launch point with y positive upward, so y(t) = v0*sin(theta)*t - (1/2)*g*t^2. If the landing point is a height h below the launch point (h > 0), landing occurs when y(t) = -h, giving (1/2)*g*t^2 - v0*sin(theta)*t - h = 0. This is a genuine quadratic in t with a nonzero constant term (-h), unlike the level-ground case where the constant term is zero and t = 0 is always one of the roots. Solving it requires the quadratic formula, not just factoring out t.

sections.heading: The trajectory is still symmetric, the ground cut is not
sections.body: It helps to remember that the underlying parabola never changes shape — it is still symmetric about its own apex, rising and falling by mirror-image amounts on either side of the peak. What changes is where the ground intersects that parabola. On level ground, the intersection points are symmetric about the apex, so time up equals time down. When the landing point is lower than the launch point, the ground intersects the falling branch further from the apex than the rising branch, so the projectile spends more time falling than it spent rising. That asymmetry is the entire reason a separate treatment is needed, and it is what the quadratic in the previous section captures automatically.
