lessons.workedExample: A ball is thrown from the edge of a 20 m cliff at v0 = 15 m/s, theta = 20 degrees above horizontal. Components: v0x = 15*cos(20) = 14.10 m/s, v0y = 15*sin(20) = 5.13 m/s. Landing condition: (1/2)(9.8)*t^2 - 5.13*t - 20 = 0, so 4.9*t^2 - 5.13*t - 20 = 0. The quadratic formula gives t = [5.13 + sqrt(5.13^2 + 4*4.9*20)] / 9.8 = [5.13 + sqrt(418.3)] / 9.8 = [5.13 + 20.45] / 9.8 = 2.61 s. Range: R = v0x*t = 14.10*2.61 = 36.8 m. Using the level-ground formula instead would have silently assumed the ball lands back at cliff height, understating both the flight time and the range.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is one of the most common traps at a science fair: a student memorizes R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g and applies it to any launch, including launches off a table, ramp, or platform where it does not belong. A judge who sees a raised launch point in a photo or diagram will often ask the student to re-derive the flight time from scratch rather than quote the formula, because that single question separates a student who understands where the formula comes from (and therefore knows when it fails) from one who has only pattern-matched a plug-in-the-numbers routine. Naming h explicitly and writing the quadratic before solving it is the tell of real understanding.

questions.prompt: Why does R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g fail for a projectile launched from the edge of a table onto the floor below?

options.text: Because gravity is weaker at table height than at floor height
Because the formula assumes launch and landing heights are equal, and here they are not
Because horizontal velocity is no longer constant once the projectile leaves the table
Because the formula only works for theta less than 45 degrees

explanations.a: The change in g over a table's height is utterly negligible; that is not the issue.
explanations.b: Correct: the formula's derivation sets y(t) = 0 at landing, which is only valid when the landing height equals the launch height.
explanations.c: Horizontal velocity stays constant throughout flight in the idealized model regardless of launch height; that assumption is unaffected by the height difference.
explanations.d: The formula's angle restriction is unrelated to this failure; it fails for any theta once launch and landing heights differ.

questions.prompt: A projectile launches from a height h above its landing point. Compared to landing at launch height with the same v0 and theta, the actual flight time is:

options.text: Longer, because the projectile must fall the extra distance h as well
Shorter, because gravity accelerates it downward sooner
The same, because horizontal and vertical motion are independent

explanations.a: Correct: the projectile must descend the additional height h beyond where level ground would have been, which strictly increases the time spent falling.
explanations.b: Gravity's acceleration g is unchanged regardless of h; a larger fall distance takes more time under constant acceleration, not less.
explanations.c: Horizontal and vertical independence explains why range and flight time can be computed separately, but it does not make flight time immune to a larger vertical drop.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding the range of a projectile launched from a height h above its landing point.

items.text: Resolve v0 into v0x = v0*cos(theta) and v0y = v0*sin(theta)
Write (1/2)*g*t^2 - v0*sin(theta)*t - h = 0 and solve for the positive root, t
Multiply v0x by the flight time t to get the range

questions.explanation: Components come first, then the vertical quadratic (which now includes the nonzero drop h) gives flight time, and only then can horizontal velocity be multiplied by that time to get range.

questions.prompt: Match each symbol in (1/2)*g*t^2 - v0*sin(theta)*t - h = 0 to what it represents.

right.text: Height of the launch point above the landing point
Initial vertical velocity component
Total time the projectile is in the air

questions.explanation: h is the extra drop distance that makes the equation a true quadratic, v0*sin(theta) is the initial vertical speed, and t is the flight duration the equation is solved for.

lessons.label: Why the Optimal Angle Drops Below 45 Degrees

sections.heading: Why 45 degrees stops being special
sections.body: On level ground, 45 degrees maximizes range because it perfectly balances two competing effects: a larger angle gives more vertical velocity (more time in the air) but less horizontal velocity (less speed covering ground), and 45 degrees is the exact angle where sin(2*theta) peaks at 1. That balance point shifts once the launch point sits above the landing point. Extra height h gives the projectile bonus hang time that has nothing to do with the launch angle — it falls that extra distance no matter which direction v0 was aimed. Because some of the flight time is now "free," the trade-off that made 45 degrees optimal on level ground no longer holds.

sections.heading: The optimal-angle formula
sections.body: Maximizing R(theta) = v0*cos(theta)*t, where t is the positive root of (1/2)*g*t^2 - v0*sin(theta)*t - h = 0, gives a closed-form result: tan(theta_opt) = v0 / sqrt(v0^2 + 2*g*h). When h = 0 this reduces to tan(theta_opt) = v0/v0 = 1, recovering the familiar 45 degrees. As h grows, the denominator grows and theta_opt shrinks, approaching 0 degrees (fully horizontal) as h becomes very large. In the limit of an extremely tall launch point, essentially all of the flight time comes from falling that huge height, so the smartest use of v0 is to point almost all of it horizontally. The same relationship can be written as sin(theta_opt) = v0 / sqrt(2*(v0^2 + g*h)), an equivalent form some references prefer because it falls out directly from the energy relation v_f^2 = v0^2 + 2*g*h; both forms give the identical angle.

sections.heading: The intuition behind the number
sections.body: Think of the total flight time as having two sources: the fraction that comes from the launch angle sending the projectile upward first, and the fraction that comes from the extra drop h it must cover regardless of angle. On level ground those two sources don't exist separately — all the hang time comes from the launch angle, so 45 degrees splits v0 evenly between height and range. Once h contributes hang time "for free," a flatter launch angle keeps most of v0 pointed horizontally without sacrificing much total flight time, because a large share of that flight time was going to happen anyway from the fall. That is why the optimal angle tilts toward horizontal as the launch height grows.

lessons.workedExample: A ball is launched at v0 = 25 m/s from a platform h = 30 m above the landing zone. tan(theta_opt) = 25 / sqrt(25^2 + 2*9.8*30) = 25 / sqrt(625 + 588) = 25 / sqrt(1213) = 25/34.83 = 0.718, so theta_opt = 35.7 degrees, about 9 degrees flatter than 45. Checking the payoff: at theta_opt = 35.7 degrees, solving the flight-time quadratic gives t = 4.37 s and R = 88.8 m. At theta = 45 degrees with the same v0 and h, t = 4.87 s but R ≈ 86.0 m. The steeper 45-degree shot is airborne longer, but the flatter 35.7-degree shot still covers more ground, because it converts more of v0 into horizontal speed without losing enough time to offset that.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use this result to test whether "45 degrees is optimal" was memorized as a universal rule or understood as a special case. A trebuchet, ski jump, or shot-put project launched from an elevated point that still claims 45 degrees as optimal is a giveaway that the student never re-derived the condition for their actual geometry. The strongest answers explain the mechanism in words before quoting the formula: extra launch height supplies flight time that does not depend on angle, so the optimal launch trades some of that angle-dependent height for more angle-independent range. A student who can say that, and who can point to their own tan(theta_opt) = v0/sqrt(v0^2+2gh) calculation, has clearly done more than look up a number.

questions.prompt: A projectile is launched from a tall tower toward a landing point far below. As the tower height h increases (v0 fixed), the optimal launch angle:

options.text: Increases above 45 degrees
Stays fixed at 45 degrees
Decreases toward 0 degrees

explanations.a: This is backward: increasing h moves the optimal angle further below 45 degrees, not above it.
explanations.b: 45 degrees is only optimal at h = 0; tan(theta_opt) = v0/sqrt(v0^2+2gh) strictly decreases as h grows, so the angle is not fixed.
explanations.c: Correct: as h grows without bound, tan(theta_opt) approaches 0, so the optimal angle approaches horizontal.

questions.prompt: What is the physical reason a flatter-than-45-degree launch can outrange a 45-degree launch when the target is below the launch point?

options.text: Gravity is weaker along a flatter trajectory
The extra height h supplies flight time independent of launch angle, so more of v0 can be spent on horizontal speed without a proportional time cost
A flatter angle experiences less air resistance
sin(2*theta) is larger for angles below 45 degrees when landing lower

explanations.a: g is constant near Earth's surface regardless of trajectory shape; this is not the mechanism.
explanations.b: Correct: because part of the flight time comes from falling the fixed height h regardless of angle, the launch can spend relatively more of v0 on horizontal speed and still stay airborne long enough to benefit.
explanations.c: This unit's model, like the level-ground model before it, assumes no air resistance; drag is not part of this result.
explanations.d: sin(2*theta) itself still peaks at theta = 45 degrees; the range-from-height formula is a different function of theta, not simply sin(2*theta).

questions.prompt: Order these launch heights h (same v0, same g) from the one with the largest optimal angle to the smallest optimal angle.

items.text: h = 0 m (level ground)
h = 10 m
h = 30 m

questions.explanation: tan(theta_opt) = v0/sqrt(v0^2+2gh) is a strictly decreasing function of h, so the optimal angle is largest at h = 0 and shrinks monotonically as h increases.

questions.prompt: Match each limiting case to the resulting optimal launch angle.

right.text: Exactly 45 degrees
Just below 45 degrees
Approaching 0 degrees (nearly horizontal)

questions.explanation: With no extra drop, 45 degrees is optimal; with an enormous drop, nearly all flight time comes from falling so the launch should be nearly horizontal; a modest drop gives a modest reduction below 45 degrees.

lessons.label: Horizontal Launches

sections.heading: The theta = 0 special case
sections.body: A horizontal launch is the cleanest possible version of launching from a height: theta = 0, so v0y = v0*sin(0) = 0 and v0x = v0*cos(0) = v0. There is no upward component at all — the object's vertical motion starts from rest and is governed entirely by gravity, exactly as if it had simply been dropped, while its horizontal motion proceeds at the full launch speed the entire time. This is the setup behind the classic lab: a ball rolls off the edge of a table with horizontal speed v0 and falls a table height h to the floor. It is also the everyday case behind a bullet fired level from a rifle, a stream of water leaving a horizontal hose, or a coin rolled off a countertop; all of them share the same reduced kinematics because none of them start with any vertical push.

sections.heading: Time of flight depends on height alone
sections.body: Because v0y = 0, the vertical equation y(t) = -(1/2)*g*t^2 = -h has no linear term in t, so solving for t does not require the quadratic formula at all: t = sqrt(2*h/g). Notice that the launch speed v0 does not appear anywhere in this expression — for a horizontal launch, how far the object travels horizontally before landing has no effect on how long it takes to fall, because horizontal and vertical motion are independent. A bullet fired perfectly horizontally and a bullet simply dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same instant, even though one has traveled a great horizontal distance and the other has traveled none. This is the single cleanest demonstration of independence of motion in the entire projectile-motion unit, because the horizontal motion is not just decoupled from the vertical motion, it contributes nothing to it at all.

sections.heading: Range follows directly
sections.body: Once t = sqrt(2*h/g) is known, the horizontal range is just R = v0*t = v0*sqrt(2*h/g). This single clean formula, with no trigonometry required, is exactly why the horizontal-launch geometry is the standard first lab exercise for projectile motion: students can predict R from a measured table height h and a measured or known launch speed v0, then fire the projectile and check the prediction directly against a landing mark on the floor, isolating exactly one variable (height) instead of juggling an angle as well. Because R is directly proportional to v0 (rather than to v0^2 as in the general angled case), doubling the launch speed off the same table exactly doubles the range, a relationship simple enough that students can verify it with just two trials and a tape measure.

lessons.workedExample: A steel ball rolls off a lab table of height h = 1.2 m with horizontal speed v0 = 2.5 m/s. Time to fall: t = sqrt(2*1.2/9.8) = sqrt(0.245) = 0.495 s. Range: R = v0*t = 2.5*0.495 = 1.24 m. If the same ball were simply dropped straight down from the same table edge with no horizontal push at all, it would still take exactly 0.495 s to hit the floor, landing directly below the table edge instead of 1.24 m away, because the vertical motion, and therefore the fall time, does not depend on v0 at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: The horizontal launch is a favorite quick check because it exposes whether a student actually understands independence of motion or has just memorized "projectile problems use trig." A judge might ask what happens to the fall time if v0 is doubled: the correct answer is nothing at all, since t = sqrt(2h/g) has no v0 in it, only the range doubles. A student who reflexively reaches for sin(theta) and cos(theta) in a horizontal-launch problem, instead of recognizing theta = 0 collapses those to 0 and 1, is signaling that the general formulas were memorized rather than understood as instances of a more general framework.

questions.prompt: A ball rolls horizontally off a table at v0 = 3 m/s. If v0 were instead 6 m/s (same table height), the time to reach the floor would:

options.text: Double
Stay exactly the same
Be cut in half

explanations.a: Fall time depends only on height and g through t = sqrt(2h/g); it has no dependence on v0 at all.
explanations.b: Correct: because vertical and horizontal motion are independent, and the vertical motion starts with zero vertical velocity regardless of v0, fall time is set entirely by h and g.
explanations.c: Fall time does not shrink with faster horizontal launch; only the range (how far horizontally it travels before landing) would double.

questions.prompt: For a horizontal launch (theta = 0) from height h, which quantity correctly gives the range?

options.text: R = v0^2*sin(2*theta)/g
R = v0*sqrt(2*h/g)
R = sqrt(2*h*g)
R = v0*h/g

explanations.a: The level-ground range formula assumes equal launch and landing heights and also assumes theta contributes vertical velocity; neither holds here.
explanations.b: Correct: fall time is t = sqrt(2h/g), and range is horizontal speed times that time, R = v0*sqrt(2h/g).
explanations.c: This has no v0 in it at all, which cannot be right since range must scale with launch speed.
explanations.d: This is not dimensionally or algebraically consistent with the correct derivation; it does not come from t = sqrt(2h/g).

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding the range of a horizontal launch off a table of height h.

items.text: Recognize v0y = v0*sin(0) = 0, so the vertical motion starts from rest
Solve -(1/2)*g*t^2 = -h for t, giving t = sqrt(2h/g)
Multiply v0 (the full launch speed, since v0x = v0) by t to get R

questions.explanation: Recognizing the zero vertical launch component comes first, then that simplifies the vertical equation enough to solve for t directly, and only then is t combined with the unchanged horizontal speed to get range.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity in the horizontal-launch geometry to what it depends on.

right.text: Height h and g only
Both v0 and h (through the fall time)
Always zero, since theta = 0

questions.explanation: Fall time comes purely from height and gravity; range multiplies that fall time by v0, so it depends on both; and the vertical launch component is zero by definition when theta = 0.

lessons.label: Landing Below the Launch Point

sections.heading: The full quadratic, this time solved
sections.body: Lesson one set up (1/2)*g*t^2 - v0*sin(theta)*t - h = 0 for a projectile landing a height h below its launch point. This lesson finishes the job: apply the quadratic formula with a = g/2, b = -v0*sin(theta), c = -h, giving t = [v0*sin(theta) +/- sqrt((v0*sin(theta))^2 + 2*g*h)] / g. Because h > 0, the quantity under the square root is strictly larger than (v0*sin(theta))^2, which means the square root itself is strictly larger than v0*sin(theta) in magnitude. That single fact determines the sign of both roots without needing to plug in numbers. It is worth noticing, too, that this is genuinely a two-root situation in a way the level-ground case never was: on level ground the constant term c is zero, so t = 0 is trivially always one root, and the quadratic formula was never really needed. Here c = -h is nonzero, so both roots require the full formula, and both need to be interpreted.

sections.heading: Why one root is always negative
sections.body: Take the minus sign first: t_minus = [v0*sin(theta) - sqrt((v0*sin(theta))^2 + 2*g*h)] / g. Since the square root term is always larger than v0*sin(theta) whenever h > 0, the numerator is always negative, so t_minus < 0 for every physically meaningful launch. A negative time is not a measurement error to be discarded arbitrarily — it has a precise meaning: it is the moment when the idealized parabola, if extended backward before the actual launch, would have crossed that same height on an imaginary earlier arc. Since the projectile did not exist before t = 0, that root describes no real event and is always dropped. This is exactly analogous to solving a quadratic for where a ball's full, unrestricted parabolic path crosses a particular height twice — once on a hypothetical rise before the object was ever launched, and once for real, on the way down, after launch.

sections.heading: The physical root
sections.body: The plus root, t_plus = [v0*sin(theta) + sqrt((v0*sin(theta))^2 + 2*g*h)] / g, is always positive by the same reasoning, and it is the one used for the actual flight time. Once t_plus is known, range follows exactly as before: R = v0*cos(theta)*t_plus. Notice this reduces correctly to the level-ground formula when h = 0: the square root becomes sqrt((v0*sin(theta))^2) = v0*sin(theta) (since v0*sin(theta) >= 0 for a launch above horizontal), so t_plus collapses to 2*v0*sin(theta)/g, the familiar level-ground time of flight. This consistency check, setting h = 0 and confirming the older formula falls out, is a useful habit any time a new formula is derived: a correct general result should always reduce cleanly to the special case it is generalizing.

lessons.workedExample: From a footbridge 15 m above a river, a rock is thrown at v0 = 10 m/s, theta = 30 degrees above horizontal. v0*sin(theta) = 10*0.5 = 5. The quadratic 4.9*t^2 - 5*t - 15 = 0 has discriminant 5^2 + 4*4.9*15 = 25 + 294 = 319, sqrt(319) = 17.86. The two roots are t = (5+17.86)/9.8 = 2.33 s and t = (5-17.86)/9.8 = -1.31 s. The negative root is discarded as unphysical; it is where the extended parabola would have crossed river height before the rock was ever thrown. Using t = 2.33 s, the range is R = v0*cos(theta)*t = 10*0.866*2.33 = 20.2 m from the bridge rail.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge handed a quadratic with two roots is testing whether a student can identify which root is physical, and more importantly, explain why the other one is not simply "wrong." The weak answer is "you throw out the negative one because time can't be negative." The strong answer explains what the negative root represents: the backward extension of the same idealized trajectory to a moment before the object was launched. That distinction, between a root being unphysical for this particular launch versus meaningless in general, is exactly the kind of reasoning a science-fair judge uses to separate memorized procedure from genuine command of the model.

questions.prompt: Solving (1/2)*g*t^2 - v0*sin(theta)*t - h = 0 for h > 0 always yields:

options.text: Two positive roots
One positive root and one negative root
Two negative roots
No real roots

explanations.a: The minus-sign root is always negative when h > 0, so both roots cannot be positive.
explanations.b: Correct: because the discriminant term always exceeds v0*sin(theta) in magnitude when h > 0, the plus root is positive and the minus root is negative.
explanations.c: The plus-sign root is always positive when h > 0, so both roots cannot be negative.
explanations.d: The discriminant (v0*sin(theta))^2 + 2*g*h is a sum of nonnegative terms with h > 0, so it is always positive and real roots always exist.

questions.prompt: What does the negative root of the landing-time quadratic physically represent?

options.text: A measurement error that should simply be ignored
The time the idealized parabola, extended backward before the actual launch, would have crossed the landing height
The time of flight if the projectile were launched downward instead of upward
The time at which the projectile reaches its maximum height

explanations.a: It is not an error; it is a mathematically meaningful root of the same equation, just one that describes an event before the object existed.
explanations.b: Correct: the quadratic describes an idealized, infinitely-extended parabola, and the negative root is where that extended curve crosses the landing height before t = 0.
explanations.c: Launching downward instead of upward would change theta and v0*sin(theta), producing a different quadratic altogether, not simply flip which root is physical.
explanations.d: Maximum height occurs at t = v0*sin(theta)/g, a different quantity from either root of the landing-time equation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding the correct flight time when a projectile lands below its launch point.

items.text: Write the quadratic (1/2)*g*t^2 - v0*sin(theta)*t - h = 0
Apply the quadratic formula to get two roots, one positive and one negative
Discard the negative root as describing a moment before launch
Use the positive root as the true flight time

questions.explanation: The quadratic must be written first, then solved for both roots, then the negative root is rejected on physical grounds, leaving the positive root as the actual flight time.

questions.prompt: Match each root sign in t = [v0*sin(theta) +/- sqrt((v0*sin(theta))^2+2gh)]/g to its physical status when h > 0.

right.text: Always positive; the actual flight time
Always negative; describes the extended parabola before launch

questions.explanation: Because h > 0 makes the square-root term strictly larger than v0*sin(theta), adding it always gives a positive result and subtracting it always gives a negative one.

lessons.label: Projectile onto an Inclined Plane

sections.heading: Landing on a slope, not a flat floor
sections.body: When a projectile is launched from the base of an incline that rises at angle phi above the horizontal, the landing surface is no longer y = 0 but the line y = x*tan(phi). "Range" now more usefully means the distance measured along the slope from launch point to landing point, not the horizontal distance. This geometry shows up in real sports and ballistics problems: a golf shot up a hillside fairway, an artillery shell fired at a target on higher ground, or a ski jumper landing on a sloped hill all share this same structure. It is also the natural generalization of the two previous lessons: launching from a height is the case where the "incline" is a vertical drop, and level ground is the case where phi = 0, so an incline problem sits on a continuum between those two extremes.

sections.heading: Using the incline as a constraint
sections.body: Rather than rotating the coordinate axes, the landing condition can be written directly by substituting the projectile's own x(t) = v0*cos(theta)*t and y(t) = v0*sin(theta)*t - (1/2)*g*t^2 into the incline's equation y = x*tan(phi), then solving for the nonzero root t (dividing through by t once, exactly as in the level-ground derivation). This gives t = 2*v0*sin(theta - phi) / (g*cos(phi)). The horizontal distance traveled is x(t) = v0*cos(theta)*t, and because horizontal distance x relates to slope distance R by x = R*cos(phi), the range measured along the incline works out to R = 2*v0^2*cos(theta)*sin(theta - phi) / (g*cos^2(phi)). Setting phi = 0 recovers the familiar level-ground range formula exactly, since cos(0) = 1 collapses the denominator to g and sin(theta - 0) = sin(theta) restores the original form. An equivalent method rotates the x and y axes so one axis runs along the incline surface; it gives the identical answer, but substituting the constraint directly avoids the bookkeeping of transforming gravity into tilted components.

sections.heading: Why the optimal angle bisects the incline and the vertical
sections.body: Using the identity cos(theta)*sin(theta - phi) = (1/2)*[sin(2*theta - phi) - sin(phi)], the incline range becomes R = [v0^2 / (g*cos^2(phi))] * [sin(2*theta - phi) - sin(phi)]. Since phi is fixed by the terrain, R is maximized exactly when sin(2*theta - phi) is maximized, which happens at 2*theta - phi = 90 degrees, giving theta_opt = 45 + phi/2. Geometrically, the incline direction sits at angle phi above horizontal and the true vertical sits at 90 degrees above horizontal; the optimal launch direction, 45 + phi/2, is precisely halfway between them, so it bisects the angle between the incline surface and straight up. The same derivation applied to a downhill target (where the ground falls away at angle phi below the launch point) gives theta_opt = 45 - phi/2 instead, bisecting the angle between the downhill slope and vertical on the other side — a mirror image of the uphill result, and a useful check that the formula is being applied with the correct sign for phi.

lessons.workedExample: A cannon at the base of a hillside that rises at phi = 20 degrees fires at v0 = 20 m/s. The optimal angle is theta_opt = 45 + 20/2 = 55 degrees. Range along the slope: R = 2*(20^2)*cos(55)*sin(55-20) / (9.8*cos^2(20)) = 2*400*cos(55)*sin(35) / (9.8*(0.9397)^2). Since cos(55) = sin(35) = 0.5736 exactly (co-function angles), this is 800*(0.5736)^2 / (9.8*0.883) = 800*0.329 / 8.65 = 263.2/8.65 = 30.4 m measured up the slope. Firing at 45 degrees instead, without adjusting for the incline, would land noticeably shorter of that mark, since 45 degrees is only optimal for phi = 0.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the most conceptually demanding lesson in the unit, and judges use it to test whether a student can extend a familiar result to unfamiliar terrain rather than just recite theta_opt = 45+phi/2 as a fact. A strong answer explains the bisection geometrically (the optimal direction splits the angle between the slope and vertical) as well as algebraically (from maximizing sin(2*theta-phi)), and can state what happens for a downhill target, where the same reasoning gives theta_opt = 45 - phi/2. A student who can derive, not just quote, this result has shown they understand optimization on a fixed constraint surface, a genuinely advanced skill for a science fair project.

questions.prompt: For a projectile launched up an incline of angle phi (from its base), the launch angle that maximizes range measured along the slope is:

options.text: theta_opt = 45 degrees, unchanged from level ground
theta_opt = 45 + phi/2
theta_opt = phi
theta_opt = 90 - phi

explanations.a: 45 degrees is only optimal for phi = 0; the incline changes the optimum.
explanations.b: Correct: maximizing sin(2*theta - phi) in the slope-range formula gives 2*theta - phi = 90 degrees, so theta_opt = 45 + phi/2.
explanations.c: theta = phi would aim the projectile parallel to the slope surface at launch, which is not the range-maximizing choice.
explanations.d: This does not follow from maximizing the range-along-incline formula; it is not the correct optimum.

questions.prompt: Geometrically, what does the optimal launch direction theta_opt = 45 + phi/2 represent relative to the incline?

options.text: It points directly along the incline surface
It bisects the angle between the incline surface and the true vertical
It is always exactly perpendicular to the incline surface

explanations.a: Pointing along the surface would mean theta = phi, which wastes the launch speed on grazing the slope rather than gaining range.
explanations.b: Correct: the incline sits at phi above horizontal and vertical sits at 90 degrees above horizontal; 45+phi/2 is exactly halfway between those two directions.
explanations.c: Perpendicular to the incline would be theta = phi + 90 degrees, a different and much steeper direction than the actual optimum.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that derive the range along an incline of angle phi.

items.text: Write the incline surface as the line y = x*tan(phi)
Substitute the projectile's x(t) and y(t) into that line equation and solve for the nonzero time root
Convert the horizontal distance x(t) into slope distance R using x = R*cos(phi)
Simplify with a product-to-sum identity to find the theta that maximizes R

questions.explanation: The incline must be defined as a constraint line first, then the landing time follows from intersecting the trajectory with that line, then horizontal distance is converted to slope distance, and only then is the result optimized over theta.

questions.prompt: Match each incline scenario to its optimal launch angle.

left.text: Launching up a phi = 20 degree incline
Launching down a phi = 20 degree incline (target below launch)

right.text: 45 degrees
55 degrees
35 degrees

questions.explanation: theta_opt = 45+phi/2 for an uphill target gives 55 degrees at phi=20; the corresponding downhill case uses theta_opt = 45-phi/2, giving 35 degrees; level ground is the phi=0 baseline of 45 degrees.

lessons.label: The Monkey and the Hunter

sections.heading: The setup: aim directly at a falling target
sections.body: A classic classroom demonstration mounts a target on an electromagnet in a tree, aims a spring-loaded dart gun directly at the target (not above it, the way you would compensate for a stationary target's drop), and wires the gun so that firing the dart simultaneously cuts power to the electromagnet, releasing the target at the exact instant the dart leaves the muzzle. Intuition says the falling target should slip out from under a straight-aimed shot. The demonstration reliably shows the opposite: the dart hits the falling target every time, regardless of the dart's speed, as long as it has enough speed to reach the target's horizontal position before either one hits the ground.

sections.heading: Why gravity cannot be aimed around
sections.body: The proof rests entirely on independence of motion. If there were no gravity, a dart aimed directly at the target's initial position would travel in a straight line and arrive exactly at that position after some time t, since nothing would deflect it. With gravity, the dart's actual vertical position at time t is its straight-line, no-gravity position minus (1/2)*g*t^2 of drop. But the target's position at time t is also its starting height minus (1/2)*g*t^2 of drop, since it too falls freely from rest starting at t = 0. Both the dart and the target lose the identical amount of height to gravity in the identical amount of time, so whatever vertical gap gravity opens up for the dart, it opens the exact same gap for the target, and the two curves meet exactly where the straight-line aim pointed.

sections.heading: What the demonstration actually proves
sections.body: The result does not depend on the dart's speed, the launch angle, or the horizontal distance to the target, only on the dart having enough speed to arrive before the target reaches the ground. This makes the demonstration a clean, direct proof that horizontal motion and vertical motion truly are independent under gravity: the horizontal motion determines only when the two objects are at the same horizontal position, while gravity acts identically on both regardless of their different horizontal speeds (zero for the target, nonzero for the dart). It is the same principle behind why a bullet fired horizontally and one simply dropped from the same height land at the same time, extended to two objects that both start falling from the same instant.

lessons.workedExample: A dart gun aims directly at a target hanging 5 m up a tree, 6 m away horizontally, so the aim angle is theta = arctan(5/6) = 39.8 degrees above horizontal. The dart launches at v0 = 15 m/s the instant the target is released. Horizontal speed: v0*cos(39.8) = 15*0.768 = 11.52 m/s, so the dart reaches the target's horizontal position at t = 6/11.52 = 0.521 s. In that time both objects fall (1/2)*9.8*(0.521)^2 = 1.33 m below their straight-line, no-gravity paths. The target's height at that instant is 5 - 1.33 = 3.67 m, and the dart's actual height (its straight-line aim height of 5 m at x=6, minus the same 1.33 m drop) is also 3.67 m: they meet.
lessons.judgeFraming: The monkey-and-hunter demonstration is a favorite because it looks paradoxical and forces a student to reach for the underlying principle rather than a formula. A judge will often ask what would change if the dart were fired faster or slower: the correct answer is that the meeting point along the aim line changes, but the two objects still meet, as long as the dart arrives before the target lands. A student who can explain why using "both objects fall (1/2)g*t^2 in the same time t, regardless of horizontal speed" is demonstrating command of the independence-of-motion principle itself, not just a memorized punchline about a monkey.

questions.prompt: A hunter aims a rifle directly at a monkey in a tree. At the instant of firing, the monkey lets go and free-falls. Assuming the bullet has enough speed to arrive before the monkey lands, the bullet:

options.text: Passes above the monkey, since the monkey drops out of the way
Still hits the monkey, because both fall the same distance under gravity in the same time
Passes below the monkey, since the bullet also drops due to gravity

explanations.a: This is the mistaken intuition the demonstration is designed to correct: the monkey's drop does not let it escape the straight-aimed shot.
explanations.b: Correct: the bullet's actual path is its straight-line aim minus (1/2)g*t^2 of drop, and the monkey's path is its starting height minus that same (1/2)g*t^2, so they always meet.
explanations.c: The bullet does drop due to gravity, but so does the monkey, by exactly the same amount in the same time, so neither passes the other.

questions.prompt: What is the essential physical principle the monkey-and-hunter demonstration proves?

options.text: Bullets travel in perfectly straight lines regardless of gravity
All objects near Earth's surface fall the same vertical distance in the same time under gravity, independent of their horizontal motion
Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones
Air resistance cancels out the effect of gravity on both objects

explanations.a: The demonstration explicitly relies on the bullet dropping due to gravity, not traveling in a straight line.
explanations.b: Correct: because both the bullet and the target lose the same (1/2)g*t^2 to gravity in the same elapsed time, their horizontal speeds (which differ) are irrelevant to how much each falls vertically.
explanations.c: This demonstration involves no comparison of falling rates by mass; both objects are governed only by g, independent of mass.
explanations.d: The idealized version of this demonstration assumes no air resistance; it is not part of why the result holds.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the monkey-and-hunter demonstration.

items.text: The gun is aimed directly at the target's initial position
The dart is fired and, simultaneously, the target is released to free-fall
Both the dart and the target fall (1/2)*g*t^2 below their respective straight-line, no-gravity paths
The dart and the target arrive at the same point at the same time

questions.explanation: The gun must be aimed before firing, firing and release happen simultaneously by design, gravity then acts equally on both over the shared flight time, and the equal drop is exactly what makes them meet.

questions.prompt: Match each object in the demonstration to its horizontal and vertical motion.

right.text: Nonzero horizontal velocity; vertical position drops by (1/2)*g*t^2 from its straight-line aim path
Zero horizontal velocity; vertical position drops by (1/2)*g*t^2 from its starting height

questions.explanation: The dart moves horizontally toward the target while also dropping under gravity relative to its straight-line aim, while the target has no horizontal motion at all and simply free-falls straight down; both lose the identical vertical distance to gravity in the same time.

units.label: Measuring Projectile Motion in the Lab

lessons.label: Launchers and Repeatable Release

sections.heading: Spring launchers vs. pneumatic launchers
sections.body: A spring-loaded launcher stores energy by compressing a spring a fixed distance against a catch, then releases it to drive a ball or dart down a barrel. Cocking to the same notch every time (most classroom launchers have 2-3 fixed compression settings) makes the stored energy, and therefore the muzzle speed, repeatable to within a percent or two. A pneumatic launcher instead stores energy as compressed air in a chamber, released through a valve when triggered; because gas pressure can be dialed to a continuous range and read off a gauge, pneumatic launchers give finer control over launch speed than a spring's fixed notches, at the cost of needing a pump and a pressure regulator. Both designs share the same physics goal: convert a fixed, measurable store of energy into projectile kinetic energy through the same mechanical path every trial, so that v0 does not drift from shot to shot.

sections.heading: Why repeatability is the whole experiment
sections.body: Projectile motion labs typically measure a downstream quantity, range, height, or time of flight, and then work backward to infer v0 or test a formula. That inference is only valid if v0 itself is treated as a controlled, known constant across trials. If the launcher's release is inconsistent, the study is not measuring the physics of projectile motion at all, it is measuring launcher noise. This is why a repeatable release is a prerequisite, not just good practice: propagated uncertainty from the launcher's own variability is often the single largest error term in a projectile lab, larger than any timing or measurement error downstream.

sections.heading: Sources of shot-to-shot variation
sections.body: Even a well-built launcher varies for identifiable reasons. Friction between the projectile and barrel changes with cleanliness, temperature, and wear, so a barrel that has not been wiped down or that has picked up grit fires inconsistently. The projectile's mass or shape can vary between individual balls in a batch, changing the mass a given spring force accelerates. Incomplete or inconsistent seating, the ball not pushed fully to the same starting position against the catch, changes the effective compression distance and thus the stored energy. Trigger technique matters too: a hand that nudges the launcher while releasing it adds a small, uncontrolled velocity component. Reducing these effects means using the same projectile every trial, cleaning the barrel periodically, mounting the launcher rigidly (clamped to a table, not hand-held) so trigger action cannot perturb aim, and always compressing to the same detent.

lessons.workedExample: A team fires a spring launcher on its middle detent 10 times at a fixed angle and photogates the muzzle speed each shot: 4.82, 4.79, 4.85, 4.81, 4.90, 4.77, 4.83, 4.80, 4.84, 4.79 m/s. The mean is 4.82 m/s with a standard deviation of about 0.04 m/s (roughly 0.8% of the mean), which the team reports as v0 = 4.82 +/- 0.04 m/s. They notice trial 5 (4.90 m/s) is the outlier and trace it to the barrel not having been wiped since the previous week, so they add barrel-cleaning to their trial protocol and rerun that block, tightening the spread to about 0.5%.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about launch repeatability because it is the assumption every downstream range or trajectory measurement rests on, and it is cheap to check: a student who reports v0 as a single number without ever firing repeated shots to characterize its spread has skipped the step that makes every later number trustworthy. A student who instead says "we fired 10 calibration shots, got a 0.8% spread, and used that spread to set our error bars on predicted range" has shown they understand that a projectile launcher is a measurement instrument with its own uncertainty, not a magic black box that outputs a fixed speed.

questions.prompt: Why is a repeatable release considered essential in a projectile motion lab, rather than just a nice-to-have?

options.text: It makes the launcher look more professional to judges
Every measurement of range, time of flight, or trajectory implicitly assumes v0 is a known, controlled constant across trials
It is required by science-fair safety rules for spring-loaded devices
It reduces the mass of the projectile

explanations.a: Repeatability is a scientific requirement, not a presentation concern; it has nothing to do with appearance.
explanations.b: Correct: if v0 varies unpredictably between trials, downstream measurements reflect launcher noise instead of the physics being tested.
explanations.c: Safety rules govern handling, not the statistical validity of the launch speed across trials.
explanations.d: Release consistency has no effect on projectile mass, which is a separate, fixed property of the ball or dart.

questions.prompt: A pneumatic launcher's main advantage over a spring launcher with fixed detents is:

options.text: It requires no calibration at all
It can dial launch speed to a continuous range via a pressure gauge, rather than a few fixed settings
It eliminates air resistance during flight
It always produces zero variance between shots

explanations.a: Pneumatic launchers still need calibration (photogating) to know their actual v0 at a given pressure.
explanations.b: Correct: compressed-air pressure is continuously adjustable and gauge-readable, unlike a spring's 2-3 discrete detents.
explanations.c: Air resistance acts on the projectile in flight and is unrelated to how the launcher stores its energy.
explanations.d: No real launcher has zero shot-to-shot variance; pneumatic launchers still show a few percent spread.

questions.prompt: Match each source of launch variation to a fix that directly addresses it.

left.text: Barrel friction changes with grit and wear
Projectile not seated to the same starting position
Hand nudges the launcher while releasing it

right.text: Clean the barrel on a fixed schedule
Use a seating gauge or fixed stop before every shot
Mount the launcher rigidly to a table

questions.explanation: Barrel friction is addressed by periodic cleaning, inconsistent seating is addressed by a fixed stop, and trigger-hand disturbance is addressed by clamping the launcher so no manual force reaches it at release.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a team should follow to establish that their launcher's release is repeatable enough to trust for a lab.

items.text: Fix the launcher rigidly and compress to the same detent every time
Fire a batch of calibration shots (e.g., 10) at that fixed setting
Time each shot's muzzle speed (e.g., with photogates)
Compute the mean and spread (standard deviation) of the calibration shots

questions.explanation: The launcher must first be set up for a fixed, repeatable configuration, then fired repeatedly, with each shot timed, before the resulting speeds can be summarized into a mean and spread.

lessons.label: Measuring Muzzle Velocity

sections.heading: Two photogates and a stopwatch you cannot mistime
sections.body: The standard way to measure a launcher's muzzle velocity is to mount two photogates, small infrared beam-and-sensor pairs, a fixed, precisely measured distance d apart right at the muzzle, in the projectile's flight path. Each photogate triggers a timer the instant the projectile blocks its beam. The projectile blocks gate 1 at time t1 and gate 2 at time t2; because d is small (often 5-15 cm) and gravity's effect on speed over that short a gap is negligible, the average speed d/(t2-t1) is an excellent estimate of the instantaneous muzzle speed v0. This beats a human with a stopwatch by orders of magnitude: human reaction time is roughly 150-250 ms, comparable to or longer than the entire flight event being timed, while photogate electronics resolve timing to microseconds.

sections.heading: Alternatives when you do not have photogates
sections.body: High-speed or even standard smartphone video (many phones now shoot 120-240 frames per second) can substitute: film the projectile passing two marked reference points a known distance apart, then count frames between the two crossings and divide by the frame rate to get elapsed time, exactly the photogate logic but with a coarser timing resolution set by 1/framerate instead of microseconds. A purely ballistic method sidesteps timing electronics altogether: launch the projectile straight up (or at a known angle) and measure the maximum height or the total range at a known angle, then solve the kinematics equations backward for v0. This trades timing precision for geometric measurement precision, so its accuracy now depends on how well height or range can be measured, not on the timer.

sections.heading: Reporting v0 with an honest uncertainty
sections.body: A single measurement is not a scientific value, a value paired with an uncertainty is. Fire the calibration set (5-10+ shots) at the intended launcher setting, compute the mean v0 and the standard deviation of the individual measurements, and report v0 as mean +/- standard deviation (or +/- the standard error of the mean, sd/sqrt(n), if you specifically want the uncertainty on the mean itself, which shrinks as you add trials). This number then propagates into every prediction the lab makes: if v0 = 4.8 +/- 0.1 m/s, a predicted range computed from it should carry its own propagated uncertainty band, not be reported as a bare, falsely precise decimal.

lessons.workedExample: Two photogates are mounted 0.100 m apart at a launcher's muzzle. A ball blocks gate 1 at t1 = 0.02184 s and gate 2 at t2 = 0.04298 s (times from the same internal clock), giving elapsed time 0.02114 s. Average speed = 0.100 m / 0.02114 s = 4.73 m/s. Repeating this 8 times gives a mean of 4.75 m/s with a standard deviation of 0.06 m/s, so the team reports v0 = 4.75 +/- 0.06 m/s (about 1.3%). They cross-check with 120 fps video of the same launcher timing a 0.20 m span, which is coarser (each frame is 8.3 ms, comparable to the whole event) but agrees within its wider uncertainty at 4.6-5.0 m/s, confirming the photogate number is not an instrumental artifact.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe muzzle-velocity measurement to see whether a student understands what limits their timing precision, not just that they used a photogate. A student who can explain why d is chosen small (gravity's effect on speed over the gap is negligible) but not too small (timing resolution and beam width start to matter), and who reports v0 with a spread from repeated trials rather than a single shot, demonstrates real metrology. A student who reports "v0 = 4.8 m/s" from one measurement with no repeat trials and no stated method has not actually measured anything defensible.

questions.prompt: Two photogates are 0.150 m apart. A projectile blocks gate 1 at t = 0.0500 s and gate 2 at t = 0.0680 s. What is the estimated muzzle speed?

explanations.a: Correct: elapsed time is 0.0680 - 0.0500 = 0.0180 s, so speed = 0.150 m / 0.0180 s = 8.33 m/s.
explanations.b: This does not match d/(delta t) using the correct elapsed time of 0.0180 s.
explanations.c: This is not the result of dividing 0.150 m by the correct elapsed time interval.
explanations.d: This confuses the distance itself with a speed; units and the division step are both missing.

questions.prompt: Why do photogates give a far more precise muzzle-velocity estimate than a human with a stopwatch?

options.text: Photogates are more expensive, and expensive equipment is always more accurate
Human reaction time (roughly 150-250 ms) is comparable to or longer than the whole flight event, while photogate electronics time to microseconds
Photogates measure distance instead of time
A stopwatch cannot be reset between trials

explanations.a: Cost is not the causal mechanism; the relevant factor is the relative size of the timing error to the event being timed.
explanations.b: Correct: when your timing error is as large as the event itself, the measurement is nearly worthless; photogates remove that error almost entirely.
explanations.c: Photogates measure time (when the beam breaks), exactly like a stopwatch does; the improvement is in timing precision, not in what quantity is measured.
explanations.d: Stopwatches can be reset between trials; this is not the source of their imprecision here.

questions.prompt: Match each muzzle-velocity method to the factor that most limits its precision.

left.text: Two photogates a known distance apart
Solving kinematics backward from measured range or height

right.text: Electronic beam-break timing (microsecond resolution)
Frame rate sets the timing resolution (1/framerate per frame)
Precision of the measured height or range itself, not any timer

questions.explanation: Photogates are limited by their electronic timing resolution (very fine), video is limited by how many frames per second it captures, and the purely ballistic method has no timer at all, so its precision is set by how well the geometric landing point or height is measured.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for reporting a defensible v0 with uncertainty.

items.text: Fix the launcher setting and photogate spacing
Fire and time a batch of calibration shots (e.g., 8-10)
Compute the mean speed across the batch
Compute the standard deviation (or standard error) and report v0 = mean +/- spread

questions.explanation: The setup must be fixed first, then a batch of shots collected and timed, before a mean can be computed, and only after the mean exists can a spread be calculated around it.

lessons.label: Video Tracking a Trajectory

sections.heading: Turning a video into x(t) and y(t)
sections.body: Frame-by-frame video analysis tools — Tracker (free, open-source software built on the Open Source Physics framework) is the standard classroom choice — let a student click the projectile's position in every frame of a recorded flight. Each click is logged as a pixel coordinate at a known time (frame number divided by frame rate), so stepping through the whole clip builds two time series: x(t), the horizontal position, and y(t), the vertical position, both in pixels and seconds. This is powerful because it recovers the entire trajectory shape, not just a single range or height number, letting a student check whether y(t) really is parabolic in t and whether x(t) really is linear in t, the two core predictions of projectile motion with negligible drag.

sections.heading: Scaling pixels into meters
sections.body: Raw tracker output is in pixels, which are meaningless without a scale. The standard fix is to place a reference object of known length in the same camera plane as the motion, a meter stick, a marked pole, or a known board width, visible in the frame, and tell the software that object's real-world length; it then computes a pixels-to-meters conversion factor and rescales every position. This only works if the reference object lies in the same plane as the projectile's motion (same distance from the camera); a reference object placed closer to or farther from the camera than the trajectory itself will be scaled wrong due to perspective, silently distorting every derived position, velocity, and acceleration.

sections.heading: Frame rate is the clock's resolution
sections.body: Video timing has a hard floor: the time between one recorded frame and the next. At 30 fps that gap is 33.3 ms; at 120 fps it shrinks to 8.3 ms; specialized high-speed cameras can push into the microseconds. This matters because a projectile in free flight for, say, half a second only gets 15 data points at 30 fps but 60 at 120 fps, and every one of those points carries a timing uncertainty of about half a frame interval. A trajectory fit (fitting y(t) to a parabola to extract g, for instance) gets systematically noisier and less precise at lower frame rates, both because there are fewer points to fit and because each point's time is less exact, so choosing the highest frame rate the camera supports is one of the cheapest precision upgrades available in a video-tracking lab.

lessons.workedExample: A student films a launched ball at 120 fps against a wall with a meter stick clamped in the same plane as the flight. In Tracker, she calibrates the meter stick (1.00 m spanning 400 pixels, so 1 pixel = 0.0025 m) and clicks the ball's position in all 42 frames it is airborne. Plotting y(t) in Tracker's built-in fit tool, the software fits y(t) = y0 + v0y*t - (1/2)g*t^2 and returns g = 9.79 m/s^2, within 0.2% of the accepted 9.81 m/s^2. She notes that at 30 fps the same flight would have given only about 10-11 points, which she checks separately and finds does return a noticeably less precise fit (g = 9.6 +/- 0.4 m/s^2 vs. 9.79 +/- 0.05 m/s^2 at 120 fps).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about video tracking because two silent failure modes are common and easy to probe: scaling error from a reference object not in the same plane as the motion, and undersampling from too low a frame rate. A student who explains that they placed the meter stick specifically in the plane of the ball's flight, and who can state their frame rate and why it was sufficient to resolve the trajectory, shows they understand video tracking is a measurement technique with its own error sources, not just a matter of clicking on a video until a nice curve appears.

questions.prompt: A reference meter stick used for scaling a Tracker video is placed noticeably closer to the camera than the actual projectile trajectory. What happens?

options.text: Nothing; scale factors are unaffected by depth in the frame
The pixels-to-meters conversion is distorted by perspective, silently skewing every derived position and velocity
The frame rate automatically corrects for the depth difference
Only the time values become inaccurate, not the position values

explanations.a: Depth strongly affects apparent pixel size (closer objects look bigger), so scale is very much affected by placement.
explanations.b: Correct: an object closer to the camera subtends more pixels per real meter than one farther away, so the scale factor derived from it is wrong for the actual trajectory's plane.
explanations.c: Frame rate governs timing resolution, not spatial scaling; it has no corrective effect on a perspective error.
explanations.d: Position values are exactly what gets distorted by an incorrect scale factor; time values, based on frame count, are unaffected.

questions.prompt: Why does raising the camera's frame rate from 30 fps to 120 fps typically improve a trajectory fit's precision?

options.text: It increases the projectile's actual speed
It changes the value of g itself
It provides more data points across the flight and reduces the timing uncertainty per point (half of a shorter frame interval)
It automatically removes air resistance from the flight

explanations.a: The frame rate is a property of the recording device, not the physical motion; it cannot change the projectile's speed.
explanations.b: g is a property of the local gravitational field, entirely unaffected by how the flight is recorded.
explanations.c: Correct: more frames per second means both more points to fit the parabola to and a tighter bound (about half a frame) on each point's time.
explanations.d: Air resistance is a physical force on the projectile, unrelated to the camera's recording rate.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of extracting x(t) and y(t) from a projectile video using tracking software.

items.text: Film the flight with a reference object of known length visible in the same plane of motion
Calibrate the software's scale using the reference object's known length
Click the projectile's position in each frame to log pixel coordinates and times
Let the software convert the logged pixel coordinates into real x(t) and y(t) in meters and seconds

questions.explanation: Filming with a properly placed reference object must happen first, then the scale is calibrated from it, then position data is logged frame by frame, and only then can that raw pixel data be converted into physical units.

questions.prompt: Match each video-tracking quantity to what it directly determines.

right.text: The timing resolution of the resulting x(t), y(t) data
The pixels-to-meters conversion factor
The raw pixel-coordinate trajectory before scaling

questions.explanation: Frame rate sets how finely time is resolved, the reference object's known length sets the pixel-to-meter scale, and the position clicks themselves are the raw, still-unscaled trajectory data that scale and timing get applied to.

lessons.label: Landing-Point Scatter

sections.heading: Carbon paper and sand as recording media
sections.body: To find exactly where a projectile lands without relying on eyesight or a moving observer, labs use a passive recording surface. Carbon paper taped face-down over plain paper leaves a small ink mark at the point of impact, cheap, precise to a few millimeters, and instantly readable. A shallow tray of fine sand (or flour) works similarly for larger or heavier projectiles: the impact leaves a small crater or divot that can be measured with a ruler against a fixed reference edge. Both methods share a key property that timing-based methods lack: they record a spatial fact (where it landed) directly, with no clock involved, so their error is purely a measurement-of-position error, not a timing error.

sections.heading: One landing point is not the answer
sections.body: A single trial's landing point is a single sample from an underlying distribution of possible landing points, not a fixed, exact answer. Even with a well-calibrated launcher (Lesson 1), small variations in v0, launch angle, spin, and air currents mean repeated shots at identical settings do not land in exactly the same spot; they scatter around some central tendency. Treating the landing point as a single deterministic number throws away this information. Instead, a defensible lab fires a batch of shots (10 or more is typical) at the same setting, marks every landing point on the same sheet, and treats the resulting cloud of marks as data: a distribution with a center and a spread, exactly as the muzzle-velocity measurements in Lesson 2 were treated.

sections.heading: Mean range and its spread
sections.body: From a batch of n landing points measured as ranges (distance from the launch point along the line of fire), compute the mean range as the arithmetic average and the spread as the standard deviation, exactly as with any repeated measurement. Any landing points with meaningful sideways (cross-range) deviation should also be checked, since a wide cross-range spread relative to the range spread can indicate a launcher that is not firing consistently along a single vertical plane, a sign of tilt or wobble worth investigating rather than ignoring. Reporting range as mean +/- standard deviation (n = however many trials) turns a scatter of ink dots into a scientific quantity that can be compared honestly against a predicted range and its own uncertainty.

lessons.workedExample: A team fires 12 shots at a fixed 30-degree angle onto carbon paper laid over graph paper with a marked launch-point origin. The measured ranges (in cm) are: 84, 87, 82, 89, 85, 83, 86, 88, 84, 85, 87, 83. The mean is 85.25 cm and the standard deviation is about 2.2 cm, so the team reports range = 85.3 +/- 2.2 cm (n = 12). They also notice the cross-range scatter (how far left-right of the centerline each mark fell) has a standard deviation of only 0.6 cm, much tighter than the 2.2 cm along the range direction, which they interpret as evidence the launcher fires consistently in a single vertical plane and that the range spread is dominated by v0 variation, not aiming drift.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges look for landing-point scatter to be treated as data, not noise to be minimized away by picking a "best" shot. A student who reports a single, cherry-picked landing point ("our best trial landed at 87 cm, so that's our range") has thrown out real statistical information and introduced selection bias. A student who fires a proper batch, reports mean +/- standard deviation, and can explain what a tight versus wide cross-range spread would tell them about their launcher's consistency demonstrates they understand that a scatter of dots is itself the experimental result, not a failure to hit one true answer.

questions.prompt: Why is it a mistake to report only the single "best" landing-point trial as the lab's range result?

options.text: Carbon paper cannot record more than one shot
It discards real scatter data and introduces selection bias by cherry-picking a favorable trial
Sand trays are more accurate than carbon paper
A single trial always overestimates the true range

explanations.a: Carbon paper can record many separate marks on the same sheet across many trials; this is not a physical limitation.
explanations.b: Correct: picking a "best" shot after the fact hides the natural scatter and biases the reported result toward whichever trial looks most favorable.
explanations.c: The relative accuracy of carbon paper versus sand is unrelated to why cherry-picking one trial is a statistical error.
explanations.d: A single trial can land anywhere in the scatter, above or below the true mean; there is no guarantee it overestimates.

questions.prompt: A batch of landing points shows a much wider cross-range (sideways) spread than range (forward) spread. This most likely indicates:

options.text: The launcher's v0 is highly consistent
The projectile has more air resistance than expected
The launcher may not be firing consistently in a single vertical plane (tilt or wobble)
The carbon paper was placed too close to the launcher

explanations.a: A consistent v0 mainly controls the forward-range spread, not sideways spread; this option does not explain the observation.
explanations.b: Air resistance primarily affects how far the projectile travels along its plane of motion, not sideways deviation.
explanations.c: Correct: if shots are drifting sideways more than they vary in range, that points to inconsistent aim direction or launcher wobble rather than random forward-speed variation.
explanations.d: Placement distance of the recording surface affects the absolute range value, not the relative width of sideways versus forward scatter.

questions.prompt: Match each recording medium to a property that distinguishes it.

right.text: Leaves a precise ink mark, best for light projectiles
Leaves a measurable divot, suited to heavier projectiles
Its error comes from timing precision, not position measurement

questions.explanation: Carbon paper gives a fine ink mark suited to light, low-impact projectiles; sand or flour records a divot suited to heavier impacts; and, by contrast, a timing-based method's error source is fundamentally about clock precision rather than spatial position.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a landing-point scatter measurement.

items.text: Fix the launcher at a chosen angle and speed setting
Fire a batch of shots (e.g., 10-12) onto carbon paper or sand
Measure the range of every individual landing mark
Compute the mean range and its standard deviation across the batch

questions.explanation: The launcher setting must be fixed first, then a batch of shots fired and recorded, then every individual mark measured, before a mean and spread across the batch can be computed.

lessons.label: Sources of Error in Projectile Labs

sections.heading: Launch-angle jitter and unwanted spin
sections.body: Even a rigidly clamped launcher has a small, real spread in its actual launch angle from shot to shot, from mechanical play in the barrel mount, from the projectile settling slightly differently each time, or from the angle-setting mechanism (a protractor and a set screw) not locking perfectly reproducibly. Because range depends on angle through sin(2*theta), which is fairly flat near 45 degrees but changes quickly near 15 or 75 degrees, angle jitter's effect on range is not uniform across the range of angles tested, it matters more at the extremes. Unwanted spin is a separate effect: a projectile leaving the barrel with backspin or sidespin experiences the Magnus effect, an aerodynamic force perpendicular to both the spin axis and the direction of travel, which can measurably curve or extend a trajectory relative to the no-spin, ideal-projectile prediction, especially for lightweight or textured projectiles (a spinning ball, notably) rather than smooth, dense ones.

sections.heading: Air resistance and timing lag
sections.body: Air resistance (drag) removes kinetic energy from the projectile throughout flight, shortening the range and flattening the trajectory relative to the idealized, no-drag parabola that R = v0^2 sin(2*theta)/g assumes. Drag scales with the projectile's cross-sectional area and roughly the square of its speed (for the turbulent-flow regime typical of classroom projectiles), so it matters most for light, large-area projectiles (a ping-pong ball) and least for dense, compact ones (a steel ball bearing), and matters more at higher launch speeds. Timing lag is a separate, purely instrumental error: photogates, video frame capture, and human reaction time (Lesson 2) all have a nonzero delay between the physical event and its recorded timestamp, and if that lag is not identical at both timing points, it introduces a small, systematic bias into every measured time interval, distinct from the random scatter that repeated trials average out.

sections.heading: Non-level ground, and ranking what dominates
sections.body: If the launch point and the landing surface are not at the same height, or if the tabletop the launcher sits on is not level, the effective launch angle and effective range both shift from their nominal values in a way that is easy to mistake for a different physical effect. A launcher tilted just 2 degrees from level, for instance, changes the effective launch angle by that same 2 degrees, comparable in size to typical angle-jitter effects. Which error source dominates depends on the setup: for a dense, compact projectile at low speed, launch-angle jitter and non-level ground usually dominate over drag and spin; for a light, fast, spinning projectile, drag and the Magnus effect can dominate instead. A rigorous lab identifies its likely dominant error sources before the trial run (based on its specific projectile and speed) rather than listing every possible error generically, and targets its mitigation effort accordingly: leveling the launcher with a bubble level, choosing a dense low-drag projectile, or damping spin, depending on which source it identified as dominant.

sections.heading: How to reduce each
sections.body: Angle jitter is reduced by a rigid, low-play angle-locking mechanism and by verifying the set angle with an independent protractor or digital inclinometer rather than trusting the launcher's built-in scale. Spin is reduced by choosing a smooth-barreled launcher and a smooth, symmetric projectile, and can be checked directly by filming the projectile in flight and looking for visible rotation. Air resistance's effect is reduced (not eliminated) by choosing a denser, more compact, more aerodynamic projectile, and its predicted effect can be estimated with a drag-included simulation for comparison against the simple no-drag formula. Timing lag is reduced by using the same type of sensor (and ideally the same physical device) at both timing points, so any fixed lag cancels out in the time DIFFERENCE even if it does not vanish in each individual timestamp. Non-level ground is checked directly with a bubble level or digital inclinometer on both the launch platform and, if relevant, the landing surface, before any trial is run.

lessons.workedExample: A team launching a lightweight foam ball at 30 degrees notices their measured ranges fall systematically about 8% short of the R = v0^2 sin(2*theta)/g prediction. They rule out non-level ground (checked with a bubble level, under 0.5 degrees off) and angle jitter (independently measured at 30.1 +/- 0.3 degrees across trials). Filming the launch at 120 fps reveals visible backspin on the foam ball. They conclude drag combined with a Magnus-effect lift from the backspin is the dominant error source for this particular light, spinning projectile, and switch to a smoother, denser rubber ball for their main data run, which closes the gap to about 2%.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask students to rank their own error sources, not just list them, because a generic list ("sources of error include air resistance, human error, and equipment limitations") signals the student never actually diagnosed their specific setup. A student who instead says "our projectile is light and visibly spinning on video, so we expect drag and the Magnus effect to dominate over angle jitter, and here is the measurement that confirms it" has done the actual diagnostic work a real experimentalist does: using evidence from their own setup to decide which error source is worth the effort to fix.

questions.prompt: Why does range's sensitivity to launch-angle jitter (via sin(2*theta)) depend on which angle is being tested?

options.text: sin(2*theta) is flatter near 45 degrees and changes more quickly near 15 or 75 degrees, so the same angle jitter shifts range more at the extremes
Angle jitter only exists at exactly 45 degrees
sin(2*theta) is constant for all theta, so angle jitter never affects range
Range does not depend on angle at all, only on v0

explanations.a: Correct: near the flat top of the sin(2*theta) curve (45 degrees) a small angle error barely moves range, but near the steep parts of the curve (15 or 75 degrees) the same angle error moves range noticeably more.
explanations.b: Angle jitter is a mechanical property of the launcher and can occur at any set angle, not just at 45 degrees.
explanations.c: sin(2*theta) varies substantially with theta, reaching a maximum at 45 degrees and falling toward 0 near 0 and 90 degrees; it is not constant.
explanations.d: R = v0^2 sin(2*theta)/g explicitly depends on theta through the sin(2*theta) term, so range clearly depends on angle.

questions.prompt: A team is choosing between a lightweight foam ball and a dense steel ball bearing for a lab where they want drag and spin effects to be as small as possible. Which should they choose, and why?

options.text: The foam ball, because it is easier to see on video
The steel ball, because it is denser and less affected by drag and Magnus lift relative to its momentum
It makes no difference; drag and spin effects are identical for any projectile shape or density
The foam ball, because lighter projectiles always travel farther

explanations.a: Visibility on video is a filming convenience unrelated to the physical size of drag or Magnus effects.
explanations.b: Correct: drag and Magnus forces scale with cross-sectional area and speed, while inertia (which resists those forces) scales with mass; a denser, more compact projectile has more inertia per unit of drag-producing area, so aerodynamic effects perturb its trajectory proportionally less.
explanations.c: Drag and Magnus effects depend strongly on shape, density, and surface texture; they are not identical across different projectiles.
explanations.d: Lighter projectiles are typically affected MORE by drag relative to their momentum, not less, so this reasoning is backward.

questions.prompt: Match each error source to its primary mitigation.

right.text: Rigid, low-play angle-locking mechanism, verified with an independent protractor
Smooth-barreled launcher and a smooth, symmetric projectile
Use the same sensor type at both timing points so fixed lag cancels in the time difference
Check with a bubble level or digital inclinometer before trials

questions.explanation: Each mechanical or instrumental error source has a targeted fix: angle jitter needs a rigid, verified angle lock; spin is reduced by smooth launcher and projectile surfaces; timing lag is neutralized by matching sensor types so a fixed lag cancels; and a non-level platform is caught by direct leveling before trials begin.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the diagnostic approach the worked-example team used to identify their dominant error source.

items.text: Notice the measured range falls systematically short of the no-drag prediction
Check and rule out non-level ground and angle jitter with direct measurements
Film the launch at high frame rate and observe visible spin on the projectile
Conclude drag and the Magnus effect from spin are the dominant source, and switch to a smoother, denser projectile

questions.explanation: The team first noticed a discrepancy, then ruled out simpler mechanical explanations with direct checks, then gathered new evidence (video) that pointed to spin, and only then concluded which effect dominated and acted on it.

lessons.label: Designing a Range-versus-Angle Experiment

sections.heading: The core design: hold v0 fixed, vary theta
sections.body: The classic testable prediction of ideal (no-drag) projectile motion is R = v0^2 sin(2*theta) / g: for a fixed launch speed, range as a function of angle is a single-humped curve, symmetric about 45 degrees, peaking there, and identical at complementary angle pairs (15 and 75 degrees should give the same range, as should 30 and 60). A defensible science-fair design isolates this relationship deliberately: pick one launcher setting and confirm via calibration (Lesson 2) that v0 stays constant across the angle range to be tested, then vary only theta, in even steps across a wide span (for example every 15 degrees from 15 to 75 degrees), firing a full batch of repeated shots (Lesson 4) at every angle so each data point carries its own mean and standard deviation rather than being a single shot.

sections.heading: Comparing data to the prediction
sections.body: With v0 measured (with uncertainty, Lesson 2) and g taken as 9.81 m/s^2 (or measured independently, Lesson 3), the formula R = v0^2 sin(2*theta)/g generates a predicted curve to overlay against the measured mean range at each angle, each point plotted with an error bar sized to its measured standard deviation (or standard error). A visually convincing overlay is necessary but not sufficient, the strongest version of this experiment explicitly computes, for each angle, whether the predicted range falls within the measured range's error bar, and reports a summary statistic (for example, what fraction of angles the prediction lands within one standard error) rather than relying on eyeballing a graph. Where the data and prediction disagree, the gap itself becomes a second, honest result to interpret using Lesson 5's error framework, rather than something to quietly leave off the poster.

sections.heading: Testing the 45-degree prediction specifically
sections.body: Because 45 degrees is the unique angle predicted to maximize range for a fixed v0, it is worth testing explicitly rather than only as one point among many: fire dedicated batches at a fine angle spacing (every 5 degrees, say, from 35 to 55 degrees) and check whether the measured mean range genuinely peaks at 45 degrees, or whether it peaks measurably elsewhere. A real experiment, with real drag and spin, can show its peak shifted a few degrees below 45, since drag reduces the range more at higher angles (where the projectile spends longer aloft exposed to drag) than the ideal formula predicts, an outcome that itself supports the physics in Lesson 5 as long as it is reported and explained rather than treated as a failed replication.

lessons.workedExample: A team calibrates their launcher at v0 = 5.10 +/- 0.05 m/s (Lesson 2) and confirms it stays within that range across all angles they plan to test (Lesson 1). Using g = 9.81 m/s^2, they predict ranges at 15, 30, 45, 60, and 75 degrees: R(15) = R(75) = (5.10^2 * sin(30))/9.81 = 1.33 m, R(30) = R(60) = (5.10^2 * sin(60))/9.81 = 2.30 m, R(45) = (5.10^2 * sin(90))/9.81 = 2.65 m. Firing 10 shots at each angle, they measure R(45) = 2.51 +/- 0.08 m, about 5% below prediction and outside one standard error, consistent with drag being more consequential at the higher, longer-hang-time 45-degree shot, matching Lesson 5's prediction that drag matters more at higher angles.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges look for a range-versus-angle project to be an actual test of a falsifiable prediction, not a demonstration that confirms what everyone already expects. A student who predicts specific numbers from R = v0^2 sin(2*theta)/g using their own measured v0, compares those numbers to their own data with error bars, and explains a measured 45-degree shortfall using the drag argument from the error-sources lesson has run a real experiment. A student who instead reports "we tested some angles and 45 degrees gave the biggest range, confirming the formula" without numbers, uncertainty, or engagement with any discrepancy has produced a demonstration, not a test.

questions.prompt: According to the ideal (no-drag) formula R = v0^2 sin(2*theta)/g, which pair of launch angles should give the same predicted range for a fixed v0?

options.text: 20 degrees and 50 degrees
25 degrees and 65 degrees
30 degrees and 45 degrees
10 degrees and 20 degrees

explanations.a: 20 and 50 degrees are not complementary (they do not sum to 90 degrees), so sin(2*20) is not equal to sin(2*50).
explanations.b: Correct: 25 + 65 = 90 degrees, and sin(2*25) = sin(50 degrees) = sin(130 degrees) = sin(2*65), so these complementary angles give equal predicted range.
explanations.c: 30 and 45 degrees do not sum to 90 degrees, so they are not a complementary pair and give different predicted ranges.
explanations.d: 10 and 20 degrees do not sum to 90 degrees, so they are not a complementary pair either.

questions.prompt: A team measures range at 45 degrees to be several percent below the R = v0^2 sin(2*theta)/g prediction, with the gap outside their error bar. What is the strongest way to handle this in their report?
