The effect becomes unmissable at true artillery range: Germany's WWI-era Paris Gun fired shells roughly 120 km with a flight time of about 177 seconds, and the Coriolis effect pushed each shell roughly 1,343 m to the right of a straight-line aim point, the first time in history gunners had to correct fire for the rotation of the Earth itself. The same rotational effect also added over 600 m to the shell's achieved range.

lessons.workedExample: A sniper zeroed at 100 m fires at a target 900 m away. Even at constant velocity, a 9x increase in range would mean a 9x increase in flight time and, since drop scales with time-squared, an 81x increase in drop. But drag also slows the bullet as range grows, so time of flight actually grows faster than 9x, from roughly 0.15 s to well over 1.5 s, meaning gravity drop grows by nearly two orders of magnitude, past the drag-free 81x figure, which is why long-range drop charts curve even more steeply than a pure time-squared relationship would predict. A 10 mph crosswind over that same 1.5+ s flight can push the bullet sideways by a foot or more. Now compare the Paris Gun: over 177 s of flight and roughly 120 km of range, the same physics scaled up produced a Coriolis deflection of about 1,343 m, far too large to ignore, unlike the roughly 3-inch Coriolis correction a rifle shooter faces at 1000 yards.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up Coriolis specifically to test scale reasoning: does the student know it is real physics applying to every projectile, but negligible at rifle ranges (a few inches at 1000 yards) and dominant at artillery ranges (over a kilometer for the Paris Gun) because deflection grows with time of flight? A student who claims Coriolis is 'always negligible' or 'always must be corrected for' has not grasped that the same formula gives wildly different answers depending on flight time, exactly the kind of scaling judgment a fair judge is checking for.

questions.prompt: Bullet drop increases faster than proportionally with range mainly because

options.text: Drag slows the projectile, so time of flight (and gravity's time-squared effect) grows faster than range does
Gravity itself becomes stronger at longer horizontal range
The projectile loses mass over its flight, reducing its resistance to gravity

explanations.a: Correct: drop already scales with time-squared while range scales with time, so drop outpaces range even with zero drag; drag then reduces average velocity over longer flights, making time of flight rise faster than range still, which steepens that growth even further.
explanations.b: Gravitational acceleration near Earth's surface does not meaningfully change over the horizontal distances involved in ballistic flight.
explanations.c: A bullet does not lose measurable mass in flight, and mass loss would not change how quickly it falls under gravity in any case.

questions.prompt: Windage correction is commonly approximated using...

options.text: 'Lag time', the difference between actual time of flight and the vacuum time of flight at muzzle velocity, multiplied by wind speed
The diameter of the projectile alone
The single strongest gust ever recorded at the range

explanations.a: Correct: lag time captures how much longer the real (drag-slowed) flight takes than an idealized constant-velocity flight, and that extra exposure time is what the crosswind acts on.
explanations.b: Diameter alone says nothing about how long the projectile is exposed to the crosswind, which is the key variable in windage.
explanations.c: Windage corrections use the actual, current wind conditions during the shot, not a historical extreme unrelated to the shot being fired.

questions.prompt: Why did the Paris Gun's Coriolis deflection (about 1,343 m) matter so much more than a rifle's does at 1000 yards (about 3 inches)?

options.text: Its flight time (about 177 s) was nearly two orders of magnitude longer, and Coriolis deflection grows with time of flight
The Paris Gun was fired at a location with a different rotation rate than the rest of Earth
Coriolis deflection only applies to explosive artillery shells, not to solid rifle bullets

explanations.a: Correct: Coriolis deflection scales with time of flight, and 177 seconds is roughly 60-90 times longer than a rifle bullet's flight to 1000 yards, which alone accounts for most of the huge difference in deflection.
explanations.b: Earth's rotation rate is the same everywhere on the planet; only the latitude-dependent component of Coriolis acceleration varies with location, not the base rotation rate.
explanations.c: Coriolis deflection is a consequence of Earth's rotation acting on any freely moving object, including solid rifle bullets, not a special property of explosive shells.

questions.prompt: Order these by typical Coriolis deflection, from smallest to largest.

items.text: Rifle bullet at 1000 yards (about 3 inches)
Extreme long-range rifle shot beyond 1500 m (several inches to about a foot)
Paris Gun shell at roughly 120 km (about 1,343 m)

questions.explanation: Coriolis deflection grows with time of flight, so the shortest, fastest rifle shot deflects least, a longer extreme-range shot deflects more, and the multi-minute Paris Gun shell deflects by well over a kilometer.

lessons.label: Case Study: Optimizing a Real Trajectory

sections.heading: Setting Up the Free-Throw Trade-off
sections.body: Take a basketball free throw as a complete case study. The hoop sits 3.05 m (10 ft) high with a rim inner diameter of 45.7 cm (18 in); a basketball is about 24 cm (9.4-9.5 in) across. A shooter releases from the free-throw line, which sits 4.6 m (15 ft) from the backboard's face, putting the shooter roughly 4.2 m (about 13 ft 9 in) of horizontal distance from the hoop's center once the rim's ~0.38 m inset from the backboard is accounted for, from a height around 2.1-2.4 m depending on the player. The shooter chooses a launch angle, a launch speed, and a backspin rate. The key extra variable is entry angle, the angle the ball's path makes with the horizontal as it crosses the rim's plane: at a shallow entry angle, the ball's circular cross-section eats into more of the rim's 45.7 cm window, shrinking the margin for both left-right and long-short error; at a steeper entry angle, more of the rim stays open, forgiving small mistakes.

sections.heading: Why Steeper Beats the Textbook 45
sections.body: Infinitely many angle-and-speed pairs will put the ball's center exactly through the hoop, so researchers modeled hundreds of thousands of simulated shots, varying angle, speed, and small human execution errors, to find which combination maximizes the probability of success rather than just hitting dead center once. That optimum comes out close to 52 degrees for a roughly 2.1 m release height, requiring enough launch speed to reach the hoop at that steep angle, but not so much that the entry angle flattens out and shrinks the effective target. Backspin of roughly 3 Hz (about 180 rpm) adds Magnus lift during flight and gives the ball a softer, more forgiving bounce if it clips the rim, both improving the odds of a make.

sections.heading: Speed Consistency Matters More Than Angle Precision
sections.body: Near the researched optimum, small errors in launch speed change the outcome (long or short) much more than equally-sized errors in launch angle do, because entry angle is fairly insensitive to small changes in launch angle near 52 degrees, but quite sensitive to launch speed, since speed sets both how far the ball travels and how steep its final entry angle is. That is the physical reason coaches emphasize a smooth, repeatable release over memorizing a 'perfect' angle: the trajectory math rewards consistent speed far more than pinpoint angle.

lessons.workedExample: A player releasing a free throw at 2.13 m (7 ft) high, 4.2 m from the hoop's center, aiming for a researched optimum near 52 degrees, needs a launch speed of roughly 7.1-7.3 m/s (about 16 mph) to reach the rim at that angle and height. If the same player instead launches at the textbook 45 degrees, a different speed reaches the same target, but the resulting entry angle is shallower, so the effective rim opening shrinks and small speed errors are more likely to send the shot long or short of a make. Simulation studies show the roughly 50-52 degree family of shots tolerates the same realistic speed error with a noticeably larger margin for success than the 45-degree family, which is the physics reason free-throw shooters are coached toward a higher, arcing shot rather than a flatter line drive.
lessons.judgeFraming: This case study is where a judge checks whether a student can synthesize the whole unit rather than recite isolated facts: naming the launch-angle-height-drag relationship from Lesson 5, backspin's Magnus lift from Lessons 3 and 4, and turning both into a concrete claim about why roughly 52 degrees beats 45 for a free throw. The strongest answers go one step further and explain that the optimum is not the angle that 'looks right' or maximizes range, it is the angle that maximizes the shooter's margin for error given realistic human inconsistency in release speed, a fundamentally different optimization problem than the vacuum range equation.

questions.prompt: A shallower ball entry angle through the basketball rim...

options.text: Shrinks the effective size of the rim's opening, reducing the margin for error
Has no effect on the probability of a make
Increases the effective size of the rim's opening

explanations.a: Correct: at a shallow entry angle the ball's circular cross-section covers more of the rim's window as seen along the ball's path, leaving less room for left-right or long-short error.
explanations.b: Entry angle directly changes how much of the rim's diameter is effectively usable for the ball to pass through, so it strongly affects make probability.
explanations.c: It is a steeper, not shallower, entry angle that opens up more of the rim's effective window.

questions.prompt: The basketball free-throw optimum near 50-52 degrees is found by maximizing...

options.text: The probability of success across many simulated shots with realistic execution error, not just hitting dead center once
The horizontal range of the shot
The backspin rate alone, independent of angle or speed

explanations.a: Correct: researchers simulate many shots with realistic human variability in speed and angle and pick the launch conditions that maximize the make probability across that variability.
explanations.b: Maximizing pure horizontal range would push the optimum closer to 45 degrees; the free-throw problem is about landing the ball IN the hoop with margin, not about maximizing distance.
explanations.c: Backspin rate alone, without a paired angle and speed, does not define a shot; the optimization varies all three together.

questions.prompt: Near the optimal free-throw angle, a shooter's outcome is generally more sensitive to small errors in...

options.text: Launch speed than launch angle
Launch angle than launch speed
Backspin rate than either speed or angle

explanations.a: Correct: near the optimum, entry angle (and thus make probability) is fairly flat with respect to small launch-angle changes but changes quickly with small launch-speed changes, which is why coaches stress a consistent release speed.
explanations.b: This is the reverse of what simulation studies find; angle precision matters less than speed precision near the optimum.
explanations.c: Backspin mainly affects lift and bounce forgiveness; it is not the dominant source of miss sensitivity near the optimal launch conditions.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to find the real optimal free-throw trajectory.

items.text: Define the geometry: rim size, ball size, release height, and horizontal distance to the hoop
Recognize that entry angle sets the effective size of the rim's opening
Simulate many launch angle and speed pairs, including small realistic execution errors
Pick the angle and speed pair that maximizes success probability, not just raw range

questions.explanation: The analysis starts from the fixed geometry, recognizes why entry angle matters for make probability, runs many simulated shots with realistic error, and finally selects the launch conditions that are most forgiving of that error.

lessons.label: Tartaglia and the Pre-Galilean Trajectory

sections.heading: The impetus picture cannon crews actually used
sections.body: Before the mid-1500s, gunners worked from a version of Aristotelian "impetus" theory: a fired ball travels in a straight line along the barrel's aim, powered by the violent impetus of the gunpowder, until that impetus is used up, at which point the ball drops into a second straight line, straight down, under its "natural" tendency to fall. A short curved arc was allowed to connect the two straight legs, but the straight-line portions were treated as the real, calculable parts of the flight. Gunnery manuals and range tables built on this picture, and because most cannons of the era fired at fairly flat, fairly fast trajectories over short ranges, the straight-line approximation was not obviously wrong to the naked eye.

sections.heading: Tartaglia's Nova Scientia (1537)
sections.body: Niccolo Tartaglia, a self-taught Venetian mathematician, published Nova Scientia ("New Science") in 1537, the first serious mathematical treatment of projectile motion. Tartaglia argued, and tried to demonstrate geometrically, that a cannonball is acted on by gravity from the very instant it leaves the barrel, so its path curves continuously rather than staying straight and then suddenly bending. He also argued that maximum range for a given muzzle speed occurs at a 45-degree elevation, a rule gunners could apply directly; the firing tables of ranges-by-elevation he promised to compile from it, however, were never actually published. Yet Tartaglia never fully broke from the older picture: in the same book he still describes the flight in practical terms as an initial "nearly straight" leg, a curved middle, and a final steep fall, and he suggests the early curvature is simply too slight to matter for aiming purposes. His science and his gunnery advice pulled in slightly different directions.

sections.heading: Why the break was incomplete
sections.body: Tartaglia lacked two things Galileo would later supply: a quantitative law relating fall distance to time, and a clean way to treat horizontal and vertical motion as independent and combinable. Without them, "the path curves continuously" was a correct qualitative claim he could not turn into an exact curve. That gap between Tartaglia's insight and Galileo's proof is roughly a century, and it is why historians credit Tartaglia as the founder of the mathematical study of ballistics while still reserving "discovery of the parabola" for Galileo.

lessons.workedExample: A 1530s gunner aiming a cannon at a fortress wall 300 meters away used range tables built on the straight-then-curved model: pick an elevation, look up the expected impact point, adjust by trial shots. Tartaglia's innovation was to show mathematically that the true path was already curving during the "straight" portion, and that 45 degrees, not the gunner's rule-of-thumb elevations, maximized range for a fixed muzzle speed. A modern check: a ball launched at 45 degrees with no air resistance travels farther than the same ball launched at 30 or 60 degrees, because range scales with sin(2*theta), which peaks at theta = 45 degrees, exactly Tartaglia's empirically-approached result, more than a century before anyone had calculus to prove it directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about Tartaglia to test whether a student understands that scientific progress is often partial and contested, not a clean jump from wrong to right. A strong answer names Nova Scientia (1537), states what Tartaglia got right (continuous curvature, the 45-degree maximum), and is honest about what he still got wrong or hedged on (the practical straight-line description he kept using). A student who claims Tartaglia "discovered the parabola" is overclaiming; a judge will immediately ask what shape Tartaglia actually proved the path was, and the honest answer is that he proved it was curved throughout, not that he identified it as a parabola.

questions.prompt: According to the pre-Tartaglia impetus theory used by 16th-century gunners, a cannonball's path consisted of:

options.text: A single smooth parabola from muzzle to impact
A straight line, then a curved arc, then a straight vertical drop
A circular arc determined entirely by the ball's spin

explanations.a: The parabola is Galileo's later result (1638), not the impetus-theory picture Tartaglia was working against.
explanations.b: Correct: impetus theory held the ball flew straight along the aim until impetus ran out, then dropped straight down, with a short connecting arc.
explanations.c: Spin-driven curving is the Magnus effect, a separate and much later topic; impetus theory did not invoke spin.

questions.prompt: What did Tartaglia's Nova Scientia (1537) establish that impetus theory denied?

options.text: That gravity acts on the ball continuously from the moment it leaves the barrel, curving the path throughout
That air resistance is proportional to velocity squared
That the trajectory is exactly a parabola

explanations.a: Correct: Tartaglia argued gravity acts from the start of flight, so the path curves continuously rather than staying straight until impetus is spent.
explanations.b: The velocity-squared drag law is a much later, separate 18th-century development (Newton, Robins, Euler), not Tartaglia's claim.
explanations.c: Tartaglia proved continuous curvature but did not identify or prove the specific parabolic shape; that came from Galileo.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the early mathematical history of ballistics.

items.text: Gunners use impetus theory: straight line, curved arc, straight drop
Tartaglia publishes Nova Scientia, arguing the path curves continuously
Tartaglia derives that 45 degrees maximizes range
Galileo later proves the path is exactly a parabola

questions.explanation: Impetus theory was the pre-existing framework; Tartaglia's 1537 book challenged it and, within the same work, derived the 45-degree maximum-range result; the exact parabolic shape was proved a century later by Galileo.

questions.prompt: Match each claim to whether it belongs to impetus theory or to Tartaglia's Nova Scientia.

left.text: Path is straight until impetus is used up, then drops straight down
Gravity curves the path from the instant of firing
Maximum range occurs at a 45-degree elevation

right.text: Impetus theory (pre-Tartaglia)
Tartaglia, Nova Scientia (1537) — continuous curvature claim
Tartaglia, Nova Scientia (1537) — 45-degree range result

questions.explanation: Impetus theory held the path was straight-then-straight with a connecting arc; Tartaglia's Nova Scientia argued for continuous gravitational curvature and derived the 45-degree maximum-range rule.

lessons.label: Galileo Proves the Parabola

sections.heading: Two building blocks, combined
sections.body: In Two New Sciences (1638), Galileo assembled two results he had developed over decades into a single proof. The first was his law of falling bodies: a body falling from rest covers a distance proportional to the square of the elapsed time (distance is proportional to t-squared), a law he had verified with inclined-plane experiments that slowed the fall enough to time it with the water clocks available. The second was the claim, radical at the time, that horizontal and vertical motion are independent: a projectile's horizontal velocity stays constant (no force acts on it horizontally, ignoring air resistance) while its vertical motion falls under gravity exactly as if the horizontal motion were not happening at all.

sections.heading: Why independence plus t-squared gives a parabola
sections.body: Combine the two: horizontal distance x grows linearly with time (x = v0*t), while vertical drop y grows with the square of time (y is proportional to t-squared). Eliminating time between those two relations gives y proportional to x-squared, which is precisely the equation of a parabola. Galileo presented this in Two New Sciences as a geometric theorem about a body undergoing simultaneously a uniform horizontal motion and a naturally accelerated vertical motion, and stated explicitly that the resulting path is a semi-parabola. This was the first time projectile motion had been reduced to a single, deductively proven geometric curve rather than a description built from qualitative stages.

sections.heading: The idealizations Galileo knew he was making
sections.body: Galileo was explicit that the parabola is an idealization: it assumes gravity acts uniformly downward (fine over cannon-range distances, wrong over planetary distances) and it ignores air resistance, which he knew distorted real cannonball and musket-ball trajectories, especially at high speed. He argued the idealized parabola was still the right starting point because it isolated the essential physics, with resistance treated as a correction to be added afterward, a strategy that became a template for physics generally: solve the clean case first, then perturb it.

lessons.workedExample: A ball is launched horizontally at 20 m/s from a 20-meter cliff, with g = 10 m/s^2 and air resistance ignored. Time to fall: y = (1/2)g*t^2, so 20 = 5*t^2, t = 2 s. Horizontal distance: x = v0*t = 20*2 = 40 m. Because x = v0*t and y = (1/2)g*t^2, eliminating t gives y = (g/(2*v0^2))*x^2, a parabola opening downward in the standard sense of increasing fall with horizontal distance. Doubling v0 to 40 m/s while keeping the same drop height leaves the fall time unchanged at 2 s (fall time depends only on height, not on horizontal speed, exactly Galileo's independence claim) while the horizontal range doubles to 80 m, a direct experimental prediction that can be checked by rolling balls off a table at different speeds and measuring where they land.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this lesson to see whether a student can derive the parabola rather than just name it. A strong answer states both ingredients (constant horizontal velocity, t-squared vertical fall) and shows how eliminating time between them produces y proportional to x-squared. A common trap is a student who says "gravity pulls the ball into a curve" without identifying that it is specifically the combination of linear-in-time horizontal motion and quadratic-in-time vertical motion that forces the curve to be a parabola rather than some other shape; a judge will ask what would happen to the shape if vertical motion also grew linearly with time, and the answer (straight line, not parabola) tests real understanding of the mechanism.

questions.prompt: In Galileo's analysis, why does a projectile's path come out as a parabola specifically (and not some other curve)?

options.text: Because horizontal position grows linearly with time while vertical drop grows with time squared, and eliminating time gives y proportional to x squared
Because air resistance bends the path into a parabolic shape
Because the ball's spin curves the path symmetrically

explanations.a: Correct: x is linear in t, y is quadratic in t; eliminating t between them algebraically produces y proportional to x squared, the defining equation of a parabola.
explanations.b: Galileo's parabola is the idealized, no-air-resistance case; real air resistance actually distorts the path away from a perfect parabola.
explanations.c: Spin-curving is the separate Magnus effect and plays no role in Galileo's geometric derivation of the parabola.

questions.prompt: A ball rolls off a table at 3 m/s; an identical ball rolls off the same table at 6 m/s at the same instant. Ignoring air resistance, which hits the floor first?

options.text: The 6 m/s ball, because it is moving faster overall
They hit at the same time
The 3 m/s ball, because it travels a shorter horizontal distance

explanations.a: Horizontal speed does not affect fall time under Galileo's independence principle; overall speed is irrelevant to when the ball reaches the floor.
explanations.b: Correct: vertical fall time depends only on drop height (y = (1/2)g t^2), which is identical for both balls, so they land simultaneously despite very different horizontal ranges.
explanations.c: Horizontal distance traveled has no bearing on fall time; that is exactly the independence of horizontal and vertical motion Galileo demonstrated.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of Galileo's proof that projectile paths are parabolic.

items.text: Establish the law of falling bodies: vertical drop is proportional to time squared
Establish that horizontal velocity stays constant (independent of vertical motion)
Write x proportional to t and y proportional to t squared
Eliminate t to get y proportional to x squared, the equation of a parabola

questions.explanation: Galileo first needed both physical laws (falling-body law and horizontal independence) before he could write the two motion equations and algebraically combine them into the parabola's equation.

questions.prompt: Match each Galilean idealization to the real-world effect it deliberately ignores.

left.text: Gravity treated as uniform and constant in direction

right.text: Gravity's direction and strength actually change over planetary-scale distances
Real projectiles slow down and their paths flatten due to drag, especially at high speed

questions.explanation: Galileo's parabola assumes uniform downward gravity, which breaks down over planetary distances, and assumes no air resistance, which breaks down for fast or light real projectiles.

lessons.label: Newton's Cannonball: Projectiles Become Orbits

sections.heading: The thought experiment
sections.body: In A Treatise of the System of the World (written around 1685, published posthumously in 1728), Newton asks readers to imagine a cannon on an impossibly tall mountain, above the atmosphere, firing a ball horizontally. At low muzzle speed the ball follows a short parabolic arc and lands nearby, exactly Galileo's picture. Fire it faster and it lands farther away, its path still curving toward Earth but over a longer arc. Newton's insight was to push this all the way: fire the ball fast enough, and the curve of its fall matches the curvature of the Earth itself, so the ball keeps falling toward the ground but the ground keeps curving away beneath it at the same rate, and it never lands. It has become a satellite.

sections.heading: Why this unifies projectiles and orbits
sections.body: Galileo's parabola works because he assumed gravity points in one constant direction (straight down) and has constant strength, an excellent approximation over a few kilometers but wrong over thousands of kilometers, where gravity's direction changes to keep pointing at Earth's center and its strength falls off with distance. Newton's cannonball scenario removes that approximation: as speed increases, the trajectory smoothly deforms from Galileo's short parabola into a much larger ellipse (or, at exactly the right speed, a circle) that closes around the Earth. The physics does not change at any point in this progression; only the geometry of the path does. This was Newton's argument that the same gravitational force governing a falling apple also holds the Moon in its orbit: an orbit is just a projectile that overshoots the ground forever.

sections.heading: The three regimes
sections.body: The thought experiment sorts outcomes by launch speed relative to two thresholds. Below the speed needed to match Earth's curvature, the ball falls back to the surface, landing farther away as speed increases. At exactly the right speed it enters a circular orbit and returns to the mountain from the opposite direction. Between that speed and Earth's escape velocity, it enters an elliptical orbit. At or above escape velocity, it never comes back at all. This mountain-top thought experiment is the conceptual bridge from the projectile-motion topics in this unit to the gravitation-and-orbits topics that follow, since orbital mechanics is, in Newton's own framing, projectile motion with the curvature of the Earth (and the corresponding change in gravity's direction) no longer ignored.

lessons.workedExample: Near Earth's surface, the speed needed for a circular orbit works out to about 7.9 km/s (roughly 17,700 mph), found by setting gravitational acceleration equal to the centripetal acceleration needed for a circular path: g = v^2/R, so v = sqrt(g*R), with g approximately 9.8 m/s^2 and R approximately 6,371 km. A real cannon firing at, say, 1 km/s falls dramatically short of this threshold: the ball's path curves back to the ground within seconds, just a very long-range version of Galileo's parabola, since it is nowhere close to matching Earth's curvature. Newton's thought experiment is why this same v = sqrt(g*R) relation, scaled to whatever body and altitude, is exactly the formula used today to compute the orbital speed of the International Space Station (roughly 7.66 km/s at its ~400 km altitude, where g is slightly weaker than at the surface).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use Newton's cannonball to test whether a student sees projectile motion and orbital motion as one continuous phenomenon rather than two separate topics memorized independently. The key insight to state clearly is that nothing about the physics changes as speed increases through the three regimes; what changes is only whether the curving path closes before or after it reaches the ground, which depends on comparing the ball's fall to the curvature of the Earth. A student who can explain why a fast enough cannonball never lands, in terms of the ground curving away as fast as the ball falls, demonstrates real grasp of gravity as a single unified force, exactly the leap Newton was making.

questions.prompt: In Newton's cannonball thought experiment, what makes a fast enough cannonball go into orbit instead of landing?

options.text: At sufficient speed the ball stops being affected by gravity
The ball's falling path curves at the same rate the Earth's surface curves away beneath it, so it never reaches the ground
Air resistance at high altitude pushes the ball upward, cancelling gravity

explanations.a: Gravity still acts on an orbiting object; that is precisely what keeps it curving toward Earth instead of flying off in a straight line.
explanations.b: Correct: this is the core of Newton's argument, the ball is continuously falling, but the ground curves away at a matching rate, so the distance between them never closes.
explanations.c: Newton's mountain-top scenario is explicitly above the atmosphere; air resistance is not part of the mechanism.

questions.prompt: What is the key idealization in Galileo's parabola that Newton's cannonball scenario removes?

options.text: That the projectile has mass
That gravity always points in the same fixed direction and has constant strength
That time passes at a constant rate

explanations.a: Mass is not an idealization Galileo made or Newton removed; both treat the projectile as having mass throughout.
explanations.b: Correct: Galileo's flat-Earth, constant-downward-gravity assumption is fine locally but breaks down at orbital scales, where gravity points toward Earth's center and weakens with distance.
explanations.c: Constant time flow is a feature of Newtonian mechanics generally and is not something the cannonball scenario changes.

questions.prompt: Order these launch speeds by increasing outcome, from shortest fall to escaping Earth entirely.

items.text: Low speed: parabolic arc, lands nearby (Galileo's regime)
Higher speed: still falls back, but lands much farther away
Exactly orbital speed: circular orbit, never lands
Above escape velocity: leaves Earth and never returns

questions.explanation: As launch speed increases from a small value toward and past escape velocity, the outcome progresses continuously from a short parabolic landing, to a longer-range landing, to a closed circular orbit, to permanent escape.

questions.prompt: Match each launch-speed regime to its resulting path shape in Newton's thought experiment.

left.text: Speed exactly equal to circular-orbit speed
Speed between orbital speed and escape velocity

right.text: Approximately parabolic arc back to the surface (for low sub-orbital speeds)
Closed circular orbit
Closed elliptical orbit

questions.explanation: Below orbital speed the ball falls back in an approximately parabolic arc (a good approximation only at low sub-orbital speeds, since the true path is technically elliptical with Earth's center at a focus); at exactly orbital speed the path closes into a circle; between orbital speed and escape velocity the closed path is an ellipse.

lessons.label: Ballistics and the Birth of Computing

sections.heading: The firing-table problem
sections.body: A WWII artillery firing table listed, for a given gun and shell, the elevation and other settings needed to hit a target at a given range, adjusted for factors like air density, wind, and propellant temperature. Producing one table required numerically solving the shell's trajectory equations, which include air resistance and are not solvable in closed form, over roughly 1,000 to 3,000 different trajectories. The U.S. Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, needed a new table for every gun-shell combination and every set of atmospheric conditions, and by the early 1940s wartime demand for new tables was outpacing the lab's capacity to compute them.

sections.heading: Human computers
sections.body: The trajectories were calculated by hand and by mechanical desk calculators, largely by teams of women mathematicians, many hired to work at the University of Pennsylvania's Moore School of Electrical Engineering, recruited via newspaper ads seeking women math majors from colleges across the country, known as "computers," a job title that predates the machine. A single trajectory, using numerical step-by-step integration, could take a trained human computer 30 to 40 hours to work through; a full firing table with over a thousand trajectories represented months of labor even with dozens of computers working in parallel, and the Army's need for new tables was growing faster than that workforce could keep up.

sections.heading: ENIAC
sections.body: To relieve this bottleneck, the Moore School, funded by the Army and the Ballistic Research Laboratory, built ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer), completed in 1945 (too late to be used during the war itself) and unveiled publicly in 1946. It is generally regarded as the first general-purpose electronic digital computer. ENIAC could compute a single artillery trajectory in about 30 seconds, work that had taken a human computer dozens of hours, roughly a several-thousand-fold speedup. It was physically operated and programmed by a team of women, including Kathleen McNulty, Jean Bartik, Betty Holberton, Marlyn Meltzer, Frances Spence, and Ruth Teitelbaum, several of whom had previously worked as human computers on the very firing-table calculations ENIAC was built to replace; their programming work went largely unrecognized publicly for decades after the war.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose the Ballistic Research Laboratory needs a firing table requiring 2,000 distinct trajectories (different ranges, elevations, and atmospheric conditions). At roughly 35 hours per trajectory by hand, that is 70,000 person-hours of computation, about 35 human computers working full-time for a full year, and that is only one table among many needed for different guns. At ENIAC's roughly 30 seconds per trajectory, the same 2,000 trajectories take about 16.7 hours of machine time, work that used to occupy dozens of people for a year could then be finished by one machine in under a day. This gap, months of skilled human labor versus hours of machine time, is the concrete, dollars-and-lives reason the U.S. Army funded electronic computing research in the first place: faster tables meant guns could be recalibrated for new ammunition and conditions far more quickly in the field.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring this up to test whether a student sees the connection between a physics topic (numerically integrating a trajectory with drag) and a technology-history topic (why ENIAC got built) rather than treating them as unrelated facts. A strong answer explains specifically why trajectories with air resistance cannot be solved with a single closed-form equation the way Galileo's ideal parabola can, so they must be integrated step by step, which is exactly the repetitive numerical work computers do well and humans do slowly. Judges are also alert to whether a student can name that the actual programming labor was performed by women whose contributions were, for decades, left out of the historical record, since that omission is itself a well-documented part of this history.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't WWII firing tables be computed with a single closed-form equation like Galileo's ideal parabola?

options.text: Because real trajectories include air resistance, which makes the equations of motion unsolvable in closed form, requiring step-by-step numerical integration instead
Because gravity was not yet precisely measured in the 1940s
Because artillery shells travel faster than the speed of sound, which Newtonian mechanics cannot describe

explanations.a: Correct: adding realistic air resistance (which depends on velocity in a complicated way) removes the closed-form solution Galileo's no-drag case has, forcing numerical, trajectory-by-trajectory computation.
explanations.b: Gravity's value was known with more than sufficient precision by the 1940s; that was never the bottleneck in firing-table computation.
explanations.c: Newtonian mechanics fully describes supersonic projectile motion (relativistic effects are irrelevant at these speeds); the real obstacle was the complexity of the drag term, not the speed regime itself.

questions.prompt: What was ENIAC originally built to do?

options.text: Break German and Japanese military codes
Compute artillery firing tables for the U.S. Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory
Simulate nuclear weapon detonations exclusively

explanations.a: Codebreaking machines like the British Bombe and Colossus were separate wartime computing efforts; ENIAC's Army funding was specifically for ballistics.
explanations.b: Correct: ENIAC was funded by the U.S. Army and the Moore School specifically to speed up production of artillery firing tables for the Ballistic Research Laboratory.
explanations.c: ENIAC did later run early nuclear-related calculations, but that was not the original purpose that secured its wartime Army funding; firing tables were.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the ballistics-to-computing history.

items.text: Demand for firing tables outpaces the human-computer workforce at Aberdeen
The Moore School, with Army funding, begins building ENIAC
ENIAC is completed in 1945, after the war has ended
ENIAC computes trajectories in about 30 seconds each, versus dozens of hours by hand

questions.explanation: Wartime demand exceeding human-computer capacity motivated the Army-funded ENIAC project; the machine was finished in 1945, just after the war, and once running it delivered the dramatic per-trajectory speedup that had been its original justification.

questions.prompt: Match each role to its description in the ballistics-computing story.

right.text: A person, overwhelmingly a woman during WWII, who calculated trajectories by hand and desk calculator
A person, again largely a woman, who physically set up and ran ENIAC's calculations, work long uncredited publicly
The Aberdeen, Maryland Army facility that needed the firing tables and helped fund ENIAC's development

questions.explanation: Human computers did the manual trajectory math, ENIAC's programmers (mostly women, several former human computers) operated the finished machine, and the Ballistic Research Laboratory at Aberdeen was the Army unit whose firing-table backlog drove ENIAC's funding.

lessons.label: The Drag-Law Debate

sections.heading: Newton's v-squared law and its limits
sections.body: Isaac Newton, working from first principles of fluid resistance, argued that the drag force on an object moving through air scales with the square of its velocity (drag proportional to v-squared), a law he derived by imagining the fluid as a swarm of individual particles struck by the moving body, with each collision's momentum transfer growing with speed, and the collision rate also growing with speed, so the total force grows as speed times speed. This v-squared law matches experiment well for fast, blunt objects like cannonballs, but at very low speeds and small sizes it does not: for slow, small, or highly viscous-flow situations, drag instead scales linearly with velocity (Stokes' drag, formalized by George Stokes in 1851, roughly a century and a half after Newton). Which power of velocity actually governs a given real projectile was not a settled matter in the 17th and 18th centuries, because no one yet had accurate experimental data at gun-shot speeds to check Newton's prediction against.

sections.heading: Robins supplies the missing measurements
sections.body: Benjamin Robins, an English mathematician and military engineer, resolved much of the uncertainty experimentally. In New Principles of Gunnery (1742), he introduced the ballistic pendulum, a large mass hung on a pendulum arm; firing a musket ball into it and measuring how far the pendulum swung let Robins calculate the ball's muzzle velocity precisely for the first time, something gunners had previously only estimated. With real muzzle velocities in hand, Robins showed that Newton's v-squared drag law, extended with an empirical correction, fit measured musket-ball trajectories far better than the older straight-line-based gunnery calculations, and he also discovered that spinning bullets curved off course, an early clue toward what would later be understood as the Magnus effect.

sections.heading: Euler's mathematical extension
sections.body: In 1745, Leonhard Euler translated Robins's book into German and added commentary and mathematical elaboration that ran to several times the length of the original (Euler's annotated edition ran to roughly five times Robins's original page count), working out the differential equations for v-squared-drag trajectories in a form gunnery officers could actually use as tables. Euler's annotated version became the standard ballistics reference across Europe; Napoleon himself reportedly studied artillery from a French edition descended from it. The Robins-Euler v-squared framework, refined further through the 19th and 20th centuries as drag also proved to depend on the object's shape, surface roughness, and (near the speed of sound) compressibility effects, remains the practical starting point for real ballistics calculations today, while the low-speed, linear-in-v Stokes regime remains correct for its own separate domain, such as dust particles settling in air.

lessons.workedExample: A slow-moving pollen grain (radius under a millimeter, speed well under 1 m/s) experiences drag that is well approximated as linear in velocity, Stokes' regime, because viscous forces dominate at that small size and low speed (the relevant Reynolds number is small). A cannonball or rifle bullet (size on the order of centimeters, speed hundreds of meters per second) is deep in the opposite regime, where drag is well approximated as proportional to v-squared, because inertial forces dominate (the Reynolds number is large). This is exactly why Newton's v-squared law worked for the artillery Robins tested but does not apply to the pollen grain: the correct power of velocity in the drag law is not a universal constant, it depends on the size and speed regime of the object, formally captured by the Reynolds number, a concept that did not exist yet when Newton and Robins were debating this in the 17th and 18th centuries.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the drag-law debate to test whether a student understands that a physical law can be correct in one regime and wrong in another, rather than treating "is drag proportional to v or v-squared" as a single fact to memorize. A strong answer names both regimes (Newton's v-squared for fast, blunt, high-Reynolds-number objects like cannonballs; Stokes' linear-in-v for slow, small, low-Reynolds-number objects), and credits Robins's ballistic pendulum as the experimental innovation that let anyone actually test which law applied to real gunfire. A judge may ask why this distinction matters practically, and the sharp answer is that using the wrong drag law for a given size and speed produces trajectory predictions that are wrong by a large factor, which is precisely the gap firing tables had to get right.

questions.prompt: What experimental device did Benjamin Robins introduce in New Principles of Gunnery (1742) that let him test drag laws against real data?

options.text: The ballistic pendulum, which let him measure a musket ball's muzzle velocity precisely
The telescope, which let him track shells visually in flight
The barometer, which let him measure air pressure at different altitudes

explanations.a: Correct: firing a ball into a hanging pendulum mass and measuring the swing let Robins back out muzzle velocity for the first time with real precision.
explanations.b: Telescopes existed well before Robins and were not his key ballistics innovation; his contribution was the velocity-measuring pendulum.
explanations.c: Barometers measure air pressure, not projectile velocity, and were not the device that let Robins test Newton's drag law against real muzzle velocities.

questions.prompt: For a fast-moving, centimeter-scale object like a cannonball, which drag law is the better approximation?

options.text: Drag proportional to velocity (Stokes' linear regime)
Drag proportional to velocity squared (Newton's regime)
Drag is negligible at that size and speed

explanations.a: Stokes' linear drag law applies to small, slow objects at low Reynolds number, like a pollen grain, not a fast cannonball.
explanations.b: Correct: at the size and speed of a cannonball, inertial effects dominate (high Reynolds number), and drag scales approximately with velocity squared, as Newton predicted.
explanations.c: Drag is very much not negligible for a cannonball; it is exactly why firing tables needed the numerical corrections discussed in this and the previous lesson.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the drag-law debate.

items.text: Newton proposes drag proportional to velocity squared from first-principles fluid reasoning
Robins invents the ballistic pendulum and measures real muzzle velocities (1742)
Euler translates and mathematically extends Robins's book into usable tables (1745)
Stokes formalizes the separate, linear-in-velocity drag law for small, slow objects (1851)

questions.explanation: Newton's theoretical v-squared law came first; Robins supplied the missing experimental velocity measurements decades later; Euler mathematically extended Robins's results shortly after; the separate low-speed linear drag regime was only formalized by Stokes over a century after Newton.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their specific contribution to the drag-law debate.

right.text: Proposed the v-squared drag law from theoretical fluid-particle reasoning
Invented the ballistic pendulum to measure real muzzle velocities (1742)
Translated and mathematically extended the v-squared law into usable gunnery tables (1745)

questions.explanation: Newton supplied the theoretical v-squared law, Robins supplied the experimental means to test it against real gunfire, and Euler supplied the mathematical machinery that turned it into a usable ballistics reference.

lessons.label: The Long Dispute Over the Magnus Effect

sections.heading: Newton notices it, but does not explain it
sections.body: In 1671, Isaac Newton observed, from watching tennis players at Cambridge, that a ball struck with spin curves noticeably in flight, and in a 1672 letter to the Royal Society he offered a qualitative explanation: the spinning surface drags the adjacent air around with it, so on the side where the spin and the ball's forward motion move the air in the same direction, the air is compressed and pushes back harder, deflecting the ball toward the opposite side. This was a real physical insight, but it was qualitative and Newton did not attempt to derive a force law from it; for well over a century afterward, the effect remained an observed curiosity noted by gunners and ballplayers rather than a solved problem in fluid mechanics.

sections.heading: Magnus gives it a controlled demonstration
sections.body: The effect gets its modern name from Heinrich Gustav Magnus, a German physicist who in 1852 ran the first controlled laboratory demonstration: he mounted a spinning brass cylinder in a moving air stream and measured a consistent sideways deflection, confirming that rotation combined with relative airflow reliably produces a transverse force, not just an occasional or ball-specific quirk. Magnus's original motivation was actually to explain the curved flight paths of spinning artillery shells, not sports balls, connecting this lesson back to Robins's earlier observation (in the same 1742 book that introduced the ballistic pendulum) that spinning musket balls veered off a straight course.

sections.heading: Rayleigh supplies the mathematics, and myths persist anyway
sections.body: In 1877, Lord Rayleigh published "On the Irregular Flight of a Tennis Ball," the first serious analytical treatment, using the pressure distribution around a rotating cylinder in a flow (later formalized in fluid dynamics as the Kutta-Joukowski-adjacent circulation argument) to derive a transverse force proportional to spin rate and forward speed. This gave the effect a real quantitative footing nearly two centuries (about 205 years) after Newton first noted it and 25 years after Magnus's demonstration made it undeniable in the lab. Despite that long, thorough resolution, a persistent popular myth claims a curveball's break is an optical illusion, that the ball does not actually curve, only appears to; high-speed photography and wind-tunnel measurements have repeatedly confirmed the curve is a real, physical lateral deflection of the ball's path, exactly the Magnus force Rayleigh's equations predict, not a perceptual trick.

lessons.workedExample: A baseball pitcher throws a curveball at about 33 m/s (75 mph) with topspin-adjusted spin around 2,000-2,500 rpm depending on grip; the Magnus force this produces is on the order of a few tenths of a newton, small compared to the ball's weight but sustained over the roughly 0.4 to 0.5 seconds of flight from mound to plate, which is enough to displace the pitch by something on the order of 20-40 centimeters (roughly 8-15 inches) from a straight-line path, depending on spin axis and rate; that is a large enough displacement, relative to the strike zone, to be the entire reason curveballs are effective pitches. This is the same physical mechanism, transverse force from spin combined with airflow, that Magnus demonstrated on a rotating cylinder in 1852 and Rayleigh analyzed mathematically for a spinning ball in 1877; it is not a different, baseball-specific effect, and it is not an illusion, as confirmed by decades of high-speed-camera tracking of real pitches.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up the Magnus effect to test whether a student can correctly attribute a multi-stage discovery (Newton's qualitative 1671 observation, Magnus's 1852 controlled demonstration, Rayleigh's 1877 mathematical analysis) instead of collapsing three centuries of work into one name or one date. A second thing judges probe is the curveball-illusion myth specifically, because a student who repeats it uncritically reveals they have not engaged with the actual physical evidence (high-speed photography, wind-tunnel data) that settles the question; the correct, judge-satisfying answer states plainly that the curve is a real physical deflection caused by the Magnus force, not a perceptual illusion, and can explain why spin plus airflow produces a genuine transverse force rather than merely an apparent one.

questions.prompt: Who first gave a controlled, quantitative laboratory demonstration of the spin-induced sideways force now called the Magnus effect?

options.text: Isaac Newton, in 1671
Heinrich Gustav Magnus, in 1852, using a spinning cylinder in an air stream
Lord Rayleigh, in 1877

explanations.a: Newton only qualitatively observed and described the effect on tennis balls in 1671; he did not run a controlled laboratory demonstration.
explanations.b: Correct: Magnus's 1852 rotating-cylinder experiment was the first controlled lab demonstration that quantified the sideways deflection.
explanations.c: Rayleigh's 1877 contribution was the mathematical, analytical treatment, coming after Magnus's earlier experimental demonstration.

questions.prompt: The popular claim that a baseball curveball's break is just an optical illusion, and the ball does not actually deviate from a straight path, is:

options.text: Correct: high-speed cameras show the path is actually straight
A myth: high-speed photography and wind-tunnel data confirm the ball undergoes a real, physical transverse deflection from the Magnus force
Correct, but only for fastballs, not curveballs

explanations.a: This is the myth itself, and it is contradicted by decades of high-speed-camera and wind-tunnel measurements showing a real deflection.
explanations.b: Correct: the curve is a genuine physical displacement caused by the Magnus force, confirmed directly by high-speed photography, not a perceptual artifact.
explanations.c: The claim in the prompt is about curveballs specifically and is false regardless of pitch type; spin-induced Magnus deflection is real for any spinning pitch.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the history of the Magnus effect.

items.text: Newton qualitatively describes spin-curving of tennis balls (1671-72)
Robins notes spinning musket balls veer off course in ballistics tests (1742)
Magnus runs a controlled spinning-cylinder demonstration (1852)
Rayleigh publishes the mathematical analysis of tennis-ball flight (1877)

questions.explanation: Newton's qualitative tennis-ball observation came first, followed by Robins's independent ballistics observation of veering musket balls, then Magnus's controlled 1852 lab demonstration, and finally Rayleigh's 1877 mathematical treatment.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher to their specific contribution to understanding the Magnus effect.

right.text: First qualitative observation and explanation, from watching tennis (1671-72)
First controlled laboratory demonstration, using a spinning cylinder in airflow (1852)
First serious mathematical/analytical treatment of the force (1877)

questions.explanation: Newton offered the earliest qualitative explanation, Magnus supplied the first controlled quantitative lab demonstration nearly two centuries later, and Rayleigh supplied the first rigorous mathematical analysis a quarter-century after that.

lessons.label: Angular Position and the Radian

sections.heading: Describing rotation with an angle
sections.body: A rotating object's position is described by an angle theta measured from a fixed reference line, usually the positive x-axis, to a reference line drawn on the rotating body. As the object spins, theta changes; that change is what rotational kinematics tracks, the same way linear kinematics tracks a changing position x. Angles can be measured in degrees, revolutions, or radians, but physics runs on radians almost exclusively, because radians are the only angular unit that makes the linear-angular equations come out clean without extra conversion factors buried in them.

sections.heading: Why the radian is defined the way it is
sections.body: One radian is the angle subtended at the center of a circle by an arc whose length equals the circle's radius. That definition is exactly what produces the arc length relation s = r*theta, where s is arc length, r is radius, and theta is in radians. There is no unit-conversion constant in that equation because radians are themselves a ratio of two lengths (arc length / radius) and are technically dimensionless, even though they get carried around like a unit for bookkeeping. A full circle has arc length s = 2*pi*r, so theta for one full revolution is 2*pi*r / r = 2*pi radians -- confirming 360 degrees = 2*pi radians, or 1 radian is approximately 57.3 degrees.

sections.heading: Why degrees break the clean equations
sections.body: If theta were measured in degrees, arc length would need an extra factor: s = r*theta*(pi/180), because a degree is an arbitrary human-chosen slice of a circle (1/360 of a revolution) rather than a ratio tied to the circle's own geometry. Every rotational kinematics equation in this unit -- s = r*theta, v = r*omega, a = r*alpha -- depends on theta being in radians to hold in that exact clean form. Working a problem in degrees is not wrong, but it requires converting to radians first or dragging the pi/180 factor through every step, which is why radians are the default unit throughout rotational mechanics and should be used unless a problem explicitly reports revolutions or degrees for readability.

sections.heading: Revolutions as a third, coarser unit
sections.body: A third common unit, the revolution, counts full 360-degree turns and is convenient for describing how many times something has spun (an odometer's wheel-rotation count, a centrifuge's total spin count) but is too coarse for equation work: 1 revolution = 2*pi radians = 360 degrees, and no kinematic equation is written directly in revolutions without first converting. Recognizing which of the three units a problem hands you, and converting immediately to radians before any calculation, is the single most reliable habit for avoiding factor-of-57 or factor-of-360 errors in rotational problems.

lessons.workedExample: A bicycle wheel has radius 0.35 m. The valve stem on the rim sweeps through an arc length of 2.2 m as the wheel turns. Using s = r*theta, theta = s/r = 2.2 / 0.35 = 6.29 radians. Converting to revolutions: 6.29 rad / (2*pi rad/rev) = 1.00 revolution, confirming the wheel made almost exactly one full turn. In degrees, 6.29 rad * (180/pi) ≈ 360 degrees, essentially one full turn (the small (<0.5 degree) difference from exactly 360 comes partly from 2.2 m being very slightly longer than one exact circumference (2*pi*0.35 ≈ 2.199 m) and partly from rounding theta to 6.29 rad), showing all three descriptions (radians, revolutions, degrees) agree -- they are just different rulers for the same rotation.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge reviewing any rotating-system project -- a wheel, a centrifuge, a turntable, a robotic joint -- will ask what unit the student used for angle and why, because a student who reports omega or alpha without confirming radians has likely introduced a silent factor-of-57 error somewhere in their analysis. Judges also probe whether the student understands radians as a ratio (arc length over radius) rather than an arbitrary unit like degrees, since that understanding is what lets a student justify why s = r*theta has no conversion constant. A student who can derive that one radian equals about 57.3 degrees from the definition, rather than reciting it, demonstrates real conceptual grounding.

questions.prompt: Why does the equation s = r*theta require theta to be measured in radians?

options.text: Because radians are defined as the ratio of arc length to radius, so no conversion constant is needed
Because radians are a larger unit than degrees, making the numbers easier to work with
Because degrees only apply to angles under 360, while radians apply to any angle
It is simply a convention with no underlying mathematical reason

explanations.a: Correct: a radian is arc length divided by radius, so s = r*theta falls directly out of that definition with no extra factor.
explanations.b: Radian size relative to degrees is irrelevant to why the equation is clean -- it is the ratio-based definition that matters.
explanations.c: Both radians and degrees can describe angles beyond 360 (multiple revolutions); that is not the distinguishing feature.
explanations.d: There is a specific mathematical reason: the ratio-based definition of the radian, not an arbitrary convention.

questions.prompt: A merry-go-round has radius 4.0 m. A rider at the rim travels an arc length of 12.0 m. What angle, in radians, did the merry-go-round rotate through?

options.text: 48 rad
3.0 rad
0.33 rad
8.0 rad

explanations.a: That is s times r (12 * 4), not s divided by r -- theta = s/r, not s*r.
explanations.b: Correct: theta = s/r = 12.0 / 4.0 = 3.0 radians.
explanations.c: That is r/s (4.0/12.0), the reciprocal of the correct ratio.
explanations.d: That is r doubled, unrelated to the s/r calculation required.

questions.prompt: One full revolution equals how many radians?

options.text: 360 radians
pi radians
2*pi radians
1 radian

explanations.a: 360 is the count in degrees, not radians -- confusing the two units gives this wrong answer.
explanations.b: pi radians is half a revolution (180 degrees), not a full one.
explanations.c: Correct: the circumference of a circle is 2*pi*r, so theta = s/r = 2*pi*r/r = 2*pi radians for a full turn.
explanations.d: 1 radian is about 57.3 degrees, a small slice of a revolution, not the whole thing.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning that derives s = r*theta from the definition of a radian.

items.text: Define 1 radian as the angle where arc length equals the radius (s = r when theta = 1 rad)
Recognize that arc length scales proportionally with the angle swept, for a fixed radius
Generalize the proportional relationship to any angle theta, giving s = r*theta
Confirm the formula against a full revolution: s = 2*pi*r matches theta = 2*pi rad

questions.explanation: The radian is defined first (arc length equals radius at theta = 1 rad), then that ratio is recognized as proportional for any angle, generalized into s = r*theta, and finally checked against the known full-circle circumference as a sanity check.

questions.prompt: Match each angle measure to its radian equivalent.

right.text: pi/2 radians
pi radians (~3.14 rad)
2*pi radians
pi radians (same as 180 degrees)

questions.explanation: 90 degrees is a quarter turn (pi/2 rad); 180 degrees and 1/2 revolution are the same angle (pi rad); a full revolution is 2*pi rad -- degrees and revolutions are just different rulers for the same underlying radian value.

lessons.label: Angular Velocity and Angular Acceleration

sections.heading: Angular velocity: how fast theta changes
sections.body: Angular velocity omega is the rotational analog of linear velocity: it measures how quickly the angular position theta changes over time. Average angular velocity is omega_avg = delta_theta / delta_t, and instantaneous angular velocity is the derivative d_theta/dt. Its SI unit is radians per second (rad/s), though it is often reported in revolutions per minute (RPM) in engineering contexts -- 1 RPM = 2*pi/60 rad/s approximately 0.1047 rad/s. Every point on a rotating rigid body shares the same omega at a given instant, regardless of how far that point sits from the rotation axis; a bolt near a wheel's hub and a point on its rim complete the same fraction of a revolution in the same time, even though (as later lessons show) their linear speeds differ.

sections.heading: Angular acceleration: how fast omega changes
sections.body: Angular acceleration alpha measures the rate of change of angular velocity: alpha_avg = delta_omega / delta_t, with instantaneous alpha = d_omega/dt. Its SI unit is radians per second squared (rad/s^2). A spinning fan speeding up from rest has positive alpha (if the rotation direction is defined as positive); a wheel skidding to a stop has alpha opposite in sign to omega, since the rotation is decelerating. Alpha is nonzero only while omega is changing -- a merry-go-round spinning at a constant rate has omega greater than zero but alpha equal to zero, exactly parallel to how a car cruising at constant speed has velocity but no acceleration.

sections.heading: Sign conventions matter as much as magnitude
sections.body: Both omega and alpha are signed quantities (they are actually vectors along the rotation axis, but for motion confined to a single plane, a plus/minus sign captures the direction fully). The standard convention used throughout this unit is that counterclockwise rotation is positive and clockwise is negative, matching how theta itself is measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis in standard math convention. Getting the sign wrong is the single most common rotational-kinematics error: a wheel slowing down while spinning counterclockwise (omega positive) has alpha negative, but a wheel slowing down while spinning clockwise (omega negative) has alpha positive -- in both cases the wheel is decelerating, but the sign of alpha depends on the sign of omega it opposes, not on the word 'slowing' alone.

lessons.workedExample: A ceiling fan speeds up from omega = 0 to omega = 15.7 rad/s (about 150 RPM) over 5.0 seconds after being switched on. Average angular acceleration alpha = delta_omega / delta_t = (15.7 - 0) / 5.0 = 3.14 rad/s^2. If the fan is then switched off and coasts to a stop over the next 12.0 seconds, alpha during coasting = (0 - 15.7) / 12.0 = -1.31 rad/s^2 -- negative because omega is decreasing from a positive value, i.e., the angular acceleration opposes the direction of spin, consistent with friction and air resistance acting as decelerating torques.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing any spinning apparatus -- a centrifuge, a flywheel energy-storage device, a robotics arm joint -- routinely ask a student to state omega and alpha separately and explain what each one physically represents, because conflating 'how fast it's spinning' with 'how fast the spin is changing' is a frequent and revealing error. A judge may also test sign reasoning directly: 'your wheel was spinning clockwise and slowing down -- was alpha positive or negative?' A student who reasons from the sign of omega rather than guessing from the word 'slowing' demonstrates they understand alpha as opposing omega's sign during deceleration, not just decreasing in magnitude.

questions.prompt: A merry-go-round spins at a constant 2.0 rad/s. What is its angular acceleration?

options.text: 2.0 rad/s^2
0 rad/s^2
4.0 rad/s^2
Cannot be determined without knowing the radius

explanations.a: 2.0 rad/s^2 confuses the constant angular VELOCITY value with acceleration; a constant omega means alpha is zero.
explanations.b: Correct: constant angular velocity means omega is not changing, so alpha = d_omega/dt = 0.
explanations.c: There is no operation on the given value that produces 4.0; alpha is zero regardless of the numeric value of omega.
explanations.d: Angular acceleration depends only on how omega changes over time, not on the radius of the rotating object.

questions.prompt: A wheel spinning clockwise (omega negative by convention) is slowing down. What is the sign of its angular acceleration?

options.text: Negative, because the wheel is slowing down
Positive, because alpha opposes the negative omega as the wheel decelerates
Zero, because 'slowing down' means no acceleration
It cannot have a sign since speed is always positive

explanations.a: This is the classic sign-error trap: 'slowing down' does not automatically mean alpha is negative -- it means alpha opposes omega's existing sign.
explanations.b: Correct: since omega is negative and decreasing in magnitude (moving toward zero), alpha must be positive to push omega toward zero.
explanations.c: Slowing down is exactly a change in omega, which by definition requires a nonzero alpha.
explanations.d: Omega and alpha are signed quantities in one-dimensional rotational motion; only speed (the magnitude) is always positive.

questions.prompt: A drill bit accelerates from rest to 300 rad/s in 2.0 seconds. What is its average angular acceleration?

options.text: 600 rad/s^2
150 rad/s^2
300 rad/s^2

explanations.a: That is 300 * 2.0, multiplying instead of dividing by the time interval.
explanations.b: Correct: alpha = delta_omega / delta_t = (300 - 0) / 2.0 = 150 rad/s^2.
explanations.c: That is 2.0 / 300, the reciprocal of the correct ratio.
explanations.d: That is just the final omega value, ignoring that the change happened over a 2.0 s interval.

questions.prompt: Match each rotational scenario to its correct description of omega and alpha.

left.text: Fan spinning at a constant rate

right.text: omega nonzero and constant, alpha = 0
omega increasing from 0, alpha nonzero and same sign as omega
omega decreasing toward 0, alpha nonzero and opposite sign to omega

questions.explanation: Constant spin means unchanging omega and zero alpha; speeding up means alpha reinforces omega's sign; slowing down means alpha opposes omega's sign, driving it toward zero.

questions.prompt: Order these angular speeds from slowest to fastest rotation rate.

items.text: 0.5 rad/s
1 RPM (about 0.105 rad/s)
10 RPM (about 1.047 rad/s)
2 rad/s

questions.explanation: Converting all to rad/s: 1 RPM is about 0.105 rad/s (slowest), then 0.5 rad/s, then 10 RPM is about 1.047 rad/s, then 2 rad/s (fastest) -- RPM and rad/s must be put on a common unit before comparing.

lessons.label: Linking Linear and Angular Motion

sections.heading: Every point on a rigid body shares omega, not v
sections.body: A rigid body is one where every point maintains a fixed distance from every other point as it rotates -- a wheel, a door, a rotor blade. All points on a rotating rigid body share the same angular velocity omega and angular acceleration alpha at any instant, because they all sweep through the same angle in the same time. But their LINEAR speed differs, because linear speed depends on how far a point sits from the rotation axis. Differentiating s = r*theta with respect to time, and holding r constant for a point fixed to the rigid body, gives v = r*omega: tangential (linear) speed equals radius times angular velocity. A point twice as far from the axis moves twice as fast in a straight-line sense, even though both points complete the same revolution in the same time.

sections.heading: Tangential acceleration: the linear partner of alpha
sections.body: Differentiating v = r*omega again gives a_t = r*alpha, the tangential acceleration -- the component of a point's linear acceleration that lies along its direction of motion (tangent to its circular path), responsible for speeding up or slowing down the point's tangential speed. Like v = r*omega, this relation holds for any point rigidly attached to a rotating body, with a_t scaling directly with r: a point on the rim of a flywheel experiences much greater tangential acceleration than a point near the hub, for the same alpha, simply because it has farther to travel in the same angular sweep.

sections.heading: Why the rim outruns the hub
sections.body: This r-dependence has real consequences. A record spinning at a constant 33.3 RPM (a fixed omega) carries a point near the center at a slow linear speed and a point near the outer edge at a much faster linear speed -- the outer point literally covers more distance per second, since v = r*omega grows with r for fixed omega. This is why tip speed is a critical design metric for spinning machinery -- v and a_t are always largest at maximum radius, for a given alpha and omega. (Stress, however, is a separate story: turbine and propeller blade stress actually peaks at the root, where the attachment must react the centrifugal load of the whole blade, and a solid rotating disk's peak stress is at its center -- so "biggest radius = most stressed" is not a safe generalization.) Engineers routinely compute tip speed (v at the outermost r) as a first check on whether a rotating component is safe.

lessons.workedExample: A wind turbine blade is 40 m long, rotating at omega = 1.5 rad/s. At the blade tip (r = 40 m), tangential speed v = r*omega = 40 * 1.5 = 60 m/s (about 134 mph). Halfway along the blade (r = 20 m), v = 20 * 1.5 = 30 m/s -- exactly half the tip speed, confirming the direct proportionality to r. If the turbine's control system ramps omega up at alpha = 0.05 rad/s^2, the tip's tangential acceleration is a_t = r*alpha = 40 * 0.05 = 2.0 m/s^2, while the same point midway along the blade only experiences 20 * 0.05 = 1.0 m/s^2 -- half the tangential acceleration, again scaling directly with r.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating any project with a rotating component -- a wind-turbine model, a centrifuge, a flywheel -- will often ask 'which point on your device moves fastest, and why?' A student who answers 'the point farthest from the axis, because v = r*omega' has correctly separated the shared angular quantity (omega, same everywhere) from the point-dependent linear quantity (v, which scales with r). Judges also probe safety and design reasoning: a student who identifies blade-tip speed as the binding engineering constraint, rather than treating the whole blade as moving 'at the same speed,' shows they grasp why rotating machinery fails at its outer radius first.

questions.prompt: A wheel of radius 0.30 m spins at omega = 10 rad/s. What is the tangential speed of a point on the rim?

explanations.a: Correct: v = r*omega = 0.30 * 10 = 3.0 m/s.
explanations.b: That is omega/r (10/0.30), the reciprocal of the correct relation.
explanations.c: That is r + omega added together, which is not how v = r*omega works.
explanations.d: That is r/omega (0.30/10), also the reciprocal of the correct relation.

questions.prompt: Two points, A and B, sit on the same rotating rigid body. Point A is at r = 1.0 m and point B is at r = 3.0 m. Which statement is true?

options.text: A and B have the same omega but B has 3 times A's tangential speed
A and B have the same tangential speed but different omega
A has a greater omega than B because it is closer to the axis
A and B have both the same omega and the same tangential speed

explanations.a: Correct: all points on a rigid body share omega; tangential speed scales with r, so B (3x the radius) has 3x A's speed.
explanations.b: Tangential speed depends on r via v = r*omega, so different radii on the same rigid body give different speeds, not the same one.
explanations.c: Omega is shared by every point on a rigid body regardless of radius -- radius affects v, not omega.
explanations.d: Omega is shared, but tangential speed is not the same since it depends on r, which differs between A and B.

questions.prompt: A centrifuge rotor accelerates at alpha = 4.0 rad/s^2. At r = 0.15 m from the axis, what is the tangential acceleration?

explanations.a: Correct: a_t = r*alpha = 0.15 * 4.0 = 0.60 m/s^2.
explanations.b: That is alpha/r (4.0/0.15), the reciprocal of the correct relation.
explanations.c: That is r + alpha added, which is not how a_t = r*alpha works.
explanations.d: That is r/alpha (0.15/4.0), also the reciprocal of the correct relation.

questions.prompt: Order these points on a spinning disk (all sharing the same omega) from slowest to fastest tangential speed.

items.text: Point at r = 0.05 m (near the hub)
Point at r = 0.10 m
Point at r = 0.20 m
Point at r = 0.40 m (at the rim)

questions.explanation: Since v = r*omega and omega is identical for every point on the same rigid body, tangential speed increases strictly with radius -- the point nearest the hub is slowest and the rim point is fastest.

questions.prompt: Match each linear-angular relation to what it connects.

right.text: Arc length to angular position
Tangential speed to angular velocity
Tangential acceleration to angular acceleration

questions.explanation: Each linear quantity (s, v, a_t) is the radius times its exactly corresponding angular quantity (theta, omega, alpha) -- position pairs with position, rate with rate, and acceleration with acceleration.

lessons.label: Centripetal Acceleration in Rotation

sections.heading: A second acceleration every rotating point has
sections.body: A point moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because its VELOCITY DIRECTION is constantly changing even if its speed is not -- and acceleration is defined as any change in velocity, direction included. This acceleration points inward, from the moving point toward the center of the circle, which is why it is called centripetal ('center-seeking') acceleration. Its magnitude is a_c = v^2/r, or equivalently, substituting v = r*omega from the previous lesson, a_c = r*omega^2. Both forms describe the same physical quantity; the v^2/r form is more natural when linear speed is known, and the r*omega^2 form is more natural when angular velocity is known and multiple radii on the same rigid body are being compared.

sections.heading: Centripetal versus tangential: two different jobs
sections.body: Centripetal acceleration and tangential acceleration are perpendicular components of a rotating point's total acceleration, and they do fundamentally different jobs. Tangential acceleration a_t = r*alpha changes the point's SPEED (it exists only when omega is changing) and points along the direction of motion. Centripetal acceleration a_c = r*omega^2 changes the point's DIRECTION (it exists whenever omega is nonzero, even at constant speed) and points perpendicular to the motion, toward the center. A point moving in a circle at constant omega (alpha = 0) has centripetal acceleration but zero tangential acceleration; a point whose omega is changing has both simultaneously, and its total acceleration is the vector sum, magnitude sqrt(a_c^2 + a_t^2).

sections.heading: Why the effect grows so fast with omega
sections.body: Because a_c = r*omega^2 depends on omega SQUARED, centripetal acceleration grows far faster with rotation speed than tangential acceleration does with angular acceleration. Doubling omega quadruples a_c, while a_t = r*alpha does not depend on omega at all -- it only changes if alpha changes. This quadratic growth is why high-speed rotating machinery -- centrifuges, jet engine turbines, ultracentrifuges used to separate biological samples -- can subject material to accelerations of tens of thousands of times Earth's gravity (expressed in units of g, where 1g = 9.8 m/s^2) at rotation rates that sound modest in RPM. A hypothetical rotor spinning at 100,000 RPM (about 10,470 rad/s) with a radius of just 0.10 m would, by the formula alone, produce a_c = 0.10 * 10,470^2 ≈ 1.1 × 10^7 m/s^2 (about 11 million m/s^2), over 1 million g -- though real 100,000-RPM ultracentrifuge rotors use much smaller radii (around 0.06-0.07 m, giving roughly 750,000g) since material burst limits constrain how large a radius can survive that speed. The idealized 0.10 m figure here is chosen purely to illustrate how fast a_c grows with omega squared, not to describe an actual device.

lessons.workedExample: A carnival ride swings riders in a horizontal circle of radius 8.0 m at a constant omega = 1.2 rad/s. Since omega is constant, alpha = 0 and there is no tangential acceleration -- but centripetal acceleration is still present: a_c = r*omega^2 = 8.0 * 1.2^2 = 8.0 * 1.44 = 11.5 m/s^2, about 1.18 times g.
