That extra energy is not free: the skater's muscles do real mechanical work pulling her arms and leg inward against the effective outward pull (technically, the centrifugal effect in the rotating frame) that resists that inward motion once she is already spinning. This is the direct bridge to angular momentum conservation as a general law, covered in a later unit: L = Iω stays fixed with zero external torque, but KE is free to change because the skater's own internal muscular work — not an external torque — is what reshapes I.

lessons.workedExample: A skater begins a spin with arms extended, angular speed ω_i = 2.0 rev/s, and moment of inertia I_i = 4.0 kg·m². She pulls her arms and free leg in, reducing her moment of inertia to I_f = 1.0 kg·m² (a factor-of-four decrease). Conservation of angular momentum gives I_iω_i = I_fω_f, so ω_f = ω_i × (I_i / I_f) = 2.0 × (4.0/1.0) = 8.0 rev/s, a factor-of-four increase in spin rate. Checking kinetic energy: KE_i = ½I_iω_i² uses ω in rad/s (ω_i = 2.0 × 2π ≈ 12.57 rad/s), giving KE_i ≈ 0.5 × 4.0 × 12.57² ≈ 316 J. After pulling in, ω_f ≈ 8.0 × 2π ≈ 50.27 rad/s, giving KE_f ≈ 0.5 × 1.0 × 50.27² ≈ 1263 J — four times the starting kinetic energy, all supplied by the skater's own muscular effort pulling her limbs inward.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the spinning-skater demonstration to test whether students actually distinguish angular momentum from angular velocity and from kinetic energy — three different quantities that behave three different ways here (L constant, ω increases, KE increases). A weak answer says only "she spins faster because she pulls her arms in"; a strong answer names L = Iω as the conserved quantity, explains why external torque is approximately zero on ice, and can additionally explain where the extra kinetic energy comes from (the skater's own muscular work), rather than treating the speed-up as a free lunch.

questions.prompt: As a spinning skater pulls her arms in, which quantity stays approximately constant?

options.text: Angular velocity, ω
Angular momentum, L = Iω
Rotational kinetic energy, ½Iω²

explanations.a: Angular velocity is exactly what changes (increases) as the skater pulls her arms in; it is not conserved here.
explanations.b: Correct: with negligible external torque about the spin axis, angular momentum L = Iω is conserved, forcing ω to rise as I falls.
explanations.c: Kinetic energy actually increases as the skater pulls in, supplied by her own muscular work; it is not conserved.

questions.prompt: Why is angular momentum approximately conserved during the skater's spin?

options.text: Because the skater's total mass never changes during the spin
Because the net external torque about the vertical spin axis is approximately zero
Because moment of inertia is constant throughout the spin

explanations.a: Mass being constant is true but is not the reason angular momentum is conserved; conservation of L follows from zero net external torque, per the rotational analog of Newton's second law.
explanations.b: Correct: gravity acts through the spin axis (no torque arm) and the ice contact cannot exert a significant twisting torque, so external torque about the vertical axis is essentially zero, conserving L.
explanations.c: Moment of inertia is exactly what changes as the skater pulls her arms in; I is not constant here, ω changes to compensate.

questions.prompt: A skater's moment of inertia drops from 5.0 kg·m² to 2.0 kg·m² as she pulls her arms in. If her initial spin rate was 1.5 rev/s, what is her final spin rate?

options.text: 0.60 rev/s
1.5 rev/s, unchanged
3.75 rev/s

explanations.a: This inverts the ratio; ω increases as I decreases, it does not decrease.
explanations.b: Angular velocity is exactly what changes to compensate for the change in I, so it cannot stay unchanged.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to how it changes as the skater pulls her arms in from an extended spin.

right.text: Stays approximately constant
Decreases
Increases
Increases

questions.explanation: With negligible external torque, L = Iω stays fixed; pulling the arms in decreases I, which forces ω to increase to keep L fixed; and because KE = L²/(2I), a fixed L with shrinking I means KE increases, powered by the skater's own muscular work.

lessons.label: Measuring Moment of Inertia

sections.heading: Method 1: known torque, measured angular acceleration
sections.body: The rotational analog of F = ma is τ = Iα, so if you can apply a known torque to an object and measure the resulting angular acceleration, you can solve directly for I = τ/α. A common lab setup hangs a known mass m from a string wrapped around a pulley or spool fixed to the object's axis; as the mass falls, it unwinds the string and spins the object. If the spool radius is r and the mass's measured linear acceleration is a (found from how fast it falls), the string tension is T = m(g − a), the torque on the object is τ = Tr, and the object's angular acceleration is α = a/r, giving I = τ/α = Tr/(a/r) = Tr²/a. This method is direct and conceptually simple, but its accuracy is limited by bearing friction and air resistance, both of which add unaccounted torques that make the measured I too large unless they are separately measured and subtracted out.

sections.heading: Method 2: torsional oscillation, no motion of the object's average position
sections.body: A more precise approach for irregularly shaped objects — an engine crankshaft, a satellite component, a human limb in biomechanics research — mounts the object on a torsion spring (a shaft or wire that twists and provides a restoring torque proportional to angle, τ = −κθ, where κ is the torsion constant). Displaced and released, the object oscillates back and forth with a period T = 2π√(I/κ), the rotational analog of a mass-on-a-spring oscillator. Solving for I gives I = κT²/(4π²). Because the object barely moves from its rest orientation and friction contributes only a small damping correction rather than a large systematic torque, torsional methods are typically far more precise than the direct torque-and-α method, and they work on objects of any shape without needing a spool or pulley at all — only a way to fix the object to the torsion spring and measure how long each oscillation takes.

sections.heading: Why this matters beyond the classroom
sections.body: Real engineered objects rarely match the clean formulas for hoops, disks, rods, and spheres closely enough for those idealized formulas to be trustworthy. Automotive engineers measure the moment of inertia of crankshafts and flywheels this way before finalizing engine designs; aerospace engineers measure spacecraft components to predict how attitude-control thrusters will affect orientation; and biomechanics researchers have used torsional and pendulum methods to measure the moment of inertia of human limb segments, since predicting how fast a swinging leg or arm can rotate requires knowing its real I, which a simple cylinder or cone approximation only estimates roughly.

lessons.workedExample: An irregular metal bracket is mounted on a torsion spring with a known torsion constant κ = 0.50 N·m/rad. Displaced slightly and released, it oscillates with a measured period T = 2.4 s (timed by averaging 20 full swings and dividing to reduce timing error). Solving I = κT²/(4π²): I = 0.50 × (2.4)² / (4π²) = 0.50 × 5.76 / 39.48 ≈ 0.0729 kg·m². The same bracket could instead be spun up with a falling mass over a spool (τ = Iα), but that setup requires a low-friction bearing and only the spool-side geometry contributes measurable torque; the torsional method sidesteps both problems, since the bracket barely moves from equilibrium and no spool or pulley is needed at all — only a way to clamp the bracket to the spring and time its swings.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe measurement methodology to see whether a student understands moment of inertia as an empirically measurable quantity, not just a formula plugged from a table. Expect a judge to ask why the torsional-oscillation method is often preferred for irregular objects over the falling-mass method (better precision, no need for a spool, friction contributes a smaller relative error), or to ask what would happen to the measured I if bearing friction in the falling-mass setup were ignored (the measured I would be systematically too large, since friction adds an extra opposing torque the calculation doesn't account for).

questions.prompt: In the torsional-oscillation method, an object's moment of inertia is found from:

options.text: I = κT² / (4π²), using the torsion constant κ and oscillation period T
I = τ / α, using an applied torque and measured angular acceleration
I = MR², assuming the object is a hoop

explanations.a: Correct: for a torsional oscillator, T = 2π√(I/κ) rearranges to I = κT²/(4π²).
explanations.b: τ = Iα is the formula for the direct torque-and-angular-acceleration method, not the torsional-oscillation method described here.
explanations.c: I = MR² is the idealized hoop formula, not an experimental measurement technique, and it does not apply to irregular objects at all.

questions.prompt: In the falling-mass method, if bearing friction at the axle is ignored in the calculation, the resulting measured moment of inertia will be:

options.text: Too high, because friction adds an opposing torque the calculation doesn't account for
Too low, because friction speeds up the fall
Unaffected, since friction only acts on the axle, not the falling mass

explanations.a: Correct: friction opposes the spin-up, effectively requiring more of the applied torque just to overcome friction, so the calculation (which attributes all torque to spinning up the object) overestimates I.
explanations.b: Friction opposes motion, so it slows the fall and the spin-up, not speeds it up.
explanations.c: Friction at the axle directly opposes the rotational motion the falling mass is driving, so it absolutely affects the torque balance used to compute I.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the torsional-oscillation method for measuring an irregular object's moment of inertia.

items.text: Mount the object on a torsion spring/shaft with known torsion constant κ
Displace the object slightly from equilibrium and release it
Time multiple full oscillations and divide to get a precise period T
Compute I = κT² / (4π²)

questions.explanation: The object must first be mounted with a known κ, then set oscillating, then timed precisely (averaging over many cycles reduces timing error), and only then can the period be converted into I.

questions.prompt: Match each measurement method to its defining formula.

right.text: I = τ / α
I = κT² / (4π²)

questions.explanation: The direct method rearranges τ = Iα into I = τ/α; the torsional-oscillation method rearranges the oscillator period formula T = 2π√(I/κ) into I = κT²/(4π²).

lessons.label: The Radius of Gyration

sections.heading: Compressing a whole mass distribution into one number
sections.body: Moment of inertia already summarizes a complicated mass distribution into a single number, I, but that number still has awkward units (kg·m²) and doesn't have an intuitive physical size attached to it. The radius of gyration, k, fixes that by defining an equivalent hoop: k is the single radius at which ALL of an object's mass could be concentrated in an infinitely thin ring and still produce the same moment of inertia. Formally, I = Mk², exactly the hoop formula from an earlier lesson, so k = √(I/M). Unlike a hoop's radius, k is not the location of any actual mass — it is a mathematical stand-in, a way of expressing I in units of length (meters) rather than kg·m², which makes it easier to compare the "rotational spread" of objects with different total masses on equal footing.

sections.heading: Radius of gyration for the standard shapes
sections.body: Because I = c·MR² (or c·ML² for a rod) for each standard shape, and I = Mk², the coefficient c and the radius of gyration are directly linked: k = R√c for shapes expressed in terms of R. For a hoop (c = 1), k = R exactly — unsurprising, since a hoop already has all its mass at radius R. For a solid disk (c = ½), k = R/√2 ≈ 0.707R. For a solid sphere (c = 2/5), k = R√(2/5) ≈ 0.632R. For a rod about its center (I = (1/12)ML²), k = L/√12 ≈ 0.289L. In every case except the hoop, k turns out smaller than the object's outer radius (or half-length), reflecting that real mass distributions have mass spread inward from the edge, not concentrated entirely at it.

sections.heading: Why engineers use radius of gyration
sections.body: Radius of gyration shows up constantly in structural and mechanical engineering, particularly for beam and column cross-sections, where a column's resistance to buckling depends on its cross-sectional moment of inertia relative to its cross-sectional area — a quantity naturally expressed as a radius of gyration because it strips away the specific area value and leaves a pure geometric "spread" measurement that can be compared directly across differently sized beams. It is also used to compare the effective rotational "reach" of different vehicle designs (a car with a low radius of gyration about its vertical axis changes direction more nimbly for the same mass), independent of exactly how much that vehicle weighs.

lessons.workedExample: A solid disk has mass M = 4.0 kg and radius R = 0.20 m. Its moment of inertia is I = ½MR² = 0.5 × 4.0 × 0.20² = 0.5 × 4.0 × 0.04 = 0.08 kg·m². Its radius of gyration is k = √(I/M) = √(0.08/4.0) = √0.02 ≈ 0.1414 m. Checking against the shortcut formula k = R/√2 = 0.20/1.414 ≈ 0.1414 m confirms the same value. Physically, this means the disk behaves rotationally as if all 4.0 kg of its mass were concentrated in an infinitely thin ring at radius 0.1414 m — noticeably smaller than the disk's actual 0.20 m radius, because much of the disk's real mass lies closer to the center than to the rim.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use radius of gyration to test whether students can move fluidly between I, M, and k in either direction — given any two, solve for the third — and to catch a specific misconception: that k marks where the mass "really is." A strong answer explicitly states that k is a mathematical equivalent-hoop radius, not a physical location, and can explain why k is always smaller than the outer radius for every standard shape except a hoop, tying the answer back to how spread out that shape's real mass distribution is.

questions.prompt: The radius of gyration k of an object is best described as:

options.text: The physical radius at which the object's mass is most concentrated
The radius of an equivalent thin hoop of the same mass that would have the same moment of inertia
Always exactly equal to the object's outer radius, for any shape

explanations.a: k is a mathematical construct, not a description of where mass is physically concentrated, except in the special case of an actual hoop.
explanations.b: Correct: k is defined by I = Mk², matching the hoop formula, so k is the radius a thin ring of the same total mass would need to reproduce the same I.
explanations.c: k equals the outer radius only for a hoop; for a disk, sphere, or rod, k is smaller than the outer radius (or half-length).

questions.prompt: A solid sphere has radius R and moment of inertia I = (2/5)MR² about a diameter. What is its radius of gyration?

options.text: k = R

explanations.a: k = R only for a hoop, where all mass sits at radius R; a solid sphere's mass is spread through its interior, so k must be smaller than R.
explanations.b: Correct: from I = Mk² = (2/5)MR², dividing both sides by M gives k² = (2/5)R², so k = R√(2/5) ≈ 0.632R.
explanations.c: This drops the square root; k² = (2/5)R², not k = (2/5)R.

questions.prompt: Order these shapes (all with the same outer radius R) from smallest to largest radius of gyration.

items.text: Solid sphere (k ≈ 0.632R)
Solid disk (k ≈ 0.707R)
Hoop (k = R)

questions.explanation: Since k = R√c and the coefficients are 0.4 (sphere), 0.5 (disk), and 1.0 (hoop), the square roots order the same way: √0.4 ≈ 0.632 < √0.5 ≈ 0.707 < √1.0 = 1.0.

questions.prompt: Match each pair of known quantities to the formula that solves for the third quantity in I = Mk².

left.text: Given I and M, find k
Given M and k, find I
Given I and k, find M

right.text: I = Mk²
M = I/k²

questions.explanation: I = Mk² rearranges directly: solving for k gives k = √(I/M); solving for M gives M = I/k²; and the base formula I = Mk² already gives I directly from M and k.

lessons.label: The Rotational Second Law: tau = I alpha

sections.heading: The angular analog of F = ma
sections.body: Newton's second law says a net force produces linear acceleration in proportion to mass: F_net = m a. Rotational motion obeys the exact same structure with three quantities swapped in. Net torque (tau_net, in newton-meters) plays the role of net force. Moment of inertia (I, in kilogram-meters-squared) plays the role of mass — it measures how hard a body is to spin, not how hard it is to push. Angular acceleration (alpha, in radians per second squared) plays the role of linear acceleration. The law reads tau_net = I alpha. Just as mass resists a change in linear velocity, moment of inertia resists a change in angular velocity, and just as F = ma can be resolved and solved along a single axis of motion in these problems, tau = I alpha is applied along a single rotation axis, with counterclockwise torques conventionally positive.

sections.heading: Why I is not just mass
sections.body: Moment of inertia depends on how mass is distributed relative to the rotation axis, not just how much mass exists. For a point mass m at radius r, I = m r squared. For extended bodies, I is the sum (or integral) of m r squared over every mass element, which is why a thin hoop of mass M and radius R has I = M R squared (all its mass sits at radius R) while a solid disk of the same mass and radius has I = (1/2) M R squared (its mass is distributed from the center outward, so on average it sits closer to the axis and resists spinning less). This is why a figure skater spins faster when she pulls her arms in: she is not changing her mass, she is shrinking her moment of inertia, and conservation of angular momentum (L = I omega, which stays constant with no external torque even as I changes, per the more general torque law tau_net = dL/dt, of which tau = I alpha is the constant-I special case) forces omega up to compensate.

sections.heading: Solving basic rotational dynamics problems
sections.body: The recipe mirrors an F = ma problem: identify every torque acting on the rotating body about the chosen axis (tau = r F sin(theta), where theta is the angle between the force and the position vector r from the axis to the point of application), sum them with sign convention, divide by the moment of inertia (looked up or computed from the body's geometry), and the result is alpha. From there, the standard angular kinematics equations (omega = omega_0 + alpha t, and so on) apply exactly as their linear counterparts do. A key subtlety: only the component of force perpendicular to the lever arm produces torque, so a force applied straight along a rod, through its axis of rotation, or radially at a wheel's center produces zero torque no matter how large it is.

lessons.workedExample: A solid disk flywheel (I = (1/2) M R squared) has mass 4.0 kg and radius 0.25 m, so I = 0.5(4.0)(0.25)^2 = 0.125 kg*m^2. A constant tangential force of 6.0 N is applied at the rim, producing torque tau = r F = (0.25)(6.0) = 1.5 N*m (the force is tangential, so sin(theta) = 1). Angular acceleration is alpha = tau / I = 1.5 / 0.125 = 12 rad/s^2. Starting from rest, after 3.0 s the disk reaches omega = alpha t = 36 rad/s, about 5.7 revolutions per second, and has swept through theta = (1/2) alpha t^2 = 54 rad, about 8.6 revolutions.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a student to explain tau = I alpha is really testing whether the student understands WHY moment of inertia depends on mass distribution and not just total mass, since that distinction is what separates a memorized formula from physical insight. A weak answer states the equation; a strong answer explains why a hoop and a disk of equal mass and radius behave differently under the same torque, and connects that to a real experimental design choice, such as why a flywheel meant to store rotational energy efficiently is built with mass concentrated at the rim.

questions.prompt: In the rotational form of Newton's second law, tau_net = I alpha, moment of inertia I plays the same role that which quantity plays in F_net = m a?

options.text: Velocity
Mass
Displacement

explanations.a: Velocity's angular counterpart is omega, not I; velocity does not appear in either second-law equation.
explanations.b: Correct: both mass and moment of inertia measure resistance to a change in motion (inertia), one linear, one rotational.
explanations.c: Displacement's angular counterpart is theta; neither displacement nor theta appears in the second law itself.

questions.prompt: A hoop and a solid disk have the same mass and radius. Under the same applied torque, which has the larger angular acceleration?

options.text: The hoop, because its I is larger
The disk, because its I is smaller
They are equal, because mass and radius are equal

explanations.a: The hoop's I = M R^2 IS larger than the disk's, but a larger I means SMALLER alpha for the same torque (alpha = tau/I), not larger.
explanations.b: Correct: the disk's I = (1/2) M R^2 is half the hoop's, so for equal torque alpha = tau/I is twice as large for the disk.
explanations.c: Mass and radius being equal does not make I equal; I also depends on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis, which differs between hoop and disk.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving a basic tau = I alpha problem.

items.text: Identify every torque acting on the body about the chosen axis
Sum the torques with a sign convention to get tau_net
Divide by the body's moment of inertia to get alpha
Apply angular kinematics equations using alpha

questions.explanation: You must first find every torque, then combine them into a net torque, then convert to angular acceleration via tau = I alpha, and only then use that alpha in kinematics.

questions.prompt: Match each linear quantity to its rotational analog.

right.text: Torque (tau)
Moment of inertia (I)
Angular acceleration (alpha)

questions.explanation: Force maps to torque, mass maps to moment of inertia, and linear acceleration maps to angular acceleration in the F=ma / tau=I*alpha correspondence.

lessons.label: The Massive Pulley

sections.heading: Why an ideal pulley is a simplification
sections.body: Introductory problems often treat a pulley as massless and frictionless: it merely redirects a string, and tension is the same on both sides. That assumption fails the moment the pulley itself has mass, because a massive pulley must undergo angular acceleration to speed up, and by tau = I alpha that requires a net torque. If the string tension were equal on both sides, the net torque about the pulley's axle would be zero and the pulley could never spin faster. So for a real pulley with moment of inertia I and radius R, the tension on the side accelerating the pulley forward (T1) must differ from the tension on the other side (T2): the string does not slip, so T1 and T2 pull with equal-magnitude, opposite-direction torques only when the pulley is not accelerating.

sections.heading: Setting up the coupled system
sections.body: A classic setup: two blocks of mass m1 and m2 hang from a string that passes over a pulley of mass M, radius R, and moment of inertia I (commonly a disk, I = (1/2) M R squared). Each block gets its own F = ma equation with its own tension: for block 1, T1 - m1 g = m1 a (if accelerating upward) or m1 g - T1 = m1 a (if accelerating downward), and similarly for block 2. The pulley gets its own tau = I alpha equation: (T2 - T1) R = I alpha, where T2 is the tension on the side of the heavier, descending block. The constraint that ties all three equations together is that the string does not slip or stretch, so the block's linear acceleration a and the pulley's angular acceleration alpha are related by a = R alpha.

sections.heading: Solving the system
sections.body: With three equations (two F = ma, one tau = I alpha) and the constraint a = R alpha, there are three unknowns: a, T1, and T2 (alpha is eliminated via the constraint). Substituting alpha = a / R into the pulley equation and adding all three equations together makes the tensions cancel, in the same way solving a standard two-block-over-a-pulley problem does, but leaves an extra I / R squared term on the effective total inertia. The heavier the pulley relative to the blocks, the more it 'soaks up' torque before releasing angular acceleration, and the smaller the system's overall acceleration compared to the massless-pulley idealization.

lessons.workedExample: A block of mass m1 = 2.0 kg hangs on one side of a pulley; a block of mass m2 = 3.0 kg hangs on the other. The pulley is a solid disk of mass M = 1.0 kg and radius R = 0.10 m, so I = 0.5(1.0)(0.10)^2 = 0.005 kg*m^2. Using a = (m2 - m1) g / (m1 + m2 + I/R^2): I/R^2 = 0.005/0.01 = 0.5 kg. So a = (3.0 - 2.0)(9.8) / (2.0 + 3.0 + 0.5) = 9.8 / 5.5 = 1.78 m/s^2, noticeably less than the 1.96 m/s^2 a massless-pulley model would predict, because the pulley's inertia absorbs some of the net torque driving the system.
lessons.judgeFraming: This topic is a favorite judge probe because it exposes whether a student actually understands WHY tensions differ across a real pulley, rather than having memorized 'tension is the same on both sides' as a universal rule. A student who can explain that unequal tension is REQUIRED to produce the net torque that spins up a massive pulley — and that assuming equal tension would force alpha to be zero — demonstrates the causal chain from tau = I alpha rather than pattern-matching a formula.

questions.prompt: For a pulley with nonzero mass and moment of inertia that is speeding up, why must the string tensions on its two sides be unequal?

options.text: Because the string always slips slightly on a real pulley
Because a net torque is required to produce the pulley's angular acceleration, and equal tensions would give zero net torque
Because friction in the axle bearing always makes one side stronger

explanations.a: The no-slip assumption is standard in these problems (that's what gives a = R alpha); slipping is not the reason for unequal tension.
explanations.b: Correct: by tau = I alpha, spinning up a massive pulley requires nonzero net torque; equal-magnitude opposing tensions would cancel to zero torque, so they cannot both be equal AND produce angular acceleration.
explanations.c: Axle friction is a separate, additional effect not required for tensions to differ; even a frictionless massive pulley needs unequal tensions to accelerate.

questions.prompt: In the two-hanging-block-over-a-massive-pulley system, what is the correct no-slip constraint linking the blocks' linear acceleration a to the pulley's angular acceleration alpha?

options.text: a = R alpha
a = alpha / R
a = I alpha

explanations.a: Correct: a point on the pulley's rim moves with linear speed v = R omega and linear acceleration a = R alpha, and the string's acceleration matches the rim's since it does not slip.
explanations.b: This has the wrong units unless R has units of 1/length; the correct relation multiplies alpha by R, not divides by it.
explanations.c: I alpha is the net torque (tau = I alpha), not an acceleration; this confuses two different equations in the same problem.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving a two-block, massive-pulley system.

items.text: Write F = ma for each hanging block using its own tension
Write tau = I alpha for the pulley using both tensions
Apply the no-slip constraint a = R alpha to relate block and pulley motion
Combine all equations to solve for a, T1, and T2

questions.explanation: Each body's own equation of motion is written first, then the constraint links the separate equations together, and only then can the combined system be solved.

questions.prompt: Match each pulley model to its correct tension behavior.

left.text: Massive pulley, system moving at constant velocity

right.text: Tension equal on both sides
Tension unequal on both sides
Tension equal because alpha = 0

questions.explanation: A massless pulley needs no net torque, so tension is always equal; a massive pulley needs unequal tension only while accelerating, and returns to equal tension once alpha = 0 even though the pulley has mass.

lessons.label: Unwinding Spools and Yo-Yos

sections.heading: A body that translates and rotates at once
sections.body: A yo-yo dropped from rest, or a spool with a string wrapped around its axle, both fall while also spinning, and the two motions are locked together by the string. As the object falls a linear distance, the same length of string unwinds from a circle of radius r (the axle radius, not necessarily the object's outer radius), so the amount the object spins is fixed by how far it falls. This produces a rolling-without-slipping-style constraint even though the object is not touching a surface: the linear acceleration of the object's center of mass, a_cm, is related to the angular acceleration of its spin, alpha, by a_cm = r alpha, where r is the radius at which the string leaves the spool.

sections.heading: Two equations, one constraint
sections.body: Solving a yo-yo or spool problem uses the same two-equation structure as any combined translation-rotation problem. Newton's second law for the center of mass, applied along the vertical, gives m g - T = m a_cm (weight down, string tension up, for a yo-yo falling and unwinding). The rotational second law about the object's own center-of-mass axis gives T r = I alpha, since only the string tension, acting at radius r, produces torque about that axis (gravity acts at the center of mass and produces zero torque about it). The constraint a_cm = r alpha ties the two equations together, leaving two equations and two unknowns (a_cm and T) once alpha is eliminated.

sections.heading: Why the acceleration is always less than g
sections.body: Substituting the constraint into the two equations of motion shows a_cm = g / (1 + I / (m r squared)), which is always less than g because the term I / (m r squared) is strictly positive whenever the object has any moment of inertia at all. Physically, some of the gravitational potential energy converts to rotational kinetic energy as the yo-yo spins up, not just translational kinetic energy, so the center of mass falls slower than a freely falling point mass would. The smaller the unwinding radius r is relative to the object's overall size, the larger I / (m r squared) becomes and the slower the fall — which is why a yo-yo unwinding from a thin axle falls far more slowly than it would if the string were wrapped around its outer rim.

lessons.workedExample: A yo-yo of mass 0.20 kg, treated as a uniform disk (I = (1/2) m R^2) of outer radius R = 0.030 m, has a string wound around a thin axle of radius r = 0.005 m. I = 0.5(0.20)(0.030)^2 = 9.0e-5 kg*m^2. Using a_cm = g / (1 + I/(m r^2)): I/(m r^2) = 9.0e-5 / (0.20 * 0.005^2) = 9.0e-5 / 5.0e-6 = 18. So a_cm = 9.8 / 19 = 0.52 m/s^2, dramatically slower than free fall, because the thin axle radius makes the I/(m r^2) term large — this is exactly why a real yo-yo appears to 'hover' down its string rather than drop like a dense stone.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this topic wants to see whether the student can identify that the string tension is what couples the object's translational and rotational motion, and explain quantitatively why the axle radius, not the outer radius, controls the fall rate. A common misconception is assuming the yo-yo falls at close to g; a strong response derives a_cm = g/(1 + I/(m r^2)) and connects the thin-axle design directly to the observed slow, sustained spin of a real yo-yo, tying the abstract equation to an everyday object the judge has actually held.

questions.prompt: Why does a falling, unwinding yo-yo accelerate downward at less than g?

options.text: Because air resistance on the string slows it down
Because some of the gravitational energy goes into rotational kinetic energy instead of only translational kinetic energy
Because the string tension exceeds the yo-yo's weight

explanations.a: Air resistance is neglected in this idealized model; the slower fall is explained by the mechanics of the constraint, not drag.
explanations.b: Correct: string tension does nonzero work rotating the yo-yo, diverting energy away from translational motion and reducing a_cm below g.
explanations.c: If tension exceeded weight, net force would be upward and the yo-yo would accelerate up, not fall; tension is less than weight here (m g - T = m a_cm with a_cm > 0 requires T < mg).

questions.prompt: In the constraint a_cm = r alpha for an unwinding yo-yo, what does r represent?

options.text: The yo-yo's outer radius
The radius of the axle the string unwinds from
The length of string still wound on the spool

explanations.a: The outer radius is irrelevant to the string constraint unless the string happens to be wound there; typically it is wound on a thinner axle.
explanations.b: Correct: r is specifically the radius at which the string leaves the spool, since that determines how much linear string length unwinds per radian of spin.
explanations.c: Remaining wound string length does not appear in the acceleration relation; only the radius at which unwinding occurs matters.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding a falling yo-yo's linear acceleration.

items.text: Write m g - T = m a_cm for the center of mass
Write T r = I alpha for rotation about the yo-yo's own axis
Substitute the constraint a_cm = r alpha to eliminate alpha
Solve the combined equations for a_cm

questions.explanation: Both equations of motion must be written first, then the geometric constraint links them by eliminating alpha, allowing the final algebraic solution for a_cm.

questions.prompt: Match each yo-yo design change to its effect on fall acceleration a_cm, holding mass and outer radius fixed.

left.text: Make the axle radius r smaller
Make the axle radius r larger (closer to outer radius)
Increase moment of inertia I (redistribute mass toward the rim)

right.text: a_cm decreases (falls more slowly)
a_cm increases (falls more quickly)
a_cm decreases (falls more slowly)

questions.explanation: Since a_cm = g/(1 + I/(m r^2)), shrinking r or growing I both increase the term I/(m r^2), pushing a_cm further below g, while growing r shrinks that term and speeds the fall toward g.

lessons.label: Combining Translation and Rotation

sections.heading: Two second laws, one body
sections.body: Many real bodies — a ball rolling down a ramp, a cylinder released on an incline, a wheel accelerating a car — both translate and rotate simultaneously, and describing their motion fully requires writing Newton's second law twice: once for translation of the center of mass (F_net = m a_cm, summing all external forces), and once for rotation about the center of mass (tau_net = I alpha, summing all torques about that same center-of-mass axis). These are not two different laws; they are the same law applied to two different aspects of the same rigid body's motion, and both must be satisfied simultaneously. Crucially, only forces that do not pass through the center of mass produce a torque about it, so gravity (acting at the center of mass) never appears in the rotational equation, while friction or an applied force offset from center often does.

sections.heading: Rolling without slipping: the third equation
sections.body: When a round body rolls without slipping — a ball or cylinder on a surface, rather than a yo-yo on a string — there is a kinematic constraint identical in form to the yo-yo case: v_cm = R omega and a_cm = R alpha, where R is the body's radius and the contact point is instantaneously at rest relative to the surface. This constraint is what makes rolling problems solvable with exactly enough equations: F_net = m a_cm (translation), tau_net = I alpha (rotation about the center of mass), and a_cm = R alpha (rolling constraint) together give three equations for three unknowns (a_cm, alpha, and typically the unknown friction force that provides the torque). Static friction is what supplies that torque in pure rolling — without it, the object could translate but never spin up, since gravity and the normal force both act through or in line with the center of mass on a ramp and cannot produce the needed torque themselves.

sections.heading: Why different shapes roll down a ramp at different rates
sections.body: A sphere, a cylinder, and a hoop, released from rest at the same height on the same frictional ramp, reach the bottom in different times, even though all have the same mass and radius, because they have different moment-of-inertia factors (I = c M R squared, where c is 2/5 for a solid sphere, 1/2 for a solid cylinder, and 1 for a thin hoop). Solving F_net = m a_cm and tau_net = I alpha together with the rolling constraint gives a_cm = g sin(theta) / (1 + c), so a smaller c produces a larger acceleration. The solid sphere (smallest c) wins the race, then the solid cylinder, then the hoop (largest c) last — a result famously demonstrable and independent of mass or radius, only the mass distribution shape factor c matters.

lessons.workedExample: A solid cylinder (c = 1/2, so I = (1/2) M R^2) of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.15 m rolls without slipping down a ramp inclined at theta = 20 degrees. Using a_cm = g sin(theta) / (1 + c) = 9.8 (0.342) / 1.5 = 2.23 m/s^2 — noticeably less than the g sin(theta) = 3.35 m/s^2 a frictionless sliding block would have on the same ramp, because part of the gravitational force's work goes into spinning the cylinder up rather than only accelerating its center of mass. The friction force providing the torque can be recovered from tau = I alpha with alpha = a_cm/R: alpha = 2.23/0.15 = 14.87 rad/s^2, tau = I alpha = 0.5(2.0)(0.15)^2(14.87) = 0.335 N*m, so f = tau/R = 2.23 N — a modest friction force, well within what a typical ramp surface (mu_s ~0.3 or higher) could supply, consistent with rolling without slipping.
lessons.judgeFraming: This concept is a favorite judge probe precisely because it is counterintuitive: students often assume friction only opposes or wastes energy, but here static friction is the ONLY thing that can make a body spin up while rolling down a frictionless-feeling ramp, and it does so with zero energy loss because the contact point does not slide. A strong answer explains why the moment-of-inertia shape factor c, not mass or radius, determines the race outcome between a sphere, cylinder, and hoop, and can explain why this result surprises most people's everyday intuition about heavier objects falling faster.

questions.prompt: On a ramp, why does a rolling solid cylinder accelerate more slowly down the incline than a frictionless block would?

options.text: Because friction dissipates energy as heat, slowing the cylinder
Because some of the gravitational force's effect goes into angular acceleration (spinning the cylinder up) rather than only linear acceleration
Because the cylinder is heavier than the block

explanations.a: In pure rolling without slipping, static friction does zero work (the contact point does not slide), so no energy is dissipated as heat; the slower acceleration is not due to energy loss.
explanations.b: Correct: solving F_net = m a_cm and tau_net = I alpha together shows a_cm = g sin(theta)/(1+c), which is always less than g sin(theta) because torque must also accelerate the spin.
explanations.c: The comparison in a_cm = g sin(theta)/(1+c) is independent of mass; a heavier cylinder of the same shape factor c has the identical acceleration.

questions.prompt: A solid sphere (c = 2/5) and a thin hoop (c = 1) of equal mass and radius are released together at the top of the same ramp. Which reaches the bottom first?

options.text: The sphere, because it has a smaller moment-of-inertia shape factor c
The hoop, because it has a larger moment of inertia and stores more energy
They tie, because they have the same mass and radius

explanations.a: Correct: a_cm = g sin(theta)/(1+c) is larger when c is smaller, and the sphere's c = 2/5 is smaller than the hoop's c = 1, so the sphere accelerates faster and arrives first.
explanations.b: A larger moment of inertia means MORE resistance to angular acceleration, which SLOWS the hoop's descent, not speeds it up; storing more rotational energy per unit speed is why it lags.
explanations.c: Equal mass and radius do not guarantee equal acceleration; the shape factor c, which depends on mass distribution, differs between a sphere and a hoop and breaks the tie.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving a rolling-without-slipping problem on an incline.

items.text: Write F_net = m a_cm along the incline, including the unknown friction force
Write tau_net = I alpha about the center of mass, using friction as the only torque source
Apply the rolling constraint a_cm = R alpha
Solve the three equations together for a_cm, alpha, and the friction force

questions.explanation: Translation and rotation equations must each be written first, then the rolling constraint links them, and only then can all three unknowns be solved simultaneously.

questions.prompt: Match each force acting on a ball rolling down a ramp to its role in the combined translation-rotation equations.

left.text: Gravity (acts at the center of mass)
Normal force (acts through the contact point, perpendicular to the ramp)
Static friction (acts at the contact point, along the ramp)

right.text: Contributes to F_net = m a_cm but produces zero torque about the center of mass
Contributes to both F_net = m a_cm and tau_net = I alpha

Contributes to F_net = m a_cm but produces zero torque, since it passes exactly through the center of mass (the radius to the contact point is always perpendicular to the surface, same as the normal force's line of action)

questions.explanation: Gravity acts exactly at the center of mass so it has zero lever arm and produces no torque about that point; the normal force's line of action also passes exactly through the center-of-mass axis for a round body on a flat or inclined surface, so it too produces no net torque about the center; only friction, acting tangentially at the contact point with a nonzero lever arm equal to the radius, supplies the torque that spins the body up.

lessons.label: Rotational Work and Power

sections.heading: Work done by a torque
sections.body: Linear work is force times displacement along the direction of the force, W = F d (for constant, aligned F). Rotational work follows the identical pattern with torque and angle: a constant torque tau doing work over an angular displacement theta (in radians) does work W = tau theta. Just as linear work requires a force to act over some distance, rotational work requires a torque to act while the body actually rotates through some angle — a torque applied to a jammed, non-rotating wheel does zero work, no matter how large the torque, exactly as pushing on an immovable wall does zero linear work despite exerting a force. The units check out: torque in newton-meters times an angle in radians (dimensionless) gives newton-meters, the same unit as linear work (joules), because radians carry no physical dimension.

sections.heading: Rotational power
sections.body: Linear power is the rate of doing work, P = F v (for aligned, constant force and velocity). Rotational power follows the same substitution pattern: P = tau omega, where omega is angular velocity in radians per second. This is the equation that governs how much power a motor, engine, or turbine delivers: a car engine's horsepower rating, for instance, is fundamentally torque times the engine's rotational speed (RPM converted to radians per second), which is why engineers report both torque and RPM curves — a high-torque, low-RPM engine and a low-torque, high-RPM engine can deliver identical peak power through entirely different tradeoffs, with direct consequences for how each is suited to towing versus high-speed cruising.

sections.heading: The rotational work-energy theorem
sections.body: Just as net linear work changes an object's translational kinetic energy (W_net = Delta KE_translational = (1/2) m v_f^2 - (1/2) m v_i^2), net rotational work changes an object's rotational kinetic energy: W_net,rot = Delta KE_rotational = (1/2) I omega_f^2 - (1/2) I omega_i^2. For a body that both translates and rotates, such as a rolling ball, total kinetic energy is the sum of both terms, KE_total = (1/2) m v_cm^2 + (1/2) I omega^2, and this is the quantity that energy-conservation problems (a ball rolling down a hill without slipping, for instance) must track in full — using only the translational term for a rolling object systematically overstates its speed, because it ignores the energy diverted into spin.

lessons.workedExample: A motor delivers a constant torque of 4.0 N*m to a flywheel initially at rest, spinning it up over 5.0 revolutions (theta = 5.0 * 2 pi = 31.4 rad). The work done is W = tau theta = 4.0(31.4) = 125.6 J. If the flywheel's moment of inertia is 0.20 kg*m^2, this work becomes rotational kinetic energy: 125.6 = (1/2)(0.20) omega_f^2, so omega_f^2 = 1256, omega_f = 35.4 rad/s (about 5.6 rev/s). If the motor delivers this work over 2.0 s, its average power is P_avg = W/t = 125.6/2.0 = 62.8 W; instantaneously, at the final angular speed, P = tau omega_f = 4.0(35.4) = 141.6 W, illustrating that instantaneous power grows as the flywheel spins faster even though torque stays constant.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe rotational work and power to check whether a student recognizes these as direct analogs of linear work and power rather than unrelated formulas to memorize separately, and to test whether the student correctly includes rotational kinetic energy in an energy-conservation analysis. A common error a judge listens for is a student computing only (1/2) m v^2 for a rolling or spinning object and forgetting the (1/2) I omega^2 term entirely, which silently violates energy conservation and produces a subtly wrong final speed.

questions.prompt: A torque is applied to a wheel that is jammed and cannot rotate at all. How much work does the torque do?

options.text: Zero, because there is no angular displacement
A nonzero amount proportional to the torque, regardless of rotation
It depends on how long the torque is applied, even with zero rotation

explanations.a: Correct: W = tau theta requires an actual angular displacement theta; with theta = 0 (jammed, non-rotating), W = 0 no matter how large tau is, exactly like pushing on an immovable wall.
explanations.b: Work always requires displacement (angular, in this case); torque alone, without any resulting rotation, cannot do work.
explanations.c: Work is not defined by duration alone; power (a rate over time) could be discussed differently, but work specifically requires angular displacement, which is zero here regardless of elapsed time.

questions.prompt: For a ball that rolls without slipping down a hill, which expression correctly gives its total kinetic energy?

options.text: (1/2) m v_cm^2 only
(1/2) I omega^2 only

explanations.a: This omits the rotational kinetic energy entirely, which would understate the total energy needed to both translate AND spin the ball as it rolls.
explanations.b: This omits the translational kinetic energy of the center of mass, leaving out most of the ball's actual kinetic energy.
explanations.c: Correct: a rolling body both translates and rotates, so its total kinetic energy is the sum of the translational term and the rotational term about its center of mass.

questions.prompt: Order the linear-to-rotational analogy from the most basic quantity to the resulting energy theorem.

items.text: Torque, the rotational analog of force
Rotational work, W = tau theta
Rotational power, P = tau omega
Rotational work-energy theorem, W_net = Delta((1/2) I omega^2)

questions.explanation: Torque is the fundamental quantity; work is built from torque acting over an angle; power is the rate of that work; and the work-energy theorem connects net rotational work to the resulting change in rotational kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: Match each linear quantity to its rotational analog.

right.text: W = tau theta
P = tau omega
KE = (1/2) I omega^2

questions.explanation: Each linear work/power/energy expression has a direct rotational analog formed by substituting torque for force, angular displacement for linear displacement, angular velocity for linear velocity, and moment of inertia for mass.

lessons.label: A Worked Rotational-Dynamics Problem

sections.heading: The setup: a hanging mass turning a wheel
sections.body: A common laboratory and exam setup: a mass m hangs from a string wrapped around the rim of a wheel or pulley of moment of inertia I and radius R, mounted on a fixed, frictionless axle (unlike the massive pulley in an earlier lesson, this wheel does not translate, only spins). As the mass falls, it unwinds the string, spinning the wheel up. Because the wheel's axle is fixed, this is simpler than the yo-yo or massive-pulley cases in one respect — the wheel itself does not accelerate translationally — but the problem still requires the same three-part structure: F = ma for the hanging mass, tau = I alpha for the wheel, and a string constraint linking the two.

sections.heading: Setting up all three equations
sections.body: For the hanging mass, taking downward as positive: m g - T = m a, where T is the string tension and a is the mass's downward linear acceleration. For the wheel, the only torque about its fixed axle comes from the string tension acting at radius R (gravity and the axle's support force both act through or at the axle and contribute no torque about it): T R = I alpha. The constraint, from the string not slipping or stretching as it unwinds: a = R alpha, identical in form to the yo-yo case but here because the wheel is fixed in place while the string end (attached to the falling mass) moves. Three equations, three unknowns (a, alpha, T), fully determined.

sections.heading: Solving simultaneously
sections.body: Substitute alpha = a / R into the wheel's torque equation: T R = I (a/R), so T = I a / R squared. Substitute this expression for T into the hanging mass's equation: m g - I a / R squared = m a. Collect all terms with a on one side: m g = m a + I a / R squared = a (m + I / R squared). Solve for a: a = m g / (m + I / R squared). This has exactly the same structural form as the massive-pulley result from an earlier lesson, because both problems share the same physics — a hanging mass's weight is opposed by an inertial reluctance to spin, expressed through the I / R squared term, which behaves like an additional effective mass added to the system.

lessons.workedExample: A mass of 0.50 kg hangs from a string wound around a wheel of moment of inertia I = 0.010 kg*m^2 and radius R = 0.080 m. First compute I/R^2 = 0.010/0.0064 = 1.5625 kg (this behaves as extra effective mass). Then a = m g / (m + I/R^2) = (0.50)(9.8) / (0.50 + 1.5625) = 4.9 / 2.0625 = 2.38 m/s^2. Tension is then T = m(g - a) = 0.50(9.8 - 2.38) = 3.71 N (check: this must be less than m g = 4.9 N, and it is, confirming the mass accelerates downward rather than hanging in equilibrium). Angular acceleration of the wheel is alpha = a/R = 2.38/0.080 = 29.75 rad/s^2, and after the mass falls 1.0 m from rest, v^2 = 2 a d = 2(2.38)(1.0) = 4.76, so v = 2.18 m/s and the wheel's final angular speed is omega = v/R = 27.3 rad/s.
lessons.judgeFraming: This problem type is a staple judge probe because it requires a student to correctly combine three separate physical relationships (a linear Newton's-law equation, an angular Newton's-law equation, and a kinematic constraint) into one coherent solution without conflating them, and because sanity-checking the result (tension must be less than the weight; the extra I/R^2 term must always reduce acceleration below g) reveals whether the student understands the physics or just manipulated algebra. Expect a judge to ask what happens to a as I grows very large or R grows very small: the answer, that a approaches zero because the wheel becomes effectively impossible to spin up, tests genuine command of the I/R^2 term's physical meaning.

questions.prompt: In the fixed-axle wheel and hanging mass system, which torque(s) act on the wheel about its axle?

options.text: Only the string tension
Both the string tension and the wheel's own weight
Only the axle's support force

explanations.a: Correct: the string tension acts at radius R and has a nonzero lever arm, producing torque; the wheel's weight and the axle's support force both act at or through the axle (zero lever arm) and produce zero torque about it.
explanations.b: The wheel's weight acts through the fixed axle (assuming a symmetric wheel), giving it zero lever arm about the rotation axis and therefore zero torque, contrary to this option.
explanations.c: The axle's support force acts exactly at the axle, so its lever arm about the rotation axis is zero; it produces no torque, contrary to this option.

questions.prompt: As the wheel's moment of inertia I grows very large (holding m and R fixed), what happens to the hanging mass's acceleration a = m g / (m + I/R^2)?

options.text: a approaches g
a approaches zero
a is unaffected by I

explanations.a: a approaches g only in the opposite limit, as I approaches zero (a massless wheel offers no rotational inertia to overcome).
explanations.b: Correct: as I grows, I/R^2 dominates the denominator, making the fraction shrink toward zero — an extremely massive-moment-of-inertia wheel is nearly impossible to spin up, so the hanging mass barely accelerates.
explanations.c: I appears explicitly in the denominator of the acceleration formula, so it directly affects a; it is not unaffected.

questions.prompt: Order the algebraic steps for solving a = m g / (m + I/R^2) starting from the three individual equations.

items.text: Write m g - T = m a for the hanging mass and T R = I alpha for the wheel
Substitute the constraint alpha = a/R into the wheel's torque equation to get T = I a / R^2
Substitute this expression for T into the hanging mass's equation
Collect terms in a and solve algebraically for a

questions.explanation: The two original equations of motion come first, then the constraint is used to eliminate alpha and express T in terms of a, then that T is substituted into the mass equation, and finally the resulting single equation is solved for a.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity in the worked wheel-and-hanging-mass problem to its correct sanity check.

right.text: Must always be less than m g (the hanging weight)
Must always be less than g (free-fall acceleration)
Behaves like an additional effective mass added to the system

questions.explanation: Since a < g, the net force on the mass must be less than its weight, so T < m g; a itself is always below g because part of gravity's effect goes into spinning the wheel; and I/R^2 enters the acceleration formula in exactly the position an extra mass would, which is why it is interpreted as effective added inertia.

lessons.label: Rotational Kinetic Energy

sections.heading: The energy hiding in a spin
sections.body: A spinning object stores kinetic energy even if its center of mass is not moving at all — a potter's wheel spinning in place, a flywheel storing energy for a bus, a figure skater pulling in her arms. Translational kinetic energy is KE = (1/2) m v^2, built from mass and how fast the center of mass moves. Rotational kinetic energy is its direct analog: KE_rot = (1/2) I omega^2, where I is the moment of inertia (how mass is distributed relative to the rotation axis, in kg*m^2) and omega is the angular speed in rad/s. The parallel is exact: mass becomes moment of inertia, linear speed becomes angular speed, and the 1/2 survives unchanged because both formulas come from the same calculus step -- integrating F dx = m v dv (or tau dtheta = I omega domega) always yields a v^2/2 (or omega^2/2) term, regardless of how the object accelerates.

sections.heading: Why moment of inertia is not just mass
sections.body: Two objects with identical mass can store wildly different rotational energy at the same omega because I depends on HOW FAR the mass sits from the axis, weighted by the square of that distance: I = sum(m_i r_i^2) for a collection of point masses, or the integral version for a continuous body. A solid disk of mass M and radius R has I = (1/2) M R^2; a thin hoop of the same M and R has I = M R^2 — twice as much, because every bit of the hoop's mass sits at the maximum radius R, while the disk's mass is spread from the center outward. This is why flywheels built for energy storage put mass in a heavy outer rim rather than a solid disk: for a fixed mass budget, pushing material outward maximizes I and therefore maximizes stored energy at a given spin rate.

sections.heading: Reading the formula in real devices
sections.body: Grid-scale flywheel energy storage systems (used for short-term frequency regulation on power grids) spin composite rotors at thousands to tens of thousands of RPM depending on design, specifically to exploit the omega^2 dependence — doubling angular speed quadruples stored energy, so engineers push speed hard while managing the centrifugal stress that scales the same way. A Beacon Power installation in Stephentown, NY reached full 20 MW of grid regulation capacity in 2011, with flywheels spinning up to 16,000 RPM. The lesson generalizes: whenever you see an object storing or releasing energy through spin rather than through straight-line motion, KE_rot = (1/2) I omega^2 is the bookkeeping tool, and I is doing the work that mass does in the translational formula.

lessons.workedExample: A solid cylinder (I = (1/2) M R^2) has mass 2.0 kg, radius 0.10 m, and spins at omega = 20 rad/s about its central axis. First find I = (1/2)(2.0)(0.10)^2 = 0.010 kg*m^2. Then KE_rot = (1/2)(0.010)(20)^2 = (1/2)(0.010)(400) = 2.0 J. Compare: if instead all 2.0 kg were concentrated in a thin hoop at r = 0.10 m, I = M R^2 = 0.020 kg*m^2 (double), so KE_rot = (1/2)(0.020)(400) = 4.0 J — twice the energy for the same mass and same omega, purely because the hoop's mass sits farther from the axis on average.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will ask a student to justify WHY I appears where mass appears in the translational formula, not just recite KE_rot = (1/2) I omega^2. A strong answer connects I to mass distribution and can compare two shapes (disk vs. hoop) of equal mass and explain which stores more energy at the same omega and why. A weak answer plugs numbers into the formula without being able to say what changes if the mass is redistributed. Expect a follow-up: 'if you doubled omega, what happens to the stored energy?' — testing whether the student registers the squared dependence, not just the existence of the formula.

questions.prompt: A thin hoop and a solid disk have the same mass M and radius R and spin at the same omega. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The hoop has more rotational kinetic energy because I = M R^2 for a hoop versus (1/2) M R^2 for a disk
The disk has more rotational kinetic energy because its mass is more concentrated
They have equal rotational kinetic energy because mass and radius are equal

explanations.a: Correct: the hoop's mass sits entirely at radius R, giving I = M R^2, twice the disk's I = (1/2) M R^2, so at equal omega the hoop stores twice the rotational KE.
explanations.b: Backwards — concentrating mass near the axis (as a disk does relative to a hoop) LOWERS I, which lowers rotational KE, not raises it.
explanations.c: Equal mass and radius do not guarantee equal I; I also depends on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis, which differs between a hoop and a disk.

questions.prompt: If the angular speed omega of a spinning flywheel is doubled while I stays fixed, the rotational kinetic energy:

options.text: Doubles
Quadruples
Stays the same

explanations.a: KE_rot depends on omega SQUARED, not omega linearly, so doubling omega does more than double the energy.
explanations.b: Correct: KE_rot = (1/2) I omega^2, so doubling omega multiplies the energy by 2^2 = 4.
explanations.c: Energy only stays the same if I decreases to compensate; with I fixed, increasing omega always increases KE_rot.

questions.prompt: Match each translational quantity to its rotational analog used in KE_rot = (1/2) I omega^2.

left.text: The factor of 1/2 in (1/2) m v^2

right.text: Moment of inertia (I)
Angular speed (omega)
Carries over unchanged to (1/2) I omega^2

questions.explanation: Moment of inertia plays the role mass plays, angular speed plays the role linear speed plays, and the 1/2 coefficient is identical in both formulas because both arise from the same quadratic energy relationship.

lessons.label: Rolling Without Slipping

sections.heading: Two motions, one constraint
sections.body: A rolling wheel is doing two things at once: its center of mass translates forward at speed v, and the wheel itself spins about that center at angular speed omega. These two motions are independent in general — a wheel could spin in place (v = 0, omega != 0, like a tire stuck in mud) or slide with no spin at all (v != 0, omega = 0, like a hockey puck). Rolling WITHOUT SLIPPING is the special case where the two are locked together by the constraint v = r*omega, with r the wheel's radius. This constraint is not a separate law of physics; it is the geometric statement that in one rotation (angle 2*pi), the wheel's rim sweeps out an arc length 2*pi*r, and if that arc length exactly matches the distance the center advances with no scuffing, the two speeds must be proportional through r.

sections.heading: Why the contact point is momentarily still
sections.body: The most useful — and most counterintuitive — consequence of v = r*omega is that the point on the wheel currently touching the ground has ZERO instantaneous velocity relative to the ground, even though the wheel as a whole is moving. Think of the wheel's motion as the sum of two velocities at the contact point: the center-of-mass translation (+v, forward) and the rotational velocity of that point about the center (-r*omega, backward, since the bottom of a forward-spinning wheel moves backward relative to the center). When rolling without slipping holds, v = r*omega exactly, so these cancel: v - r*omega = 0. This is why a rolling tire does not screech or scuff the road, while a spinning, slipping tire (peeling out) does — the contact point is sliding against the ground precisely when v != r*omega.

sections.heading: A velocity profile across the wheel
sections.body: Because the contact point has zero velocity and the center has velocity v, every other point on the wheel has a velocity that can be found by adding translation and rotation with the contact point as an instantaneous pivot. The very top of the wheel, twice as far from the contact point as the center, moves at 2v — this is a textbook result confirmed by everyday observation: the top of a rolling bicycle wheel is a blur while the bottom, for an instant, is not moving at all. This 'instantaneous axis of rotation' picture (treating the contact point as a momentary pivot) is a standard tool AP Physics C students use to find velocities of arbitrary points on a rolling body without re-deriving the constraint from scratch each time.

lessons.workedExample: A bicycle wheel of radius 0.35 m rolls without slipping at v = 4.2 m/s. Find omega and the speed of the topmost point. From v = r*omega, omega = v/r = 4.2/0.35 = 12 rad/s. The contact point has speed 0 (rolling constraint). The center has speed v = 4.2 m/s. The top point, at distance 2r = 0.70 m from the contact point (the instantaneous pivot), moves at omega * (2r) = 12 * 0.70 = 8.4 m/s = 2v, exactly double the center's speed — consistent with the instantaneous-axis picture where every point's speed is omega times its distance from the momentarily-stationary contact point.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love asking 'what is the velocity of the point touching the ground?' because the answer (zero) feels wrong to most students on first encounter, and defending it separates surface-level from real understanding. A strong response derives it from v = r*omega rather than asserting it, and can extend the reasoning to find the speed of the top of the wheel (2v) without being fed the instantaneous-axis trick. A judge may also probe the difference between a wheel's own spin rate and how fast a marked point on its rim traces out a path in the ground frame (a cycloid) — a strong student recognizes rolling without slipping is a constraint linking two otherwise-independent motions, not a separate kind of motion.

questions.prompt: For a wheel of radius r rolling without slipping with center-of-mass speed v, the instantaneous velocity of the point in contact with the ground is:

options.text: v, the same as the center
2v, twice the center's speed

explanations.a: The contact point's rotational velocity (-r*omega) exactly cancels the translational velocity (+v) under the rolling constraint v = r*omega, so it is not moving at the center's speed.
explanations.b: Correct: translation (+v) and the contact point's rotational velocity about the center (-r*omega = -v) sum to zero — this is why a rolling wheel does not scuff the ground.
explanations.c: 2v is the speed of the TOP of the wheel (twice as far from the contact pivot as the center), not the contact point itself.

questions.prompt: A wheel spins with omega != 0 while its center of mass stays fixed at v = 0 (like a tire spinning in mud). This wheel is:

options.text: Rolling without slipping, since it is still rotating
Not rolling without slipping, since v = r*omega is violated
Rolling without slipping only if omega is small

explanations.a: Rotation alone does not satisfy the constraint; v = r*omega requires the translational and rotational speeds to be linked, and here v = 0 while omega != 0.
explanations.b: Correct: with v = 0 and omega != 0, v = r*omega only holds if omega = 0 too, so the constraint fails — this is a pure spin-in-place (slipping) case.
explanations.c: The size of omega does not matter; any nonzero omega paired with v = 0 already violates v = r*omega.

questions.prompt: Order these points on a rolling wheel from slowest to fastest instantaneous speed (ground frame): contact point, center of mass, top of wheel.

items.text: Point touching the ground
Center of mass (axle)
Topmost point of the wheel

questions.explanation: Treating the contact point as the instantaneous pivot, speed scales with distance from it: the contact point itself has speed 0, the center at distance r has speed v, and the top at distance 2r has speed 2v.

lessons.label: The Role of Static Friction in Rolling

sections.heading: Friction as the torque source
sections.body: Imagine a ball released from rest on a frictionless ramp: gravity pulls the center of mass downhill, but there is no force applied off-center to produce a torque about the center of mass, so the ball would slide down without ever starting to spin — it reaches the bottom translating but not rotating. Real ramps are not frictionless, and the force that converts sliding into rolling is STATIC friction acting at the contact point. Because that force acts at the rim, a distance r from the center, it produces a torque tau = r * f_s about the center of mass, and that torque is exactly what spins the object up as it accelerates down the ramp. Without static friction, gravitational potential energy would convert entirely into translational kinetic energy; with it, some of that energy is diverted into rotational kinetic energy as well.

sections.heading: Why this friction force does zero work
sections.body: It seems paradoxical that a force can change an object's motion (supplying torque, changing omega) while doing zero work, but the rolling-without-slipping constraint makes this exact. Work done by a force equals force times the displacement of the POINT OF APPLICATION in the direction of the force. Static friction acts at the contact point, and — as shown in the rolling-without-slipping lesson — that point has zero instantaneous velocity, hence zero displacement over any instant. Force times zero displacement is zero work, no matter how large the friction force is. This is why energy conservation (KE_initial + PE_initial = KE_final + PE_final, with no friction-loss term) works perfectly well for objects rolling without slipping down a ramp, even though a torque-producing friction force is clearly present and essential to the motion.

sections.heading: How large a coefficient of friction is 'enough'
sections.body: Static friction only need be as large as required to maintain the rolling constraint; it self-adjusts up to its maximum value f_s,max = mu_s * N (mu_s the coefficient of static friction, N the normal force). For a uniform sphere or cylinder rolling down an incline of angle theta, applying Newton's second law for both translation and rotation shows the required friction force is f_s = (I / (I + m r^2)) * m g sin(theta). If mu_s is too small to supply this force, the object cannot maintain pure rolling and begins to slip — which is why icy or oily ramps make rolling objects skid rather than roll cleanly, and why the required mu_s is larger for hoops (larger I) than for solid spheres (smaller I) at the same ramp angle.

lessons.workedExample: A solid sphere (I = (2/5) m r^2) rolls without slipping down a ramp inclined at theta = 20 degrees. The required static friction is f_s = (I / (I + m r^2)) m g sin(theta) = ((2/5) m r^2 / ((2/5) m r^2 + m r^2)) m g sin(theta) = (2/7) m g sin(20 deg). With m = 1.0 kg, g = 9.8 m/s^2: f_s = (2/7)(1.0)(9.8)(0.342) = 0.96 N. The normal force is N = m g cos(theta) = (1.0)(9.8)(0.940) = 9.2 N, so the minimum coefficient of static friction needed is mu_s,min = f_s / N = 0.96/9.2 = 0.10. If the actual mu_s of the ramp is below 0.10, the sphere slips instead of rolling cleanly.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is one of the most commonly misunderstood ideas in rotational mechanics, and judges probe it directly: 'if friction is doing no work, why is it necessary at all?' A strong student separates the two roles of a force cleanly — supplying torque (which changes omega) versus doing work (which changes kinetic energy) — and explains that these are decoupled here specifically because the contact point does not move. A weaker answer conflates 'friction is present' with 'friction dissipates energy,' missing that static (non-slipping) friction is fundamentally different from kinetic friction in this respect. Expect a follow-up about what happens to energy conservation the moment the object starts to slip.

questions.prompt: A ball rolls without slipping down a ramp. The static friction force at the contact point:

options.text: Does no work, but supplies the torque that spins the ball up
Does negative work, slowing the ball's translation
Does no work and produces no torque, since it is a reaction force

explanations.a: Correct: the friction force acts at the contact point (zero instantaneous velocity, so zero work) but acts at a lever arm r from the center, producing torque tau = r f_s that spins the ball up.
explanations.b: Static friction here does zero work, not negative work — the contact point does not move, so force times displacement is zero regardless of the force's direction.
explanations.c: Static friction absolutely produces torque (that is precisely why the ball starts spinning); it is the WORK that vanishes, not the torque.

questions.prompt: Why does static friction do zero work on a ball rolling without slipping down a ramp?

options.text: Because static friction forces are always smaller than kinetic friction forces
Because the contact point where friction acts has zero instantaneous velocity
Because friction only acts perpendicular to the direction of motion

explanations.a: The relative sizes of static and kinetic friction have nothing to do with whether work is done; work depends on displacement of the point of application, not the magnitude comparison between friction types.
explanations.b: Correct: work = force times displacement of the point of application; the rolling-without-slipping contact point has zero velocity, hence zero displacement over any instant, hence zero work.
explanations.c: Static friction on a rolling object acts along the ramp surface (horizontal-ish, in the plane of motion), not perpendicular to it; perpendicularity is not why the work is zero here.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity in f_s = (I / (I + m r^2)) m g sin(theta) to what happens to the required friction if that quantity increases (others fixed).

right.text: Required f_s increases
Required f_s also increases
Required f_s is unaffected (mu_s only sets the MAXIMUM available friction)

questions.explanation: Both I and sin(theta) appear in the numerator direction of the required-friction formula, so increasing either raises the friction needed to maintain rolling; mu_s does not appear in that formula at all — it only caps how much friction the surface CAN supply (f_s,max = mu_s N), determining whether slipping occurs, not how much friction is required.

lessons.label: The Ramp Race: Hoop versus Disk versus Sphere

sections.heading: A race decided before it starts
sections.body: Release a hoop, a solid disk, and a solid sphere from rest at the top of the same ramp, same mass, same radius, and let them roll without slipping. Every time, the sphere wins, the disk is second, and the hoop finishes last — and the outcome does not depend on the mass, the radius, or even the ramp angle. The reason is the dimensionless ratio I/(m r^2), called beta, which captures how an object's mass is distributed relative to its axis independent of its actual size: beta = 2/5 for a solid sphere, 1/2 for a solid disk or cylinder, and 1 for a thin hoop or ring. A smaller beta means a smaller fraction of the object's kinetic energy budget gets diverted into spinning, leaving more for translation — so smaller-beta objects race downhill faster.

sections.heading: Deriving the split with energy conservation
sections.body: Applying energy conservation from top to bottom of a ramp of height h: m g h = (1/2) m v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2. Using the rolling constraint omega = v/r and writing I = beta * m r^2, the rotational term becomes (1/2)(beta m r^2)(v/r)^2 = (1/2) beta m v^2. So m g h = (1/2) m v^2 (1 + beta), and solving gives v = sqrt(2 g h / (1 + beta)). This single formula explains the whole race: h and g are the same for every object on the same ramp, so the only thing distinguishing final speeds is (1 + beta) in the denominator — larger beta means a larger denominator means a smaller final v. A sphere (beta = 2/5) reaches v = sqrt(2gh/1.4); a hoop (beta = 1) only reaches v = sqrt(2gh/2), noticeably slower for identical h.

sections.heading: The counterintuitive part: mass and radius do not matter
sections.body: Because m and r cancel completely out of v = sqrt(2gh/(1+beta)), a bowling-ball-sized solid sphere and a marble-sized solid sphere reach the SAME speed at the bottom of the same ramp, and a heavy steel hoop ties a light cardboard hoop of the same shape category. This is a genuinely famous classroom demonstration and a favorite conceptual-physics teaching point — the mass/radius-independence part echoes Galileo's inclined-plane experiments in the early 1600s, which established that acceleration under gravity doesn't depend on an object's mass, while the shape-dependent (beta) spread between hoop, disk, and sphere is a later result of rotational dynamics that Galileo's experiments didn't address. Students who expect 'heavier wins' or 'bigger wins' are consistently surprised. What DOES matter is purely the shape category via beta: how far the mass sits from the axis, not how much of it there is or how big the object is.

lessons.workedExample: A solid sphere (beta = 2/5) and a thin hoop (beta = 1) are released from rest together at the top of a ramp of height h = 0.80 m. Sphere: v = sqrt(2(9.8)(0.80)/(1 + 0.4)) = sqrt(15.68/1.4) = sqrt(11.2) = 3.35 m/s. Hoop: v = sqrt(2(9.8)(0.80)/(1+1)) = sqrt(15.68/2) = sqrt(7.84) = 2.80 m/s. The sphere reaches the bottom about 20% faster despite identical mass, radius, and starting height — entirely because less of its kinetic energy budget (a fraction beta/(1+beta) = 2/7 for the sphere vs. 1/2 for the hoop) is diverted into rotation rather than translation.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson is a judge favorite for testing whether 'more mass wins' misconceptions have been replaced by real understanding. A strong student predicts the finish order from beta alone before doing arithmetic, and can explain WHY mass and radius cancel (they appear identically in both the m g h term and the (1/2) m v^2 (1+beta) term). A judge may ask what happens if the objects instead SLIDE frictionlessly down the ramp with no rotation at all — testing whether the student recognizes that without the rotational energy sink, all objects (any beta) would tie, which isolates rotation as the entire cause of the spread in the rolling case.

questions.prompt: A solid sphere (beta = 2/5) and a solid disk (beta = 1/2) of DIFFERENT masses and DIFFERENT radii are released together from rest on the same ramp and roll without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first?

options.text: Whichever has the larger mass
The sphere, regardless of mass or radius
They tie, since mass and radius are different

explanations.a: Mass cancels completely out of v = sqrt(2gh/(1+beta)); a heavier object does not roll faster than a lighter one of the same shape category.
explanations.b: Correct: v depends only on h, g, and beta, and beta = 2/5 for the sphere is smaller than beta = 1/2 for the disk, so the sphere always wins regardless of the specific mass or radius of either object.
explanations.c: They do not tie — differing beta (2/5 vs 1/2) produces differing final speeds via v = sqrt(2gh/(1+beta)), independent of the mass/radius values, which is precisely why the race has a predictable winner.

questions.prompt: In m g h = (1/2) m v^2 (1 + beta), what does a LARGER value of beta physically represent?

options.text: A larger fraction of kinetic energy going into rotation rather than translation
A larger total mass of the rolling object
A larger coefficient of friction between the object and the ramp

explanations.a: Correct: beta = I/(m r^2) measures how far mass is distributed from the axis; a larger beta means more of the available energy m g h is diverted into (1/2) I omega^2 (rotation), leaving less for (1/2) m v^2 (translation), which is why larger-beta objects arrive slower.
explanations.b: Beta is dimensionless and mass-independent by construction (it divides out m entirely); it says nothing about total mass.
explanations.c: Beta is a shape/mass-distribution property of the rolling object; friction coefficient is a separate property of the two surfaces in contact and does not appear in beta.

questions.prompt: Order these three objects (same mass, same radius, released together, rolling without slipping) from FASTEST to SLOWEST at the bottom of the ramp.

items.text: Solid sphere (beta = 2/5)
Solid disk/cylinder (beta = 1/2)
Thin hoop/ring (beta = 1)
