questions.explanation: Final speed v = sqrt(2gh/(1+beta)) decreases as beta increases, and beta increases in the order sphere (2/5) < disk (1/2) < hoop (1), so the sphere finishes fastest and the hoop finishes slowest.

lessons.label: Rolling versus Sliding

sections.heading: When the constraint breaks
sections.body: Rolling without slipping (v = r*omega) is not automatic — it holds only as long as available static friction is enough to enforce it. Push a bowling ball onto a lane with too little friction, or floor the gas pedal on a low-traction road, and v and r*omega stop matching: the object's translational speed and its rotational speed become independently free, decoupled from each other. This is SLIDING, and it is the default state whenever required friction exceeds what the surface's mu_s can supply (f_s,max = mu_s N). A bowling ball thrown down a lane typically starts by sliding (high v, low omega, because the bowler imparts mostly translational velocity) and only transitions to rolling without slipping partway down the lane, once friction has had enough time to spin it up to match v = r*omega.

sections.heading: Kinetic friction takes over, and now it dissipates
sections.body: The instant slipping begins, the friction at the contact point switches character: it is no longer static friction (which can be any value up to mu_s N and adjusts to prevent slipping) but KINETIC friction, with a fixed magnitude f_k = mu_k N acting to oppose the RELATIVE sliding velocity at the contact point. Because the contact point is now genuinely moving relative to the ground (that is the definition of slipping), kinetic friction acts through a nonzero displacement and therefore does nonzero (negative) work, converting mechanical energy into heat. This is the crucial contrast with the static-friction case: static friction can supply torque for free (zero work) only because the contact point does not move; the moment it does move, friction stops being free and starts eating into the total kinetic energy budget.

sections.heading: The approach to rolling: an example from bowling
sections.body: A classic case is a bowling ball released with forward velocity v0 and initial omega0 = 0 (pure sliding, backspin-free). Kinetic friction acts backward on the ball's linear motion (decelerating v) while simultaneously producing a forward torque about the center (accelerating omega upward from zero), because the ball's bottom is sliding forward relative to the lane, so kinetic friction there points backward on the ball, which is a torque that spins the ball forward. Both v decreasing and omega increasing continue until they satisfy v = r*omega, at which point relative sliding at the contact point stops, kinetic friction switches off (no more relative motion to oppose), and rolling without slipping takes over for the rest of the ball's path — matching the visibly observable slide-then-roll transition partway down a bowling lane.

lessons.workedExample: A solid sphere (beta = 2/5, so I = (2/5) m r^2) is launched across a floor with v0 = 6.0 m/s and omega0 = 0 (pure sliding). Kinetic friction mu_k decelerates translation: a = -mu_k g. It also creates torque tau = mu_k m g r about the center, giving angular acceleration alpha = tau/I = (mu_k m g r)/((2/5) m r^2) = (5 mu_k g)/(2 r), so omega(t) = alpha t. Rolling begins when v(t) = r omega(t): v0 - mu_k g t = r * (5 mu_k g t)/(2r) = (5/2) mu_k g t. Solving: v0 = mu_k g t (1 + 5/2) = (7/2) mu_k g t, so t = 2 v0 / (7 mu_k g). With mu_k = 0.30, g = 9.8: t = 2(6.0)/(7 * 0.30 * 9.8) = 12.0/20.6 = 0.58 s — after which the sphere rolls without slipping and kinetic friction (and its energy loss) stops.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use rolling-versus-sliding to test whether a student truly separates static and kinetic friction's roles rather than treating 'friction' as one undifferentiated force. A strong answer identifies which type of friction is active at each phase, explains why kinetic friction does work while static (non-slipping) friction does not, and can reason through the physical picture of a spinning-up, decelerating object converging toward v = r*omega. A common judge probe: 'does the object's kinetic energy increase, decrease, or stay the same during the slide-to-roll transition?' — the correct answer is that it strictly decreases, since kinetic friction is dissipative, distinguishing this phase sharply from steady rolling without slipping where energy is conserved.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown across a floor with v0 != 0 and omega0 = 0. During the phase before it begins rolling without slipping, its total mechanical (kinetic) energy:

options.text: Stays constant, since only friction acts and friction conserves energy
Decreases, because kinetic friction is doing negative work at the sliding contact point
Increases, because friction spins the ball up

explanations.a: Friction does not generically conserve energy; only STATIC (non-slipping) friction is work-free here, and this phase is explicitly sliding, so kinetic friction is active and dissipative.
explanations.b: Correct: the contact point is sliding relative to the ground during this phase, so kinetic friction acts through a real displacement there, doing negative work and converting kinetic energy to heat.
explanations.c: Friction spinning the ball up (increasing rotational KE) is outweighed by friction simultaneously decelerating translation (decreasing translational KE); the net effect during sliding is always a loss of total mechanical energy.

questions.prompt: What physically distinguishes kinetic friction from static friction at a rolling/sliding contact point?

options.text: Kinetic friction only occurs on ramps, static friction only on flat ground
Kinetic friction acts when there is relative sliding at the contact point; static friction acts when there is none
Kinetic friction always points in the direction of motion; static friction always opposes it

explanations.a: Both types of friction can occur on ramps or flat ground; the distinction is about relative motion at the contact point, not the surface's orientation.
explanations.b: Correct: static friction applies when the contact point has zero relative velocity (no slipping); kinetic friction applies when the contact point IS sliding relative to the surface, and it opposes that relative sliding.
explanations.c: Kinetic friction opposes relative sliding (so its direction depends on which way the contact point slides, not simply 'the direction of motion'), and static friction's direction is whatever is needed to prevent slipping, not always opposing overall motion.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of a bowling ball released with forward v0 and omega0 = 0 as it travels down the lane.

items.text: Ball released: pure sliding, v0 != 0, omega = 0
Kinetic friction decelerates v and increases omega simultaneously
v and r*omega become equal; sliding at the contact point stops
Ball rolls without slipping for the remainder of the lane

questions.explanation: The ball begins sliding, kinetic friction simultaneously slows translation and speeds up rotation, the two converge until v = r*omega is satisfied, and only then does the ball transition into rolling without slipping.

lessons.label: Total Kinetic Energy of a Rolling Body

sections.heading: Adding the two energy budgets
sections.body: A rolling object's total kinetic energy is simply the sum of its translational and rotational pieces: KE_total = KE_trans + KE_rot = (1/2) m v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2. This is not an approximation or a special rule for rolling objects — it follows from a general theorem that a rigid body's kinetic energy always splits cleanly into the kinetic energy of the center of mass moving plus the kinetic energy of rotation about the center of mass, valid whether or not the object is rolling. What makes ROLLING specifically useful is that the rolling constraint v = r*omega links the two terms together into a single-variable expression, letting KE_total be written purely in terms of v (or purely in terms of omega), which is exactly what makes energy-conservation problems on ramps tractable with one equation instead of two.

sections.heading: The energy-conservation recipe
sections.body: For any object rolling without slipping down a ramp of height h, starting from rest, the recipe is: (1) write total mechanical energy conservation, m g h = KE_trans,final + KE_rot,final = (1/2) m v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2; (2) substitute the rolling constraint omega = v/r to eliminate one variable; (3) solve for v. This produces the general result v = sqrt(2 g h / (1 + I/(m r^2))), matching the beta-based formula from the ramp-race lesson but emphasizing that it is a direct application of energy bookkeeping, not a separate law specific to racing shapes. The same recipe extends naturally to problems where the object starts with some initial speed, rolls up an incline and decelerates, or has friction doing additional (non-conservative) work — the bookkeeping principle is always: account for every term in the total KE_trans + KE_rot budget.

sections.heading: A sanity check: the split at the bottom
sections.body: Because I = beta m r^2 and omega = v/r, the rotational share of total KE at any instant is a FIXED FRACTION for a given shape: KE_rot/KE_total = beta/(1+beta), independent of v. For a solid sphere (beta = 2/5), rotational energy is always 2/7 (about 29%) of the total, no matter how fast it is going; for a hoop (beta = 1), it is always 1/2 (50%). This fixed-ratio property is a useful check on any rolling-energy calculation: if a calculated KE_rot and KE_trans do not divide in the beta/(1+beta) ratio appropriate to the shape, something in the calculation is inconsistent with the rolling constraint.

lessons.workedExample: A solid cylinder (I = (1/2) m r^2, so beta = 1/2) of mass 3.0 kg and radius 0.15 m rolls without slipping down a ramp from height h = 1.2 m, starting from rest. Total energy: m g h = (3.0)(9.8)(1.2) = 35.3 J. This splits as KE_trans = (1/(1+beta)) * m g h = (1/1.5)(35.3) = 23.5 J and KE_rot = (beta/(1+beta)) * m g h = (0.5/1.5)(35.3) = 11.8 J (check: 23.5 + 11.8 = 35.3 J, and 11.8/35.3 = 1/3 = beta/(1+beta) = 0.5/1.5, consistent). From KE_trans = (1/2) m v^2: v = sqrt(2(23.5)/3.0) = sqrt(15.7) = 3.96 m/s, and omega = v/r = 3.96/0.15 = 26.4 rad/s.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson tests whether a student can execute the full energy-conservation pipeline cleanly under pressure: set up m g h = (1/2) m v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2, correctly substitute the rolling constraint, and solve for the requested unknown without dropping a term. Judges also probe the conceptual side — asking what fraction of total kinetic energy is rotational for a given shape, or what changes if the object is sliding instead of rolling (then KE_rot = 0 and all of m g h becomes translational, so v = sqrt(2gh), the familiar frictionless result). A student who can move fluidly between the shape-specific beta, the constraint, and the final speed demonstrates the kind of integrated understanding that a good judge scores highly for depth.

questions.prompt: For a rolling object, KE_total = (1/2) m v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2. Using the rolling constraint v = r*omega, this can be rewritten purely in terms of v as:

options.text: KE_total = (1/2) m v^2 (1 + I/(m r^2))
KE_total = (1/2) m v^2 + I v^2
KE_total = (1/2)(m + I) v^2

explanations.a: Correct: substituting omega = v/r gives (1/2) I (v/r)^2 = (1/2)(I/r^2) v^2; factoring (1/2) m v^2 out of both terms leaves (1/2) m v^2 (1 + I/(m r^2)), the standard compact form.
explanations.b: This drops the 1/2 factor and the required 1/r^2 from substituting omega = v/r into (1/2) I omega^2, giving an expression with the wrong units and wrong coefficient.
explanations.c: Mass and moment of inertia cannot simply be added (m + I) — they have different units (kg vs kg*m^2), so this expression is dimensionally invalid.

questions.prompt: For a hoop (beta = I/(m r^2) = 1) rolling without slipping, what fraction of its total kinetic energy is rotational?

explanations.a: 1/3 would correspond to beta/(1+beta) = 1/3, i.e. beta = 1/2 (a solid disk), not a hoop.
explanations.b: Correct: KE_rot/KE_total = beta/(1+beta) = 1/(1+1) = 1/2 for a hoop, since its I = m r^2 splits energy evenly between translation and rotation.
explanations.c: 2/7 is the fraction for a solid SPHERE (beta = 2/5, giving 0.4/1.4 = 2/7), not a hoop.

questions.prompt: An object slides (no friction, no rotation) down the same ramp of height h that a rolling object of the same mass descends. Compared to the rolling object, the sliding object's final speed at the bottom is:

options.text: The same, since both start from the same height
Higher, since none of m g h is diverted into rotational kinetic energy
Lower, since sliding always loses more energy than rolling

explanations.a: Same height does not guarantee the same final speed; how the available energy m g h is split between translational and rotational forms differs between the two cases.
explanations.b: Correct: with no rotation, all of m g h converts to (1/2) m v^2, giving v = sqrt(2gh) — faster than any rolling object, whose formula v = sqrt(2gh/(1+beta)) always has (1+beta) > 1 in the denominator.
explanations.c: Frictionless sliding loses no mechanical energy at all (no kinetic friction is present since there is no sliding-with-friction here); it simply never spins up, so it is not a lossy process in this idealized case.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to find the speed of a solid sphere at the bottom of a ramp of height h, released from rest, rolling without slipping.

items.text: Write m g h = (1/2) m v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2
Substitute I = (2/5) m r^2 and omega = v/r
Simplify to m g h = (1/2) m v^2 (1 + 2/5) = (7/10) m v^2
Solve for v = sqrt(10 g h / 7)

questions.explanation: Energy conservation is written first with both KE terms present, the sphere's specific I and the rolling constraint are substituted next, the expression is simplified into a single v^2 term, and finally solved algebraically for v.

lessons.label: Angular Momentum L = I omega

sections.heading: Angular momentum for a rigid body: L = I omega
sections.body: Just as linear momentum p = mv measures how hard a moving object is to stop, angular momentum L measures how hard a rotating object is to stop spinning. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, angular momentum is L = I omega, the product of the moment of inertia I (how mass is distributed relative to the axis) and the angular velocity omega (how fast the object is spinning, in radians per second). L is a vector, with units of kilogram-meters-squared per second (kg·m²/s), and it points along the rotation axis according to the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of spin, and the thumb points along L. A flywheel spinning counterclockwise as viewed from above has L pointing straight up out of it; reverse the spin and L flips to point down.

sections.heading: Angular momentum for a single particle: L = r x p
sections.body: The rigid-body formula L = I omega is a special case of a more general definition that applies to any moving particle, rotating or not: L = r x p, the cross product of the particle's position vector r (measured from the chosen origin or axis) and its linear momentum p = mv. The magnitude is L = r p sin(theta), where theta is the angle between r and p, and the direction again follows the right-hand rule, curling from r toward p. Crucially, a particle moving in a straight line still has nonzero angular momentum about any point not on that line — a car driving past a street corner at constant velocity has nonzero, constant angular momentum about the corner throughout its pass, even though nothing about the car's motion is 'rotating' in an everyday sense — the perpendicular distance from the corner to the car's path (and hence L) never changes. This r x p definition is what lets angular momentum apply seamlessly to orbits, collisions, and rigid rotation alike, and summing r x p over every particle in a rigid body reduces exactly to L = I omega.

sections.heading: Why the distinction matters for problem-solving
sections.body: Choosing the right form saves enormous algebra. When a problem involves a rigid, symmetric object spinning about a fixed or symmetry axis (a disk, a rod, a planet), L = I omega is fastest, since I can be looked up or computed once. When a problem involves a point mass, a projectile, or an object orbiting a force center (a planet around the sun, a ball on a string), L = r x p is the natural tool, because there may be no well-defined 'moment of inertia' for a single particle beyond mr² at that instant. Both descriptions must agree wherever they overlap, and mixing them incorrectly, such as trying to apply L = I omega to an object that is not rigid or not rotating about a fixed axis, is a common source of error.

lessons.workedExample: A 2.0 kg solid disk of radius 0.30 m spins about its central axis at 4.0 rad/s. Its moment of inertia is I = ½MR² = 0.5 × 2.0 × 0.30² = 0.090 kg·m², so L = I omega = 0.090 × 4.0 = 0.36 kg·m²/s, directed along the spin axis by the right-hand rule. Now compare a 0.50 kg ball on the end of a 1.2 m string, swung in a horizontal circle at 3.0 m/s. Treating the ball as a point particle, r and p (=mv) are perpendicular, so L = r p sin(90°) = 1.2 × (0.50 × 3.0) = 1.8 kg·m²/s. If the ball's string is instead modeled as a point mass (or thin hoop) at radius r, I = MR² = 0.50 × 1.2² = 0.72 kg·m², and omega = v/r = 3.0/1.2 = 2.5 rad/s, then L = I omega = 0.72 × 2.5 = 1.8 kg·m²/s — the two methods agree, because a point mass orbiting at radius r has moment of inertia exactly mr² about that axis.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this topic to check that a student understands L = I omega as a special case of L = r x p, not two unrelated formulas. A common weak answer treats angular momentum as always requiring a spinning object; a strong answer recognizes that a particle moving in a straight line still carries angular momentum about a chosen point, and can compute it either way when the two methods should agree, as with a point mass on a string. Judges may also press on units (kg·m²/s) and direction (right-hand rule) since both are easy to state vaguely but reveal whether the vector nature of L was actually understood.

questions.prompt: Which formula for angular momentum applies most directly to a single point particle moving in a straight line, evaluated about some fixed origin?

options.text: L = I omega
L = r x p
L = ½mv²

explanations.a: Incorrect: L = I omega describes rigid-body rotation about a fixed axis and requires a well-defined moment of inertia; it is not the natural tool for a single moving particle.
explanations.b: Correct: L = r x p is the general definition and applies to any particle with position r and momentum p, whether or not it is 'rotating' in the everyday sense.
explanations.c: Incorrect: ½mv² is kinetic energy, a scalar with no directional or rotational meaning; it is not an angular momentum formula at all.

questions.prompt: A particle moves in a straight line at constant velocity, never curving. About a point not on that line, its angular momentum is:

options.text: Zero, because the particle is not rotating
Constant and nonzero
Constantly increasing without bound

explanations.a: Incorrect: angular momentum does not require circular motion; a straight-line path still has nonzero r x p about an off-line point.
explanations.b: Correct: L = r p sin(theta) stays constant for straight-line, constant-velocity motion because the perpendicular distance from the point to the line (the 'lever arm') never changes, even as r and theta individually do.
explanations.c: Incorrect: while r grows as the particle moves away, sin(theta) shrinks proportionally, so the product r sin(theta), the perpendicular distance, stays fixed and L stays constant.

questions.prompt: Match each angular momentum quantity to its description.

right.text: Depends on how mass is distributed relative to the axis
Measured in radians per second
Found using the right-hand rule along the rotation axis

questions.explanation: Moment of inertia captures the geometry of mass distribution, angular velocity is the spin rate in rad/s, and the right-hand rule fixes the vector direction of L along the axis.

lessons.label: Conservation of Angular Momentum

sections.heading: The conservation law: zero net external torque means constant L
sections.body: Just as linear momentum is conserved when net external force is zero, angular momentum is conserved when net external torque is zero: if tau_net,ext = 0, then L_total stays constant over time, in both magnitude and direction. This follows directly from tau = dL/dt (covered fully in a later lesson): no net torque means no rate of change, so L cannot change. The law applies to a single rigid body, to a system of interacting bodies (like a person and a spinning wheel they are holding), and even to systems whose parts are exchanging angular momentum internally, as long as no outside torque acts on the system as a whole. Internal torques, forces between parts of the system, always come in equal-and-opposite pairs by Newton's third law and cancel when summed over the whole system, so they cannot change the system's total L.

sections.heading: Why this is a genuinely independent conservation law
sections.body: Angular momentum conservation is not a restatement of linear momentum or energy conservation; it is a separate law that can hold even when the other two look complicated. A skater pulling her arms in conserves L (no external torque about her spin axis, since gravity and the ice's normal force act through or symmetrically about that axis) while her kinetic energy actually increases, supplied by the work she does pulling her arms inward against the outward-flying tendency of her hands. This is a frequent point of confusion: conserved angular momentum does NOT mean conserved kinetic energy, because KE = L²/2I, and if I changes while L is fixed, KE must change too. Recognizing which quantity is conserved, and why, is often the entire content of a rotational dynamics problem.

sections.heading: Sources of external torque that break conservation
sections.body: Real systems are never perfectly torque-free forever: friction at a bearing or axle, air resistance, or an applied push all exert external torques that slowly bleed angular momentum away. A spinning bicycle wheel eventually stops because friction at the axle and air drag apply a small but persistent external torque opposing the spin. Over the short timescale of a classroom demonstration or a diver's half-second tuck, these torques are small enough to treat as zero, which is why the conservation law is such a powerful approximation even though it is not, in the strictest sense, ever perfectly exact for a real, friction-and-air-filled system.

lessons.workedExample: A 4.0 kg cylindrical merry-go-round of radius 1.0 m (I = ½MR² = 2.0 kg·m²) spins at 2.0 rad/s. A 20 kg child at the center (contributing negligible I) walks out to the rim, adding I_child = mr² = 20 × 1.0² = 20 kg·m² to the system. With no external torque about the vertical axis (the support bearing is assumed frictionless and provides no torque about that axis), L is conserved: L_initial = I_initial × omega_initial = 2.0 × 2.0 = 4.0 kg·m²/s. After the child reaches the rim, I_total = 2.0 + 20 = 22 kg·m², so omega_final = L/I_total = 4.0/22 ≈ 0.18 rad/s — the platform slows dramatically because I grew more than tenfold while L stayed fixed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use this concept to test whether a student can identify when a torque-free assumption is justified, and to catch the common misconception that conserved angular momentum implies conserved kinetic energy. A strong answer explains why the vertical-axis torque is zero (gravity and the frictionless bearing's normal force both act through or symmetrically about that axis) before applying L_i = L_f, rather than treating conservation as an automatic rule. Judges may also ask what happens to kinetic energy in a case like the skater or platform example, checking whether the student can show KE changes even though L does not.

questions.prompt: Angular momentum of a system is conserved whenever:

options.text: The system's kinetic energy stays constant
The net external torque on the system is zero
All internal forces are frictionless

explanations.a: Incorrect: kinetic energy can change (as in the skater pulling her arms in) even while angular momentum is conserved, because KE = L²/2I depends on I as well as L.
explanations.b: Correct: this is the direct statement of the conservation law, following from tau_net,ext = dL/dt = 0.
explanations.c: Incorrect: internal friction affects how energy is distributed within the system but does not by itself create an external torque; conservation depends specifically on external torque, not internal friction.

questions.prompt: A figure skater conserves angular momentum while pulling her arms in and spinning faster. What happens to her kinetic energy?

options.text: It stays exactly constant, since L is conserved
It decreases
It increases, because she does work pulling her arms inward

explanations.a: Incorrect: KE = L²/2I; if L is fixed but I decreases as her arms come in, KE must increase, not stay constant.
explanations.b: Incorrect: KE increases in this scenario, not decreases; the muscular work she does pulling her arms in against the effective outward tendency adds energy to the rotation.
explanations.c: Correct: her muscles do work overcoming the arms' tendency to fly outward, and that work converts to rotational kinetic energy, so KE rises even though L stays fixed.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to whether angular momentum is conserved over the timescale described.

left.text: A diver tucking mid-air during a half-second dive
A bicycle wheel spinning for ten minutes on a real axle
A frictionless lab turntable with a person pulling in weights

right.text: Conserved: negligible external torque over the short airborne time
Not conserved: axle friction and air drag apply external torque over minutes
Conserved: no external torque acts about the frictionless vertical axis

questions.explanation: Gravity during free fall exerts no torque about the diver's own center of mass, so a short dive is effectively torque-free; a real axle bleeds L away over minutes through friction and drag; an idealized frictionless turntable has no external torque about its vertical axis regardless of internal rearrangement.

lessons.label: The Figure Skater and the Diver

sections.heading: Changing I to change omega: the trade at the heart of the trick
sections.body: Because L = I omega is conserved when no external torque acts, and L stays fixed, any change in moment of inertia I must be met by an inverse change in angular velocity omega, so that their product stays constant. This is the entire mechanism behind a figure skater's spin: pulling the arms and a leg in toward the body's rotation axis dramatically shrinks I, since moment of inertia depends on mass times the square of its distance from the axis (I equals the sum of m r² over all mass elements), and even a modest reduction in average radius produces a much larger reduction in I because of that squared dependence. With L fixed, omega must rise by the same factor I falls, which is why skaters can visibly multiply their spin rate several-fold within a second or two of drawing their limbs in.

sections.heading: The diver's and gymnast's tuck
sections.body: A diver or gymnast performing a somersault uses the identical principle in the air, where gravity (acting through the body's own center of mass) exerts no net torque about that center of mass, so angular momentum about the center of mass is conserved throughout the flight. Extending the body into a long, straight 'layout' position maximizes I and produces a slow, graceful rotation; pulling into a tight tuck, knees to chest, arms wrapped in, can shrink I to roughly a third or a quarter of the layout value, multiplying the somersault rate correspondingly. Elite divers time the tuck-and-extend sequence precisely: tucking early in a dive buys extra rotations for a triple or quadruple somersault, and extending back out just before entry both slows the spin for a clean, controlled entry and increases I so the diver's angular velocity at splashdown is small and manageable.

sections.heading: The quantitative relationship: same principle, different magnitude
sections.body: Both cases obey the identical relation, I_1 omega_1 = I_2 omega_2, meaning omega_2/omega_1 = I_1/I_2, so the spin-rate multiplier equals the ratio by which I shrank. A skater who reduces I by a factor of 3 (a typical figure-skating estimate, from an extended position to a tight tuck) triples her spin rate; a diver who reduces I by a factor of 4 in a tight tuck quadruples the somersault rate. The mechanism has nothing to do with any external push, and everything to do with redistributing the body's own mass closer to or farther from the rotation axis while L, set once at the start of the free spin or free fall, remains untouched.

lessons.workedExample: A figure skater has moment of inertia 4.0 kg·m² with her arms extended and spins at 2.0 rad/s (about 0.32 rev/s). She pulls her arms and one leg in, reducing I to 1.2 kg·m². Angular momentum is conserved (ice friction under the skate at the pivot exerts negligible torque about the vertical spin axis): L = I_1 omega_1 = 4.0 × 2.0 = 8.0 kg·m²/s. After the pull-in, omega_2 = L/I_2 = 8.0/1.2 ≈ 6.7 rad/s, about 1.1 rev/s — her spin rate rises by the same factor (4.0/1.2 ≈ 3.3) that I fell. A diver doing a similar tuck from I_layout = 12 kg·m² down to I_tuck = 3.0 kg·m² would see their somersault rate quadruple, since 12/3.0 = 4.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges expect a quantitative, not just qualitative, grasp of this trick: 'she pulls her arms in and spins faster' is true but shallow, while explaining that I depends on r² so a modest radius change produces a much larger I change (and thus omega change) demonstrates real command of the physics. A strong answer also identifies where the torque-free assumption comes from in each case (a low-friction ice pivot for the skater, gravity acting through the center of mass for the diver), since that assumption is what licenses using L = constant in the first place.

questions.prompt: A skater's moment of inertia drops from 5.0 kg·m² to 1.0 kg·m² as she pulls in her arms, conserving angular momentum. By what factor does her angular velocity change?

options.text: It increases by a factor of 5
It decreases by a factor of 5
It stays the same, since only I changed

explanations.a: Correct: with L = I omega fixed, omega_2/omega_1 = I_1/I_2 = 5.0/1.0 = 5, so omega increases fivefold as I drops fivefold.
explanations.b: Incorrect: this inverts the relationship; a smaller I with fixed L requires a LARGER omega, not a smaller one.
explanations.c: Incorrect: omega cannot stay the same, because L = I omega is fixed and I changed; omega must change inversely to keep the product constant.

questions.prompt: Why does a diver's somersault rate increase in a tight tuck compared to a straight layout position?

options.text: The diver's mass increases when tucked
Moment of inertia decreases because mass is pulled closer to the rotation axis, and L is conserved
Air resistance pushes the diver into faster rotation

explanations.a: Incorrect: mass does not change during a tuck; only its distribution relative to the rotation axis changes.
explanations.b: Correct: I depends on mass times distance-squared from the axis; tucking pulls mass inward, shrinking I, and with L conserved (no external torque about the center of mass during free fall), omega must rise to compensate.
explanations.c: Incorrect: air resistance is a small external torque that if anything slightly reduces angular momentum over time; it is not the mechanism behind the tuck's speed-up, which is purely a redistribution of the diver's own mass.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a diver's tucked somersault, from takeoff to entry.

items.text: Diver leaves the board with a fixed angular momentum L about her center of mass
Diver tucks tightly, shrinking I and sharply increasing omega
Diver completes multiple fast rotations while tucked
Diver extends back into a layout, increasing I and slowing omega for a controlled entry

questions.explanation: L is set once at takeoff and stays fixed throughout the free-fall flight; tucking early shrinks I to gain rotation speed for multiple somersaults, and extending late grows I back to slow the spin for a clean entry.

lessons.label: Angular Momentum in Interacting Bodies

sections.heading: The rotating stool and spinning wheel demonstration
sections.body: A classic physics demonstration seats a person on a low-friction rotating stool, initially at rest, holding a bicycle wheel that has been spun up so its own axis points vertically. When the person flips the spinning wheel upside down, reversing the direction its angular momentum vector points, the person and stool begin spinning rapidly in the same direction the wheel was originally spinning. The explanation is angular momentum conservation for the whole person-plus-wheel-plus-stool system: no external torque acts about the vertical axis (gravity and the stool's support act through or symmetrically about that axis), so total L about that axis must stay constant. Before the flip, L_total = L_wheel (pointing up, say) plus L_person = 0 (not yet spinning). After the person flips the wheel so its L now points down, the person's body must acquire enough angular momentum pointing up to keep the vector sum unchanged, and that new person-plus-stool angular momentum shows up as visible spinning.

sections.heading: Transfer, not creation, of angular momentum
sections.body: The demonstration is often misdescribed as the wheel 'giving' the person its spin, but more precisely, angular momentum is neither created nor destroyed; it is transferred, and the total is conserved throughout. The torque the person's hands exert on the wheel to flip it is matched, by Newton's third law, by an equal and opposite torque the wheel exerts back on the person's hands and body. That reaction torque is what spins the person and stool up. If the person instead flipped the wheel only partway, or spun it at a different rate, the resulting spin of the person and stool would change correspondingly, always in whatever way keeps the vector sum of all the angular momenta in the system exactly equal to what it was before the flip.

sections.heading: Generalizing to any two interacting rotating bodies
sections.body: The same logic governs any pair of bodies exchanging angular momentum through internal torques: a helicopter's main rotor and its fuselage (which is why a tail rotor, or counter-rotating blades, is needed to prevent the body from spinning opposite the main rotor), two ice skaters pushing off each other while holding hands, or a space station reorienting itself using an internal reaction wheel without firing any thrusters. In every case, summing the angular momentum of all interacting parts before and after the internal interaction gives the same total, because internal torques between the parts are equal and opposite and cancel out of the system-wide sum, leaving only external torques (which are assumed zero or negligible) able to change the grand total.

lessons.workedExample: A student of moment of inertia 3.0 kg·m² (about the stool's vertical axis, including her own body) sits at rest on a frictionless stool holding a bicycle wheel spinning at 20 rad/s with wheel moment of inertia 0.10 kg·m², wheel-L pointing up: L_wheel = 0.10 × 20 = 2.0 kg·m²/s. She flips the wheel completely upside down, so its L now points down: L_wheel,new = -2.0 kg·m²/s. Conservation requires the total to stay at +2.0 kg·m²/s (the original value), so: L_wheel,new + L_student = 2.0, giving L_student = 2.0 - (-2.0) = 4.0 kg·m²/s. Her angular velocity is omega_student = L_student/I_student = 4.0/3.0 ≈ 1.3 rad/s, and she spins in the same direction the wheel originally pointed — a full flip transfers twice the wheel's original L to her, compared to only stopping the wheel, which would transfer just its original 2.0 kg·m²/s.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the rotating-stool demonstration to test whether a student truly understands conservation as a vector statement about a whole system, not a vague claim that 'spin gets passed along.' A strong answer sets up L_before = L_after as vectors (noting the wheel's L reverses sign on a full flip, so the student must absorb twice the original magnitude, not just cancel it), and identifies the internal, equal-and-opposite torque between hands and wheel as the transfer mechanism licensed by Newton's third law. Judges may also ask what happens if the wheel is flipped only 90 degrees instead of 180, checking whether the student can reason about the vector components rather than reciting a memorized outcome.

questions.prompt: In the rotating-stool demonstration, why does the seated person begin spinning when they flip the spinning wheel upside down?

options.text: The wheel's spin is magically transferred to the person's body
Total angular momentum of the person-wheel system is conserved, so the person must gain angular momentum equal and opposite to the wheel's change
Air currents from the spinning wheel push the person around

explanations.a: Incorrect: there is no 'magic' transfer; the effect follows precisely from conservation of the system's total angular momentum vector.
explanations.b: Correct: with no external torque about the vertical axis, L_total stays fixed; reversing the wheel's L requires the person's L to change to compensate, and that shows up as visible spin.
explanations.c: Incorrect: air currents are negligible; the effect works identically in a vacuum chamber and is due to the mechanical torque transmitted through the person's hands, not aerodynamics.

questions.prompt: A person flips a spinning wheel completely upside down (180 degrees) versus just stopping it (bringing it to rest). Compared to stopping the wheel, fully flipping it transfers:

options.text: The same amount of angular momentum to the person
Half as much angular momentum to the person
Twice as much angular momentum to the person

explanations.a: Incorrect: stopping the wheel only removes its original L (a change of magnitude L), while flipping it reverses the sign, a change of magnitude 2L; these are not equal.
explanations.b: Incorrect: this has the ratio backwards; flipping produces a larger transfer than stopping, not a smaller one.
explanations.c: Correct: stopping the wheel changes its L by L_wheel (from L to 0), but flipping it changes its L by 2×L_wheel (from +L to -L), and by conservation the person must absorb whatever change the wheel undergoes, so flipping transfers twice as much.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world system to the interacting-body angular momentum principle it illustrates.

left.text: A helicopter needs a tail rotor or counter-rotating blades
Two skaters pushing off each other while holding hands, then spinning apart
A space station reorients using an internal reaction wheel, no thrusters fired

right.text: Without it, the fuselage would spin opposite the main rotor to conserve total L
Internal push forces are equal and opposite, redistributing but not creating angular momentum
Angular momentum is exchanged between station and wheel internally, with zero external torque, so the total stays fixed

questions.explanation: A helicopter's fuselage would counter-rotate without a tail rotor to conserve total system L; skaters pushing off exchange momentum via equal-and-opposite internal forces; a station's reaction wheel exchanges angular momentum internally while total L stays fixed with no thrusters firing.

lessons.label: Gyroscopes and Precession

sections.heading: Why a spinning top does not simply fall over
sections.body: A stationary top, balanced on its point, falls over almost immediately, because gravity exerts a torque about the contact point that tips it. A rapidly spinning top, however, does something that looks almost magical: instead of falling, its axis slowly sweeps out a cone, a motion called precession, while the top stays upright far longer than intuition suggests it should. The key is that the top already has a large angular momentum L pointing along its spin axis, and gravity's torque tau does not act to simply topple this L the way it would topple a non-spinning object; instead, because tau = dL/dt, the torque changes L by adding a small increment dL in the direction of tau at each instant, and that direction is perpendicular to L, not aligned with it.

sections.heading: The vector picture: torque perpendicular to L causes rotation of L, not collapse
sections.body: Gravity's torque about the contact point, tau = r x F_gravity, points horizontally, perpendicular to the top's tilted spin axis (and therefore perpendicular to L). Because dL is added in the direction of tau, and tau is perpendicular to L, the L vector's magnitude stays essentially constant while its direction slowly rotates, tracing a cone around the vertical, exactly the way a velocity vector perpendicular to itself produces circular motion rather than speeding up or slowing down. This is precisely analogous to uniform circular motion: a centripetal force perpendicular to velocity changes the direction of v without changing its magnitude, keeping an object in a circle; here, a torque perpendicular to L changes the direction of L without changing its magnitude, keeping the spin axis sweeping out a cone (precessing) rather than toppling.

sections.heading: Why faster spin means slower, more stable precession
sections.body: The precession rate omega_p for a gyroscope or top can be shown to be approximately omega_p = tau / (I omega), where I omega is the magnitude of the spin angular momentum. This inverse relationship explains a familiar observation: a top spinning very fast precesses slowly and appears remarkably stable, resisting toppling for a long time, while a top that has slowed down (energy bled away by friction) precesses faster and wobbles more visibly just before it finally falls over, since I omega has shrunk while gravity's torque tau stays essentially the same. This is also the principle behind gyroscopic stabilization in ship navigation systems and spacecraft attitude control: a large spin angular momentum makes an axis strongly resistant to being reoriented by outside torques. (Bicycle wheels are often cited here too, but experiments with counter-rotating wheels that cancel the wheels' gyroscopic angular momentum show a bicycle can still be self-stable — Kooijman et al., Science, 2011 — so geometry and mass distribution, not gyroscopic effects, are the primary reason a rolling bicycle stays upright.)

lessons.workedExample: A toy gyroscope has a rotor of moment of inertia 5.0 x 10⁻⁵ kg·m² spinning at 300 rad/s, giving spin angular momentum L = I omega = 5.0×10⁻⁵ × 300 = 0.015 kg·m²/s. Its center of mass sits 0.040 m horizontally from the pivot point, and its mass is 0.050 kg, so gravity's torque about the pivot is tau = r F = 0.040 × (0.050 × 9.8) ≈ 0.0196 N·m. The precession rate is omega_p = tau / L = 0.0196 / 0.015 ≈ 1.3 rad/s, meaning the gyroscope's axis sweeps a full circle roughly every 4.8 seconds — noticeably slower than the rotor's own spin (300 rad/s), illustrating why a fast-spinning gyroscope's axis drifts only sluggishly even under a steady gravitational torque.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe precession because it is one of the most counterintuitive results in mechanics, and a shallow 'it just spins around' answer reveals a student has not internalized the vector reasoning. A strong answer explains specifically why the gravitational torque is perpendicular to L (not aligned with it), so it rotates L's direction rather than growing or shrinking it, drawing the direct analogy to a centripetal force producing circular motion. Judges may also ask what happens as friction slows the top's spin over time, testing whether the student can connect the inverse relationship omega_p proportional to 1/(I omega) to the visibly increasing wobble just before a top finally falls.

questions.prompt: Why does a rapidly spinning top precess (its axis sweeps a cone) instead of immediately toppling over under gravity?

options.text: Gravity's torque on a spinning top is zero
Gravity's torque is perpendicular to the top's angular momentum L, so it rotates the direction of L rather than collapsing it
The spinning motion cancels out the force of gravity

explanations.a: Incorrect: gravity's torque about the contact point is nonzero (that is what would topple a non-spinning top); the difference is what that torque does to a large existing L.
explanations.b: Correct: because tau = dL/dt and tau is perpendicular to L, the torque changes L's direction, not its magnitude, producing a slow rotation of the spin axis (precession) rather than a fall.
explanations.c: Incorrect: gravity is not cancelled; the top's weight is still fully supported by the normal force at the pivot, and gravity's torque is what actively drives the precession.

questions.prompt: As friction slows a top's spin rate over time, its precession rate omega_p = tau/(I omega) will:

options.text: Increase, since I omega (spin angular momentum) shrinks while tau stays roughly constant
Decrease, since less energy is available
Stay constant, since precession does not depend on spin rate

explanations.a: Correct: omega_p = tau/(I omega); as the spin omega drops, the denominator I omega shrinks, and with tau roughly unchanged, omega_p (and the visible wobble) increases — matching the common observation of a top wobbling faster just before it falls.
explanations.b: Incorrect: less spin angular momentum makes the top MORE susceptible to the same torque, increasing precession rate, not decreasing it.
explanations.c: Incorrect: the formula omega_p = tau/(I omega) shows precession rate depends directly, inversely, on the spin angular momentum I omega.

questions.prompt: Match each vector quantity in the precessing-top system to its direction or behavior.

left.text: Gravitational torque tau about the pivot
Change in angular momentum dL over a small time dt

right.text: Points along the top's tilted spin axis
Points horizontally, perpendicular to L
Points in the same direction as tau, rotating L's direction without changing its magnitude

questions.explanation: L points along the spin axis; the gravitational torque about the pivot is horizontal and perpendicular to L; and since dL = tau dt, the infinitesimal change in L points along tau, which is perpendicular to L, so L's direction rotates (precesses) rather than growing or shrinking.

lessons.label: Torque as the Rate of Change of Angular Momentum

sections.heading: The general law: tau = dL/dt
sections.body: The most general and fundamental statement of rotational dynamics is tau_net = dL/dt: the net external torque on a system equals the rate at which its angular momentum changes over time. This is the exact rotational analog of F_net = dp/dt for linear motion, and just as F = ma is the constant-mass special case of F = dp/dt, tau = I alpha (torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration) is the special case of tau = dL/dt that applies when I stays constant, since then dL/dt = d(I omega)/dt = I(domega/dt) = I alpha. When I itself changes over time, such as a skater pulling in her arms or a rotating system losing mass, tau = dL/dt is required, because the product rule adds an extra term from dI/dt that tau = I alpha alone misses entirely.

sections.heading: Angular impulse: the rotational counterpart to linear impulse
sections.body: Just as linear impulse J = integral of F dt equals the change in linear momentum Delta p, angular impulse, the integral of torque over time, equals the change in angular momentum: integral of tau dt = Delta L. This lets torque problems be solved the same way impulse-momentum problems are: a torque applied for a longer time, or a larger torque applied briefly, produces the same change in L, exactly mirroring how a smaller force applied longer can produce the same impulse as a larger force applied briefly. This equivalence is why tau = dL/dt is considered the deeper, more fundamental law: F = dp/dt and tau = dL/dt share an identical mathematical structure, one for translational motion and one for rotational motion, and both reduce to conservation laws (constant p, constant L) precisely when their respective net external influence, force or torque, vanishes.

sections.heading: How tau = dL/dt underlies precession
sections.body: The precession seen in gyroscopes and spinning tops (previous lesson) is a direct, visible consequence of tau = dL/dt: a torque perpendicular to L, applied continuously, does not change L's magnitude but continuously adds a small dL in the direction of tau, causing L's direction to slowly rotate. This same law, stated with full generality, also governs the everyday case of a torque aligned with (or opposed to) L, which simply speeds up or slows down the existing spin, the rotational equivalent of a force aligned with velocity speeding up or slowing down straight-line motion. Every problem in rotational dynamics, from a wrench tightening a bolt to a planet's orbit sweeping around the sun, is in the end an application of this single equation, tau_net = dL/dt, evaluated in whatever way the geometry of that particular problem calls for.

lessons.workedExample: A merry-go-round with I = 250 kg·m² starts at rest. A constant tangential force of 80 N is applied at the rim, radius 2.0 m, giving a constant torque tau = rF = 2.0 × 80 = 160 N·m, for 5.0 seconds. Using angular impulse, Delta L = tau × Delta t = 160 × 5.0 = 800 kg·m²/s, so L_final = 800 kg·m²/s (starting from L_initial = 0). Since I is constant here (no one is moving on the platform), omega_final = L_final/I = 800/250 = 3.2 rad/s, which matches the special-case formula tau = I alpha: alpha = tau/I = 160/250 = 0.64 rad/s², and omega_final = alpha × t = 0.64 × 5.0 = 3.2 rad/s, confirming both approaches agree exactly when I is constant.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use this lesson to test whether a student sees tau = I alpha as a special case rather than the fundamental law, and can correctly reach for tau = dL/dt (or angular impulse, integral of tau dt = Delta L) whenever I is changing during the process, such as a skater pulling in her arms while a torque is also being applied. A strong answer draws the explicit F = dp/dt versus F = ma parallel, and can explain, using tau = dL/dt, why a torque perpendicular to L produces precession while a torque aligned with L simply speeds up or slows down the spin. Judges may probe with a scenario combining a changing I and an applied torque simultaneously, which only tau = dL/dt handles correctly.

questions.prompt: Which equation is the more general, fundamental statement of rotational dynamics, valid even when moment of inertia I changes over time?

options.text: tau = I alpha
tau = dL/dt
L = I omega

explanations.a: Incorrect: tau = I alpha is only valid when I is constant; it misses the extra term from dI/dt that arises when I changes over time.
explanations.b: Correct: tau = dL/dt is the general law from which tau = I alpha follows as the constant-I special case (since then dL/dt = I domega/dt = I alpha).
explanations.c: Incorrect: L = I omega is a definition of angular momentum for a rigid body, not a dynamical law relating torque to changing motion.

questions.prompt: A skater is simultaneously pulling her arms inward (changing I) while a small friction torque acts on her from the ice. Which approach correctly accounts for both effects on her angular momentum?

options.text: tau = I alpha alone, since it directly relates torque to angular acceleration
tau_net = dL/dt, integrated over time to find the total change in L from the friction torque
L = I omega alone, ignoring the torque entirely

explanations.a: Incorrect: tau = I alpha assumes constant I, but her I is changing as she pulls her arms in, so this formula alone misses part of the dynamics.
explanations.b: Correct: tau_net = dL/dt (or its integrated form, angular impulse) is the only version of the law that correctly handles a changing I together with an applied external torque simultaneously.
explanations.c: Incorrect: ignoring the torque would incorrectly treat the situation as perfectly conservation, when in fact the small friction torque IS changing her total angular momentum over time, just slowly.

questions.prompt: Order these from most specific (most restrictive assumptions) to most general (fewest assumptions).

items.text: tau = I alpha (assumes I constant)
tau_net = dL/dt (valid always, the general law)
L = constant (requires zero net external torque)

questions.explanation: tau_net = dL/dt is the fully general law; L = constant and tau = I alpha are two independent special cases of it, not a nested hierarchy. L = constant restricts the torque to zero but I need not be constant (the skater example: L stays fixed while I drops as she pulls in her arms). tau = I alpha instead holds I fixed but does not require zero torque.

lessons.label: Angular Momentum Beyond Rigid Bodies

sections.heading: One law, many kinds of systems
sections.body: Every example so far, spinning disks, skaters, gyroscopes, tops, has treated angular momentum as a property of a solid object spinning about an axis. But the deeper law, tau_net,ext = dL/dt, and its conservation special case, was derived from L = r x p, a definition that applies to any particle with position and momentum, rigid body or not. This means angular momentum conservation reaches into systems that involve no rigid rotation at all: fluids swirling in a vortex, a cloud of gas collapsing under its own gravity, or a single planet tracing an elliptical path around the sun, none of which is a rigid body spinning about a fixed axis, yet all of which obey the identical L = r x p and tau = dL/dt framework.

sections.heading: Kepler's second law as angular momentum conservation
sections.body: The clearest bridge to orbital mechanics is Kepler's second law: a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times as it orbits the sun, moving faster when close (at perihelion) and slower when far (at aphelion). This is angular momentum conservation in disguise. The sun's gravitational force on the planet always points directly along the line connecting them (a 'central force'), which means r and F are parallel, so the torque tau = r x F is exactly zero at every point in the orbit. With zero net torque, the planet's angular momentum L = r x p about the sun is conserved throughout the orbit, and it can be shown geometrically that the rate at which the position vector r sweeps out area is exactly proportional to L. Constant L therefore directly forces constant areal sweep rate, which is precisely Kepler's second law, discovered empirically by Johannes Kepler around 1609 from Tycho Brahe's observational data, decades before Newton showed why it had to be true.

sections.heading: The conceptual bridge forward
sections.body: This is why angular momentum, though introduced here through spinning rigid objects, is one of the most far-reaching ideas in mechanics: the exact same conservation principle that lets a skater spin up by pulling in her arms is what lets a planet speed up as it swings closer to the sun, and what governs how a collapsing gas cloud, conserving its initial small angular momentum as it shrinks, is forced to spin up dramatically, flattening into the rotating disk that astronomers believe is how solar systems and galaxies take shape. Recognizing L = r x p and tau_net = dL/dt as the truly general statements, with L = I omega as a convenient special case for rigid bodies, is what allows this single idea to carry all the way from a merry-go-round demonstration to the orbital motion covered in gravitation and orbits.

lessons.workedExample: A comet orbits the sun on a highly elliptical path. At perihelion, it is 0.60 AU from the sun and moving at 45 km/s (perpendicular to its position vector at that point, the closest approach). Its angular momentum per unit mass is L/m = r v sin(theta) = 0.60 × 45 × sin(90°) = 27 AU·km/s. At aphelion, 30 AU from the sun, its velocity is again perpendicular to r (aphelion and perihelion are both points where velocity is purely tangential), so conservation gives r_aphelion × v_aphelion = 27, meaning v_aphelion = 27/30 = 0.90 km/s — the comet crawls through the outer solar system fifty times slower than it whips through perihelion, exactly the speeding-up-when-close, slowing-down-when-far behavior described by Kepler's second law, arising here purely from L = r x p being conserved because the sun's gravity is a central force.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use this lesson to test whether a student can generalize angular momentum conservation beyond the rigid-spinning-object examples that dominate instruction, connecting it explicitly to Kepler's second law via the zero-torque argument for central forces. A strong answer explains specifically why gravity produces zero torque about the sun (r and F are parallel, since gravity points along the line connecting the two bodies), rather than just asserting that orbits 'happen to' sweep equal areas. Judges may also ask for another example of angular momentum conservation in a non-rigid-body system, such as a collapsing gas cloud, testing whether the concept has been generalized past the classroom demonstrations or remains tied to just skaters and gyroscopes.

questions.prompt: Why is a planet's angular momentum about the sun conserved throughout its orbit?

options.text: The sun's gravitational force is a central force, always along the line connecting sun and planet, so r x F = 0 and there is zero torque
The planet's moment of inertia never changes
The orbit is a perfect circle, so speed never changes

explanations.a: Correct: because gravity is a central force, r and F are always parallel or antiparallel, making the torque tau = r x F exactly zero at every point in the orbit, which conserves L = r x p.
explanations.b: Incorrect: a planet is not a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis in this context, and 'moment of inertia' as such is not the relevant quantity; L = r x p is the correct, general definition here.
explanations.c: Incorrect: most real orbits are ellipses, not circles, and speed does change around the orbit (faster near perihelion, slower near aphelion); it is precisely this speed variation that Kepler's second law and angular momentum conservation explain.

questions.prompt: Kepler's second law states that a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. This is best understood as:

options.text: A coincidence of orbital geometry unrelated to any conservation law
A direct consequence of angular momentum conservation, since zero torque from a central force keeps L = r x p constant
A consequence of energy conservation alone

explanations.a: Incorrect: it is not a coincidence; it follows rigorously from the zero-torque, central-force argument and conservation of L.
explanations.b: Correct: the areal sweep rate is directly proportional to L = r x p; since gravity's central force gives zero torque, L is conserved, and constant L forces constant areal sweep rate.
explanations.c: Incorrect: energy conservation alone governs the speed-versus-distance trade via the orbit's total energy, but the specific equal-areas-in-equal-times statement follows from angular momentum conservation, not energy conservation.

questions.prompt: Match each non-rigid-body or astronomical system to the angular momentum principle it demonstrates.

left.text: A comet speeding up near perihelion, slowing near aphelion
A collapsing gas cloud spinning up as it shrinks
A fluid vortex (not a rigid rotating solid)

right.text: L = r x p conserved under a central gravitational force, producing Kepler's second law
L conserved as radius shrinks, forcing angular velocity to rise, by the same logic as a skater's spin-up
L = r x p applies to fluid elements even though there is no single rigid body or fixed axis

questions.explanation: A comet's speed variation is Kepler's second law, itself a consequence of conserved L under gravity's zero torque; a collapsing cloud spins up as its L stays fixed while its radius (and thus I) shrinks; a fluid vortex obeys L = r x p at the level of its individual fluid elements even without any single rigid body.

lessons.label: Euler and the Equations of Rigid-Body Motion

sections.heading: A body that is more than a point
sections.body: Newton's second law, F = ma, treats an object as a single point mass, which works fine for a thrown ball but says nothing about a spinning top or a tumbling wrench, where different parts of the object move at different velocities and the object's shape matters. Leonhard Euler, the Swiss mathematician who dominated 18th-century physics, spent decades building the mathematics for extended rigid bodies. His 1765 treatise Theoria motus corporum solidorum seu rigidorum ("Theory of the Motion of Solid or Rigid Bodies") laid out the modern framework: every rigid body has three mutually perpendicular principal axes through its center of mass, each with its own moment of inertia (I1, I2, I3) describing how mass is distributed relative to that axis. Choosing coordinates that rotate with the body and align with these axes turns a messy three-dimensional rotation problem into three coupled but tractable equations.

sections.heading: Euler's equations
sections.body: For a rigid body with angular velocity components (omega1, omega2, omega3) along its principal axes, Euler's equations state I1 (domega1/dt) - (I2 - I3) omega2 omega3 = tau1, and its two cyclic permutations for axes 2 and 3, where tau is the applied external torque. Set torque to zero and you get the torque-free rotator: for a body tumbling with angular velocity not aligned to a single principal axis, like a satellite or a thrown wrench, the coupling terms (I2 - I3) omega2 omega3 generically do not vanish unless two of the three moments of inertia are equal, so the angular velocity keeps changing over time -- though rotation purely about one principal axis is always a steady solution regardless, which is exactly what the next lesson's tennis-racket theorem examines for stability. This single fact, that free rotation is not automatically steady, is the seed of everything else in this unit: the intermediate-axis instability, the falling cat's shape changes, and the gyrocompass's precession all trace back to solutions of Euler's equations under different constraints.

sections.heading: The symmetric top and Poinsot's geometric picture
sections.body: When two moments of inertia are equal (I1 = I2, a symmetric top like a spinning coin or a gyroscope wheel), Euler's equations simplify enormously: the spin axis traces a cone around the fixed angular momentum vector at a constant rate, called torque-free precession, with no wobble growth or decay. Nearly seven decades after Euler, the French mathematician Louis Poinsot (1834) gave a beautiful geometric visualization for the fully asymmetric case: the tip of the angular velocity vector traces a curve called the polhode on an ellipsoid built from the moments of inertia, and that curve's shape, closed loops near the largest and smallest axes, an unstable saddle near the intermediate one, is exactly what predicts the tennis-racket instability covered in the next lesson.

lessons.workedExample: A satellite tumbling in torque-free space has principal moments of inertia I1 = 20, I2 = 15, I3 = 8 kg*m^2 (arbitrary units) and starts spinning almost purely about axis 1 (the largest) with a tiny nudge on axis 2. Plugging into Euler's equations, the coupling term (I2 - I3) omega2 omega3 stays small because omega2 and omega3 both stay small, so the small nudge oscillates but never grows: rotation about the largest axis is stable. If instead the satellite starts spinning almost purely about axis 2 (the intermediate value, 15), the same algebra shows the coupling terms for the OTHER two axes reinforce each other rather than restoring the original spin, and the small nudges in omega1 and omega3 grow exponentially at first. That asymmetry between the largest/smallest axes and the middle one is not a special case; it falls directly out of the signs of (I1-I3), (I2-I1), and (I3-I2) in Euler's three coupled equations.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about Euler's equations because they are the load-bearing wall under the rest of rigid-body dynamics, and a student who can only quote F=ma has not actually engaged with rotation. A strong answer names the three coupled equations, explains why the coupling terms (I2-I3)omega2omega3 and its permutations only vanish for symmetric bodies, and connects that directly to why free rotation can be unstable. A student who describes rotation only in terms of a single scalar moment of inertia, as if a rigid body had just one axis that mattered, will be pushed by a sharp judge to explain what happens when the body has three DIFFERENT principal moments, which is precisely where the single-axis picture breaks down.

questions.prompt: What did Euler's 1765 treatise contribute that F = ma alone cannot handle?

options.text: A framework using three principal axes and three moments of inertia to describe how an extended rigid body rotates
A correction to Newton's law of gravitation for spinning masses
The first measurement of the speed of light using a rotating mirror

explanations.a: Correct: Euler's principal-axis framework and his three coupled equations describe how mass distribution governs rotational motion, something point-mass F=ma cannot capture.
explanations.b: Euler did not revise Newtonian gravitation; the light-speed measurements of Fizeau and Foucault (a toothed-wheel measurement in 1849 and a rotating-mirror measurement in 1850/1862) came a century later and are unrelated.
explanations.c: A toothed-wheel measurement (Fizeau, 1849) and a rotating-mirror measurement (Foucault, 1850/1862) of the speed of light are a separate 19th-century achievement, unrelated to Euler's 1765 rigid-body framework.

questions.prompt: In Euler's equations for torque-free rotation, the coupling term (I2 - I3) omega2 omega3 vanishes only when:

options.text: Two of the three principal moments of inertia are equal
The body is rotating at exactly one revolution per second
The center of mass is at the geometric center

explanations.a: Correct: if I2 = I3 (or the corresponding pair in a cyclic term), that coupling term is identically zero regardless of angular velocity, which is exactly the symmetric-top case.
explanations.b: The rotation rate is irrelevant to whether the coefficient (I2-I3) is zero; that depends only on the geometry of the mass distribution.
explanations.c: Center-of-mass location affects where the principal axes are centered, but equal moments of inertia is the specific condition that zeroes this term.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the history of rigid-body rotation theory.

items.text: Newton publishes point-mass dynamics (F = ma) in the Principia (1687)
Euler publishes Theoria motus corporum solidorum, introducing principal axes and the coupled rotation equations (1765)
Poinsot publishes the geometric polhode construction for visualizing torque-free rotation (1834)

questions.explanation: Newton's point-mass mechanics came first; Euler extended it to extended rigid bodies with principal axes seventy-eight years later; Poinsot's geometric picture of Euler's solutions followed another sixty-nine years after that.

lessons.label: The Intermediate-Axis (Tennis-Racket) Theorem

sections.heading: Three axes, two stable, one not
sections.body: Any rigid body has three principal axes with three moments of inertia, conventionally ordered I1 > I2 > I3. The intermediate-axis theorem, also called the tennis-racket theorem, states that free rotation about the axis with the LARGEST moment of inertia (I1) and the axis with the SMALLEST (I3) are both stable: a small wobble away from either axis stays small and the object keeps spinning cleanly. Rotation about the MIDDLE axis (I2), the intermediate one, is unstable: any tiny perturbation grows, and the object executes an unexpected half-flip partway through its spin before settling back toward rotation about roughly the same axis, now inverted. You can see this with a tennis racket, a smartphone, or a book flipped end over end with a rubber band around it: spin it about the axis through the handle or the axis perpendicular to the strings (largest and smallest moment) and it flips cleanly; spin it about the third axis, in the plane of the strings and running crosswise through the head, perpendicular to the handle, and it does an uncontrolled twist mid-flight.

sections.heading: The mathematics behind the asymmetry
sections.body: The instability falls directly out of Euler's equations from the previous lesson. Linearizing the equations around rotation purely about axis 2 shows the perturbation in the other two components grows like an exponential rather than oscillating, because the product of coefficients (I1-I2)(I2-I3)/(I1 I3) is positive when linearizing about the intermediate axis I2 (with the convention I1 > I2 > I3, both factors are positive), which produces exponential growth rather than oscillation, while the analogous coefficient is negative when linearizing about the largest or smallest axis, giving oscillation, i.e. stability. Poinsot's polhode construction shows the same result geometrically: the trajectory traced on the inertia ellipsoid forms closed small loops around the axes of largest and smallest inertia, but near the intermediate axis the loops open into a long path called a separatrix that carries the tip of the angular velocity vector far from its start, which is the flip.

sections.heading: The Dzhanibekov effect: a cosmonaut confirms 19th-century math in orbit
sections.body: The effect is named for Soviet cosmonaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov, who noticed it in 1985 aboard the Salyut 7 space station: unscrewing a wing nut in zero gravity, he flicked it to send it spinning down a guide wire, and watched it rotate cleanly, then abruptly flip 180 degrees, then flip back, repeating at regular intervals with no forces or torques acting on it. The observation struck Soviet engineers as strange enough to be studied and, for a time, kept out of public reporting, even though the underlying mathematics, that intermediate-axis rotation is unstable, had already been known to rigid-body theorists for over a century as a direct consequence of Euler's 18th-century equations and Poinsot's 19th-century geometric picture. Zero gravity did not create new physics; it just removed air resistance and support forces that normally damp the effect out too fast to notice on Earth.

lessons.workedExample: A rigid rectangular block (like a book) has principal moments of inertia I1 (about the shortest, thinnest axis, largest I) > I2 (about the axis through the front cover) > I3 (about the long spine axis, smallest I, given how mass is distributed for a book roughly). Actually for a uniform rectangular block with side lengths a > b > c, the axis through the CENTER perpendicular to the largest face (length a by b) has the largest moment of inertia, and the axis along the longest dimension has the smallest. Spin the book about either extreme axis with a rubber band holding it shut and toss it: it completes clean end-over-end or barrel rolls. Spin it about the third, intermediate axis, perpendicular to the spine but lying in the plane of the covers, running from the spine to the page edges, and it will not complete a clean rotation; partway through the toss it visibly twists and lands with its cover facing the opposite way it started, then can flip back on a longer toss, which is the observable signature of the exponential instability predicted by linearizing Euler's equations about that axis.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges reach for this topic because it is a rare case where a strange, YouTube-famous phenomenon has an exact, checkable mathematical explanation, and it tests whether a student can connect a cool demo to the underlying equations rather than just describing the flip. A strong answer states which axis is unstable (the intermediate, middle-moment-of-inertia one, not simply 'the weird one'), explains that the instability is a direct consequence of the sign of (I1-I2)(I2-I3) in the linearized Euler equations, and correctly notes that Dzhanibekov observed rather than discovered the underlying physics in 1985. A student who claims zero gravity is what CAUSES the flip, rather than merely revealing it by removing damping, has the causality backwards, and a judge will ask directly whether the same flip can be reproduced with a tossed book on Earth (it can).

questions.prompt: For a rigid body with principal moments of inertia I1 > I2 > I3, free rotation is unstable about:

options.text: The axis with moment of inertia I2, the intermediate value
The axis with the largest moment of inertia, I1
The axis with the smallest moment of inertia, I3

explanations.a: Correct: rotation about the middle principal axis is unstable; small perturbations grow, producing the mid-flip characteristic of the tennis-racket theorem.
explanations.b: Rotation about the largest-moment axis is one of the two STABLE cases; perturbations there oscillate rather than grow.
explanations.c: Rotation about the smallest-moment axis is the other stable case, exactly analogous to spinning about the largest axis.

questions.prompt: What did cosmonaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov actually contribute in 1985?

options.text: He observed the intermediate-axis flip in orbit on a wing nut, drawing attention to an effect already implied by 19th-century rigid-body mathematics
He mathematically proved the tennis-racket theorem for the first time
He discovered that gravity is required for the flip to occur

explanations.a: Correct: the flip he saw was a striking real-world observation of an instability already predictable from Euler's and Poinsot's earlier work; he did not discover new physics.
explanations.b: The mathematical proof follows from linearizing Euler's equations, work that predates Dzhanibekov by well over a century.
explanations.c: The opposite is true: gravity and air resistance on Earth tend to damp the flip out quickly, which is why zero gravity made it easy to notice, not why it happens.

questions.prompt: Match each rotation axis (by its moment-of-inertia rank) to its stability behavior.

right.text: Stable: perturbations oscillate and stay small
Unstable: perturbations grow, causing a mid-flip
Stable: perturbations oscillate and stay small

questions.explanation: Both extreme axes (largest and smallest moment of inertia) give stable rotation with bounded oscillations; only the intermediate axis produces the exponentially growing perturbation responsible for the observed flip.

lessons.label: The Falling-Cat Problem

sections.heading: A puzzle that looked like it broke conservation of angular momentum
sections.body: Drop a cat upside down from a modest height and, almost every time, it lands on its feet. That is unremarkable as a feat of animal reflexes, but it is a genuine puzzle in physics: the cat starts falling with zero angular momentum (it was held still, then released, with no one imparting a spin), and angular momentum is conserved for a body in free fall because gravity, acting through the center of mass, exerts no net torque about that center. A body with zero angular momentum should not be able to rotate at all, and yet the cat clearly reorients itself by roughly 180 degrees before it lands. Nineteenth-century physicists, aware of conservation of angular momentum but without a resolution, genuinely debated whether the cat was cheating: pushing off the dropper's hand, or exploiting air resistance.

sections.heading: Marey's 1894 chronophotography settles the empirical question
sections.body: French physiologist Etienne-Jules Marey, a pioneer of chronophotography (capturing a rapid sequence of images of a single moving subject, a forerunner of cinema), photographed a falling cat in 1894 at roughly 12 frames per second. The sequence showed two things decisively: the cat had zero rotational motion at the very start of the fall, ruling out a push-off from the dropper's hand, and the cat completed most of its reorientation while its body was clearly not resisting air in any way that could explain the twist, ruling out air resistance as the mechanism. The images were widely reproduced and made the puzzle harder, not easier: the cat was demonstrably rotating with zero net angular momentum, using nothing but its own body.

sections.heading: The resolution: shape change, not torque
sections.body: The trick is that conservation of angular momentum constrains the TOTAL rotation of the system to stay zero, but it does not forbid different PARTS of a flexible body from rotating in opposite directions, as long as they cancel. A falling cat bends sharply at the waist, effectively splitting itself into a front half and a back half that can be rotated somewhat independently. It then tucks the front legs in close to its body (reducing that half's moment of inertia so it can rotate through a larger angle for a given tiny angular momentum) while extending the back legs outward (increasing that half's moment of inertia so it rotates through a smaller angle), twists the front half one way and the back half the other, and then reverses the tuck-and-extend on each half to bring the body back straight, having achieved a net rotation with zero net angular momentum throughout. The complete, rigorous mechanical model, matching Marey's photographic evidence to Euler-style equations for the two connected body segments, was published by T.R. Kane and M.P. Scher in 1969, seventy-five years after Marey's photographs, in "A dynamical explanation of the falling cat phenomenon."

lessons.workedExample: Model the cat as two cylinders (front half, back half) connected at a flexible waist joint, with zero total angular momentum. Phase 1: bend at the waist so the two halves' rotation axes are no longer aligned; tuck the front cylinder's limbs in (small moment of inertia, so it can spin through a large angle, say 90 degrees, for a small angular impulse) while extending the back cylinder's limbs out (large moment of inertia, so it only spins a few degrees the opposite way to keep total angular momentum at zero). Phase 2: straighten the waist, now with the front half rotated relative to the back half. Phase 3: reverse the limb postures, tucking the BACK half and extending the FRONT half, and twist back, which now moves the back half through the larger angle while the front barely moves further, since the roles of the two halves' moments of inertia have swapped. The net result after both phases: the whole body has rotated roughly 180 degrees, even though at every instant the two halves' angular momenta summed to exactly zero.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the falling-cat problem to test whether a student actually understands what conservation of angular momentum forbids and what it permits, since the intuitive but WRONG answer is 'the cat must be violating conservation of angular momentum, or getting help from somewhere external.'
