The correct, and more interesting, answer is that a multi-segment body can reorient with zero NET angular momentum by having its parts rotate oppositely while differing in moment of inertia, exactly as astronauts, divers, and gymnasts do mid-air. A strong answer cites Marey's 1894 photographic evidence ruling out push-off and air resistance, and names Kane and Scher's 1969 two-segment model as the mechanism, rather than vaguely gesturing at 'cats are flexible.'

questions.prompt: Why is a falling cat righting itself a genuine physics puzzle rather than just an animal reflex story?

options.text: The cat starts with zero angular momentum and gravity exerts no net torque about its center of mass in free fall, so the total rotation should stay zero
Cats are heavier than air, so they should not be able to rotate at all while falling
The cat's fur creates enough air resistance to violate Newton's third law

explanations.a: Correct: with zero starting angular momentum and no external torque, conservation of angular momentum says total angular momentum must stay zero throughout the fall, yet the cat clearly reorients.
explanations.b: Weight relative to air has nothing to do with whether angular momentum is conserved; this option misidentifies the actual constraint.
explanations.c: Marey's photographs specifically ruled out air resistance as the mechanism, and nothing about fur resistance would violate Newton's third law regardless.

questions.prompt: What did Marey's 1894 chronophotography of the falling cat demonstrate?

options.text: The cat had zero rotation at the start of the fall and reoriented without pushing off the dropper's hand or relying on air resistance
The complete dynamical equations explaining how the cat rotates with zero angular momentum
That cats violate conservation of angular momentum

explanations.a: Correct: the photographic sequence ruled out the two leading alternative explanations (push-off and air resistance), sharpening the puzzle rather than solving it.
explanations.b: The full dynamical model came 75 years later, from Kane and Scher in 1969; Marey provided decisive evidence, not the mechanism.
explanations.c: No experiment showed a violation of conservation of angular momentum; the eventual resolution (Kane and Scher) is fully consistent with it.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the falling-cat problem's history.

items.text: 19th-century physicists debate whether a falling cat's self-righting violates conservation of angular momentum
Marey's 1894 chronophotography shows the cat starts with zero rotation and rotates without push-off or air resistance
Kane and Scher publish the complete two-segment dynamical model in 1969

questions.explanation: The debate predates Marey's photographic evidence, which sharpened the puzzle in 1894 without resolving the mechanism; the rigorous mechanical resolution followed another seventy-five years later, in 1969.

questions.prompt: Match each phase of the cat's shape-changing maneuver to its effect.

left.text: Tucking one half's limbs in close to the body
Extending the other half's limbs outward

right.text: Lets the front and back halves rotate somewhat independently about different axes
Reduces that half's moment of inertia so it rotates through a larger angle for the same small angular impulse
Increases that half's moment of inertia so it rotates through a smaller angle, keeping total angular momentum near zero

questions.explanation: Bending at the waist decouples the two halves' rotation axes; tucking shrinks moment of inertia so that half can spin further, while extending grows moment of inertia so the other half barely moves, letting the net angular momentum stay zero while the body still reorients.

lessons.label: The Gyrocompass and Gyroscopic Navigation

sections.heading: Foucault's gyroscope: proving Earth spins without watching the stars
sections.body: In 1852, French physicist Leon Foucault (already famous for his 1851 pendulum demonstration of Earth's rotation) built a fast-spinning wheel mounted in gimbals that let it point freely in any direction, and coined the term "gyroscope" (from Greek for "to see rotation") for it. Conservation of angular momentum means a rapidly spinning, freely mounted wheel resists changes to the direction its spin axis points; it behaves like a rigid pointer fixed relative to distant space rather than to the room around it. Foucault used this gyroscopic rigidity to show, in a laboratory over a period of minutes rather than his pendulum's hours, that the Earth itself was rotating beneath the wheel's fixed-in-space axis. That first, freely mounted (three-degrees-of-freedom) gyroscope was a beautiful demonstration, but it was not yet a compass: it simply held whatever direction it started in, useful for detecting rotation, not for finding north on its own.

sections.heading: Turning gyroscopic rigidity into a north-seeker
sections.body: In a companion 1852 paper, Foucault himself went further: he built a second gyroscope with only two degrees of freedom, its spin axis constrained to stay in the local horizontal plane. He showed that this constrained axis does not merely hold a fixed direction; it actively settles toward true north, behaving, in his own words, similar to a magnetic needle. This constrained device is considered the original form of the north-seeking gyroscope, more than fifty years before anyone built a practical compass from the idea. What was still missing was engineering: a damped, self-correcting instrument robust enough for a pitching ship. German inventor Hermann Anschutz-Kaempfe patented a workable design in 1904-1906 and had the first functional marine gyrocompass in naval service by 1908; American inventor Elmer Sperry independently developed a competing design, patented starting in 1908 and adopted by the US Navy from 1911 onward. Both designs use a pendulous mounting that constrains the spinning rotor's axis to stay in the local horizontal plane, exactly as Foucault's constrained gyroscope had. Because Earth is itself rotating, a spin axis confined to the horizontal plane experiences a small torque unless it happens to align with Earth's own rotation axis component in that plane, which points toward true north; that torque produces a slow precession that damps out over a period of hours until the axis settles pointing at true north, not magnetic north, and stays there as the ship or aircraft turns.

sections.heading: A patent fight and an unlikely expert witness
sections.body: Because Anschutz-Kaempfe's and Sperry's designs emerged so close together, a bitter patent dispute followed: when Sperry tried sailing his compass into the German market around 1914, Anschutz sued for infringement. The German court hired Albert Einstein as a neutral, independent expert, engaged with the agreement of both Anschutz and Sperry, and Einstein wrote technical opinions analyzing the damping mechanisms of the competing designs (specifically how each design used friction or fluid damping to settle the north-seeking oscillation), an unusual but well-documented episode of the century's most famous physicist doing applied consulting on rigid-body mechanics. Gyrocompasses, unlike magnetic compasses, are unaffected by a ship's steel hull or electrical wiring and point to TRUE rather than magnetic north, which is why they became standard for naval and later aircraft and spacecraft inertial navigation.

lessons.workedExample: A ship's gyrocompass rotor spins at anywhere from a couple thousand up to roughly 12,000 rpm depending on the design, to build up enough angular momentum, since a larger spin angular momentum L means a given disturbing torque tau produces a slower, more controlled precession rate (precession rate = tau / L, so large L resists disturbance and settles more predictably). If the ship turns 90 degrees while underway, the pendulous mounting senses the resulting small misalignment between the rotor's horizontal-plane axis and true north, generates a restoring torque, and the axis precesses back toward north over a damped oscillation lasting on the order of an hour rather than snapping back instantly, which is why real gyrocompasses include damping (as Einstein's testimony analyzed) to prevent that restoring oscillation from overshooting and settling on a heading east or west of true north instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the gyrocompass because it is a rare case where an everyday-sounding instrument runs entirely on angular momentum conservation plus precession under torque, connecting straight back to Euler's equations from the first lesson of this unit. A strong answer distinguishes Foucault's original 1852 freely mounted gyroscope (proves Earth's rotation, but merely holds a fixed direction) from his own companion 1852 horizontal-plane-constrained gyroscope (which genuinely seeks north, the ancestor of the modern gyrocompass), and from Anschutz-Kaempfe's and Sperry's early-1900s designs, whose real contribution was engineering that north-seeking principle into a damped, self-correcting, practical marine instrument rather than discovering north-seeking behavior itself. A student who says a gyrocompass 'just points north because it's a compass' has not engaged with the mechanism, and a judge will ask directly why a gyrocompass, unlike a magnetic compass, still works accurately inside a steel-hulled submarine.

questions.prompt: What did Foucault's original 1852 (freely mounted) gyroscope demonstrate, and what could it NOT yet do?

options.text: It demonstrated Earth's rotation via the spin axis's resistance to reorientation, but was not yet a practical, damped compass
It actively sought true north using a pendulous mount, functioning as a full gyrocompass
It measured the exact value of Earth's rotational period to the second

explanations.a: Correct: Foucault's original three-degrees-of-freedom gyroscope used angular momentum conservation to hold a fixed direction in space, revealing Earth's rotation beneath it. In a companion 1852 paper Foucault himself built a horizontal-plane-constrained (two-degrees-of-freedom) version that did settle toward true north, but turning that north-seeking principle into a damped, practical navigation instrument took Anschutz-Kaempfe and Sperry another half-century.
explanations.b: That description fits Foucault's own companion 1852 constrained gyroscope, and later Anschutz-Kaempfe's and Sperry's engineered gyrocompasses, not his original freely mounted device.
explanations.c: Foucault's gyroscope demonstrated rotation qualitatively; precise timing of Earth's rotational period was not its purpose or result.

questions.prompt: Why does a gyrocompass point to true north rather than magnetic north?

options.text: Its spin axis is constrained to the horizontal plane and precesses to align with Earth's rotation axis component in that plane, which is a geometric effect unrelated to magnetism
It contains a magnet that has been calibrated to correct for magnetic declination
It is simply less accurate than a magnetic compass, and true north is a coincidental average of its readings

explanations.a: Correct: the gyrocompass's north-seeking behavior comes from angular momentum and precession geometry tied to Earth's rotation, not from any magnetic sensing, which is why steel hulls do not affect it.
explanations.b: A gyrocompass contains no magnet at all; magnetic declination correction is a separate procedure used with ordinary magnetic compasses.
explanations.c: Gyrocompasses are generally MORE accurate and stable aboard steel ships than magnetic compasses, not less; the true-north alignment is a deliberate mechanical result, not a coincidence.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their role in gyroscope and gyrocompass history.

right.text: Built the first gyroscope (1852) and used it to demonstrate Earth's rotation
Developed the first functional marine gyrocompass, in German naval service by 1908
Served as an expert witness analyzing damping mechanisms in the Anschutz-Sperry patent dispute

questions.explanation: Foucault built and named the original 1852 gyroscope to reveal Earth's rotation; Anschutz-Kaempfe turned that principle into the first working gyrocompass by 1908; Einstein later gave technical expert testimony on damping design during the resulting Anschutz-Sperry patent litigation.

lessons.label: Newton's Rotating Bucket

sections.heading: The setup: a bucket, a rope, and a puzzle about what 'rotating' means
sections.body: In the Scholium to the Definitions at the start of his Principia (1687), Isaac Newton described a thought experiment to argue that rotation is absolute, meaningful in itself, and not merely relative to other objects. Hang a bucket of water from a twisted rope and release it. At the instant of release, the bucket starts spinning relative to the water (their surfaces are in relative motion) but the water's surface stays flat, showing no sign of the spin. Gradually, friction between the bucket's walls and the water drags the water into spinning too; as it catches up to the bucket's rotation, its surface climbs the sides and curves into a concave paraboloid. Eventually bucket and water spin together at the same rate, in relative rest with each other, yet the water's surface stays concave the whole time it is doing so.

sections.heading: Newton's argument for absolute space
sections.body: Newton's key move is to notice that the water's curved surface does NOT track its relative motion with respect to the bucket: at the start, bucket and water are in relative motion (bucket spinning, water still) and the surface is flat; at the end, bucket and water are in relative REST (both spinning together) and the surface is curved. If curvature depended only on the relative motion between water and bucket, it should be the reverse. Newton concluded the water's curvature tracks something else entirely: its rotation relative to absolute space itself, a fixed background against which true motion (and the centrifugal effects it produces) can be measured, independent of any other object in the universe.

sections.heading: Why this became a foundational, and contested, argument
sections.body: The bucket argument was Newton's strongest piece of evidence for treating space as a real, physical entity rather than just a relationship between objects, a position opposed at the time by Gottfried Leibniz, who argued space was nothing but the relative ordering of objects and had no independent existence. Newton's bucket seemed to settle the debate empirically: here was a measurable physical effect (the paraboloid surface) that could not be explained by relative motion between the water and any nearby object, only by rotation relative to something absolute. That argument stood largely unchallenged for nearly two centuries until Ernst Mach's critique, covered in the next lesson, reopened the question of what, exactly, absolute rotation is rotation relative TO.

lessons.workedExample: Trace the bucket experiment through four stages. Stage 1 (release): bucket spins, water still; relative motion is high, water surface is flat. Stage 2 (transition): friction drags the water into spinning; relative motion decreases as the water speeds up toward the bucket's rate; the surface progressively curves into a paraboloid as it does. Stage 3 (co-rotation): bucket and water spin together at the same angular velocity; relative motion is now zero, yet the surface remains a curved paraboloid, its steepest, most concave state. Stage 4 (if the bucket is now stopped while the water keeps spinning by inertia): relative motion between bucket and water reappears, this time with water spinning past a still bucket, and the surface stays curved, tracking the water's own rotation, not its relative motion to the bucket. Newton's point: the ONE thing that correlates with curvature throughout all four stages is the water's rotation relative to space itself, not its rotation relative to the bucket.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up Newton's bucket because it is the classic entry point into the question of what 'rotating' even means, and it tests whether a student can track WHICH quantity correlates with the observed effect. A strong answer walks through why relative bucket-water motion fails as an explanation (it is high when the surface is flat, and zero when the surface is most curved, exactly backwards from what a relative-motion account would predict) and correctly identifies that Newton used this to argue for absolute space. A student who simply says 'the water spins so it curves' has not engaged with the actual puzzle, which is specifically about what the curvature is caused BY, given that it does not track the bucket-water relative motion.

questions.prompt: In Newton's bucket experiment, what happens to the water's surface at the moment the bucket and water are rotating together at the same rate (relative rest between them)?

options.text: The surface remains a curved paraboloid, its most concave state
The surface returns to flat, since bucket and water are no longer in relative motion
The surface oscillates unpredictably between flat and curved

explanations.a: Correct: once bucket and water co-rotate, the surface is at its most curved, even though the water and bucket are in relative rest with each other, which is the crux of Newton's argument.
explanations.b: This is the intuitive but WRONG prediction if curvature depended only on relative bucket-water motion; the actual observation contradicts it.
explanations.c: The surface's curvature is a steady, predictable function of the water's rotation rate once co-rotation is reached, not an oscillation.

questions.prompt: What did Newton conclude the water's curvature was caused by, given that it does not track relative bucket-water motion?

options.text: The water's rotation relative to absolute space, an independently existing background against which true rotation can be measured
The friction force between the bucket's wooden walls and the water alone, at all times
The Coriolis effect caused by Earth's own rotation beneath the bucket

explanations.a: Correct: Newton argued that since relative bucket-water motion fails to explain the curvature pattern, the curvature must track rotation relative to absolute space instead.
explanations.b: Friction is the MECHANISM that transfers spin from bucket to water over time, but it is not what Newton says the curvature ultimately measures; friction is at its lowest once co-rotation is reached, precisely when curvature is greatest.
explanations.c: Earth's own rotation is far too slow to produce the bucket's curvature and was not part of Newton's argument; the bucket's own spin rate dominates.

questions.prompt: Order the four stages of Newton's bucket experiment.

items.text: The twisted rope is released; the bucket begins spinning while the water surface stays flat
Friction gradually transfers spin from the bucket to the water; the surface begins curving
Bucket and water reach the same rotation rate (relative rest); the surface is now a fully curved paraboloid
Newton compares the curvature pattern to the relative-motion pattern and finds they do not match

questions.explanation: The physical stages (release, transition, co-rotation) happen in that order, and Newton's analytical conclusion, that curvature does not track relative motion, is drawn only after observing all three stages.

lessons.label: Mach's Principle and the Origin of Inertia

sections.heading: Mach's challenge: rotation relative to WHAT, exactly?
sections.body: In his 1883 book Die Mechanik in ihrer Entwicklung (The Science of Mechanics), Austrian physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach attacked Newton's bucket argument at its foundation. Mach's objection was not that the water curves, which is an observed fact, but that Newton had no way to actually POINT to absolute space, measure it, or interact with it; it was, in Mach's view, an unobservable and therefore scientifically empty concept smuggled in to explain an otherwise mysterious effect. Mach's famous rhetorical challenge: what if the bucket's walls were miles thick, so thick and massive that they dominated the local surroundings? Would the water still climb the walls if the bucket, not the water, were held still while everything else, including the distant stars, rotated around it? Newton's framework could not even in principle answer that question, since it treated absolute space as an unmeasurable backdrop rather than something built from the arrangement of actual matter.

sections.heading: Mach's alternative: inertia from the distant stars
sections.body: Mach proposed instead that inertial effects, the resistance a mass shows to acceleration, and the centrifugal curvature of the bucket's water, are not caused by motion relative to empty absolute space at all, but by motion relative to the totality of all the OTHER matter in the universe, popularly summarized as "the distant stars." On this view, a lone bucket of water spinning in an otherwise completely empty universe (no stars, no other matter at all) would show NO curvature whatsoever, because there would be nothing for it to be rotating relative to. Inertia itself, not just the appearance of centrifugal force, would be a relational property that emerges from the gravitational (or otherwise physical) influence of all the mass in the universe, rather than a built-in property of space itself. This idea came to be called Mach's principle, a name Einstein himself coined decades later, though Mach never formalized it into an equation.

sections.heading: An unresolved influence on Einstein, and general relativity's partial answer
sections.body: Mach's principle deeply influenced the young Einstein, who wanted general relativity to fully realize it: gravity and inertia should emerge entirely from the distribution of matter, with no absolute background space left over. General relativity (1915) partially delivers on this, since spacetime geometry does respond to the presence of matter, and a striking related effect, frame dragging (a rotating mass slightly drags spacetime, and any nearby free-falling frames, around with it, predicted by Lense and Thirring in 1918 and confirmed by satellite experiments including Gravity Probe B in 2011), is exactly the kind of matter-causes-inertial-effects phenomenon Mach's principle calls for. But general relativity also admits solutions, such as an empty, matterless rotating universe, that Mach's principle strictly forbids, so physicists still debate today whether GR fully embodies Mach's principle, only partially embodies it, or is a fundamentally different, non-Machian theory that happens to share some of Mach's intuitions. The question Mach raised in 1883, what does 'rotating' mean in a universe with nothing else in it, remains genuinely open.

lessons.workedExample: Imagine two versions of Newton's bucket thought experiment. Version 1 (Newton's universe): a bucket spins in a universe otherwise filled with ordinary matter, including distant stars; the water curves, and Newton says this proves absolute space is real, since the curvature tracks the water's rotation relative to that background, not relative to nearby objects. Version 2 (Mach's universe): strip away every other object in existence, leaving only the bucket and the water, alone in a truly empty universe, then spin the bucket. Newton's framework predicts the water STILL curves, because it is still rotating relative to absolute space; Mach's framework predicts the water does NOT curve at all, because there is no other matter left for the rotation to be relative to, and Mach held that inertial (centrifugal) effects require the presence of that other matter to exist in the first place. No experiment can actually empty the universe to test this directly, which is exactly why the debate stayed a live theoretical question for over a century, testable only indirectly through effects like frame dragging.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges raise Mach's principle because it is one of the cleanest examples in physics of an idea that changed how a later, greater theory (general relativity) was built, without ever being fully confirmed or resolved itself. A strong answer explains specifically what Mach objected to in Newton's bucket argument (the unmeasurability of absolute space, illustrated by the thick-walled-bucket challenge), states Mach's alternative (inertia relative to the distribution of all matter, not absolute space), and can name at least one modern echo, frame dragging, confirmed by Gravity Probe B in 2011, as a partially Machian effect. A student who claims Mach's principle was 'proven right' or 'proven wrong' is overclaiming in either direction; a judge will press on whether general relativity fully satisfies Mach's principle, and the honest, defensible answer is that it is still debated, since GR admits some explicitly non-Machian solutions.

questions.prompt: What was Mach's core objection to Newton's absolute-space explanation of the bucket experiment?

options.text: Absolute space is unmeasurable and cannot be pointed to or interacted with, so it is scientifically empty as an explanation
The water in Newton's bucket does not actually curve, contradicting Newton's own reported observation
Newton's mathematics for the paraboloid shape contained an algebraic error

explanations.a: Correct: Mach's objection was philosophical and methodological, that absolute space cannot be observed or measured, not that the observed curvature itself was wrong.
explanations.b: Mach did not dispute the observed curvature; he disputed Newton's explanation for WHY it occurs, accepting the phenomenon while rejecting the absolute-space account of it.
explanations.c: There was no claimed mathematical error in Newton's geometry; the dispute was entirely about the physical interpretation of the cause.

questions.prompt: According to Mach's principle, what would happen to a spinning bucket of water in an otherwise completely empty universe (no other matter at all)?

options.text: The water would not curve, because Mach held inertial effects require rotation relative to other matter, which would not exist
The water would curve exactly as it does in our universe, since curvature depends only on the bucket's own spin rate
The water would curve even MORE than in our universe, because there would be no other matter to dampen the effect

explanations.a: Correct: Mach's principle holds that inertial (centrifugal) effects arise from rotation relative to the rest of the universe's matter; remove that matter and, by Mach's account, the effect should vanish.
explanations.b: This is Newton's prediction (absolute space still produces the effect regardless of other matter), which is exactly the position Mach's principle was formulated to contradict.
explanations.c: Mach's principle does not predict amplification from removing matter; if anything, removing the source of inertial effects should reduce or eliminate them, not increase them.

questions.prompt: Match each concept or event to its description.

right.text: Mach's book criticizing Newton's absolute space and proposing that inertia derives from the distribution of all matter
Prediction that a rotating mass drags nearby spacetime and free-falling frames around with it
Satellite experiment that measured and confirmed frame dragging around Earth

questions.explanation: Mach's 1883 book originated the critique of absolute space; Lense and Thirring's 1918 theoretical prediction of frame dragging is a partly Machian effect within general relativity; Gravity Probe B experimentally confirmed that predicted effect in 2011, offering partial but not complete support for Mach's principle.

units.label: Applications: Gyroscopes, Flywheels, and Spinning Sports

lessons.label: Flywheel Energy Storage

sections.heading: Storing energy as spin
sections.body: A flywheel stores energy the same way a spring or a battery does, but the energy lives in rotation instead of stretch or chemistry: KE_rot = (1/2) I omega^2, where I is the rotor's moment of inertia and omega is its angular speed in rad/s. Because the energy depends on omega SQUARED, doubling the spin rate quadruples the stored energy, which is why flywheel designers push omega as high as they can rather than just adding mass. Shape matters too: a thin ring (I = MR^2) stores twice the energy of a solid disk of the same mass and radius (I = (1/2)MR^2) at the same omega, because more of the ring's mass sits far from the axis. Real flywheel rotors are usually rim-heavy for exactly this reason, with a lightweight hub and spokes carrying the load to a dense outer rim.

sections.heading: Why the rotor cannot spin forever faster
sections.body: The limit is not the motor, it is the material. Every particle of the spinning rim needs a centripetal force pulling it toward the axis, and at high omega that force is enormous; the rim itself supplies it through internal tensile stress, roughly stress ~ (density) x (tip speed)^2 for a thin hoop. Once that stress exceeds the material's tensile strength, the rotor fails catastrophically. This is why flywheel energy density (energy stored per unit mass) scales with the material's SPECIFIC strength, tensile strength divided by density, almost independent of the rotor's actual size or mass -- a key design insight. It is also why modern flywheels use carbon-fiber composites rather than steel: composites have a much higher strength-to-density ratio, so they can spin faster before bursting and store more energy per kilogram, even though steel is individually the stronger material by raw tensile strength.

sections.heading: From lab curiosity to grid hardware
sections.body: Beacon Power's Gen4 flywheels, deployed for grid frequency regulation in New York and Pennsylvania, use composite rotors levitated on magnetic bearings inside a vacuum enclosure (to kill air-drag and friction losses) and operate between about 8,000 and 16,000 rpm, delivering roughly 25 kWh of extractable energy per unit. Two hundred of these units, connected in parallel at the Stephentown, NY site, form a 20 MW / 5 MWh plant that can absorb or inject power in well under 4 seconds, far faster than a conventional generator can ramp -- exactly the speed grid operators need to counter second-to-second imbalances between supply and demand.

lessons.workedExample: A Beacon Power Gen4 rotor delivers 25 kWh of USABLE energy as it slows from its top speed of 16,000 rpm down to its cutoff speed of 8,000 rpm (below that, the power electronics can no longer extract useful power). Since KE proportional to omega^2, the fraction of the rotor's TOTAL kinetic energy remaining at 8,000 rpm (half the top speed) is (8,000/16,000)^2 = 0.25, so 25% of the total energy is left unused at cutoff and 75% was extracted. That means the rotor's total stored energy at full speed is 25 kWh / 0.75 = 33.3 kWh -- a direct consequence of the omega^2 scaling, not an arbitrary design choice.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating a flywheel project will push past 'it stores energy when spinning' to ask what actually limits how much energy the rotor can hold. A student who only cites motor power or bearing friction has described secondary effects; a student who identifies rotor burst stress and specific strength has identified the real physical ceiling. Judges also listen for whether a student can explain why only part of a flywheel's stored energy is usable (the operating speed window), since that distinction between total and extractable energy is exactly the kind of subtlety separating memorized formulas from genuine engineering understanding.

questions.prompt: A thin ring and a solid disk have the same mass M and radius R and spin at the same angular speed omega. Which stores more kinetic energy, and why?

options.text: The ring, because its mass sits farther from the axis on average, giving it a larger moment of inertia
The disk, because solid objects always have more inertia than hollow ones
They store the same energy, because KE_rot depends only on mass and omega

explanations.a: Correct: I_ring = MR^2 is twice I_disk = (1/2)MR^2, and since KE_rot = (1/2)I omega^2 at equal omega, the ring stores twice the energy.
explanations.b: This has it backwards -- moment of inertia depends on how mass is DISTRIBUTED relative to the axis, not on whether the object is solid, and here the hollow ring has the larger I.
explanations.c: KE_rot = (1/2)I omega^2 depends on I as well as omega, and I differs between the two shapes even though M and R match.

questions.prompt: Why do flywheel designers prefer carbon-fiber composite rotors over steel rotors of the same mass, even though steel has a higher raw tensile strength?

options.text: Composites have a higher strength-to-density ratio, so they can spin faster before bursting and store more energy per kilogram
Composites have a lower moment of inertia, which is always desirable
Composites are cheaper to manufacture, which is the only reason for the choice

explanations.a: Correct: burst stress scales with density x tip-speed^2, so the material property that sets the achievable energy density is specific strength (strength/density), which composites win on even when steel's absolute strength is higher.
explanations.b: A lower moment of inertia at the same omega means LESS stored energy, which is the opposite of the design goal -- rotors are made rim-heavy to increase I.
explanations.c: Cost may factor into real decisions, but the physics reason given in the lesson is the strength-to-density ratio governing burst speed, not manufacturing cost.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning chain that explains why a flywheel rotor eventually fails as omega increases.

items.text: Angular speed omega increases toward the rotor's design limit
Each mass element needs a larger centripetal force to stay on its circular path
The rotor material supplies that force through internal tensile stress, which rises with omega
Once stress exceeds the material's tensile strength, the rotor fractures

questions.explanation: Higher omega demands more centripetal force per mass element, which the rotor supplies as internal stress; that stress climbs with omega until it exceeds the material's strength and the rotor bursts.

questions.prompt: Match each flywheel design feature to the physical reason it is used.

left.text: Rim-heavy rotor shape (mass concentrated at the outer edge)

right.text: Eliminates air drag, which would otherwise bleed off stored kinetic energy
Maximizes moment of inertia I for a given rotor mass, increasing stored energy at a fixed omega
Removes mechanical contact friction, extending spin-down time and cycle life

questions.explanation: A vacuum removes air drag losses, concentrating mass at the rim raises I (and thus KE_rot at fixed omega), and magnetic bearings eliminate contact friction, all serving the same goal of keeping stored rotational energy from leaking away.

lessons.label: Reaction and Momentum Wheels in Spacecraft

sections.heading: Turning without touching anything
sections.body: A spacecraft in orbit has no ground to push off and firing thrusters burns limited propellant, so many satellites reorient using internal reaction wheels instead. A reaction wheel is a small flywheel spun up or down by an electric motor mounted inside the spacecraft. Because no external torque acts on the spacecraft-plus-wheel system, its TOTAL angular momentum L is conserved. If the motor spins the wheel one way, the spacecraft body must rotate the other way so that the sum L_wheel + L_body stays constant (starting from zero, if the spacecraft began at rest). Reversing the motor spins the wheel back down and rotates the body back -- this lets a satellite point its camera, antenna, or solar panels precisely, repeatedly, and without consuming any fuel.

sections.heading: Reaction wheels versus control moment gyroscopes
sections.body: A plain reaction wheel changes the spacecraft's orientation by changing the WHEEL's spin rate, which limits how much torque it can deliver (torque = I_wheel x angular acceleration of the wheel, and motors are power-limited). A control moment gyroscope (CMG) instead keeps its rotor spinning at a large, constant, high rate and mounts it on a gimbal that TILTS the spin axis. Tilting a large angular momentum vector produces a torque on the spacecraft (torque = the rate of change of L, and since a CMG keeps |L| large and constant, tilting L's direction quickly produces a large torque) that can be far larger than a reaction wheel could produce for the same electrical power, because the energy goes into repointing an already-spinning mass rather than speeding one up from scratch. This is why large, heavy platforms like the International Space Station use CMGs: its four double-gimbal CMGs each spin a 100 kg rotor at about 6,600 rpm, storing roughly 4,760 N*m*s of angular momentum apiece and each able to output about 258 N*m of control torque -- enough to slowly reorient a structure with the mass of a small building using only gimbal motors, not thrusters.

sections.heading: Saturation: the catch
sections.body: Reaction wheels and CMGs cannot absorb angular momentum forever. Small, persistent external torques on a real spacecraft -- from gravity-gradient effects, solar radiation pressure, or residual atmospheric drag in low orbit -- slowly transfer angular momentum into the wheels, spinning them faster and faster until they hit their maximum rpm and 'saturate,' losing the ability to provide more control authority in that direction. Mission designers must periodically desaturate (or 'dump') that momentum using an external torque source, typically small thrusters or, for satellites in Earth's magnetic field, magnetic torquer coils that push against the geomagnetic field. Sizing the wheels and planning the desaturation schedule is itself a rotational-dynamics design problem.

lessons.workedExample: A small satellite has body moment of inertia I_body = 0.05 kg*m^2 about its spin axis and carries a reaction wheel with I_wheel = 2 x 10^-4 kg*m^2, both initially at rest. To slew the body, the motor spins the wheel up to 6,000 rpm (628 rad/s). Conservation of angular momentum, starting from L_total = 0, requires I_wheel*omega_wheel + I_body*omega_body = 0, so omega_body = -(I_wheel/I_body)*omega_wheel = -(2x10^-4 / 0.05)(628) = -2.5 rad/s. The satellite body rotates at 2.5 rad/s (about 0.4 rev/s) in the direction opposite the wheel -- precise, repeatable, and fuel-free, but limited: the wheel is now near its maximum speed and has little spare momentum capacity left before it must be desaturated.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe reaction-wheel projects to see whether a student understands that the spacecraft and wheel are ONE system whose total angular momentum is conserved, rather than treating the wheel as a magic steering knob. A strong answer explains why the body must rotate opposite the wheel, and can also explain saturation: what happens as the wheel approaches its rpm limit and why real missions need thrusters or magnetic torquers as a backup. A student who cannot explain saturation has described the effect without engaging with the engineering constraint that makes it a genuinely hard design problem.

questions.prompt: A satellite at rest spins up an internal reaction wheel clockwise (as viewed from a fixed external frame). What happens to the satellite's body?

options.text: The body stays perfectly still, since the wheel is internal to the spacecraft
The body rotates counterclockwise, so that total angular momentum remains zero
The body rotates clockwise, in the same direction as the wheel

explanations.a: No external torque acts on the system, but the WHEEL gained angular momentum, so the body must gain equal and opposite angular momentum to keep the total at zero -- it cannot stay still.
explanations.b: Correct: with L_total conserved at zero, I_wheel*omega_wheel + I_body*omega_body = 0 forces omega_body to be opposite in sign to omega_wheel.
explanations.c: This would make L_total nonzero with no external torque to have produced it, violating conservation of angular momentum.

questions.prompt: Why can a control moment gyroscope (CMG) produce much more torque per watt of motor power than a plain reaction wheel of similar size?

options.text: The CMG's rotor is made of denser material
The CMG repoints an already large, constantly-spinning angular momentum vector by gimbaling it, rather than spending power to speed a wheel up from rest
The CMG is not subject to conservation of angular momentum

explanations.a: Rotor material density affects I, but the torque advantage described in the lesson comes from the gimbaling mechanism, not from material choice.
explanations.b: Correct: torque is the rate of change of the momentum vector's direction, and tilting a large, already-spinning L vector produces large torque for modest gimbal-motor power, unlike spinning a wheel up from scratch.
explanations.c: CMGs obey the same conservation law as any rotating system; their advantage is mechanical (gimbaling), not an exemption from physics.

questions.prompt: Order the sequence of events that leads a reaction wheel to 'saturate' and require desaturation.

items.text: A small, persistent external torque acts on the spacecraft (e.g. gravity-gradient or drag)
The wheel continuously speeds up to counteract that torque and hold attitude
The wheel approaches its maximum rated rpm and can no longer absorb more momentum
Ground controllers fire thrusters or use magnetic torquers to dump momentum from the wheel

questions.explanation: A persistent external torque forces the wheel to keep speeding up to hold attitude, which eventually saturates the wheel near its rpm limit, requiring an external torque source to desaturate it.

questions.prompt: Match each spacecraft attitude-control component to its role.

right.text: Spins a wheel up or down for fine, moderate-torque attitude control
Gimbals a large, constantly-spinning rotor to produce high torque efficiently
Pushes against Earth's magnetic field to desaturate wheel momentum without using propellant

questions.explanation: Reaction wheels provide fine control by changing their own spin rate, CMGs provide large torque by gimbaling an already-spinning rotor, and magnetic torquers offload accumulated wheel momentum against Earth's field.

lessons.label: Gyroscopic Sensors in Phones and Vehicles

sections.heading: A gyroscope with no spinning wheel
sections.body: Classic gyroscopes sense rotation using a large, continuously spinning mass, but the gyroscope inside a smartphone has no wheel at all. It is a MEMS (micro-electromechanical systems) device: a silicon proof mass, smaller than a grain of rice, is electrically driven to vibrate back and forth at high frequency along one axis. When the whole chip rotates, the Coriolis effect deflects the vibrating mass sideways, perpendicular to both its vibration direction and the rotation axis, by an amount proportional to the rotation rate. Tiny capacitive plates sense that sideways deflection and convert it into an electrical signal reporting angular velocity, typically in degrees per second, on each of three axes.

sections.heading: What phones do with a rotation-RATE signal
sections.body: A raw MEMS gyroscope reports how fast the device is rotating right now, not its absolute orientation, so a phone must integrate that signal over time to track how much it has turned. This feeds screen auto-rotation and augmented-reality overlays that must track head or device motion within milliseconds. It is also the core of optical image stabilization (OIS): the gyroscope detects the small, fast rotations of a hand-held camera during a shot, and a control loop shifts the lens or image sensor in the opposite direction fast enough to cancel the blur, all within the exposure time of a single photograph.

sections.heading: Drift, fusion, and vehicle stability control
sections.body: Because orientation is obtained by integrating a rate signal, any small constant bias error in the gyroscope accumulates without bound -- a real MEMS gyroscope with even a tiny 0.01 deg/s bias will report 0.6 degrees of false rotation after just one minute of standing still. Devices correct this by fusing the gyroscope with an accelerometer (which senses gravity's direction, giving an absolute up/down reference) and often a magnetometer, using a complementary or Kalman filter to combine the gyroscope's fast, drift-prone response with the accelerometer's slow, drift-free one. The same MEMS yaw-rate gyroscope is mandatory automotive safety hardware: electronic stability control (ESC) systems compare the car's ACTUAL rotation rate about its vertical axis, measured by the gyroscope, against the rotation rate a computer predicts from the steering angle and wheel speeds. When the two disagree, indicating a skid, the system automatically brakes individual wheels to correct the car's path -- a feature required on all new light vehicles sold in the United States since the 2012 model year.

lessons.workedExample: A car enters a turn and its steering angle and speed predict a yaw rate of 12 deg/s, but the MEMS gyroscope measures the car is actually rotating at 20 deg/s -- the rear end is sliding out faster than the driver's steering input alone would produce, a classic oversteer skid. The electronic stability control computer detects this 8 deg/s discrepancy in real time and briefly brakes the outer-front wheel, applying a corrective torque about the car's vertical axis that opposes the excess rotation, bringing the measured yaw rate back toward the predicted 12 deg/s and helping the driver stay on the intended path -- entirely from a rotation-rate measurement, not a picture of the road.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will want to know whether a student understands that a MEMS gyroscope measures a RATE (deg/s), not an absolute angle, since that distinction explains both why phones need sensor fusion and why the signal is directly useful for something like stability control, which cares about rotation rate, not absolute heading. Expect a question like: 'if you only had the gyroscope and no accelerometer, what would go wrong over time?' A strong answer names integration drift specifically, not just a vague 'it gets less accurate.'

questions.prompt: What physical effect does a MEMS vibrating-structure gyroscope actually use to detect rotation?

options.text: The Coriolis effect deflecting a vibrating proof mass sideways when the chip rotates
Conservation of angular momentum in a large spinning flywheel, as in a classic mechanical gyroscope
A change in electrical resistance caused directly by rotation

explanations.a: Correct: the driven vibration plus rotation produces a Coriolis-induced sideways deflection, which capacitive plates sense and convert into an angular-rate signal.
explanations.b: Classic mechanical gyroscopes use a large spinning rotor, but MEMS gyroscopes have no continuously spinning wheel at all -- they use a vibrating mass and the Coriolis effect instead.
explanations.c: The sensing mechanism is capacitive (from the mass's physical displacement), not a direct resistance change from rotation.

questions.prompt: A MEMS gyroscope has a small constant bias error and is used ALONE (no accelerometer) to track a device's orientation by integrating its rate signal over time. What happens?

options.text: The reported orientation drifts further from the true orientation the longer the device runs
Nothing -- a rate sensor with a bias error still gives a perfectly accurate integrated angle
The error stays bounded and constant no matter how long you integrate

explanations.a: Correct: integrating a constant bias over time produces an error that grows without bound, which is exactly why gyroscopes are fused with an absolute reference like an accelerometer.
explanations.b: A bias in the rate signal accumulates once integrated into an angle -- it does not cancel out, and the lesson gives a concrete number: a 0.01 deg/s bias yields 0.6 degrees of drift in one minute.
explanations.c: Because the error is being INTEGRATED, longer run times produce larger accumulated drift, not a constant bounded error.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which an electronic stability control (ESC) system responds to a car beginning to skid.

items.text: The onboard computer predicts an expected yaw rate from the steering angle and wheel speeds
The MEMS gyroscope measures the car's actual yaw rate about its vertical axis
The computer detects that measured yaw rate disagrees with the predicted yaw rate
The system automatically brakes an individual wheel to apply a corrective torque

questions.explanation: ESC continuously compares a model-predicted yaw rate to the gyroscope's measured yaw rate, and only once it detects a disagreement does it brake a specific wheel to correct the skid.

questions.prompt: Match each smartphone or vehicle application to the gyroscope role it depends on.

right.text: Detects fast hand-shake rotation so the lens/sensor can be shifted to cancel blur during exposure
Corrects the gyroscope's long-term integration drift using gravity's absolute direction
Compares measured yaw rate to a steering-predicted yaw rate to detect and correct a skid

questions.explanation: OIS uses the gyroscope's fast rotation-rate signal to cancel hand-shake blur, sensor fusion corrects gyroscope drift with an absolute gravity reference, and ESC compares measured versus predicted yaw rate to catch a skid.

lessons.label: Spin in Sport

sections.heading: Shrinking your shape to spin faster
sections.body: Once a diver or gymnast leaves the board or the floor, no external torque acts about their center of mass (gravity acts AT the center of mass and produces zero torque about it, and air resistance is negligible over such short flights), so their angular momentum L = I*omega is conserved for the rest of the flight. Athletes exploit this directly: pulling the arms and legs into a tight tuck dramatically reduces the body's moment of inertia I, and since L stays fixed, omega must increase to compensate -- the same athlete who left the board rotating slowly in a layout position can spin two or three times faster once tucked. Extending back out of the tuck before landing or entering the water increases I again, slowing the rotation back down for a controlled, vertical entry.

sections.heading: How much does tucking actually change I
sections.body: Physicist Cliff Frohlich's classic 1979 analysis of springboard divers (American Journal of Physics) estimated that a diver's moment of inertia in a tight tuck is roughly four to five times smaller than in a fully extended layout position -- a factor large enough to turn a single somersault into a triple. Frohlich's paper is also famous for resolving a different apparent paradox: how a diver can start TWISTING in midair -- rotating about their body's long axis -- with essentially zero angular momentum about that axis, something that looks impossible if you think of angular momentum conservation too literally. His analysis showed the diver can initiate a twist with no external torque by moving their arms asymmetrically (raising one, lowering the other) -- this 'angular-momentum twist' works because the diver already has nonzero TOTAL angular momentum from the somersault; the arm-throw only redistributes it so a component appears about the twist axis, which started at zero, without ever changing the total. (Frohlich describes a separate, true 'cat twist' for the case of zero TOTAL angular momentum, achieved by bending the body into two segments and twisting them against each other -- the actual falling-cat mechanism, distinct from the simple arm-throw used here.)

sections.heading: Scratch spins and the discus: two ends of the same trade-off
sections.body: A figure skater's scratch spin shows the same physics from a standing position: with arms and the free leg extended, I is large and omega is modest; pulling both tight to the body's axis can shrink I enough to roughly triple or quadruple the spin rate, converting muscular work done against the resulting centripetal forces into extra rotational kinetic energy. The discus throw uses the SAME lever in reverse: during the 1.5 to 1.75 turns of the throw, keeping the throwing arm close to the body minimizes I so the thrower can rotate quickly and build angular momentum efficiently; only in the final instant before release does the thrower extend the arm outward, trading some rotation rate for the large radius that maximizes the discus's tangential release speed, v = omega*r.

lessons.workedExample: A figure skater in a scratch spin starts with arms and one leg extended, giving I_initial = 4.0 kg*m^2 at omega_initial = 3.0 rad/s. She pulls her arms and leg tight to her body's axis, reducing her moment of inertia to I_final = 1.2 kg*m^2. Conservation of angular momentum (I_initial*omega_initial = I_final*omega_final) gives omega_final = (4.0)(3.0)/1.2 = 10.0 rad/s, roughly 1.6 revolutions per second, versus 0.5 rev/s before -- more than a threefold increase in spin rate. Her rotational kinetic energy rises from (1/2)(4.0)(3.0)^2 = 18 J to (1/2)(1.2)(10.0)^2 = 60 J, more than tripling even though no external torque did work on her; that extra energy comes from the muscular work she does pulling her limbs inward against the centripetal force.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges expect a student presenting sports-physics work to correctly identify WHY tucking increases spin rate (angular momentum conservation, not 'because it's more aerodynamic' or other vague claims), and to notice that the resulting kinetic-energy increase requires the athlete to do real muscular work -- energy is not free just because momentum is conserved. A sharper follow-up judges like to ask is why the discus thrower does the opposite of a tucking diver at the moment of release, testing whether the student can distinguish 'minimize I to spin up' from 'maximize r to maximize release speed' as two different phases of the same motion.

questions.prompt: A diver leaves the springboard rotating slowly in a layout (extended) position, then pulls into a tight tuck mid-air. What happens to her rotational kinetic energy during the tuck, and where does that energy come from?

options.text: It increases, supplied by the muscular work she does pulling her limbs inward against centripetal force
It stays exactly the same, since angular momentum is conserved
It decreases, because tucking reduces her moment of inertia

explanations.a: Correct: L = I*omega is conserved, but since I drops and omega rises, KE_rot = (1/2)I*omega^2 actually increases -- and that extra energy comes from real muscular work, not from nowhere.
explanations.b: Angular momentum L is conserved, but kinetic energy is NOT automatically conserved along with it -- KE_rot changes because I and omega change in a way that increases (1/2)I*omega^2.
explanations.c: A smaller I combined with a larger omega (which conservation of L guarantees) produces MORE kinetic energy, not less -- the (1/2)I*omega^2 relationship is not linear in I alone.

questions.prompt: According to Cliff Frohlich's 1979 analysis, how can a diver start TWISTING (rotating about their body's long axis) in midair even though they have essentially zero angular momentum about that axis at takeoff?

options.text: By moving their arms asymmetrically (one up, one down), which redistributes their existing (nonzero total) angular momentum onto the twist axis without ever changing the total
Air resistance from the board's recoil pushes them into a twist
They are secretly pushing off the board with a small sideways torque without the audience noticing

explanations.a: Correct: this was Frohlich's actual resolution -- an asymmetric arm motion (his 'angular-momentum twist') lets a diver initiate a twist with no external torque, redistributing their already-nonzero total angular momentum onto an axis that started with none.
explanations.b: Air resistance is negligible over such a short flight and was not the mechanism Frohlich identified; the effect is purely about body-shape changes, not aerodynamic force.
explanations.c: Frohlich's point was that NO external torque (from the board or otherwise) is needed to produce the twist -- it is explainable entirely from internal shape changes, which is what made the finding notable.

questions.prompt: Match each rotational-sport moment to what the athlete is doing to their moment of inertia and why.

left.text: Discus thrower keeping the arm close during the turns
Discus thrower extending the arm just before release

right.text: Minimizes I to maximize spin rate for more rotations in the air
Minimizes I to rotate quickly and build angular momentum efficiently during the turns
Maximizes radius r to maximize tangential release speed v = omega*r, even at the cost of some rotation rate

questions.explanation: A tucking gymnast and a spinning discus thrower both shrink I for a fast, efficient rotation, but at release the discus thrower reverses the strategy, extending the arm to maximize radius and therefore release speed.

questions.prompt: Order a diver's body configuration through a tucked somersault dive, from takeoff to entry.

items.text: Leaves the board in an extended layout position, rotating relatively slowly
Pulls into a tight tuck, sharply reducing moment of inertia
Spins rapidly through the required somersault rotations while tucked
Extends back out before entry, increasing moment of inertia and slowing the rotation for a controlled entry

questions.explanation: The dive begins extended and slow, tucks to shrink I and spin fast through the required rotations, then re-extends to raise I and slow the rotation for a clean, vertical entry.

lessons.label: Designing a Rotational Experiment

sections.heading: The basic apparatus: known torque, measured angular acceleration
sections.body: A defensible rotational-dynamics project measures a rigid body's moment of inertia experimentally and compares it to a theoretical prediction from its geometry. The standard setup hangs a known mass m from a string wound around a pulley of known radius r, which is coupled to the rotating object under test (a disk, wheel, or turntable). As the mass falls, it unwinds the string and spins up the rotating body under a torque supplied by the string tension T: torque = T*r. Newton's second law for the falling mass gives m*g - T = m*a, where a = r*alpha links the mass's linear acceleration to the body's angular acceleration alpha -- so T is NOT simply m*g unless a is negligible, and a careful experiment measures or accounts for it rather than assuming the string tension equals the weight.

sections.heading: The friction correction that most rushed projects skip
sections.body: Real bearings and axles have friction, so the true relationship is torque_applied = I*alpha + torque_friction, not the idealized torque = I*alpha alone. A single trial that ignores friction and solves I = torque/alpha will systematically OVER-estimate I, because part of the applied torque was actually spent overcoming friction rather than accelerating the rotor. The fix is to run the experiment at several different hanging masses (several different torques), measure alpha for each, and plot torque versus alpha: the slope of that line is I (from torque = I*alpha + torque_friction, a linear relationship in torque vs. alpha with slope I and intercept torque_friction), which cleanly separates the two effects instead of lumping friction losses into the moment-of-inertia estimate. An independent check -- letting the rotor spin freely and decelerate under friction alone, then measuring that deceleration -- gives a second, corroborating estimate of torque_friction.

sections.heading: Comparing to theory and reporting error honestly
sections.body: The predicted moment of inertia comes from the object's geometry: I = (1/2)MR^2 for a uniform disk, I = MR^2 for a thin ring, and the parallel-axis theorem I = I_cm + Md^2 for combining pieces or off-axis rotation. A strong project reports the measured I alongside the theoretical I, states the percent difference, and discusses SPECIFIC sources of systematic error -- the string and pulley's own small moments of inertia (which add to the effective inertia being spun up), the string's mass, air resistance, and any non-uniformity in the test object's density -- rather than a vague catch-all like 'experimental error.' Naming which assumption is most likely violated, and by roughly how much, is what turns a plug-and-chug lab into real experimental science.

lessons.workedExample: A student hangs m = 0.050 kg from a string over a pulley of radius r = 0.015 m, spinning up a disk with theoretical I = (1/2)(0.400 kg)(0.100 m)^2 = 0.0020 kg*m^2. She times the disk's angular acceleration with a photogate and measures alpha = 2.3 rad/s^2. If she (incorrectly) assumes T = m*g = 0.4905 N and ignores friction, she gets torque = 0.4905*0.015 = 0.00736 N*m and I = 0.00736/2.3 = 0.0032 kg*m^2 -- about 60% higher than the 0.0020 kg*m^2 theoretical value. Repeating the run with a second, larger hanging mass and comparing the two (torque, alpha) pairs reveals a nonzero intercept in the torque-vs-alpha line: a friction torque of about 0.0027 N*m that the single-trial calculation had folded entirely into I. Subtracting it brings the measured I back within about 10% of theory, a defensible result with an honestly identified error source.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges specifically probe whether a student ran ONE trial and called it done, or recognized that a single (torque, alpha) pair cannot separate a real moment of inertia from friction losses. Expect the question: 'how do you know your measured I isn't just inflated by bearing friction?' A student who describes the multi-mass torque-vs-alpha regression (or an independent free-deceleration check) has designed a genuinely defensible experiment; a student who only ran one hanging mass and compared a single number to theory has not controlled for a known confound, which is exactly the gap fair judges are trained to find.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to assume the string tension T equals the hanging mass's weight m*g when computing the applied torque?

options.text: Because the mass is accelerating (a = r*alpha), so Newton's second law gives m*g - T = m*a, meaning T is less than m*g whenever the system is accelerating
Because gravity does not act on a mass that is attached to a string
Because the pulley reverses the direction of the tension force

explanations.a: Correct: applying Newton's second law to the falling mass shows T = m(g - a), which is less than m*g whenever a is nonzero, i.e. whenever the system is actually accelerating rather than moving at constant speed.
explanations.b: Gravity acts on the mass regardless of the string; the issue is that the NET force (gravity minus tension) is what produces the mass's acceleration, not that gravity somehow stops acting.
explanations.c: The pulley changes the direction the string pulls, but the tension magnitude relationship comes from Newton's second law on the falling mass, not from any directional effect of the pulley.

questions.prompt: A single trial computes I = torque_applied / alpha, ignoring bearing friction entirely. How does this bias the measured I compared to the true moment of inertia?

options.text: It overestimates I, because part of the applied torque was actually spent overcoming friction rather than accelerating the rotor
It underestimates I, because friction always speeds up the rotor
It has no effect, because friction and moment of inertia are independent quantities

explanations.a: Correct: the true relation is torque_applied = I*alpha + torque_friction, so solving I = torque_applied/alpha while ignoring torque_friction attributes friction's share of the torque to I, inflating the estimate.
explanations.b: Friction opposes motion and REDUCES alpha for a given applied torque, not speeds it up -- and the resulting bias in the naive calculation is an overestimate of I, not an underestimate.
explanations.c: They are not independent in the measurement: since both torque_friction and I*alpha add up to the same measured applied torque, failing to separate them corrupts the I estimate.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a defensible moment-of-inertia experiment that correctly separates friction from I.

items.text: Predict the theoretical I from the object's geometry (e.g. I = (1/2)MR^2 for a disk)
Run the apparatus at several different hanging masses, measuring alpha for each applied torque
Plot torque versus alpha and take the slope as I and the intercept as friction torque
Compare the friction-corrected measured I to the theoretical prediction and report percent difference with named error sources

questions.explanation: A sound design predicts I from theory first, gathers multiple (torque, alpha) pairs to enable separating friction from I via the line's slope and intercept, then compares the corrected result to theory with named error sources.

questions.prompt: Match each systematic error source in this experiment to its physical effect on the measurement.

left.text: The pulley itself has a small but nonzero moment of inertia
Only one hanging mass is tested, with no free-deceleration check

right.text: Adds a small extra inertia to the system that gets lumped into the measured I of the test object
Changes the effective mass and torque being delivered to the system as it unwinds, a usually-small but real deviation from the idealized point-mass model
Leaves friction torque unseparated from I, biasing the single-trial I estimate high

questions.explanation: A massive pulley adds its own inertia to what is being measured, a massive string subtly changes the falling system's dynamics as it unwinds, and skipping the multi-trial or free-deceleration check leaves friction hidden inside the I estimate.
